MLT.name: Malta
MLT.summary:
Malta decriminalised same-sex conduct on 29 January 1973 and now operates one of the strongest legal frameworks for transgender people in its regional bloc. On 15 April 2014 parliament approved a constitutional amendment naming gender identity as a protected ground, the first European state to do so, and introduced civil unions in the same sitting. Statutory discrimination protections extend to sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics, and legal gender recognition requires no surgery. Nonbinary identity is recognised, and hate-crime provisions cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity offences.

Rules governing everyday access are settled rather than contested: same-sex marriage since 2017, full joint adoption since 2014, open military service, protected bathroom access, a ban on conversion therapy and a full ban on intersex infant surgery. Equaldex records no restrictions on legal gender change and reports that 84% of respondents consider the country a good place for gay people.

Physical risk to visitors is low. A 2025 academic chapter in the Routledge Companion to Gender and Crime, by Mary Grace Vella, records one of the lowest rates of physical or sexual victimisation of LGBTIQ+ people among the 27 EU member states, and the Malta Police Force operates hate-crime procedures for sexual-orientation and gender-identity incidents. The same research finds that non-physical harassment and online hatred make up a comparatively larger share of what LGBTIQ+ people experience, and that reporting of violence to the Malta Police Force remains significantly low despite institutional reform.

Border handling is the sharpest documented exposure. In M.S. v. Malta, an LGBTI asylum seeker was detained on arrival in April 2023 and served with a return decision and removal order to Bangladesh in May 2024; on 30 July 2025 the International Commission of Jurists and partner organisations filed observations at the European Court of Human Rights raising non-refoulement under Article 3, detention conditions and the absence of an individualised assessment before detention under Articles 5 and 13. The case concerns an asylum seeker rather than a visa-holding traveller, but it is direct evidence of how an LGBTI arrival can be screened, held and ordered removed.

Detention inside the country is the weakest documented point. On 29 May 2018 the Maltese civil court, Judge Silvio Meli, awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison €5,000 each after prison authorities held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, used the men's showers and were subjected to insults and what the proceedings described as continuous sexual abuse and violence. The court found that the authorities had knowingly and repeatedly placed the women in situations of high risk of sexual and psychological violence; the only alternative offered, transfer to the female section, would have cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, and warders and inmates there were hostile. The director of prisons was ordered to pay, with the Aditus Foundation representing the seven women.

A 2024 University of Malta dissertation by Oriana Vidal, drawing on interviews with four current and former transgender and gender-diverse inmates of the Correctional Service Agency across a 25-year cohort, finds that agency practice, policies and procedures lag the national gender-identity law: participants now hold individual cells in the female section but report residual misgendering by officers using masculine birth names, along with gaps in gender-appropriate clothing and healthcare, and the study records problems after release as well as deficiencies in healthcare, legislation and staff knowledge.

Social climate is the remaining caution. Despite the legal position, Maltese respondents rank first of 30 EU regions for hiding being LGBTIQ at work, and harassment and online hatred remain more prevalent than physical violence.
MLT.outOfScopeNotes:
Petty crime around nightclubs and tourist spots, and general regional terrorism guidance, are ordinary travel risks that affect everyone.

Routine border handling of trans visitors is not documented beyond the asylum-seeker case, and no source describes visa or document scrutiny for trans visitors specifically.

Prison axis: the 2024 study rests on four interviews spanning 25 years; the earlier separate-dormitory segregation is documented from that study alone; no source in this record documents current solitary or special-unit practice for trans prisoners beyond what the study describes, and the abuse documented in the 2018 ruling predates the post-2013 reform practice.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D13.

sources.title: Seven transgender prison inmates awarded €5,000 each in damages for 'truly disgusting' treatment (Malta Today)
sources.summary: Malta Today (29 May 2018): the Maltese civil court (Judge Silvio Meli) awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison €5,000 each (€4,000 for breach of rights plus €1,000 for damage to personal dignity) after the prison authorities held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, were forced to use the men's showers (often forgoing washing) and suffered insults and 'continuous sexual abuse and violence'. The court found the authorities had 'knowingly and repeatedly' placed them in situations of high risk of sexual and psychological violence; the only alternative offered, transfer to the female section, would have cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, and female inmates and warders were said to be hostile, so they stayed in the male section. The director of prisons was ordered to pay; the Aditus Foundation human-rights NGO represented the seven women.

sources.title: The lived experiences of transgender inmates at Malta's Correctional Service Agency (Oriana Vidal, University of Malta, 2024)
sources.summary: University of Malta master's dissertation (Oriana Vidal, 2024) interviewing four current and former transgender/gender-diverse inmates of Malta's Correctional Service Agency (CSA), a cohort spanning the last 25 years. It records that after Malta's 2013 gender-law reform CSA practice allowed TGD inmates to transfer to the female section, whereas earlier practice had segregated them in a separate dormitory (staff described the rationale as 'the risks of pregnancies'); participants now receive individual cells in the female section but report residual misgendering by officers (masculine birth names), gender-appropriate clothing and healthcare gaps, and conclude that CSA practice, policies and procedures lag Malta's progressive national gender-identity law. It also cites the 2018 newspaper report (Agius, Malta Today) of seven TGD inmates winning a court award after rights breaches including strip searches, showering-privacy issues and being treated as males.

ISL.name: Iceland
ISL.summary:
Iceland ranks first of 121 jurisdictions surveyed by Equaldex as a good place for gay and lesbian people, at 93 per cent. Same-sex sexual activity is legal for men and women, same-sex marriage is recognised, gender change carries no restrictions, and non-binary identity is recognised in law.

Legal gender recognition operates through a self-determination process introduced by the 2019 reform, which replaced an earlier statute that had itself been among the most progressive in Europe. Reporting on that reform by the Reykjavík Grapevine in August 2019 records that, alongside the liberalisation, campaigners including the chair of Trans Ísland continued to map practical obstacles that the change did not resolve.

Statutory protections cover discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, hate-motivated offences, and access to sex-segregated facilities. Equaldex also records a full ban on intersex infant surgery and a ban on conversion therapy. Outright International's Iceland profile, last updated 12 March 2026, describes the legal framework as progressive while noting acknowledged gaps in protection, and confirms that LGBTI organisations can register.

Reporting routes exist at national level. 112.is, Iceland's national emergency service, treats hate crime as an umbrella term covering offences committed from prejudice or hatred and publishes guidance for victims and perpetrators, alongside a dedicated page on abuse against queer people that states queer people are more likely to be victims of violence.

Recorded incidents have risen even as the statutory framework has widened. Police-recorded potential hate crimes numbered 16 in 2023, three times the previous year, 11 in 2024, and 7 in the current year at the time of reporting. Samtökin 78, the queer rights organisation, is publicly calling for stronger hate-crime legislation in response.

For British visitors, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office states that same-sex sexual activity is legal and same-sex relationships are recognised in Icelandic law, and links dedicated LGBT+ traveller advice.
ISL.outOfScopeNotes:
The specific statutory penalties attaching to hate-motivated offences and to discrimination are not stated in the available inventory; the sources confirm that the protections exist without giving sentencing ranges.

Whether the police-recorded potential hate crimes from 2023, 2024 and the current year resulted in charges or convictions is not sourced here, so outcomes downstream of recording remain unresolved.

The scope and conditions of the ban on intersex infant surgery, including any age limit or consent threshold, are not detailed in the inventory; only Equaldex's characterisation of it as a full ban is available.

Two sources intended to document legislation directly, the OSCE hate-crime legislation and national-frameworks pages for Iceland, yielded no usable findings in this pass, so the underlying statutory text was not examined.

The extent to which the Equality Complaints Committee's procedures differ from the criminal hate-crime route in timing, remedy and evidentiary threshold is not sourced, and neither is the practical accessibility of the 2019 gender recognition process to foreign nationals or visitors.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Iceland's 1996 Penal Code amendments made it illegal to publicly attack a person or group with mockery, defamation, abuse or threats because of their sexual orientation, and a 2014 amendment added gender identity to anti-discrimination grounds. Public expression is visibly supported: Reykjavík Pride drew about 100,000 people in 2015 (roughly 30% of the population), and in 2016 President Guðni Th. Jóhannesson became the first president to attend a gay pride parade. The country has a visible gay scene of bars and cafés in Reykjavík, though elsewhere the sparse population means there is almost no gay scene (Akureyri has no gay bars). Wikipedia country coverage: Stepchild adoption (a person adopting their partner's biological child) has been permitted since 2000, and on 27 June 2006 same-sex couples gained equal access to joint adoption of children alongside public IVF insemination treatment. Registered partnerships from 1996 already granted same-sex couples many of the same rights, responsibilities and benefits as marriage, including the ability to adopt stepchildren. A 2000 Gallup poll found 53% of Icelanders supported lesbian and gay adoption rights, with 35% against. Wikipedia country coverage: Section 178 of the Penal Code criminalized same-sex relations between 1869 and 1940, and public antipathy towards LGBT people remained high until the 1980s: some of the earliest Icelanders to come out publicly, Hörður Torfason and Anna Kristjánsdottir, initially faced public discrimination and ridicule. State hostility has since reversed — the 1996 anti-discrimination amendments, the 2010 unanimous (49–0) same-sex marriage vote, and the 2023 conversion therapy ban (53–0, 3 abstentions) mark the shift. One lingering restriction was the blood donation ban on men who have sex with men, challenged by a lawsuit in 2014, relaxed to a 4-month deferral in September 2021, and lifted entirely from September 2026. Wikipedia country coverage: Since 2008 it has been illegal to discriminate against people on the basis of their sexual orientation in education. Since 2016 the town of Hafnarfjörður has included information about same-sex relationships in its eighth-grade (ages 14–15) sex education lessons, and the Queer Student Association of Iceland runs social activities and field trips for University of Iceland students. On gender, the 2019 self-determination law (effective 1 January 2020, implemented January 2021) lets minors change their legal gender with parental consent, adds an 'X' third-gender option, and bans medical interventions on intersex children against their will except for health-related reasons. The age of consent was set at 14 in 1992 and raised to 15 in 2007, regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Discrimination complaints on equality grounds are handled by the Equality Complaints Committee, the established domestic redress mechanism, rather than requiring a criminal-law route.

Samtökin 78 campaigns domestically for strengthened hate-crime legislation, and its public calls in response to rising recorded incidents indicate an ongoing legislative push that residents may be able to support or feed into.

Legal gender recognition is administered on a self-determination basis without medical preconditions, and non-binary identity has legal standing, so residents are not required to obtain a diagnosis or surgical intervention to change registered gender.

Iceland's first-place ranking on Equaldex sits alongside a documented increase in police-recorded potential hate crimes, so legislative standing and experienced hostility are not measuring the same thing. A visitor weighing the two should treat the legal assessment and the incident counts as separate evidence.

ESP.name: Spain
ESP.summary:
Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route that replaces the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The law also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions. With administrative self-declaration, Spain stands alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Courts are applying the aggravation in practice. sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The source documents a long history of state and political hostility toward LGBTQ people in Spain, alongside pockets of present-day backlash. Under Franco's dictatorship (1936–1975), thousands of gay men and women were jailed, put in camps, or locked in mental institutions; some were sent to special prisons called galerías de invertidos ('galleries of inverts'), and vagrancy laws were used arbitrarily against suspected dissidents using actual or perceived homosexuality. Trans people were persecuted under 'public scandal' crimes and municipal legislation until the end of the 1980s. In 2023, a newly elected far-right government in Madrid repealed that region's non-discrimination law, repealed the local conversion therapy ban insofar as it applies to trans people, removed any penalties for conversion therapy, and repealed several trans legal recognitions. In 2013, Interior Minister Jorge Fernández Díaz stated that same-sex marriage endangered the survival of the human species and opposed equal legal protection for such marriages. Media and official hostility is not extensively covered; the article notes public opinion is overwhelmingly accepting (88% acceptance per a 2013 Pew poll, the highest of 39 countries), though it reports conflicting violence statistics — a 4% decrease reported by the Secretary of State for Security in 2018 versus a 7% increase reported by the Observatorio Madrileño and a 30% increase by Catalonia's Observatori contra l'Homofòbia in early 2019.

NLD.name: Netherlands
NLD.summary:
Entry requirements for transgender and non-binary visitors to the Netherlands are set out in the official WorldPride Amsterdam 2026 safety and travel guidance: visa requirements depend on nationality alone, and gender identity plays no part in the application. A passport carrying a gender marker different from the one assigned at birth, or an 'X' marker, is accepted provided it was officially issued, and no additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border.

Discrimination on grounds of gender identity is prohibited under Dutch law. Since 1 July 2025 a discriminatory motive has been written into the Criminal Code as a ground for increasing penalties, following a private-member's bill by Timmermans and Bikker, alongside expanded rights for victims and protection of victim data. Same-sex marriage is legal, non-binary people are legally recognised, conversion therapy is banned, and Equaldex records bathroom access as protected.

Official victimisation data published by the Dutch government shows that over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence, including 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people. The 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism recorded a sharp rise in incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence; in 2022, one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation.

Reported anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination is climbing. Police figures relayed by Transgender Netwerk and reported by NL Times in April 2026 show 4,800 discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people in the previous year, up 7.5% on 2024 and up 81% from 2,654 in 2022. Reports concerning transgender people rose 51% in a single year, from 264 to 399. COC described the trend as extremely worrying and noted that only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination were secured that year.

During WorldPride Amsterdam itself, more than 70 people filed discrimination reports through the RITA platform in the opening days, mostly from festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and from Pride Walk participants; RITA warned that the reports represent only a fraction of the total. Amsterdam expanded its 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during the event, covering the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief and hotels, plus a central RITA location, against an expected 1.4 million visitors. Mayor Halsema told the city council that discrimination and violent incidents would be handled as a priority during World Pride, with police, enforcers and organisers agreeing to act quickly; recent Prides drew 25 to 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene.
NLD.outOfScopeNotes:
Two sourced statements on the scope of hate-crime protection do not line up: Equaldex records hate-crime protections as covering sexual orientation only, while the government's 1 July 2025 package writes discriminatory motive into the Criminal Code as a general aggravating ground. Whether the 2025 mechanism extends to gender identity in charging and sentencing practice is not resolved by the sources held here.

NJCM states that no official figures exist on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands, and that the DIZ placement guidelines were unpublished as of February 2024; the current status of those guidelines is not sourced. The OSCE/ODIHR framework page confirms the absence of a statutory definition of 'hate crime', which limits how far police recording data can be read as a legal count. RITA's own caution that the 70-plus WorldPride reports are only a fraction of the total means incident volume during the 2026 event remains unquantified.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2, D8, D13.

sources.title: NJCM adviseert demissionair Minister voor Rechtsbescherming over plaatsing van transgender gedetineerden (Nederlands Juristen Comité voor de Mensenrechten)
sources.summary: The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights (NJCM), criminal-law working group, announced (site date 22 Feb 2024) that it had advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection on the placement of transgender detainees: no law or regulation currently governs their placement, which NJCM calls worrying and undesirable. The note highlights the group's vulnerable position (international research documents human-rights violations including discrimination and sexual violence), the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands, and the relevance of CPT standards, pointing to the full letter (PDF) to Minister Weerwind (21 Feb 2024).

sources.title: Advies plaatsing transgender gedetineerden — brief aan de Minister voor Rechtsbescherming (NJCM Werkgroep Strafrecht, 21 februari 2024)
sources.summary: NJCM letter to Minister Weerwind (Leiden, 21 Feb 2024) documenting Dutch placement practice for transgender detainees: there is no law, regulation or official policy governing their placement — the Penitentiary Principles Act only separates male and female detainees — and DJI (Prison Service) confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in the BRP (municipal records) together with case-by-case factors (gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, physical/mental health), while DIZ said it was (unpublished) drafting guidelines. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'Extra Care Facility' (EZV) wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. The letter cites documented cases: a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing at arrival then moved to an EZV; a parole-board appeals ruling (21 Mar 2016, 15/4323/GB) on a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation in the men's prison; and sentencing rulings by the Limburg court (17 Oct 2017, ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624, trans woman facing placement in a men's prison) and The Hague appeals court (29 Jun 2020, ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108, trans man in a women's prison) treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM asks the minister to create CPT-aligned rules placing transgender detainees by gender identity.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Gender expression became an explicitly protected ground under the Equal Treatment Act in March 2019 (bill passed the House 127–23 in 2018 and Senate 64–11 on 12 March 2019), following earlier cases in which the Dutch Institute for Human Rights treated transgender people as covered by the word 'gender'. Since February 2023, sexual orientation (and disability) are formally written into Article 1 of the Netherlands Constitution. Open service in the military has been permitted for gay people since homosexuality's declassification as a mental illness in 1973 and for transgender people as well. Legal gender recognition has been administrative since a December 2013 law took effect in 2014, removing the earlier requirement of surgery and sterilization imposed by the 1984–85 laws. Wikipedia country coverage: Access to care includes full Dutch coverage of PrEP and related care for gay and bisexual men from 1 August 2019, available at all Municipal Health Services (GGD) offices, projected to save €33 million in HIV treatment costs. Assisted insemination for infertility is covered by health insurance regardless of whether the patient is single, in an opposite-sex couple, or a lesbian couple; the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport's 2016 guidelines (endorsed by eight medical organizations, including the Dutch Psychiatry Association and Transvisie) recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, and top surgery is available to patients over 16. In July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate. Conversion therapy has been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012, and the practice was ultimately banned by a bill ratified on 8 September 2026. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth-specific findings are mixed: a 2018 Statistics Netherlands survey found 11.4% of LGBTQ youth faced online bullying and harassment, more than double the rate for heterosexual young people, and a 2020 Movisie estimate put homeless LGBTQ youth at 900–2,000, three times the rate for heterosexual youth, with rejection at home a stated cause. In education, the government-financed religious-school 'single fact construction' loophole that let schools fire staff — as in a 2005 case of a teacher in a same-sex relationship — was closed by bills passed in 2014 (House 141–9) and 2015 (Senate 72–3), effective 1 July 2015, so LGBTQ students and teachers cannot be fired over sexual orientation. The age of consent was equalised at 16 in 1971, ending the 1911 Article 248bis rule that set 21 for same-sex activity. However, acceptance is falling among adolescents: the Utrecht University/Trimbos HBSC study found positive attitudes toward homosexuality among secondary-school boys dropped from 40% to 22% and among girls from 78% to 51% between 2021 and 2025.

USA.name: United States
USA.summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk for a trans visitor to the United States. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

Screening at US checkpoints carries an outing risk: TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Multiple foreign governments have responded. In April 2025 CNN reported that several countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules; Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the US.

Facilities access is restricted in a growing number of states. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol in what civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

State document rules are tightening. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences and invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template for other states, with further targeting bills pending in state legislatures. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.

Visa screening carries its own exposure. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the US to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban on grounds of fraud.

Federal custody presents documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication, and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes, with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.

Care access is constrained for visitors needing it. Executive Order 14187 (January 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

Whether a foreign visitor's own national passport carrying an X marker or a marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth will be accepted for entry, or will trigger secondary screening, is not directly addressed in the inventory. The sources document US-issued passport policy and foreign travel advisories, not port-of-entry treatment of third-country documents.

The "SWS25" visa marking and the fraud-based permanent ban are reported in connection with the sports-related State Department announcement of February 2025; whether the marking or the fraud finding extends to non-athlete visa categories is not stated in the sources.

sources.title: Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration
sources.summary: Wikipedia survey: EO 14168 (sex-as-binary, documents, facilities clause, care-funding halt), EO 14183 (military ban), EO 14187 (care for minors), EO 14190 (schools), EO 14201 (sports), January 2025 federal funding freeze; several orders blocked or enjoined in court. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates: their hair would be cut short, they would be taken off hormone medication, and instead put into psychiatric therapy and given psychiatric drugs. Imprisoned transgender individuals reported being denied access to care, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced labor programs, with guards justifying it with statements like "If you wanna be a man, I'll treat you like a man"; those who refused faced punishments including beatings and solitary confinement, and many also reported severe sexual abuse. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): In December 2025 Attorney General Pam Bondi instructed the FBI to begin offering cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called "radical gender ideology," describing such activists as "domestic terrorist groups." In May 2026 the White House's "United States Counterterrorism Strategy" stated that national counterterrorism activities would "prioritize the rapid identification and neutralization of violent secular political groups whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." The source text also reports beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse against transgender people in ICE custody, and notes that advocates have compared the administration's actions to the early stages of genocide. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): Executive Order 14168 (January 20, 2025) redefined sex for the federal government as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). On the same day Trump rescinded Executive Order 13988, which had sought to protect LGBTQ rights in federal prisons and prevent discrimination. Other measures include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers providing gender-affirming care to transgender youth; the Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): The source text states that during the second Trump presidency the US government has taken actions to persecute transgender people, accompanied by anti-transgender rhetoric and misinformation often to dehumanize and scapegoat them. Anti-transgender campaigning was a large part of the 2024 Trump campaign, with spending on anti-transgender advertising exceeding spending on housing, immigration, or the economy; Trump repeatedly made false claims that schools were performing "gender-affirming surgeries on children without their parents' consent," claims conservative groups called "valid" while acknowledging they were untrue. Censorship measures include a January 2025 list of "forbidden terms" including "gender," "transgender" and "LGBT" in health agencies, removal of words from federal websites including the Stonewall National Monument site, and revocation of scientific grants mentioning LGBT topics. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): Executive Order 14190 (January 29, 2025), "Ending Radical Indoctrination in K-12 Schooling," directs law enforcement to investigate schools for promoting "gender ideology" and to criminally prosecute teachers who facilitate a transgender minor's social transition — including using preferred names or pronouns — potentially as sexual exploitation of a minor and/or practicing medicine without a license, with federal funding revoked for violating schools. Executive Order 14187 (January 28, 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care, and in summer 2025 the DOJ subpoenaed "over 20" hospitals for full records of patients under 19 including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialized LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline; in August 2025 it threatened to pull federal funding from sex education programs mentioning transgender people (11 states and 2 territories complied by November 2025); and in October 2025 proposed HHS rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18, with gender-affirming care for children already banned in 27 states. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): In January 2025 a list of "forbidden terms" was distributed within government health-related agencies instructing employees to avoid words including "gender," "transgender," or "LGBT," and such words were widely removed from federal agency websites including the National Park Service Stonewall National Monument site. Executive Order 14168 mandated federal agencies use "sex" instead of "gender," remove materials that "promote gender ideology," and rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in federal workplaces. Executive Order 14190 additionally directs law enforcement to criminally prosecute educators who refer to a student using preferred name and pronouns or describe a student as "non-binary," and the counterterrorism strategy frames "radically pro-transgender" ideology as a security threat.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Expression has been both suppressed and asserted in U.S. history: during the reservation era, Christian missionaries and federal agencies forced Native American LGBTQ people into prescribed dress and grooming, such as making males cut their hair and females wear dresses, while both Native and non-Native LGBTQ people lived in hiding because homosexuality was a criminal offense. Open expression also carried risk — William Dorsey Swann, born enslaved in Maryland, organized drag balls in Washington, D.C. in the 1880s and 1890s and was arrested repeatedly, including the first documented case of arrests for female impersonation on April 12, 1888. The military's Don't Ask, Don't Tell policy (1990s–2011) explicitly barred soldiers from coming out, and gender expression-related bullying contributed to a wave of teenage and young adult suicides in 2009–2010 that prompted the It Gets Better Project. Wikipedia country coverage: Partner recognition has advanced unevenly: Berkeley, California became the first jurisdiction to recognize same-sex unions in 1984 through domestic partnership health benefits for city employees, California passed the first state domestic partnership law in 1999, and Vermont was the first state to legalize civil unions. The federal Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) barred federal recognition of same-sex unions until it was ruled unconstitutional in 2013, and Obergefell v. Hodges legalized same-sex marriage nationwide on June 26, 2015; the Respect for Marriage Act of December 2022 repealed DOMA and required all states to recognize existing same-sex marriages. Recognition still varies: same-sex marriages are not licensed or recognized in American Samoa, and status differs across sovereign Native American tribal nations. Adoption policy also remains state-dependent, with some states allowing same-sex couple adoption and others banning all unmarried couples. Wikipedia country coverage: Social climate and visibility have shifted markedly over time: Gallup found 7.6% of U.S. adults identified as LGBTQ or another non-heterosexual orientation in 2024, rising to 22.3% among Gen Z (born 1997–2012) and 9.8% among Millennials, versus 1.1% of the Silent Generation. Visibility grew through media — Ellen was cancelled in 1998 after its star came out, while Will & Grace premiered that same year and is credited with helping increase public acceptance — and through institutions like Gay Straight Alliance clubs, which research links to greater safety, inclusion, wellbeing and educational attainment for LGBTQ students. At the same time, climate remains hostile: the FBI reports bias against sexual orientation has consistently accounted for between one-seventh and one-fifth of single-bias reported hate incidents this century, 37 states still lacked anti-bias statutes for gender-identity crimes as of 2019, and the Transgender Day of Remembrance is held annually for transgender murder victims.

USA.comparisons: Compared to the UK (0.66): the US shares bathroom-law enforcement and border hostility but adds foreign-government traveler warnings and documented foreign-visitor detention, which the UK lacks. The US scores above Peru (0.48) — Peru's higher baseline street violence is offset by the US's unique institutional hostility (traveler warnings, border detention, bathroom arrests) — and level with Mexico (0.50): Mexico's far higher lethal anti-trans violence (~50+ murders/year, police extortion) is balanced against the US's documented traveler-detention cases and state-level legal enforcement, which Mexico lacks. Different risk profiles converging at the same score.

USA.tangentialFactors:
The federal posture differs from state practice in ways a visitor may notice at different points of a trip. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia impose no state-level ban on trans people using facilities consistent with their gender identity, while nine states and one territory restrict such use in schools and some government buildings; the practical environment therefore varies sharply by itinerary. Kansas's February 2026 law is described by rights groups as a template, and a July 2026 assessment flagged four states as "Do Not Travel" for trans people, suggesting the sub-national picture is moving in one direction rather than stabilising.

Foreign governments treat the United States as a changed destination. Advisories issued in early 2025 by multiple countries, and adjusted travel guidelines from at least eight European states, place the US in a category where allied governments formally warn their own trans citizens. That is unusual for a destination of comparable diplomatic standing and is a reasonable proxy for how seriously document and data rules are taken abroad.

Several federal measures remain contested in court. The passport sex-marker restrictions were allowed to proceed by the Supreme Court in November 2025, but the Wikipedia survey records that a number of the executive orders have been blocked or enjoined, and the ACLU suit on behalf of seven plaintiffs is pending. The legal position is therefore active rather than settled, and a visitor's experience may differ from a reading of any single order.

USA.localsOnly:
State identity-document rules govern what a resident can hold, independent of federal passport policy. MAP's identity-document map sets out which states allow gender-marker changes on a driver's licence or birth certificate and under what conditions; Kansas has closed both routes as of February 2026 and invalidated existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth.

Executive Order 14168 also reaches federal workplaces: it rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in federal workplaces, and mandated that federal agencies use "sex" rather than "gender" and remove materials that "promote gender ideology." A January 2025 list of "forbidden terms" circulated within government health-related agencies instructed employees to avoid words including "gender," "transgender" and "LGBT," and such words were removed from federal agency websites including the National Park Service Stonewall National Monument site; scientific grants mentioning LGBT topics were revoked.

Education and sport carry criminal and administrative exposure for residents. Executive Order 14190 (29 January 2025) directs law enforcement to investigate schools for promoting "gender ideology" and to criminally prosecute teachers who facilitate a transgender minor's social transition, including using preferred names or pronouns, potentially as sexual exploitation of a minor or practising medicine without a licence, with federal funding revoked for violating schools. Executive Order 14201 (5 February 2025), "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports," underpins the visa marking described above. An October 2025 rule blocks student loan forgiveness for public workers providing gender-affirming care to transgender youth, and an August 2025 threat to pull federal funding from sex education programmes mentioning transgender people led 11 states and two territories to comply by November 2025.

Residents in custody face the Federal Bureau of Prisons and ICE policies described above, and the Bureau of Prisons no longer publishes the count of transgender prisoners it holds. Residents under 18 seeking care face bans in 27 states and the proposed Medicaid exclusion; adults' access is not addressed by these particular measures.

BRA.name: Brazil
BRA.summary:
Brazil pairs a broad legal framework for LGBTI people with persistent violence against them in practice. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and a federal anti-discrimination framework covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds.

After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. Courts have applied those provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists. In the October 2024 municipal elections, close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

Protection machinery has also widened. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.

Detention carries a specific and contested regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons, carried out between April and June 2021, interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region. It documents that in that system travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.
BRA.outOfScopeNotes:
Access to sex-segregated facilities such as restrooms and changing rooms is not addressed by any source in the present inventory. Whether official guidance affirms a trans person's right to use facilities matching their identity, and on what legal basis, remains unresolved here.

The gap between the National Council of Justice's placement rules and conditions on the ground is documented for one state system only. Whether Resolution 348 and Resolution 366 are applied as written at custody hearings elsewhere in the country is not sourced in this inventory, and the Rio de Janeiro census covers eleven units in one metropolitan region rather than the national prison population.

The enforcement record for the 2019 hate-crime provisions is illustrated by a single civil damages ruling against a nightclub. Criminal prosecutions and convictions for transphobia under those provisions are not sourced here.

The travel advisory material in the inventory concerns general crime, gang activity and demonstrations. It offers no trans-specific assessment, so the extent to which official advisories address anti-LGBTI violence is unresolved.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D5, D6, D8, D11, D13.

sources.summary: Overview: same-sex marriage legal nationwide since 2013; legal gender change without surgery allowed since 2018 (STF); age of consent equal; plus federal anti-discrimination framework. Wikipedia country coverage: Brazil was the first country in Latin America to recognize same-sex unions for immigration benefits: on November 25, 2003, Judge Ana Carolina Morozowski of the 5th Civil Court of Curitiba granted permanent residency to the British partner of gay activist Toni Reis, and a week later the National Immigration Council issued Administrative Resolution No. 3 granting temporary or permanent visas to partners 'without distinction of sex.' The Brazilian government was slow to cable consulates, leaving binational same-sex couples confused about how to apply; Immigration Equality and the Brazilian Rainbow Group met officials at the New York consulate in February 2004 to press for clarity. A Florianópolis judge also barred immigration authorities from deporting an Italian woman partnered with a Brazilian lesbian. Identity documents also reflect gender: passports and ID cards allow an 'unspecified'/X marker under ICAO standards (mandatory for state-issued ID cards since January 11, 2024), and the 2025 Superior Court of Justice decision permitting a neutral gender on the civil registry affects only the plaintiff but sets a precedent. Wikipedia country coverage: Brazil's public health system (SUS) provides free sex reassignment surgery as a basic constitutional right, per a 2007 4th Regional Federal Court ruling; roughly 250 such surgeries were performed between 2000 and 2007 at three university hospitals. Access is constrained in practice: the Health Ministry left qualification decisions to local officials, and the text notes that long lines and poorly equipped public facilities push those who can afford it toward private hospitals and clinics. Partners in registered stable unions are recognized as dependents on health plans and insurers. In July 2026, the 3rd Panel of the Superior Court of Justice ruled that health insurance plans must cover facial feminization surgeries, and in March 2024 the Supreme Court extended five-day paid paternity leave to the non-pregnant mothers of lesbian couples. Wikipedia country coverage: Gender-affirming care for minors was banned by Brazil's Federal Council of Medicine (CFM) in April 2025, alongside a reduction of the minimum age for gender-affirming surgery from 25 to 21; LGBTQ+ advocates filed a Direct Action of Unconstitutionality at the Supreme Court. The Federal Court of Acre blocked the resolution on July 25, 2025, restoring care for minors nationwide, but on October 2, 2025 Federal Judge Flávio Dino overturned that block and reinstated the ban — making youth medication continuity and cross-state travel a live issue. Adult access to surgery within the public system requires patients to be at least 21, diagnosed with no personality disorder, and to undergo at least two years of psychological evaluation. Conversion therapy has been forbidden by the Federal Psychology Council since 1999, though a Brasília federal judge briefly approved it in September 2017 before reversing course in December 2017; the Supreme Court ultimately banned it, and in 2019 Justice Cármen Lúcia issued an injunction overturning the judge's decisions. Blood donation restrictions on gay and bisexual men (12 months without same-sex activity) were struck down as unconstitutional by the Federal Supreme Court in May 2020. Wikipedia country coverage: Hostility is documented both in violence and in legislative opposition: Senator Marcelo Crivella attacked the pending federal anti-discrimination bill, arguing homosexuals would receive a protection that 'should have been given to women, the elderly and children,' while conservative senators framed the law as an aggression on religious freedom. In January 2019 openly gay representative Jean Wyllys left Brazil after death threats, replaced in February by David Miranda. Grupo Gay da Bahia reported 343 LGBTQ murders in 2016, 387 in 2017 and 420 in 2018, but the figures are disputed: Veja columnist Reinaldo de Azevedo called the GGB methodology 'unscientific' because it counts all media-reported murders of LGBTQ people regardless of motive, and scholars note international comparisons are flawed because figures reflect documentation capacity rather than crime totals. The text also notes the Catholic Church and radical evangelical groups have been identified as sources of rising intolerance, and documents a 2007 incident in which a judge was brought before São Paulo's Justice Council for calling soccer a 'virile, masculine sport and not a homosexual one.' Wikipedia country coverage: Education is a direct battleground: the Supreme Federal Court ruled in June 2024 (recorded as 2024 elsewhere in the text) that public and private schools must fight discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, sexist bullying against cisgender and transgender girls, and homotransphobic bullying. Since 2020 the Court has been overturning state and municipal laws banning 'gender and sexuality courses' in schools, and since 2023 it has been overturning laws banning gender-neutral language in schools. Youth-specific risks include the April 2025 CFM ban on gender-affirming care for minors (see D8) and labor exploitation: in the central, north and northeastern regions, transgender people from extremely poor families sometimes begin sex work as early as age 12 after expulsion from home, and travestis commonly work the streets as young as 16 or 17 in southern/southeastern regions and major capitals. On the more favorable side, the 2004 government initiative Brasil Sem Homophobia was designed to protect LGBTQ students, and a 2010 Rio de Janeiro State University/University of Campinas survey found 95% of homosexual youth had revealed their orientation by age 18, many by 16, versus after 21 for the 1980s generation.

Country overview (updated Mar 2026): constitutional and federal criminal provisions — after the 2019 Supreme Court ruling — prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds, yet LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination in practice.
Expat legal guide (updated 5 Apr 2026): same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules apply nationwide, forming the entry and family framework for a trans visitor or partner.
Investigation (May 2024): 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies victimise LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo; the city prepares for a Pride drawing thousands of tourists.

AP (Oct 2024): 'Death threats assail Brazil's trailblazing trans candidates as they campaign' — nearly 1,000 transgender politicians run in municipal elections across every state amid threats and intimidation, as the number of trans officeholders has tripled since the last cycle.

São Paulo Court of Justice (27th Private Chamber) upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing — the Barra Bonita first instance had ordered R$4,000 compensation.

Analysis (2022): lower courts pushed the Superior Court of Justice (STJ) toward unanimously extending Maria da Penha Law and Feminicide Law remedies to trans women — inclusion of trans people in violence-prevention law.
São Paulo Municipal Council parliamentary inquiry (CPI) on Violence Against Trans and Travesti Persons: final report carrying 189 recommendations.

Canada travel advisory (updated Aug 2026) for Brazil: exercise a high degree of caution because of high crime rates and gang-related urban violence; avoid demonstrations and border drug-trafficking zones. Country-wide guidance covering all visitors.
Tour operator guide: Brazil 'progressive' on LGBTQIA+ rights and generally safe, but flags that practical safety issues can arise for LGBTQIA+ travellers.
Historical essay (Mar 2000): historian James N. Green on early-1900s Rio homosexual subculture — Glória monument site functioning as a meeting venue in the 'tropical Paris' era.

sources.summary: Brazil's National Council of Justice (CNJ) Resolution 348 of 13 Oct 2020, as amended by Resolution 366 of 20 Jan 2021, is the national framework for where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed: a person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing (Art. 4º); on arrest, the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person is consulted about their preference (Art. 7º), and the judge must inform them of the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it general population or specific wings/cells (Art. 8º); the declared preference is recorded and a later change of placement is possible, with transfers prioritised in cases of violence or serious threat (Art. 9º). LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited (Art. 11, VI–VII). The resolution entered into force after publication (120 days, extended to 180 days by Res. 366/2021).

RUS.name: Russia
RUS.summary:
Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression — including, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Since the November 2023 extremist designation, arrests have occurred for displaying the rainbow flag or its colors, and between March and May 2026 nine LGBTQ organizations (including Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out, and Centre T) were outlawed as extremist.

SAU.name: Saudi Arabia
SAU.summary:
Saudi Arabia is among the most dangerous countries in which a transgender person can be discovered. The kingdom has no codified penal code: judges apply an uncodified interpretation of sharia drawn from the Quran and Sunnah, and same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity are prosecuted under that framework. Penalties range from fines and flogging through lengthy or indeterminate imprisonment to death in the most severe cases.

Transgender expression is itself treated as an offending act. Deviation from traditional gender norms is prosecuted as a criminal offence rather than merely tolerated as conduct accompanying a charge, and police and morality-enforcement officers apply the provisions with wide discretion. There is no legal gender recognition, no legal status for same-sex relationships, and no discrimination protections.

Enforcement is documented and lethal. Mohammad Amin, a Pakistani transgender woman known as Meeno, died in Saudi custody in 2017 after a roundup that ended with her held in Azizia prison in Riyadh alongside 34 others; Pakistani activists said she was beaten with clubs and hosepipes aggravating a chronic heart condition, while Saudi authorities attributed the death to a heart attack, an account her family and trans-rights activists dispute. In October 2021, five Saudi men were arrested in the Northern Borders province after filming themselves in women's clothing and posting the footage online. In 2005, dozens of men caught dancing and behaving as women at a Jeddah party described as a gay wedding were sentenced in a closed trial without defence lawyers to a combined 14,200 lashes and up to two years in prison.

Enforcement reaches travellers for expression as well as conduct. Amnesty International reported in June 2026 that visitors have been imprisoned over social media posts, including a business analyst arrested at Riyadh airport on 31 August 2024 as he was returning to the United Kingdom with his family, targeted for posts published before he entered the country.

Official travel guidance is inconsistent with this record. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office states that same-sex relations are illegal although legal action is uncommon, advises couples against public affection, and warns that transgender status is not recognised, exposing trans travellers to difficulties with dress codes and access to medical care. VisitSaudi states that all visitors are welcome and that privacy will be respected.
SAU.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the death penalty has actually been carried out for consensual same-sex conduct in recent years, as opposed to being available in theory, is not resolved by the sources assembled here.

The UK FCDO assertion that legal action is uncommon is not quantified and is not reconciled with the documented arrest cases; the frequency of prosecution remains unresolved.

The specific legal status of gender-affirming care is not sourced in this inventory. The only care-related finding is the UK FCDO warning that trans travellers may face difficulties with access to medical care.

The competing accounts of Mohammad Amin's death, beating versus heart attack, remain disputed and unresolved; no independent adjudication of the cause is available in these sources.

VisitSaudi's statement that all visitors are welcome and privacy will be respected has no stated legal effect and is not corroborated by any enforcement or policy document in this inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D6, D13.

Wikipedia country coverage: In May 2023 the Saudi Tourism Authority's FAQ page was updated to state that all visitors, including LGBTQ visitors, are welcome, though homosexuality remains illegal and enforcement is described as not universal. Entry and exit visa paperwork does not ask about sexual orientation, but does ask nationality, sex, religion and marital status; tourist visas were introduced in 2019 alongside a Public Decency Law fining public displays of affection and immodest clothing. In September 2013 Gulf states discussed a proposal to test and ban gay foreigners, which officials later downplayed as a mere proposal. Foreigners face deportation as a penalty for homosexuality, and work-visa applicants must pass an HIV test on arrival and before permit renewal, with infected foreigners deported. Wikipedia country coverage: Bars and nightclubs are illegal, and public movie theaters—permitted only since 2018—have LGBTQ themes edited out of films, with customs maintaining a banned list of films and TV shows. The government has designated several hospitals to treat people with AIDS/HIV, but other hospitals often refuse care or treat patients without compassion, and condoms were until recently rarely available outside certain hospitals or medical supply stores. In June 2022 officials in Riyadh seized rainbow-colored products in a crackdown framed as curbing promotion of homosexuality. Observers reported that MDLBeast Soundstorm, an annual multi-day music festival in Riyadh, included public display of LGBTQI+ culture, while appearing to support homosexuality can result in prosecution for individuals and clubs alike. Wikipedia country coverage: Public education is required to teach Islamic values strongly condemning homosexuality, and Ministry of Education textbooks stated that homosexuality is "one of the most disgusting sins and greatest crimes" with capital punishment as the penalty for public homosexual intercourse—though in 2020 the Ministry was found to have removed the death-penalty condemnation from textbooks. In 2012 the government asked the CPVPV to help expel students judged to be gay or lesbian based on their mannerisms and fashion taste. The June 2022 rainbow-goods seizure explicitly targeted "the young generation," confiscating children's hair accessories, backpacks, pencil cases and rainbow-striped crayon packs. HIV prevention education for men who have sex with men is minimal, though a 2024 Saudi AIDS National Program report makes some mention of them; private schools, mainly serving expatriates, have discretion over curriculum on homosexuality.

BBC News: 'Meeno' — Mohammad Amin, a Pakistani transgender woman — died in Saudi custody after a roundup with 34 others in Azizia prison, Riyadh; Pakistani activists say she was beaten with clubs and hosepipes aggravating a chronic heart condition, while Saudi authorities attributed the death to a heart attack; family and trans-rights activists dispute the official account. Directly relevant to how Saudi enforcement treats trans people.

Gulf News (25 Oct 2021): five Saudi men were arrested in the Northern Borders province after filming themselves in women's clothing and posting the footage on social media — cross-dressing/gender-nonconformity enforced as a criminal matter.

Amnesty International (29 Jun 2026, updated 17 Jul 2026): documents visitors imprisoned over social media posts — including a business analyst arrested at Riyadh airport on 31 Aug 2024 as he was returning to the UK with his family, targeted for posts published before he even arrived in the country. Enforcement reaches travellers for expression, not only conduct on the ground.

UK FCDO Saudi Arabia safety advice (current): same-sex relations are illegal although legal action is uncommon; couples should avoid public affection; VisitSaudi states all visitors are welcome and privacy will be respected; being transgender is not recognised — trans travellers could face difficulties with dress codes and access to medical care.

A3M Global Monitoring LGBTQ+ Risk Map (2024/25): Saudi Arabia appears among the least safe destinations for LGBTQ travellers in a ranking that also lists Somalia, Yemen, Uganda, Afghanistan, UAE, Tanzania, Malaysia and Pakistan.

The Guardian (April 2005) by Brian Whitaker: 'Saudis' tough line on gays' - dozens of Saudi men caught dancing and 'behaving like women' at a Jeddah party described as a 'gay wedding' were sentenced to a total of 14,200 lashes plus up to two years' jail, after a closed trial without defence lawyers; HRW's Scott Long: 'Prosecuting and imprisoning people for homosexual conduct are flagrant human rights violations.'

AFG.name: Afghanistan
AFG.summary:
Afghanistan under the Taliban is the most hostile environment on this map for a transgender person. No legal protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity existed before the 2021 takeover and none exists after it, according to the EUAA COI Report of February 2026. The Taliban's Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice Law of 31 July 2024, in its Article 22, obliges the regime's overseers to prevent listed evils including lesbianism and homosexuality "even if with one's own spouse", placing same-sex conduct under continuous moral surveillance alongside adultery and gambling.

Criminalisation is layered. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, updated 19 January 2026, records that Afghanistan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women: Penal Code 2017 provisions on "sodomy" and "inciting sodomy" carry up to two years' imprisonment, while the Code's Sharia-reference clause permits the death penalty for same-sex activity. Amnesty International, cited in the EUAA COI Report, states that same-sex relations are punishable by death, and reporting from October 2021 records the same conclusion as applied by the ruling movement.

Enforcement has intensified and is public. OHCHR reported in March 2026 that UN human-rights experts condemned a surge in corporal punishment, with at least 1,110 people flogged during 2025 alone, nearly double the 2024 figure, and warned that women, girls and LGBT+ people face heightened punishment for moral crimes including adultery, illicit relationships and sodomy. OutRight International reported in February 2023, from interviews conducted with LGBTIQ Afghans still in the country in September and October 2022, that Taliban security officials pursue gay men and trans women more systematically than in the early months of rule, using physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations; the Taliban Supreme Court has confirmed such punishments on social media.

Detention is documented as abusive. CNN reported in November 2024 first-person accounts of arbitrary detention, beatings and sexual abuse in Taliban custody as the crackdown intensified. The Human Rights Watch and OutRight report of 26 January 2022, based on 60 interviews, found that Taliban members and their supporters attack, threaten and expel LGBT people from their homes, that abuse by family, neighbours and partners surged after the takeover, and that many went into hiding or fled. Reporting from Kabul in October 2021 documented street attacks on men coded as gay, with victims changing their clothing and confining themselves indoors.

Visibly transgender people carry the gravest risk. The JURIST feature of 8 November 2024, drawing on the Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan formed by Afghan LGBTQ refugees in Bremen, reports systematic persecution after August 2021 and notes that even the post-2001 constitution provided no protective framework. Transgender residents describe years of hiding in windowless rooms. A discovered trans visitor would be processed by the same apparatus as local LGBTIQ people: moral-police surveillance under the 2024 law, arbitrary detention, corporal punishment, and abuse in custody, with no legal recognition, no protection machinery, and no consular recourse that operates for LGBTIQ detainees.
