sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Under the Islamic Republic, Afghanistan's Law of Marriages (1971) required a legal marriage to be between two Muslim adults of the opposite sex, with Article 41 directing that gaps in the law be resolved by Islamic law principles, so no same-sex marriage, civil union or domestic partnership was recognized; the 1949 Law on Marriages, Weddings and Circumcision likewise framed marriage as between a Muslim man and woman. Under Taliban rule post-2021, same-sex relationships and marriages are not recognized at all. Additionally, Article 430 made it an 'Instigation of Delinquency' for an adult to promote or assist a minor in adultery, homosexuality or prostitution, a document that can criminalize any adult (including a caregiver or partner) involved with a same-sex partner or family. Wikipedia country coverage: Health and support facilities are severely limited: in 2017 the U.S. State Department reported that LGBTI community members 'did not have access to certain health services' and could be fired from jobs because of sexual orientation, and that organizations protecting LGBTI freedom 'remained underground because they could not legally register with the government.' The first HIV-AIDS treatment center opened in Kabul in 2009 with more clinics promised, but access to anti-retroviral drugs is 'at best limited,' and the government only permits condom distribution to married couples (2020 report), excluding same-sex couples. Wikipedia country coverage: Care access is constrained by law, stigma and limited infrastructure: before 2003 little or no HIV-AIDS education or treatment existed; the 2008 official count was 504 people living with HIV-AIDS though the true number was suspected to be in the thousands, with low literacy, weak infrastructure and social taboos blocking comprehensive public health education. The 2017 U.S. State Department report documented that LGBTI people lacked access to certain health services, and Article 373 of the criminal code imposes fines or murder-equivalent penalties for spreading a 'dangerous disease.' Youth-specific: Article 430 of the marriage law (which the source cites alongside the 1971 Marriage Law) treats any adult who promotes or assists minors (under 18) in adultery, homosexuality or prostitution as committing 'Instigation of Delinquency,' which can deter adults from seeking care for minors; in bacha bazi cases under the Islamic Republic, young victims were often charged rather than the adult perpetrators, while Article 427 increased punishment where the victim was under 18, and Article 398 offered lesser punishment for vigilante honor killings that can target minors found engaging in homosexuality. Wikipedia country coverage: Partner recognition is legally non-existent: under the 1971 Law of Marriages, Article 41 directed that unaddressed issues be decided by Islamic law, so Afghanistan family law never recognized same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, and the Taliban government does not recognize same-sex relationships or marriages. Civil-society partnership is also barred — no law addressed discrimination or harassment on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, political parties were prohibited from advocating anything opposing Islamic morality, and by the 2017 and 2020 State Department reports LGBTQ organizations could not legally register and remained underground. On 23 January 2025, ICC Prosecutor Karim Ahmad Khan requested arrest warrants against Taliban leaders Hibatullah Akhundzada and Abdul Hakim Haqqani for persecution of women, girls and the LGBTQ community — the first time the court has recognized crimes against the LGBTQ community. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth are a documented target: bacha bazi involves teenage boys kidnapped, dressed in women's clothing, made to dance in competitions and forced into sexual acts; when the Taliban came to power in 1996 they banned bacha bazi alongside homosexuality, both carrying the death penalty, and under the Islamic Republic young victims were often charged rather than the adult perpetrators. A law was enacted prohibiting Afghan soldiers from having their 'ashna' ('friend') live with them, and President Karzai signed an agreement to ban the practice, but it was rarely enforced, police were reportedly complicit, and neither the U.S. Department of Defense nor the Afghan government took action despite being aware. Education access is hampered by low literacy, weak infrastructure, taboos, abstinence-only sex education programs, censorship provisions (Article 32 of the 2002 Press Law prohibiting 'incitement to depravity' and Article 27(D) of the 1973 Postal Law barring material 'repugnant to public decency'), and a 2009 memoir about growing up gay in Afghanistan (Hamid Zaher's It Is Your Enemy Who Is Dock-Tailed) that cannot be distributed within the country. A 2011 survey found young men displaying rainbow symbols unaware of their meaning, and in 2017 and 2020 the State Department noted that awareness of sexual orientation or gender identity remained limited and homosexuality was widely seen as taboo. Wikipedia country coverage: Facilities are effectively closed to LGBTQ Afghans: the 2017 U.S. State Department report found LGBTI people 'did not have access to certain health services,' and organizations protecting LGBTI freedom 'remained underground because they could not legally register with the government' — a status the 2020 report confirmed. On the health side, the country's first HIV-AIDS treatment center only opened in Kabul in 2009, with more clinics promised, and access to anti-retroviral drugs remains 'at best, limited.' Persons convicted of homosexuality were generally sentenced to prison in the cities under the Islamic Republic. Wikipedia country coverage: Care access is severely restricted and stigmatized. The 2017 U.S. State Department report found LGBTI community members 'did not have access to certain health services,' while the 2020 report noted the government only permits condom distribution to married couples and that there is stigma against people living with HIV. Prior to 2003 little or no HIV-AIDS education or treatment existed; as of 2008 the official count was 504 people living with HIV-AIDS, with the true figure suspected to be in the thousands, and low literacy, weak infrastructure and traditional social mores impede public health education. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth are the primary targets of sexual exploitation and of the law. Militia members without access to women kidnap boys to be humiliated and raped, and other boys become prostitutes regardless of sexual orientation — a practice known as bacha bazi, prevalent in big cities and reported in 2007 as still common in northern Afghanistan, involving teenage boys dressed in women's clothing made to dance and perform sexual acts. GBR.name: United Kingdom
GBR.summary:
The United Kingdom's post-April 2025 Supreme Court regime now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery rather than executive decree. In August 2026 the equality watchdog's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. The code is the daily, nationwide consequence of the ruling: trans visitors use facilities designated by biological sex, and organisations are instructed on how to lawfully enforce that division.

Prison placement has been litigated to the same end. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, ruled the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory custody guidance unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis; the guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in prisons matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The preceding hearing had been told by the challengers that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard. Any visitor arrested in the United Kingdom should therefore expect placement by sex at birth, with contested suicide-risk arguments surrounding that outcome.

Searching and strip-searching follow the same rule. British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court ruling, with trans women searched by officers of their sex at birth as an interim position; the prior policy had permitted a trans woman staff member to conduct an intimate search of a woman holding a Gender Recognition Certificate. Police Scotland's interim guidance of 25 June 2025 states that in custody and stop-and-search, any search involving removal beyond a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear is conducted on the basis of biological sex, though where a person's lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request.

The direction of travel is a court- and watchdog-led rollback rather than executive hostility, and it is contested at international level: on 18 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.
GBR.outOfScopeNotes:
Surrey Police's FOI-released searching/biological-sex policy (a Surrey and Sussex document) could not be retrieved at research time because the source returned HTTP 403; its contents are therefore unverified here and no claim in this record rests on it.

Whether the interim search policies issued by British Transport Police and Police Scotland have been made permanent, or replaced by a national consolidated policy, is not sourced in this inventory. The inventory also does not record whether the Scottish Prison Service issued replacement custody guidance after the 19 June 2026 ruling, nor whether the reported revisions to the Equality Act 2010 have been enacted in the form the UN experts criticised.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D1, D2.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: In December 2023, the UK government said it would no longer accept gender recognition certificates issued by 50 countries and U.S. states (including Sweden, New York State, and Belgium), due to concerns those jurisdictions allowed people to transition 'too easily'; individuals from these locations would have to apply for a new GRC under British law to legally change their gender in the UK. Women and Equalities Minister Kemi Badenoch called the changes 'long overdue', while Shadow Equalities Minister Anneliese Dodds warned of diplomatic consequences since the list excluded Canada, the US, Australia and New Zealand. Wikipedia country coverage: In November 2021, a lesbian couple launched a judicial review against Frimley NHS Clinical Commissioning Group over a 'discriminatory' fertility policy: heterosexual couples only need to 'try to conceive' for 2 years before NHS-funded treatment, while same-sex female couples must undergo 12 rounds of private IVF first. For trans youth specifically, NHS England said in March 2024 that gender identity clinics would no longer prescribe puberty blockers to children or young people (renewed indefinitely in December 2024, to be reconsidered in 2027), and in April 2025 it was reported the NHS had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year since the Cass Review, with families sometimes turning to black-market or overseas hormones instead. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex marriage was legalised in England and Wales in 2014 (Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013, in force 13 March 2014), in Scotland in 2014, and in Northern Ireland on 13 January 2020 after UK Parliament intervention. However, transgender people seeking a Gender Recognition Certificate have historically been required to divorce or annul their marriage first, and under current law a GRC will not be issued unless the spouse consents; if the spouse does not consent, the marriage must be terminated. Civil partnerships, available since 2005, give most but not all rights of marriage and have recognition issues in other countries. Wikipedia country coverage: Section 28, which prohibited the 'promotion of homosexuality' by schools and local authorities, was repealed in 2003. Transgender youth are covered by the Equality Act 2010, but the Bell v Tavistock ruling (December 2020) found children under 16 could not independently consent to puberty blockers (overturned on appeal September 2021); the Cass Review (April 2024) led NHS England to stop prescribing puberty blockers to minors and close the Tavistock GIDS in March 2024, with only two of eight planned regional centres opened and many 16-17 year olds transferred to adult services. In January 2022, the Girls' Day School Trust barred admissions for trans girls without a Gender Recognition Certificate, and in July 2022 the RFU/RFL implemented a single-sex policy for under-12s excluding trans girls from girls' teams. Wikipedia country coverage: Anti-trans rhetoric in UK media has been described as 'increasing and becoming more vitriolic' since 2016 and 'super-charged' since 2018; a 2019 study by Paul Baker found numerous UK press articles from 2018-2019 were written to be critical of trans people and cast them as 'unreasonable and aggressive'. ILGA-Europe rankings show the UK fell from 1st in Europe (86% score) in 2015 to 9th in 2020 (66%, with concern about a 'hostile climate on trans rights') to 22nd in 2025 (45%, third steepest drop in Europe). Despite this, 86% of UK respondents agreed homosexuality should be accepted (2019 Pew poll) and 77% support same-sex marriage (2017 poll); large LGBT communities exist in Brighton, Blackpool, Manchester, London and other cities with gay villages and annual pride festivals.

DEU.name: Germany
DEU.summary:
Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several states have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all.

How the exception is applied in practice remains unsettled. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025; authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility, and critics called the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law.

DW reported on 23 August 2023 that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates, a finding illustrated by the case of climate activist Penelope Frank of Last Generation, legally recorded male, who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted. The Berlin prison service maintains an official page in German with information and contacts for trans, inter and non-binary persons held across the city's facilities.

Screening is a documented flashpoint. In June 2025 the DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which officers allegedly deliberately disregarded her gender identity; she characterised the incident as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment and gave Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a debate about registered trans women's access, in which trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic. Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel reported on how Berlin saunas and similar venues now treat trans women, after months of public argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

Reporting and support machinery exists for hostility encountered in country. The STOP the HATE campaign site, run by the Prevention and Empowerment organisation in northern Germany, provides a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.
DEU.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether identity-based placement is applied uniformly across the 16 states is unresolved in these sources. No national figure for the number of trans prisoners, and no data on the outcomes of intake placement reviews, is sourced here.

The legal weight of the Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline against the Self-Determination Act is unresolved. The sources document the debate and individual venue practice, but no court ruling on whether a private association may restrict women's saunas by sex characteristics is available.

The outcome of BASHKKA's complaint under the Equal Treatment Act is not sourced, and no source states whether Frankfurt Airport screening procedures were revised after 23 November 2024.

Whether a visitor's gender marker is checked at entry in general, as distinct from the documented airport incident, is not addressed by any source in this inventory.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity between men was recriminalized under Paragraph 175 of the German Empire's Penal Code in 1871. Nazi Germany extended these laws during World War II, resulting in convictions multiplying to about 8,000 per year and 5,000–15,000 suspected offenders interned in concentration camps. East Germany decriminalized in 1968 and West Germany in 1969. In 2002 the government overturned Nazi-era convictions, and in 2017 the Bundestag unanimously passed a bill to pardon around 50,000 men convicted after WWII, with compensation of €3,000 per conviction plus €1,500 per year of jail time. A compensation scheme was implemented in September 2021. Wikipedia country coverage: Transgender people have been allowed to change their legal gender since 1980 under the Transsexuals Act, which originally required genital surgery and sterilization. In January 2011 the Federal Constitutional Court ruled those requirements unconstitutional. Effective 1 November 2024, the Self-Determination Act (passed April 2024, 374–251) allows adults to change gender by self-determination with three months' notice. The Act applies to transgender, intersex, and nonbinary adults. Separately, since 1 January 2019, an intersex 'divers' (miscellaneous) option is available on birth certificates, passports, and driver's licenses under the Third Gender Act, though a doctor's statement confirming intersex status is required, which LGBT groups criticized. The 'divers' option was clarified in April 2019 as applying to intersex people only, not transgender people. Wikipedia country coverage: Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is illegal in health services throughout Germany under the General Act on Equal Treatment (in force 18 August 2006). Since May 2020 Germany has had a nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors, making it the fifth country to do so, with penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting, or referring minors to conversion therapy. Regarding blood donation, MSM were previously banned; a one-year deferral took effect in summer 2017, reduced to four months in September 2021, and an individual risk-based assessment replaced the deferral from 1 April 2023. The German Medical Association is against explicit legalisation of assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and directs members not to perform such procedures, though this directive is not legally binding. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples have been legally recognized since 2001 through registered life partnerships, providing rights in inheritance, alimony, health insurance, immigration, hospital and jail visitations, and name change. Same-sex marriage became legal on 1 October 2017 after the Bundestag passed the bill on 30 June 2017 (393–226), granting full marital and adoption rights. Same-sex stepchild adoption became legal in 2005 and expanded to 'successive adoption' in 2013. However, a Federal Court of Justice ruling in October 2018 held that the non-biological mother in a married lesbian couple is not automatically recognized on a child's birth certificate and must adopt — unlike heterosexual couples where the non-biological father is automatically recognized. A bill to rectify this inequality (initiated by the Greens in June 2018) was pending in the Bundestag. Wikipedia country coverage: Conversion therapy for minors was banned nationwide in May 2020, protecting LGBTQ youth. In May 2019 the Federal Minister of Family Affairs recommended teachers use gender-neutral forms ('parent 1 and parent 2' instead of 'mother and father'). The age of consent was equalized at 14 years in East Germany in 1989 and unified Germany in 1994. According to the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2013 survey, two-thirds of 20,000 German LGBT respondents concealed their sexual orientation at school and in public life. Discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is illegal in education under the 2006 General Act on Equal Treatment.

JPN.name: Japan
JPN.summary:
Most visitors to Japan report little direct hostility or discrimination in daily contact, particularly in major tourist destinations, and the everyday risk posture for a transgender traveller is low. LGBTQ visibility remains limited, social attitudes can be reserved, and legal equality still lags behind other developed countries.

The statutory framework is the Act on Promotion of Public Understanding of Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity. The official translation defines gender identity, obliges the government to publish the annual implementation status of policies promoting understanding of sexual orientation and gender identity diversity, and sets out the national basic plan. Parliament enacted the law in June 2023 after months of debate.

No national anti-discrimination statute stands alongside that Act, and no statutory guarantee against violence on grounds of gender identity exists. Full marriage equality for same-sex couples is also absent, so a trans visitor's marital or partner status has no national recognition to rely on.

On workplace and facilities access, Japan's Supreme Court ruled in July 2023 that government restrictions on a transgender employee's use of restrooms were illegal. The Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry was found to have violated public-service law by barring a transgender woman from the women's bathroom at work. She had challenged the denial in 2015, and a Tokyo district court ruled for her in 2019 on the basis of her important legal interest in living by her self-identified gender, awarding damages; the Supreme Court upheld that outcome.

On legal documents, a Japanese court has ruled unconstitutional the requirement of sterilising surgery for a change of gender on official documents, in the case brought by Gen Suzuki against the surgical precondition for a legal gender-marker change. Visitors should note that the ruling addresses the surgical precondition itself; the wider procedural route for marker changes and its application to foreign documents is not described in these sources.

Bathhouses are the most concrete everyday friction point. Onsen, sento and super-sento establishments can be daunting for non-binary and trans visitors, and guides aimed at gender-diverse travellers set out LGBTQ+-friendly venues, private-bath and co-ed-pool options and the etiquette involved. First-person accounts from trans travellers published in 2023 describe what to expect from venue norms and transition-related concerns in practice.
JPN.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in these sources: whether Gifu Prefecture adopted a policy on clothing, hair and housing for trans inmates after the bar association's September 2023 warning, and whether any national prisons directive now governs placement by legal sex.

Unresolved: the current statutory procedure for changing a gender marker after the surgery requirement was struck down, and whether the ruling extends to documents presented by foreign nationals at entry.

Not sourced in this inventory: any account of immigration or border screening that could reveal a traveller's trans status, visa application questions on gender, or entry refusal on that basis. Nor is there sourced material on the availability of gender-affirming medication to short-term visitors, insurance coverage for it, or access to competent care beyond the bathhouse and venue guidance.

The onsen and bathhouse material is drawn from guidebooks and first-person travel writing rather than official regulation, so the practical norms it describes are reported expectations, not enforceable rules.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D5.

sources.title: Prison warned over treatment of transgender inmate | The Asahi Shimbun
sources.summary: Asahi Shimbun (9 Sep 2023): Gifu's Kasamatsu Prison — a women's prison — holds an inmate who is listed as female on her family register but identifies as a man (diagnosed with gender identity disorder). The Gifu Prefecture Bar Association demanded the prison allow him male clothes and a male hairstyle; after years with no policy change, the bar association issued a formal 'warning' to the prison in Sep 2023. The case shows Japan places convicted trans inmates in facilities matching their registered (family-register) sex rather than their gender identity, while treatment conditions inside remain contested at the prefecture level.

sources.title: Japan Should End Abusive Detention Conditions for Transgender People | Human Rights Watch
sources.summary: HRW (11 Jun 2025): Tomoya Asanuma, a prominent transgender activist, was arrested in March 2024, held for more than 100 days in pre-trial detention and charged with assault; he was detained among men at a pre-trial detention centre, initially denied hormone treatment (until a doctor recommended it), mocked for his transgender identity in interrogations, and only allowed to shower away from other detained men after requests. HRW frames this as part of Japan's 'hostage justice' detention abuse and the legal limbo trans people face. For the prison-housing axis, it documents that a trans man's custodial placement followed his male legal sex, with accommodations (hormones, segregated showers) granted only grudgingly.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Japan only briefly, first in 1872 (early Meiji era) and repealed by the Penal Code of 1880, in force from 1882, in line with the Napoleonic Penal Code; the source elsewhere dates the criminalised period to 1873–1881. Since then Japan has had no laws against homosexuality, so sexual activity between consenting adults in private is legal regardless of gender or sexual orientation. The age of consent has been set at 16 years since June 2023, applying equally to same-sex and opposite-sex relations. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex marriages performed abroad are not legally recognised in Japan, and bi-national same-sex couples cannot obtain a visa for the foreign partner based on their relationship. However, the Ministry of Justice applies a general rule of granting the discretionary "designated activities" visa to same-sex married spouses. Since March 2009, Japanese nationals have been allowed to marry same-sex partners abroad, with the Justice Ministry instructing local authorities to issue the required single-status certificates. On gender markers, foreign nationals change their registered gender with their country of nationality and then report the change to the Immigration Services Agency for their residence card — a conflict-of-laws situation the source says can lead to bureaucratic breakdown, illustrated by the 2018 case of US national Elin McCready, whose gender change was refused recognition by Tokyo ward offices.

Placement of convicted trans people in custody follows the family register rather than gender identity. At Kasamatsu Prison, a women's prison in Gifu Prefecture, an inmate listed as female on her family register but identifying as a man, diagnosed with gender identity disorder, was held in the women's facility. The Gifu Prefecture Bar Association demanded that the prison permit male clothes and a male hairstyle, and after years without a policy change issued a formal warning to the prison in September 2023. Conditions of treatment inside therefore remain contested at prefecture level.

Pre-trial detention exposes trans detainees to the same placement rule. Tomoya Asanuma, a prominent transgender activist, was arrested in March 2024, held for more than 100 days and charged with assault. Human Rights Watch reported in June 2025 that he was detained among men, initially denied hormone treatment until a doctor recommended it, mocked for his transgender identity during interrogations, and allowed to shower away from other detained men only after requests. The report frames this within Japan's hostage-justice detention practices and the legal limbo trans people face, and notes that custodial accommodations such as hormones and segregated showers are granted grudgingly.
JPN.blindSummary:
Most visitors to the state report little direct hostility or discrimination in daily contact, particularly in major tourist destinations, and the everyday risk posture for a transgender traveller is low. LGBTQ visibility remains limited, social attitudes can be reserved, and legal equality still lags behind other developed countries.

The statutory framework is the Act on Promotion of Public Understanding of Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity. The official translation defines gender identity, obliges the national government to publish the annual implementation status of policies promoting understanding of sexual orientation and gender identity diversity, and sets out the national basic plan. The national legislature enacted the law in June 2023 after months of debate.

No national anti-discrimination statute stands alongside that Act, and no statutory guarantee against violence on grounds of gender identity exists. Full marriage equality for same-sex couples is also absent, so a trans visitor's marital or partner status has no national recognition to rely on.

On workplace and facilities access, the Supreme Court ruled in July 2023 that government restrictions on a transgender employee's use of restrooms were illegal. A national economic ministry was found to have violated public-service law by barring a transgender woman from the women's bathroom at work. She had challenged the denial in 2015, and a district court ruled for her in 2019 on the basis of her important legal interest in living by her self-identified gender, awarding damages; the Supreme Court upheld that outcome.

On legal documents, a national court has ruled unconstitutional the requirement of sterilising surgery for a change of gender on official documents, in the case brought by Gen Suzuki against the surgical precondition for a legal gender-marker change. The ruling addresses the surgical precondition itself; the wider procedural route for marker changes and its application to foreign documents is not described in these sources.

Bathhouses are the most concrete everyday friction point. Public bathhouses can be daunting for non-binary and trans visitors, and guides aimed at gender-diverse travellers set out LGBTQ+-friendly venues, private-bath and shared-pool options and the etiquette involved. First-person accounts from trans travellers published in 2023 describe what to expect from venue norms and transition-related concerns in practice.
JPN.blindOutOfScope:
Unresolved in these sources: whether the province adopted a policy on clothing, hair and housing for trans inmates after the bar association's September 2023 warning, and whether any national prisons directive now governs placement by legal sex.

Unresolved: the current statutory procedure for changing a gender marker after the surgery requirement was struck down, and whether the ruling extends to documents presented by foreign nationals at entry.

Not sourced in this inventory: any account of immigration or border screening that could reveal a traveller's trans status, visa application questions on gender, or entry refusal on that basis. Nor is there sourced material on the availability of gender-affirming medication to short-term visitors, insurance coverage for it, or access to competent care beyond the bathhouse and venue guidance.

The bathhouse material is drawn from guidebooks and first-person travel writing rather than official regulation, so the practical norms it describes are reported expectations, not enforceable rules.

A dated 2009 shadow report documents invisibility, marginalisation, silent prejudice and stigmatisation plus discrimination across education, employment, housing and health care with little governmental attention at the time.

No national statute, regulation or policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary or segregation) is documented; the custody findings rest on press and human-rights documentation of individual cases rather than official policy texts.

JPN.tangentialFactors:
The SOGI-promotion Act was enacted in June 2023 after months of parliamentary debate, and the text was watered down amid a culture-war dispute over transgender issues. The political contestation behind the statute is documented by Kyodo News, and it bears on how strongly the Act can be invoked in practice.

Institutional protection has nonetheless advanced on two axes at once: Chambers' Global Practice Guide records enactment of the SOGI-promotion law, two pro-transgender Supreme Court decisions and one decision favourable to same-sex couples, while confirming that marriage equality and violence-protection guarantees remain unattained. THA.name: Thailand
THA.summary:
The Immigration Bureau operates 'Welcome Pride by Immigration', launched on 5 August 2024 to address concerns of foreign LGBTQ+ travellers whose passports do not match their current appearance or gender, and to ease immigration scrutiny on arrival. It is the one entry-side measure a trans visitor should know about before landing.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 22 January 2025, after the bill passed its final Senate reading in June 2024, making Thailand the first country in Southeast Asia to do so; the statute uses gender-neutral 'marriage partners' terms. The change closes the practical exclusions couples previously faced from property regimes, succession, hospital visitation and pension survivor claims.

Legal gender recognition remains absent. There is no mechanism to change the sex marker on a birth certificate, national ID or passport, and title prefixes remain locked to the sex assigned at birth; the Name Act 1962 offers only a partial workaround for personal names. A trans visitor's documents therefore stay as their issuing authorities recorded them, which is the mismatch 'Welcome Pride' was designed to soften at the border. Human Rights Watch found in December 2021 that even affirmative steps such as first-name changes leave discretion with officials, and that anti-discrimination protections are not fully enforced.

Thai law carries no hate-crime designation. When a Chinese tourist murdered a trans woman in Pattaya in April 2025 after she refused his request for sex, the community described the killing as a hate crime, but bias-motivated violence is handled as an ordinary offence with no enhanced penalties and no dedicated data collection. LGBTQ+ groups pressed for new hate-crime protections in the wake of the killing.

Detention carries documented risk. The Department of Corrections has separated LGBT prisoners from other inmates nationwide since 1993, and Pattaya Remand Prison holds transgender inmates in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men; a trans woman stopped by police in 2017 and expecting placement with men because her documents still read 'Mr.' was instead held in the separated wing. The department was at the same time considering an exclusively LGBTQ facility at Min Buri, while acknowledging that transgender women elsewhere generally face a choice between men's cells and solitary confinement.
THA.outOfScopeNotes:
The operational detail of 'Welcome Pride by Immigration' — which airports handle it, what inspection or referral it involves, and how consistently it is applied — is not sourced beyond the launch announcement, so its practical effect at the border is unresolved here.

Whether the Min Buri LGBT facility proceeded beyond the pilot stage, and the current status and staffing of dedicated or separated wings at Pattaya Remand Prison, are not established by the available sources, which date from 2016 and 2017.

The current national count of LGBT prisoners is not sourced; the figures above are from 2016 and 2017 reporting. No source in the inventory reports post-2025 data on bias-motivated violence against trans people or on the outcome of any prosecution in the April 2025 Pattaya killing.

Whether any hate-crime or gender-recognition bill has been tabled or enacted after the November 2025 reporting is unresolved in this inventory.

sources.title: Thailand Separates LGBTQ Inmates, Considers Segregated Prison (NBC News/AP)
sources.summary: NBC News/AP (29 Jan 2017): the Thai Department of Corrections says LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993; at Pattaya Remand Prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men. sources.title: Exclusion or protection? Activists skeptical about LGBT prison (Coconuts Bangkok)
sources.summary: Coconuts Bangkok (30 Aug 2016): trans activist Nachacha Kongudom, arrested in June 2015 while protesting the junta, was sent to a men's prison against her request for a women's facility; prison officials told her that under Thai law 'she remains a man' and no Thai document can identify a trans woman as female, and during intake she was harassed and ordered to expose her body. The Department of Corrections then announced a pilot using Bangkok's Min Buri prison as an LGBT facility to prevent abuse of trans inmates, after Pattaya men's prison had already begun separating trans prisoners from cis men following reports of abuse. DOC figures: ~4,448 of ~300,000 prisoners identified as LGBT, 34 of them transgender. Activists welcomed the pilot but feared it 'could encourage exclusion' and insisted placement 'should be an option, not an obligation.'

MEX.name: Mexico
MEX.summary:
Extending legal gender recognition to trans people remains the central unfinished task of Mexican equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many of Mexico's states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition, while calling on the states that lack such procedures to adopt them and warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Barriers are documented concretely. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. The same report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Violence against trans people intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

One legislature has moved to close a specific gap. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe the law as critical to their sense of safety.

Inter-American authorities have pressed the same point. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

The gap between statute and practice is the recurring finding. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice; the analysis explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.
MEX.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in the sources assembled here: whether any recognition procedure exists at the national level as opposed to state level, and how many of Mexico's 32 federative entities currently operate an administrative legal gender recognition procedure. Human Rights Watch states only that many states do and that implementation varies.

Not sourced: rules governing gender markers on passports and other documents presented at the Mexican border, and whether entry or visa screening can expose a traveller's trans status.

Not sourced: any restriction on gender-affirming medical care, any law or policy on access to sex-separated facilities, and any hate-crime statute covering anti-trans motivation beyond the transfemicide offence enacted in Mexico City.

Unresolved: the sources contain no data on housing placement of trans prisoners in Mexico, whether placement follows birth sex or lived identity, or on special units, segregation or solitary confinement as applied to trans detainees. The Mexico City conjugal-visit policy is the only prison-specific item located.

Not sourced: the outcome of the prosecutions sought by the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, and whether impunity levels have changed since that 2024 statement.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5.

sources.title: LGBTQ people in prison (Wikipedia; Mexico section)

The article contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement (birth-sex vs identity placement), special units, or solitary/segregation practice for Mexico.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The source references historical sodomy executions (1658) and the 1901 Dance of the Forty-One scandal, but does not describe a current statutory criminalisation of homosexuality. Street prostitution is noted as illegal in certain jurisdictions such as Mexico City. Same-sex marriage was legalized in Mexico City effective 4 March 2010, with Coahuila state legalizing civil unions in January 2007. Wikipedia country coverage: LGBT Pride Parades have been held annually since 1979 in Mexico City (over 1,000 people in 1979, 350,000 in the XXXI edition), and regularly in Guadalajara since 1996 and over a dozen other cities. However, the source notes that due to expectations of "sexual silence" and fear of discrimination, it is common for gay men and lesbians to be cautious about disclosing their sexual orientation, and leading "double lives" is seen as necessary. Government operatives have targeted Zona Rosa nightclubs since 2007 for drug, prostitution, and safety enforcement, which LGBT groups denounced as homophobic. Wikipedia country coverage: The source notes that some Zona Rosa sites of cohabitation lack safety measures such as emergency exits, targeted by government enforcement. It also mentions signs that Mexican youth are being committed to psychiatric clinics after coming out to their family. Mexican police are described as notorious for corruption and extortion, and transvestites are subject to police abuse. Wikipedia country coverage: A UAM study found that 27% of LGBTQ persons studied suffer mental disorders and risk of alcoholism, some 40% have thoughts of suicide, and 25% have attempted it. The National Center for the Prevention and Control of HIV/AIDS is listed as an official resource, and Pride events include consciousness-raising about AIDS and HIV. There are signs that Mexican youth are committed to psychiatric clinics after coming out to families, with some 16% rejected by family and a greater percentage physically attacked by relatives — highlighting youth-specific vulnerability in accessing safe care.

MEX.tangentialFactors:
Third-gender traditions sit alongside the statutory framework. Oaxaca's indigenous muxé community is documented as a long-standing third-gender presence, a social fact distinct from the legal recognition procedures available to trans people elsewhere in the country.

Tourist centres and the rest of the country are not equivalent. Intrepid Travel's LGBTQIA+ guide identifies Mexico City's Zona Rosa as a gay hub with an annual Pride march and LGBT-friendly hotels, bars and tours, and Cancún as a mainstream destination, while advising caution outside tourist hubs.

Comparative counts place Mexico second among jurisdictions tracked by Transgender Europe for transfeminicide in the year to September 2023, behind Brazil.

Partnership recognition has advanced unevenly across jurisdictions and over a long period: Coahuila approved gay civil unions in January 2007 by a 20–13 vote, after Mexico City and Buenos Aires, with adoption and custody excluded for those couples.
MEX.localsOnly:
Prison policy in Mexico City addresses conjugal visits rather than trans status directly. In July 2007, following the efforts of the Mexico City Human Rights Commission (CDHDF), the city's prison system began allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation; visitors are not required to be married to the inmate, and the practice applies across all Mexico City prisons.

Residents of states without an administrative recognition procedure must pursue recognition through slower or judicial routes, and the Human Rights Watch dispatch of March 2025 is addressed specifically to the states that have yet to adopt such procedures.

Enforcement of the transfemicide offence created by the Paola Buenrostro law will be handled by the Mexico City authorities that enacted it, and the unpunished 2016 case that gave the law its name indicates the starting point for that enforcement record.
MEX.blindSummary:
Extending legal gender recognition to trans people remains the central unfinished task of equality law in the country. a human rights organisation reported on 31 March 2025 that many of the country states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition, while calling on the states that lack such procedures to adopt them and warning that implementation differs sharply from one state/province to another. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Barriers are documented concretely. a human rights report of 6 March 2024 found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in one state/province leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. The same report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in a river in August 2023.

Violence against trans people intensified over the year to mid-2024. a news agency reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them an activist shot in the capital city; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. a second agency reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTQ+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. International monitoring records 593 transfemicides in the country between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to the highest-count jurisdiction's 100.

One legislature has moved to close a specific gap. The Congress of the capital city approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe the law as critical to their sense of safety.

Inter-American authorities have pressed the same point. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged national and state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTQ+ violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

The gap between statute and practice is the recurring finding. an academic analysis of 22 November 2024 concludes that the country progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice; the analysis explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state/province or private violence, including murder and torture.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009, with the capital city the pioneering jurisdiction.

BRN.name: Brunei
BRN.summary:
Section 198 of Brunei's Syariah Penal Code creates the trans-specific offence of "a man posing as a woman or vice versa". Official guidance on the code states that it binds all persons in the country including tourists, and travel agents are briefed to that effect.

The US State Department's 2017 report on human rights practices in Brunei describes the provision as banning men from dressing as women and women from dressing as men "without reasonable excuse", with no known convictions recorded in 2017. Morality provisions covering cross-dressing were among those enforced under the code at that time, while the sharia implementing regulations had not been issued.

Human Rights Watch's #OUTLAWED survey places Brunei among at least two countries, with Oman, whose national laws expressly criminalise "posing as" or "imitating" a person of a different sex. That trans-specific offence appears in only nine of the countries that criminalise gender expression, against at least 67 countries that criminalise same-sex relations. A state-sharia analogue exists in Malaysia.

Stage three of the Syariah Penal Code took effect on 3 April 2019 under the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013, which was brought into force in stages. It provides for death by stoning for anal sex, adultery and abortion, amputation for theft, and 40 strokes of the cane for lesbian sex. Homosexuality was already an offence carrying up to 10 years' imprisonment under the previous law. The 2017 State Department report separately records that 'liwat' between men carries death by stoning if implemented.

The code applies chiefly to Muslims, roughly two-thirds of an estimated population of 420,000 to 450,000. First-person reporting published as the penalties took effect describes anonymous accounts of a climate of fear and no assurance of enforcement against foreigners.

The sultan stated that Brunei's capital-punishment moratorium covers the new sharia provisions. The country has carried out no execution since 1957, and a freshness check dated 27 September 2026 found the law still in force with the 2019 moratorium intact. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights urged Brunei to halt the code, Human Rights Watch described it as barbaric, and the United Nations and foreign governments condemned it.

The 2017 State Department report also records LGBTI-reported discrimination in employment, housing, recreation and services.
BRN.outOfScopeNotes:
Four sources in the inventory could not be retrieved at research time and returned HTTP 403: the Norwegian government's hosted copy of Brunei's Penal Code including the Syariah Penal Code provisions, the Human Dignity Trust's April 2019 briefing on implementation of the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013, a France24 report of April 2019 on fear among Brunei's gay community, and an SSRN paper on the sharia penal code. Their specific claims remain unresolved against the primary text.

No source in the inventory reports a conviction under Section 198 after 2017; the only conviction figure available is the US State Department's "no known convictions" finding for 2017, and whether that position has since changed is unresolved.

Whether the sharia implementing regulations that were unissued in 2017 have since been made is not sourced here, and no source addresses legal gender recognition, the text or marker on identity and travel documents, visa or border screening that could expose a visitor's gender history, bathroom or facility rules, access to transition-related healthcare, or recognition of partners or marriages. These gaps are not findings of permissiveness.

Population estimates differ between sources, with 420,000 and 450,000 both appearing in the inventory, and the Muslim share is given as roughly two-thirds.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6, D7, D8, D12, D13.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Brunei does not allow a person to change their name or gender on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not allowed. On 11 March 2015, a civil servant was fined B$1,000 under the Syariah Penal Code Order for cross-dressing. The SPC also prohibits men from dressing as women or women dressing as men 'without reasonable excuse' or 'for immoral purposes', with no known convictions reported in 2017. Wikipedia country coverage: LGBTI individuals reported intimidation by police, including threats to make their sexuality public, to hamper their ability to obtain a government job, or to bar graduation from government academic institutions. State-imposed corporal punishment is prescribed: under the SPCO, if evidentiary standards are not met, the maximum penalty for sex between men is seven years imprisonment and thirty strokes of whipping; for unmarried men, one year in prison or 100 lashes; and sex between women is punishable by any two of forty lashes of caning, up to 10 years' imprisonment, and a fine of up to B$40,000. Bruneian society tends to associate homosexuality with 'effeminate men'. Wikipedia country coverage: Members of the LGBTI community reported that the government monitored their activities and communications, and events on LGBTI topics were subject to restrictions on assembly and expression, with the government reportedly refusing to issue permits for such events. Media outlets described the Sharia provisions as 'medieval' and 'uncivilized', and the UN urged Brunei to review its laws when the move to Sharia law was announced. OutRight Action International has described Brunei as 'the country that has the most worrisome state of rights for LGBT people in Southeast Asia', and anyone convicted of 'tarnishing the image of Islam' may be heavily punished.

BRN.tangentialFactors:
Brunei sits in a small group of jurisdictions: Human Rights Watch identifies at least two states, Brunei and Oman, whose national laws expressly criminalise posing as or imitating a person of a different sex, with a comparable provision operating through state sharia in Malaysia. Of the at least 67 countries that criminalise same-sex relations, only nine criminalise gender expression in statute, which places Brunei's Section 198 among the narrower set of trans-specific offences worldwide.

International reaction to stage three was sharp and public. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights called for the law to be halted, Human Rights Watch labelled it barbaric, and the United Nations together with foreign governments issued condemnations as the penalties took effect on 3 April 2019.

The enforcement picture is not uniform on its face. Brunei has not carried out an execution since 1957, the sultan has said the moratorium extends to the stoning provisions, and reporting from April 2019 records uncertainty about how far the code would be applied to foreigners. A freshness check on 27 September 2026 found the code still in force and the moratorium undisturbed.

The wider criminal framework already reached same-sex conduct before stage three, with homosexuality punishable by up to 10 years, so the 2019 additions extended penalties rather than creating the underlying prohibition.

PRT.name: Portugal
PRT.summary:
Portugal remains among the safer European destinations for transgender visitors. Homosexuality is legal, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2010, gender-affirming care is lawful, and legal gender and name change currently runs under the 2018 self-determination law, which allows self-declaration from age 16 without a medical requirement. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, conversion therapy has been banned since 2024, surgical intervention on intersex infants is prohibited, and access to facilities matching a person's gender is protected.

The Penal Code treats sexual orientation and gender identity as explicit grounds for aggravated offending. Under Articles 132, 144 and 145, an offence determined by hatred on those grounds is aggravated, with aggravated assault punishable by up to four years, and organising discrimination on those grounds carrying penalties of one to eight years.

That baseline is under active legislative pressure. On 19 and 20 March 2026 the Assembleia da República debated and approved three bills tabled by the PSD, Chega and CDS-PP, the first parliamentary vote to roll back self-identification in legal gender recognition. The proposals passed by 124 votes to 79 and were referred to the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees. At first reading Parliament backed reinstating a mandatory medical opinion for any change of legal gender and name, undoing the 2018 reform.

As recorded in the sources, the bills have cleared only their first reading and have not been enacted, so the 2018 framework remains the operative law for legal gender and name change. The package also puts the ban on forced medical interventions on intersex children in question. A European Parliament written question, E-001183/2026, put the health and safety of transgender people in Portugal and the repeal process to the Commission. Nothing in the record indicates criminalisation of trans people or any restriction on their entry or presence in the country.
PRT.outOfScopeNotes:
The final outcome of the three bills is unresolved in the sources: only the first reading of 20 March 2026 and the referral to the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees are documented, and no source records a final vote, promulgation or entry into force.

Whether the 2018 self-determination law's provisions, including self-declaration from age 16, and the prohibition on surgical intervention on intersex infants survive the package is not sourced. Nor is the fate of the Provedor de Justiça's request for constitutional review of Article 176-C.

Entry, visa and document-screening practice for transgender visitors, including how foreign passport gender markers are handled at the border, is not covered by the inventory. Enforcement rates for the Penal Code's hate-crime aggravation and for the discrimination ban are likewise not sourced here.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map 2026: Portugal drops one place to 12th at 67%; no affirmative legislation since the 2024 conversion-practices ban, while a new draft bill threatens legal gender recognition based on self-determination and the ban on forced medical interventions on intersex children. No score 67% below Malta/Iceland/Belgium but above most of Europe.
Público (March 2026, in Portuguese): the Portuguese Parliament (AR) approved PSD, Chega and CDS bills reversing the gender-identity law - first vote to roll back self-ID legal gender recognition.

Observador (Mar 2026): parliament debates rolling back the gender-identity regime; psychologists' order and trans groups call it 'retrocesso'; socialists invoked the 2006 murder of Gisberta (trans woman killed by youths in Porto) against the rollback, drawing protests from Chega's Hugo Soares. Documents the political fight around the three roll-back bills.

Joint statement: IGLYO, ILGA-Europe, OII Europe, TGEU, EL*C and Bi+ Equal warn three bills debated 19 March, voted 20 March 2026 would seriously attack trans/intersex rights, bodily autonomy and legal gender recognition; if adopted Portugal would lose at least 4 Rainbow Map places, dropping below Sweden, Netherlands, Ireland and France - regression from a European reference point.

Forbidden Colours (20 Mar 2026): Parliament passed the roll-back proposals 124 to 79 (backed by Chega, governing PSD and CDS-PP), sending them to the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees; the proposals directly target Portugal's 2018 self-identification law. Called a dangerous turning point for fundamental rights.

KET Brussels (26 Mar 2026): in first reading Parliament backed reintroducing a mandatory medical opinion for any legal gender and name change, undoing the 2018 reform that allowed self-declaration from age 16; human rights groups say it is dismantling the self-determination law.

TVI/IOL: committee-stage analysis (CIG) of the bills warns they worsen suffering and negative outcomes for trans people and defends schools' existing discrimination-prevention duties; Bloco de Esquerda bill assessed as compatible with school human-rights obligations. Legislative-process detail on the roll-back package.

The Portugal Brief (16 Aug 2026): Justice Ministry data show legal sex/name changes climbing back toward the two-years-prior high-water mark, most in Lisbon (per Expresso) - even as Parliament advances bills to reimpose the medical requirement the 2018 self-determination law scrapped. Uptick before the expected tightening.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Portugal's Parliament formally adopted 17 May as the 'National Day Against Homophobia and Transphobia' in 2015, committing to national and international obligations to combat such discrimination. Annual pride parades in Lisbon and Porto attract thousands of participants and spectators, and Lisbon hosts Queer Lisboa, one of Europe's largest LGBT film festivals. However, three draft bills given preliminary approval on 20 March 2026 (151–79) would ban the inclusion of 'gender ideology' in school curricula, and hundreds protested outside the Assembly against them. Wikipedia country coverage: Portugal was fined by the European Court of Human Rights in 1999 after a domestic court made homophobic statements in ruling against a gay father's custody of his daughter; the ECHR ruled in the father's favour and ordered custody returned to him. Same-sex couples were barred from adopting and informally forbidden from fostering children until adoption rights took effect on 1 March 2016, after a presidential veto was overridden by Parliament.

PRT.tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map 2026 places Portugal 12th on 67%, one place down, with no affirmative legislation adopted since the 2024 ban on conversion practices. The score sits below Malta, Iceland and Belgium but above most of the continent. The joint statement by IGLYO, ILGA-Europe, OII Europe, TGEU, EL*C and Bi+ Equal warned that adoption of the three bills would cost Portugal at least four further places, dropping it below Sweden, the Netherlands, Ireland and France and ending its standing as a regional reference point.

The political contest is unusually open. The Ordem dos Psicólogos and trans organisations described the bills as a retrocesso, while socialist deputies invoked the 2006 murder of Gisberta, a trans woman killed by youths in Porto, against the rollback, drawing protests from Chega's Hugo Soares. Forbidden Colours called the vote a dangerous turning point for fundamental rights.

Public opinion runs against the legislative direction. Equaldex records high public support for same-sex parenting in Portugal, ranked first among 30 EU regions, alongside its ratings of legal homosexuality, marriage, unrestricted gender change, lawful gender-affirming care, the intersex surgery ban, hate-crime coverage, the discrimination ban, the conversion-therapy ban and protected bathroom access.

The package also puts the ban on forced medical interventions on intersex children in question. IRL.name: Ireland
IRL.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Ireland rests on the Gender Recognition Act 2015 (No. 25 of 2015), commenced on 4 September 2015 by S.I. 369/2015 and amended by subsequent statutory instruments through 2026. Adults change their legal gender by self-declaration, with no psychological evaluation or medical requirement, and the operative text is the statute itself rather than any discretionary approval process.

GCN's anniversary reporting records that Ireland is one of only 11 European countries permitting gender recognition through self-determination without a psychological evaluation requirement, with activists marking the milestone while flagging gaps that remain. A Guardian retrospective of 23 December 2025, marking the decade since the Act, carries first-person accounts of self-declaration and updated documents and frames the statute as a move away from Ireland's Catholic past, alongside renewed calls over remaining gaps in trans rights and healthcare.

The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 explicitly covers gender identity and sex characteristics as protected characteristics. Garda reports of hate crimes rose 15% in 2025, with racism and xenophobia recorded as the most common motives, according to an Irish Times report of August 2026. A University College Dublin study published on 3 July 2025 found that discrimination against sexual and gender minorities in Ireland has increased, documenting a rise in prejudice despite the protective statutory framework.

Access to gender-affirming care is constrained by waiting times rather than by a legal prohibition. The Journal's April 2025 investigation reports years-long waiting lists for multidisciplinary assessment at the National Gender Service, with some trans people turning away from official channels as a result; the HSE defends its comprehensive multidisciplinary model of care.

Equaldex records gender change as legal with no restrictions, but no legal recognition of non-binary identity, gender-affirming care that is legal yet restricted for minors, no statutory ban on conversion therapy, and no ban on intersex infant surgery. Hate-crime protections there cover sexual orientation and gender identity, while employment and housing discrimination protections cover sexual orientation only.

Belong To LGBTQ+ Youth Ireland operates an anonymous online hate-crime reporting form alongside rights information and links to protections under the Equal Status Acts, giving young LGBTQ+ people a route to report incidents short of a formal complaint.
IRL.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposed limitation on the effect of a Gender Recognition Certificate during imprisonment has since been enacted, and what the amended text would provide, is unresolved in the available sources; only its passage at first legislative stage as of late 2025 is documented.

Enforcement of the Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 in cases where gender identity is the recorded motive is unresolved: the published statistics break down hate-crime reports by overall motive, with racism and xenophobia most common, and no trans-specific charge or conviction data is sourced here.

The Telegraph's September 2024 account of Ireland backing down on hate-speech laws amid the trans debate was paywalled (HTTP 402) and could not be read at research time; no claim from it is carried into this record. Two further sources, the Garda hate-crime statistics release for 2025 and a Diaspora Support page on returning to Ireland, were too thin to yield findings.

The reported rise in discrimination rests on a single UCD study; its methodology, sample and the specific categories of discrimination measured are not detailed in the inventory and remain unverified.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5.

sources.title: Transgender history in Ireland (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Wikipedia 'Transgender history in Ireland' (rev. 2 Oct 2026): documents Barbie Kardashian, a trans woman who held a Gender Recognition Certificate and a Department of Social Protection certificate recognising her as female — found guilty at Limerick Circuit Court in May 2022 of seven counts of threatening to kill or cause serious harm to her mother, and acquitted in October 2024 of separate alleged threats to a fellow prisoner and a prison officer at Limerick Prison; the article records that as of late 2025 a proposed amendment to the Gender Recognition Act 2015 that would limit the effect of a GRC 'for the purposes of imprisonment' had passed its first legislative stage, and cites the historical 1889 case of John Bradley (assigned female at birth), imprisoned at Grangegorman prison after disclosing.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Ireland forbids incitement to hatred based on sexual orientation under the Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act 1989, with penalties up to a €1,000 fine or 6 months' imprisonment on first offence, rising to €10,000 or 2 years on indictment; gender identity was formally added to protected grounds by the Cabinet in October 2022. The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024, described as the toughest and broadest hate crime legislation in Europe, has been in force since 31 December 2024 and explicitly covers sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics. Open expression is visible: Dublin Pride drew an estimated 60,000 people in 2018, alongside the Dublin Gay Theatre Festival, the GAZE International LGBT Film Festival and gay-friendly venues nationwide. However, in April 2019 Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown County Council cancelled Glitter Hole's Drag Storytime, first calling it "not age-appropriate" and then citing a high level of homophobic abuse on social media. Wikipedia country coverage: Community facilities include the Outhouse LGBTQ+ Centre, gay and gay-friendly pubs, restaurants, clubs, bars and saunas across Ireland, with visible LGBT scenes in Dublin, Cork, Galway, Limerick and Waterford. Health facilities are a serious gap: a November 2022 Transgender Europe study found wait times for a first gender-affirming healthcare appointment in Ireland of 2.5 to 10 years, with only one public trans health provider, which was severely understaffed. Patients there were reportedly denied care for reasons including being on social welfare, having an ADHD diagnosis, or not answering "highly sexualized questions" in "the right way", pushing many to the private sector or self-administered hormone therapy. A free PrEP programme through community pharmacies was established by the Department of Health in November 2019. Wikipedia country coverage: The Irish state itself was the historical source of hostility: male homosexual acts were criminalised under the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 and Criminal Law Amendment Act 1885 until decriminalisation in 1993, and in Norris v. Attorney General (1983) the Chief Justice invoked the "Christian nature of [the Irish] State" to uphold those laws. On 19 June 2018 Taoiseach Leo Varadkar and Justice Minister Charles Flanagan issued formal public apologies to the LGBT community for state-caused suffering and criminal convictions. Residual state hostility persists in policy: Section 81E(5) of the Pensions Act 1990 bars pensioners who retired more than a year before the 2010 civil partnership law from claiming a survivor's pension for their civil partner, and Labour Minister Brendan Howlin defended refusing equal pension opt-in rights to gay men, a stance condemned by the Irish Examiner on 24 June 2015. In the courts, Judge McKechnie in Foy's case reproached the government for inaction and said Ireland was "very much isolated" among Council of Europe members on transgender recognition. Wikipedia country coverage: Sex education in Ireland has been described by students and teachers as "archaic", "inadequate", "biased" and "largely religious based", with reports of non-virgin students being humiliated and LGBT issues never mentioned. The Provision of Objective Sex Education Bill 2018, which would have covered consent, contraceptives, abortion, LGBT issues and sexuality, passed second reading in the Dáil in April 2018 but lapsed with the dissolution of the Oireachtas in 2020. The source notes that many LGBT youth still experience bullying, and that before the 1970s LGBT individuals would mostly stay in the closet, move to England, or commit suicide. Youth-specific legal gaps: a November 2019 report by Minister Regina Doherty recommended extending self-declaration gender recognition to 16- and 17-year-olds with parental consent, and Senator Fintan Warfield's March 2018 bill to ban conversion therapy (which explicitly would not ban supportive practices for questioning LGBT youth) remained stalled in the Seanad as of April 2022 despite a coalition pledge to ban it.

BEL.name: Belgium
BEL.summary:
Belgium is among the more protective jurisdictions in Europe for transgender visitors. Discrimination, hate crimes and hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are prohibited; same-sex marriage and adoption are legal; and legal name and gender-marker change rests on self-determination.

Since 1 January 2018, under the Law of 25 June 2017, transgender people have been able to change their registered gender and first names by declaration to the civil registrar, without medical conditions. The Federal Justice Department records that the Constitutional Court partially annulled that law on 19 June 2019 and that, pending replacement provisions, applications continue to be handled under the current procedure.

Hate crime and hate speech on grounds of gender identity are criminal offences, and transphobia is recorded as a hate-crime motive. One qualification matters for expectations of the justice system: the OSCE/ODIHR national framework page states that hate crimes are not defined in Belgian legislation and that no code exists to record them as such, so breaches of non-discrimination law that constitute criminal offences are prosecuted under general provisions.

Belgium passed Europe's first femicide law in 2023, covering all gender-based homicide and including protections for gender minorities, and a 2023 law banning conversion practices. Medically unnecessary surgeries on intersex infants remain legal, although a Brussels court held a hospital accountable for non-consensual interventions.

The principal visitor-facing risk is violence rather than law. The equality bodies Unia and the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men reported in May 2025 that violence and intimidation targeting LGBTQI people are rising, with gay men and transgender people especially affected. Of 136 sexual-orientation discrimination cases Unia handled in a year, 35% involved physical assault and 35% serious intimidation. An RTBF investigation documented a recurring pattern in which perpetrators use fake dating-app profiles to arrange meetings, then ambush victims in isolated locations to rob, humiliate or assault them; police have recorded an alarming number of incidents, many unreported through fear or shame. A case against three men accused of targeting at least eight victims went to the Brussels Criminal Court in May 2025.

The formal-law position is confirmed by the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map country page, which scores Belgium across legal gender recognition, hate crime, equality and non-discrimination, family law, civil society, asylum and intersex protection.
