sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Belgium's age of consent has been equal at 16 regardless of orientation since 1795, though article 372bis raised it to 18 for same-sex acts between 1965 and 1985 before repeal on 18 June 1985 after debate sparked by the case of lesbian teacher Eliane Morissens. For minors seeking legal gender change, those aged 12–16 may change first name only, while 16–17-year-olds may apply for a sex change with parental consent plus a psychological opinion confirming free decision-making. Conversion therapy, which targets minors disproportionately, was banned on 20 July 2023 with penalties of 8 days to 2 years imprisonment and fines of 208–2400 euros. In 2019, Flemish Ministry of Health-funded LGBT groups launched the suicide prevention project lumi.be and a dedicated transgender youth suicide prevention site, gendervonk.be, and pride march demands have included including gay relationships in high school sex education. Wikipedia country coverage: The source describes adoption and parental recognition rather than custody per se: since 2006 same-sex couples have held the same adoption rights as opposite-sex couples, and lesbian couples can access IVF. Until 2015 a legal inequality persisted because the husband of a biological mother was automatically recognized as father (Civil Code art. 135), while a mother's female partner had to complete an adoption procedure to be recognized as co-mother; a bill fixing this was approved in 2014 (Senate 48–2, Chamber 114–10) and took effect 1 January 2015. Between 2006 and 2014 there were 70 LGBT domestic adoptions recorded in Belgium (58 male couples in Flanders, 2 female couples there, plus 12 adoptions in the French Community). No custody-specific provisions are addressed. Wikipedia country coverage: State hostility is essentially absent at the level of major institutions, but right-wing political hostility has existed: the Flemish Block/Vlaams Belang and the National Front voted against same-sex marriage, though Flemish Interest has softened its stance — its leader stated in 2015 the party would not campaign to repeal same-sex marriage, and in 2019 the party chairman condemned an MP who criticized same-sex marriage and adoption after public outcry. N-VA was criticized for joining a European parliamentary group containing homophobic parties. On the crime side, on 22 December 2014 a Liège court jury convicted four people of the homophobic murder of Ihsane Jarfi — the first Belgian crime officially qualified as hate-motivated on sexual orientation grounds — and in May 2018 a human rights body reported 125 homophobic discrimination cases (17 physical attacks, 42 public insults, 17 housing cases, 31 online attacks), with a 2019 study finding 90% of LGBT people in Brussels had suffered verbal or psychological harassment. Media is described as broadly accepting: homosexuality is widely accepted in media, Will Ferdy came out on TV in 1970, and transgender journalist Bo Van Spilbeeck's 2018 coming-out received widespread coverage; conversion therapy was banned in July 2023.

FRA.name: France
FRA.summary:
The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings: detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments, and accounts collected in a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

France's national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010, together with ministry and association input, and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations: placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure during strip searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

The national preventive mechanism explained to the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Sodomy was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791, but a 1960 ordinance (the Mirguet amendment, article 330, 2nd alinea) doubled penalties for indecent exposure when homosexual in nature and was only repealed in 1980; the Vichy government's 1942 article 334 set age of consent at 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual ones, equalised at 15 in 1982 under Mitterrand. LGBTQ people in Alsace and Lorraine were persecuted and interned in concentration camps after the 1940 Nazi annexation, and were also persecuted under the Vichy Regime despite no laws criminalising homosexuality. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 before 1980, still awaiting a Senate vote. Conversion therapy was banned effective 1 February 2022, punishable by two years' imprisonment and/or a €30,000 fine. Wikipedia country coverage: A 31 December 2004 amendment made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; civil liberty groups including Reporters Without Borders criticised it as a serious infringement on free speech, while the Chirac government cited rising anti-gay violence. MP Christian Vanneste of Chirac's own UMP party became the first person convicted under the law in January 2006, though the conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Historically, homosexuality and cross-dressing were treated as immoral and LGBTQ people faced legal harassment under public morality and order laws. Since 2017, transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and LGBT people may serve openly in the French Armed Forces. Wikipedia country coverage: The source text contains no provisions on visas, asylum or border entry for LGBTQ people. The closest entry-related finding concerns citizenship of children born abroad: France refused to recognise surrogate children as French citizens until 2015, leaving many in legal limbo, and the Court of Cassation ruled in December 2019 that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France. Wikipedia country coverage: A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems with gender-affirming healthcare in France: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times, and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent and self-determination model. Transsexualism is covered under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979, but French trans rights organisations said the 2010 decree removing gender identity disorder as a diagnosis changed nothing in practice. The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" and a "primarily social problem" and advised extreme caution, though this did not change actual practice. Assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state coverage for women under 43, the MSM blood donation deferral was removed entirely on 16 March 2022, and intersex people retain significant gaps in protection from non-consensual medical interventions. Wikipedia country coverage: The December 2004 law amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, and penalties are increased when a physical assault or murder is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation. A report released on 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims versus around 1,380 in 2018; in October 2018 President Macron denounced the violence as "unworthy of France" and promised unspecified "concrete measures". Transphobia became an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison in 2017. Overseas, Mayotte sees frequent reports of family rejection, harassment and discrimination, and a 2006 Lifou Island proposal for a "family code" envisaged eviction or lynching of LGBTQ people (it was not approved). Wikipedia country coverage: In March 2024, centre-right Republican senators commissioned The Little Mermaid Observatory — a group opposed to all forms of gender transition for minors — to report on youth gender-affirming care, which called such care a "health scandal" and youth transness a "social contagion"; the resulting bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, provoking large-scale protests, but is opposed by the Macron government and has had no update since 23 July 2024. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, the interministerial body fighting anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of The Little Mermaid Observatory, which had called gender-affirming healthcare "mutilation"; one committee member resigned and the president stepped away. The Académie Nationale de Médecine's "epidemic-like" framing of trans people seeking care is a further state-actor hostility marker. Historically the National Assembly voted 293–222 against same-sex marriage in June 2011, and conservative outrage greeted the use of "parent 1" and "parent 2" on French school enrolment forms reported in February 2019. Wikipedia country coverage: In March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos made fighting discrimination including homophobia one of 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009, and in January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign Tous égaux, tous alliés, which gives students reporting services and a helpline and requires all French schools to provide guidance about LGBTQ issues, with 17 May as a sensitisation day. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced that all higher education institutions must use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms. Youth are the direct target of the pending under-18 medical transition ban (Senate, May 2024), while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for medical care of trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 alongside calcium and vitamin D. The Vichy-era discriminatory age of consent (21 for homosexual relations versus 15 heterosexual) was equalised at 15 in 1982, and the association Le Refuge estimated 3–4% of its helpline calls concerned conversion therapy before the 2022 ban. Wikipedia country coverage: A 2013 Pew Research Center survey found 77% of the French population believed homosexuality should be accepted, one of the highest of 39 countries polled, with 81% acceptance among 18–29 year-olds; the 2019 Eurobarometer found 79% backed same-sex marriage across Europe and 85% believed LGBT people should have equal rights, and the 2023 Eurobarometer found 79% and 84% respectively. Gabriel Attal was one of the few openly gay heads of government in the world during his January–September 2024 premiership, and Paris Mayor Bertrand Delanoë came out publicly in 1998 before his 2001 election. Paris Pride drew 500,000 people in 2019 — the city's third-largest event after the marathon and Techno Parade — and pride events now run in dozens of cities nationwide, with Le Marais, Quartier Pigalle and Bois de Boulogne hosting a thriving LGBTQ nightlife. Acceptance is markedly lower overseas: a 2014 study found about 20% of overseas residents saw homosexuality as a sexuality like any other versus 77% in metropolitan France, with Mayotte particularly taboo and the first same-sex marriages in Saint Martin and French Polynesia triggering public demonstrations.

A report on the nation's first same-sex wedding, performed days after the marriage-equality law took effect — dating the legal equality baseline relevant to partner travel and marriage recognition for visitors.

CHE.name: Switzerland
CHE.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Switzerland operates by self-declaration. Since 1 January 2022 any person registered in a Swiss municipality can change their sex marker and/or first name by personal declaration before a civil registrar, with no surgery and no court proceeding. In the first months of the route about 350 people had used it.

Same-sex marriage has been in force since 1 July 2022 under the 'Marriage for All' reform, which also opened adoption and IVF to same-sex couples; the reform was approved by 64.1% of voters in referendum.

Public incitement to hatred, denigration or discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been punishable under Article 261bis of the Criminal Code since 1 July 2020. That provision does not cover gender identity, so a person targeted specifically for being trans does not receive the criminal-law aggravation available on sexual-orientation grounds. The Criminal Code contains no general hate-crime provision; offences are addressed through the anti-discrimination provisions instead.

Recorded anti-LGBTIQ+ violence is rising. Monitoring by the LGBTIQ Helpline reports roughly six hate crimes per week, 309 cases in the reference year, with reports up fivefold since 2020. OSCE/ODIHR's 2024 Hate Crime Report records that Swiss police do not record bias motivation and that national recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes, so official statistics understate the picture.

On 28 January 2026 the Federal Council adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan to combat hate crimes against LGBTIQ persons, covering 2026 to 2030. Its three pillars are support and protection of victims, prevention of hate crime, and monitoring of violence, with the Federal Office for Gender Equality coordinating implementation.

Non-discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is recognised in Swiss law, and same-sex couples have been able to marry since 1 July 2022.

Placement of transgender detainees is governed cantonally rather than nationally. The canton of Basel-Stadt's detention law, adopted by the Grand Council on 13 November 2019, requires separation of female and male detainees and states that the gender identity of the detained person is respected as far as possible, with the prison directorate permitted to deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority. No federal trans-prisoner placement rule is recorded and no Swiss case law on the question is recorded; placement practice varies by canton.
CHE.outOfScopeNotes:
The numeric value of the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map index for Switzerland is not present in the inventory and is therefore not stated here.

No federal rule governing the placement of trans prisoners is recorded, nor is any Swiss case law, specialised trans units in places of detention, or federal practice on solitary confinement for trans prisoners; whether such material exists elsewhere is unresolved.

Entry and visa rules, border or airport document screening, gender markers on passports and other identity documents, access to gender-affirming healthcare, and rules on access to sex-segregated facilities such as bathrooms are not addressed by the sources supplied and remain unsourced for this record.

The hate-crime figures derive from LGBTIQ Helpline monitoring rather than police statistics, and official police recording does not code bias motivation, so the relationship between the two data sets is unresolved.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D14.

sources.title: Gesetz über den Justizvollzug (Justizvollzugsgesetz, JVG) vom 13. November 2019 — Basel-Stadt detention law (TGNS)
sources.summary: Primary legal text of the canton of Basel-Stadt's detention law (JVG, adopted 13 Nov 2019 by the Grand Council). §2 Trennungsvorschriften requires separation of female and male detainees and stipulates that 'the gender identity of the detained person is respected as far as possible' (Die Geschlechtsidentität der eingewiesenen Person wird soweit möglich beachtet); the prison directorate may deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority. This is the explicit 2019 inclusion of gender identity in a Swiss detention law aimed at protecting transgender people's placement in correctional facilities.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Switzerland — placement of transgender people in correctional facilities (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Wikipedia overview of Swiss LGBTQ rights records that in November 2019 the Grand Council of Basel-Stadt voted to include 'gender identity' in its law on detention to better protect transgender people in regard to placement in correctional facilities, citing the TGNS-documented JVG. No federal trans-prisoner placement rule is recorded; placement practice is cantonal. No Swiss case law, special trans units or federal solitary-confinement practice for trans prisoners are recorded. Wikipedia country coverage: In November 2019 the Grand Council of Basel-Stadt voted to include 'gender identity' in its cantonal law on detention, in order to better protect transgender people with regard to their placement in correctional facilities. No federal-level provision on trans placement in detention is described in the source. Wikipedia country coverage: Conversion therapy remains unregulated at federal level, though the National Council adopted a national ban on 12 December 2022 (143 for, 37 against, 11 abstentions) that is still pending in the Council of States; Neuchâtel banned it in 2023 and Valais and Vaud in 2024. The Federal Council has stated such therapies are 'ineffective and cause significant suffering to young people subjected to them' and would breach professional duties — a direct youth-specific framing — and a 2026 report confirmed it condemns the practice while leaving further federal regulation open. Blood donation rules moved to a 4-month deferral after last new sexual contact for gay men from 1 November 2023 (down from 1 year since 2017). Support services include a helpline launched by Swiss LGBT groups in November 2016, Dialogai (founded 1982) offering helplines and advice, and Transgender Network Switzerland advising on legal sex and name changes, the armed forces and asylum. Wikipedia country coverage: A 2018 survey of 1,700 Neuchâtel schoolchildren aged 14–15 found 10% of girls and 5% of boys identified as LGBT; among these, 38% reported receiving slaps, kicks or punches, 25% reported frequent harassment, 16% reported being a victim of physical violence, and 7% reported discrimination by a teacher. Since the mid-1990s an annual Coming Out Day has been observed in schools, high schools and universities, often via seminars, films and group discussions, and LGBT youth groups operate at EPFL, ETH Zurich, Lausanne and St. Gallen. In June 2023 the Federal Supreme Court upheld a cantonal school's firing of a teacher who refused to call a transgender student by his chosen male first name, ruling the school's duty to protect the student's privacy and self-determination outweighed the teacher's religious objections. On legal sex change, minors aged 12–18 originally required guardian consent, but the National Council suppressed that requirement and the Council of States set 16 as the age below which guardian consent is needed.

AUT.name: Austria
AUT.summary:
Outright International's country overview, updated March 2026, records a permissive statutory baseline: same-sex relations have been legal since 1971, marriage equality has applied since 2017, and same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since 2016.

Legal gender recognition is available without mandatory medical procedures. A person may obtain an 'X', indeterminate or absent gender marker, and intersex people may choose 'diverse', 'inter' or no designation at all.

The non-binary marker carries a documented restriction. The Constitutional Court ruled in June 2018 that official documents must reflect gender identity accurately, and Austria issued its first 'X' passport and 'divers' birth certificate in 2019; the Interior Ministry limited 'divers' registration to applicants holding a medical panel certificate of intersexuality.

The Equal Treatment Act covers discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and recent amendments broadened 'gender' to encompass gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics.

Violence is an active and documented risk. In March 2025 police uncovered a network that used fake dating-platform accounts to lure at least 17 gay, bisexual and queer people to remote locations, where masked groups ambushed them, filmed the attacks and falsely accused them of being paedophiles. Fifteen people aged 14 to 26 were arrested, and investigators state that the real victim count is considerably higher.

National police data for 2025 records 6,751 suspected hate crimes, 7,327 prejudice motives and 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence, with official and media commentary acknowledging that the figures under-record.

A visitor who is detained falls under national rules on the housing of transgender prisoners, set out in Justice Ministry answer to parliamentary question XXVIII. AB 774 of May-June 2025, a German-language document. A 2025 Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report covers the legal framework for LGBTIQ people in Austrian prisons, including gender self-determination and anti-discrimination protection.
AUT.outOfScopeNotes:
Hate-crime totals for 2025 are police figures, and under-recording is acknowledged in the sources; the split between rising homophobic and falling transphobic incidents rests on that same administrative data.

Whether an 'X' or 'divers' marker on a foreign passport is accepted at Austrian border control, and how gender markers are screened on entry, is unresolved: the inventory contains no source stating a border or visa position on markers.

The precise scope of the Interior Ministry's restriction of 'divers' registration to holders of a medical panel certificate of intersexuality, including any subsequent change to that policy, is unresolved in these sources.

Justice Ministry answer XXVIII. AB 774 is available only in German and is cited here for its subject and date rather than for a reviewed reading of its provisions.

The rejected sauna petition and the Ministry of Education rules on outside sex-education providers are reported in a single source and are not corroborated elsewhere in the inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5.

Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report (2025) on LGBTIQ detainees in Austria, part of an EU-funded project. Covers the legal framework for LGBTIQ people in detention, gender self-determination, anti-discrimination protection, and the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in Austrian prisons.

Austrian Justice Ministry answer to parliamentary question XXVIII. AB 774 (May-June 2025): official rules on housing transgender people in Austrian penal institutions — the authority to cite if a trans visitor is detained; German-language.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Austria permits LGBT people to serve openly in the Austrian Armed Forces, and since 2014 transgender people have been allowed to serve openly (policy reportedly still in effect in 2017). The Equal Treatment Act has covered anti-discrimination in employment on the basis of sexual orientation since 2004; gender identity and intersex status are not explicitly listed but are perceived as covered under "gender." As of January 2017, every federal state (the last being Lower Austria) had anti-discrimination laws covering sexual orientation in goods and services, and from 1 January 2016 hate speech based on sexual orientation is banned with crimes committed on account of a victim's sexual orientation treated as an aggravating factor. The 1993 Security Police Act obliges police to avoid actions that could be perceived as biased on sexual orientation grounds. LGBT advocacy operates openly, e.g. HOSI Wien (founded 1979), HOSI Salzburg, ALGF, and Afro Rainbow Austria, and the National Council passed a non-binding resolution on 2 July 2019 calling for a government bill banning conversion therapy on minors, with all parties voting in favor by the final vote. Wikipedia country coverage: Austrian trans people can change legal gender and name without prior sex-reassignment surgery, but the change is bound on submission of a psychiatric opinion, and public health insurance payment for sex-change treatment is likewise bound to submission of various psychiatric opinions. Puberty blockers for youth experiencing gender dysphoria have been endorsed by the Austrian Society of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (ÖGKJP) and the Austrian Society of Gynecology and Obstetrics (OEGGG). Lesbian couples can access artificial insemination and IVF treatments. Youth-specific risk: in 2018 the ultra-conservative association TeenSTAR was found offering minors conversion therapy classes teaching that sexual orientation was "changeable"; the Education Directorate Salzburg banned TeenSTAR workshops pending review, the association was finally banned in April 2019, and Parliament passed a resolution in July 2019 calling for a legal ban on conversion therapy on minors. Wikipedia country coverage: Despite progressive laws, the text notes "there are still many LGBT minorities who think that being different is a problem," a sentiment shaped by the country's Catholic influence. Political visibility is high: seven politicians in the National Council are openly gay since the 2019 election, Iris Eliisa Rauskala became the first openly LGBT government minister (June 2019), and Georg Djundja became Austria's first openly gay mayor in April 2019; President Alexander Van der Bellen took part in the 2019 EuroPride parade in Vienna. Community infrastructure exists in all larger cities (Vienna, Linz, Innsbruck, Salzburg, Graz) with annual Vienna Gay Pride/Regenbogenparade; conservative parties ÖVP and FPÖ have historically opposed LGBT rights, and historical prosecutions were harsh (lesbianism criminalised under Austrian law after the Anschluss, with 1940 court alignment to Paragraph 175). Public opinion as of 2023: 65% of Austrians supported same-sex marriage and 66% agreed nothing is wrong with a same-sex relationship; as of July 2020 no expungement or compensation scheme for historical convictions had been implemented. Wikipedia country coverage: Transgender people in Austria can change legal gender and name to match their gender identity without prior sex reassignment surgery, but the change is conditional on submitting a psychiatric opinion, and payment of sex-change treatment by public health insurance is likewise bound to submission of various psychiatric opinions. Endorsing a youth-specific angle, two professional bodies — the Austrian Society of Gynecology and Obstetrics (OEGGG) and the Austrian Society for Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (ÖGKJP) — have endorsed the use of puberty blockers for youth experiencing gender dysphoria. Regarding minors, the National Council approved a resolution (preliminary vote 13 June 2019, final vote 2 July 2019) calling on the government to submit a bill banning conversion and reparative therapies on minors, with FPÖ initially opposing but later agreeing. The source also notes that lesbian couples can access artificial insemination and IVF treatments.

AUT.tangentialFactors:
The far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) took the largest vote share in the September 2024 national election at 29.2 percent, its first such result since the Second World War, and monitoring bodies and commentators recorded concern about the consequences of an FPÖ-led government for LGBTQ+ people.

ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2026, covering 2025, documents Ombuds guidance on gender-inclusive forms for intersex and non-binary people, new Ministry of Education rules restricting outside sex-education providers, and a rejected municipal petition for queer sauna time slots. The first of these bears on how a person's marker is handled by public bodies; the third concerns access to a city leisure facility.

Recorded trends move in opposite directions: for the reporting year, homophobic offences rose while transphobic incidents declined.

Statutory terms on decriminalisation, partnership and gender recognition are open by comparison with neighbouring jurisdictions, but the practical position on the 'X' marker and the volume of recorded violence are narrower than the statute alone implies.

The Ludwig Boltzmann Institute's 2025 national report, part of an externally funded project, sets out the framework for LGBTIQ detainees in Austria: gender self-determination, anti-discrimination protection, and the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in the country's prisons. It is the working reference for residents, families and their representatives.

Justice Ministry answer XXVIII. AB 774 of May-June 2025 states the official rules on housing transgender people in Austrian penal institutions. The text is in German.

Ombuds guidance on gender-inclusive forms is directed at administrative practice and affects how residents complete official paperwork when their marker is 'diverse', 'inter' or absent.

GGG's July 2026 reading of the official hate-crime statistics for the reporting year shows homophobic offences rising and transphobic incidents falling, within a national total of 6,751 suspected hate crimes and 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence.

ITA.name: Italy
ITA.summary:
Outright International records same-sex relations as legal throughout Italy for men and women. That legal baseline has not prevented recurring violence against LGBT people, and in particular against transgender people. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Annual Review documents that homophobic and transphobic violence continued in 2025, including organised dating-app entrapment schemes in which groups lure victims and then assault or rob them. Progetto Gionata characterises transphobia as the most severe and most widespread discrimination confronting transgender people in Italy, which is consistent with the pattern of violence recorded by monitors rather than with isolated incidents.

The most serious traveller-specific finding is the sexual assault of young transgender tourists in Campania. ANSA reports that the convictions for the assault were upheld on appeal in April 2026, an outcome that affirms accountability for violence against trans visitors, while also confirming that the assault took place and that the victims were targeted while in Italy. Organised entrapment schemes of the kind ILGA-Europe records for gay men present a comparable risk surface for transgender visitors who use dating and hookup applications, where victims are deliberately isolated before being attacked.

Police violence against transgender people is documented and has been prosecuted. On 5 July 2024 tgcom24 reported that a Milan traffic officer was sentenced to ten months in prison for stopping and then beating a transgender woman with batons. The conviction shows that such conduct reaches criminal sanction, and it also shows that transgender people in Italy face the risk of physical violence from the officers who stop them.

Transgender people who are detained in Italy are held in an institutional environment that monitor reports describe as lacking consistent gender-affirming provision. The Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report of July 2025 sets out the legal and policy framework governing LGBTIQ detainees in Italy, the pathways available for gender affirmation in custody, and the treatment of same-sex relationships in prison. A 2026 study in Frontiers in Psychiatry, drawing on a thematic analysis of transgender identity and psychiatric care in Italian prisons, records systemic gaps and institutional challenges in the care provided to incarcerated trans people.

The political and institutional climate is openly hostile. ILGA-Europe reports that Italy's Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from its Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second consecutive year, and that a cardinal described homosexual acts as a mortal sin. Human Rights Watch's 2025 World Report chapter on Italy records sustained hostile political rhetoric about LGBT people as contributing to a hostile environment, within a wider account of rule-of-law and civil-society constraints in the country. Progetto Gionata's assessment of transphobia as the most pervasive discrimination facing trans people is consistent with this official climate.

One judicial development points the other way. In March 2025 the Civil Court of Asti recognised, for the first time in that court, the physical and psychological harm caused by homophobic mistreatment. The recognition concerns mistreatment of LGBT people in the setting the case arose from, and its reach beyond that court is not established by the source.
ITA.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in this source inventory: nothing here addresses entry or visa screening that could expose a visitor's transgender status, the rules on gender markers in passports or identity documents, whether a visitor may obtain gender-affirming healthcare in Italy, or how Italian authorities treat foreign court documents recording a change of gender. No source covers same-sex marriage or the recognition of foreign civil unions or marriages for visiting couples, beyond the baseline that same-sex relations are legal.

The inventory does not state the prison placement rule for trans women in Italy, so this summary does not assert that they are held with men or that any exception applies. What the sources do support is that gender-affirming pathways in custody exist in law and that gaps in delivery, including in psychiatric care, are documented by the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute and by the Frontiers in Psychiatry study.

The status of the Milan officer's conviction on appeal is not stated by the source; only the first-instance sentence of ten months, reported on 5 July 2024, is documented. The Asti ruling is described by ILGA-Europe as a first for that court, and the inventory does not establish its precedential effect on other Italian courts.

The sources cited for the assault convictions and for the dating-app entrapment schemes do not establish whether either pattern is rising or falling over time. A tour-operator assessment of Italy as an LGBTQIA+ destination makes no jurisdiction-specific safety finding and is not relied on here.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D5.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Cross-dressing is legal in Italy, though during fascist rule (1920s–1940s) the penal code banned it and police targeted trans people, and in 2006 a police officer was reportedly fired for cross-dressing in public off duty. A bill banning homophobic and transphobic advertising in streets and on vehicles passed the Chamber of Deputies 271–16 on 28 October 2021 and the Senate 190–34 on 4 November, signed by President Mattarella and in force 10 November 2021; the government forced a single up-or-down vote on the whole bill, so MPs opposing that provision had to vote for it. A broader anti-discrimination/hate-crime bill passed the Chamber on 4 November 2020 (265–193) but died in the Senate on 27 October 2021 by a 131–154 secret ballot. Wikipedia country coverage: Transgender people have been able to change legal gender since 1982, when Italy became the sixth country worldwide to allow it, and since 21 May 2015 sterilisation and sex reassignment surgery are no longer required for legal gender change. On 23 July 2024 (judgment no. 143) the Constitutional Court first recognised non-binary individuals as rights-holders under Articles 2, 3 and 32, but refused to add a "non-binary" registry marker, saying only Parliament can change Italy's male/female binary system; the same judgment struck down the requirement of judicial authorisation for gender-affirming surgery after legal sex change. Courts in Trento (15 February 2023) allowed legal gender change for transgender minors with parental consent and psychological consultation, and Trapani (6 July 2023) allowed a name and gender change with no surgery or hormones. On 14 April 2025 the Supreme Court of Cassation ordered Italian ID cards to use the gender-neutral term "genitori" (parents) instead of "mother" and "father" for children with same-sex parents, finding the old wording discriminatory. Wikipedia country coverage: The Supreme Court of Cassation, citing the Constitutional Court's 2010 ruling recognising same-sex couples as a "legitimate social formation," ordered a questura (police office issuing residence permits) to grant a residence permit to an Algerian citizen married to a same-sex Spanish spouse. Italy recognises persecution based on sexual orientation or gender identity as grounds for asylum under the 1951 Geneva Convention and EU Qualification Directive 2011/95/EU, and Decree-Law No. 130/2020 (in force 22 October 2020) simplified asylum procedures and reinforced protection for vulnerable groups including those persecuted for SOGI. Same-sex marriages performed abroad are not recognised as marriages but must be registered as civil unions (Court of Cassation, May 2018). Wikipedia country coverage: Gay and bisexual men have been allowed to donate blood since 2001. Since February 2019 puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones are provided free of charge and covered by the National Health Service, and since 2020 hormone therapy has been fully covered by national healthcare, free of charge. However, gender identity is not mentioned in Italy's anti-discrimination laws, so transgender people may face discrimination in access to goods and services, housing, education and health services. Wikipedia country coverage: Sexual-orientation discrimination in employment has been illegal nationwide since July 2003 under Legislative Decree no. 216 of 2003 (implementing EU Directive 2000/78/EC); exemptions for police, armed forces and rescue services were removed by Law no. 101 of 2008. No other nationwide anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity has been enacted — the Zan bill passed the Chamber 265–193 on 4 November 2020 but died in the Senate on 27 October 2021, and ILGA-Europe's 2021 report notes Italy lacks nationwide protection for goods and services. No Italian law explicitly bans transphobic discrimination, though a Rome court ruled on 15 January 2023 that firing a trans professor amounted to sex discrimination. Regions have legislated instead: Tuscany (2004), Liguria (2009), Marche (2010), Sicily (2015), Piedmont (2016), Umbria (2017), Emilia-Romagna (2019), Campania (2020) and Apulia (2024). Wikipedia country coverage: The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, and Italy has had an equal age of consent for homosexual and heterosexual acts since before the 20th century. A court in Trento ruled on 15 February 2023 that transgender minors could change their legal gender on documents with parental consent and after consulting a psychologist. In 2018 the Italian National Bioethics Committee and Italian Medicines Agency backed puberty blockers for adolescents with gender dysphoria case-by-case with safeguards; from February 2019 blockers and cross-sex hormones are free under the National Health Service, though access still requires medical evaluations, parental consent and exhaustion of other interventions — supported by the Italian Society of Endocrinology, Italian Academy of Pediatrics and six other paediatric and adolescent medical societies. In May 2026 AGESCI, Italy's largest Catholic scout association, decided sexual orientation and gender identity can no longer exclude adults from leadership and educational roles after three years of internal debate; Pew (2013) found 86% of Italians aged 18–29 accepted homosexuality versus 67% of those over 50.

Same-sex relations are legal nationwide, yet ILGA-Europe's 2025 coverage describes continued homophobic and transphobic violence and institutional hostility, including the second consecutive omission of LGBTI persecution from Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars by the Education Ministry. Human Rights Watch places this within a broader pattern of hostile political rhetoric about LGBT people and of rule-of-law and civil-society constraints, which bears on how reliably protection is delivered when a visitor seeks it.

Religious authority statements form part of the same climate. A cardinal's description of homosexual acts as a mortal sin, reported in ILGA-Europe's review, sits alongside state-level hostility rather than apart from it, and indicates that stigma is voiced from institutions with reach over public opinion and education.

Judicial treatment of mistreatment claims appears to be shifting at provincial level. The Civil Court of Asti's March 2025 recognition of physical and psychological harm from homophobic mistreatment is described as a first for that court, which is a signal of movement in claims practice while falling short of an established national rule.

Violence risk is structured rather than random. ILGA-Europe's documentation of organised dating-app entrapment schemes, which target gay men through arranged meetings followed by assault or robbery, indicates an organised predation pattern in which the dating app is the lure. Transgender visitors face a comparable exposure, given the additional targeting visible in the Campania assault cases whose convictions were confirmed on appeal in April 2026.

A 2026 study in Frontiers in Psychiatry, presenting a thematic analysis of transgender identity and psychiatric care in Italian prisons, records systemic gaps and institutional challenges in the care delivered to incarcerated trans people, including in the psychiatric dimension of that care.

Residents who encounter police violence against trans people have a criminal-law route, and the Milan case shows that it has been used.

POL.name: Poland
POL.summary:
Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in Poland. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals; her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may be exposed to both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and links general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance.

The wider legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.
POL.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the March and October 2024 hate-speech bills have since been enacted by the Sejm is unresolved in the source inventory, which records drafts, a cleared legislative-centre stage and postponement only. The inventory does not state the requirements Polish courts apply to a legal gender-marker change, nor whether a court-ordered sterilisation or surgical requirement persists; the Przegląd Sejmowy analysis is cited as evidence that the regime exists and is contested, not for its specific conditions.

Implementation of the September 2024 European Court of Human Rights partnership ruling is unresolved, as is whether Poland has since adopted the recognition framework the court called for. The inventory does not establish whether gender identity is a protected ground in Poland's general anti-discrimination statute independent of the pending bills. It also does not establish how Border Guard or prison placement decisions are made for trans detainees after the 2024 cases, beyond the fact that no specialised section exists and that intervention was required in the documented instances.

The trans detainee case's reference to a prior history of violence and sexual assault is specific to that individual and should not be generalised to trans travellers, who have no reason to expect similar screening.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D1, D2, D6, D14.

Przeglad Sejmowy 2024/5, Podgorska-Rykala & Kepa: scholarly legal analysis of Poland's administrative regime for transgender persons under the Civil Status Records Law, Population Register Act and Identity Cards Act; asks whether citizens are equally treated and whether protection is sufficient, especially on civil status. Evidence of how gender-marker documents work in practice in Poland.

HRW news release (18 Mar 2007): the then government proposed fast-track legislation 'punishing anyone who promotes homosexuality' in schools - dismissal, fines or prison for teachers/students, banning LGBT organisations and safer-sex HIV education, with deputy minister Orzechowski announcing teachers who reveal homosexuality would be fired; HRW wrote to PM Kaczynski. sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Homosexuality was decriminalised in independent Poland in 1932, but under partition it had been criminalised in Congress Poland (1818), Austria (1852), Prussia (1871) and Russia (1845, penalised by forced resettlement to Siberia), and during the German occupation it was recriminalised from 1939 — Polish men in same-sex relationships were punished under Article 175, especially in annexed areas, with the General Government's criminal police able to deport or impose the death penalty, and camp prisoners under Paragraph 175 classified as 'political prisoners' with red triangles. Earlier, only two known sodomy sentences were carried out: Wojciech Skwarski of Poznań, burned at the stake in 1561 (the sentence also counted theft and murder), and Agnieszka Kuśnierczanka in 1642, publicly beaten and exiled; the 1925 Suwałki case saw Stefan Góralski and Marjan Kuleszyński sentenced to three months under paragraph 516 of the 1903 Russian Penal Code. Post-war, the 1948 law set the age of consent at 15 for all sexual acts and otherwise left the liberal interwar law intact, but the Security Service's Operation Hyacinth of 15 November 1985 registered around 11,000 suspected gay men in a national database, with 'pink files' still held by the Institute of National Remembrance as of 2005 despite activists' requests to destroy them. Since EU accession a 1 January 2004 law barred workplace discrimination on sexual orientation, and on 8 July 2024 the Tusk government added a registered-partnership bill (no joint adoption) to the Sejm agenda after its October 2024 presentation by Equality Minister Katarzyna Kotula. Wikipedia country coverage: Open discussion of homosexuality remained taboo outside literary circles: the Second Republic magazine Wiadomości Literackie and figures such as Tadeusz Boy-Żeleński and Irena Krzywicka broke taboos on contraception and homosexuality, founding the Liga Reformy Obyczajów in 1935, and 1933 saw three novels with openly lesbian themes including The Well of Loneliness with Krzywicka's preface. Communist authorities actively censored information about the Kinsey Report, while a 1985 Polityka article 'Jesteśmy inni' ('We are different') triggered a national discussion and Selerowicz's conspiratorial 1983–84 meetings produced the samizdat bulletin Etap; press came-outs followed with actor Marek Barbasiewicz in Kobieta i Życie (September 1992) and Izabela Filipiak in Viva (1998). Media expression has also been a vehicle for hostility: the right-wing Gazeta Polska distributed 'LGBT-free zone' stickers (later reworded 'LGBT Ideology-Free Zone') after a court ordered distribution halted, President Andrzej Duda stated in the 2020 election that 'LGBT is not people, it's an ideology, which is more harmful than Communism', and Lech Kaczyński opposed official Pride in 2004–05. Cultural visibility includes the 1987 Polish premiere of Larry Kramer's The Normal Heart in Poznań with a 4 May 1989 TVP broadcast, Karolina Breguła's 2023 'Let Them See Us' billboard campaign (frequently vandalised), and Lambda's Queer Museum in Warsaw, opened 6 December 2024 as the first of its kind in Central and Eastern Europe. Wikipedia country coverage: The first official gay club in Poland, Café Fiolka at Puławska 257 in Warsaw, opened on 7 October 1990 and was closed in 1992 after repeated acts of vandalism, while earlier police targeted cruising spots — in 1927 Warsaw's 6th Sanitary-Moral Brigade, joined by the female 1st Brigade in 1925, hunted local cruising areas and arrested mostly working-class men identifying as 'ciota'. Health and support infrastructure developed around the AIDS crisis: the Ministry of Health established a Plenipotentiary for AIDS and a ten-person expert team in 1985 (a year before Poland's first recorded AIDS case), Lambda was registered by the Warsaw Voivodeship Court on 23 February 1990 to spread tolerance and prevent HIV, and the Kochaj, nie zabijaj (Love, don't kill) campaign began in spring 1990. Community organisations include Campaign Against Homophobia (2001), the Polish Feminist Lesbian Archive OLA-Archiwum (registered 1998, publishing Furia Pierwsza), the Trans-Fuzja foundation co-founded by MP Anna Grodzka, and the Razem group for Polish LGBT immigrants in New York (1995, part of the Lesbian & Gay Community Services Center). Medical services are documented from the first sex reassignment surgery in 1963 at Szpital Kolejowy in Międzylesie (infrequent for another ~20 years), the first recorded transgender meeting on 10 December 1985 at Warsaw's Department of Sexology, and the 6 December 2024 opening of the Queer Museum in Warsaw. Wikipedia country coverage: Homophobia is described as a common public attitude driven by the Catholic Church's influence on Polish public life and widespread social conservatism, with homosexuality a taboo for most of Polish history; the Church later became 'a factor in making homosexuality something scandalous in many social circles' and influenced the 1988 blocking of the Warsaw Gay Movement's legal registration. Political hostility escalated after 2015: several municipalities and four voivodeships declared 'LGBT-free zones' (partly in response to mayor Rafał Trzaskowski's pro-LGBT declaration), and in August 2019 multiple LGBT community members said they felt unsafe, amid a 2019 rise in violence including attacks on the first Białystok Equality March and a foiled bombing attempt at a Lublin march; at a Kalisz rally on 11 November 2021 the organizer called 'LGBT, pederasts and Zionists' enemies of Poland. ILGA-Europe's 2020 report ranked Poland worst among EU countries for LGBT rights, and on 7 August 2020 47 people were arrested in the Rainbow Night mass arrest (some peacefully protesting activist Margot's arrest), drawing criticism from the Polish Ombudsman; 50 ambassadors and representatives wrote an open letter on 27 September 2020 affirming that 'Human Rights are not an ideology'. Visibility milestones run from the first Equality Parade in Warsaw in 2001 (over 300 attendees), through banned 2004–05 Prides (the 11 June 2005 march drew about 2,500 in civil disobedience with several brief arrests and a 600–1,000-person 2004 Freedom Veche), to the 2011 election of Poland's first out LGBT MPs, Robert Biedroń and Anna Grodzka; by contrast, questioned villagers in the 1925 Suwałki case reported no 'abnormality' and accepted the two men in their community.

POL.localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition for Polish citizens operates under the Civil Status Records Law, the Population Register Act and the Identity Cards Act. A scholarly analysis by Podgorska-Rykala and Kepa in Przegląd Sejmowy 2024/5 examines whether that administrative regime treats citizens equally and whether protection of civil status is sufficient, and its framing indicates continuing disputes over how marker changes are handled in practice.

Resident-facing protections remain incomplete. The hate-speech bills extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation had cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May 2024 but approval was postponed, with a second bill introduced in late October, so at the time of the source inventory the expanded penalties were not yet enacted. The Prosecutor General's special response team and its guidelines for law enforcement were operating as an executive measure.

Same-sex couples resident in Poland gained the June 2024 revocation of the directive blocking recognition of foreign marriage certificates, and the September 2024 European Court of Human Rights judgment requires a partnership recognition framework that the legislature had not yet delivered. Trans people in custody rely on litigation rather than internal complaint procedures, as the July 2024 judgment shows, and there is no specialised trans prison section to request.
POL.blindSummary:
Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor. In a case publicised by a legal-aid NGO on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender foreign national in a guarded centre for male foreigners; her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may be exposed to both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the human rights court found that national prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in national custody is litigable and winnable, though the country operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: a national travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and links general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance.

The wider legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the sitting government as slow and insufficient through 2024. The deputy justice minister announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Criminal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 the justice minister revoked a predecessor's directive that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the human rights court ruled that the absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.
POL.blindOutOfScope:
Whether the March and October 2024 hate-speech bills have since been enacted by the legislature is unresolved in the source inventory, which records drafts, a cleared legislative-centre stage and postponement only. The inventory does not state the requirements courts apply to a legal gender-marker change, nor whether a surgical requirement persists; the parliamentary review analysis is cited as evidence that the regime exists and is contested, not for its specific conditions.

Implementation of the September 2024 partnership ruling is unresolved, as is whether a recognition framework has since been adopted. The inventory does not establish whether gender identity is a protected ground in the general anti-discrimination statute independent of the pending bills. It also does not establish how detention or prison placement decisions are made for trans detainees after the 2024 cases, beyond the fact that no specialised section exists and that intervention was required in the documented instances.

The trans detainee case's reference to a prior history of violence and sexual assault is specific to that individual and should not be generalised to trans travellers, who have no reason to expect similar screening.

POL.tangentialFactors:
The social climate carries a legacy that shapes what a trans visitor may encounter. Amnesty International's 2025 report 'A Thousand Cuts' documents technology-facilitated gender-based violence against LGBTI people in Poland on X, set against the LGBT-free-zone declarations adopted by dozens of local authorities between 2019 and 2023 and what the report characterises as a lack of legal inclusion. The report also tracks platform policy reversals: X removed its rule against misgendering and deadnaming in April 2023 and reinstated a version of it in 2024, so online abuse exposure varies with platform enforcement rather than Polish law.

A historical precedent for state-led censorship sits alongside the current reform debate. In March 2007 the then government proposed fast-track legislation punishing anyone who promoted homosexuality in schools with dismissal, fines or prison, banning LGBT organisations and safer-sex HIV education, with a deputy minister announcing that teachers who revealed homosexuality would be fired; Human Rights Watch wrote to Prime Minister Kaczyński in response. For comparison, reform pace is the recurring criticism across sources: Human Rights Watch called the Tusk government's 2024 output slow and insufficient, while ILGA-Europe's Annual Review records legislative drafts passing the Government Legislation Centre only to be postponed. Momentum is upward from a low baseline rather than settled.

HUN.name: Hungary
HUN.summary:
Hungary's statutory position on trans people has not changed with the political turnover of the 12 April 2026 election, in which Péter Magyar's Tisza party won 138 seats and ended 16 years of Viktor Orbán's government. Analysts describe the outcome as a restoration of the democratic baseline rather than a repeal of the legal architecture built during the previous era, and Tisza has not published an LGBTQ+ programme. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal in Hungary since 1961.

Legal gender recognition is explicitly prohibited. In May 2020, while ruling by emergency decree during the COVID-19 pandemic, the Orbán government pushed through a bill barring passports and identity cards from reflecting an acquired gender, including for people already legally recognised, and redefined the word nem (sex) in the civil code as immutable biological sex. Administrative refusal had already made recognition effectively impossible from 2018. Trans Hungarians therefore carry identity documents that do not match their presentation, and a visitor whose papers were issued under this regime should expect document checks to expose the mismatch at border control and in any transaction requiring identification.

One correction route operates at European level. In Case C-247/23 Deldits, judgment of 13 March 2025 on a reference from the Budapest High Court in an immigration matter, the Court of Justice of the European Union held that Article 16 GDPR obliges the national register authority to rectify recorded gender data where that data has changed and no longer satisfies the accuracy principle of Article 5(1)(d). In September 2024 the same court's Advocate General had called on Hungarian authorities to correct a transgender refugee's gender marker in national registries. Neither holding reinstates the domestic power to issue new documents bearing an acquired gender.

In April 2026 the Court of Justice ruled that Orbán-era anti-LGBTQ legislation, including the prohibition on gender change for under-18s argued under child-protection law, breached EU rules on several levels, and found a breach of Article 2 of the EU Treaty, which sets out the union's founding values. The judgment was delivered nine days after Hungarians voted.

Public assembly is the most contested area for a visitor. Budapest Pride spokesperson Johanna Majercsik identified restoration of the right to assembly as the most urgent issue after the election and noted that anti-queer laws can be repealed with a two-thirds parliamentary majority, while the Tisza party's silence on LGBTQ+ rights under Péter Magyar has raised questions about the pace of change. The 31st Budapest Pride, held in June 2026, was the first since Orbán was voted out; tens of thousands marched against the backdrop of the anti-LGBT laws still in force, and international coverage recorded community expectations that changes will be made.

Detention remains a documented exposure point. A 2025 national report on LGBTIQ detainees in Hungary, produced by the Hungarian Helsinki Committee and the Háttér Society as part of the EU-funded Strengthening the rights of LGBTIQ detainees in the EU project, sets out the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people held in Hungarian detention under the current legal and political climate. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records that LGBT people in Hungary continue to face discrimination and demonisation.
HUN.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in this source set: whether the constitutional restriction on LGBTQ public events and the child-protection content legislation have been amended, suspended or left untouched in the months since the April 2026 election. The sources record the repeal mechanism and the organisers' demands, not the legislative outcome.

Unresolved: whether the Court of Justice holdings on registry rectification and on the under-18 gender-change prohibition have been applied in practice by Hungarian registry authorities, and how border and police officials treat documents that do not match presentation during routine checks. No source in this inventory reports enforcement data.

Not sourced here: access to gender-affirming healthcare, facilities and restroom access for visitors, and the operation of hate-crime or anti-discrimination protections in prosecutions. Any statement on those points would rest on material outside the current inventory.

The 2025 detention report is cited at the level of its subject and authorship; individual findings on conditions, complaints handling and staff conduct are not reproduced in this record.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: In January 2018 the European Court of Justice ruled that asylum seekers may not be subjected by authorities to psychological tests in order to determine their sexual orientation. The source otherwise contains no material on border controls, entry screening, or documentation checks specific to trans or LGBTQ travellers; the only related policy rhetoric noted is the May 2020 National Assembly resolution rejecting the Istanbul Convention, which attacked the treaty's measures as promoting "destructive gender ideologies" and "illegal migration." Wikipedia country coverage: The source documents sustained political hostility rather than recorded hate-crime statistics: in October 2020 PM Orbán said "gays are to leave our children alone," and in 2017 he welcomed the World Congress of Families, a group designated a hate group by the Southern Poverty Law Center, at the National Parliament. After a 2021 children's book by the Labrisz Lesbian Association, Fidesz launched a smear campaign confusing homosexuality with pedophilia, and the government-linked media giant Mediaworks published an article calling Labrisz pedophiles without proof; Labrisz won at first instance but the Curia ruled in November 2022 that the article did not violate its right to good reputation, prompting an appeal to the Constitutional Court. In 2014 Jobbik displayed a sign reading "The Parliament Does Not Want Any Deviants" at Budapest Pride and verbally abused attendees. The ECJ found in April 2026 that the 2021 child protection law discriminated against and scapegoated LGBTI residents. Wikipedia country coverage: Unregistered cohabitation has been recognised since 1996 for any couple, including same-sex couples, giving specified rights with inheritance only by testament and a widow's pension after 10 years. Registered partnerships for same-sex couples have been available since 1 July 2009, carrying the same rights as spouses except adoption, assisted reproduction and taking a surname, while same-sex marriage was banned by the 1 January 2012 constitution. Same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly, stepchild adoption is limited to married different-sex couples, and IVF and donor insemination are unavailable to lesbians in a registered partnership; a December 2020 constitutional amendment further banned adoption by same-sex couples and restricted single-parent adoption. In September 2026 PM Péter Magyar announced intent to repeal the ban on adoption by same-sex couples.

HUN.localsOnly:
Hungarian citizens cannot obtain legal gender recognition at all: the 2020 emergency-decree legislation removed the route and locked identity documents to sex assigned at birth, and the redefinition of sex as immutable biological sex in the civil code forecloses domestic litigation on the point.

Registry rectification under Article 16 GDPR remains available for correcting recorded gender data, following the Deldits judgment of 13 March 2025, but that mechanism addresses the accuracy of an existing record rather than authorising the issuance of a new passport or identity card.

Repeal of the anti-queer statutes is a two-thirds majority question in the National Assembly, and the Budapest Pride organisers have framed restoration of assembly rights as the first objective. The 2025 report by the Hungarian Helsinki Committee and the Háttér Society is the reference document on the treatment and rights of LGBTIQ detainees, produced under an EU-funded project covering the situation in Hungarian places of detention.

Human Rights Watch's 2025 country chapter documents continuing discrimination and demonisation of LGBT people in public life, which shapes how a resident's documents and presentation are read by officials even where no offence is committed.

European litigation has run ahead of domestic implementation. The Court of Justice has now found a breach of Article 2 of the EU Treaty, a provision that sets out founding values, in addition to the GDPR and free-movement holdings, which raises the pressure on Budapest but does not itself alter what a border officer or registry clerk does on a given day.

Compared with neighbouring jurisdictions where legal gender recognition operates through an administrative procedure, Hungary stands out for having converted a de facto administrative blockage dating from 2018 into an express statutory prohibition in 2020, so the document problem is structural rather than a matter of processing delay.

GRC.name: Greece
GRC.summary:
Greece's statutory framework is among the stronger ones in the region. Law 5089/2024 legalised same-sex marriage in February 2024, making Greece the first state with a majority Orthodox Christian population to do so, and added SOGIESC equal-treatment guarantees covering social protection, education, healthcare, housing and goods and services. Civil unions have been available since 2015, with adoption and foster care permitted, and the age of consent is 15 for everyone. Legal gender change has been possible on a self-declaration basis since 2017. Conversion practices have been banned for minors and intersex genital mutilation criminalised since 2022, employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity has been prohibited since 2023, and hate-crime and hate-speech provisions cover gender identity. ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map placed Greece 7th in its 2025 rankings.

There are no trans-specific restrictions at the border or on bathroom use, and legal gender recognition is available. The UK Foreign Office updated its Greece travel advice for LGBTQ+ travellers in April 2024, noting that same-sex relations are legal, civil unions date from 2015 and marriage from February 2024, and advising visitors to remain alert.

Enforcement and street-level violence tell a harder story. In March 2024 a mob of roughly 150 people attacked two transgender people in Thessaloniki; 21 people were arrested, 11 of them minors, and a masked attack on counter-protesters followed. The European Court of Human Rights found in Koutra and Katzaki v. Greece (2017) that police stopped and mistreated transgender sex workers and their lawyer in Athens in 2013, pulling them from cars in street stops, and that complaints against the officers were discontinued. In 2025 the same court condemned Greece for detaining an LGBTI Iranian refugee pending deportation, finding a violation of Article 3. In July 2025 the Crete Court of Appeal convicted three French tourists over a 2017 attack, and a criminal case was opened over an online post inciting discrimination against immigrants and LGBTI people.

The social climate lags the statute. EU Fundamental Rights Agency survey data from 2024 shows 63% of LGBTIQ respondents avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner against an EU-27 average of 53%, 36% avoid certain locations for fear of assault against 29%, only 35% are open about being LGBTIQ against 51%, and 28% felt discriminated against at work against 19%. The Orthodox Church officially opposed marriage equality, and transphobic comments were directed at Greece's Eurovision contestants in 2024.

Trans-specific gaps remain measurable. The TGEU Trans Rights Index and Map 2025, which recorded backsliding outpacing progress across Europe for the first time, counts Greece at 21 of 32 indicators, with shortfalls including age restrictions on legal name changes, the absence of a national action plan, and no legal recognition of trans and non-binary parenthood.
GRC.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not state how Greek border officials handle a passport whose gender marker does not match the holder's presentation, whether additional document checks are applied to trans travellers, or whether any entry refusal or secondary screening on gender-identity grounds has been recorded. This is unresolved in the inventory.

No sourced material addresses access to hormone therapy or other trans-specific healthcare for short-term visitors, the availability of gendered facilities in tourist accommodation, or whether the healthcare equal-treatment guarantee in Law 5089/2024 has been tested in practice for a visitor.

The UK Foreign Office advice is reported as an alertness recommendation rather than a warning of a specific threat; the inventory does not reproduce the full text or any regional caveat it may contain.

Enforcement outcomes are unevenly sourced. The Thessaloniki arrests, the Crete appeal conviction and the discontinued police complaints in the 2017 Strasbourg judgment are documented, but there is no inventory data on conviction rates for gender-identity hate crimes nationally, nor on whether the criminal case opened over the discriminatory online post resulted in charges.

The TGEU count of 21 of 32 indicators is given without the full indicator list, so the eleven unmet measures beyond the three named cannot be enumerated from this inventory.
