CZE.name: Czechia
CZE.summary:
Czechia's rules for legal gender recognition have been rewritten twice in eighteen months. On 24 April 2024 the Czech Constitutional Court, in judgment PL. US 52/23, struck down the requirement that an official sex change be conditional on surgery disabling reproductive function, holding compulsory sterilisation for legal recognition unconstitutional; by June 2025 the surgery requirement had been dropped in practice. The European Court of Human Rights then found a violation of Article 8 against Czechia in T.H. v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 33037/22, judgment 12 September 2025), holding the surgical and sterilisation conditions and the related civil-registry treatment incompatible with private-life rights and framing Convention-guaranteed gender recognition on self-determination, with Transgender Europe and ILGA-Europe intervening.

Detention remains the weakest point for a trans visitor. Administrative courts clashed in public over the handling of an HIV-positive trans man in transition held by immigration police: in March 2023 the Supreme Administrative Court rebuked the Prague Municipal Court for 'sarcastic moral lectures' toward the detainee and ruled that authorities must first assess whether a person is 'potentially vulnerable' before deciding placement. Practice has not caught up with that standard. In November 2025 reporting, judges described Czech prisons as unprepared for trans people and lacking clear rules; the Supreme Court is pressing for a national prison concept that explicitly addresses the needs of people in or after transition, the human-rights commissioner is pushing a binding regulation, and the Justice Ministry maintains that the existing framework is sufficient, with consultation ongoing.

Social hostility is measurable and politically amplified. The ILGA-Europe 'Being LGBTQ+ in Czechia' survey found 43% of respondents discriminated or harassed in the previous five years, over a third within twelve months, with trans and non-binary respondents reporting the highest rates, and 51% targeted by insults, assault or threats over five years. Politicians' anti-LGBT speech rose from 43% in 2018 to 71% in 2023, and 63% of respondents attributed rising intolerance to politicians. In 2024 the Justice Minister publicly stated that his goal was 'to prevent men from giving birth' after the Constitutional Court repealed the surgical prerequisite, and the far-right SPD circulated election leaflets promising to take money from 'LGBT activists' and 'give more to families, take it away from the deviants'.

Enforcement machinery exists but is thinly quantified. Police recorded 94 hate crimes in 2024, with 46 prosecuted and 42 sentenced, and LGBTI-motivated incidents appear in the bias breakdown; the OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report notes that recorded statistics still do not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other offences. The government has approved a Criminal Code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to disability, sexual orientation and gender identity, which remains pending in Parliament, while a Constitutional Court ruling weakened 'particularly vulnerable victim' status.

Entry and protection channels carry no trans-specific obstacle on the record: the new Asylum Law includes sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds and offers an opposite-gender interview option. Facilities and public-space conduct are not restricted by any trans-specific rule in the sources.

Where a visitor goes matters. Prague and Brno rate highest for LGBTQ+ solo travellers, with formal nondiscrimination policies, queer districts in Vinohrady and Žižkov, and hostels providing concierge support, private rooms and organised socials; harassment risk concentrates in rural areas and late-night settings. In June 2023 a group disrupted Brno Pride drag story-time with homophobic slurs.

Partner recognition is unresolved. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2018 by a cross-party group of 46 MPs from six parliamentary clubs (ANO, Pirates, KSČM, ČSSD, TOP 09, STAN) to replace registered partnerships was backed by the caretaker government and cleared committees on 29 June 2023, while a constitutional ban on same-sex marriage moved to second reading with SPD, ODS, KDU-ČSL and ANO support estimated at 80–90%.
CZE.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the Criminal Code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to sexual orientation and gender identity has been adopted remains open; the sources record government approval and the bill pending in Parliament.

Unresolved: whether the national prison concept or a binding regulation on trans detainees has been issued after the November 2025 reporting. The sources document competing positions between the Supreme Court, the human-rights commissioner and the Justice Ministry, with consultation ongoing.

Unresolved: the final status of the same-sex marriage bill. The inventory records committee clearance on 29 June 2023 and a constitutional ban proposal in second reading, with no later outcome sourced.

Unresolved: whether the 2024 hate-crime figures break out LGBTI-motivated incidents numerically. OSCE/ODIHR states that LGBTI-motivated incidents are included in the bias breakdown but also that recorded statistics do not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other crimes.

Not sourced: the UK Foreign Office travel advice for Czechia produced no trans-specific safety finding, so no assessment from that channel is reflected here. The sources also do not address bathroom access, identity-document presentation at borders, or medication import rules beyond general traveller guidance.

Unresolved: whether the vulnerability-assessment standard set by the Supreme Administrative Court in the 2023 immigration-detention case is applied consistently by lower courts; the reporting documents disagreement between courts rather than a settled practice.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1962, following research by Kurt Freund concluding that homosexual orientation cannot be altered; homosexual prostitution was decriminalised in 1990. The age of consent was equalised in 1990 at 15, having previously been 18 for homosexuals. A separate criminalisation-adjacent strand hits trans people: in May 2024 the Constitutional Court ruled that forced surgery and sterilisation of transgender individuals is unconstitutional and gave the government until June 2025 to change the laws, after which (July 2025) the Health Ministry announced trans people would no longer be required to undergo surgery or hormone treatment to change their legal gender. State rhetoric also framed trans bodies as criminal: on 27 June 2021 President Miloš Zeman said sex-reassignment surgery means 'you are committing a crime for inflicting self-harm' and that 'these transgenders truly disgust me.' Wikipedia country coverage: Public expression is legal and visible but carries social risk. The first Prague Pride parade was held in August 2011 with mayoral support and drew negative responses from religious conservative groups and the far-right; it has run annually since 2012, and since 2014 organisers have barred pedophile promotional activity at Pride venues. Brno has hosted the Mezipatra gay and lesbian film festival every November since 2000, and a Prague City Council-produced gay guide and map appeared in late 2010. Self-censorship remains common: in a 2012 EU Fundamental Rights Agency survey of 93,000 LGBTQ people, only one in five Czech respondents was open about their orientation to all colleagues or classmates, 71% were selectively open at work or school, and 52% of gay men and 30% of lesbian women avoided holding hands in public outside gay neighbourhoods for fear of assault, threat or harassment. Wikipedia country coverage: Facilities are highly concentrated in the capital: Prague has a large, well-developed gay nightlife scene centred on the Vinohrady district with at least 20 bars and clubs and 4 saunas, while gay venues are much more sparsely spread in other Czech towns, and the city acts as a magnet for the country's gay youth. Since 2001 the Czech Republic has granted 'persons living in a common household' hospital and prison visitation rights similar to married heterosexual couples, alongside inheritance and succession rights in housing. Blood donation opened to all citizens regardless of partner gender on 1 July 2024, replacing the previous ban on people with a same-gender partner, though people reporting anal sex with a new partner in the past four months are still excluded. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth-specific findings: the age of consent was equalised in 1990 at 15, previously having been 18 for homosexuals. Anti-discrimination protection under the 2009 Anti-Discrimination Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in education as well as employment, housing and access to goods and services. Acceptance is markedly higher among younger Czechs — a 2013 Pew Research Center survey found 84% of 18–29-year-olds thought homosexuality should be accepted, versus 72% of those over 50 — and a January 2020 Median poll showed younger respondents overwhelmingly supporting same-sex marriage while those aged 55 and above were mostly opposed. Prague's gay scene draws the country's gay youth to the capital, and in the 2012 FRA survey only one in five respondents was open about their orientation to all classmates, indicating school-level concealment.

Discrimination exposure is concentrated among trans and non-binary residents, who report the highest rates in the national survey: 43% discriminated or harassed over five years, more than a third within twelve months, 51% subjected to insults, assault or threats.

Residents seeking protection can invoke sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds under the new Asylum Law, which also provides an opposite-gender interview option.

Relationship recognition still runs through registered partnerships. The 2018 cross-party marriage bill cleared committees in June 2023 but no enacted marriage equality is recorded in these sources, and a constitutional ban proposal advanced to second reading.

CZE.blindSummary:
The state's rules for legal gender recognition were rewritten twice in eighteen months. On 24 April 2024 the national Constitutional Court, in judgment PL. US 52/23, struck down the requirement that an official sex change be conditional on surgery disabling reproductive function, holding compulsory sterilisation for legal recognition unconstitutional; by June 2025 the surgery requirement had been dropped in practice. The regional human-rights court then found a violation of Article 8 against the state in T.H. (Application no. 33037/22, judgment 12 September 2025), holding the surgical and sterilisation conditions and the related civil-registry treatment incompatible with private-life rights and framing guaranteed gender recognition on self-determination, with two international NGOs intervening.

Detention remains the weakest point for a trans visitor. Administrative courts clashed in public over the handling of an HIV-positive trans man in transition held by immigration police: in March 2023 the Supreme Administrative Court rebuked the municipal court for 'sarcastic moral lectures' toward the detainee and ruled that authorities must first assess whether a person is 'potentially vulnerable' before deciding placement. Practice has not caught up with that standard. In November 2025 reporting, judges described the national prisons as unprepared for trans people and lacking clear rules; the Supreme Court is pressing for a national prison concept that explicitly addresses the needs of people in or after transition, the human-rights commissioner is pushing a binding regulation, and the Justice Ministry maintains that the existing framework is sufficient, with consultation ongoing.

Social hostility is measurable and politically amplified. A national LGBTQ+ survey found 43% of respondents discriminated or harassed in the previous five years, over a third within twelve months, with trans and non-binary respondents reporting the highest rates, and 51% targeted by insults, assault or threats over five years. Politicians' anti-LGBT speech rose from 43% in 2018 to 71% in 2023, and 63% of respondents attributed rising intolerance to politicians. In 2024 the Justice Minister publicly stated that his goal was 'to prevent men from giving birth' after the Constitutional Court repealed the surgical prerequisite, and a far-right party circulated election leaflets promising to take money from 'LGBT activists' and 'give more to families, take it away from the deviants'.

Enforcement machinery exists but is thinly quantified. Police recorded 94 hate crimes in 2024, with 46 prosecuted and 42 sentenced, and LGBTI-motivated incidents appear in the bias breakdown; the international hate-crime monitoring body notes that recorded statistics still do not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other offences. The government has approved a Criminal Code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to disability, sexual orientation and gender identity, which remains pending in the national legislature, while a Constitutional Court ruling weakened 'particularly vulnerable victim' status.

Entry and protection channels carry no trans-specific obstacle on the record: the new Asylum Law includes sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds and offers an opposite-gender interview option. Facilities and public-space conduct are not restricted by any trans-specific rule in the sources.

Where a visitor goes matters. The largest urban centres rate highest for LGBTQ+ solo travellers, with formal nondiscrimination policies, designated queer districts and hostels providing concierge support, private rooms and organised socials; harassment risk concentrates in rural areas and late-night settings. In June 2023 a group disrupted a Pride drag story-time in a large city with homophobic slurs.

Partner recognition is unresolved. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2018 by a cross-party group of 46 MPs from six parliamentary clubs to replace registered partnerships was backed by the caretaker government and cleared committees on 29 June 2023, while a constitutional ban on same-sex marriage moved to second reading with far-right, conservative and people's party support estimated at 80–90%.

SVN.name: Slovenia
SVN.summary:
Slovenia's legal framework for trans visitors is among the more permissive in the region. Same-sex relations are legal nationwide, legal gender recognition is available without surgery or a psychiatric diagnosis, and the Health Ministry confirmed to the Interdisciplinary Council for Gender Recognition in 2024 that medical treatment is not required for legal gender recognition, formally asking the Interior Ministry to amend the relevant Civil Registry Act sub-article. Comprehensive anti-discrimination laws in force since 2016 explicitly cover sexual orientation and gender identity, and LGBTI organisations can be registered.

On 29 October 2022 the Ministry of the Interior announced that the local-jurisdiction step in the gender-change procedure had been abolished on the recommendation of the Advocate of the Principle of Equality. The stated effect is that transgender people are no longer exposed to involuntary disclosure of their transgender identity in their local environment, a change that removes a specific outing risk at the administrative stage of recognition.

Bias-motivated violence remains documented. In 2023 Legebitra recorded 17 cases of bias-motivated speech and TransAkcija recorded 25 cases of direct bias-motivated incidents. The US State Department's 2023 report found no laws criminalising consensual same-sex conduct and no reports of state-condoned violence, but noted that authorities recorded violence incidents without tracking case numbers and that local NGOs called violence against LGBTQI+ persons prevalent and under-reported. In June 2023, near the Ljubljana Pride route, a woman wearing a rainbow flag was assaulted, marchers had eggs thrown at them and rainbow flags were burned on video. After Pride, LGBTIQ+ organisations held a press conference describing attacks and rising hate; the Prime Minister took three days to respond and the Interior Minister made no statements.

Support machinery exists but has gaps. The ENACT national report of January 2025 found that civil society provides counselling, advocacy and safe spaces for LGBTI hate-crime victims, while LGBTI people using generic victim-support services face heteronormative hurdles; the report documents institutional shortcomings in the anti-LGBTI hate-crime framework.
SVN.outOfScopeNotes:
The F and M Global Barometers entry for Slovenia records no substantive finding, so no independent barometer score corroborates or contradicts the other sources.

Incident figures for 2023 are NGO-recorded (Legebitra, TransAkcija) rather than police statistics; the US State Department reports that authorities record violence without tracking case numbers, so official hate-crime volumes against LGBTI people are unresolved in these sources.

Whether the Interior Ministry carried out the Civil Registry Act sub-article amendment requested in 2024 is not sourced here.

The sources reviewed do not address entry, visa or border-screening treatment of trans travellers, nor the recognition of foreign gender markers on Slovenian documents.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6, D7, D8.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Expression rights are exercised publicly but contested: the annual Pride Parade in Ljubljana on 17 June 2023 drew roughly 3,500 participants under the slogan 'Več skupnosti, en boj' and was attended by President Nataša Pirc Musar. During and after the march attendees faced threats, violence, insults, flag burnings and property destruction; police received a report of an unidentified suspect who physically assaulted two people, causing minor injuries, and were investigating attacks, theft and public-order disturbances. A Pride Parade Association representative said there had not been such hostility for years, and condemnations came from the Human Rights Ombudsman, the National Assembly president, the president and, on 20 June, the prime minister, while opposition leader Janez Janša and two ministers stayed silent. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth-specific findings are limited to the political and educational sphere: anti-discrimination rules in place since 2003 bar sexual-orientation discrimination in education, and the anti-discrimination bill approved 21 April 2016 and promulgated 9 May 2016 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. The 2016 law and the earlier rules are described as vague, open to interpretation and very rarely enforced. Youth wings are also a source of hostility: members of the youth wing of the Slovenian Democratic Party used biblical arguments at the June 2023 Pride Parade, and social media posts associated with them carried anti-LGBTIQ+ sentiment.

SVN.tangentialFactors:
Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, places Slovenia among the most progressive countries in Central and Eastern Europe on LGBTIQ rights, a regional standing that separates it from several neighbours where legal recognition is contested or conditional.

Public opposition has a documented history. A 2006 law legalising same-sex marriage restricted the ceremony to the two partners and a local community registration official, with no friends or relatives present; gay and lesbian organisations welcomed it as a concrete step while calling it insufficient. In December 2015 Pope Francis urged Slovenian politicians to 'support the family' four days before a referendum on the gay-marriage law adopted by parliament that March, a referendum the law later lost after a conservative challenge. The 2022 gender-change reform and the 2016 anti-discrimination statutes sit within this contested political environment.
SVN.localsOnly:
The 2022 abolition of local jurisdiction applies to residents undertaking the gender-change procedure, removing the requirement to process the change through the local community where a person lives and the associated exposure to neighbours and local officials.

The Health Ministry's 2024 instruction to the Interior Ministry to amend the Civil Registry Act sub-article on gender recognition is an internal administrative step affecting how recognition is recorded for residents. SRB.name: Serbia
SRB.summary:
Serbia does not criminalise transgender people, but the documented pattern of violence and official mistreatment makes it a high-risk destination. The most acute traveller-facing exposure is police conduct: in February 2024 Serbian authorities opened an investigation into allegations that officers beat, tortured and sexually harassed two LGBT people during an apartment raid in Belgrade. The interior ministry's probe was still characterised as an investigation, with no sanction reported.

Recorded hostility is persistent. About 105 incidents motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity were registered in 2024, and the civil-society association Da se zna! presented the eighth annual hate-crime report, 'Transphobia and Homophobia in Serbia 2024', in September 2025 as the standing register of such cases. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records intolerance and violence against LGBT people as a significant concern through 2024, and notes that the state response to the July and August 2024 protests, including activist arrests and smear campaigns, exposed rule-of-law weaknesses. The US State Department's human-rights reporting has separately listed violence targeting LGBTI individuals among the country's human-rights problems.

LGBT venues and public events carry specific risk. The Pride Info Centre was attacked in January 2024 and announced its closure in September after more than twenty attacks since 2018, none properly sanctioned. Pride marches in Belgrade proceed under heavy police protection, which itself indicates the level of organised hostility they attract.

Official hostility is documented at political level: an analysis covered 70 instances of politicians' hate speech between April 2023 and April 2024. In custody, the Association for the Prevention of Torture has recommended that the Penal and Correctional Institution in Padinska Skela allow transgender women at intake to choose a female officer for searches and body inspection rather than a male or combined search, a finding that indicates searches by male staff have been the practice.

Serbia lies outside the Schengen border-free travel area, so passport controls apply on entry and on travel onward to Schengen states. The practical bottom line: no criminalisation, but police-brutality exposure, high incident levels and weak sanctioning of attacks make this a high-risk destination, with Belgrade manageable only under sustained situational awareness.
SRB.outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the February 2024 police-assault investigation is unresolved in the sources available here; no disciplinary result, charge or clearance has been sourced, and the record should not be read as either prosecution or exoneration.

The figure of about 105 orientation- or gender-identity-motivated incidents in 2024 is carried from the existing record; the underlying Da se zna! report text was not re-verified in this pass, and the count's methodology, including whether it reflects police-recorded or self-reported cases, is not sourced.

Whether the Association for the Prevention of Torture recommendation on searches of transgender women at Padinska Skela has been implemented is not sourced; the inventory establishes the recommendation, not compliance.

The US State Department evidence dates from the 2018 reporting year and is used here only as historical corroboration of a continuing pattern; current US government characterisation of conditions is not sourced.

Whether any identity-document marker change, legal gender recognition procedure or hate-crime sentencing enhancement applies to trans visitors is not sourced in this inventory and remains unresolved.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D3, D4, D5.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity is legal in Serbia today, but the source documents a long criminalising history: the 1860 'Kaznitelni zakon' (Penalty Act) of the Principality punished intercourse 'against the order of nature' between males with 6 months to 4 years' imprisonment, and lesbian sexuality was simply not mentioned. The 1929 Yugoslav Criminal Code banned 'lewdness against the order of nature' between heterosexuals and homosexuals alike; the SFRY narrowed it in 1959 to homosexual anal intercourse with the maximum cut from 2 to 1 year. Same-sex intercourse was legalised in Vojvodina in 1977 but male homosexuality was re-criminalised when Vojvodina was reincorporated into Serbia's legal system in 1990. Male homosexual intercourse was officially decriminalised in 1994 by amending article 110 (act against order of nature), though a new subsection 4 then banned male same-sex acts for males aged 14 to 18 with up to one year's prison, setting the age of consent at 18 for anal intercourse between males and 14 otherwise; an equal age of consent of 14 regardless of sexual orientation or gender took effect on 1 January 2006 under the current Criminal Code. Wikipedia country coverage: Public expression of LGBT identity has repeatedly been suppressed: the first Belgrade Gay Pride in 2001 ended in extreme violence, and Pride events in Belgrade (2004, 2009) and Novi Sad (2007) were cancelled because police could not guarantee safety against violent opponents. The 2010 Belgrade Pride went ahead with about a thousand participants but was met by the Belgrade anti-gay riot, attended by 6,000 anti-gay protesters and extreme nationalist group members; Amnesty International noted in May 2014 that public authorities had repeatedly banned pride parades on the basis of violent threats from homophobic groups and had failed to protect LGBTQ individuals and organisations from verbal, social media and physical attacks. Belgrade Pride successfully took place in September 2014 and has been held annually since (except 2020, moved online for COVID-19), with local mayors and some ministers attending. EuroPride in September 2022 was initially banned by authorities on security grounds and opposed by President Vučić, but proceeded on 17 September along a shortened route under heavy police protection, with organisers reporting almost 10,000 attendees; Novi Sad held its first gay pride rally on 17 May 2019. On speech, the Broadcasting Act (2002) and Information Act (2003) bar media content encouraging discrimination or hate based on sexual orientation, though the Radiodiffusion Agency never effectively acted against offenders, and the Anti-Discrimination Act of 2009 prohibits hate speech on that basis across society; a Penal Code hate crime provision covering sexual orientation and gender identity was adopted on 24 December 2012, with the first conviction in 2018. Wikipedia country coverage: Sex change surgeries have been partially covered by Serbia's statewide basic medical insurance since a Health Insurance Act change approved on 28 July 2011 (effective 2012), with government-financed insurance covering up to 65% of surgery costs and the patient paying the remainder; hormone replacement therapy, which some choose instead, is not financed by health insurance. Belgrade was described by The New York Times in 2012 as a hub for sex reassignment surgery because prices were far lower than in neighbouring and Western countries. Access remains poor in the eyes of those affected: a reported 90% of LGBT individuals in Serbia say medical institutions are not adequately responding to their needs, and according to Jovanka Todorović of Gayten-LGBT about 80% of Serbian transgender people are not willing to undergo surgery. The Ministry of Health also barred people with a 'history of homosexual relations during the last five years' from donating reproductive cells for artificial insemination or IVF in early 2019, removing the provision on 23 April 2021; official medical textbooks circulated classifying homosexuality under 'sexual deviations and disorders' until the Serbian Medical Society confirmed in a 2008 letter to Labris that same-sex orientation is not a disease (homosexuality had been removed from the official disease list in 1997 with ICD-10). Wikipedia country coverage: Serbia had no legal protections specifically aimed at LGBTQ rights until 2002, when the Broadcasting Act barred broadcasters from spreading information encouraging discrimination, hate and violence based on sexual orientation. In 2005 the Labor Act banned sexual-orientation discrimination in employment and the Act on Higher Education guaranteed equal rights regardless of sexual orientation in higher education institutions. On 26 March 2009 Parliament approved the unified Anti-Discrimination Act, prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and transgender status in all areas, with 2021 amendments adding sex characteristics — making Serbia one of the first Western Balkan countries to do so. Enforcement is weak: Amnesty International noted in 2014 that authorities had failed to protect LGBTQ individuals and organisations from discrimination including verbal and social media threats and physical attacks, and the Radiodiffusion Agency took no action against media offenders under the 2002/2003 provisions. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Map ranked Serbia 29th of 49 European countries with a 34% score, down from 27th in 2024. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples have never been recognised by law, and the Serbian Constitution adopted in November 2006 effectively bans same-sex marriage through Article 62, which defines marriage as entered into based on the free consent of a man and a woman; other forms such as civil unions or domestic partnerships are neither explicitly mentioned nor prohibited. Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and same-sex couples cannot legally adopt. Plans to legalise domestic partnerships by amending the Civil Code were announced in June 2019 (covering joint property and alimony but not inheritance, adoption or surrogacy); in July 2019 a Novi Sad lesbian couple, Jelena Dubović and Sunčica Kopunović, were turned away when they tried to register a civil partnership and sued, with legal experts doubting they would win. Minister Gordana Čomić announced in November 2020 that a same-sex partnership law would reach parliament in the first half of 2021 and a draft went to public consultation in February 2021, but President Vučić said in May 2021 he would not sign it as unconstitutional, the bill stalled without a vote, and he reaffirmed in August 2023 he would sign no such law in his term. In September 2024 the Green–Left Front submitted a new Draft Law on Civil Partnership covering maintenance, inheritance and health and social insurance, still unscheduled for a vote as of 2026; the 2023 ECHR Grand Chamber ruling in Fedotova and Others v. Russia holds that Council of Europe states including Serbia have a positive obligation to provide some form of legal recognition for same-sex couples. Public opinion is split: 2021 Civil Rights Defenders data shows 26% support for same-sex marriage but 80% believing LGBTI+ persons should have at least some of the rights in a same-sex union law (second-highest in the Western Balkans after Montenegro), with 2018 data cited by the U.S. State Department showing 70% opposing an LGBT person inheriting a deceased partner's property. Wikipedia country coverage: The Act on Higher Education, approved by Parliament in 2005, guarantees equal rights regardless of sexual orientation in higher education institutions, and on 5 July 2011 Parliament approved a youth act prohibiting discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation, regulating measures and activities undertaken by local governments to improve the social status of youth and address their needs and interests. The criminal law history directly shaped minors: a provision banning male same-sex acts for males aged 14 to 18 (up to one year's prison) was added in 1994, and an equal age of consent of 14 regardless of sexual orientation or gender only came in on 1 January 2006. Attitudes toward LGBT young people and parenting remain hostile: 2018 data cited in the U.S. State Department human rights report found 48% of parents would seek medical treatment for their LGBT child and 90% opposed child adoption by an LGBT person, while a 2022 World Values Survey found 65% of Serbians disagreed that homosexual couples are as good parents as other couples. Support is markedly higher among younger (18–29) and university-educated respondents in Belgrade and Vojvodina, and 2021 Civil Rights Defenders data records a general improvement in attitudes toward LGBTI+ issues over the preceding five years, though 57% still believe homosexuality is a disease.

SRB.localsOnly:
Discrimination in employment shapes daily life for trans Serbians: a Zoomer survey found that three-quarters of trans and non-binary people fear job interviews because they expect discrimination.

Transphobia and homophobia are tracked annually by Da se zna!, whose 2024 hate-crime report was presented in September 2025; roughly 105 orientation- or gender-identity-motivated incidents were registered for the year, giving residents a documented baseline for reporting and advocacy.

The closure of the Pride Info Centre in September 2024, after more than twenty attacks since 2018 with no attack properly sanctioned, removed a long-standing point of support and reporting in Belgrade.

For trans people in detention, the Association for the Prevention of Torture has issued a national-preventive-mechanism recommendation that the Penal and Correctional Institution in Padinska Skela let transgender women choose a female officer for searches and body inspection at intake.
SRB.blindSummary:
The country does not criminalise transgender people, but the documented pattern of violence and official mistreatment makes it a high-risk destination. The most acute traveller-facing exposure is police conduct: in February 2024 the country authorities opened an investigation into allegations that officers beat, tortured and sexually harassed two LGBT people during an apartment raid in the national capital. The interior ministry's probe was still characterised as an investigation, with no sanction reported.

Recorded hostility is persistent. About 105 incidents motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity were registered in 2024, and a civil-society association presented its eighth annual hate-crime report covering that year in September 2025 as the standing register of such cases. The country chapter in a leading international human-rights report records intolerance and violence against LGBT people as a significant concern through 2024, and notes that the state response to the July and August 2024 protests, including activist arrests and smear campaigns, exposed rule-of-law weaknesses. The parent nation's annual human-rights reporting has separately listed violence targeting LGBTI individuals among the country human-rights problems.

LGBT venues and public events carry specific risk. a Pride information centre was attacked in January 2024 and announced its closure in September after more than twenty attacks since 2018, none properly sanctioned. Pride marches proceed under heavy police protection, which itself indicates the level of organised hostility they attract.

Official hostility is documented at political level: an analysis covered 70 instances of politicians' hate speech between April 2023 and April 2024. In custody, a national preventive mechanism has recommended that a penal and correctional institution allow transgender women at intake to choose a female officer for searches and body inspection rather than a male or combined search, a finding that indicates searches by male staff have been the practice.

The country lies outside the parent nation's border-free travel area, so passport controls apply on entry and on travel onward. The practical bottom line: no criminalisation, but police-brutality exposure, high incident levels and weak sanctioning of attacks make this a high-risk destination, with the major-tourist city manageable only under sustained situational awareness.
SRB.blindOutOfScope:
The outcome of the February 2024 police-assault investigation is unresolved in the sources available here; no disciplinary result, charge or clearance has been sourced, and the record should not be read as either prosecution or exoneration.

The figure of about 105 orientation- or gender-identity-motivated incidents in 2024 is carried from the existing record; the underlying annual report text was not re-verified in this pass, and the count's methodology, including whether it reflects police-recorded or self-reported cases, is not sourced.

Whether the preventive-mechanism recommendation on searches of transgender women at the penal and correctional institution has been implemented is not sourced; the inventory establishes the recommendation, not compliance.

The parent nation's evidence dates from the 2018 reporting year and is used here only as historical corroboration of a continuing pattern; current parent-nation characterisation of conditions is not sourced.

Whether any identity-document marker change, legal gender recognition procedure or hate-crime sentencing enhancement applies to trans visitors is not sourced in this inventory and remains unresolved.

SRB.tangentialFactors:
Access to gender-affirming care is constrained: ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records shortages of testosterone supply, specifically Testosteron Depo, for trans patients in Serbia during 2024. Visitors who depend on regular injections should carry adequate supplies and written prescriptions, and should not assume local pharmacy stock.

The country's wider governance environment bears on how a trans visitor's complaint would be handled. Human Rights Watch links the 2024 protest response, including activist arrests and smear campaigns, to broader rule-of-law weaknesses, and the US State Department has listed government corruption and violence against journalists alongside violence targeting LGBTI individuals. Complaints against police therefore enter a system with a documented record of failing to sanction such conduct.

Compared with jurisdictions where identity-document markers and criminalisation drive risk, Serbia's exposure is enforcement-side rather than statute-side: the law does not prohibit trans people, but the officers, institutions and crowds a visitor may encounter are the hazard.

HRV.name: Croatia
HRV.summary:
Same-sex conduct has been legal in Croatia since 1977, and open military service is available. Registered life partnerships have existed since 2014, but a 2013 constitutional referendum barred same-sex marriage, and full same-sex adoption rights were confirmed only by a final court ruling in 2022. Hate-crime legislation covers sexual orientation and gender identity.

Legal gender recognition rests on a 2013 legislative amendment that allows a gender marker to be registered without altering sex characteristics. A Croatian legal analysis works through the Criminal Procedure Act, the Police Powers Act, the Customs Act and the law governing prison sentences to set out how police, customs and court officers must conduct searches of trans and gender-nonconforming people, and records case studies of the difficulties that arise in practice.

Formal protection outpaces enforcement. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report records minority representatives saying that anti-discrimination provisions covering employment, housing, education and health are not consistently enforced, and NGOs describing uneven judicial handling of discrimination cases, limited access to justice, and victims reluctant to report for fear of inefficiency and victimisation during trial; hate-crime investigations are flagged as inadequate. Zagreb Pride's 2018 documentation report on Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 records under-reporting of homophobic and transphobic crimes alongside its compiled hate-crime data and case studies on hate speech, freedom of assembly, legal gender recognition, partnership recognition and employment discrimination. The European Commission's 2024 country report assessed transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives, including the sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds.

Protection machinery has produced at least one concrete result: a Zadar prosecutor charged a man over the refusal of a gay couple's accommodation booking, an incident dating from 2018 and reported in ILGA-Europe's 2025 Annual Review.

Official hostility is visible in organised form rather than in street-level attacks. The same review reports escalating anti-gender disinformation, including a Croatian Parliament session on 'Gender Ideology' at which speakers spread misinformation and no LGBTI organisations were invited, and disruption directed at the first Pula Pride march the day before it took place. No case of mob violence, trans-tourist rape, police brutality or detention of a foreign trans visitor surfaced in the sources reviewed.

On the visitor axis, public displays of affection may draw unwelcome responses in less-populated cities, and gay venues have been described as virtually non-existent outside Zagreb, though new venues have opened in Split, Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik. Pride events are held in Zagreb, Split, Osijek, Karlovac and Pula, alongside the Balkans Trans Inter March.
HRV.outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the Zadar prosecution is not stated in the sources reviewed; only the charge and the 2018 date of the underlying incident are documented.

Whether the 2013 gender-marker registration route operates as a self-declaration process, and which documents it covers, is unresolved in this inventory; the 2018 Council of Europe report and the 2026 legal analysis address the framework from different angles without settling current practice at counters and border posts.

No source in this inventory reports a trans-specific violent offence against a visitor, and absence of such a case in the reviewed material is not evidence of absence on the ground.

Enforcement data post-dating the 2024 European Commission reporting period, which covered 2023, is not available here; the anti-gender and Pride-disruption accounts derive from a single monitoring review.

Search and detention practice for trans people is analysed in academic sources for 2013 onward, with no official statistical breakdown of how often officers deviate from the prescribed procedure.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D6, D8, D13.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex conduct legal since 1977; life partnerships since 2014 while the 2013 constitutional referendum banned same-sex marriage; full same-sex adoption rights since 2022 (final court ruling); open military service; hate-crime legislation; Pride events incl. Zagreb, Split, Osijek, Karlovac, Pula and the Balkans Trans Inter March; legal gender recognition framework. Wikipedia country coverage: In March 2014 Croatia granted asylum for the first time to a person persecuted on the basis of sexual orientation — a young man from Uganda who fled under the Uganda Anti-homosexuality Act. The text otherwise says nothing about visa rules, passport gender markers, or entry procedures for transgender travellers. Wikipedia country coverage: Croatia has three LGBT centres: the first in Zagreb, a second opened in Split on 24 May 2014, and a third in Rijeka on 16 October 2014 (LGBTIQ+ Druga Rijeka). Zagreb has the biggest gay scene, with clubs, bars and Queer Zagreb programming, while gay-friendly venues and beaches are noted in Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik. On health facilities, the blood transfusion institute's rules effectively bar gay and bisexual men from donating blood indefinitely — a 2007 bylaw places MSM under categories of permanent rejection, and as of 2021 this is framed as 'behaviors or activities that expose them to risk of contracting blood-borne infectious diseases'. Wikipedia country coverage: Article 68 of the Life Partnership Act grants life partners the same health insurance and healthcare rights as married heterosexual couples and prohibits adverse treatment of life partnerships in those areas. Reproductive care is unequal: the Medically Supported Fertilization Law limits IVF to married heterosexual couples and single infertile women, effectively excluding same-sex couples (a 2012 law allowed single women but not lesbian couples). Foster care access for same-sex couples only came via courts — the Constitutional Court ruled on 7 February 2020 that excluding them was unconstitutional and discriminatory, and Mladen Kožić and Ivo Šegota became Croatia's first same-sex foster parents in September 2020 after a three-year legal battle; as of January 2024 no national law yet regulates same-sex adoption, protections coming only from court rulings. Youth-specific: children's placement decisions and partner-guardianship (permanent parental rights for a non-biological life partner, first case July 2015) directly shape minors' family lives, and the Center for Social Welfare initially rejected the Kožić/Šegota application twice. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2009 the European Committee on Social Rights found discriminatory statements in a mandatory Croatian school biology textbook, ruling they violated the European Social Charter; on 1 March 2013 the Minister for Science, Education and Sports announced an action to strip homophobic content from elementary and high school books, especially religious education texts. Age of consent was equalised at 14 in 1998 and raised to 15 under the Penal Code of 1 January 2013. Youth/family education support exists: Zagreb Pride's 2016 guide "We Have a Family!" for LGBT parents, and the 2018 picture book "My Rainbow Family" for preschool-age children with same-sex parents (first 500 copies free, French Embassy funding; crowdfunded reprint raised over $7,000). A Eurobarometer-style survey found 64% of Croatians agreed school lessons should include information about sexual orientation diversity and 63% about gender identity; a 2016 study on children in LGBT families found psychosocial adaptation and experiences of stigmatisation. In 2023 the opposition Možemo! party proposed easier legal gender change and IVF inclusivity, but none of those bills had passed as of January 2024.

Intrepid Travel country guide: Croatia 'widely accepts' LGBTQIA+ travellers (legal since 1977, partnership/protection laws) — but PDA may draw unwelcome responses in lesser-populated cities and gay venues are 'virtually non-existent outside Zagreb', now improving with new venues in Split, Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik. Visitor-facing nightlife/PDA guidance.

European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination in Croatia (2024, reporting period 2023): transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives, including SOGI grounds.

CroL (May 2014, Croatian): Split got an LGBT Centre (second in Croatia, first in Dalmatia) a month before the 4th Split Pride (7 June 2014), run by association Risp-et; organisers demanded equal treatment of same-sex families (marriage, joint adoption) and said institutions create 'second-class citizens'; mayor Ivo Baldasar attended the press conference. Documents organised community infrastructure on the coast.

CroL (Oct 2014, Croatian): presentation of LGBTIQ+ centre 'Druga Rijeka' in Rijeka — founded to develop the community in Primorsko-goranska county and network with national/international organisations, backed publicly by mayor Vojko Obersnel and cultural institutions; goals include visibility, anti-discrimination work and quality-of-life advocacy. Second major community centre documented.

EST.name: Estonia
EST.summary:
Estonia decriminalises same-sex relations nationwide and has had marriage equality since June 2023, the first Baltic state to reach that point, with joint adoption included. Opposition filed more than 700 amendments to block the bill and every one failed. Public support for marriage equality stood at 53% in 2023, reaching 75% among people in their twenties, against 34% in 2012.

Legal gender recognition remains medicalised. A psychiatric diagnosis and physiological alteration are required, and no nonbinary identity is recognised. Advocacy continues for recognition based on self-determination, and the national action plan adopted in 2025 commits the state to updating the legal framework so that gender identity and expression are protected.

Anti-discrimination coverage is uneven. Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, as is discrimination in healthcare. One source records housing protection extending to gender identity while another records housing protection on sexual orientation only, a discrepancy the sources do not resolve. Hate-speech and hate-crime legislation does not include gender identity, and no hate-crime protection is recorded for trans people. Conversion therapy is not banned. Access to sex-separated facilities is recorded as protected.

The social climate is more guarded than the legal framework. LTU.name: Lithuania
LTU.summary:
Lithuania is workable for a trans visitor but carries one of Europe's most restrictive legal-gender-recognition regimes. The Civil Code grants unmarried adults the right to change gender through medical intervention, yet no implementing legislation has ever been adopted. The Lithuanian Gay League describes the resulting gap as 18 years old; the public broadcaster has counted 17. Either figure describes the same condition: the statutory right exists on paper, with no procedure behind it.

The courts have declined twice to break the deadlock in 2025. In August, the Ukmergė Chamber of the Vilnius Regional District Court suspended a civil case concerning the amendment of civil-status gender documents and referred to the Constitutional Court the question of whether the relevant provisions comply with the Constitution. In September, the Constitutional Court declined to examine that referral and also declined to hear the lower court's request to review the absence of legal provisions allowing trans people to change gender markers and personal identification codes in official documents. The practical result for a visitor is straightforward: Lithuania has no accessible route to amend a gender marker or the personal identification code on a civil-status document, and the constitutional question has been left unanswered rather than resolved.

Documentation is therefore the central risk. A visitor whose passport or identity documents do not match their presentation or stated gender should expect that mismatch to be visible to any official who inspects identification, with no domestic legal remedy available to correct the record in advance of travel.

Conditions on the ground are documented by national authorities rather than inferred. The Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson published its second National Review of the Situation of Transgender People in Lithuania in 2024, following an earlier review in 2019. It covers the legal framework, document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination, data protection and public attitudes, and records both the absence of a legal framework and the absence of any strategic approach to trans rights in Lithuania.

Trans people themselves describe routine, systemic mistreatment in employment. Reporting published in May 2025 documented open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse at work, with experts pointing to systemic labour-market discrimination. This is not confined to the private sphere of the workplace; it is described as a pattern across the labour market.

Public assembly carries documented risk of official under-protection. In April 2024 the Seimas Ombudsperson found that police had failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to peaceful assembly, citing an inadequate police response to hostile provocateurs at an assembly organised by the Lithuanian Gay League, and recommended measures to secure effective assembly rights. A trans visitor attending a public event or a Pride march should expect that hostile counter-protesters may act without effective police protection.

Support structures are thin. An international LGBTI rights organisation's Annual Review 2025 identifies a systemic lack of targeted support for LGBTI hate-crime victims in Lithuania. The same review records that LGBTI asylum seekers from Cameroon were granted protection only after a four-year wait, during which they faced dire camp conditions, and that a psychologist was convicted of coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts.

Anti-LGBTI legislation has a live parliamentary history. In 2013 the Seimas was reported to be considering five bills on LGBTI people, including a ban on gender reassignment justified on the assertion that gender is determined genetically from the moment of conception, a ban on same-sex adoption, fines of up to €1,800 for organisers of events deemed to denigrate constitutional moral values, and the legalisation of anti-gay speech. In 2009 the Seimas passed the Law on the Protection of Minors, banning information on homosexuality in schools and in media accessible to minors by overriding President Valdas Adamkus's veto 87 to 6; Amnesty International called it a huge step backwards. The inventory does not establish the current status of the 2013 bills, and this dossier does not assume any of them passed.
LTU.outOfScopeNotes:
The current procedural status and outcome of the prosecution of former Seimas member Petras Gražulis for anti-LGBTI ridicule are unresolved in the source inventory, which records only that his immunity complicated the proceedings.

The fate of the five bills the Seimas was reported to be considering in 2013 is not sourced here. This dossier states only that the bills, including a proposed ban on gender reassignment and legalisation of anti-gay speech, were put before parliament for consideration in that year, and does not assert that any were enacted.

Whether the Law on the Protection of Minors as enacted in 2009 has since been amended, narrowed or struck down in relation to LGBTI content is not sourced in the inventory; the dossier reports only its enactment against a presidential veto by a vote of 87 to 6 and Amnesty International's contemporary response.

Two different figures appear across the sources for the length of the period without implementing legislation, 17 years and 18 years, depending on publication date. Both are reported as characterisations by their respective publishers rather than as a court finding.

The source inventory does not address entry, visa or border-screening procedures for trans travellers, nor whether border or airline officials inspect gender markers on documents. Any expectation about entry screening here is inferred from the absence of a domestic legal gender-recognition procedure and is not drawn from a documented policy source.

The healthcare barriers identified in the 2024 national review are recorded in summary form only in the inventory; the specific medical requirements, waiting periods or eligibility criteria for gender-affirming care in Lithuania are not resolved here.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults has been legal in Lithuania since 1993, two years after the end of Soviet occupation; it had been criminal during the interwar period and under Soviet rule. The age of consent was equalised at 14 in 2003 to meet EU accession criteria, then raised to 16 on 2 July 2010 regardless of gender or sexual orientation — a rule that applies equally to gay and straight youth. Public instigation of violence against LGBT people is explicitly banned under Section 170(3) of the Criminal Code; a 2010 preliminary investigation found 160 of roughly 180 hate-speech instances (mostly online) concerned the LGBT community, with perpetrators usually fined and computers occasionally confiscated. Two attempts to criminalise 'public propagation of homosexual relations' with fines of 2,000–10,000 litas were made (2011, unanimously rejected by Parliament; again in 2013, also rejected). Wikipedia country coverage: Lithuania's most prominent expression restrictions targeted minors: a 16 June 2009 amendment to the Law on the Protection of Minors banned the 'propaganda of homosexual, bisexual or polygamous relations' for under-18s; the presidential veto was overturned by Parliament, but on 22 December 2009 the anti-LGBT clauses were replaced with a broader ban on information promoting conceptions of marriage or family other than those in the Constitution. That provision was used to restrict a Vilnius Pride 2013 advertisement to night-time broadcast with an adult-content logo (over a T-shirt reading 'For the diversity of families'), and in 2014 the children's book 'Gintarinė širdis' was age-labelled and then banned by the Ministry of Culture because two stories involved same-sex relationships — the ECHR Grand Chamber ruled in January 2023 that this violated Article 10. On 18 December 2024 the Constitutional Court struck down the anti-LGBT provisions as violating Article 25 (freedom of speech). Article 39.1 of the Public Information Act (amended 30 September 2010) briefly barred messages that 'depict or promote a sexual orientation'; this was described as a translation error and removed on 16 June 2011, with sexual orientation added as a protected ground. Pride events have been repeatedly obstructed: Vilnius City Council refused permission in 2007 citing security; Baltic Pride 2010 was halted by a court shortly before it began (overturned one day prior, then held amid heavy policing and violence, 12 protesters arrested); the 2013 march required litigation through all judicial instances to be allowed on Gedimino Avenue (about 500 participants, 28 arrests including MP Petras Gražulis). Participation has since grown — around 10,000 at the 2019 Vilnius Pride and around 5,000 in 2023. In 2014 all major TV stations refused a pro-tolerance LGBT video clip over fears of breaching the Minors law. Wikipedia country coverage: In January 2019 the Lithuanian Constitutional Court ruled that foreign same-sex spouses must be granted residence permits, following the 2018 European Court of Justice ruling in Coman and Others. No further visa, entry, or residence provisions for LGBT visitors appear in the source text. Wikipedia country coverage: Marriage is limited to opposite-sex couples by Article 38 of the 1992 Constitution and Article 3.12 of the Civil Code, and Article 3.229 had restricted partnerships to heterosexual couples. On 17 April 2025 the Constitutional Court ruled that the absence of legal regulation of partnership institutions (including for same-sex couples) contradicts the Constitution, and granted same-sex couples the right to register partnerships through the courts until the Seimas adopts a comprehensive registered-partnership law. A partnership bill had been preliminarily approved 46–17 in May 2017 but remained pending as of 2019, and in May 2021 more than 10,000 people protested against partnership legislation in Vilnius. Adoption remains closed to same-sex couples because marriage is required; although single applicants are theoretically eligible, adoption by single gay people is 'in practice not legally possible', and President Gitanas Nauseda stated in September 2021 he would do his best to block adoption demands from Kaunas Pride organisers. Only 24 same-sex households were declared in the 2011 census.

The healthcare barriers identified in the 2024 national review are recorded in summary form only in the inventory; the specific medical requirements, waiting periods or eligibility criteria for gender-affirming care in this country are not resolved here.
blindSourceSummaries: The top court refused to address the country's trans rights gap — a significant setback; the civil code grants unmarried adults the right to medically change gender, but implementing legislation has never been adopted, leaving trans people in legal limbo.

A regional district court suspended a civil case on amending civil-status gender documents and referred the laws' compliance with the constitution to the top court — asking whether courts could finally end 17 years of legal limbo.

The top court declined to examine a lower court's request to review the absence of legal provisions allowing trans people to change gender markers and personal identification codes in official documents.
Trans people in the country detail workplace harassment — open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse; systemic labour-market discrimination per experts.

The parliament's ombudsperson found police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to peaceful assembly — inadequate police response to hostile provocateurs; recommended measures to guarantee effective assembly rights.

The equal-opportunities ombudsperson's summary of the 2024 national review on the situation of transgender people covers public attitudes, the legal framework, document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination, data protection and negative public attitudes; it notes the lack of a legal framework and strategic approach.

An annual review chapter reports a systemic lack of targeted hate-crime victim support; LGBTI asylum seekers granted protection after a four-year wait, with dire camp conditions and a psychologist convicted of coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts; prosecution of a former MP for anti-LGBTI ridicule was complicated by his elected-official immunity.

A report on parliament considering five anti-gay and anti-trans bills — including a ban on gender reassignment, a same-sex adoption ban, fines for organisers of events 'denigrating constitutional moral values', and legalisation of anti-gay speech.

A report that parliament passed a law banning information on homosexuality in schools and media accessible to minors, overriding a presidential veto; a rights organisation called it a huge step backwards.
LTU.blindLocalsOnly:
The national equal-opportunities ombudsperson is the principal domestic monitor of trans conditions in this country. Its 2024 National Review, the second after 2019, assesses the legal framework, civil-status document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination, data protection and public attitudes, and records that the state has neither a legal framework for trans recognition nor a strategic approach to trans rights.

The national ombudsperson has issued a recommendation requiring the police to take measures guaranteeing effective assembly rights for the LGBT community, following its 2024 finding of an inadequate police response to provocateurs at an assembly organised by a national LGBTI rights organisation. Residents and organisers may rely on that recommendation as a formal accountability instrument.

Legal recognition for residents remains unresolved after the constitutional court's September 2025 refusal to enter the question referred by the civil division of a regional district court. The court declined both to review the compliance of the provisions with the constitution and to review the absence of provisions permitting changes to gender markers and personal identification codes, leaving the referral unanswered.

Resident-facing concerns extend to healthcare access, data protection and public attitudes, all of which the 2024 national review treats as documented problem areas, alongside workplace harassment characterised as open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse.

Prosecution of a former member of the national parliament for anti-LGBTI ridicule has been complicated by his immunity as a member of the international parliament. LGBTI asylum seekers have been granted protection, in at least one documented case, only after multi-year delays marked by severe camp conditions, and a psychologist was convicted of coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts.
LTU.tangentialFactors:
Legal gender recognition is the clearest comparison point for this jurisdiction. Where many neighbouring states have adopted either administrative or court-based procedures for amending gender markers, Lithuania has neither a procedure nor a court willing to impose one, having twice declined to enter the question in 2025. The gap is a legislative and constitutional failure rather than a judicial reversal.

The 2013 parliamentary package, including a proposed statutory ban on gender reassignment and the criminalisation of anti-gay speech, sits within a longer pattern of legislative turbulence around LGBTI rights rather than isolated incident. The 2009 Law on the Protection of Minors was enacted against a presidential veto, indicating that the Seimas has been willing to override the executive on this subject matter, and Amnesty International's characterisation of it as a huge step backwards frames how international observers read such measures.

Assembly and protest risks are uneven rather than uniform. Police protection at LGBTI events has been formally found deficient by the national ombudsperson, and hostile provocateurs are documented as having disrupted peaceful assemblies without an adequate official response.

Economic conditions carry a trans-specific drag. Systemic labour-market discrimination, described by trans people and experts in 2025 reporting, compounds the absence of legal recognition: there is no administrative status to rely on when employment discrimination occurs, and the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson's 2024 review identified labour-market discrimination as a standing field of concern.

Hate-crime response is a structural weakness. The absence of targeted support for LGBTI hate-crime victims has been identified by an international monitoring body for 2024, which affects how incidents are recorded, referred and supported.

LVA.name: Latvia
LVA.summary:
Latvia has no procedure for legal gender recognition. Transgender and nonbinary Latvians cannot obtain a corrected gender marker, and no targeted legislation has been adopted; coalition members of parliament said in June 2025 that trans rights "have not emerged as a major issue yet." One trans immigrant interviewed by LSM stated that acquiring legal recognition of his gender would invalidate both his marriage and his residency status.

Registered partnerships for same-sex couples have been in force since 1 July 2024. They do not constitute marriage, and same-sex couples cannot marry.

There is no criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct, and no legal restriction on access to sex-segregated facilities is documented in the sources.

The most significant institutional failure concerns hate-crime enforcement. In Hanovs v. Latvia, decided unanimously on 18 July 2024, the European Court of Human Rights found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14. A 2020 attack on a gay couple in Riga was not prosecuted as a hate crime even though the aggressor admitted using anti-gay slurs; the matter was reduced to a minor public-order offence carrying a lenient fine. The Court held that the failure to prosecute inhuman treatment and the discriminatory handling of the case violated the prohibition of inhuman treatment, the right to private life and the non-discrimination guarantee, and the Strasbourg Observers analysis of the judgment notes that states must investigate and punish hate-motivated attacks thoroughly as a positive obligation.

Enforcement failures are documented beyond that case. In Daugavpils, two people were attacked and police closed the matter until the Prosecutor General ordered the investigation reopened. Following the ECtHR ruling, the Prosecutor General also reopened criminal proceedings in the Hanovs case. Former MEP Tatjana Mamikins faced an investigation over homophobic posts and left for Russia.

Protection machinery does function in some channels. In 2025 an administrative court overturned the denial of asylum to a Ghanaian LGBTI applicant.

Public hostility remains visible from senior religious figures: in 2007 Cardinal Jānis Pujats of Riga described homosexuality as "total corruption in the sexual arena" and demanded a referendum on same-sex marriage and large counter-demonstrations against Pride.
LVA.outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific travel advisory; ordinary crime is low.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Male homosexuality was decriminalized in Latvia in 1992, while female homosexuality was never criminalized. In 1999 the age of consent was equalized and set at 16 regardless of gender and/or sexual orientation. Wikipedia country coverage: Only in the capital Riga is there a small gay scene; elsewhere in Latvia the sparse population means there is no gay scene at all. The democratization process has allowed LGBT people to establish organizations and infrastructural elements such as bars, clubs, stores and libraries, concentrated in Riga. Wikipedia country coverage: Latvian law allows any person over 25 to adopt, but persons not married to each other may not adopt the same child, so in unmarried couples only one partner may adopt. Registered partnerships, codified in November 2023 and effective 1 July 2024, carry rights similar to marriage except for adoption and inheritance rights. In April 2023 the Saeima passed amendments to the Law on the Protection of the Children's Rights banning adoption of Latvian children by foreign same-sex couples. Wikipedia country coverage: It is possible to surgically affirm gender in Latvia and to legally change identity, with a medical certificate required by authorities; Latvian law does not define 'sex change'. In 2004 authorities denied a legal identity change to a transgender person after a partial sex change, but the Supreme Court ruled in 2008 that the change should have been granted; a 2009 legislative proposal that would have required sterilization to change legal gender was rejected by the Saeima. Lesbian couples can access IVF and assisted insemination treatment, and a 2020 court ruling favored parental leave rights for same-sex couples, prompting a Justice Ministry draft law on civil unions in 2022. Wikipedia country coverage: In September 2006 Latvia's Parliament passed amendments to the Labour Code prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in the workplace; President Vaira Vīķe-Freiberga refused to sign the bill until that protection was added. In 2023 ILGA-Europe ranked Latvia 24th out of 27 European Union countries for protection of LGBT rights. The source text describes no discrimination protections on the basis of gender identity. Wikipedia country coverage: The age of consent was equalized at 16 in 1999 regardless of gender and/or sexual orientation, and the 2006 constitutional amendment defining marriage as a union between a man and a woman shapes the family framework children are raised in. In April 2023 the Saeima amended the Law on the Protection of the Children's Rights to ban adoption of Latvian children by foreign same-sex couples, and a 2020 court ruling in favor of parental leave rights for same-sex couples led to a Justice Ministry draft civil-union law in 2022. The Ombudsman's 2018 call for a partnership law cited that about half of Latvian children are born out of wedlock and should enjoy legal protections. No education-specific findings appear in the source text.
