TUR.name: Turkey
TUR.summary:
Turkey presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors, driven by hostility that has become formal state policy rather than residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — together with systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people.

The Erdoğan government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Under that framing a draft legislative package that would effectively criminalise LGBT people was before the government as of October 2025. The measure had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Street-level enforcement in Istanbul illustrates that point. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The passport-carrying rule for foreigners compounds these risks. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Turkish rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex — a trans man had been held in a women's prison — and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care, with online framing contested as an "LGBT opening".

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited here as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.
TUR.outOfScopeNotes:
The draft legislative package that would effectively criminalise LGBT people was under active government consideration as of October 2025 and had not been passed when reported. Its current status is unresolved on the sources available, and enforcement described here precedes its adoption.

The 2008 Human Rights Watch report covers a period before Turkey's post-2018 legal changes to gender recognition. It is used as evidence of historical pattern and institutional continuity, not as a statement of current statute, and the extent of its continued applicability is not sourced here.

The Istanbul figures on trans-women detentions in 2025 derive from a single district and a small number of identified cases; the reporting notes that the true scale of GBT checks is not established. The annual violation totals come from media monitoring and civil-society complaints rather than official statistics, so they represent documented incidents rather than a complete count.

The treatment of LGBT detainees inside Turkish prisons is documented through the Prison Insider country profile and prison-insider testimony rather than through official inspection data. Official policy on gender-matched placement for trans prisoners is not stated in the sources reviewed; the Poyraz case indicates placement by registered sex, but no comprehensive rule is cited.

The Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 is described as creating profiling and access risk. The extent to which its provisions are binding on facilities treating foreign patients, including short-stay medical contact by visitors, is not resolved in the available material.

Pride-week monitoring covers the Istanbul event specifically. Whether comparable violations occurred at Pride events elsewhere in Turkey in 2025 is not sourced here.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D6, D10, D12, D13.

sources.title: LGBTQI+ prisoners are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches (Kaos GL), reporting the Prison Insider 'Country Profile' on Turkey (with CİSST data)
sources.summary: Kaos GL (7 May 2024), covering the Prison Insider Country Profile report on Turkey prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association (CISST) and using ILGA World data: LGBTI+ prisoners in Turkish prisons are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches and to de facto isolation, being placed in solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and sometimes refusing to go to hospital out of fear of other male prisoners during transfers. CISST observations quoted in the article state that there is no policy or staff training to identify and address LGBTI+ prisoners' needs, that Turkish prison administration is built on a binary, heteronormative system, that LGBTI+ prisoners are frequently transferred (disrupting visits and solidarity), and that complaints are ineffective and can lead to further violence. The piece documents that Turkey manages trans and LGBTI+ prisoners through segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The source text contains no visa, entry, or border rules for LGBTQ travelers to Turkey. The closest material concerns people already seeking protection in the country: LGBT individuals are described as among the most vulnerable asylum seekers and refugees in Turkey, whose access to rights and services is limited by anti-LGBTQ sentiment among state actors and the general public. Wikipedia country coverage: Sex reassignment surgery is available in Turkey's major cities — Istanbul, Ankara, İzmir and Antalya — and the minimum age for the procedure is 18. In order to change the gender marker on an identity card, the procedure must be conducted at a state hospital. Hormone replacement therapy for transgender individuals is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors needing continued medication must arrange and pay for it privately. Wikipedia country coverage: Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no direct discrimination protection regarding gender identity in Turkish law. The EU Commission's 2025 annual report wrote that legal protection of LGBTIQ persons is insufficient and not aligned with the EU acquis, and that authorities were granting official permissions for demonstrations promoting exclusion and discrimination. Bills to introduce such protections have been repeatedly proposed (CHP, February 2015) and constitutional protection agreed in 2013 draft talks, but the drafts were cancelled; KAOS GL has a case pending since 2023 alleging ineffective remedies against discrimination such as Pride bans. Separately, the government considered legislation criminalizing public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex" with one to three years' imprisonment, though it was not included in the 2026 judicial package. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition: same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unavailable, and same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly or as joint parents. When the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026, provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people were removed from the bill, which made symbolic same-sex weddings possible — but these carry no legal marital status. Because Turkish marriage law determines eligibility by the gender recorded in a person's civil registry rather than by trans status, individuals who have legally changed their registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender; LGBT marriage for non-trans people remains legally impossible. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth opinion is notably more accepting: a 2020 Pew Research Center survey found acceptance of homosexuality higher among youth (34%) and educated respondents (41%) than the 25% national figure, and Kadir Has University polling showed support for equal rights rising from 33% in 2016 to 45% in 2020. Student organizing exists — the Lesbian and Gay Inter-University Organization (LEGATO) formed in 1996 with groups at several universities by 2014 — but in May 2019 police broke up a student Pride march at Middle East Technical University, arresting at least 25 students. Minors are a stated focus of the crackdown: Erdoğan's May 2025 "Decade of Family and Population" declaration (starting 2026) attacked the LGBTQ movement as a threat to children, and the September 2026 "My Family is Safe" raids against LGBTQ+ and HIV support organizations were framed as protecting children, with 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses under investigation; in April 2026 the İzmir group Genç LGBTI+ was ordered to dissolve with eleven founders put on trial, and RTÜK's stated goal includes "protecting children, youth and the family structure," backing fines against Amazon Prime Video, Disney+, HBO Max, Netflix and Mubi for LGBTQ+ content. For trans youth specifically, the minimum age for sex reassignment surgery is 18 and the procedure must be performed at a state hospital to change an identity-card gender marker.

TUR.localsOnly:
Trans residents of Turkey face systematic detention. Kaos GL's annual report for 2025 counted 299 detention decisions in one year, the majority recorded through formal channels and a substantial minority taken off the record, against a backdrop of documented privacy attacks. The GBT check used on the approximately 20 trans women stopped in Beyoğlu in 2025 is a routine police instrument and, on the view of legal experts, breaches the ECHR's detention provisions.

Custody conditions for transgender prisoners are contested. Poyraz died at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 amid allegations of delayed medical care, delayed investigation and absent witness statements. Human Rights Association branches across six cities demanded an independent inquiry and changes to detention practices affecting trans prisoners, and a trans man was confirmed to be held in a women's prison on the basis of registered sex.

LGBT prisoners are placed in isolation rather than matched to gender-identified facilities. Arbitrary body and strip searches, restricted healthcare access, refusals of hospital transfer, frequent transfers that break solidarity networks, and ineffective complaint procedures are documented in the Prison Insider country profile prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association.

Transition care has become a site of administrative surveillance. The Kayseri circular adding "gender reassignment" to official medical-board report reasons, and the accompanying requirement for e-reports, closes off the neutral "other" option in hospital records and introduces profiling risk into routine medical paperwork.

Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of them classified as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately represented among the victims.
TUR.blindSummary:
The country presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors, driven by hostility that has become formal state policy rather than residual prejudice. The annual LGBTI+ Human Rights Report recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the preceding year's total, with 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people.

The national government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language human-rights monitors identify as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Under that framing a draft legislative package that would effectively criminalise LGBT people was before the government as of October 2025. The measure had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Street-level enforcement in a major city illustrates that point. In 2025 police there stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in one central district and held them at a police station in that district for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate the detention provisions of the applicable regional human-rights treaty. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

Violence against trans people in the country is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in a residential district of the same major city by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by a national memory-and-justice centre found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The passport-carrying rule for foreigners compounds these risks. The country requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 national lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. a transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at a women's prison in the national capital region on 1 December 2025. National rights groups coordinated from a human-rights association's branches in six cities demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by an opposition MP on 12 December 2025, confirmed that trans prisoners are placed according to their registered sex — a trans man had been held in a women's prison — and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. a prison-insider country profile prepared with a civil-society association on penal system affairs and using international monitoring data documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. a Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a provincial health directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required electronic reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care, with online framing contested as an "LGBT opening".

The underlying pattern is longstanding. a national human-rights organisation's 2008 report, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited here as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

TUR.tangentialFactors:
The hostility visible in Turkey is not confined to policing. It runs through public rhetoric at the highest level of government and through administrative measures that touch healthcare records, so that a trans visitor's exposure is not limited to any single encounter. A Health Ministry regulation that forces "gender reassignment" into the stated reasons for medical-board reports converts a health contact into an entry in an official record.

Detention decisions account for the overwhelming majority, which points to the street stop as the characteristic site of contact between trans people and the Turkish state.

Where police routinely process trans people through identity checks, an assault victim can end up in the same processing system as her attacker, as occurred in the Bakırköy knifing case. DNK.name: Denmark
DNK.summary:
Denmark permits legal gender recognition by self-declaration, with no medical evaluation required, a regime in force since 2014 and the first of its kind in Europe. Non-binary people may obtain an 'X' marker in passports, and trans people determine their own legal gender markers.

Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics is prohibited. The Equal Treatment Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in employment and services; workplace protection on the basis of gender identity has been in place since 2015, and fair-housing protection on that ground has held throughout the monitored period.

Same-sex couples may marry and adopt. Denmark was the first country to recognise same-sex partnerships, in 1989, and marriage equality followed in 2012.

On 10 September 2024 the Danish Supreme Court held that serving a sentence in a men's prison department does not violate the human rights of a trans inmate. That judgment is the leading Danish authority on where trans detainees are placed, and it is the single most consequential ruling for a visitor who is remanded or convicted.

The Danish Institute for Human Rights reports that police under-investigate hate crimes and are not obliged to flag hate-crime motivation at the time a report is made, which bears directly on a visitor who is targeted. Its LGBT+ barometer records that 38% of homosexual and bisexual respondents report differential treatment based on gender, sexual orientation or appearance, and that hate speech directed at sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics recurs every year.

Violence against trans people is documented. In July 2024 a migrant trans woman was murdered in a hotel room in Copenhagen. The UN Committee Against Torture, in its eighth periodic review, found that some trans people, QTIBIPOC and migrants report denial of access to spaces and services as well as threats.

Denmark's record on arrest and asylum is favourable on the available indicators: freedoms against arbitrary arrest based on gender identity were affirmed in every year from 2011 to 2024, and in February 2013 a Guatemalan trans woman became the first transgender person granted asylum in Denmark, refused return over her gender identity after citing police attacks and threats tied to her trans activism.
DNK.outOfScopeNotes:
Conversion-therapy status is unresolved in the sources. One source records a ban in force since 2023, while another states there is no ban and that a bill was revived in August 2026. The current legal position should be verified against the Danish statute before publication.

Whether Danish police have since been required to flag hate-crime motivation at the point of reporting is not sourced; the inventory only establishes the Danish Institute for Human Rights finding that no such obligation existed.

The scope of the Supreme Court's 10 September 2024 prison-placement ruling — whether it extends to pre-operative, non-binary or intersex detainees, and to remand rather than convicted prisoners — is not addressed in the available material.

The sources do not state whether Denmark's asylum practice toward trans claimants after the 2013 Fernanda Milan decision has been consistent; only that single early case is documented here.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Denmark's 1996 Act on Prohibition of Unequal Treatment in the Labor Market lists discrimination grounds including sexual orientation but does not explicitly name gender identity or expression; a 2015 court ruling, brought by a transgender woman suing her former employer, held that gender identity or expression is covered by the law. Danish law also prohibits discrimination based on gender identity or expression in other categories, and hate crime legislation since 2004 Penal Code amendments adds penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation. In the workplace, a 2019 report found 69% of LGBT respondents were open about their sexual orientation to colleagues and only 9% felt they could not be.

NOR.name: Norway
NOR.summary:
Norwegian law contains no offence targeting trans people. The Penal Code was amended in 2020 to make hate speech against trans people a criminal offence, and the hate-crime framework recorded by OSCE/ODIHR defines hate crimes as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or disability, with any offence so motivated recorded under that framework.

Legal gender recognition runs on self-declaration with no medical-intervention requirement: the change of legal gender is decided at the tax office on the basis of the individual's own perception of their gender identity, from age 16 on the person's own application.

Violence is the principal offset to that legal position. A gunman killed two people at Oslo Pride in 2022; the perpetrator, Zaniar Matapour, an ISIS sympathiser, was sentenced to 30 years, the strictest penalty available. Reported hate crimes rose 18% in 2023, with the largest increases in offences motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, and antisemitism. A knife attack on two people was investigated as a hate crime, and a drag bingo event drew online threats.

Recorded figures understate the scale. Police-reported hate-crime cases against queer and trans people reached record numbers in 2023, yet the clearance rate fell from 52% to 45% and more cases were dropped. A HATECYCLE study drawing on more than 3,000 survey responses from LGBTQI people found that only 8% of those who experienced a hate crime reported it to police, citing mistrust, procedural obstacles, fear of personal costs, and, among those who did report, dismissive treatment.

The Police Security Service (PST) reports a significant decline in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, while warning that hate speech and intimidation risks persist, particularly during Pride, and that most threat actors aim to spread fear rather than act. Organised anti-trans hostility is concentrated among political extremists and religious fundamentalists: the Nordic Resistance Movement's 2017 Kristiansand march advocated "crushing the gay lobby", and research interviews with far-right activists frame gender diversity as degeneracy. That is a movement phenomenon rather than street-level risk for an ordinary visitor.
NOR.outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and border treatment of trans visitors is not sourced in this inventory. Nothing here establishes how Norwegian border officials or visa authorities handle trans passport holders, mismatched markers, or screening that could disclose a person's trans status; the current record's claim of no trans-specific border friction is not backed by any source listed for this pass.

Facility access is likewise unresolved: no source addresses bathroom or changing-room rules for visitors, and none addresses whether anti-discrimination coverage of gender identity extends to service refusal in practice beyond the statutory text.

Healthcare access for visitors is not covered. The gender-recognition material describes the legal document route only; it does not state whether hormone therapy or other gender-affirming care is available to non-residents, nor what documentation a visitor would need at a pharmacy or clinic.

Partner and marriage recognition, next-of-kin rights and inheritance treatment for trans visitors' families are absent from the inventory and remain unverified here.

Two figures carry dating caveats. The 18% hate-crime increase and the 52%-to-45% clearance drop both describe 2023; no hate-crime statistics for 2024 or 2025 are supplied, so the current-year picture is unresolved. The PST threat assessment is reported in April 2025 as covering "the past year" without a precise measurement period, and the underlying PST document was not consulted directly.

The 8% reporting rate comes from a survey of 3,000+ LGBTQI respondents rather than a census, and the inventory does not state the sampling frame or whether trans respondents were separately weighted; treating it as a precise national rate would overstate what the study supports.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6, D7.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity between men has been legal since 1972; same-sex acts between women were never penalized. In April 2022, the government made formal apologies to victims of the ban on sex between men. Conversion therapy was banned effective 1 January 2024, approved by Parliament 85–15 on 12 December 2023. Wikipedia country coverage: Hate speech based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 1981 (Paragraph 135a of the Penal Code). In November 2020, the Storting amended the hate speech law to also protect bisexual and transgender people. 15% of LGBT respondents reported being targets of personal threats, mostly online, compared to 4% of the general population (2019 Norwegian Institute of Social Research report). Wikipedia country coverage: Access to gender-affirming healthcare in Norway still requires a psychiatric diagnosis, with referral to the National Treatment Centre for Gender Incongruence (NTCGI) at Oslo University Hospital. Only a quarter of referred patients are allowed access to gender-affirming healthcare, with those disqualified having no alternative options. Non-binary people were still without treatment as of a 2023 report, despite a 2020 guideline explicitly calling for equal access. Minors aged 6–16 may change legal sex with parental consent under the 2016 self-determination law, and 2020 guidelines recommend puberty blockers between Tanner stage 2 and age 16 following interdisciplinary assessment. Wikipedia country coverage: In 1981, Norway became the first country to enact a law preventing discrimination against LGBT people by amending Paragraph 349a of the Penal Code, prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation in goods/services and public gatherings. Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation has been banned since 1998. Since 2013, Norway has a law prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity and expression (Section 5 of the Act on the Prohibition of Discrimination on the grounds of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression), and is one of the few countries explicitly protecting intersex people from discrimination. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2021, anti-transgender groups such as Kvinneaktivistene and a Norwegian branch of Women's Declaration International formed. In 2023, 2611 feminists including Norway's minister of equality called for a reckoning with transphobia. Some tabloid newspapers have been criticized for regularly publishing transphobic content, with journalism expert Jon Martin Larsen criticizing Klassekampen for contributing to 'incitement and hatred against transgender people.' Bufdir found 11% expressed hostile attitudes towards transgender people in 2017, versus 7.8% towards gay people. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 January 2009, granting lesbian and gay couples the same rights as heterosexuals including religious weddings, adoption, and assisted pregnancies. A registered partnership law had been in effect since 1993, and unregistered same-sex cohabitation has been recognized since 1991 for limited rights such as next-of-kin medical decisions. In 2024, Norway was ranked the best country for same-sex couples to legally marry. Wikipedia country coverage: Homosexual boys reported a six times higher occurrence of bullying in schools than heterosexual boys (2013 University of Bergen survey). Queer Youth (Skeiv Ungdom) is among LGBT associations offering helplines and counselling to LGBT youth. Minors aged 6–16 may change legal sex with parental consent under the 2016 law, and 2020 health guidelines recommend puberty blockers between Tanner stage 2 and age 16.

NOR.localsOnly:
Change of legal gender is an administrative act handled at the tax office, not a medical or judicial one. From age 16 a person applies alone; between 6 and 16 the application requires parental involvement; below age 6 it is possible only for documented congenital differences of sex development. A 2017 regulation extends the procedure to Norwegian citizens resident abroad.

Barriers to reporting are documented and specific: mistrust of police, procedural obstacles, fear of personal costs, and dismissive treatment from officers among those who did report. Only 8% of LGBTQI survey respondents who experienced a hate crime filed a police report. The clearance rate for recorded hate crimes dropped from 52% to 45% in 2023, with a rise in cases dropped.

National support and community organisations listed for LGBT and trans people include FRI, Skeiv Ungdom, the Transgender Association and Oslo Pride. A dedicated hate-crime group within the police is the designated point for reporting and is described as encouraging victims to come forward.
NOR.blindSummary:
The country has no offence targeting trans people. The Penal Code was amended in 2020 to make hate speech against trans people a criminal offence, and the hate-crime framework recorded by the international monitoring body defines hate crimes as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or disability, with any offence so motivated recorded under that framework.

Legal gender recognition runs on self-declaration with no medical-intervention requirement: the change of legal gender is decided at the tax office on the basis of the individual's own perception of their gender identity, from age 16 on the person's own application.

Violence is the principal offset to that legal position. a gunman killed two people at a Pride march in 2022; the perpetrator, an ISIS sympathiser, was sentenced to 30 years, the strictest penalty available. Reported hate crimes rose 18% in 2023, with the largest increases in offences motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, and antisemitism. a knife attack on two people was investigated as a hate crime, and a drag bingo event drew online threats.

Recorded figures understate the scale. Police-reported hate-crime cases against queer and trans people reached record numbers in 2023, yet the clearance rate fell from 52% to 45% and more cases were dropped. a study drawing on more than 3,000 survey responses from LGBTQI people found that only 8% of those who experienced a hate crime reported it to police, citing mistrust, procedural obstacles, fear of personal costs, and, among those who did report, dismissive treatment.

The national security service reports a significant decline in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, while warning that hate speech and intimidation risks persist, particularly during Pride, and that most threat actors aim to spread fear rather than act. Organised anti-trans hostility is concentrated among political extremists and religious fundamentalists: a far-right march in 2017 advocated "crushing the gay lobby", and research interviews with far-right activists frame gender diversity as degeneracy. That is a movement phenomenon rather than street-level risk for an ordinary visitor.
NOR.blindOutOfScope:
Entry and border treatment of trans visitors is not sourced in this inventory. Nothing here establishes how border officials or visa authorities handle trans passport holders, mismatched markers, or screening that could disclose a person's trans status; the current record's claim of no trans-specific border friction is not backed by any source listed for this pass.

Facility access is likewise unresolved: no source addresses bathroom or changing-room rules for visitors, and none addresses whether anti-discrimination coverage of gender identity extends to service refusal in practice beyond the statutory text.

Healthcare access for visitors is not covered. The gender-recognition material describes the legal document route only; it does not state whether hormone therapy or other gender-affirming care is available to non-residents, nor what documentation a visitor would need at a pharmacy or clinic.

Partner and marriage recognition, next-of-kin rights and inheritance treatment for trans visitors' families are absent from the inventory and remain unverified here.

Two figures carry dating caveats. The 18% hate-crime increase and the 52%-to-45% clearance drop both describe 2023; no hate-crime statistics for 2024 or 2025 are supplied, so the current-year picture is unresolved. The security service threat assessment is reported in April 2025 as covering "the past year" without a precise measurement period, and the underlying document was not consulted directly.

The 8% reporting rate comes from a survey of 3,000+ LGBTQI respondents rather than a census, and the inventory does not state the sampling frame or whether trans respondents were separately weighted; treating it as a precise national rate would overstate what the study supports.

SWE.name: Sweden
SWE.summary:
Sweden's parliament approved new acts on legal gender recognition and on medical procedures performed on genitalia in April 2024, as recorded by a Library of Congress global legal monitor entry of April 2024.

The Legal Gender Recognition Act came into force on 1 July 2025. TGEU reports that the new act simplifies the procedure for changing legal gender but falls short of a full self-determination model, with medical barriers remaining, so a person seeking to update legal documents may still be required to satisfy medical conditions.

Sweden's main national board decided on 28 January 2017 that transgender people would no longer be classified as mentally ill, the depathologisation step that governs diagnostic status for trans residents.

The clearest documented everyday-facility friction concerns changing rooms. SVT reported in October 2025 that the swimming-pool chain Medley stopped trans customers from choosing their changing rooms, a restriction on facility access that a trans visitor to such a venue would encounter directly.

On hate crime, Brå (the National Council for Crime Prevention) published report 2024:13, which supplements Swedish hate-crime statistics with a descriptive analysis of persons suspected of offences in which police identified LGBTQI-related hate-crime motives. This is the national dataset on anti-LGBTQI offending.

On protection machinery, the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 covering 2025 records a bill that would extend protection of victims of conversion practices when these are carried out through coercion, threats or sustained psychological pressure.
SWE.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains nothing on criminalisation, on the law governing bathroom access, or on visa, entry and border-screening procedures, so those points are unresolved here rather than assessed.

The scope of the Medley changing-room restriction is not stated: whether it applies across all of the chain's venues, whether it has been challenged in court, and whether comparable policies exist at other Swedish swimming facilities are unresolved on these sources.

Brå report 2024:13 is described in the inventory only by subject; the number of hate-crime reports, the number of suspects and any conviction outcomes are not sourced here.

The conversion-practices measure is recorded as a bill, and whether it was enacted is not stated in the inventory.

The military article ends at 2014, so current service conditions for trans personnel in the Swedish armed forces are not sourced.

The Spartacus Gay Travel Index reference dates from 2019 and is a third-party ranking, not an official assessment.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D5, D7.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity was legalized in Sweden in 1944 (age of consent 18), and in 1972 an equal age of consent of 15 was set alongside legal gender recognition. Homosexuality was declassified as an illness in October 1979 and being transgender was declassified as an illness (the text dates this to 2017 in one place, 2009 in another). A 1987 law banning sex in gay saunas and prostitution, passed to combat HIV, was repealed in 2004. Until 2013, legal gender change required sterilization and sex reassignment surgery — requirements ruled unconstitutional in January 2013 and removed by the Riksdag in July 2013, with roughly 600–700 people later compensated 225,000 SEK each (law passed March 2018) for forced sterilization. Wikipedia country coverage: Sweden's hate speech law covers sexual orientation (added by Riksdag vote in 2002, effective 1 January 2003) and 'transgender identity and expression' (added effective 1 January 2019); transgender identity and expression were added to hate crime legislation on 1 July 2018, with sexual orientation added in 2010. The law has been criticised as 'selectively applied': authorities refused to prosecute a Halmstad imam who called homosexuality a 'virus' in 2015, and Pentecostal preacher Åke Green was convicted then acquitted through to the Supreme Court, which held European Convention religious-speech protections barred punishment. Anti-gender actors also target expression through knowledge production, labelling gender studies and intersectional feminist scholarship 'ideological or unscientific'. Wikipedia country coverage: The source contains no visa or entry rules for LGBTQ travellers; the nearest material is that a 1978 state inquiry into the living conditions of gays and lesbians suggested granting refugee status to persecuted LGBTQ people, and that RFSL counselling centres in Stockholm, Gothenburg and Malmö assist people with contact to authorities and 'legal assistance with, for example, asylum and wills'. A 2021 study found migrant LGBTQ people have worse sexual health, avoid healthcare more, are more exposed to sexual violence and are more dissatisfied with their sexual life than other groups. Wikipedia country coverage: Sweden has seen a rise in domestic anti-gender campaigns tied to a transnational movement opposing gender equality and transgender rights, mobilising around the pejorative concept of 'gender ideology'. Actors include the far-right Sweden Democrats and Christian Democrats, who oppose trans-rights legal reforms while framing opposition as protecting women's rights and Swedish values, and 'gender-critical' radical feminist groups — notably the Swedish Women's Lobby (SWL, founded 1997, umbrella for 57 associations representing over 130,000 women and girls), which in 2025 launched the Women's Platform for Action International (WoPAI) promoting 'sex-based rights'. Scholars document 'insidious de-democratization' and report growing political violence and intimidation against trans advocates, feminist scholars and racialized activists, including online harassment, threats and public vilification. Separately, misinformation that Sweden had banned gender-affirming care for minors spread on social media and was cited by US Republican politicians to justify outright bans. Wikipedia country coverage: In March 2021 the Karolinska Institute stopped providing puberty blockers or gender-affirming hormone therapy to children and teens under 16, and to 16–18-year-olds outside approved clinical trials; on 22 February 2022 the National Board of Health and Welfare said puberty blockers should be used only in 'exceptional cases' backed by 'uncertain science' (guidance, not a ban). In 2021 the Board cut gender-affirming clinics from seven to three (those three yet to be chosen). In April 2024 the Riksdag approved new laws (234 for, 94 against) effective 1 July 2025 lowering the minimum age for legal gender change without a gender-dysphoria diagnosis from 18 to 16, requiring a doctor/psychologist statement plus National Board approval, and guardian approval for 16–17-year-olds; genital surgery is limited to 18+ and gonad removal to 23+ absent exceptional reason. Nationwide Board data released in 2026 showed trans children prescribed puberty blockers had slightly increased since the 2022 guidance. Anti-gender efforts also target gender studies and feminist scholarship in education, and Sweden's age of consent has been equal at 15 since 1972.

FIN.name: Finland
FIN.summary:
Finland does not criminalise trans people, and the sources reviewed document no trans-specific violence against a visitor: no assault, mob attack or police-brutality case involving a trans traveller is recorded. The hate-crime material below is aggregate national reporting, not an incident series involving visitors.

Police recorded 1,808 suspected hate-crime offences, the highest total ever logged, with defamation and assault the most common types. The Police University College reports the sexual-orientation and gender-identity-or-expression category climbing across six reported years, from 72 cases to 241. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2026 gives the same headline total of 1,808 suspected hate crimes and identifies sexual orientation and gender identity as recurrent motives, present in 12% of cases.

The Criminal Code contains no hate-crime offence. Motive is captured only in police reports, so sexual-orientation and gender-identity-motivated incidents are counted as reported suspicions rather than as charges, and the recorded figures measure reporting behaviour as much as offending.

Finland's first conversion-practices case was prosecuted as assault, with convictions in March. Parliament endorsed a citizens' initiative to ban conversion practices by 125 votes to 49 in March, while a full statutory ban remained pending at the time of the review.

Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since 1 March 2017. Since 28 February 2018 the Maternity Act recognises both women in a same-sex partnership as mothers from the moment of the child's birth, with the second parent registered at birth rather than through adoption.
FIN.outOfScopeNotes:
The two sources give the same total of 1,808 suspected hate crimes but attribute it to different years, 2024 in the Police University College release and 2025 in the ILGA-Europe review. The discrepancy is unresolved in the sources reviewed and neither document reconciles it.

Restroom and facility rules, gender-marker changes on identity documents, entry and visa screening, and access to gender-affirming care for short-term visitors are not addressed in the sources reviewed for this revision.

The status of a full statutory ban on conversion practices is unresolved: the citizens' initiative was endorsed in March but the review states a complete ban remained pending, with no later enactment sourced here.

No source in the inventory reports an incident count for hate crimes against foreign visitors specifically; the 1,808 figure is not disaggregated by victim residency or nationality.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D11.

Finland's Police University College (Polamk, Nov 2025): record 1,808 suspected hate-crime offenses reported in 2024 — highest figure ever recorded; defamation and assault the most common types. The sexual-orientation/gender-identity-or-expression category climbed 72 -> 68 -> 126 -> 140 -> 215 -> 241 across the six reported years. The Criminal Code has no hate-crime category, so motive is only recorded in police reports — meaning SOGI-motivated incidents are counted via reported suspicion, not charge.

The Guardian (21 Mar 2025): Finland and Denmark updated their travel advice for transgender citizens travelling to the United States after reports of border difficulties following the US 'two genders' executive order. Denmark advises trans travellers to contact the US embassy in Copenhagen before departure over document issues. Finland's advice is outbound guidance issued to its own travellers, not an assessment of risk within Finland.

Investigate Europe, 'The Cruel Condition' (10 Sep 2025): Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden explicitly wrote infertility requirements into law for legal gender recognition; at least 11,000 people subjected to such conditions across the six countries investigated, Sweden first (1972, in force 40 years); the last requirement was phased out at end-June 2025 — Finland's statutory sterilisation-era requirement is history, but the legacy cohort is documented.

Yle (28 Feb 2018): Parliament approved a citizens'-initiative-inspired change to the Maternity Act recognising both women in same-sex partnerships as mothers from the moment of the child's birth — second-parent registration fixed at birth rather than via adoption.

Yle (1 Mar 2017): same-sex marriage and joint adoption became legal in Finland. The western Finland register office alone had about 41 same-sex couples scheduled to marry in the first week. The operative date for marriage equality in Finland is 1 March 2017.

Yle (19 Sep 2013): the 'Tahdon2013' citizens' initiative for same-sex marriage collected 162,000+ certified signatures — largest Finnish initiative ever, far above the 50,000 threshold forcing parliamentary consideration; organiser target had been 250,000. The process route that produced the 2017 marriage law.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity between both men and women has been legal in Finland since 1971, with 'promotion' of homosexuality decriminalised and the age of consent equalised at 16 in 1999; homosexuality was declassified as an illness in 1981 and transvestism in 2011. Discrimination based on sexual orientation was criminalised in 1995 and on gender identity in 2005. Until April 2023, trans people seeking legal gender recognition had to be sterilised or otherwise infertile and hold a mental disorder diagnosis. Wikipedia country coverage: Civic and public expression is protected in practice: a citizens' initiative ('Tahdon2013') gathered over 166,000 signatures in 2013 and became the first citizens' initiative passed by Parliament, legalising same-sex marriage in December 2014. A 2010 gay rights panel on state broadcaster Yle TV2 and Pride parades in numerous cities (an estimated 100,000 attended 2018 Helsinki Pride) mark open public visibility, alongside the first public gay demonstration in 1981. Finland's Constitution allows citizens' initiatives with 50,000 valid signatures to be put to Parliament. Wikipedia country coverage: There is a visible gay scene in Helsinki with gay bars, clubs and cafés, and support organisations operate nationwide — Seta (founded 1974), Trasek for trans and intersex rights, and Rainbow Families. Gender-affirming care for minors is delivered through the country's two centralised gender identity units, and a Seta survey found over 40% of trans respondents were entirely unable to access the care they needed, with most reporting extended waiting times. Since December 2023 there is no extra deferral period on blood donation for men who have sex with men. Wikipedia country coverage: Registered partnerships from 2002 to 1 March 2017 gave same-sex couples the same rights as married couples except adoption and joint surname, with immigration rights for a foreign same-sex partner. Stepchild adoption became legal in 2009 and joint adoption by same-sex couples on 1 March 2017 alongside same-sex marriage (passed 101–90 in December 2014). Surrogacy remains illegal for all couples, and in April 2019 a law passed 122–42 gave lesbian couples full maternity pay and parentage rights without intra-family adoption. Wikipedia country coverage: Section 8(1) of the Discrimination Act prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and other personal characteristics, whether based on fact or assumption, and gender identity/expression has been covered since 2005 (sexual orientation since 1995). The Act on Equality between Women and Men also covers sex and gender identity, and Parliament amended the law in 2014 to extend protections in employment, goods and services, education and health services. Finnish police reported 73 violent attacks and assaults against LGBT people in 2018, a 27% increase on 2017 — the only hate-motive category to rise that year. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2020 the Council for Choices in Health Care revised clinical recommendations for gender dysphoria under age 25, prioritising psychosocial therapy over medical transition and restricting puberty blockers and hormone treatment, though these are recommendations not mandates — puberty blockers remain available case-by-case and cross-sex hormones can be considered if identity is of a permanent nature causing severe dysphoria, through two centralised gender identity units for minors. The 2023 gender recognition law set the age limit at 18 (up from a proposed 15 with guardian permission), with a 30-day reflection period and a limit of one change per year. In November 2019 the Institute of Health and Welfare reported that LGBT children and youth face significantly more bullying, physical, psychological and sexual violence than heterosexual peers and are more likely to suffer violence at home.

TWN.name: Taiwan
TWN.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Taiwan remains gated by a 2008 executive order requiring sex-reassignment surgery before a gender marker can be changed on the national ID. An estimated 90% of trans people are blocked from obtaining an ID matching their presentation, which makes every ID-requiring interaction, including clinic visits and airport security checks, a potential site of distress and discrimination. The Ministry of Health and Welfare has recognised gender self-determination as a human right since 2013, but the surgical requirement stands. In August 2024 a Taipei court denied a transgender woman's request to change her ID marker without surgery or psychological evaluation, with the supporting rights group indicating an appeal was likely.

No tangible policy change on abolishing the surgery requirement or expanding assisted reproduction access occurred during 2025, and the government has continued to fail to act on trans rights amid persistent transphobia. Pending changes to conscription criteria could actively harm trans people, including trans women who may be drawn into military service on the basis of their marker.

Public facilities are a documented friction point. The Ministry of Environment is investing NT$280 million over four years to double gender-neutral public bathrooms nationwide from 623 to 1,246 by 2029, but 17% of trans and gender-neutral survey respondents who reported discrimination said it occurred in public restrooms or changing rooms. A rights group's November 2025 inspection found that only 5 of 149 government-listed all-gender toilets met the required standards, including clear all-gender signage, so the practical availability of safe facilities is far below the official count.

An anti-gender discourse wave has been building since at least 2024, with movement activity rising and organisations aligning themselves with Donald Trump's anti-trans policies; a political party has called for an official 'two genders' position. Against this, the 7th annual Taiwan Transgender March in Taipei drew an estimated 3,000 people in November 2025 despite rain, including international participants, and called for an end to discrimination.

Taiwan legalised same-sex marriage in 2019, the first jurisdiction in Asia to do so, and regularised adoption for same-sex parents on 16 May 2023. It is widely described as the most liberal jurisdiction of the Chinese diaspora on LGBT rights. No severe incidents targeting trans visitors, such as mob violence or organised predation, are documented in the sources reviewed.
TWN.outOfScopeNotes:
One source addressing Taiwan's transgender rights laws, protections and gaps returned HTTP 404 at research time and could not be read; any protections it described are unresolved and not reflected here.

The outcome of the appeal flagged by the rights group after the August 2024 Taipei court denial is not sourced. Whether the court's reasoning was narrowed, upheld or overturned on appeal remains unresolved.

The pending conscription-criteria changes are described as pending; whether they were finalised, and what the final text requires of trans conscripts, is not sourced.

Whether the 5-of-149 all-gender toilet finding prompted remediation, and whether the NT$280 million bathroom programme has met any of its interim milestones toward 2029, is not sourced.

The sources reviewed do not document incidents of violence against trans visitors, but absence of documentation in this inventory is not evidence that none occurs; a dedicated incident check was not available.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Private, consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Historically, a 1740 Qing decree criminalised voluntary homosexual intercourse between adults (punishable by a month in prison and 100 heavy blows), while the Republic of China's provisional criminal code abolished explicit prohibitions on 'consenting ji jian' around 1912 and sodomy was decriminalised when the ROC took over Taiwan after World War II under the 1935 criminal code. During martial law, LGBT people were harassed and detained under general public order laws (Temporary Provisions against the Communist Rebellion), repealed in 1991. Wikipedia country coverage: Public expression is open and expanding: the first Taiwan Pride was held in Taipei on 1 November 2003 with over 1,000 attendees, growing to about 80,000 by 2015, 137,000 in 2018 and 170,000 by 2019, with pride events also held in Kaohsiung (since 2010) and Taichung (20,000 in 2016). LGBTQ representation in literature and film — from Pai Hsien-yung's novel Crystal Boys in the 1970s to Ang Lee's Brokeback Mountain (2005) and Zero Chou's Spider Lilies (2007 Berlin Teddy Award winner) — is described as instrumental in raising public awareness. In 2022 Taiwan withdrew from hosting WorldPride 2025 over the disputed name 'WorldPride Kaohsiung,' which the public and government considered offensive, and the event moved to Washington, D.C. in June 2025. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples can legally adopt, and since May 2023 legislation has granted full adoption rights, replacing the partial (stepchild-only) adoption rights in place since 2019. Until 2023 they could only adopt the biological child of their partner; a January 2022 court order had already allowed a same-sex couple to adopt before the legislature codified full rights. Taiwan law also permits single individuals, including individual LGBT people, to adopt depending on circumstances, while the Artificial Reproduction Act limits IVF and other assisted reproductive technologies to legally married heterosexual couples, specifically excluding same-sex female couples and single women. Wikipedia country coverage: Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender characteristics has been banned in education nationwide since the Gender Equity Education Act of June 2004 (fine of NT$100,000 for schools discriminating in admission, instruction or assessment). Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 2007–08 amendments to the Employment Service Act and the Act of Gender Equality in Employment, with fines of NT$300,000 to NT$1,500,000. The Long-Term Care Services Act (January 2017) contains an anti-discrimination clause covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and Judicial Yuan Interpretation No. 748 (24 May 2017) held that the Constitution's Article 7 grounds of discrimination are 'illustrative, rather than exhaustive,' so sexual orientation is protected by the right to equality. Wikipedia country coverage: Discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in education has been banned since the Gender Equity Education Act of June 2004, with sexual-bullying prevention and reporting duties added in June 2011. In November 2018 voters passed a referendum question to ban LGBT-inclusive sex education in schools (Question 11) and rejected the pro-inclusion Question 15; Education Minister Yeh Jiunn-rong said LGBT content would be reviewed against the result, and an earlier Ministry of Education curriculum reform (announced March 2010, effective 2011) had already been watered down to 'respecting diverse sexual orientations' after anti-LGBT opposition. Following that referendum, suicide hotlines reported a 40% surge in calls from LGBT individuals, particularly adolescents and young adults. Youth-relevant health measures include the 22 February 2018 Ministry of Health and Welfare letter effectively banning conversion therapy, with violators liable under the Criminal Code or the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act.

TWN.tangentialFactors:
The anti-gender movement in Taiwan is organised and politically connected rather than a diffuse social mood: analysis published in November 2024 describes a distinct wave of anti-gender discourse, and by 2025 the movement's organisations were taking cues from United States policy under Donald Trump. The Taiwan Solidarity Party's call for a 'two genders' position shows the discourse has reached party-level programme rather than remaining online commentary.

Reform stagnation is a procedural pattern, not an isolated ruling. The August 2024 Taipei court refusal to grant a marker change without surgery or psychological evaluation sits alongside a full calendar year of 2025 in which no legislative or administrative change to the surgery requirement or to assisted reproduction was delivered, which suggests a visitor should not expect the legal position to shift during a short stay.

Facility investment and facility quality diverge. The state is funding a doubling of gender-neutral bathrooms by 2029, yet an independent audit in November 2025 found that almost all listed all-gender toilets failed basic standards such as signage, so a count of facilities on paper overstates what a trans traveller will find in practice.

Conscription criteria are an adjacent exposure that does not apply to short-term visitors but shapes the environment for residents and for anyone with longer-term obligations.

KOR.name: South Korea
KOR.summary:
South Korea does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available and the requirement of surgery is falling. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years that forcing surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. The Supreme Court has also allowed a transgender person with minor children to change their gender in the family relations register.

Trans visitors have a documented, judicially enforced right to public restrooms. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in South Korea (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: South Korea's Wikipedia article on LGBT rights contains no information on how transgender prisoners are housed in the civilian prison system. Its most prominent trans state-placement case is military: Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, a transgender conscript, was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty. The article records that consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel is criminalised under Military Criminal Act article 92-6 (up to two years' imprisonment; a gay soldier was sentenced to six months in 2017) and that transgender people are excluded from military service. No birth-sex versus identity placement rule, special unit, or solitary or segregation practice for transgender prisoners is described. Wikipedia country coverage: South Korean national law does not recognize same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court's en banc panel ruled that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognized provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children. Wikipedia country coverage: Violence and hostility at LGBTQ events is documented: in Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organizers later filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender, June Green, told NBC News he feels "threatened to just walk on the street" absent a nondiscrimination bill.

IND.name: India
IND.summary:
India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
IND.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory does not state when the March 2026 amendment takes effect, whether rules or forms under it have been notified, or how it affects identity documents already issued to trans people.

Unresolved: whether the narrowed recognition scheme changes passport endorsements, visa applications or gender markers for foreign visitors is not addressed in any source here.

Unresolved: the inventory gives no figures on penalties for anti-trans violence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, nor on prosecution rates for the offences the old Indian Penal Code did cover.

Unresolved: the frequency of airport, railway and passport incidents beyond the cited cases is not quantified, so the four documented encounters cannot be read as a rate.

Not sourced here: any count of state-level protection cells or other sub-national implementation machinery.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Constitutional protection covers expression: the Supreme Court has ruled that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls under Article 15's prohibition of discrimination by "sex," and the Allahabad High Court extended this in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. Academic expression is protected too — the University Grants Commission prohibits bullying and ragging aimed at students based on sexual orientation or gender identity in higher education. Counter-currents exist: conservative groups such as the Vishva Hindu Parishad and Bajrang Dal have labelled same-sex marriage a "Western attack on Indian culture" and have occasionally targeted Pride events. Wikipedia country coverage: Facilities for trans people are largely state-level: Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards that coordinate housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pension schemes, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Federally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries. Wikipedia country coverage: Intersex minors face coercive surgery: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male via non-consensual operations, prompting the Madras High Court in April 2019 to order Tamil Nadu to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants. On campus, the University Grants Commission bars bullying and ragging based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and acceptance is notably higher among urban youth and students at top-tier universities such as the IITs, which host support groups like Indradhanu (IIT Delhi) and Saathi (IIT Bombay). Colleges such as the American College in Madurai teach specialised curricula on genderqueer and intersex human rights using works by transgender activists A. Revathi and Kalki Subramaniam. Bans on conversion therapy (Madras High Court 2021, National Medical Commission 2022) coexist with clandestine networks still operating nationwide. Wikipedia country coverage: Public opinion is mixed and shifting: a 2025 Pew Research Center survey found 59% of respondents still call homosexuality "morally unacceptable," while a 2023 Gallup poll showed 53% support same-sex marriage, and a 2021 Ipsos survey of urban internet users found 17% identifying as non-heterosexual or non-cisgender. Demographic studies report a high prevalence of verbal abuse and physical violence against sexual minorities, and the 2011 census recorded roughly 480,000 people identifying as transgender. Community visibility has grown quickly: organisations like GayBombay, Good as You (Bangalore) and Sappho for Equality (Kolkata) operate alongside Pride events held annually in dozens of cities since the first parade in Kolkata in 1999. Political visibility includes Shabnam Mausi (first transgender elected official, 1998), transgender mayors and judges, and Menaka Guruswamy, who in March 2026 became India's first openly LGBTQ+ member of the national Parliament.

IND.tangentialFactors:
The March 2026 amendment is contested on opposite readings of the same text. The government frames the shift away from self-identification as widening welfare access and strengthening anti-trafficking protection, while opponents inside and outside Parliament, including LGBTQ-community protesters, read it as exclusion of trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people from legal personhood.

Urban checkpoints are not exempt from the pattern the country note treats as peripheral.

Courts and the legislature are moving in opposite directions. The Supreme Court's 2018 decriminalisation, the Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines and the Allahabad High Court's 2026 relief on passport medical examinations sit against a Parliament that narrowed recognition in the same period, so the protective floor is judicial rather than statutory.

Scale matters for expectations: an estimated two million transgender people live in India, and the 2026 amendment determines which of them can evidence legal recognition at all.
IND.blindTangential:
The March 2026 amendment is contested on opposite readings of the same text. The national government frames the shift away from self-identification as widening welfare access and strengthening anti-trafficking protection, while opponents inside and outside the national legislature, including LGBTQ-community protesters, read it as exclusion of trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people from legal personhood.

Assessments of police conduct diverge in degree rather than in fact. a foreign government's December 2025 note characterises police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited and not systemic, and likelier in conservative rural areas, while the incident record from railway stations, an airport terminal and passport offices shows specific, named encounters with railway police, airport security and passport officials. Urban checkpoints are not exempt from the pattern the note treats as peripheral.
