CHN.name: China
CHN.summary:
China is authoritarian without criminalising trans identity: there is no criminal offence attaching to being transgender, no law restricting bathroom use by gender identity, and courts have awarded compensation to a trans claimant. Against that, the legal framework offers no anti-discrimination protection, legal gender recognition is unavailable, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. A visitor should expect a state that does not prosecute trans people but does not protect them either.

The most directly visitor-relevant evidence concerns the border. In May 2025 the Thai trans YouTuber Nisamanee 'Nut' Lertvorapong alleged that Chinese immigration officials laughed at, mocked and questioned her during a family trip, posting video to Instagram with the statement that no one should be treated differently on the basis of gender. A visibly trans traveller should anticipate intrusive or humiliating handling by immigration officers, with no complaint mechanism on offer.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable in China, and gender-affirming surgery for adults requires parental consent, with proof of parental death where that applies; disagreements are pushed back into the family to resolve. This is a practical barrier for trans residents and for anyone staying long enough to need medical care.

Trans-specific violence and coercive treatment are documented. A New York Times investigation in December 2024 set out transgender 'conversion' practices in the country, and in November 2024 the 28-year-old performance artist Ling'er won a record monetary payout after being subjected to electroshock 'conversion' treatment under family pressure — the first successful legal challenge to such treatment by a trans person in China. She said she hoped the case would help other LGBTQ+ people protect their rights. The case shows both that the medical system has permitted forced commitment and electroshock, and that a court will now hear a claim.

Public expression is tightly constrained. Around Pride month in 2026 platforms scrubbed prominent LGBT social media accounts, foreign films and events with LGBT themes, which Human Rights Watch read as evidence of a deteriorating rights situation and deepening repression of expression and association. Displaying rainbow flags or accessories is no longer permitted even inside venues, and in August 2023 officials removed an LGBTQ+ anthem titled 'Rainbow'. The broadcast regulator SAPPRFT's 2016 guideline banning depictions of 'abnormal sexual behaviour', including same-sex romance, established the censorship baseline that has since extended from television to social platforms.

Foreign gender-nonconforming performers meet the same squeeze: a Zurich drag artist on tour found the space for queer subcultures shrinking first-hand in August 2026, and the cancellation of nationwide shows by the transgender dancer Jin Xing in early 2025 led observers inside the country to fear a wider crackdown. Visible queerness by a visitor, performer or resident carries a real risk of cancellation, refusal or removal rather than prosecution.
CHN.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa screening of trans travellers, including whether officials inspect passport gender markers or ask transition-related questions at the border beyond the reported treatment of Nisamanee Lertvorapong. That question is unresolved here.

There is no sourced material on bathroom or facility access for visitors, on hate-crime or hate-speech protection for trans people, or on whether any anti-discrimination remedy exists outside the civil claim Ling'er brought. These are not established either way by the available sources.

Whether the parental-consent requirement for gender-affirming surgery applies to foreign patients treated in China, and whether it affects short-stay visitors needing emergency care, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

Enforcement is reported at national and platform level; variation between provinces and cities, and the practical treatment of trans residents by police outside documented cases, are not covered by the inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D6, D7, D9, D12, D13.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Beijing currently provides dependent residency status to the same-sex partners of legal residents, such as expats — the only entry/residence-related recognition noted for same-sex partners in the source. Separately, the Chinese government requires parents adopting children from China to be in heterosexual marriages, and adoption of Chinese children by foreign same-sex couples and homosexual individuals is prohibited by the Chinese authorities. No other visa, entry, or border provisions for LGBTQ travelers appear in the text. Wikipedia country coverage: Healthcare and community facilities remain hostile: psychiatric facilities and psychiatry textbooks across the country still de facto treat homosexuality as a mental disorder and continue to offer conversion therapy, because the 2001 declassification by the Chinese Society of Psychiatry was never reflected in National Health and Family Planning Commission regulations. Gender-affirming care is limited by a conservative environment; in December 2022 Chinese authorities banned online sale of estradiol and androgen blockers even with valid prescriptions, forcing in-person purchase. As of 2025 there are 7 medical centers treating transgender youth, 3 of which offer puberty suppression, with the first such clinic opened in 2021 at the Children's Hospital of Fudan University in Shanghai. LGBTQ social venues have also been closed or forced to shut: Shanghai Pride cancelled all activities in 2020 and has not resumed, and the Roxie, one of the country's last lesbian bars (Shanghai), was forced to close in 2024. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples cannot marry or adopt, and households headed by such couples are ineligible for the legal protections available to heterosexual couples; foreign same-sex couples and homosexual individuals are barred from adopting Chinese children. Since the October 2017 National People's Congress amendment allowing adults to appoint guardians by mutual agreement (yìdìng jiānhù), some same-sex couples have used this 'legal guardianship' route for limited protections, but face outright refusal or discriminatory conditions — one Hunan notary office held a six-hour meeting on whether approval would 'disrupt public disorder or morality', a Guangzhou office demanded a 100,000 yuan deposit not required of heterosexual applicants, and a 2021 China Notary Association report says some notary employees were disciplined for providing voluntary guardianship services to same-sex couples. On 12 April 2021 the Shenyang Intermediate People's Court ruled that a 79-year-old woman could not sue her female partner of 50 years over 294,000 yuan because their relationship is not recognized as a marriage. Wikipedia country coverage: Chinese law contains no explicit anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people, and hate crime laws do not cover sexual orientation or gender identity. Physical attacks are documented: days before the International Day Against Homophobia in 2018, two women wearing rainbow badges were attacked and beaten by security guards in Beijing, and the security company dismissed the three guards involved shortly thereafter. During the Cultural Revolution homosexuals were regarded as 'disgraceful' and 'undesirable' and heavily persecuted, with individuals such as Zhu Zhenhua publicly humiliated in 1983 for 'hooliganism and sodomy' and Chen Baoping sentenced to nine years in 1962. Under Xi Jinping, LGBTQ rights activists face greater scrutiny under mass surveillance, authors of boys' love works are routinely arrested and criminally prosecuted (one woman received 10 years 6 months for a gay-themed novel), and in 2025 China voted against renewing the UN Independent Expert on Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity mandate. Wikipedia country coverage: The Marriage Law of the PRC, adopted 10 September 1980, defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, so same-sex couples cannot marry. The first mainland same-sex marriage lawsuit — Sun Wenlin against the Furong District Bureau of Civil Affairs, filed December 2015 — was rejected by the Changsha court on 13 April 2016, though Sun and Hu Mingliang held a private wedding ceremony on 17 May 2016. The 2017 guardianship-agreement reform gives same-sex couples only partial, unevenly applied protections, and a 2021 Shenyang court refused to recognize a 50-year same-sex partnership in a property dispute. Beijing does provide dependent residency status to same-sex partners of legal residents such as expats; public support is rising, with a July 2024 William Institute poll finding 52% of Chinese agree same-sex couples should be able to marry (43% in a May 2021 Ipsos poll). Wikipedia country coverage: Education is a major pressure point: a 2016 UNDP survey found less than five percent of LGBT people are fully out at school, work, or in their religious community, and about fifteen percent are out to their families. In July 2021, LGBT accounts run by university students on WeChat — including Purple (Tsinghua), Colorsworld (Peking), Zhihe (Fudan) and Rainbow of Jin (19 Tianjin universities) — were deleted for violating account regulations, and a campaign marking the International Day Against Homophobia on school campuses was forbidden by public officials in 2018. Qiu Bai's five lawsuits against the Ministry of Education over homophobic teaching materials all failed, ending with a 2 March 2017 Beijing High Court rejection, and in 2021 a Jiangsu court upheld calling homosexuality a mental disorder in a 2013 university textbook as 'perceptual differences' rather than factual error — that textbook is used by a number of Chinese universities. A Peking University survey found trans female students face strong discrimination across sex-segregated enrollment, uniforms, bathrooms, dormitories, PE exams and conscription, all tied to legal gender marker; for trans youth specifically, the minimum age for sex reassignment surgery was lowered to 18 (from 20), Shanxi Province has allowed minors to apply for gender-marker change since 2014 with a guardian's ID, the 2022 Chinese expert consensus recommends puberty blockers for transgender youth, and as of 2025 seven medical centers treat transgender youth with three offering puberty suppression. A September–October 2016 Varkey Foundation survey found 54% of 18–21-year-olds in China supported same-sex marriage.

MYS.name: Malaysia
MYS.summary:
Malaysia criminalises both same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at two levels. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Every one of the 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintains Sharia enactments that criminalise cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These state offences reach Muslims only. Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed such enactments, and three of them also bar women from posing as men. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the laws contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and public. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Queue-and-venue raids carry acute exposure risk for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B in the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

The wider climate is one of state-backed restriction. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, but the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.
MYS.outOfScopeNotes:
The United Nations Development Programme and Asia Pacific Transgender Network joint publication on Malaysia is hosted as an image-based PDF; no extractable text was available from it, so its specific findings are unresolved rather than absent.

The Malaysia4U legal guide is a non-governmental compilation, updated July 2026, and its statements on the rarity of enforcement against consenting adults in private and on tourists rarely being targeted are not corroborated in the inventory by an official enforcement source.

Whether the Home Minister's 2 December 2025 suggestion of revisiting section 377B produced any legislative amendment is not sourced here. The outcome of the Negeri Sembilan constitutional challenge filed after the June 2014 arrests, expected to be decided on 7 November 2014, is likewise not stated in the inventory.

Police mistreatment and impunity in the 2019 killing cases are documented as allegations in the Human Rights Watch reporting; no prosecution outcome for any of the three killings is available in the inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D5, D13.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Identity documents are a live battleground: in August 2016 the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the National Registration Department (NRD) to update a trans man's identity card with his gender identity and chosen name, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity as a male — but this judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017. The only successful documented gender-marker change is historical: in 1975 NRD recognised Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim (formerly Mohd Fauzi bin Abdul Karim) as female, and the Johor Deputy Mufti allowed her to marry under sharia law. The 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holds that sex is determined at birth and remains so even after sex reassignment surgery, though it was never gazetted and so is not legally binding. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2001 then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad stated Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay, and warned gay foreign ministers not to bring their partners while visiting. This is the only entry/deportation policy stated in the source; there is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors. Artist pressure has also affected entry: in July 2023 The 1975 was forced to cut short its Good Vibes Festival set after Matty Healy criticised the country's anti-LGBTQ laws and kissed a bandmate, with Healy saying he had not researched the country before booking. Wikipedia country coverage: Custodial and 'rehabilitation' facilities are explicitly prescribed: shariah courts may commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to 6 months (Federal Territories s.56, Kedah s.52, Selangor s.54, Sarawak s.53), and may order cross-dressing or other offenders into counselling/rehabilitation in a religious institution — up to 6 months in Kelantan (s.19-20) and Pahang (s.66), extended to up to 1 year by Terengganu's 2022 amendment. Public-facing venues are also targeted: a Kuala Lumpur gay bar was raided by police and religious enforcement in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants was raided in 2022, and 11 shopping malls were raided in May 2023 over Swatch Pride watches. In November 2024 Kelantan approved amendments to its entertainment law banning activities that promote LGBTQ behaviour. Wikipedia country coverage: Human Rights Watch reports that transgender people face 'discriminatory denial of health care and employment' alongside arbitrary arrest, physical and sexual assault, and imprisonment. Conversion therapy is 'practiced regularly' and openly promoted by politicians and religious leaders, and the 1982 fatwa bars Muslims from sex reassignment surgery unless intersex. The National Blood Centre of Malaysia prohibits homosexuals and bisexuals from donating blood, in a policy that appears gender neutral. No youth-specific health-care or medication-carrying finding appears in the source. Wikipedia country coverage: The source states plainly that 'there are no Malaysian laws that protect the LGBTQ community against discrimination and hate crimes.' By contrast, hate speech rules do cover orientation: the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Content Code 2022, s.6.1(ii), defines hate speech as material that denigrates or devalues a person on grounds including sexual orientation, enforced via s.211 of the Communications and Multimedia Act. Media exclusion is statutory-adjacent: in 1994 the government banned anyone homosexual, bisexual or transsexual from state-controlled media, and Section 377D of the Penal Code (gross indecency, undefined, up to 2 years) remains a discretionary tool. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples have no route to recognition: the source states LGBTQ rights are not pursued by any political party, and at Cambridge Union in June 2019 Mahathir said Malaysia cannot accept same-sex marriage, calling it 'a regressive way of thinking'. The 1982 fatwa additionally ruled that marriages involving transgender people are invalid, though not gazetted. The single exception is the 1975 sharia marriage of transgender woman Sari Kartina to Abdul Razak Othman in Johor Bahru. Adoption is orientation-neutral: under the Adoption Act 1952 and Registration of Adoption Act 1952 there is no restriction on a single person adopting regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.

MYS.tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's 10 August 2022 report "I Don't Want to Change Myself" rests on interviews with 73 LGBT people in Malaysia conducted between 2018 and 2021 across seven states, together with journalists and lawyers, and is the principal evidence base for the finding that every state and the federal territories maintain Sharia codes criminalising gender nonconformity alongside the federal penal penalty of up to 20 years plus mandatory whipping for oral and anal sex.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile places Malaysia among jurisdictions that criminalise same-sex conduct, and lists active litigation there alongside cases from Mauritius and Namibia; its account of the state layer cites the Selangor and Kelantan codes and the Sharia Criminal Code (I) Enactment 2019 covering "sodomy" and "sexual intercourse against the order of nature".

Reuters reported on 21 August 2023 that fears among LGBT people in Malaysia were growing as Islamist opposition foreclosed reform, a political condition that shapes how existing law is enforced rather than altering the text of it.

Human Rights Watch's 24 September 2014 report "I'm Scared to Be a Woman" records that the Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes, that a 1982 National Fatwa Council fatwa ended domestic sex-reassignment surgery, and that a woman was arrested more than 20 times. These are resident-facing barriers, but they also mean a visitor presenting documents with a mismatched gender marker is unlikely to obtain any local correction.
MYS.blindSummary:
The state criminalises both same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at two levels. Sections 377A and 377B of the national penal code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to residents and apply to visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Every one of the 13 provinces and the national capital state/province maintains religious enactments that criminalise cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These provincial offences reach members of the majority faith only. Since the 1980s all 13 provinces have passed such enactments, and three of them also bar women from posing as men. Enforcement is carried out by provincial religious departments, and the laws contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

Litigation has narrowed the provincial layer without loosening the national one. The High Court denied a request to declare the religious prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional, and the national court struck down one province's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 provisions of another province's religious code in February 2024 on division-of-powers grounds, leaving penal code offences fully intact. a constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and public. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the national capital state/province religious enforcement department had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In one high-profile case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue a trans woman for "insulting religion" before she fled abroad and received refugee protection.

Venue raids carry acute exposure risk for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in the national capital and arrested 208 men under section 377B in the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. a magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. a legal support organisation mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Interior Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in a second province.

Trans people face lethal violence and official indifference to it. a transgender woman was killed on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

The wider climate is one of state-backed restriction. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, government-funded "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the religious cross-dressing offences do not apply, but the penal code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.

SGP.name: Singapore
SGP.summary:
Trans identity and same-sex relations are not criminalised in Singapore. Section 377A, which had criminalised sex between men, was repealed in 2022, and Reuters reported in June 2023 that the LGBT community felt safer in the change's wake. There is no religious-police apparatus, and the country records one of the lowest crime rates internationally.

Legal gender recognition is available, but the process is difficult and, according to the MPSC report of February 2025, carries prohibitive cost because genital surgery is a precondition. The same report identifies discrimination, abuse and restrictions affecting transgender students, discrimination in employment, and discrimination and harassment in healthcare settings that discourages transgender people from seeking care.

Statutory protection remains partial. The Workplace Fairness Legislation gives Singapore its first statutory anti-discrimination framework, but gender identity and expression are not protected grounds, so workplace exposure for transgender staff continues; more than 65% of trans Singaporeans report negative workplace experiences. Outright International's overview, updated March 2026, records a further structural gap: LGBTI organisations cannot register, even though same-sex relations are legal and legal gender recognition is possible.

Official data on incarcerated transgender people exists in narrow form. The Singapore Prison Service told the Straits Times on 15 November 2023 that 10 transgender inmates were behind bars and that no cases of assault against them had been recorded.

Media regulation still carries pre-repeal residue. In July 2025 the South China Morning Post reported that a clause of the radio broadcast code groups homosexuality with paedophilia and incest as forbidden lifestyles, prompting calls for review, including from a former radio DJ and actor who argued the grouping has no place in a post-377A Singapore.

The Freedom and Marriage Barometers profile is cited for the existence and coverage of its indices; the actual score values and their trend direction are not present in the available material and remain unresolved here.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The Media Development Authority limits the "promotion or glamorisation of the homosexual lifestyle" on television and radio, including imposing higher age ratings (NC16, M18, R21) on shows or films depicting same-sex sexual activity; in 2019 rapper Joshua Su (The G3sha) withdrew from a TEDx radio talk after being asked not to make "sensitive" comments about his sexuality. Expression in public remains policed under public order provisions: gay men were charged with soliciting in 11 cases between 1990 and 1994 (fines of $200–$500), and Section 294 of the Penal Code covers obscene acts in public places (max three months' imprisonment, fine, or both). Pride expression has nonetheless continued, with Pink Dot SG held annually since 2009 and record crowds of approximately 28,000 attending in recent years. Wikipedia country coverage: Yale-NUS College and Tembusu College of the National University of Singapore provide gender-neutral toilets for their students. During Wikimania 2023 at the Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre (16–19 August 2023), a female toilet was temporarily converted to a gender-neutral one, drawing a public backlash: the Facebook group "We Are Against Pinkdot in Singapore" threatened a boycott of Suntec and users sought petitions against it. Pink Dot SG and non-profit group Oogachaga responded that gender-neutral toilets complement gendered toilets rather than replace them. Government representatives also noted in 2014 that gay bars and clubs operate in Singapore. Wikipedia country coverage: In January 2006 the Ministry of Community Development, Youth and Sports granted S$100,000 (US$61,500) to Liberty League, an "ex-gay" conversion-therapy organisation; activists pressured the group into returning the grant and it has been defunct since 2014. In May 2020 Health Minister Gan Kim Yong wrote that the Ministry of Health expects doctors to practise evidence-based best practice and to respect patients' preferences and circumstances including sexual orientation, with complaints to the Singapore Medical Council as the recourse — though no such complaint had been received from self-declared LGBTQ patients in the prior three years. A May 2019 National University of Singapore study estimated 210,000 men who have sex with men in Singapore, more than double the previous estimate of 90,000, who "could be at risk of a concentrated epidemic of HIV." Same-sex couples also cannot access the same healthcare benefits as heterosexual couples because their relationships are unrecognised. On youth acceptance, a 2021 TODAY Youth Survey found 80% willing to work with LGBTQ people (6% disagreed), 75% willing to form close friendships (10% disagreed) and 58% willing to accept LGBTQ family members (18% disagreed). Wikipedia country coverage: Singapore does not recognise same-sex relationships in any form — marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships — and does not recognise adoption of children by same-sex couples generally. On 29 November 2022 Parliament passed both the repeal of Section 377A and a constitutional amendment protecting Parliament's right (not the judiciary's) to define marriage, leaving open a future simple-majority legalisation of same-sex marriage or civil unions; combined with the Women's Charter precedent that a marriage not between a woman and a man is void, only heterosexual marriages are recognised. One exception: in December 2018 a gay Singaporean man won a landmark appeal to adopt his son fathered through surrogacy in the United States, after which Social and Family Development Minister Desmond Lee said in January 2019 the government does not support "the formation of family units with children of homosexual parents through institutions and processes such as adoption" and would seek to strengthen adoption laws — a statement not yet made into law. Without recognition, same-sex couples cannot access healthcare benefits, inheritance rights or social security benefits.

SGP.tangentialFactors:
Comparison with neighbouring Malaysia is the useful regional frame: Malaysia retains criminalisation and a religious-police presence, which makes Singapore markedly less hazardous for a trans visitor on the same itinerary.

Singapore functions as a medical hub for the wider area, and gender-affirming care is available locally, which matters for visitors needing continuity of prescriptions or care while travelling.

The social environment is visible rather than hidden. Operator and community listings describe a thriving LGBTQIA+ scene with gay-friendly bars such as Backstage Bar in Chinatown, alongside pop-ups and exhibitions, and visitor-facing guidance on solo travel and room sharing is published by tour operators.

The Freedom and Marriage Barometers country profile carries interactive scores across unified, gay and transgender rights indices and an LGBTQI+ perception index covering 2011 to 2024, tracking de jure protections against lived experience; the direction of those scores is not itemised in the available material.

IRN.name: Iran
IRN.summary:
Iran is among the most severe environments in the world for a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor. The Islamic Penal Code criminalises all same-sex activity for men and women, with penalties running from flogging to execution, and Human Rights Watch has recorded executions carried out for homosexual conduct, most recently documenting two men put to death in November 2005. The UK Home Office's December 2025 country report notes that convictions are also brought under more severe charges used as a pretext, and that the code contains no discrimination protections of any kind.

The country's position is bifurcated. Transsexuality is legally recognised, following a 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Khomeini, and gender-reassignment surgery is permitted and may be state-subsidised after a diagnosis of "gender identity disorder." Recognition of a person's acquired gender, however, comes only after surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process. Surgery is described by the UK Home Office as invasive and frequently carried out to a sub-standard level.

For a trans visitor the practical consequence is that legal recognition does not travel with you. An LGBT+ person living openly in Iran without recognised surgery is assessed by the UK Home Office as likely to face persecution, and the same report places trans people who have not completed the surgical and legal pathway under immorality and indecency provisions carrying imprisonment, fines and corporal punishment.

Custodial violence is documented. Ghazal Marzban, an imprisoned trans rights activist, recounted in an open letter published by HRANA being raped while held in a Ministry of Intelligence detention facility. Public space is also restricted by administrative pressure: Tehran authorities issued a public warning instructing transgender people to avoid "busy" areas of the capital, an official advisory that narrows where gender-nonconforming people may appear.

Coercion shapes the recognition system itself. Reporting in 2025 describes pressure on Iranian trans people to conform to a binary transition or face legal penalty, with state funding for surgery presented as protection while functioning as the price of tolerance. Human Rights Watch's country analysis frames the same arrangement as state-funded surgery purchased at the cost of dignity. At the same time, foreign patients travel to Iran for the subsidised procedure, and trans medical tourism has grown into a visible industry.

Documented persecution is systematic rather than incidental. A 6Rang submission to the UN Independent Expert on Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression, filed in February 2025, surveyed 25 LGBTIQ+ people who had fled Iran and found 96% of them from ethnic minorities, describing forces driving displacement from the country. 6Rang's January–February 2025 submission to Iran's Universal Periodic Review separately catalogued human-rights violations against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people, including violence and legal discrimination.
IRN.outOfScopeNotes:
The current status and terms of the Tehran advisory warning transgender people to avoid busy areas are not resolved here: the inventory confirms the warning was issued but does not establish whether it remains formally in force or how it is enforced.

The outcome of Ghazal Marzban's criminal case and her custody location at the time of the HRANA publication are not sourced in this inventory; the account of the assault in a Ministry of Intelligence detention facility is documented, the subsequent proceedings are not.

No source in this inventory addresses passport or visa screening of gender markers for entry into Iran, airport treatment of trans travellers, or the availability of names and pronouns in official documents. Any statement about entry screening would be unsourced.

Figures specific to executions or imprisonments of trans people as distinct from same-sex conduct are not available here; the inventory supports execution records for homosexual conduct and imprisonment under immorality provisions for people without recognised surgery, but not a combined count.

The extent to which state-subsidised surgery meets clinical standards rests on the UK Home Office's characterisation of procedures as invasive and often sub-standard; no independent clinical audit is present in the inventory.

Whether the UPR and UN Special Procedures submissions produced any change in Iranian law or practice by the date of this record is unresolved; the inventory documents the filings, not their effect.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Under Article 20, Clause 14, a person who has had sex reassignment surgery can legally change their name and gender on birth certification upon a court order, and the government reportedly provided these corrected identity documents efficiently and transparently. Supporters of gender reassignment also invoke Article 215 of Iran's civil code (acts subject to 'rational benefit'), though medical approval from a doctor is required. One documented downside: new military identity cards listed the subsection of law exempting gay men and transgender individuals, who are classified as having mental disorders — a disclosure 6Rang warned identifies them and puts them at risk of violence and discrimination. Wikipedia country coverage: The source documents asylum pathways but not visa regimes: many LGBTQ Iranians seek UNHCR refugee status to be resettled in Australia, Canada, or the United States, and some middle-class Iranians have received education in Western nations. Asylum outcomes have been mixed — the UNHCR rejected a plea in 2001 from an Iranian man who had entered the country illegally and was later convicted of killing his boyfriend; Japan rejected an Iranian gay man's asylum claim in 2005, and Sweden rejected a similar appeal that same year. One case resolved the other way: LGBTQ activist Zahra Seddiqi Hamedani was reported to be living in Cologne, Germany in December 2023. Wikipedia country coverage: The Netherlands stopped deporting gay men back to Iran temporarily in 2006; in March 2006 Dutch Immigration Minister Rita Verdonk stated there was 'no question of executions or death sentences based solely on the fact that a defendant is gay,' but after internal and external pressure she reversed course in October 2006 and announced Iranian LGBTs would not be deported. The United Kingdom drew criticism for continued deportations, with news reports documenting gay Iranians who committed suicide when faced with deportation; some campaign-backed cases such as Kiana Firouz and Mehdi Kazemi ended in asylum grants. Separately, the 2017 US State Department report noted that security forces raided houses, monitored internet sites for information on LGBTI persons, and that 6Rang documented forced 'anal' or 'sodomy' tests and degrading treatment on persons charged with homosexual conduct. Wikipedia country coverage: The 2017 US State Department report describes custodial facilities used against LGBTI people: following an April 13, 2017 IRGC raid on a private party in Isfahan Province in which agents reportedly fired weapons and used electric Tasers, the Canadian nonprofit Iranian Railroad for Queer Refugees reported those arrested were taken to Dastgerd Prison in Isfahan, where they were led to the prison yard and told they would be executed. Earlier, in February 2008, police in Isfahan raided a party and arrested 30 men who were held indefinitely without a lawyer on suspicion of homosexual activity. On the health side, since the mid-2000s the Iranian government has provided transgender persons grants of up to 45 million rials (about $1,240) and loans up to 55 million rials (about $1,500) for gender reassignment surgery, and the Ministry of Cooperatives, Labor, and Social Welfare required health insurers to cover such surgery; HIV/AIDS medication is given free of charge to all Iranian citizens and several clinics offer free testing and counselling. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legally recognized in Iran, and no legislation exists to address discrimination or bias-motivated violence on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Because the government does not allow any political party or organization to endorse LGBTQ rights, vague support has fallen to exiled groups such as the Green Party of Iran, the Worker Communist Party of Iran, the Worker's Way, the Glorious Frontiers Party, and the Constitutionalist Party of Iran. Enforcement is severe: in 2016 Mullah Taha, an Iranian Shia gay cleric, was forced to flee Iran after conducting same-sex marriages, and gay Iranian couples report being afraid to be seen together in public while traditional families strongly influence who and when their children marry. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth-specific findings are prominent: the 2017 US State Department report noted concerns about LGBTI minors, and the law sets the death penalty as legal for those above 18, and for murder, at the age of 15. Documented cases involving young people include the January 2008 arrest of Hamzeh Chavi (18) and Loghman Hamzehpour (19) in Sardasht on sodomy and mohārebe charges, the reported 2006 hanging of two youths in north-eastern Iran for 'sex crimes,' the 2022 case of two gay men in Maragheh whose death sentences for 'sodomy by force' — a charge stemming from an accusation by a 16-year-old boy — were later commuted to life in prison, and the May 2021 murder of 20-year-old Ali Monfared allegedly by relatives. On education, the government approved a booklet explaining condoms and distributed it to high school students and ran comprehensive HIV/AIDS education by the late 1990s, but no educational campaign for LGBTQ people has been allowed to exist; Kaveh Khoshnood noted that without acknowledging homosexuality's existence, no programs for LGBTQ people can be developed. Youth-facing cultural resources include the 2015 graphic novel Yousef and Farhad, published in English and Persian by OutRight Action International, and Maryam Keshavarz's 2011 film Circumstances about changing Iranian youth mores on sex and dating.

IRN.tangentialFactors:
Iran is a regional outlier in two directions at once: it combines one of the world's harshest criminal regimes for same-sex conduct with formal state recognition and public funding for gender-affirming surgery, an arrangement found in almost no neighbouring jurisdiction. Visitors comparing the country with other regional destinations should not read the availability of surgery as an indicator of general safety.

The medical-tourism trade is a point of contrast between visitors and residents. Foreign patients arrive for subsidised, low-cost procedures that Iranian trans people are pushed toward under penalty, so clinics catering to international clients coexist with domestic pressure to complete a binary transition. LGBTQ Nation's 2025 reporting on the boom is the clearest documentation of that split.

Persecution documented against LGBTIQ+ people overlaps substantially with ethnic and minority status: 96% of the 25 people surveyed by 6Rang for its February 2025 UN submission were from ethnic minorities, which suggests that a trans visitor perceived as belonging to a minority group faces an added layer of exposure.

The enforcement backdrop includes state execution for same-sex conduct, recorded by Human Rights Watch over two decades, and periodic spikes in official statements against LGBT people. 6Rang's UPR submission, timed to the 48th session in January–February 2025, indicates that the international review mechanism is an active channel for this documentation, though it does not itself change conditions on the ground.
IRN.localsOnly:
Iranian residents must obtain a diagnosis of "gender identity disorder" before surgery can proceed, after which the state may subsidise the cost of the operation. Full legal recognition of a person's acquired gender depends on completing that surgery, undergoing sterilisation and passing through a lengthy legal process; until every step is finished, the prior legal status continues to apply.

The pathway is not free choice. Reporting by LGBTQ Nation and Business Insider describes forced or strongly coerced transitions for Iranian citizens, where pressure to conform to a binary male/female outcome replaces the option of living outside that framework, and where refusal carries legal penalty. State funding for surgery is presented publicly as protection while operating as the condition of tolerance.

Residents who live openly as LGBT+ without recognised surgery are treated under immorality and indecency provisions, with imprisonment, fines and lashing available as penalties, and the UK Home Office records that charges may be brought under more severe provisions as a pretext. There are no statutory discrimination protections covering sexual orientation or gender identity.

Trans people face restrictions on movement and assembly in practice as well as in law: Tehran authorities publicly instructed transgender residents to stay out of busy areas of the capital. Detention carries documented risk of sexual violence, as the account of activist Ghazal Marzban of rape in a Ministry of Intelligence facility demonstrates.

Displacement is a common outcome. 6Rang's February 2025 survey of 25 LGBTIQ+ people who left the country found 96% were from ethnic minorities, and its UPR submission documents the pattern of persecution, violence and legal discrimination that drives people out.
IRN.blindSummary:
The state is among the most severe environments in the world for a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor. The national penal code criminalises all same-sex activity for men and women, with penalties running from flogging to the death penalty, and an international human-rights organisation has recorded executions carried out for homosexual conduct, most recently documenting two men put to death in November 2005. The parent nation's asylum office reports in its national country assessment that convictions are also brought under more severe charges used as a pretext, and that the code contains no discrimination protections of any kind.

The jurisdiction's position is bifurcated. Transsexuality is legally recognised under a 1987 religious ruling by the country's founding supreme leader, and gender-reassignment surgery is permitted and may be publicly subsidised after a diagnosis of "gender identity disorder." Recognition of a person's acquired gender, however, comes only after surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process. Surgery is described by the parent nation's asylum office as invasive and frequently carried out to a sub-standard level.

For a trans visitor the practical consequence is that legal recognition does not travel with you. a LGBT+ person living openly without recognised surgery is assessed by the parent nation's asylum office as likely to face persecution, and the same assessment places trans people who have not completed the surgical and legal pathway under immorality and indecency provisions carrying imprisonment, fines and corporal punishment.

Custodial violence is documented. a trans rights activist imprisoned in the country recounted in an open letter published by a domestic human-rights group being raped while held in a national intelligence detention facility. Public space is also restricted by administrative pressure: the municipal authorities of the capital issued a public warning instructing transgender people to avoid "busy" areas, an official advisory that narrows where gender-nonconforming people may appear.

Coercion shapes the recognition system itself. Reporting in 2025 describes pressure on residents to conform to a binary transition or face legal penalty, with state/province funding for surgery presented as protection while functioning as the price of tolerance. The same international human-rights organisation's country analysis frames the arrangement as publicly funded surgery purchased at the cost of dignity. At the same time, foreign patients travel to the country for the subsidised procedure, and trans medical tourism has grown into a visible industry.

Documented persecution is systematic rather than incidental. a national LGBTIQ+ organisation's February 2025 submission to the national-level UN expert on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression surveyed 25 people who had fled the state and found 96% of them from ethnic minorities, describing forces driving displacement. The same organisation's submission to the state's universal periodic review, filed for the January–February 2025 session, separately catalogued human-rights violations against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people, including violence and legal discrimination.
IRN.blindOutOfScope:
The current status and terms of the capital's advisory warning transgender people to avoid busy areas are not resolved here: the inventory confirms the warning was issued but does not establish whether it remains formally in force or how it is enforced.

The outcome of the imprisoned activist's criminal case and her custody location at the time of the human-rights group's publication are not sourced in this inventory; the account of the assault in a national intelligence detention facility is documented, the subsequent proceedings are not.

No source in this inventory addresses passport or visa screening of gender markers for entry into the state, airport treatment of trans travellers, or the availability of names and pronouns in official documents. Any statement about entry screening would be unsourced.

Figures specific to executions or imprisonments of trans people as distinct from same-sex conduct are not available here; the inventory supports execution records for homosexual conduct and imprisonment under immorality provisions for people without recognised surgery, but not a combined count.

The extent to which state/province-subsidised surgery meets clinical standards rests on the parent nation's asylum office characterising procedures as invasive and often sub-standard; no independent clinical audit is present in the inventory.

Whether the universal periodic review and national-level UN expert submissions produced any change in law or practice by the date of this record is unresolved; the inventory documents the filings, not their effect.

ISR.name: Israel
ISR.summary:
Israel does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct, and its legal framework carries anti-discrimination protections alongside publicly funded transition healthcare. Legal gender recognition runs through the courts, and as of 2025 registration of a person's previous name has been abolished for transgender people, removing the old-name traceability that previously followed a document change. Tel Aviv functions as a regional queer hub, and the country is widely regarded as the most progressive destination in its part of the world for trans visitors.

Border screening is the sharpest visitor-specific risk. A first-person account published by Haaretz in May 2023 documents a transgender traveller subjected to gender-identity humiliation at an Israeli airport, with security personnel insisting "if you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male". The Israel Police adopted a new regulation governing searches of transgender people in 2023, in response to complaints about humiliating searches of trans detainees and travellers. That change governs search protocol; it does not establish that border screening will be conducted with respect for a visitor's stated gender.

Violence against LGBT people rose in Israel during 2025, according to official data reported by the Jerusalem Post, and Ynet reported anti-LGBTQ violence reaching a record high, with dating-app traps and organised ambushes used to lure victims into assaults. Haaretz reported in February 2025 that inflammatory messaging from the United States was feeding into the local climate, with trans Israelis describing heightened fear as a result.

Custody remains the weakest point of the protection framework. Documentation in a law-journal article establishes that Israel's response to transgender prisoners' vulnerability has been isolation or segregation from the general prison population rather than placement in facilities matching gender identity, and trans women have at least at times been held in men's prisons. Courts have intervened case by case: in October 2019, following a petition by ACRI, an Israeli court ordered the Israel Prison Service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and transfer her from a male prison to a female one. She was initially housed in a separate wing of the women's prison, and ACRI prepared a further petition seeking her placement with the general population.

On partner recognition, a Channel 10 survey found most Israelis favour same-sex marriage while half of Members of the Knesset declined to state a position, including a culture minister who has marched in the Pride parade.
ISR.outOfScopeNotes:
Two sources in the inventory could not be used. The LegalClarity page on trans rights in Israel returned HTTP 404 at research time and its content is unresolved; nothing from it is reflected here.

A direct conflict between sources is unresolved: Outright International's profile states there is no legal gender recognition in Israel, while the Jerusalem Post reports that registration of a previous name has been abolished for transgender people. The inventory does not reconcile the two, and the scope of the 2025 change (whether it covers full marker change or only removal of the prior-name trace) is not sourced.

Not sourced: whether Israel issues a non-binary or third gender marker; whether the 2023 police search regulation extends to airport border screening or applies only to police searches in custody; trans-specific breakdowns of the 2025 violence statistics; and any post-2025 court rulings on prison placement.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2, D4, D6, D8, D13.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Public expression has expanded but repeatedly drawn violence: Israel's first LGBT pride march (Alizada) was held 17 September 1977, Tel Aviv's first Pride parade in 1993, and Eilat Pride began in 2001. Jerusalem Pride was initially banned by municipal order until a court overturned it; the 2005 march was attacked by Haredi man Yishai Schlissel (3 stabbed, 10-year sentence), and after his 2015 release he stabbed six marchers, killing teenage girl Shira Banki. The 2018 Aguda-organized LGBTQ strike drew over 100,000 to a Tel Aviv rally, and an estimated 250,000 marched in Tel Aviv Pride in June 2022. The 2025 Tel Aviv Pride (13 June) was cancelled by the municipality after Israeli strikes on Iranian targets, while in 2026 the Jerusalem Municipality raised the Pride flag for the first time along the route from Sacher Park to the Knesset. Wikipedia country coverage: In December 2004 the Tel Aviv District Court ruled the government acted illegally in trying to deport the Colombian partner of a gay Israeli soldier, extending a 1999 Supreme Court rule barring deportation of foreign nationals married to Israeli citizens to common-law and same-sex couples. In March 2008 the Interior Ministry granted a rare residency permit to a gay Palestinian from Jenin to live with his partner of 8 years in Tel Aviv, citing danger to his life in the West Bank. In December 2016 Attorney General Avichai Mandelblit instructed the Interior Ministry to give same-sex couples the same citizenship rights as opposite-sex couples; previously same-sex spouses of Israeli citizens waited up to seven years for citizenship and typically received only permanent residency. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2008 the City of Tel Aviv opened the Municipal LGBT Community Center, the first of its kind in the country. On 1 August 2009 an armed attacker killed two people and injured 15 at a lesbian and gay centre in Tel Aviv, condemned by PM Netanyahu and President Peres. Community infrastructure also includes the Jerusalem Open House, which staged the 21 June 2007 Jerusalem parade after police allocated thousands of personnel to secure the area, and a central Jerusalem square to be renamed "Tolerance Square" in memory of Shira Banki. In 2026 the Jerusalem Municipality hung Pride flags with the Hebrew inscription "equality in life" along the parade route. Wikipedia country coverage: On 14 February 2022 Health Minister Nitzan Horowitz issued an executive directive banning licensed medical professionals (psychologists, social workers, Ministry of Health-licensed therapists) from conducting conversion therapy, though it does not bind rabbis, clergy or alternative practitioners and has not been codified into law by the Knesset. Reproductive care was restricted: a July 2018 surrogacy law excluded single men and same-sex couples, but the High Court of Justice ruled on 27 February 2020 and the Supreme Court unanimously on 11 July 2021 that the ban violated equality and the right to parenthood, effective 12 January 2022. Trans healthcare was historically denied — Attorney General Haim Cohn blocked Rina Natan's sex reassignment surgery in 1954, and legal recognition of sex reassignment only came in 1986; in July 2025 the High Court blocked a fast-track attempt to undo a gender change, holding the 2021 certificate "remains valid." Youth-specific: the governing coalition defeated a bill to ban conversion therapy on 24 February 2016, and the same day defeated a bill to train health professionals on gender and sexual orientation issues. Wikipedia country coverage: Under the British Mandate, official questionnaires documented "unnatural" sexual expression including sodomy between school boys, and Britain pushed criminalization into Palestinian schools and society, a policy carried into the Israeli state. In 1943 the Acre district court tried Mustafa Naif, aged 16, alongside Mustafa Zaharan for sodomy; Naif recanted to protect his friend, was convicted of perjury instead, and faced a sodomy charge carrying up to 10 years' imprisonment. Youth are also direct targets of violence: Shira Banki, a teenage girl, was stabbed to death at the 2015 Jerusalem Pride parade. On family formation, between 2008 and 2017 only 3 of 550 same-sex couples seeking to adopt succeeded (versus over a thousand heterosexual couples), until the government reversed course in August 2017 under Supreme Court pressure; the Knesset also voted in July 2018 to keep single men and same-sex couples out of surrogacy.

ISR.tangentialFactors:
Israel's regional standing cuts both ways. The absence of criminalisation, the court route to document change and publicly funded transition care place it ahead of every neighbouring jurisdiction, but the practical experience of a trans arrival is shaped by security screening rather than by statute, and the airport account shows a border officer applying a surgical criterion to a person's legal sex.

The violence trend is documented at the aggregate LGBT level rather than the trans level. Official figures for 2025 show an increase in anti-LGBTQ attacks, and the record totals reported by Ynet include lure-by-dating-app ambushes, a tactic that targets individuals who are identifiable as queer or trans through their profiles. The sources do not break the assault totals down by victim gender identity.

Outright International's at-a-glance profile for Israel, last updated 12 March 2026, lists no legal gender recognition and states that LGBTI organisations cannot register, a baseline that sits uneasily beside the documented abolition of previous-name registration. Public opinion and legislative opinion on same-sex marriage diverge, with majority support recorded in polling and half of lawmakers unwilling to commit to a position.
ISR.localsOnly:
Residents can change their legal gender through the courts, and since 2025 the previous name is no longer registered for transgender people, so the old name does not remain traceable on official records after a change.

Transition healthcare is publicly funded, and anti-discrimination protections apply in ordinary civilian life. The Israel Police search regulation adopted in 2023 governs how searches of transgender detainees are conducted and was a direct response to complaints from trans people about humiliating treatment in custody.

Trans residents face the same documented rise in anti-LGBTQ violence recorded for 2025, including organised ambushes, and report heightened fear linked to imported political rhetoric. Custody practice defaults to isolating transgender prisoners from the general population; court orders have forced individual reviews, as in the 2019 hormone therapy and transfer ruling, but segregation remains the standard management approach rather than placement by gender identity with the general population.

LGBTI organisations in Israel cannot register, which constrains the resident advocacy machinery that would otherwise absorb complaints of this kind.

ARG.name: Argentina
ARG.summary:
Argentina's statutory framework remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, passed by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, was promulgated on 24 May 2012 and allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was also the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree modifying the Gender Identity Law as it applies to minors, and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prisons. Reuters reported that the decree bans gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for the rights of adolescents, and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented peak in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes described the figure as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated aggravation is therefore not currently applied in that line of cases.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.
ARG.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the February 2025 decrees survive constitutional challenge is unresolved in the available sources. Legal experts are recorded as calling them illegal and unconstitutional and as intending to petition the courts, but no ruling is sourced here.

The inventory does not state whether the core self-identification provisions of Law 26.743 for adults remain fully operative after the decrees, or only the provisions touching minors and prison housing. The distinction is not sourced and should be verified against the decree texts.

No source records how the current framework is applied to foreign nationals seeking document changes or entry on the basis of a changed gender marker, and no data is available on screening of trans travellers at Argentine border points.

The removal of the travesticidio aggravating circumstance in 2020 and its rejection by the Supreme Court in 2025 are sourced to one case; whether the aggravator is unavailable across all gender-motivated homicide prosecutions is not established here.

ARE.name: United Arab Emirates
ARE.summary:
The United Arab Emirates subjects trans visitors to gender-document screening at the border. In 2025, two Israeli trans women were detained for hours at Dubai airport, X-rayed to check whether their genitals matched the female sex recorded in their passports, mocked by staff, and denied entry with their passports confiscated.

Entry refusals on identity grounds are documented across a decade. In August 2016 the trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was denied entry and detained at Dubai airport. In March 2022 the Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon, 2014 Miss Tiffany Universe runner-up, was stopped at Dubai immigration and interrogated for nine hours before being deported to Thailand ahead of her Expo 2020 appearance; her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman.

The legal framework underpinning these encounters explicitly acknowledges and penalises nonconformity with traditional gender roles, and transgender expression or unconventional appearance frequently results in arrest, confinement or expulsion. A new federal criminal code enacted in early 2022 criminalised consensual same-sex relations with up to six months' imprisonment, and charges under it require a complaint basis.

There is no legal gender recognition in the UAE, so a visitor's documents cannot be brought into line with lived gender before travel. Foreign nationals also face prolonged custody: a Brazilian trans woman has been detained since September 2022, arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test, and in April 2023 she accused the consulate of negligence over her case.
ARE.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether genital X-ray screening at Dubai airport is a written procedure or an ad hoc practice by individual officers is not resolved by the available sources; the 2025 account establishes that it occurred, not that it is codified.

No source in the inventory gives conviction or sentencing data under the 2022 code's six-month provision, so the frequency of enforcement is unresolved.

The inventory does not address hate-crime protection, healthcare access, bathroom or facilities rules, or partner recognition for trans visitors; nothing should be inferred about those from the entries above.

Cairo 52 describes legal mechanisms penalising gender nonconformity without naming the specific articles relied on, so the statutory basis of those provisions remains unresolved here.

The outcome of the Brazilian detainee's case, and whether her consulate responded to the negligence allegation, are unresolved.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: No LGBTQI+ support or advocacy organizations operate openly in the country; social attitudes toward homosexuality and varied gender expression, together with the likelihood of state repression, prevent the establishment of such organizations or community education on related issues. In Dubai, legal and social sanctions mean that no formal LGBTQ organizations or nightclubs exist — one nightclub that sponsored a special night for the LGBTQ community was shut down by the government. Sex reassignment surgery is severely restricted to limited circumstances that are highly regulated by the state. Wikipedia country coverage: Involuntary medical and psychological 'treatments', including administration of hormonal therapies and detention for forced psychological treatments, have occurred in relation to suspected or established same-sex sexual conduct. Gay conversion practices are not prohibited or discouraged by any law or regulation. Health care access is also implicated in the 2007 Dubai case, where the family of a raped 16-year-old French-Swiss boy accused UAE authorities of failing to notify them that one of the rapists was HIV-positive, delaying medical attention. Gigi Gorgeous, a transgender woman, was detained for five hours at Dubai International Airport in August 2016 because authorities did not recognise her gender as legitimate, and her passport was confiscated. Wikipedia country coverage: There have been reports of mistreatment in detention — beatings and forced rectal examinations amounting to torture — as a consequence of suspected or established same-sex sexual conduct. In 2012 police raided and broke up a gay party of 30 men in Dubai; two Indian men arrested for consensual sex in a public toilet that year received six months each plus deportation. In a 2007 Dubai case, a 16-year-old boy who was kidnapped and raped was initially treated by police as a suspect, and fear of being charged under Article 177 drove him and his family to leave the country; he was later awarded AED 15 million (US$4 million) in civil compensation. In December 2013, two Brazilian transgender women who called police about prejudice they witnessed in a nightclub were themselves arrested for 'imitating women', held until March 2014, fined AED 10,000 and ordered deported. Wikipedia country coverage: There are no protections under any UAE law or policy against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. Same-sex conduct remains explicitly criminalised under Article 409(1)(b) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law (2021), carrying a minimum sentence of six months' imprisonment with no maximum prescribed. Wikipedia country coverage: The UAE does not recognise same-sex marriage. Under Article 409(5) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law (2021), no criminal action for same-sex conduct may be brought except upon a complaint by the spouse or guardian of the complainant, who may withdraw it at any time. Because civil guardianship ends at age 18, no eligible complainant exists for consensual male-male sexual conduct between adults, so federal prosecution is not possible; for female-female relations, an unmarried Muslim woman's father or male relative may qualify as guardian under the Islamic wali concept and a married woman's husband as spouse, so prosecution remains possible where such a complainant exists. Wikipedia country coverage: Censorship heavily targets youth-facing material: the UAE's Media Regulatory Office banned Pixar's Lightyear in June 2022 for depicting a same-sex relationship, and in the same month the popular Arabic-language children's comic Majid came under investigation for allegedly promoting homosexuality, with its May 2022 edition withdrawn over dialogue using the Arabic word مثلي (mithli). In June 2023 the UAE banned Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse over a scene showing a 'Protect Trans Lives' transgender flag, and Amazon blocked search results for 150 terms (including 'lgbtq', 'pride', 'closeted gay') on its UAE site under threat of penalties. The country's internet provider blocks sites on dating, marriage and LGBTQ issues, and any site containing the word 'gay' or 'sex', limiting young people's access to information. Youth are also directly criminalised and vulnerable: in 2005 Abu Dhabi police raided a gathering where 26 young men were accused of cross-dressing and preparing a 'gay wedding' (11 sentenced to five years, one to one year), and a 16-year-old boy was raped in Dubai in 2007 and treated as a suspect. Gay conversion practices are not prohibited, no community education on LGBTQ issues can be established, and the UAE ranked 85th with a score of 37 on PlanetRomeo's 2015 Gay Happiness Index. Wikipedia country coverage: No LGBTQI+ support or advocacy organizations operate openly anywhere in the UAE; in Dubai, no formal LGBTQ organizations or nightclubs exist, and a nightclub that sponsored a special night for the LGBTQ community was shut down by the government. Social attitudes plus the likelihood of state repression prevent establishment of such organizations or community education. Medical facilities are also constrained: sex reassignment surgery is severely restricted to limited, state-regulated circumstances, and detainees have been held in cells designated for 'effeminate' people. Wikipedia country coverage: Involuntary medical and psychological 'treatments' — including administration of hormonal therapies and detention for forced psychological treatments — have occurred in connection with suspected or established same-sex sexual conduct, and beatings and forced rectal examinations amounting to torture have been reported in detention. Youth-specific: a 16-year-old French-Swiss boy raped in Dubai in July 2007 was initially treated by police as a suspect, and fear of being charged under Article 177 drove him and his family to leave the country. Wikipedia country coverage: In July 2007 in Dubai, a 16-year-old French-Swiss boy was kidnapped and raped by a group of men; he was initially treated as a suspect and his family left the country, though he was later awarded AED 15 million (US$4 million) in civil compensation. Reports of mistreatment in detention — beatings and forced rectal examinations amounting to torture — have been consequences of suspected or established same-sex sexual conduct. Police raids and arrests for same-sex conduct and cross-dressing have occurred, including the 2005 Abu Dhabi desert resort raid on 26 young men and the 2012 raid breaking up a gay party of 30 men in Dubai. Under Article 412(2), men who disguise themselves as women to enter a women-only space may be imprisoned for up to one year and fined up to AED 10,000; this replaced a broader previous ban on wearing clothing 'inappropriate for one's sex'. Prosecution under Article 409 requires a complaint from a spouse or guardian, who may withdraw it at any time. ZAF.name: South Africa
ZAF.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075), a challenge brought against the Department of Correctional Services with the assistance of Lawyers for Human Rights. The court held that refusing a transgender inmate prescribed gender-affirming health care falls below the required standard of health care, and that refusing feminising clothing and accessories is likewise unlawful. Orders compelling the Department to provide hormone treatment at state expense, permit clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, implement the accommodations required by its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and deliver prescribed medical care were granted. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling the same day.

Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling; reporting in August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice. Detention therefore remains a site of elevated risk for trans visitors and residents despite the binding remedies now in place.

Outside prison, everyday exposure is shaped by documents. The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Costs of affirming one's gender through the process are described as dauntingly high. Where documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman who was met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month. Violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 examining whether the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act read with section 9 of the Constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.
