The extent to which the Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure is implemented across facilities after the November 2025 orders is not resolved by the available sources; rights organisations expressed doubt before the ruling and no post-ruling compliance reporting is available here.

Whether exclusion from gender-segregated bathrooms constitutes unfair discrimination remains an open question: the source is a 2024 academic analysis of the issue rather than a reported court holding, and no binding precedent on facility access is sourced.

The status and timing of the pending reform toward self-determining legal gender recognition, and whether the medical requirements will be removed, are not sourced and should be checked against current legislation before travel.

Whether the 2024 Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act has produced prosecutions in cases involving gender identity is not evidenced in the inventory, so its enforcement record remains unverified here.

Sentencing outcomes in the Tshwane tavern assault and the identity of those detained in the December 2024 killings are not sourced beyond the report of an arrest.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D1, D2, D4, D5, D13, D14.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Sex between men was a common-law crime of 'sodomy' and 'unnatural sexual offence' inherited from Roman-Dutch law; under the National Party (1948-1994) homosexuality carried up to seven years in prison, used to break up gay events and harass activists (e.g. the January 1966 Forest Town raid), and a 1969 amendment to the Immorality Act barred men from erotic conduct with more than two people present. Male same-sex conduct was legalised in 1994 (female same-sex conduct was never illegal), and in 1998 the Constitutional Court confirmed in National Coalition for Gay and Lesbian Equality v Minister of Justice that sodomy and 'unnatural sexual act' offences were unconstitutional, applying retroactively to 27 April 1994. A residual Sexual Offences provision kept the age of consent at 19 for homosexual acts versus 16 for heterosexual acts until the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Related Matters) Amendment Act equalised it at 16 in gender-neutral terms in 2007 (the inequality was declared unconstitutional in Geldenhuys v NDPP in 2008, retroactive to 1994). As of a 2017 ILGA poll, 24% of South Africans still said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals, while 57% disagreed. Wikipedia country coverage: The Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (2000) prohibits hate speech and harassment on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds and set up Equality Courts; before this, South Africa had no statutory hate-crime penalty regime and courts treated homophobic hatred only as an aggravating sentencing factor. The Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Bill was passed by the National Assembly in March 2023 and the National Council in November 2023 and signed into law by President Ramaphosa in May 2024, its hate-speech wording tightened after 2016 public consultation so that it requires a 'clear intention' to be harmful, incite harm or promote hatred on grounds including gender or gender identity and sexual orientation. Human Rights Watch and other legal experts warned the bill is vague, threatens freedom of expression, and has been likened to the Suppression of Communism Act, 1950. The Department of Justice's National Task Team (2011) and National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities (April 2014) addressed sex- and gender-based violence, with a rapid response team for unsolved cases. Wikipedia country coverage: The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act lets a person change their sex status in the population registry and obtain identity documents and passports indicating their gender identity, requiring medical or surgical treatment such as hormone replacement therapy (sex reassignment surgery is not required); hormone therapy is available from age 16 and surgery from 18, or younger with parental consent. In October 2021 the Department of Home Affairs announced plans to introduce gender-neutral identification on South African ID cards — the first African country to do so — with an identity-management document estimating 530,000 non-binary residents, though the head of policy confirmed changes will take a few years as they move through consultation to legislation. Court decisions extending to same-sex couples before and after the Civil Union Act include immigration benefits, employment and pension benefits and joint adoption. South Africa ranks among the world's best in the 2025 Spartacus Gay Travel Index and Equaldex LGBT Equality Index, and the official South African Tourism site offers in-depth travel tips for gay travellers. Wikipedia country coverage: The source text contains no provisions on border checks, entry screening or security screening of travellers. The only screening-type policy described is blood donation: until 2014 the South African National Blood Service required men who have sex with men to abstain from sex for six months before donating, replaced by a gender-neutral rule barring any donor with a new sexual partner in the last six months or more than one partner. Wikipedia country coverage: Age-of-consent rules hit young people directly: homosexual acts were gated at 19 versus 16 for heterosexual acts until the 2007 Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Related Matters) Amendment Act set a uniform 16 in gender-neutral terms (inequality declared unconstitutional in Geldenhuys, 2008, retroactive to 1994). South Africa has no specific anti-bullying law, though the Protection from Harassment Act 17 of 2011 and Child Justice Act 75 of 2008 cover homophobic harassment and youth offenders; per the Department of Basic Education, South African pupils are the 'most bullied kids in the world' — a 2015 TIMSS survey found 44% of Grade 5 pupils (age 10-11) bullied weekly and 34% monthly, the highest of 38 countries, 48% of public-school pupils bullied weekly, and Grade 9 pupils (14-15) third-most bullied at 17% weekly and 47% monthly. A bill introduced in 2021 would ban conversion therapy on children — still not prohibited under the Children's Act 38 of 2005 — after three teens aged 15-19 died at a conversion therapy camp whose owners were convicted of murder and child abuse in February 2015. Transgender minors access hormone therapy from 16 and surgery from 18 (or younger with parental consent), with private care mostly urban and public systems facing long waits, forcing rural youth to travel to major cities; a non-binary teenager, Zade de Kock, petitioned Home Affairs over being forced to use inaccurate gender markers throughout his schooling. Active LGBT student organisations exist at Wits, UCT, Stellenbosch, UJ and UWC. Wikipedia country coverage: Visibility is high: the first Lesbian and Gay Pride march was held in Johannesburg on 13 October 1990 (about 800 people), and Pride is now held annually in Cape Town, Johannesburg, Durban, Pretoria and Soweto, with smaller cities including Bloemfontein, Polokwane, Port Elizabeth, Mbombela, East London, Pietermaritzburg and Knysna hosting LGBT events — Knysna's Pink Loerie Mardi Gras draws visitors nationwide. Cape Town is called one of the world's friendliest LGBTQ+ cities, with the De Waterkant gay village, a permanent rainbow crosswalk and the Pink Lane. Public opinion is mixed but comparatively favourable: the 2015 Progressive Prudes study found 55% would accept a gay family member and 51% that gay people should have the same human rights; Afrobarometer (2016) put South Africa second in Africa at 67% comfortable with a same-sex couple next door versus a 21% Africa-wide average; ILGA (2017) found 67% back equal rights for gay and lesbian people and 72% for transgender people; and an Ipsos poll in May 2021 found 71% support some legal recognition for same-sex couples, 18% having attended a same-sex wedding. Violence remains a gap: lesbians have been murdered, beaten and subjected to 'corrective rape' (including among pupils), activists accuse police of negligent handling including nine allegedly related murders of gay men between 2010 and 2013, and ActionAid has condemned impunity; in 2012 Contralesa petitioned to remove LGBT rights from the Constitution, but the ANC parliamentary caucus rejected it.

ZAF.tangentialFactors:
The trajectory of state recognition runs back more than a decade: Justice Minister Jeff Radebe launched a programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence citing the Constitution's equality clause, an early government framing of LGBTI violence as a policy problem that preceded the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024.

South Africa's statutory package compares with the small group of jurisdictions combining constitutional sexual-orientation protections, statutory gender recognition, marriage equality and an operative equality court; the divergence between that package and enforcement is the pattern the Mokoena litigation and the Frere Hospital memorandum illustrate.

The prison ruling is a data point within a wider correctional pattern rather than an isolated finding: a standard operating procedure existed, implementation was contested by practitioners, and a court then ordered the Department of Correctional Services to comply with its own rules.

Academic and civil-society debate continues over whether legal gender recognition should be reframed as a right grounded in dignity rather than a medical procedure, and over the exclusion of non-binary identities from a binary marker system.
ZAF.localsOnly:

Only two sex markers are available on official documents, so non-binary residents have no route to a matching marker through the existing statute, and reform toward self-determination has been proposed but is not yet law.

Residents who present with documents that do not align with their appearance report being refused service and threatened with arrest for fraud, and Gender Dynamix's 2024 report records police mocking a trans woman who sought to open a domestic-violence case.

Residents in correctional facilities are covered by the Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure for transgender inmates and, since the Equality Court judgment of 14 November 2025, by court orders requiring hormone treatment at state expense, gender-expressive clothing and the delivery of prescribed care.

Township residents, particularly Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people, bear a disproportionate share of the recorded violence, and community organisations reported five LGBTQIA+ murders in December 2024 alone.

Public healthcare for trans residents is available but unevenly delivered, with documented treatment delays of up to a year prompting direct action against a provincial hospital in the Eastern Cape.

IDN.name: Indonesia
IDN.summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level provisions targeting morality. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveler in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing directly to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.
IDN.outOfScopeNotes:
The scope of the October 2025 presidential decree is not resolved here. The sources describe it as framing LGBTQ+ people within national defence doctrine and as encouraging official and vigilante hostility; none of them records a prosecution or administrative action brought against an individual under the decree itself.

Enforcement of the same-sex provisions recorded for South Sumatra is not evidenced in these sources. The Human Dignity Trust profile states that the provisions exist, but no recent case from that province is documented here, so the practical enforcement picture outside Aceh remains unresolved.

The reported demand of up to US$100,000 in the Ventocilla case rests on the family's account of a WhatsApp call and is not independently corroborated in the sources available; the police position in that case is a denial of violence rather than a response to the payment demand.

Quantitative totals for vigilante attacks on trans women following the October 2025 decree are not established by these sources. Reporting characterises a clear surge and names the decree as a contributing cause, but the aggregate count and its geographic spread are unresolved.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Indonesia censors expression deemed to promote homosexuality: the 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction criminalizes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations (up to 7 years prison), and in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned TV/radio programs making LGBTQ behavior appear 'normal.' The government has banned websites and apps containing 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words (including Grindr), shut down the Instagram account of the comic Alpantuni, and in 2025 a new bill was being discussed to explicitly prohibit online content presenting 'lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behavior.' In October 2025, President Prabowo Subianto declared the spread of LGBTQ culture a 'non-military national threat' in a presidential decree, placing it alongside separatism and terrorism. Wikipedia country coverage: Transgender Indonesians can change their legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and receiving a judge's approval, after which they may marry someone of the opposite legal gender. Since June 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identification papers (Kartu Tanda Penduduk) across multiple provinces including Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung, and Papua, because many were undocumented — especially where families disapproved — leaving them without access to work or social services. However, only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognized (no third gender/X option), and transgender Indonesians have their gender at birth printed unless they have already obtained court recognition. Wikipedia country coverage: Since 2018, the Jakarta Social Agency has declared transgender women (waria) 'socially dysfunctional,' regularly conducted raids against them, and taken detained trans individuals to city-owned 'rehabilitation' centres where they are incarcerated alongside homeless people and released only after signing a promise not to repeat their 'offence' — officials stated this is meant as a deterrent against being transgender. Conversion therapy is widely practiced and openly advertised in rehabilitation centres, including corrective rape from family members against lesbian women. LGBTQ groups are working on setting up safe houses and evacuation plans, and the Yayasan Srikandi Sejati organization provides HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers at a free health clinic; Yogyakarta has the only madrasa for transgender people in the world. Wikipedia country coverage: As of 2019, no specific law exists to protect Indonesian citizens from discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people. Theoretically, protection against discriminatory employment practices on any ground is guaranteed in the Constitution and Human Rights Law (No. 39/1999), and the Attorney General's Office rescinded a public job offer declaring LGBTQ persons need not apply after advice from the National Commission on Human Rights. A police brigadier (TT) was fired for being gay after colleagues outed him; his lawsuit was rejected by the Semarang State Administrative Court in May 2019 on procedural grounds. The police have issued a circular since 2015 to process hate speech related to sexual orientation and gender identity, and Regulation of the Head of National Police Number 8 of 2009 stipulates the duty to protect minority groups' special rights including sexual orientation.

IDN.tangentialFactors:
Indonesia's institutional anti-LGBT posture has a documented origin point. In August 2016 the Indonesian Psychiatric Association proclaimed same-sex orientation and transgender identities to be mental illnesses and recommended psychological "rehabilitation"; the Jokowi government remained mostly silent at the time.

Human Rights Watch has documented discriminatory regulations, arrests and criminal trials against LGBT people in Indonesia since 2016. Its 7 July 2026 report, "Surge in Abuse Against LGBT Students", follows official condemnation of a student group at Universitas Indonesia; Arus Pelangi, Indonesia's LGBT umbrella organisation, documented 94 cases. In early July 2026 officials called on parents to monitor their children in relation to what they described as a lifestyle.

The escalation described by The Diplomat and ABC News is presented as continuous rather than sudden: analysts state that attacks on trans women did not suddenly appear, and trace the current surge to officials' verbal attacks and to the October 2025 defence decree.
IDN.blindSummary:
The country is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, and prosecutions are reported as selective rather than systematic.

The national human rights trust profile records that two provinces criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level provisions targeting morality. In one province, where religious law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Those punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present there, including foreign visitors.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, national police raided a privately rented villa after public reports of a gathering and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. The deputy director of the international rights organisation that reported the operation described it as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy, stating that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveler in custody. a foreign trans activist studying at a university abroad was arrested at an airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in 2022. During a call to his mother, she was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while national police have denied that violence was used.

Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing directly to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted in that reporting state/province that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

The reported demand of up to US$100,000 in the custody-death case rests on the family's account of a call and is not independently corroborated in the sources available; the police position in that case is a denial of violence rather than a response to the payment demand.

PAK.name: Pakistan
PAK.summary:
Pakistan's legal framework for transgender people is progressive on paper and broken in enforcement. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 recognised self-perceived gender identity, barred discrimination in education, employment and healthcare, and the 2020 Rules added a neutral 'X' marker for administrative documents. Those protections remain formally in force, but the Federal Shariat Court ruled on 19 May 2023, across 12 shariat petitions, that sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the Act — covering the definition of gender identity, the right to self-perceived gender identity, and inheritance — do not conform with the petitioners' reading of Islamic principles. In its reasoning the court speculated that the Act could facilitate the rape and sexual assault of women by men disguised as transgender women. The UK Home Office country note of November 2025 records the 2023 ruling as leaving ongoing legal disputes over which provisions survive.

Amnesty International called the ruling a blow to the rights of an already beleaguarded group and had warned the Pakistani government on 17 May 2023 against adopting amendments that violate human-rights standards. Justice Project Pakistan's assessment is that the central failure is implementation rather than absence of law: statutory protections have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment, and its policy brief makes specific recommendations on custody and police safeguards.

Lethal violence against transgender women is continuing and recent. In November 2024 gunmen shot three transgender women at close range near Karachi, the largest city, the second deadly attack on the community there within a week. On 21 September 2025 police found the bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead by unidentified assailants on a roadside highway at Memon Goth, Karachi. In a separate night-time attack reported in February 2026, activists Zehrish Khanzadi and Bindiya Rana were fired at through a door with three bullets and narrowly escaped; the same report describes a wave of violence leaving Pakistani transgender people afraid to go out. Estimates cited in 2025 put the transgender citizen population at around 500,000.

Police conduct compounds the risk. Accounts published in October 2025 describe transgender Pakistanis facing street harassment, rejection by landlords, dismissal at hospitals and suspicion and ridicule at police stations, alongside the violence itself. A legislator, Senator Mushtaq Ahmad, has proposed a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control trans people's official gender identity, an active retrograde legislative push against the self-identification model.

On sexual conduct, the UK Home Office note of November 2025 states that consensual same-sex acts are criminalised under section 377 of the Pakistan Penal Code, carrying two years to life, with the definition unclear and covering male-to-male sex; Human Dignity Trust (December 2024) records only men as criminalised. The same note assesses that LGBT+ people are unlikely to face state persecution. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report likewise records section 377 criminalisation, societal violence and discrimination, and notes that transgender people (khwaja sira) have some legal recognition while facing harassment and violence. No trans-traveller-specific entry or screening rules are recorded in the sources reviewed.
PAK.outOfScopeNotes:
The scope of section 377 remains unresolved in the sources: the UK Home Office note calls the definition unclear, and Human Dignity Trust records that only men fall within the offence. Whether the provision would be applied against a transgender visitor, as opposed to cisgender men, is not sourced.

Which sections of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 remain operative after the Federal Shariat Court's 19 May 2023 ruling is subject to ongoing legal disputes per the November 2025 UK Home Office note; the sources do not establish the final legislative or appellate position on sections 2(f), 3 and 7.

No source in this inventory addresses visa conditions, airport or border screening, gender-marker checks at entry, or detention conditions specific to foreign transgender visitors. Nothing is recorded here about prison or immigration-detention placement policy for trans detainees, nor about the availability of hormone treatment or trans-related healthcare for short-term visitors.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Pakistani media strictly censors LGBTQ-related news stories: the government blocked the website Queerpk.com in late 2013, and the Pakistani edition of the International New York Times (Express Tribune) left a blank space where a photo accompanying a same-sex marriage story should have appeared. Penal Code provisions reinforce this: Article 292 bans sale, distribution, exhibition, ownership or importation of 'obscene' books, pamphlets or images, and Article 294 prohibits 'obscene' public acts, songs, music or poems, while Article 153 penalises inducing students to political activity that disturbs public order with up to two years' imprisonment. Article 141 designates an assembly of five or more persons an 'unlawful assembly' if its common object is to commit any offence. Open expression carries personal risk: LGBTQ Pakistanis are generally reluctant to be open about their sexuality for fear of forced marriage, honour killings, humiliation, blackmail or violence, and a person living openly as LGBTQ is likely to face treatment from non-state actors such as Islamist and terrorist groups. A 2016 article by a young Pakistani man in the UK-based Gay Star News had his surname omitted for his security. Wikipedia country coverage: Healthcare access is a documented failure point for trans people. In 2016, 23-year-old transgender activist Alisha was shot seven times and left to bleed to death at Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar while staff argued over whether to take her to the men's or women's ward; men there discriminated against and taunted her friends and asked whether her blood was 'HIV-positive'. Some transgender women use hormones and silicone under terrible medical conditions without proper equipment or supervision, since expensive sex change surgery is rarely available in Pakistan due to lack of education and social taboos. In 2010 the Supreme Court ordered provision of free medical and educational facilities, microcredit schemes and job quotas for transgender people, and the 2018 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act prohibits discrimination in healthcare, education, employment, housing and access to goods and services, though the source notes locals often deny trans people basic education and healthcare. On HIV/AIDS: the epidemic began in Pakistan in 1987, government estimates (2004) put nearly 3,000 people living with HIV while critics suggest 70,000–80,000 and UNAIDS reports possibly up to 210,000; a 2009 survey found male and transgender sex workers at high risk, and Pakistani prostitutes lack access to condoms with little public health education provided. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex partnership has no legal recognition: the Constitution does not mention sexual orientation or gender identity, Part II 37 pledges to protect marriage and the family and oppose obscenity, and Part IX 227 requires all laws to be compatible with Islam as defined by a government-appointed Islamic council. Article 496 of the Penal Code punishes dishonestly going through a marriage ceremony knowing one is not lawfully married with up to seven years' imprisonment. Same-sex couples can live together only in secret — the source notes the LGBTQ community can socialise, organise, date and, in rare cases, live together as couples, if done mostly in secret — and in 2005 tribal council in the Khyber region ordered a man who married a fellow tribesman to leave the area or face death. For trans people, a small clerical body in Lahore (Tanzeem Ittehad-i-Ummat) declared transgender marriages legal under Islamic law in June 2016, while in May 2023 the Federal Shariat Court struck down sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the 2018 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act on self-perceived gender, with provisions remaining in force pending appeals.

Inheritance rights secured by the same Act were among the provisions struck down by the Federal Shariat Court in May 2023.

Discrimination in education, employment and healthcare is prohibited by statute, but residents report dismissal at hospitals, rejection by landlords and employment barriers in practice. Police stations are described as places of suspicion and ridicule rather than protection, and Justice Project Pakistan documents torture and ill-treatment in custody as an implementation failure of the existing law.

The estimated transgender population is around 500,000 citizens facing social exclusion and abuse. The community's most visible activists have been targeted directly: Zehrish Khanzadi and Bindiya Rana survived a shooting in which three bullets were fired through a door. A proposal by Senator Mushtaq Ahmad for a government gender re-assignment board would place control of official gender identity in state hands and would narrow the current self-identification model if adopted.

PHL.name: Philippines
PHL.summary:
The Philippines does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity, and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender. Social visibility is high: gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy are long-standing, Pride events and nightlife are prominent in the capital, and LGBTQ+ themes carry substantial media presence. A 2026 travel-risk assessment rates Manila 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers overall at 69 of 100 but scores trans travellers lower, at 62, in the 'Exercise Caution' band.

There is no legal gender recognition process available administratively. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people, so a court order is the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A pending bill would open recognition to applicants including consenting minors and would allow markers beyond male and female, such as X or nonbinary; its drafter links the absence of recognition to social exclusion, forced disclosure of trans status and violence. The Commission on Human Rights has described the trans killings recorded in a single year as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide, and allies have signalled endorsement of the recognition bill to the 20th Congress.

No national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity exists. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed and stalled in Congress for 25 years, a blockage cited by campaigners as the direct reason two killings in June 2025 produced no legislative remedy. Protections that do exist are sub-national or sectoral: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances cover eight provinces (Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo) and 32 cities and municipalities; the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers punishes SOGIE harassment with a fine of PHP 20,000 to 40,000 and up to one year's penalty; and the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act reach slurs and ridicule, with fines of PHP 1,000 to 10,000, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar.

Two access rules turn on documents rather than on identity. The armed forces have permitted openly gay and bisexual personnel since 2009 and transgender personnel since 2017, with the uniform policy following the legal gender shown on the birth certificate. The Code of Professional Responsibility governing lawyers was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent. Kierra Apostol, an 18-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a river in Cagayan on 23 June 2025 after being reported missing; on the same day a trans woman who was a former journalist and activist was shot by an unidentified gunman inside a clinic in General Santos. A foreign national was arrested in May 2025 on a charge of raping a trans woman at a Batangas resort. In April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd during a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan; the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community.

Detention removes what protections exist on paper. Transgender women are held with male inmates according to birth sex: at Manila City Jail, arrivals to the male dormitory have their heads shaved, and survival against abuse is organised through inmate hierarchies and informal same-sex 'weddings' with male inmates rather than through policy. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's documented response at Davao City Jail is administrative segregation, transferring LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex 'to prevent abuse', alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, with three LGBT groupings housed there since the annex was established. Schools are a further documented site of harm: a 2017 Human Rights Watch investigation recorded bullying and discrimination against gender-diverse students across Philippine schools while noting that law offered few remedies at the time.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The source reports that gender diverse people in the Philippines have been refused entry and service by establishments, and that cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from some private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence. Marawi City's December 2004 ordinance bans men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. After the 2017 Marawi siege, individuals perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps. Wikipedia country coverage: The source describes LGBTQ-friendly counseling services and therapy sessions used to help people escape dangerous and hostile environments, and notes that from the 2000s organizations formed around sexual health (particularly HIV), psychosocial support and spiritual needs; LGBTQ Filipinos have a higher rate of suicidal ideation or attempts. Republic Act 11166 prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and in June 2023 Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other, rolling out first to government-owned hospitals. Youth-specific: the DSWD and Department of Education allowed students in late 2016 to wear uniforms matching their gender identity, the July 2017 Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy reviews curricula for gender stereotypes and sets June as Pride Month, and the 2013 Anti-Bullying Law's rules list sexual orientation and gender identity as prohibited bullying grounds. The source also reports hate crimes and forced conversion therapy committed by family members against Iglesia ni Cristo LGBTQ teenagers, backed by the church's central establishment.

The protection picture is a patchwork rather than a single national rule, and its coverage is geographic: a trans visitor in Albay, Bataan or Iloilo stands under a provincial ordinance with a stated penalty, while a visitor outside the eight covered provinces and 32 covered localities has no SOGI-specific discrimination complaint to file. Whether these local ordinances are applied to foreign complainants is not addressed in the sources.

The gap between social acceptance and legal status is the defining pattern. Cultural visibility, Pride attendance and media presence coexist with a quarter-century of legislative inaction, and the sources treat that inaction as the proximate cause of the violence rather than as background: campaigners used the June 2025 killings to demand passage of the SOGIE Equality Bill, and the drag artist assaulted in 2024 made the same demand from the stage.

Document status carries practical weight beyond the recognition question. Because birth-certificate gender governs military uniform policy and because administrative correction is closed off, a trans visitor whose documents do not match presentation should expect screening to be resolved on the paper record, with no administrative correction available even with surgery.

The jail findings illustrate how safety is actually delivered to gender-diverse people in state custody: Manila City Jail relies on inmate hierarchies, Davao City Jail relies on segregation into an annex. Neither model is a legal protection, and both place the burden of safety on the detainee.

CHL.name: Chile
CHL.summary:
Chile's statutory framework for trans people is among the more developed in the region. Legal gender recognition has operated since 2019 on a self-determination basis, with no medical or surgical conditions attached. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and since 2012 the criminal code has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences. Birth certificates also offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Detention carries specific protections. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing trans detainees the recognition of their assumed gender, including placement and segmented housing by gender identity, entry examinations, and rules on access for trans visitors; a standing committee with Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives monitors implementation.

The policy record has stalled. A Chilean advocacy group's annual assessment judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTIQ+ rights, the first such reversal since the return of democracy in 1990, attributing the failure of equality and trans-rights bills to the rise of the ultra-right and to government inaction. Movilh's 24th Annual Human Rights Report, published in 2025, describes a breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus around LGBTIQ+ rights, with non-discrimination law reform rejected by lawmakers.

Documented violence remains a live risk. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered by an acquaintance and hidden for 24 hours; the case is treated as the country's benchmark anti-trans killing and was described in the national press as Chile's biggest hate crime. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour in a transphobic attack at a hotel in Santiago, during which the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Institutional hostility is also visible inside state employment. Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in 2025 alleging she was relegated to administrative duties, had her private life exposed without consent, and was denied support.
CHL.outOfScopeNotes:
The F&M Global Barometers profile is cited as a source of comparative indices, including a specific trans rights barometer, but no numerical scores or ranking positions were carried in the inventory; those values remain unverified here.

Movilh's 24th Annual Human Rights Report (2025) is identified by title and publisher, but its underlying incident counts, methodology and specific findings beyond the consensus-breakdown assessment were not extracted and are therefore unresolved.

Whether the hate-crime aggravating circumstance in force since 2012 has produced convictions or sentencing uplift in trans-specific cases is not sourced. Likewise, no evidence was available on how the Gendarmería protocol has performed in practice, on outcomes of the Panes litigation, or on whether the stalled non-discrimination reform will be reintroduced.

Policies on entry screening, passport gender markers for foreign visitors, and recognition of foreign documents in Chilean institutions were not covered by the inventory and remain unsourced.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2, D4, D5, D6, D8, D13.

BioBioChile investigation (2 Jan 2024): profile of Ever, a young trans man murdered in 2023 and hidden for 24 hours — described as Chile's 'biggest hate crime'; the killer, an acquaintance, confessed. The country's benchmark anti-trans homicide case.

Chilevisión (23 Sep 2021): a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for nearly an hour in a transphobic attack at a Santiago hotel; the victim recounts 'he told me he wanted to kill me'. sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The 2012 anti-discrimination law (Zamudio Law) protects against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and since 2018 also gender expression, and it added hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. A bill criminalizing incitement to hatred or violence on grounds including sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression was passed by the Chamber of Deputies on 9 January 2020. Historically, Article 373 of the Penal Code ('offenses to morals and good customs') was used by police to harass homosexuals even for holding hands in public; a 2015 Movilh report noted that for the first time in seven years no police abuses against LGBT people were reported, credited to the Carabineros Human Rights Department. Wikipedia country coverage: The Migration and Immigration Law, enacted 11 April 2021, bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that unrecognized asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection. No foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk because of, among other grounds, sexual orientation or gender identity. Wikipedia country coverage: The Migration and Immigration Law (11 April 2021) bars removal of foreigners with complementary protection to a country where their life, physical integrity or personal freedom would be at risk due to sexual orientation or gender identity. The source text provides no further detail on border screening procedures, detention, or entry screening specific to trans travelers. Wikipedia country coverage: A Ministry of Education circular of April 2017, 'Rights of girls, boys and trans students in the field of education,' requires schools nationwide to provide bathroom and shower facilities that respect the gender identity of trans students, alongside guarantees of social name use and gender-conforming uniforms; non-compliance is sanctionable. A 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centers in Chile to call and register transgender people by their social name. Since 2009 the National Organization of Gendarmeries has ended disciplinary sanctions against inmates that prevented them from dressing according to their gender identity. Wikipedia country coverage: Since 2013, sex reassignment surgeries and hormone therapy have been funded by Chile's public health system (Fondo Nacional de Salud), and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular requires all care centers to register trans people by social name. Youth-specific: in June 2024 the Ministry of Health's Circular 7 suggested deferring initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, though the Medical College noted physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court (7-3) annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law that had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents; in November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) via the 2026 Budget Law, but the Ministry of Health-run program continues providing support in medical centers. The Gender Identity Support Program 'Crece con Orgullo' has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17. Wikipedia country coverage: The Gender Identity Law 21.120 (effective 27 December 2019) lets those over 18 change name and sex by request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery, while 14-to-18-year-olds must go before family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents; under-14s cannot use the law but are recognized as transgender. In April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, though the ruling applies only to that case. Education protections include the 2009 General Law of Education, the 2011 School Violence Law requiring Good School Coexistence Committees, the 2013 Superintendence of Education handbook ordering non-discriminatory treatment, the 2015-2018 National School Coexistence Policy incorporating the International Day Against Homophobia and Transphobia into the 2016 School Calendar, the School Inclusion law effective March 2016, and the April 2017 ministerial circular on trans students' rights. Law 21,430 (published 15 March 2022) is the first regulation explicitly protecting LGBTIQA+ children and adolescents, including non-discrimination on sex characteristics and the right to develop gender identity, and obliges state bodies to create programs on sexual rights and diversity. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report (56-30-6), a non-binding recommendation proposing to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors, and repeal Circular 812 protecting gender identity in schools.

CHL.tangentialFactors:
The equality gains on record are the product of sustained movement campaigning rather than settled consensus: Movilh's own achievements index lists the anti-discrimination law, inclusive questions in the 2012 national census, the 'El amor es amor' marriage campaign, and local-level 'Comuna Diversa' work carried out through regional branches. The fragility of that consensus is the turbulence now visible in the legislative record.

Comparative measurement exists and should be read alongside the legal text. The F&M Global Barometers country profile for Chile publishes composite scores on LGBT rights perception, including a dedicated Global Barometer of Transgender Rights index, which ranks formal legal protections against lived conditions.

Violence reporting is concentrated in the capital region, where the 2021 hotel assault took place, while the killing of Ever in 2023 sets the national reference point for anti-trans homicide. Both remain cited as the standard cases of transphobic violence.
CHL.localsOnly:
Discrimination claims brought by trans residents reach the courts. Isabella Panes's 2025 lawsuit against Carabineros covers reassignment to administrative tasks, non-consensual disclosure of her private life, and refusal of institutional support, and stands as the leading test of the national police force's obligations toward trans personnel.

The Gendarmería protocol is administered through a standing committee with representatives of the prison authority and the undersecretariat, which oversees implementation, housing segmentation, entry examinations and the access rules that apply when trans visitors attend a facility.

Documentation routes are open without medical prerequisites: since 2019 trans Chileans amend their gender marker through self-declaration, and intersex children can be registered with a third sex option on the birth certificate. Movilh continues to publish an annual human rights report on sexual and gender diversity, the 24th edition covering 2025.

blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex marriage and adoption legal since March 2022; hate-crime law includes SOGI as aggravating circumstances since 2012; civil unions since 2015; comprehensive self-determination-based legal gender recognition law passed 2019; third-sex option for intersex children on birth certificates since 2006; non-binding intersex-affirming health guidance (2023) recommends against unnecessary surgeries; in 2025 a court issued the country's first lesbophobic femicide conviction.
An LGBTQ+ news outlet (Mar 2025): an annual rights report finds this country's 2024 was a 'year of regression' for LGBTQ rights, with stalled equality and trans-rights legislation.
Investigative outlet (Jan 2024): profile of a young trans man murdered and dismembered in 2023 - described as the country's 'biggest hate crime'; the killer, an acquaintance, confessed.

National TV network (Sept 2021): a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for nearly an hour at a hotel in the capital in a transphobic attack; the victim recounts fearing for his life.

National daily: the country's prison service signed a new protocol for trans inmates - placement according to gender identity, segmented housing, medical examination on entry to determine hormonal/surgical treatment needs, and respect for assumed-gender expression.
International survey group's country profile for this country: composite scores measuring LGBT rights perception, including a dedicated transgender-rights barometer index.

Foreign newspaper (April 2025): the country's first trans police officer sued the national police for discrimination - relegated to administrative tasks, private life exposed without consent, denied support against online hate, and transition-related surgery refused.

Main national LGBT organisation's achievements page: lists the organisation's historical milestones across legal, judicial, public-policy, human-rights, mobilisation and international sectors benefiting lesbians, gays, bisexuals and trans people in this country - institutional-culture context.
CHL.blindLocalsOnly:
Discrimination claims brought by trans residents reach the courts. Isabella Panes's 2025 lawsuit against the national police force covers reassignment to administrative tasks, non-consensual disclosure of her private life, and refusal of institutional support, and stands as the leading test of that force's obligations toward trans personnel.

The prison protocol is administered through a standing committee with representatives of the national prison authority and the undersecretariat, which oversees implementation, housing segmentation, entry examinations and the access rules that apply when trans visitors attend a facility.

Documentation routes are open without medical prerequisites: since 2019 trans residents amend their gender marker through self-declaration, and intersex children can be registered with a third sex option on the birth certificate. The national LGBT integration movement continues to publish an annual human rights report on sexual and gender diversity, the 24th edition covering 2025.
CHL.blindTangential:
The equality gains on record are the product of sustained movement campaigning rather than settled consensus: the national LGBT integration movement's achievements index lists the anti-discrimination law, inclusive questions in the 2012 national census, a national marriage-equality campaign, and local-level diversity work carried out through provincial branches. The fragility of that consensus is the turbulence now visible in the legislative record.

Comparative measurement exists and should be read alongside the legal text. The national country profile in the global rights barometers publishes composite scores on LGBT rights perception, including a dedicated national barometer of transgender rights index, which ranks formal legal protections against lived conditions.

Violence reporting is concentrated in the largest city, where the 2021 hotel assault took place, while the killing of Ever in 2023 sets the national reference point for anti-trans homicide. Both remain cited as the standard cases of transphobic violence.

COL.name: Colombia
COL.summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice".

Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The courts have also intervened directly in detention. A Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

The sharpest risk sits where armed groups operate, including in territories under their control. In the department of Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns announced through flyer campaigns targeting "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots", and threatened a further wave. Trans women in that department reported few options beyond sex work; Tatiana Cespedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after receiving death threats from armed men, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed. In the department of Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Targeted killings of trans people continue in the country's ordinary, urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025. A 28-second video of the assault went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands, flailing in a creek unable to swim, before she drowned; her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities. One report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.
COL.outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the comprehensive trans law legislated in 2025 is unresolved in the source inventory: it is reported as being under consideration, but no source confirms enactment, its scope, or whether it is in force at the time of publication.

Full-year 2025 homicide totals for trans and LGBTI people are not sourced. Available figures are partial and differently defined, so they are not directly comparable: the Attorney General's Office counted 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, while a separate report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, and a 2024 report counted more than 40 transgender women killed in 2023.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa rules for trans visitors, the treatment of foreign trans documents at Colombian border and airport controls, whether screeners or officials may question a traveller's gender presentation, or whether the domestic notary-based marker procedure is available to non-residents or visitors.

Healthcare, asylum and hate-crime sentencing provisions for trans people are not sourced here. There is no inventory item on whether Colombia maintains trans-specific hate-crime aggravation in the criminal code, and none on access to gender-affirming care, insurance coverage, or waiting lists.

Facilities, such as access to gendered bathrooms, changing rooms and shelters on the basis of identity documents, are not covered by the inventory, and neither are detention conditions beyond the single court ruling on trans detainees, which is reported without its case number, date or court name.

Whether the notary-based ID change procedure operates consistently across the national territory is unresolved; the sources describe the rule change and its rationale but contain no implementation data.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D5.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized in Colombia in 1981, and law reforms in the 1990s equalized the age of consent at 14 for both homosexual and heterosexual sex. In 1999 the Constitutional Court declared unconstitutional the military rule prohibiting "homosexual acts" (Judgment C-507 of 1999), and in 2011 Congress passed a law penalizing discrimination based on sexual orientation with one to three years' imprisonment plus fines. Efforts to ban conversion therapy (Ecosieg) have not yet succeeded: Congressperson Mauricio Toro's "Inconvertibles" bill of 10 May 2022 failed by 2024, and Congressperson Carolina Giraldo proposed a similar bill, "Quiérele siempre," in 2025. Wikipedia country coverage: The Constitutional Court has repeatedly protected public expression of same-sex affection: in 1994 it disapproved the National Council of Television's refusal to air a commercial featuring a same-sex couple; T-268 of 2000 permitted a gay pride parade the Mayor of Neiva had blocked; T-301 of 2004 ordered Santa Marta police to stop harassing homosexuals at the city boardwalk; T-314 of 2011 held the Tequendama Hotel's refusal of access to homosexuals at two events as discriminatory; and T-909 of 2011 ordered Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali to take a course so as not to repress homosexuals expressing affection in public. By contrast, as of 2020 military culture still discourages discussion of same-sex attraction under a "se puede ser, pero no demostrar" (you can exist, but not show off) norm. Wikipedia country coverage: In March 2016 the first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Wikipedia country coverage: Access to public and commercial facilities has been protected by court order: T-314 of 2011 ruled the Tequendama Hotel's refusal to admit homosexuals to two events discriminatory, T-909 of 2011 ordered Cosmocentro mall's guardianship officials and security firm to take a course on not repressing homosexual affection, and T-301 of 2004 ordered Santa Marta police to stop harassing homosexuals at the boardwalk. The 2016 Ministry of Interior presidential decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup. A May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture, while Bogotá and Medellín have thriving gay neighbourhoods, bars and counselling/legal advice centres. Wikipedia country coverage: The Constitutional Court extended social security (health insurance) benefits to same-sex couples on 5 October 2007 and pension rights on 17 April 2008, so same-sex couples now enjoy the main benefits heterosexual couples have under the same terms. In 2012 the Court found that sexual orientation cannot be a criterion for preventing blood donation and ordered the Ministry of Health and Social Protection to rewrite donation regulations so they assess risk by sexual behaviour rather than orientation. The 2016 government decree specifically addresses LGBTI rights in health care, and a 2016 report (Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS at Universidad de los Andes) recommended ending psychiatric pathologization of transgender identity and abandoning sterilization as a prerequisite for other physical changes; conversion therapy bans remain unpassed as of 2025. Wikipedia country coverage: Despite supportive media coverage — gay characters in programmes such as the prime-time soap opera Dr Mata and a lesbian scene in A corazón abierto — Colombian society remains generally conservative, and a bloc of conservative senators defeated the civil union bill in Congress on 19 June 2007. The country's Inspector General asked the Constitutional Court in 2015 to invalidate all same-sex marriages approved in Colombia, and by 31 March 2016 a campaign to force a referendum repealing the November 2015 same-sex adoption ruling had gathered 1.8 million signatures including 45 members of Congress (a Congress committee shelved it 20–12 in May 2017). Polling shows the split: an Invamer poll of October 2019 put same-sex marriage support at 50% versus 47% opposed and adoption at 36% in favour versus 62% opposed, while 2016 polls showed 37–40% support for marriage and only 22% for adoption. Wikipedia country coverage: In 1998 the Constitutional Court ruled that public school teachers cannot be fired for revealing their sexual orientation and that private religious schools cannot ban gay students from enrolling. After student Sergio Urrego committed suicide in August 2014 following discrimination by his teachers, the Constitutional Court ruled for his family and ordered the Ministry of Education to review, within a year, the "manuals of coexistence" of all schools nationwide so they contain no articles discriminating against children by sexual orientation or gender identity, meaning schools across the country cannot discriminate against students on those grounds. Youth-relevant family policy has also shifted: since 2014 LGBTQ individuals can adopt their partner's biological child, the 4 November 2015 ruling granted full same-sex adoption rights barring agency discrimination, and a 12 November 2015 ruling required birth registration listing two mothers or two fathers — though the 1.8-million-signature referendum drive targeted exactly these rights for children of same-sex couples.

COL.tangentialFactors:
Colombia's situation is distinctive for how much of the protection it extends comes from the judiciary and transitional justice rather than from the statute book alone. The 2015 notary-based marker change, the 1993 Constitutional Court recognition doctrine, and the 2023 Special Jurisdiction for Peace indictment are all products of courts and peace-process bodies, and the Attorney General's Office is the institution recording LGBTI homicides while the courts recognise gender persecution.

The President Petro government has positioned itself as aligned with LGBTIQ+ equality, which is why the UN Independent Expert Reid found the reforms themselves credible even as he documented the violence. The political direction and the security outcome point in opposite directions, and the mismatch is documented by UN bodies rather than asserted by advocacy groups.

Colombia's decades-long armed conflict is the structural context for the most severe documented risks. Kill-lists and "social cleansing" campaigns are attributed to armed groups, not to private individuals acting alone, and they intersect with the country's history of persecution of people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities in the context of conflict.

Within Latin America the country pairs one of the region's broadest document and family-law regimes with homicide figures of a scale that most other regional jurisdictions with comparable legal recognition do not report.

NGA.name: Nigeria
NGA.summary:
Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct nationally under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), and the law reaches far beyond marriage. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) documents that the SSMPA also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case surfaced in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
NGA.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the cross-dressing criminalisation proposals reported by Reuters in September 2022 have since been enacted. The available sources describe them as proposals and do not record a final legislative outcome.

Unresolved: whether Bobrisky was assigned to a male or a female prison section during her 2024 term. The source available does not record the decision, only that the choice was reported as discretionary at the time of sentencing.

Unresolved: the current status of the investigation into the killing of Abuja Area Mama. The sources record that no suspects had been charged six months after the August 2024 killing, despite an announced investigation by the Abuja police chief; no later outcome is sourced here.

Not sourced in this inventory: whether Nigeria's entry or visa screening involves any question about gender identity or transition history, or whether foreign consular officials require documents that match gender presentation at the border. Any claim on border screening would need a dedicated source.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D3, D4, D5.
