sources.title: Bobrisky — Wikipedia (Nigerian transgender woman; 2024 imprisonment at Kirikiri)
sources.summary: Wikipedia biography of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, documents the only trans-imprisonment case the search surfaced: she pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine. She served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, and was released on 5 August 2024. At sentencing, press coverage (BBC Pidgin, cited in the article) openly asked 'which prison they will keep the crossdresser in', reflecting discretionary placement; the article does not record whether she was assigned to a male or female section. Outcome/ruling: an October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Detention and raid sites are the main facilities described: men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held in jail for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by end-2011, and mass arrests occurred at hotels (Asaba, Delta State, June 2018, 100+ party-goers; Egbeda, Lagos, August 2018, 57 young men; Warri, Delta State, August 2023, the 'Warri 67'). LGBTQ-friendly venues also face closure risk — the House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church in Lagos cancelled conferences after its members' names and addresses were published in four newspapers on 12 September 2008 and some were threatened, beaten and stoned. Outside Nigeria, Housing Works in Brooklyn provides housing, legal representation and medical care to LGBTQ asylum seekers from Nigeria. Wikipedia country coverage: Many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes because of arrest and 'kito' extortion risk, and activists say the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work. The 2015 survey by Bisi Alimi's organisation found only 30% of Nigerians agree LGBTQ persons should receive education, healthcare and housing, while the Constitution (Section 17(3)(d)) nominally guarantees adequate medical and health care to all citizens. Historically, NGOs Global Rights and The Independent Project provided LGBT groups with HIV/AIDS awareness training (US State Department 2011 report). No youth-specific healthcare finding appears in the source text. Wikipedia country coverage: The Federal Ministry of Education has a national policy on safety, security and violence-free schools in all Nigerian schools that prohibits discrimination explicitly including on 'sexual orientation' — though there is no enacted legislation protecting against discrimination generally, and no political party endorses LGBTQ rights. Youth are heavily targeted by enforcement: in August 2018 police raided a birthday party in Egbeda, Lagos, arresting 57 young men alleged to be undergoing an 'initiation into the LGBTQ community' (the 'Egbeda 57'), and in October 2023 76 people were arrested at a party in Gombe state. Religious institutions also play a crucial role in education, and mainstream interpretations of Islam and Christianity drive stigmatization of LGBTQ students.

NGA.tangentialFactors:
The Thomson Reuters Foundation's August 2024 assessment, marking ten years of the SSMPA, finds that the law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its statutory scope and has effectively sanctioned abuse; LGBTQ+ Nigerians report lost job prospects and a rise in attacks since its passage.

Community infrastructure exists because state protection does not. Queer Nigerians counter app-based entrapment with exposure forums and sting operations; one administrator's alert page drawing 43,000 followers is cited as the scale of that self-policing.

Two official foreign assessments point in the same direction across a decade: the UK Home Office's 2025-2026 country policy note sets out penalties as they stand in law, while the UK foreign office's 2026 travel advice sets out the consequences for visitors, including attacks, blackmail and death-penalty exposure. The gap between the statute's text and its enforcement practice is itself a safety variable: police extortion is reported against people stopped for appearance rather than conduct.

Where trans identity is not named in the criminal statute, discretion fills the gap. The prison-placement question raised in the Bobrisky case shows that transgender detainees face unregulated outcomes under general correctional rules, and the cross-dressing proposals reported by Reuters show that expression, not identity, is the legislative target.
NGA.blindSummary:
The jurisdiction criminalises same-sex conduct nationally under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, and the statute extends well past marriage. Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public display of a same-sex amorous relationship, and gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have invoked it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

a foreign government's country policy and information note (June 2025, updated April 2026) states that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that twelve state-level jurisdictions apply religious criminal law, under which same-sex acts between men and between women are criminalised and male sodomy carries the death penalty under state/province Zina provisions.

Trans identity is not named in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender residents fear proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in the jurisdiction face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known by an online nickname, was found on a highway in the capital city hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the capital's police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. a February 2025 report records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against people perceived as gay is a routine feature of enforcement. a March 2025 report describes a 24-year-old man stopped by police in the country's largest city, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the national statute as a weaponised law that produces hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ residents through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The jurisdiction offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the national statute reinforced historic-era criminalisation. a foreign foreign office's 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under religious criminal law.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns a widely known transgender public figure. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served the term in a maximum-security prison and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, showing that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. an October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the national correctional service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Unresolved: whether the cross-dressing criminalisation proposals reported in September 2022 have since been enacted. The sources describe them as proposals and record no final legislative outcome.

Unresolved: whether the transgender public figure was assigned to a male or female prison section during her 2024 term. The available source records only that the choice was reported as discretionary at sentencing.

Unresolved: the current status of the investigation into the killing of the 33-year-old trans TikToker. The sources record that no suspects had been charged six months after the August 2024 killing, despite an announced investigation; no later outcome is sourced here.

Not sourced: whether entry or visa screening involves any question about gender identity or transition history, or whether border officials require documents matching gender presentation. Any claim on screening would need a dedicated source.

KEN.name: Kenya
KEN.summary:
Kenya criminalises consensual sex between men under the colonial-era Penal Code, with imprisonment of up to 14 years, and the provision applies regardless of the nationality of those involved. There is no statute governing gender identity and no codified pathway for legal gender recognition, although intersex people are legally recognised as a third gender.

Police conduct is the most immediate risk for a trans visitor. Twenty-six trans and intersex interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi described routine detention on pretexts such as being drunk and disorderly, followed by on-the-spot extortion, including demands to "look for 5,000 shillings". Several of those interviewed use traditionally male names as pseudonyms to move through public space safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

Document access is obstructed in practice. Evidence placed before the High Court showed that 94% of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans were refused corrections by civil registration offices, with some spending close to four years' wages on attempts that failed.

Violence against sexual and gender minorities is documented rather than alleged. The Kenya Human Rights Commission's Lives on the Line report, published in September 2025, covers October 2023 to September 2024, was built with more than 14 community organisations, and expressly challenges the 2019 High Court ruling in Petition 16/2019 that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence.

The courts have moved in the opposite direction from the police. On 12 August 2025 the Eldoret High Court found that prisons fail dignity and privacy protections for transgender Kenyans and directed the state to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act; the petition was brought by a trans Kenyan subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and court-ordered gender determination while incarcerated. On 20 May 2026 the Milimani High Court in Nairobi, in a decision delivered by Justice Bahati Mwamuye in Petition 27 of 2020, ruled on the constitutional right to legal gender recognition. The Mombasa Court of Appeal had held forced anal testing unconstitutional in 2018, with compensation awarded in 2024, and the Supreme Court upheld freedom of association allowing LGBTQ organisation registration in 2023. A man was sentenced to 50 years' imprisonment in December 2024 for killing an LGBTQ activist.
KEN.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Transgender Protection Rights Act directed by the Eldoret High Court on 12 August 2025 has been drafted, introduced or enacted is unresolved in the sources available here.

The operative remedy of the Milimani High Court decision of 20 May 2026 is not specified in the inventory: the sources confirm that the court ruled on the constitutional right to legal gender recognition but do not state what relief was granted or whether a statutory recognition process was ordered.

No sourced material in this inventory records prosecutions of the criminal provisions against foreign nationals or visitors, so the practical likelihood of charge rather than extortion cannot be assessed from these sources.

The outcome of the petition filed against incitement to hatred and discrimination is unresolved.

The US State Department human rights report used here covers the 2010 reporting year and describes conditions more than a decade old; it is retained only as evidence of the long-standing pattern of societal discrimination and of the registration status of LGBTQ organisations at that time.

The inventory does not state whether the 2019 High Court ruling in Petition 16/2019 has been appealed, varied or remains binding notwithstanding the Kenya Human Rights Commission's challenge to it.

CNN 'A Equals' interactive on trans and intersex Kenyans: 26 interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi describe routine police harassment — detention on pretexts like 'drunk and disorderly', on-the-spot extortion ('look for 5,000 shillings...'), and using traditionally male names as pseudonyms to navigate society safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

KHRC 'Lives on the Line' (Sep 2025): the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in Kenya, covering Oct 2023–Sep 2024; explicitly challenges the 2019 High Court ruling (Petition 16/2019) that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence; built with 14+ community organisations.

GATE.ngo on Nairobi Milimani High Court decision delivered 20 May 2026 (Justice Bahati Mwamuye, Petition 27 of Jan 2020): follows evidence that 94% of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans were refused by civil registration offices, some spending nearly four years' wages on failed document corrections; Kenya has never had a codified legal framework for gender recognition.
Reuters (Dec 2024): a Kenyan man was sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist.

OutRight International Kenya profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): a decade of court-driven progress — 2018 Mombasa Court of Appeal ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional (compensation awarded 2024); 2023 Supreme Court upheld freedom of association allowing LGBTQ organisation registration; petition filed against incitement to hatred and discrimination.

The Star (23 Sep 2025) on the KHRC 'Lives on the Line' report: purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision; quotes the finding that despite Constitution Article 28's dignity guarantee, the data 'paints a blunt picture' — active LGBTIQ+ organisations raise awareness and provide community spaces amid documented violence.

US State Department Human Rights Report for Kenya (2010 reporting year): LGBT advocacy organisations such as the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya (GALCK) were permitted to register and operate; societal discrimination based on sexual orientation was widespread, causing loss of employment and education; in Feb 2010 Mtwapa religious leaders demanded closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute.

KEN.tangentialFactors:
LGBTI civil-society groups may operate in Kenya, but only within a restrictive civic space, according to the UK Home Office country policy note of February 2025. The Kenya Human Rights Commission's data collection relied on purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision, and those organisations continue to raise awareness and provide community spaces despite the documented violence.

Societal discrimination is long-standing and reaches beyond legal exposure. The US State Department human rights report for the 2010 reporting year recorded widespread discrimination based on sexual orientation causing loss of employment and education, and noted that in February 2010 religious leaders in Mtwapa demanded the closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute, a demand bearing on access to health services for men who have sex with men. The same report recorded that the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya was permitted to register and operate.

Kenya's trajectory over the past decade has been court-driven rather than legislative: judicial decisions have struck down forced anal testing and affirmed freedom of association, while the legislature has produced no framework for gender recognition. The Constitution's Article 27 and Article 28 guarantees of equality and dignity sit alongside a criminal statute that has not been repealed.
KEN.localsOnly:
Kenyan residents live under the same criminal provisions as visitors, and the absence of a codified legal framework for gender recognition applies to them directly: civil registration offices refuse marker corrections in the overwhelming majority of cases, and the courts have yet to see that practice translated into a statutory process.

The Eldoret High Court's 12 August 2025 judgment addresses conditions that fall on residents in state custody. The petition established that prisons fail dignity and privacy protections for transgender detainees, and that the petitioner had been subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and a court-ordered gender determination during incarceration.

Community infrastructure exists and is documented. The Lives on the Line report was produced with more than 14 community organisations, and active LGBTIQ+ organisations provide both awareness work and physical community space. A petition against incitement to hatred and discrimination has been filed; its outcome is not recorded in the sources available here.

Intersex Kenyans hold a distinct legal position, recognised as a third gender, which does not extend to transgender or gender-diverse people seeking marker change.

ROU.name: Romania
ROU.summary:
Romania is broadly workable for a transgender visitor, with same-sex relations legal nationwide and a protection apparatus that functions unevenly. Domestic legal gender recognition exists and is court-based, but civil-status authorities resist it in practice. In the Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi case, the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate reflecting the trans man's UK-recognised identity, and the Bucharest Tribunal rejected the appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates, making the decision definitive in March 2026. ACCEPT Romania announced the outcome on Trans Day of Visibility and urges others who have changed their documents in another European Union member state to pursue transcription in Romania.

The legal anchor is the Court of Justice of the European Union's ruling of October 2024, reported by Reuters, that Romania infringed a transgender man's rights in refusing recognition of a UK gender recognition certificate. ACCEPT Romania describes the underlying obligation as a duty on member states to transcribe legal gender recognition obtained in another EU member state. Whether the same duty extends to recognition obtained outside the Union is not established by the sources reviewed.

One definitive ruling does not amount to uniform practice. The Mirzarafie-Ahi order shows that a Romanian court will issue a corrected birth certificate where a foreign certificate is recognised, and it also shows that regional civil-status directorates were prepared to appeal rather than comply.

The country's anti-discrimination statute, Government Ordinance 137/2000, covers sex and sexual orientation but does not name gender identity. Enforcement runs through the National Council for Combating Discrimination (CNCD), which has investigated printing houses that refused to produce LGBT and gender-equality materials. Outright International records institutional follow-through on LGBTI complaints as limited.

There is no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions in Romania. The 2018 referendum proposing a constitutional definition of marriage as between a man and a woman failed on low turnout, and the Romanian Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017.

Official rhetoric toward transgender people grew harsher during the 2025 electoral period. Presidential candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself against LGBTQ people in February, Prime Minister Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes, and a deputy mayor from the AUR party in Ploiești made further derogatory announcements. The National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August 2025 after ACCEPT complained about anti-Pride framing presented as provocation. ILGA-Europe and partners reported that eight of nine country submissions to the European Union's 2025 Rule of Law Report documented smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people, with the Romanian election period cited as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.

Visible hostility coexists with visible organising. Tens of thousands marched at Bucharest Pride in June 2025 as it marked its twentieth anniversary, at a point organisers described as growing right-wing hostility toward LGBTQ+ Romanians.
ROU.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Romanian courts will transcribe gender recognition obtained outside the European Union, including from the United Kingdom, is unresolved by the sources reviewed. The CJEU ruling and the Romanian court order both turn on recognition obtained within or attached to the Union's framework, and no source here addresses non-EU certificates.

No source reviewed states whether Government Ordinance 137/2000 will be amended to name gender identity as a protected ground, or whether the civil-partnership bill will advance. Both are presented as current obstacles, not as pending developments with dates.

Whether the hate-crime legal framework has been applied to offences against transgender people is not established by this inventory. The Council of Europe thematic review documents a framework and implementation reporting, and the sources record no prosecution outcomes.

BGD.name: Bangladesh
BGD.summary:
Bangladesh is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The protests that ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024, known as the Monsoon Revolution, mark the inflection point: hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground afterwards, and trans people who were previously visible now live in hiding. A Washington Blade assessment of 5 August 2025, one year after the ouster, found Bangladesh's LGBTQ community increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats.

The current national incident baseline is set by the advocacy group JMBF, whose annual report published in April 2026 documents 260 human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals across the country in 2025. JMBF describes this as a sharp increase continuing an upward trend recorded since 2022, and the violations include murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion.

Lethal violence against visible trans people is ongoing. Shila, a prominent trans advocate originally from Chattogram district and widely known for humanitarian work, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 February 2025. Five unidentified individuals were accused in the case.

Police extortion is a routine hazard for visibly trans people. After hijra refused to pay extortion money on 10 September 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack at Gomdondi Phultala. On 17 September 2025 police arrested twelve hijras in Narayanganj while they collected money from vehicles carrying expatriates, a traditional livelihood. In April 2024, five transgender and hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, which places the country's main transit hub among the documented policing hotspots.

Legal exposure is governed by an ambiguous framework. The Penal Code 1860 criminalises intercourse against the order of nature with a penalty of up to life imprisonment; Outright International reports that the provision is rarely enforced as a prosecution but is used by police to harass people presumed to be LGBTIQ. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity (September 2023, updated April 2026) states that it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within Section 377. A UK Upper Tribunal decision of February 2019 (PA/07096/2017) reproduces Home Office country material recording Islamist groups calling for the prosecution of LGBT people under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues.

Bangladesh has officially recognised third-gender identity since 2013, but that formal recognition has not prevented the rollback of safety in practice since 2024.
BGD.outOfScopeNotes:
The scope of Section 377 as applied to lesbianism is unresolved in the sources. The UK Home Office country policy note records that it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within the provision, while ILGA's 2019 State-Sponsored Homophobia report read female-female activity as not criminal and elsewhere described the provision as relevant to all genders. No source in the inventory settles the question.

Whether the murder of Shila on 3 February 2025 was motivated by her trans advocacy is not established in the available material; five unidentified individuals stand accused and the sources do not record a motive or a conviction.

No source in the inventory addresses entry and visa screening of trans visitors, acceptance of passports with altered gender markers at Bangladeshi ports of entry, or access to gender-affirming care while visiting. Those points are not sourced here and should not be read as either permitted or prohibited on the basis of this record.

The 260 incidents and 426 affected individuals for 2025 are JMBF tallies rather than government figures, and no official Bangladeshi crime statistic for anti-trans offences appears in the inventory for comparison.

VNM.name: Vietnam
VNM.summary:
Same-sex conduct is not criminalised in Vietnam. The 2015 Civil Code, Article 37, recognised transgender people's right to change their legal gender, and a November 2015 milestone allowed people who had changed gender to apply for a civil-status change. The implementing legislation has not followed. A draft law protecting transgender people's legal status was expected to be discussed by the National Assembly with completion targeted for 2020, and a recognition draft law was still under consideration as of February 2026. The right to legal gender recognition therefore exists in statute without an operative procedure.

No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, according to Freedom House as cited by the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada. Amnesty International's 2025 report finds that LGBTI people's rights lack meaningful protection in both law and practice.

Same-sex marriage was removed from the list of forbidden acts in 2015, but the unions it permits confer no legal rights and are not registered by the state.

Public space for LGBTI organising narrowed during 2025. Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march, and at least five other Pride events were cancelled that year. Human Rights Watch Asia director Patricia Gossman described the cancellations as worrying signs of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, against Vietnam's long-standing reputation for tolerance toward sexual minorities.

Healthcare access is impeded by administration rather than by provider hostility in many accounts. Transgender women report routine discrimination at healthcare encounters, including staff asking why their appearance does not match their identity documents, alongside heightened scrutiny. Four trans Vietnamese patients described respectful providers whose care was undone by administrative red tape. The Ministry of Health declared in August 2022 that same-sex attraction and transgender identity are not mental disorders.

Trans women face economic- and stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence, reported most acutely for trans women in northern provinces and ethnic-minority communities. No trans-specific killing has been documented here.

Conversion efforts (SOGICE) are documented in the Vietnamese context. A Lighthouse Vietnam study published in October 2024 set out the lived experiences and forms of SOGICE among LGBTIQ people and identified data needs.

Detention carries a specific unresolved risk. In January 2015 the Social, Economic and Environmental Institute proposed to the Ministry of Public Security that homosexual and transgender prisoners be housed separately from the general prison population to protect them from sexual harassment, citing a 2014 survey in which most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails. It stated that existing prison infrastructure allowed transgender prisoners to be held only in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population, with no housing wing matched to a prisoner's gender identity, and asked that prisoners be permitted to determine their own gender identity. No enacted outcome has been documented.

Wider repression forms the backdrop. Vague Penal Code articles 109, 116, 117 and 331 were used to arrest at least 43 people in 2025, and proposed press-law rules would require disclosure of sources. Vietnam was re-elected to the UN Human Rights Council for a term running to 2028.

For a visitor: no criminalisation, no trans-specific border friction documented, and unrestricted bathroom access, but no practical route to legal gender recognition and no statutory protection against discrimination.

sources.summary: VietnamNet (16 Jan 2015) reports a proposal by the Social, Economic and Environmental Institute to Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security to house homosexual and transgender prisoners in jails separate from the general prison population, to protect them from sexual harassment. sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults is legal and has never been criminalized in Vietnamese history, and the Penal Code sets the age of consent at 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Historically, the 1812 Gia Long Code (Article 332) banned prostitution and illicit sexual activity including extra-marital sex, which in rare cases allowed homosexuality to be prosecuted under labels such as "extramarital sex" or "rape", though pre-colonial enforcement was so inconsistent that little to no known state action was taken. In 2002 the Ministry of Labour – Invalids and Social Affairs declared homosexuality a "social evil" comparable to prostitution, gambling and drug use and promised legislation to combat homosexuality and arrest same-sex couples; fines on same-sex marriages were abolished by government decree on 24 September 2013 (effective 11 November 2013). Since 3 August 2022 conversion therapy has been outlawed via Dispatch No. 4132/BYT-PC from the Ministry of Health, which states that homosexuality, bisexuality and being transgender are not illnesses and that LGBTQ+ people may not be forced into "treatment". Wikipedia country coverage: Vietnam's first gay pride parade was held in Hanoi on 5 August 2012, and by 2017 pride events were held in around 34 other cities and provinces, with over 35 similar events held annually in cities including Haiphong, Da Nang, Ho Chi Minh City and Cần Thơ. Hanoi Pride ran for a fifth consecutive year from 18–24 September 2017 drawing thousands (versus about a hundred at the first parade), and its sixth edition in November 2018 saw more than 1,000 participants cycling to campaign for transgender rights and same-sex marriage; several events were aired on state channels VTV4, VTV6 and VTV9. Media coverage has shifted: in 2002 publications such as Thế Giới Phụ Nữ and Tiếp thị & Gia đình described homosexuality as a disease and "deviant behavior", while in September 2010 Tuoi Tre Online became the first major state media outlet to agree that "homosexuality is normal". The 2013 sitcom My Best Gay Friends was published on YouTube because Vietnamese broadcasters were reluctant to air it. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2006 the government enacted legislation protecting citizens infected with HIV and people living with AIDS from discrimination, and health care is provided free to all Vietnamese citizens. The 2022 conversion-therapy dispatch (No. 4132/BYT-PC) mandated enhanced public communication and dissemination among medical facilities nationwide so staff and patients better understand LGBTQ+ individuals, and advised that psychological support be provided by people with an understanding of gender identity. Sex reassignment surgery was previously illegal, forcing transgender people to travel to nearby Thailand for the procedure; the 2015 Civil Code amendment (passed 24 November 2015 by 282–84, effective January 2017) allows those who have undergone sex reassignment to register under their preferred sex, but a further implementing bill is still required, so the law is not fully enforced. Under the Law on Citizen Identification effective 1 July 2024, transgender citizens may change their ID card when undergoing gender transition but must present confirmation documents, and legal effect depends on the Gender Affirmation Law being passed first. Wikipedia country coverage: The age of consent is 16 under the Vietnamese Penal Code, regardless of gender or sexual orientation. A 2015 study found around 44% of Vietnamese LGBT students aged 14–22 faced stigma, discrimination and violence because of their identities, and a 2014 USAID report showed 54% of LGBT students said their school was not safe, with many dropping out; of those who experienced violence, one third thought about committing suicide and half of those attempted it. 85% of transgender students said they dropped out because of assault and bullying, while a 2015 UNESCO study found 19% of students perceived bullying against LGBT students as "harmless" and 70% of Hanoi parents said they would not allow their children to talk to gay students, with some believing conversion therapy could "cure" LGBT children. A 2007 poll of 300 junior-high and high-school pupils at Ho Chi Minh City Pedagogical University found 80% answered "no" to "Is homosexuality bad?", and 2023 Pew data shows support for same-sex marriage is highest among 18–34-year-olds at 79% versus 57% for those aged 35 and above.

UGA.name: Uganda
UGA.summary:
Uganda is a destination trans and gender-nonconforming visitors should avoid. The Anti-Homosexuality Act of 2023 provides the death penalty for "aggravated homosexuality," lengthy prison terms for the promotion of homosexuality, and penalties reaching 20 years for other offences under the Act. In April 2024 Uganda's Constitutional Court upheld the Act's core provisions, including the death penalty in certain circumstances, and dismissed challenges arguing that public participation requirements had not been met. The same court had previously voided a comparable 2013 statute on procedural grounds, leaving the 2023 Act fully in force.

The Act's offences are written around same-sex conduct and the promotion of homosexuality, but the enforcement climate treats gender nonconformity and perceived LGBT identity as grounds for suspicion, violence and detention. Human Rights Watch recorded arrests, shelter raids, evictions and public outings after the Act's passage, with many LGBT people in hiding. Reuters reported in June 2024 that rights violations against the LGBT community were escalating according to a Ugandan pressure group, and in February 2026 the Associated Press reported that two women were detained in Arua after neighbours reported them for kissing in public, described as one of the first known arrests under the 2023 Act.

The Guardian reported in January 2024 that fear had spread across Kampala, where a transgender woman was mobbed and beaten into a two-week coma after a false allegation posted on TikTok; she was sheltering with some 20 other people in a Kampala safe house. Human Rights Watch's May 2025 report "They're Putting Our Lives at Risk" documented the same pattern, including a small group of Ugandan mothers who have chosen to speak publicly in defence of their LGBT children, and described how abuse is enabled by public rhetoric from the government itself.

Digital activity carries its own exposure. Access Now reported in May 2025 that authorities use digital entrapment, obtaining evidence against LGBTQ+ people through dating apps and other platforms, while the companies behind popular apps do too little to prevent it. Amnesty International's October 2024 report "Everybody Here Is Having Two Lives or Names" found that criminalisation has shrunk online civic space, producing widespread technology-facilitated gender-based violence, including doxxing, impersonation, hacking and disinformation, and forcing people and organisations to change how they present themselves online.

The United States State Department's travel advisory for Uganda is a "Do Not Travel" advisory that includes specific warnings for LGBT travellers, including that the law applies to both visitors and residents. The advisory page could not be retrieved at the time of research, so its current wording is cited from the underlying advisory content rather than from a live reading of the page. A United States State Department human rights report from 2011, published during the debates over what became the 2023 Act, identified violence and discrimination against marginalised groups, including the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender community, among the three most serious problems facing the country.
UGA.outOfScopeNotes:
The United States State Department travel advisory for Uganda returned HTTP 403 at the time of research and could not be read live. The characterisation of that advisory used here, a "Do Not Travel" level with LGBT-specific warnings covering both visitors and residents, comes from the advisory's underlying content and is unverified against a current page.

The number of prosecutions brought under the 2023 Act is not established by the sources reviewed. The February 2026 report of the Arua arrest describes those two women as one of the first known arrests under the Act, but no official tally of charges or convictions is available in the inventory.

Whether the death penalty has been imposed in any case under the Act is unresolved. The sources confirm that the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in April 2024 and that it applies in defined circumstances, but none reports a sentence handed down or carried out under the 2023 statute.

Whether conduct limited to gender expression alone, without sexual conduct, can be charged under the Act is not addressed in the sources reviewed. The 2011 United States State Department human rights report predates the Act by more than a decade and describes the pre-Act environment of discrimination and violence rather than the current enforcement regime.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D7.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: In October 2021, trans woman Cleopatra Kambugu Kentaro was issued new identification documents identifying her as female, making her the first Ugandan to have a change of gender legally recognised. The source does not address broader document or legal gender recognition processes beyond this single case. Wikipedia country coverage: In June 2021, a raid on the Happy Family Youth Shelter in Kampala resulted in forty-four arrests, with police claiming an illegal same-sex wedding was being held; several detainees alleged police performed invasive anal examinations. Additionally, under the Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023, people convicted of homosexuality or attempted homosexuality cannot be employed in childcare facilities even after release. Wikipedia country coverage: Human Rights Watch reported in 2005 that Uganda's abstinence-until-marriage programs discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation, denying young LGBTQ people information that could save their lives and reinforcing stigma. A 2018 article in African Health Sciences stated that Uganda's high HIV rate has roots in stigma against same-sex sexual behavior and sex work. The source does not address healthcare access barriers specifically for trans people. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex marriage has been constitutionally banned in Uganda since 29 September 2005, when President Museveni signed a constitutional amendment stating 'Marriage between persons of the same sex is prohibited.' Under the Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023, 'purporting to contract a same-sex marriage' or knowingly attending a purported same-sex marriage ceremony carries imprisonment of ten years. Wikipedia country coverage: Under the Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023, minors convicted of homosexuality face three years imprisonment, and sexual intercourse with a person younger than 18 is classified as 'aggravated homosexuality' punishable by death. The June 2021 raid on the Happy Family Youth Shelter in Kampala targeted a youth facility, resulting in forty-four arrests. The proposed but ultimately excluded provision of the 2023 bill would have criminalised merely identifying as gay or non-binary with ten years in prison, directly targeting youth who may be exploring gender identity. Human Rights Watch noted that abstinence programs deny young LGBTQ people safe sex information, conveying messages of intrinsic wrongfulness that reinforce stigma. Wikipedia country coverage: LGBTQ people in Uganda face severe discrimination actively incited by conservative political, religious and community leaders, with violent attacks and harassment common and often performed or incited by state officials. Media outlets have outed individuals: in October 2010, tabloid Rolling Stone published names, addresses, photographs and hangouts of 100 allegedly gay and lesbian Ugandans with a call for their execution; activist David Kato was murdered in 2011 shortly after winning a lawsuit against the paper. Pride Uganda was cancelled in August 2017 after threats of arrest, and in June 2012 the government banned 38 NGOs accused of promoting homosexuality. A 2013 Pew survey found 96 percent of Ugandans believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society, while a 2017 ILGA poll showed 59 percent agreed gay, lesbian and bisexual people should enjoy the same rights as straight people, indicating some attitudinal shift.

UGA.tangentialFactors:
The 2023 Act did not survive judicial challenge in its entirety by coincidence: the Constitutional Court struck down the 2013 statute on procedural grounds and upheld the 2023 Act on public-participation grounds. The distinction between the two cases shows that the current statute was drafted to withstand legal attack, so visitors should not expect the Act to be struck down during their stay or shortly after.

Reporting on the situation comes from a broad base rather than a single outlet. Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, Reuters, the Guardian, the Associated Press and Access Now have each documented different facets of the same regime: arrests and evictions, mob violence, digital entrapment, and the shrinking of online space. Access Now's finding that app companies are doing too little is relevant to visitors who rely on dating and social apps to meet people.

Violence is not confined to police action. The Guardian's account of a transgender woman beaten into a coma after a false TikTok allegation, and the report that mobs have gathered outside people's homes and shouted that they needed to die, point to a risk of community-level attack that no visa or accommodation arrangement addresses. Public officials have amplified this climate by spreading misinformation and hatred about LGBT people.

The Act's death-penalty provision is real but its application is limited to defined circumstances, and the sources reviewed do not establish that a death sentence has been carried out under the Act. Penalties up to 20 years and lengthy prison terms for promotion are the provisions most likely to affect a visitor who is accused of advocacy, support or same-sex conduct.

A parent-nation human rights report from 2011, published during the debates over what became the 2023 Act, identified violence and discrimination against marginalised groups, including the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender community, among the three most serious problems facing the country.

The number of prosecutions brought under the 2023 Act is not established by the sources reviewed. The February 2026 report of the provincial-town arrest describes those two women as one of the first known arrests under the Act, but no official tally of charges or convictions is available in the inventory.

Whether the death penalty has been imposed in any case under the Act is unresolved. The sources confirm that the national Constitutional Court upheld the provision in April 2024 and that it applies in defined circumstances, but none reports a sentence handed down or carried out under the 2023 statute.

Whether conduct limited to gender expression alone, without sexual conduct, can be charged under the Act is not addressed in the sources reviewed. The parent-nation human rights report from 2011 predates the Act by more than a decade and describes the pre-Act environment of discrimination and violence rather than the current enforcement regime.

A human-rights organisation (4 Apr 2024): the national constitutional court upheld the 2023 law's core provisions — including the death penalty in certain circumstances and penalties up to 20 years — rejecting public-participation challenges; contrasted with the same court voiding a similar 2013 law on procedure.

A digital-rights organisation (15 May 2025): the country's anti-LGBTQ+ laws are used to entrap people online — digital entrapment is one of the main tactics authorities use against LGBTQ+ people via apps, while the companies behind popular apps do too little; shares 2025 case research and safety recommendations — directly relevant to visitor device and app risk under the law.

An international rights organisation (23 Oct 2024) report: the devastating impact of criminalisation on digital spaces for LGBTQ people in the country — widespread technology-facilitated gender-based violence (doxxing, impersonation, hacking, disinformation); the 2023 law fostered a climate of impunity forcing people and organisations to alter how they present themselves online.
A news outlet (Feb 2026): police arrested two women for allegedly kissing in public — they were detained in a town after neighbours reported them; one of the first known arrests under the 2023 law.

A foreign government's 2011 human-rights report for the country: the most important problems included violence and discrimination against marginalised groups — women, children, persons with disabilities, and the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender community — from the era of the anti-homosexuality bill debates.
UGA.blindTangential:
The 2023 Act did not survive judicial challenge in its entirety by coincidence: the national Constitutional Court struck down the 2013 statute on procedural grounds and upheld the 2023 Act on public-participation grounds. The distinction between the two cases shows that the current statute was drafted to withstand legal attack, so visitors should not expect the Act to be struck down during their stay or shortly after.

Reporting on the situation comes from a broad base rather than a single outlet. Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, Reuters, the Guardian, the Associated Press and Access Now have each documented different facets of the same regime: arrests and evictions, mob violence, digital entrapment, and the shrinking of online space. Access Now's finding that app companies are doing too little is relevant to visitors who rely on dating and social apps to meet people.

Violence is not confined to police action. The Guardian's account of a transgender woman beaten into a coma after a false TikTok allegation, and the report that mobs have gathered outside people's homes and shouted that they needed to die, point to a risk of community-level attack that no visa or accommodation arrangement addresses. National officials have amplified this climate by spreading misinformation and hatred about LGBT people.

The Act's death-penalty provision is real but its application is limited to defined circumstances, and the sources reviewed do not establish that a death sentence has been carried out under the Act. Penalties up to 20 years and lengthy prison terms for promotion are the provisions most likely to affect a visitor who is accused of advocacy, support or same-sex conduct.
UGA.localsOnly:
LGBT Ugandans now operate under a permanent risk framework. Amnesty International documented people and organisations altering how they present themselves online, adopting false names and identities, as a direct response to the 2023 Act, and recorded technology-facilitated gender-based violence including doxxing, impersonation, hacking and disinformation as daily features of that environment.

Human Rights Watch described shelter raids, evictions and public outings, and recorded that a small group of Ugandan mothers have publicly defended their LGBT children despite the risks of doing so. Many LGBT people are living in hiding, moving between safe houses in Kampala and elsewhere, as in the January 2024 case of a transgender woman recovering from a mob attack in a safe house shared with around 20 other people.

A pressure group reported to Reuters in June 2024 that violations were escalating, and the February 2026 arrest of two women in Arua, reported by the Associated Press, shows that prosecutions are being initiated by neighbours rather than by investigative bodies alone. Residents who are known or suspected to be LGBT face eviction, physical attack and reporting to police by people in their immediate neighbourhoods.

EGY.name: Egypt
EGY.summary:
Egypt presents a direct and documented entry risk to trans visitors. The Ministry of Interior holds broad powers under the immigration law to refuse entry to, or deport, anyone whose presence is said to disturb public order and morality, and those powers have been applied to travellers perceived as queer. The Cairo 52 study "Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here" (27 November 2023) analyses that law and the case law built on it alongside 12 documented incidents between 2018 and 2022. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights separately records the deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even where no charge is ever upheld. Removal therefore does not require any offence under Egyptian law.

Same-sex conduct is not expressly written into the penal statutes, but prosecutions are a routine outcome rather than a theoretical one. Economic Courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation by reading Penal Code provisions together with Article 9(C) of the Anti-Sex Work Law 10/1961, and Court of Cassation interpretations dating from the 1970s had already stripped out the requirement of a financial exchange, so habitual conduct or multiple partners is enough to sustain a charge. The cybercrime legislation adds six months' imprisonment and a fine for content held to violate "social and family values". The penalties that follow arrest are custodial.

Arrests are manufactured by police work rather than generated by complaints. The BBC investigation into how Egyptian police hunt LGBT people on dating apps describes officers running entrapment operations online, with victims recounting blackmail and detention, and the EIPR documentation identifies fake accounts used to draw in individuals, transgender women especially, on LGBTQ dating apps and websites. A visitor using those same apps is exposed to the same tactic. People taken into custody are subjected to coerced anal examinations, recorded by Bedayaa and by Human Rights Watch in its reporting on the Queen Boat-era crackdown, and the EIPR material notes violations continuing inside police stations after arrest.

Document handling at the border and in administrative dealings is tightening. A Ministry of Interior directive issued to civil-registry heads nationwide in December 2024 closes the Civil Status Law 143/1994 loophole that had allowed transgender people to correct their gender markers through governorate committees, which means corrected documents are increasingly difficult to obtain and mismatches between presentation and papers are more likely to be flagged.

Healthcare carries the same exposure. TIMEP's submission for Egypt's fourth Universal Periodic Review cycle (6 January 2025) finds discriminatory laws, policies and practices that violate the right to health for transgender and intersex people, pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in health services, and barriers to equitable care that persist since the preceding cycle. Egypt rejected all UN recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity at its 2025 Universal Periodic Review.
EGY.outOfScopeNotes:
This inventory contains no source addressing restroom or facility access, nor any source describing how consular or border officers treat identity documents during routine screening; those questions remain unresolved here rather than answered negatively.

The 12 incidents analysed in "Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here" are reported as a set without individual outcomes, so the length of detentions and the number of deportations actually carried out are not established. The app-entrapment cases in the BBC reporting are anonymised at the victims' request, which leaves convictions and sentences unverifiable from this material.

The Ministry of Interior directive closing the gender-marker loophole is reported through civil-society documentation; whether a formal instrument has been published, and its exact text, is not confirmed in this inventory. The specific UN recommendations Egypt rejected at its 2025 Universal Periodic Review are cited in summary form here without the underlying session record.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D6.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Egyptian morality and public order provisions criminalize 'any behavior, or the expression of any idea' deemed immoral or offensive to religious teachings, giving police broad leeway to prosecute LGBTQ expression. In 2017, the Supreme Media Regulatory Council issued an order preventing 'the appearance of the homosexuals' or 'promoting their slogans' in media. In August 2018, Al Sisi's government introduced legislation placing any social network user with more than 5,000 followers under increased scrutiny and prosecution under media laws. In 2013, comedian Bassem Youssef was charged by the Morsi government with 'propagating and promoting homosexuality and obscenity.' Wikipedia country coverage: State officials and police routinely harass, abuse, and torture LGBTQ people, particularly trans people, leading to unfair arrests and abuse in custody. After the September 2017 rainbow flag incident, TV hosts Ahmed Moussa and Mohamed Al Gheity repeatedly incited violence against the LGBTQ community; Moussa shared personal information of flag-raisers, leading to at least 84 arrests between 25 September and end of November 2017, many subjected to forced anal tests. In December 2014, TV presenter Mona Iraqi collaborated with police to raid a public bathhouse, arresting around 26 men (later acquitted). In January 2019, host Mohamed El Gheity was jailed for one year for hosting a gay man on his TV show. A 2009 newspaper (Al Balagh Al Gadid) was shut down and two reporters jailed for printing a story about actors' involvement in homosexual prostitution. Wikipedia country coverage: Personal and family law in Egypt is governed by religious law of the person's recognized religion (Islam, Coptic Orthodox Christianity), none of which recognize homosexual relationships. Egyptian law therefore only recognizes marriage between a man and a woman. Reports suggest that if a same-sex relationship becomes public, police may use it as evidence in criminal indictment under laws against Satanism, prostitution, and public immorality. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2004, a seventeen-year-old private university student received a 17-year prison sentence (including two years' hard labor) for posting a personal profile on a gay dating site. The September 2017 rainbow flag incident involved Egyptian youth raising flags at a concert; the resulting crackdown caused 'a state of trauma and despair among young Egyptian LGBTQ individuals,' with many attempted suicides by Egyptian LGBTQ youths. Sarah Hegazi, detained for three months after the incident, fled to Canada, was granted asylum, and died by suicide in 2020. Many Egyptian LGBTQ youths and individuals had to leave the country due to social and political threats. Wikipedia country coverage: According to Pew Research Center, 95% of Egyptians believe homosexuality should not be accepted by society, and polling data suggests only a minority support LGBTQ rights — so Egyptian political parties and human rights NGOs do not express public support. The term 'khawalat' (historically male cross-dressing dancers) has been stigmatized and used as a derogatory term for passive and gay men. Egyptian cinema has portrayed queer characters 'almost exclusively in a mode of stereotyping and defamation.' After the 2011 revolution, LGBTQ activists became more visible and organized online campaigns against homophobia and transphobia went viral on Twitter and Facebook by 2013, though this did not translate into legal reform. In August 2021, the Central Bank of Egypt had to confirm that rainbow holograms on new banknotes were an anti-counterfeiting feature after online critics suggested they were covert LGBTQ support.

EGY.tangentialFactors:
The enforcement pattern has a long documented history. Human Rights Watch's report In a Time of Torture (29 February 2004) set out arbitrary arrests, beatings and confinement in dark cells on suspicion of homosexual conduct during the Queen Boat-era crackdown, with testimony from defendants, and the EIPR material on continuing violations inside police stations shows the same treatment logic still present two decades later.

Outright's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, states the gap plainly: homosexuality is not explicitly criminalised, yet vague public-morality and debauchery provisions are used to secure prison sentences. Bedayaa's February 2023 briefing adds that authorities turn a blind eye to harassment while arresting the people being harassed, and that Egypt maintains no anti-discrimination policy or law covering sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics. The absence of any such statute removes the principal route to redress for a visitor who is stopped, searched or detained.
EGY.localsOnly:
For Egyptian residents, legal gender recognition has been actively foreclosed. The Civil Status Law 143/1994 had permitted correction of gender markers through governorate committees, and a Ministry of Interior directive distributed to civil-registry heads across the country in December 2024 was issued specifically to close that route.

Residents face the same health system described in TIMEP's January 2025 UPR submission: discriminatory laws, policies and practices, and widespread gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare that leaves transgender and intersex Egyptians without equitable access. Bedayaa's briefing documents rising arrests of homosexual and transgender people, deteriorating detention conditions, and the complete absence of anti-discrimination law or policy at national level.

PER.name: Peru
PER.summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. In February 2025 a congressional committee approved unanimously, for plenary debate, the dictamen of bills on bathroom access presented by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia, restricting trans people's use of public bathrooms; the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents then mandated that restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru found the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Enforcement of the restriction reaches private and public life. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are also constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
PER.outOfScopeNotes:
The bill numbers are reported inconsistently across sources: one account cites bills 6506 and 8457 approved in committee in February 2025, another cites 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR approved by Congress in April 2025. Which instrument carried the bathroom restriction through to law is unresolved in the material reviewed.

Whether the February 2025 committee dictamen was enacted independently of the April 2025 sexual-integrity law, and whether the bathroom provision has been challenged in court, is not sourced here.

Enforcement practice of the biological-sex restroom rule, including whether security staff or public authorities have applied it against visitors, is not documented in the material reviewed.

The figure of 54 transgender and gender-diverse people killed between 2020 and 2023, and the report of a consumer-protection body dismissing a trans woman's complaint against a gym, are carried from the record without a source attached in this inventory; both remain unverified here.

Whether the 17-year sentence against the three officers has been appealed, and whether the officers remained in custody pending appeal, is not stated in the sources reviewed.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5.
