sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Peru since the 1924 Penal Code; the 1863 code had criminalized sodomy with penalties akin to rape. Age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation per a 2012 Constitutional Court decision — relevant to trans and cis youth. Discrimination and hate crimes on sexual orientation and gender identity were criminalized by a 2017 governmental decree (Nº 1323, in effect 7 January 2017) under Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code; Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip the provisions but Kuczynski's veto stood. Law 32331 (enacted 13 May 2025) prohibits trans people from using public restrooms — a state-imposed restriction on trans people's daily movements that could intensify hostile interactions in transit spaces. Wikipedia country coverage: Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity; in 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, but reversed itself in a 21 October 2016 ruling (published 8 November), permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law — covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity — was introduced 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem to cover trans healthcare; after protests, in June 2024 MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' for health-insurance classification purposes. Wikipedia country coverage: Peru's 2016 national education curriculum includes information on sexual orientation, sex and gender issues, describing sexual orientation as the result of complex biological, cognitive and environmental circumstances and 'not a voluntary choice'. Opinion polls show age-based variation: 18–24-year-olds (66%) were markedly more favourable toward homosexuals than the population overall (49%), and younger people showed higher approval of same-sex marriage (8.3% approval among Peruvians in 2010, higher among younger respondents). Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases — a protection with specific relevance to trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

PER.localsOnly:
Health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance in June 2024, a change directed at residents navigating healthcare settings rather than at visitors.

A 2012 study by the Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a structural fact shaping economic and policing exposure for trans residents.

The bathroom legislation also bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity' in public facilities, affecting everyday use of schools, workplaces and public buildings for trans residents.

Congressional pressure continues against therapeutic abortion at the Instituto Nacional Materno Perinatal, an issue raised by trans and feminist organisers alongside the LGBTIQ+ demands.

The 2017 repeal of LGBT hate-crime coverage means residents must rely on general criminal provisions rather than an aggravating ground for bias-motivated violence.
PER.blindSummary:
This country demands real caution for trans visitors, with a nationally-legislated bathroom ban and documented police violence, but no criminalisation of trans identity. The national legislature approved (February–April 2025) a bathroom ban prohibiting trans people from using public bathrooms matching their gender — a nationally-legislated restriction comparable to bans passed in other countries. A consumer-protection body dismissed a discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy.

Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed — trans women most affected. In one documented case, three police officers were sentenced to 17 years in prison for torture and sexual abuse of a trans woman (December 2025), an unprecedented conviction. An official decree briefly classified trans identity as a "mental disorder" (May 2024) before being walked back after mass protests.

For a visitor: no border friction or criminalisation, but the bathroom ban creates daily legal exposure whenever public facilities are used. Same-sex or partner recognition does not exist, so marriage-based protections cannot be assumed.
PER.blindOutOfScope:
General crime (theft, robbery) and political instability affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: how the bathroom ban is enforced in practice at public facilities and how it applies to visitors is not documented in the sources.
blindSourceSummaries: A news outlet (Feb 2025): a national-legislature committee in this country approved unanimously a bill threatening trans people's rights by restricting their use of public bathrooms; the article also records community demands — HIV medication supply, scrapping outdated medical rules, recognition of diverse families, equal marriage, and quotas in public office.

A university human-rights institute analysis: the bathroom-restriction provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing trans people as harassment risks — the institute cites a regional human-rights court advisory opinion that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee full rights.

A regional news platform (Jul 2024): hate crimes rose and trans women are the most affected; recorded numbers are only a sub-registry; a 2012 university study found the majority of trans women in the two largest cities work in sex work.

A foreign broadcaster's world service (Dec 2025): three police officers sentenced to 17 years for torture and sexual abuse of a trans woman — this country's first conviction in a sexual-discrimination-motivated case and, per the article, the first torture-by-discrimination case of a regional human-rights court in the region's history.
A news outlet (Dec 2025): the officers sentenced to 17 years for the rape and torture of a trans woman — the sentence landing nearly 20 years after the attack.

An international human-rights organisation (May 2025): an April-2025 law mandates public-restroom entry be restricted by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their identity; vague child-protection articles enable censorship; the organisation says child protection is used as a pretext for repression and scapegoating.

An international human-rights organisation (Jun 2024): the health system walked back anti-trans guidance — authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as 'a step toward dignity'.

An international LGBTIQ organisation's country overview: public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a court in the capital ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional; an April-2025 law restricts restrooms by 'biological sex'; an April-2025 law lets authorities revoke registrations on public-order grounds, risking weaponisation against queer organising; Pride marches held annually.

A foreign solidarity-group briefing (Apr 2025): a week of setbacks — the national legislature approved bills banning bathroom use contrary to birth sex and inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'; a media personality publicly harassed the first openly lesbian member of the national legislature; pressure continues against abortion rights.

An activist news digest (May 2017): the national legislature voted to strip LGBT protections from the new penal code's hate-crime provisions — carried after a constitutional-committee vote and amid a claimed petition with a million signatures; the outcome left the country among only a few in its region lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.
PER.blindLocalsOnly:
The court-based legal gender recognition process (expensive, years-long, no self-identification law) is resident-facing; the 54 killings and the torture case concern residents.

The consumer-protection dismissal, the official decree classifying trans identity as a "mental disorder", and its walk-back after mass protests are resident-facing facts a visitor would not encounter directly.
PER.tangentialFactors:
Public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination in Peru, according to Outright International's current country overview, so official channels are not reliably protective for a trans visitor who reports an incident.

An April 2025 law on foreign funding for NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order' and 'security' grounds, which Outright International assesses risks being weaponised against queer organising. Combined with the censorship articles in the sexual-integrity law, the space for advocacy that a visitor might rely on for support is narrowing.

The bathroom restriction is comparable to measures passed in other countries, and the removal of LGBT hate-crime coverage in 2017 places Peru alongside only Paraguay and Guyana in South America in lacking such statutory protection.

Pride marches have been held annually in Peru since 2002, with a recorded march as early as 1984, indicating visible community presence alongside the documented risk.

Community demands recorded alongside the bathroom bills include reliable HIV medication supply, scrapping outdated medical rules, recognition of diverse families, equal marriage, and LGBTIQ+ quotas in public office.
PER.blindTangential: The bathroom ban is a nationally-legislated restriction that sources compare to similar limitations passed in parts of other countries. National-level legal and policy developments colour the climate around a visit: an anti-equality decree struck down in July 2025 by a court in the capital, congressional bills restricting bathroom use and inclusive signage, and a 2017 removal of hate-crime protections from the penal code.

URY.name: Uruguay
URY.summary:
Uruguay's trans-protection regime rests on the Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law No. 19684), dated 26 October 2018 and promulgated by the Executive, which sets out state-guaranteed identity, health and anti-discrimination rights for trans persons. It provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration, with no surgery or diagnosis required, alongside a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence and a state employment quota for trans people.

Same-sex relations are legal nationwide, and same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013. Uruguay was the first country in Latin America to recognise same-sex civil unions, in legislation signed by President Tabaré Vázquez in December 2007 that gave couples cohabiting five years or more rights equivalent to marriage.

Non-discrimination protection, a ban on conversion therapy, an equal age of consent and hate-crime rules covering sexual orientation and gender identity are all in force. The status grid compiled for Montevideo reflects national law rather than any municipal rule, so the same baseline applies elsewhere in the country.

Detention is governed by an explicit placement right: the National Rehabilitation Institute states that a trans person entering the prison system may decide whether to be held in a men's or a women's prison, and trans women are currently placed in women's prisons. A new prison under construction in Montevideo will include a dedicated sector for trans inmates, and the new women's prison at Punta de Rieles will for the first time account for the trans population. The Parliamentary Commissioner for the Prison System recorded 28 trans women and nine trans men among 14,965 people deprived of liberty.

Lethal violence against trans people continues despite that framework. Joana, a 29-year-old trans woman, was shot dead in her home in Montevideo on 28 July 2025; a suspect was subsequently sentenced to seven years for the murder, giving the case judicial follow-through.

Discrimination complaints in public services are being litigated. In May 2024 the trans health-service user Andreina Stuart denounced mistreatment and discrimination at the hospital in San Carlos, Maldonado; a criminal complaint is pending, the hospital director pledged an administrative investigation once the judicial stage concludes, and local officials pressed for updates to the health system. Beccah Rivas, a trans woman, has sued the state bank BROU over discriminatory handling by a Prosegur guard and alleges the bank withheld the key camera footage; prosecutor Tania Vidal compelled the bank to produce material, and Rivas says she was dismissed after publicising the case.

Outright's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records same-sex relations legal, legal gender recognition available and LGBTI organisations registrable as the civil-rights baseline a visitor enters, while flagging intersex bodily-autonomy protections as incomplete.
URY.outOfScopeNotes:
The Equaldex status grid for Montevideo is an undated compiled page; the underlying dates of the non-discrimination, conversion-therapy and hate-crime provisions are not sourced here and remain unresolved.

Whether the dedicated trans sector in the new Montevideo prison has been completed is unresolved: the July 2023 report gives an official estimate of under two years, and no later confirmation appears in the inventory.

The outcome of Andreina Stuart's criminal complaint and of the hospital's promised administrative investigation is not sourced beyond the pending stage reported in May 2024.

The disposition of Beccah Rivas's discrimination suit against BROU, and the veracity of her allegation that footage was withheld, are unresolved; only the prosecutor's compulsion of material and her dismissal claim are documented.

The motive in the killing of Joana, and whether the homicide was prosecuted or treated as a hate crime, are not sourced; only the seven-year sentence is recorded.

The scope of the incomplete intersex bodily-autonomy protections flagged by Outright is not specified in the inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5.

sources.title: Uruguay to build prison for transgender inmates — MercoPress
sources.summary: MercoPress (29 Jul 2023), citing Uruguayan authorities and officials: as part of a new prison planned for Montevideo there will be a specific sector for the trans population, which Parliamentary Commissioner for the prison system Juan Miguel Petit called 'good news for a very vulnerable population' and estimated would be ready in less than two years. National Rehabilitation Institute (INR) Director Luis Mendoza told a parliamentary hearing that 'if the trans person enters the system they have the right to decide if they want to go to a men's or women's prison,' and that while trans women are currently placed in female prisons, cohabitation entails 'a whole process' of adaptation; he also noted the new women's prison at Punta de Rieles would for the first time account for the trans population, adding 'the laws are very advanced in Uruguay, but the mentality and infrastructure are not in line.' The article cites official figures of 14,965 people deprived of liberty, including 28 trans women and nine trans men (Office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Prison System).

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Incitement to hatred on the grounds of sexual orientation and 'sexual identity' has been prohibited since 2003, and Penal Code article 149ter provides enhanced penalties for crimes motivated by those characteristics. Gay, lesbian and bisexual people may serve openly in the military (open service since May 2009, per a Defence Minister decree) and the 2018 Comprehensive Law for Trans Persons stipulates the 'free development of personality according to their chosen gender identity' while calling on the government to ensure trans people are treated respectfully by authorities. The 2017 Mental Health Law (Law No. 19529) bars any mental-health diagnosis being made on the exclusive basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Since October 2018 no surgery, hormone therapy or diagnosis is required to change legal gender on official documents; name and legal gender changes have been possible for adults since October 2009, and for minors with parental consent since the October 2018 law. A non-binary marker still does not exist — only female and male — even though Law 19,684 (article 4c) recognises non-binary people in its definitions. Wikipedia country coverage: The 2018 Comprehensive Law for Trans Persons calls on the government to ensure transgender people are included in housing programmes and are not denied health services, and in July 2019 the state water company Obras Sanitarias del Estado began offering jobs to transgender people in compliance with the law. From 16 December 2020 gay and bisexual men have been able to donate blood under the same conditions as the rest of the population, ending the previous 12-month abstinence requirement. The 2004 anti-discrimination law created an Honorary Commission to Combat Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and other forms of Discrimination to investigate allegations of unlawful discriminatory conduct, covering sexual orientation and sexual identity. Wikipedia country coverage: The Comprehensive Law for Trans Persons, passed in October 2018 (62–26 in the Chamber, 17–12 in the Senate), allows minors to change legal gender with parental consent and mandates that transgender people receive 1 percent of public and private educational scholarships. Youth-specific harm is severe: 25 percent of transgender Uruguayans left home before age 18 after family rejection, 87 percent did not finish secondary school, and other studies show about 75 percent have been expelled from the education system. Same-sex couples have been able to jointly adopt since September 2009 (Uruguay first in Latin America), and same-sex marriage has been legal since August 2013; the age of consent has been equal at 15 regardless of orientation or gender since 1934. Article 22 of Law No. 19580, in force since January 2018, prohibits unnecessary medical procedures on intersex children and teenagers. Wikipedia country coverage: A 2014 poll found about 71 percent of Uruguayans supported same-sex marriage — the highest in South America — and in 2016 Americas Quarterly named Uruguay the most LGBT-friendly country in Latin America, calling it 'a model for social inclusion'. Uruguay hosted the region's first international LGBT rights conference in July 2016, with hundreds of diplomats, politicians and activists attending; the Montevideo Pride parade has run annually since the 1990s and drew an estimated 120,000 people in 2018, alongside Punta Pride in Punta del Este each February, and Montevideo has several gay bars, restaurants and pubs. The 2015 Gay Happiness Index ranked Uruguay fifth with a score of 73, on par with Canada and Nordic countries. Opposition exists: the Archbishop of Montevideo called same-sex adoption a 'serious error', and between November 2018 and March 2019 about 69,360 signatures were gathered for a pre-referendum against the trans law, though only about 10 percent of voters turned out on 4 August 2019, short of the 25 percent needed. Against this, about two-thirds of transgender Uruguayans report having been victims of physical violence, and their life expectancy is around 45 years versus a national average of 77.

URY.tangentialFactors:
Freedom House rated Uruguay Free in its 2024 Freedom in the World report at 96/100, with political rights at 40/40 and civil liberties at 56/60, a general rights climate that sits behind the trans-specific statutes rather than replacing them.

The gap between statute and practice is acknowledged by the authorities themselves. National Rehabilitation Institute Director Luis Mendoza told a parliamentary hearing that the laws are very advanced in Uruguay but that mentality and infrastructure are not in line, noting that housing trans women in female prisons entails a whole process of adaptation. Parliamentary Commissioner Juan Miguel Petit called the planned trans sector good news for a very vulnerable population and estimated it would be ready in under two years.

Intersex bodily-autonomy protections remain incomplete even where LGB and trans provisions are in place, so the umbrella term LGBTI covers uneven ground in this jurisdiction.

Enforcement outcomes vary across the documented cases: a murder produced a seven-year sentence, a hospital complaint sits at the criminal-complaint stage with an administrative investigation deferred behind it, and a discrimination suit against a state bank has turned on disclosure of evidence.
URY.localsOnly:
Law No. 19684 operates as resident-facing statute as well as visitor protection: it guarantees identity, health and anti-discrimination rights, and it carries a state employment quota for trans people plus a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence.

Legal gender recognition is administrative and based on self-declaration, so residents can change their registered gender without surgical or psychiatric prerequisites.

LGBTI organisations can be registered, which underpins the domestic advocacy and service infrastructure available to residents.

Prison placement is a right exercisable by residents: the National Rehabilitation Institute holds that a trans person entering the system may choose between a men's and a women's prison, and the new women's prison at Punta de Rieles is designed to account for the trans population for the first time. Official counts list 28 trans women and nine trans men among 14,965 people deprived of liberty.

Residents pursuing complaints through the courts face open proceedings: Andreina Stuart's criminal complaint against the San Carlos hospital is pending, and Beccah Rivas's suit against BROU is contested over the production of camera footage, with a prosecutor having compelled disclosure.
URY.comparisons: Uruguay's comprehensive legal framework places it above Chile and Argentina, around the Japan/Taiwan level — above the UK (which has an in-force daily bathroom code, strip-search policies, and men's-prison placement post-Supreme-Court) by approximately 0.10, reflecting the five axes on which Uruguay is systematically better (bathrooms protected, no strip-search, no men's-prison rollback, self-ID vs court-GRC, stable vs deteriorating climate).

QAT.name: Qatar
QAT.summary:
Qatar criminalises consensual same-sex relations, with a sentence of up to three years available to Muslim and non-Muslim defendants alike, while Sharia permits a capital penalty that has never been imposed. The sources record no statute repealing or legalising this exposure and no legal change to the framework governing gender non-conformity.

Human Rights Watch reported on 24 October 2022 that Qatar's security forces arrested and abused LGBT people between 2019 and 2022, documenting six cases of severe repeated beatings and five cases of sexual harassment in police custody. Arrests took place in public places on the sole basis of gender expression and were accompanied by unlawful searches. Mistreatment was recorded as recently as September 2022, in the period when Qatar was preparing to host the 2022 World Cup under international scrutiny.

Transgender women interviewed by Human Rights Watch described punitive handling from the moment of arrest. One was detained for wearing makeup; officers made her wipe it off, kept the stained wipes as evidence, photographed her and shaved her head. Another was beaten until her lips and nose bled. All reported sexual harassment in custody, forced unlocking of their phones in order to identify other LGBT people, and conversion-therapy sessions imposed as a condition of release.

Detention was carried out in an underground prison in the capital, Doha. One woman spent two months in solitary confinement, and forced surgical removal of breast tissue was reported as a means of imposing physical detransition.

Beatings, torture and forced conversion therapy by police are documented independently of the individual cases above, and cultural norms are described as treating homosexuality and cross-dressing harshly. Visible non-conformity therefore carries exposure to both the criminal provisions and police practice described here.
QAT.outOfScopeNotes:
Rules governing passport and identity-document gender markers, and whether Qatari border or visa screening inspects them, are not addressed by these sources and remain unresolved here.

No information in the inventory covers entry refusal, deportation grounds, or any screening at the point of entry that could reveal a traveller's trans status. The same is true of access to gender-affirming healthcare, use of gendered facilities, hate-crime charging practice, and recognition of partners or marriages.

The counts of six beating cases and five sexual-harassment cases come from Human Rights Watch's interview sample rather than a national total. The sources do not establish how many people were interviewed overall or how many arrests based on gender expression occurred in Qatar in the same period.

Whether any provision of Qatari law offers anti-discrimination or legal-recognition protection to transgender people is not stated in these sources, and no such protection can be asserted or ruled out from this inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D13.

Wikipedia LGBTQ rights in Qatar: same-sex acts illegal (up to 3 years for Muslims and non-Muslims; Sharia allows a capital sentence never imposed); documented beatings/torture and forced 'conversion therapy' by police; cultural norms view homosexuality and cross-dressing harshly. Baseline legal-persecution picture.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Qatar's Penal Code Article 296 (Law 11/2004) punishes sodomy with one to three years' imprisonment, replacing Article 201 of the 1971 code (which had carried up to five years) and, before that, Article 171 (1956) and the Indian Penal Code imposed via Order in Council 1938. Trans people can be arrested for "impersonating the opposite gender" under "violating public morality" and "community protection" provisions, with detention of up to six months without trial or charge. In the 2024 Grindr case, the detainee was forced to sign documents in Arabic without a translator and denied a lawyer. There is no legal recognition of same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, and cohabitation is illegal. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2013 Kuwait proposed banning gay foreigners from entering any Gulf Cooperation Council country and the GCC agreed to discuss it, but backtracked, possibly over concerns about the effect on Qatar's 2022 World Cup hosting. In May 2022 the Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said LGBTQ visitors would be welcomed to the World Cup but must respect the nation's culture, and in 2013 bid chief Hassan Al-Thawadi said all were welcome provided they refrained from public displays of affection. In the 1990s the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration told Philippine workers that gay workers were prohibited in Qatar after mass arrests and deportations. In 2023 Qatar Airways employee Gilbert Ignatius was deported, fired and banned from Qatar without official explanation. Wikipedia country coverage: On 4 February 2024 a dual British-Mexican citizen was arrested after police ran a fake Grindr profile; he was held 44 days, interrogated about other gay men, and the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention raised concerns about his treatment. In 2016 Polish Instagram star King Luxy spent two months in custody on suspicion of being homosexual, and in 1998 an American visitor was sentenced to six months in prison and 90 lashes for homosexual activity. In May 2023 Gilbert Ignatius was detained by Qatar's Criminal Investigation Department over his appearance — tinted moisturizer, designer clothing and bag cited as evidence of prostitution — and an officer told him "You have no rights. This is Qatar." He reported that post-World Cup secret police crackdowns especially target people who appear to be from the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand, and trans detainees may be held up to six months without charge. Wikipedia country coverage: In May 2022 some hotels on FIFA's official recommended accommodation list outright refused to serve same-sex couples, while others accepted them only if they hid their relationship in public; FIFA said it would remind hotels of non-discrimination requirements. Detainees in the 2024 Grindr case were denied access to antiretroviral medicines needed to live with HIV, a denial the UN Working Group flagged. Trans detainees are required to undergo forced physical detransition (including surgical removal of breast tissue) while held, and must attend conversion "therapy" on release, per BBC-sourced information that Qatari authorities "categorically rejected." Wikipedia country coverage: Abuse including beatings, torture and forced "conversion therapy" has been used by police and other authorities against LGBTQ people. An October 2022 Human Rights Watch report alleged systemic police brutality against LGBTQ people in Qatar based on eyewitness accounts from 2019 to 2022. A May 2022 account by Naser Mohamed, the first Qatari to publicly come out as gay, described LGBTQ people being held and physically abused, then promised safety from further torture if they agreed to become informants against others. In May 2023 an officer struck Gilbert Ignatius when he asked to contact the Indonesian embassy. Wikipedia country coverage: Sexual acts between males and between females are illegal, punishable by up to three years in prison for Muslims and non-Muslims alike, and for Muslims duly convicted in sharia courts a capital sentence remains a theoretical possibility though never imposed. The government does not allow people in Qatar to campaign for LGBTQ rights, and in 2022 police arrested protesters who criticised Qatari law. Trans people may be detained for up to six months without trial on suspicion of "impersonating the opposite gender" or violating public morality/community protection laws. In 1998 an American citizen received six months' imprisonment and 90 lashes for homosexual activity. Wikipedia country coverage: Qatar voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity at the Human Rights Council in 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025. In 2018 nine articles on gay and transgender rights were censored from the Doha edition of The New York Times International Edition, prompting the Government Communications Office to pledge an investigation; a 2016 Doha News opinion piece by a gay Qatari man writing as "Majid Al-Qatari" drew extremely strong reactions for allowing the topic to be discussed. In June 2019 state-linked AJ+ marked LGBTQ Pride Month, prompting criticism of the paradox with domestic censorship, and in 2022 Transport for London banned Qatari advertising after Qatar moved to block rainbow armbands, with Qatar subsequently reviewing its London investments. Senior officials repeatedly framed restrictions as cultural: Nasser Al Khater said in December 2021 that public display of affection "is frowned upon" and Major General al-Ansari warned rainbow flags could be confiscated to "protect" fans. Wikipedia country coverage: The Qatari government does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil partnerships, and Qatari family law, influenced by traditional Islamic morality, means no legal recognition exists for same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships — cohabitation is itself illegal. This absence of recognition has practical effects: some World Cup hotels refused same-sex couples or required them to conceal their relationship, and the Australian men's national team publicly called in October 2022 for Qatar to recognise same-sex marriage. Because same-gender couples cannot marry, the local death penalty for same-gender sex is argued to apply only to Muslims through extramarital-sex provisions.

QAT.comparisons: Unlike Kuwait (statute repealed, courts awarding compensation) or Bahrain (rare enforcement), Qatar's targeting of gender expression is systematic, current, and unreformed — placing it below both despite their shared Gulf context.
QAT.blindSummary:
The jurisdiction criminalises consensual same-sex relations, with a sentence of up to three years available to Muslim and non-Muslim defendants alike, while religious law permits a capital penalty that has never been imposed. The sources record no statute repealing or legalising this exposure and no legal change to the framework governing gender non-conformity.

Human Rights Watch reported on 24 October 2022 that the national security forces arrested and abused LGBT people between 2019 and 2022, documenting six cases of severe repeated beatings and five cases of sexual harassment in police custody. Arrests took place in public places on the sole basis of gender expression and were accompanied by unlawful searches. Mistreatment was recorded as recently as September 2022, in the period when the jurisdiction was preparing to host a major international sporting event under global scrutiny.

Transgender women interviewed by Human Rights Watch described punitive handling from the moment of arrest. One was detained for wearing makeup; officers made her wipe it off, kept the stained wipes as evidence, photographed her and shaved her head. Another was beaten until her lips and nose bled. All reported sexual harassment in custody, forced unlocking of their phones in order to identify other LGBT people, and conversion-therapy sessions imposed as a condition of release.

Detention was carried out in an underground prison in the national capital. One woman spent two months in solitary confinement, and forced surgical removal of breast tissue was reported as a means of imposing physical detransition.

Beatings, torture and forced conversion therapy by police are documented independently of the individual cases above, and cultural norms are described as treating homosexuality and cross-dressing harshly. Visible non-conformity therefore carries exposure to both the criminal provisions and the police practice described here.
QAT.blindOutOfScope:
Rules governing passport and identity-document gender markers, and whether border or visa screening inspects them, are not addressed by these sources and remain unresolved here.

No information in the inventory covers entry refusal, deportation grounds, or any screening at the point of entry that could reveal a traveller's trans status. The same is true of access to gender-affirming healthcare, use of gendered facilities, hate-crime charging practice, and recognition of partners or marriages.

The counts of six beating cases and five sexual-harassment cases come from Human Rights Watch's interview sample rather than a national total. The sources do not establish how many people were interviewed overall or how many arrests based on gender expression occurred in the jurisdiction in the same period.

Whether any provision of law in the jurisdiction offers anti-discrimination or legal-recognition protection to transgender people is not stated in these sources, and no such protection can be asserted or ruled out from this inventory.
blindSourceSummaries: An international human-rights organisation (Oct 2022): security forces arrested and abused LGB people — six cases of severe repeated beatings and five sexual-harassment cases in police custody between 2019 and 2022, with arrests in public places based solely on gender expression and unlawful searches; mistreatment as recent as September 2022 as the country prepared to host the 2022 global sporting event.

An encyclopedia article on LGBTIQ rights in this country: same-sex acts illegal (up to 3 years); a religious-law capital sentence exists but has never been imposed; documented beatings, torture and forced 'conversion therapy' by police; cultural norms view homosexuality and cross-dressing harshly.

An LGBTIQ news outlet (2018): taboo around homosexuality in this country — an essay by a gay citizen drew extreme reactions; commentators on expected conduct during the upcoming global sporting event; no legal change.
QAT.tangentialFactors:
The police practice documented by Human Rights Watch is among the most severe recorded in the Gulf, and its continuation into September 2022 shows that it was not suspended while the country hosted a tournament under global scrutiny.

Public hostility to non-conformity predates the tournament period. A first-person essay by a gay Qatari man published by Doha News in 2016 drew extreme reactions that the writer described as jarring and as causing irreparable damage to mental health. Reporting in July 2018 recorded an entrenched taboo around homosexuality alongside no legal change, and commentary published ahead of the 2022 World Cup addressed the conduct visitors could expect to be held to. The harsh treatment of cross-dressing described in the sources is the element of that climate that bears directly on trans visitors rather than on gay and bisexual travellers alone.

QAT.localsOnly:
The criminal provisions and the documented arrest practice operate inside Qatar without regard to nationality: residents face the same exposure to arrest on the basis of gender expression, the same custodial conditions, and the same requirement to attend conversion-therapy sessions before release.

Police demand for phone access during custody has implications that extend past the individual detained, since the stated purpose was to identify other LGBT people known to them. Residents, and anyone whose contact list is held by a resident, fall within that risk.

The custodial conditions recorded by Human Rights Watch, including an underground facility in Doha and prolonged solitary confinement, apply to people held in the country indefinitely as well as to those transiting it.

KWT.name: Kuwait
KWT.summary:
Kuwait criminalised "imitating the opposite sex in any way" in 2007, when the National Assembly added Article 199 bis to Penal Code Article 198, punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine of 1,000 dinars (about US$3,500). Human Rights Watch reported that the only known targets of the provision were transgender people, who could neither change their legal documents nor find protection from such policing. Within two weeks of the law taking effect, at least 14 people were arrested at checkpoints, coffee shops and taxis; three were beaten, one into unconsciousness, and heads were shaved as punishment. HRW's 2012 report "They Hunt Us Down for Fun" documented police violence against trans women under the provision.

The 2007 amendment was proposed by MP Waleed Al-Tabtabaei and passed with overwhelming parliamentary support. In February 2022 the Constitutional Court struck it down as unconstitutional, after an individual targeted by police brought the challenge; the ruling is recorded by both Human Rights Watch and the Library of Congress. HRW urged the National Assembly to repeal the statute outright, observing that the judgment removed criminal exposure without ending the underlying dress-code policing practice. A cisgender woman arrested over a short haircut was later awarded 4,000 dinars in compensation, with the Court of Cassation finding that police had detained her "without justification." Being visibly trans is no longer a crime in Kuwait, and Kuwait is the only Gulf state to have repealed its cross-dressing statute.

Criminal exposure elsewhere in the penal code is unchanged. Article 193 still punishes consensual sexual relations between men by up to seven years, and adultery by up to five years. There is no route to changing gender markers on legal documents, so a visitor whose papers do not match their presentation has no domestic remedy for the mismatch.

Discrimination did not end with the ruling. Writing a year after the Constitutional Court decision, DAWN MENA reported that transgender people continue to face social and employment discrimination in practice, and that the judgment was not a first step toward recognition of transgender rights.

Regional conditions shape the risk. Gender segregation and enforced dress codes make trans people especially vulnerable across the area, according to Brian Whitaker's 2016 overview. Human Rights Watch's 2018 study of LGBT activism across 22 jurisdictions in the region, based on interviews with 34 activists, found that six interviewees from Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Oman, Syria and Morocco had relocated to Europe for security reasons tied to their identity or their activism.
KWT.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the National Assembly has since enacted a replacement or amending statute after the Constitutional Court struck Article 198 is not resolved by the sources held here; HRW's February 2022 appeal for outright parliamentary repeal is the last word available on the legislative track.

Enforcement data after February 2022 is thin. The inventory contains no post-ruling arrest figures, so the frequency of dress-code stops, raids, or administrative harassment of transgender people since the ruling is not sourced and should be treated as unknown rather than as absent.

How Article 193 is applied in practice to transgender people, as distinct from cisgender men who have sex with men, is not documented in these sources; the seven-year penalty is stated for consensual relations between men without further specification.

The compensation award to the cisgender woman detained over a short haircut is carried from the existing record; the case number and the date of the Court of Cassation judgment are not verified against a primary source in this inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D5, D6, D12.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: In September 2013 it was announced that all Gulf Cooperation Council states had agreed to discuss a proposal for some form of 'testing' to detect homosexuality in order to deny entry to gay foreigners; officials later insisted it was only a proposal, with concern over hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar cited as a reason for backtracking. Separately, foreigners found to be infected with HIV/AIDS are deported from Kuwait, while Kuwaiti citizens who are infected remain entitled to outpatient care. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity between men is illegal under Kuwait's penal code with penalties of up to seven years in prison, and public morality laws are strictly enforced, leading to regular prosecutions of LGBTQ people. In 2017 Instagram star King Luxy was arrested in Kuwait for allegedly looking too feminine and spent two weeks in custody before release. A 2022 Constitutional Court ruling overturned the criminalisation of 'imitation of the opposite sex', though discrimination by officials persists. Wikipedia country coverage: Foreigners found to be infected with HIV/AIDS are deported, whereas Kuwaiti citizens who are infected are entitled to outpatient medical care organised by a specialised infectious disease hospital. HIV incidence has remained under 0.1 percent through to the latest 2021 figures, with males aged 25–49 making up 47 percent of those with HIV, and in 1992 the National Assembly criminalised intentional transmission of HIV. No youth-specific or minor-specific care access findings appear in the source. Wikipedia country coverage: No known association or charity exists in Kuwait to campaign for LGBTQ rights or to organise educational and social events for the LGBTQ community. In 2007 a group of Kuwaitis applied to the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs to form such an association and never received a formal reply, and in July 2019 they announced they would reapply after a Ministry of Commerce crackdown on LGBTQ symbols such as rainbows in shops. In August 2023 Kuwait banned the film 'Barbie', claiming it promoted homosexuality. No youth- or education-specific findings about minors appear in the source.

KWT.tangentialFactors:
Censorship narrows access to information. The communications regulator CITRA blocked LGBTQI+ material, including advocacy content and legal information, according to the US State Department's 2023 country report; censors also banned the film "The Danish Girl" in Kuwait alongside other regional states. A visitor researching rights or support networks before or during travel may find those resources unreachable on local networks.

Political visibility is effectively absent. No candidate in the National Assembly election openly acknowledged an LGBTQI+ orientation, a finding from the same State Department report. The Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute's July 2024 analysis sets out the steps it considers still necessary after the abolition of the 2007 provision, indicating that the repeal settled the criminal-law question without delivering a wider framework of protection.

Kuwait's position relative to its neighbours is unusual rather than protective: it retains the region's general criminalisation of consensual same-sex relations while having removed the cross-dressing offence that its neighbours still hold on the books.

BHR.name: Bahrain
BHR.summary:
Bahrain decriminalised same-sex sexual activity in 1976, repealing a British colonial-era statute, and is the only Gulf state that does not explicitly penalise same-sex intimacy. No statute criminalises transgender expression. A foreign government's official guidance records that arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare.

Decriminalisation has not removed exposure. Authorities continue to arrest gender and sexual minorities under broadly-phrased indecency and debauchery provisions, which carry imprisonment, fines and deportation. Nine cross-dressers were arrested at a hotel discotheque party in Manama on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. In February 2024 the Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation, extending the framework under which such charges are brought.

Legal gender recognition is refused by the courts. In a May 2023 judgment a Bahraini lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and for gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia, and declined his request for a Ministry of Health medical-committee examination. The same pattern appears in the treatment of identity documents: a foreign trans woman arrested on drug charges was tried "as a man" despite carrying a passport marked female, indicating that corrected documents may not be respected by the judicial system.

For a visitor, the practical exposure sits in the morality provisions rather than in a dedicated statute, and in a court that has shown it will disregard a foreign passport's gender marker. Arrest risk is documented but infrequently reported; the consequences of an arrest, including deportation and public charges of this kind, are severe.
BHR.outOfScopeNotes:
Two source baselines conflict on the fundamental question of legality. The Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada record BHR105575.E (August 2016) reports that "according to sources, homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain," citing Canadian government material of 14 July 2016 and Gulf News of 5 February 2011, while the Wikipedia infobox sourced to ILGA, Outright International and the 2023 US State Department report the 1976 decriminalisation. This conflict is unresolved and is not settled by the sources in hand; the 1976 reading is the more consistently sourced of the two.

Sourcing for this jurisdiction is thin and partly remote. Bahrain has denied entry to or impeded independent human-rights researchers for roughly a decade, including bodies of the United Nations and Amnesty International, so local media frequently serve as the only source of documentation, and many findings rest on second-hand reporting.

The scale of active enforcement is not established. The available material gives individual arrests and a general foreign-government statement that arrests are relatively rare, but no arrest totals, conviction rates or sentencing data for gender-based charges.

No sourced information was found on prison conditions for trans detainees, on access to legal representation, or on whether any administrative appeal lies against the May 2023 gender-recognition refusal.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2, D5, D6, D7, D9.

sources.summary: Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Bahrain' (continuously updated): legal status 'decriminalised since 1976' per ILGA-sourced infobox, with recognition limits and no SOGIESC discrimination protections. Orientation and recognition source, consistent with the Outright and State Department baseline. Wikipedia country coverage: The Interior Minister stated that 'suspected' (effeminate) homosexuals are banned from entering Bahrain through airport checks, and pending bills proposed to expressly ban LGBTQ foreigners from entering the kingdom or receiving residency permits. In September 2013, all Gulf Cooperation Countries agreed to discuss a proposal to establish testing to ban gay foreigners from entering, though officials later backtracked. Penalties under indecency provisions include deportation for non-Bahrainis. Wikipedia country coverage: In response to parliamentary questions about lesbianism in schools, the Assistant Under-Secretary for Educational Services stated the Education Ministry is not responsible for addressing sexuality and that 'The public shouldn't make a big deal out of this problem because it does not exist,' adding that students whose appearance is contrary to school values should be disciplined. Pending bills proposed to instruct children's teachers in warning signs of homosexuality or cross-dressing so that children can be punished. In February 2024, the Ministry of Education referred a private school's administration and board to investigation and dismissed its general manager after a video showed students performing a scene with two male students pretending to propose to each other. Wikipedia country coverage: No LGBTQ-specific facilities, shelters, or community organizations exist: the US Department of State reports there are no approved LGBTQ-related organizations, and ILGA concludes it is 'improbable' that any sexual- or gender-diversity group would be registered, since the body controlling association registration may refuse any group judged contrary to morality or public order. Gender-affirming medical care is heavily restricted: courts require medical documentation of a 'sex change operation' or medical necessity to change legal gender markers, and a 2023 court ruling held that sex-reassignment procedures are against Islamic law where cases are considered solely related to gender dysphoria, limiting eligibility to people with intersex traits. Article 330 of the penal code also mandates that anyone charged with prostitution or 'fujoor' be taken to a hospital for sexually transmitted disease testing and potentially relocated to a medical facility. Wikipedia country coverage: Bahrain has no legal protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, and hate speech against the LGBTQ+ community remains widespread with no legal consequences — partly because Article 309 protects religious groups but does not extend equivalent protection to LGBTQ+ people. Enforcement hits individuals through morality and indecency provisions (Articles 324, 329, 350), which carry 3 months to 2 years' imprisonment, fines up to 200 BHD, and deportation for non-Bahrainis; the government used these against people suspected of being LGBTQI+ or of 'cross-dressing', including a 2009 one-month jail sentence for a man wearing an abaya and purse in public and a 2011 police raid on a party described as a same-sex wedding. False accusations of homosexuality are also used as a tool to discredit and bully government critics and protesters, including human rights advocate Nabeel Rajab and 2011 Pearl Square demonstrators. Media hostility compounds this: a widely-viewed August 3, 2024 Albilad caricature depicted a pride-flag roll of toilet paper captioned 'the correct place'. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth are a direct policy target: a bill proposed in October 2021 would have criminalized promoting or inviting others to homosexual gatherings with up to 5 years' imprisonment, and other pending bills proposed instructing children's teachers to spot warning signs of homosexuality or cross-dressing so that children could be punished. The Education Ministry disclaims responsibility for sexuality issues — Assistant Under-Secretary Khalid Al Alawi said it is parents' job and that 'the public shouldn't make a big deal out of this problem because it does not exist', while adding that students whose appearance is contrary to school values should be disciplined. On February 14, 2024, the Ministry referred a private school's administration and entire board to investigation and dismissed its general manager after a video showed two male students pretending to propose to each other in class; a 2022 incident in which a private school distributed material perceived as promoting homosexuality also triggered calls for stricter laws. Note also that the age of adulthood under the 1976 penal code is 21 for consensual same-sex acts, and the Gulf Daily News has published articles on female homosexuality in girls' high schools.

Cairo 52 (7 Feb 2024): in a May 2023 judgment a Bahraini lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia — including refusal of a Ministry of Health medical-committee examination he requested. For this record: the documented judicial-refusal practice blocking legal transition at first instance.

Cairo 52 country review: Bahrain has denied entry to or impeded independent human-rights researchers for a decade, including UN human-rights bodies and Amnesty International, so local media often serve as the only source. Most findings for this jurisdiction rest on thin, partly remote sourcing.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Bahrain decriminalised same-sex relations in 1976, repealing a British colonial-era law, and is the only Gulf state not explicitly penalising same-sex intimacy, but authorities still use 'indecency' and 'debauchery' provisions to arrest queer and trans people; the Feb 2024 Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation. Decriminalisation coexists with arrests under morality provisions.

Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada RIO BHR105575.E (Aug 2016, covering 2011-Jul 2016): reports that 'according to sources, homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain' (citing Canada 14 Jul 2016 and Gulf News 5 Feb 2011) plus societal-attitude and treatment-by-authorities research. This contradicts the 1976-decriminalisation reading of Wikipedia, Outright and the 2023 US State Department. The conflict is unresolved and requires intake follow-up.

BHR.comparisons: Bahrain scores above Qatar, Oman, and the UAE because it lacks both a codified gender-expression statute and a documented pattern of systematic targeting.
BHR.blindSummary:
The state decriminalised same-sex sexual activity in 1976, repealing a historic-era statute, and is the only state/province among its neighbouring peers that does not explicitly penalise same-sex intimacy. No statute criminalises transgender expression. a foreign government's official guidance records that arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare.

Decriminalisation has not removed exposure. Authorities continue to arrest gender and sexual minorities under broadly-phrased indecency and debauchery provisions, which carry imprisonment, fines and deportation. Nine cross-dressers were arrested at a hotel discotheque party in the capital on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. In February 2024 the national legislature adopted further moral legislation, extending the framework under which such charges are brought.

Legal gender recognition is refused by the courts. In a May 2023 judgment a lower court of the state rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and for gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia, and declined his request for a medical-committee examination by the national health authority. The same pattern appears in the treatment of identity documents: a foreign trans woman arrested on drug charges was tried "as a man" despite carrying a passport marked female, indicating that corrected documents may not be respected by the judicial system.

For a visitor, the practical exposure sits in the morality provisions rather than in a dedicated statute, and in a court that has shown it will disregard a foreign passport's gender marker. Arrest risk is documented but infrequently reported; the consequences of an arrest, including deportation and public charges of this kind, are severe.

Sourcing for this jurisdiction is thin and partly remote. The scale of active enforcement is not established. The available material gives individual arrests and a general foreign-government statement that arrests are relatively rare, but no arrest totals, conviction rates or sentencing data for gender-based charges.

OMN.name: Oman
OMN.summary:
Oman is a destination trans and gender-nonconforming travellers should avoid. The Penal Law (Royal Decree 7/2018) criminalises same-sex conduct with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, and its provisions on impersonation and gender non-conformity reach presentation as well as acts. The Public Prosecution has stated that any male who appears in female clothing or demeanour may be fined up to OMR 3,000 and jailed for up to one year, with additional charges available for publishing such material on social media. These provisions are applied to foreign nationals.

The statute set is broad. Article 265 covers public indecency (10 days to 3 months plus an OMR 100–300 fine); Article 266 covers impersonation and entry into women-only venues while disguised (1 month to 1 year); Articles 267 and 268 cover producing or sharing content held to violate public morals, offline and online (up to 1 year, or 10 days to 1 month). Gender non-conformity is punished through Article 266(d). The 2011 Cyber Crime Law, Articles 17 and 31, has been used against LGBT expression, carrying 1 month to 3 years plus an OMR 100–3,000 fine.

Enforcement against gender presentation is documented rather than theoretical. In January 2018 the Royal Oman Police announced the arrest of a group of men for dressing as women after photographs circulated on social media; Human Rights Watch wrote to Oman's authorities in an open letter of 13 July 2020 about arrests and convictions under the Penal Code's cross-dressing provision, including arrests of men in women's clothing after Snapchat photos from a private party in Salalah and the arrest of an Asian expatriate wearing an abaya and niqab during a women-only hour at a park in Al Buraimi.

Courts have imposed custodial sentences. A Salalah preliminary court sentenced two men to four years' imprisonment and OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and sharing photographs of themselves in women's clothing on social media, and sentenced two further men to three years with the same fine for appearing in the video, with additional charges for publishing immoral acts on social media.

At the border, a genderqueer non-binary Indian model and activist arriving at Muscat International Airport on a 10-day tourist visa on 27 February 2023 reported that friends cleared immigration while she was held for separate examination, made to remove her shirt, and touched inappropriately by officers. That is direct first-hand evidence of how a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor can be treated on arrival, alongside refusal of entry.

Prosecution does not require a complaint from family. Cases are often triggered by digital evidence surfaced during unrelated investigations, and Oman's Article 49 exception removes the usual dual-criminality protection, so conduct abroad can still be pursued. Article 60 requires deportation of foreign nationals convicted of a felony (permanent exclusion) and permits it for misdemeanours (3–15 years). The state ISP enables surveillance, and outing a person carries both social and criminal consequences.
OMN.outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile at humandignitytrust.org/country-profile/oman/ returned HTTP 403 at research time and could not be read directly; its content on criminalisation of same-sex activity and gender expression is described second-hand in the inventory and is not independently verified here.

Reported article numbering for the cross-dressing offence is inconsistent across sources: the 2018 Penal Code provision is cited as Article 266(d) in statute-level extraction and as Article 22 in coverage of the Public Prosecution's announcement. Which numbering appears in the operative text is unresolved.

The date of the Muscat airport examination is unresolved. The source inventory dates the account to 27 February 2023; other references to the same incident give February 2024.

No source states where inside the prison system people convicted of the cross-dressing offence were housed, including whether they were held in facilities matching their gender presentation. This remains unsourced.

The Shafiqa Ahmadi article on Islam and homosexuality offers general scholarly framing on the distinction between acts and identity but contains no Oman-specific or transgender-specific findings, and is not relied on for any claim above.

Unsourced dimensions after this research pass: D7, D12, D13.

BGR.name: Bulgaria
BGR.summary:
Bulgaria is an EU member state that imposes no traveler-facing restrictions on gender expression. There is no criminalisation of gender identity or presentation, no law governing which public facilities a person may use on the basis of gender, and no document, entry, or border screening that turns on a visitor's gender marker. Same-sex relations have been decriminalised since 1968. Entry and visa rules are applied to foreign passports on ordinary terms, and a foreign visitor's recorded gender raises no separate question at the border.

The statutory baseline offers a partial shield. Anti-discrimination legislation in force since 2004 prohibits both direct and indirect discrimination in housing, education and medical treatment, and a 2015 amendment extended coverage to 'sex' as including 'sex change'. A visitor refused a room, a treatment or a service on that ground therefore has a named statutory ground to invoke, though the practical value of that hook depends on institutions that have shown little appetite for pursuing bias cases.

Recognition of a visitor's own documents is where Bulgaria is under active legal pressure. In September 2025 the Court of Justice of the European Union heard the opinion of Advocate General Richard de la Tour, who concluded that EU law precludes national legislation of the kind Bulgaria maintains refusing identity documents that match a trans person's presented gender; the court indicated agreement with the Advocate General's reasoning. The Shipov case remains pending a full judgment, and EU free-movement law supplies a backstop for anyone holding documents issued or recognised in another member state.

The Strasbourg court has already ruled against Bulgaria on the same question. In Y.T. v Bulgaria (2020) the European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8 over the refusal of legal gender recognition, and it made clear in December 2024 that those obligations were unaffected by the registry revision adopted that year, consistent with P.H. v Bulgaria. Judge Šimáčková dissented, judging the revision decision over-formalistic. The Bulgarian Supreme Court of Cassation nonetheless ruled in 2023 that legal gender recognition is impossible, treating gender as an unchangeable biological factor.

The social environment is markedly harsher than the travel rules. Parliament passed a law in August 2024 banning 'propaganda' of non-traditional sexual orientation in schools, on the model of Russian legislation. The EU Agency for Fundamental Rights survey records that 75% of LGBTIQ people in Bulgaria avoid holding hands in public and 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault. Organised hostility to visible LGBT events is documented: in June 2017 Human Rights Watch reported that a group calling itself the National Resistance rallied counter-demonstrators to 'cleanse Sofia from garbage' ahead of the Sofia Pride march on 10 June, prompting the organisation to call on authorities to protect the march.

Public LGBT events are policed rather than prohibited. The fourth annual Sofia Pride parade in June 2011 passed without incident under heavy police guard, drawing only a protest from a 'Family NGO', after far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 editions. Amnesty International's 2015 'Missing the point' review found that authorities consistently fail to identify and adequately investigate hate crimes: bias attacks spiked in 2013 according to the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee, legislation exists but such attacks go unpursued, and the Sofia Prosecution opened only some cases. That institutional non-response is the pattern later reporting inherits, and it is the main practical variable behind the risk of bias violence.
BGR.outOfScopeNotes:
The full Court of Justice judgment in the Shipov proceedings had not issued as of the latest source, which reports only the Advocate General's September 2025 opinion and the court's concurrence with that reasoning. Whether the final judgment adopts the reasoning unchanged, and what transition period Bulgaria is given, is unresolved here.

The relationship between the Supreme Court of Cassation's 2023 holding and the pending EU-law proceedings is not settled in these sources: whether the national ban falls automatically on judgment, or requires a legislative amendment, is not sourced.

The absence of a facilities or bathroom statute, and the absence of gender-based document screening at entry, are stated as the current baseline in this record; no Bulgarian statute or border directive was located in the inventory that imposes either, and no source affirmatively audits border practice for trans arrivals.

The FRA survey figures (75% avoiding hand-holding, 46% avoiding locations) are carried without a survey year in this inventory; the fieldwork date is unresolved. The Amnesty International hate-crime findings date from February 2015 and the underlying spike to 2013, so current prosecution rates are not sourced and are inferred from continuity rather than measured.

Whether the August 2024 school statute has been challenged in the Constitutional Court, and its effect on adult education or on private venues, is not sourced.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D5, D6, D7.
