sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Expression is heavily restricted: on 7 August 2024 Bulgaria's parliament passed an amendment to the education law banning 'propaganda, promotion, or incitement... directly or indirectly' of ideas about 'non-traditional sexual orientation and/or gender identity other than the biological one', signed by President Rumen Radev and in force from 16 August 2024, introduced by the Revival party and backed by GERB. In November 2009 the District Council of Pazardzhik voted to forbid the 'public demonstration of sexual or any other orientation' (struck down by the Administrative Court in October 2010 for procedural errors, upheld on appeal July 2011). Hate speech based on sexual orientation has been banned since the Protection Against Discrimination Act took effect 1 January 2004, but gender expression and gender identity are not explicitly named in the 2015 revision. Billboards promoting tolerance toward same-sex couples in Varna and Burgas were vandalised in December 2018, and the Bulgarian Orthodox Church calls pride events a 'sinful demonstration'. Wikipedia country coverage: Entry and residency: citing Coman and Others v General Inspectorate of Immigration (the Romanian ECJ case requiring full EU residency rights for same-sex couples), a Sofia court on 29 June 2018 granted an Australian woman and her French wife — married in France in 2016 — the right to live in Bulgaria, after they had been denied residency a year earlier when they tried to move there. In September 2023 the European Court of Human Rights held that Bulgaria's refusal to recognise same-sex couples is an 'infringement of human rights'; that case is subject to appeals and awaiting a government response. No text addresses visas, asylum, or entry screening for LGBT visitors as such. Wikipedia country coverage: Health services are covered by the anti-discrimination ban on sexual-orientation discrimination in force since 1 January 2004, and same-sex couples are denied the right to make medical decisions for each other. Gay and bisexual men are not explicitly barred from donating blood: the donor form (per a Ministry of Healthcare ordinance of 19 July 2004) does not ask orientation but requires confirmation of no HIV/STI-risk practices. Intersex newborns routinely have male genitalia removed as the 'easier operation', with parents 'rarely informed' of later harm to the child's gender identity, and there are no laws concerning intersex people. Youth-specific: Single Step Foundation launched Bulgaria's first licensed online support chat in October 2017 for LGBTI youth, families and allies. Wikipedia country coverage: State hostility is documented in law and courts: the 2024 education 'propaganda' amendment, the 2009 Pazardzhik council ban on public demonstration of orientation, the Constitutional Court's Istanbul Convention verdict condemning legislation for legal gender recognition, and the Supreme Court of Cassation's 20 February 2023 interpretative decision that 'the only meaning of the term sex should be its biological one' and that the legal system rests on 'the binary existence of humankind', effectively barring legal gender change. Hate crimes against LGBT people 'are often ignored and go uninvestigated by authorities' — including the 2008 killing of a 25-year-old student in a Sofia park by a group intending to 'cleanse' the park of gays, and the 27 September 2020 assault in Plovdiv on children as young as 14 or 15 by ultra-fans of Botev; a January 2014 government commitment to outlaw such hate crimes was dropped by the government formed after the October 2014 elections, though heavier penalties for sexual-orientation-based crimes were adopted on 28 July 2023. Media and political hostility includes the 1964 show trial of 26 men (including actor Georgi Partsalev and singer Emil Dimitrov) described by experts as 'a masquerade for the public' about 'decadent Western culture', the 2020–2021 rise in anti-LGBT rhetoric where 'gender became a slur', far-right National Resistance advocating brooms and shovels against pride attendees, and the Ataka party's protests. ILGA-Europe ranked Bulgaria 37 of 49 European countries for LGBT rights protection in 2020. Wikipedia country coverage: Article 46 of the Constitution has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 1991, explicitly banning same-sex marriage, and the Constitution does not ban civil unions — but none exist, so same-sex couples are denied inheritance, medical decision-making and joint property rights. A Bulgarian court recognised a same-sex marriage performed in France in 2019, and a Sofia court granted residency rights in June 2018 under the Coman ruling; by contrast, a couple who married in the UK had their recognition claim rejected by the Sofia Administrative Court in January 2018, an appeal pursued by the LGBT organisation Deystvie. In September 2023 the ECtHR found Bulgaria's non-recognition an 'infringement of human rights', pending appeal. Same-sex couples are banned from adopting, and a 2021 ECJ ruling forced Bulgaria to issue an ID to a child of a lesbian couple after it refused a birth certificate. Wikipedia country coverage: On 7 August 2024 parliament amended the education law to prohibit 'propaganda, promotion, or incitement... in the education system' of ideas about non-traditional sexual orientation or non-biological gender identity, defined as attraction 'contrary to Bulgaria's legal concept of... opposite sexes', in force 16 August 2024. The age of consent has been 14 regardless of sex since 2002, and since 2026 it is 16. A 2008 survey of 15 schools in Sofia, Varna and Plovdiv found 10.5% of students identified as bisexual and 1.8% as gay, with 29% saying they would refuse to sit next to a gay classmate, 5% saying they would bully gay classmates and 39% saying they would protect them. Children as young as 14 or 15 were assaulted in Plovdiv on 27 September 2020 in an anti-LGBT 'cleansing action', and the first Sofia Pride in 2008 (about 150 participants) was attacked with petrol bombs, rocks and glass bottles with over 60 hooligans arrested. Single Step Foundation (founded 2016) works specifically with LGBTI youth on coming out and affirmation.

BGR.tangentialFactors:
Bulgaria sits at the harsh end of EU member states on legal gender recognition while remaining inside the union's protective machinery. Its outright statutory ban on recognition has no parallel in most member states, and it is the specific target of both a pending Court of Justice case and a settled European Court of Human Rights judgment, which is why the country's position is legally unstable even as its social climate stays hostile.

The gap between written protection and enforcement is the defining turbulence. Anti-discrimination law has covered 'sex change' since 2015 and hate-crime provisions exist on the books, yet the documented pattern is of bias attacks going unpursued and prosecutions opened only sporadically. Visitors should read formal protections as a complaint route rather than as a preventive guarantee.

Visibility carries more risk than legality suggests. Survey data on avoidance behaviour, organised counter-demonstrations at Pride, and far-right disruption of the 2008 and 2010 marches all point to a threat environment concentrated around public LGBT presence rather than around private conduct or documentation.

Police posture at large LGBT events has historically been the difference between an orderly march and violence, which makes the security arrangement around any scheduled event a live consideration rather than a background assumption.
BGR.localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition is unavailable in practice. The Supreme Court of Cassation held in 2023 that gender is an unchangeable biological factor and that recognition cannot be granted, and Bulgarian authorities continue to refuse identity documents matching a person's presented gender. The European Court of Human Rights found this incompatible with Article 8 in Y.T. v Bulgaria (2020) and confirmed in December 2024 that the registry revision adopted that year did not alter those obligations, consistent with P.H. v Bulgaria; Judge Šimáčková dissented on the ground that the revision decision was over-formalistic.

EU law is the operative pressure point. The Advocate General's September 2025 opinion in the Shipov proceedings at the Court of Justice of the European Union concluded that EU law precludes legislation such as Bulgaria's, and the court concurred with that reasoning; a full judgment remains pending. Until it lands, recognition claims rest on the Strasbourg judgment and on free-movement rights derived from residence in another member state.

Residents have statutory anti-discrimination protection dating to 2004, covering direct and indirect discrimination in housing, education and medical treatment, extended in 2015 to 'sex' including 'sex change'. The weakness is institutional: Amnesty International's 'Missing the point' review found that authorities consistently fail to identify and adequately investigate hate crimes, with bias attacks spiking in 2013 per the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee and the Sofia Prosecution opening only some cases.

Since August 2024 a statute banning 'propaganda' of non-traditional sexual orientation in schools, modelled on Russian legislation, constrains what can be said in educational settings. Public assembly is not restricted as such: Sofia Pride has run annually under heavy police guard, and the June 2011 edition passed without incident apart from a 'Family NGO' protest, after far-right disruption in 2008 and 2010. Human Rights Watch called on authorities ahead of the 10 June 2017 march to protect participants from the National Resistance counter-rally.
BGR.comparisons: Bulgaria scores below Romania (0.67, no propaganda law, less hostile FRA numbers) and level with Serbia (0.64, similar climate, no EU backstop but no propaganda law either).
BGR.blindSummary:
The country is a member of the supranational union and imposes no traveler-facing restrictions on gender expression. There is no criminalisation of gender identity or presentation, no statute governing which public facilities a person may use on the basis of gender, and no document, entry, or border screening that turns on a visitor's gender marker. Same-sex relations have been decriminalised since 1968. Entry and visa rules are applied to foreign passports on ordinary terms, and a foreign visitor's recorded gender raises no separate question at the border.

The statutory baseline offers a partial shield. Anti-discrimination legislation in force since 2004 prohibits both direct and indirect discrimination in housing, education and medical treatment, and a 2015 amendment extended coverage to 'sex' as including 'sex change'. a visitor refused a room, a treatment or a service on that ground therefore has a named statutory ground to invoke, though the practical value of that hook depends on institutions that have shown little appetite for pursuing bias cases.

Recognition of a visitor's own documents is where the country is under active legal pressure. In September 2025 the union's top court heard the opinion of an advocate general, who concluded that union law precludes national legislation of the kind maintained here refusing identity documents that match a trans person's presented gender; the court indicated agreement with that reasoning. The case remains pending a full judgment, and free-movement law supplies a backstop for anyone holding documents issued or recognised in another member state/province.

The regional human rights court has already ruled against the country on the same question. In a 2020 judgment it found a violation of the right to private life over the refusal of legal gender recognition, and it made clear in December 2024 that those obligations were unaffected by the registry revision adopted that year, consistent with an earlier judgment. One judge dissented, judging the revision decision over-formalistic. The national supreme court nonetheless ruled in 2023 that legal gender recognition is impossible, treating gender as an unchangeable biological factor.

The social environment is markedly harsher than the travel rules. The national legislature passed a law in August 2024 banning 'propaganda' of non-traditional sexual orientation in schools, on the model of comparable foreign legislation. The union's fundamental-rights survey records that 75% of LGBTIQ people in the country avoid holding hands in public and 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault. Organised hostility to visible LGBT events is documented: in June 2017 a monitoring organisation reported that a group calling itself the National Resistance rallied counter-demonstrators to 'cleanse the capital from garbage' ahead of the annual Pride march on 10 June, prompting the call on authorities to protect the march.

Public LGBT events are policed rather than prohibited. The fourth annual Pride parade in June 2011 passed without incident under heavy police guard, drawing only a protest from a 'Family NGO', after far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 editions. A 2015 international review found that authorities consistently fail to identify and adequately investigate hate crimes: bias attacks spiked in 2013 according to a national monitoring committee, legislation exists but such attacks go unpursued, and the capital's prosecution service opened only some cases. That institutional non-response is the pattern later reporting inherits, and it is the main practical variable behind the risk of bias violence.
BGR.blindOutOfScope:
The full top-court judgment in the pending recognition proceedings had not issued as of the latest source, which reports only the advocate general's September 2025 opinion and the court's concurrence with that reasoning. Whether the final judgment adopts the reasoning unchanged, and what transition period the national legislature is given, is unresolved here.

The relationship between the national supreme court's 2023 holding and the pending union-law proceedings is not settled in these sources: whether the national ban falls automatically on judgment, or requires a legislative amendment, is not sourced.

The absence of a facilities statute, and the absence of gender-based document screening at entry, are stated as the current baseline in this record; no national statute or border directive was located in the inventory that imposes either, and no source affirmatively audits border practice for trans arrivals.

The fundamental-rights survey figures (75% avoiding hand-holding, 46% avoiding locations) are carried without a survey year in this inventory; the fieldwork date is unresolved. The hate-crime findings date from February 2015 and the underlying spike to 2013, so current prosecution rates are not sourced and are inferred from continuity rather than measured.

Whether the August 2024 school statute has been challenged by constitutional review, and its effect on adult education or on private venues, is not sourced.

SVK.name: Slovakia
SVK.summary:
Slovakia carries no traveller-facing legal exposure for trans visitors. Legal gender recognition has been available for more than forty years, though the procedure is medicalised and the rules in force require surgical sterilisation before identity documents can be amended. There is no bathroom law and no border obstacle under the free-movement rules of the regional union to which the country belongs.

The security climate is the material concern. On 12 October 2022 a 19-year-old attacker whose primary target was then-prime minister Eduard Heger arrived in the capital at about 18:35; at 19:11 he fired eight shots at the LGBT bar Teplaren, killing two people and injuring a third. The bar was his stated fallback target. The incident is classified as the country's first modern terrorist attack, and the national authorities responded with terrorism charges and official condemnation.

Rights groups assessed the shooting as marking a new era for trans people in the country. A February 2023 assessment found the trans community's position precarious: transition rules were already burdensome, and the aftermath deepened fears about what lay ahead.

Six months after the attack, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Dunja Mijatović wrote to the Slovak National Council reporting no discernible progress and concluding that the human rights of LGBTI people appeared more at risk rather than less. She raised concern about regressive legislative proposals, including a bill that would make legal gender recognition impossible.

Street violence and political rhetoric compound the picture. In July 2022 teenagers beat two men perceived as gay in the capital, and anti-LGBT political rhetoric intensified after October 2022 rather than receding. Police protect Pride events, so the gap lies between functioning institutional protection and the street and political climate a visitor actually moves through.
SVK.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the bill making legal gender recognition impossible advanced, was amended or became law is not sourced in the material available here and remains unresolved.

Enforcement of hate-crime provisions, including any sentence or conviction arising from the July 2022 assault on two men perceived as gay, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The outcome of the terrorism proceedings arising from the 12 October 2022 shooting, including convictions and sentences, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

Two of the supplied sources, an Amnesty International statement and a Pew Research Center survey, yielded no usable finding for this record.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6, D7.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity was legalised in Czechoslovakia in 1962 and the age of consent was equalised to 15 in 1990, previously having been 18 for same-sex activity. In May 2013 the Criminal Code was amended to add sexual orientation as a hate-crime ground allowing harsher penalties, and hate speech on that basis was outlawed. Bills were repeatedly tabled to criminalise trans lives: amendments in 2021 (ĽSNS, 12 Feb; Republic Movement, 23 Sep) and 13 Jan 2023 sought to ban legal gender change and, in the 2023 version, outlaw medical transition with a prison sentence of at least four years — all failed, mostly on abstentions. Wikipedia country coverage: Slovakia's first gay Pride on 22 May 2010 in Bratislava drew about a thousand attendees confronted by right-wing groups who threw stones at speakers, dispersed tear gas and infiltrated the march, forcing cancellation of the city-centre route; 29 people were arrested. Hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation was outlawed in the May 2013 Criminal Code amendment. By contrast, the serving Minister of Culture Martina Šimkovičová made a public homophobic and racist statement on 3 July 2024 claiming Europe is dying because of 'an excessive number of LGBT people'. Wikipedia country coverage: Transgender people in Slovakia have difficulty accessing healthcare; following the 18 May 2022 revocation of the Ministry of Health's standards of care under pressure from the Conference of Slovak Bishops and MPs, there were no valid standards, and as of 18 November 2022 healthcare providers were refusing transgender care, forcing trans people to seek treatment abroad. Standards were republished on 3 March 2023 but their implementation in care access and civil registries 'remains to be seen', and the guideline allowing document change without surgery was revoked on 21 November 2023 on grounds of 'government coalition stability'. In practice surgical sterilisation has usually been required for legal gender change, and gay and bisexual people are barred from donating blood if they had unprotected sex within one year. Registry offices refuse to process gender changes pending new standards, and any existing marriage is invalidated on change of legal gender. Wikipedia country coverage: The Anti-Discrimination Act was adopted in 2004 to meet EU requirements and broadened in 2008, outlawing discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity across employment, education, housing, social care and the provision of goods and services; Article 2 lists sexual orientation among protected grounds. In May 2013 the Criminal Code was amended to cover sexual orientation as a hate-crime ground with harsher penalties and to outlaw related hate speech. The Act also applies to the military, where LGBT people may serve openly, though a 2005 Pravda report described a 'very homophobic environment' in the armed forces. Wikipedia country coverage: Slovakia recognises no civil unions or same-sex marriage; bills introduced in 1997, 2000, 2012, 2018, 2021 and 2022 were all rejected (2012: 94 against to 14 for; 2018: 31 of 150 in support; 2021: 7 for, 67 against). Since 1964 law recognises only a 'close person' (sibling or spouse) with limited rights, mainly inheritance. In June 2014 a constitutional amendment (Article 41) defining marriage as 'a unique union between a man and a woman' passed 102–18, potentially rendering future recognition laws unconstitutional. As of 2025 only married couples may adopt, barring same-sex couples, single people and unmarried partners. Under the ECJ's 5 June 2018 Coman ruling, same-sex couples resident in Slovakia who married in an EU state where one partner is an EU citizen enjoy full residency rights, and the Interior Ministry announced immediate compliance. Wikipedia country coverage: The age of consent was equalised at 15 in 1990 (previously 18 for same-sex activity). The Alliance for the Family's 2014 petition demanded a ban on same-sex adoption and the prohibition of sex education in schools, plus a fourth referendum question barring schools from requiring children to take sexual-behaviour education — the third question was ruled unconstitutional, and the 7 February 2015 referendum on the rest passed but was invalid at 21.07% turnout after opponents urged a boycott. As of 2025 only married couples may adopt, excluding same-sex couples and single people from parenting altogether. A 24 February 2023 bill restricting legal gender change to those whose sex was 'wrongly assigned at birth', provable only by karyotype test, passed first reading with 87 votes, and the 2017 survey found family disclosure reactions mixed — 54% of mothers, 42% of fathers and 49.5% of grandparents accepting, with 28.5% of fathers and 29% of grandparents indifferent. Wikipedia country coverage: On 12 October 2022 a shooting outside Tepláren, a well-known Bratislava gay bar, killed two people plus the perpetrator and wounded a third. Slovakia is described as having some of the worst LGBTQ rights in the EU and less supportive public opinion than the Czech Republic; support is volatile, from 66% acceptance in a 2007 Pew survey to 29–57% backing civil unions in 2019, falling to 40% after the 2022 attack, with the 2015 Eurobarometer putting Slovakia fourth-lowest in the EU on same-sex marriage at 24%. PlanetRomeo's 2015 Gay Happiness Index ranked Slovakia 47th versus Czechia 18th. In the 2017 Iniciatíva Inakosť survey nearly 40% of LGBT respondents had faced active discrimination (15.2% in the last year), many reported low self-esteem, anxiety, depression, alcohol abuse and suicidal feelings from homophobic persecution, and fewer than half were willing to hold a partner's hand in public; there is only a small gay scene of a few bars and clubs in Bratislava.

External oversight is active. a regional human rights commissioner addressed the national legislature directly in April 2023, an unusual step that signals how far the body assessed the situation as having deteriorated.

The direction of legislative traffic is the open question. Proposals to restrict legal gender recognition were live enough to draw commissioner concern, while the existing framework already imposes sterilisation.

BLR.name: Belarus
BLR.summary:
Belarus presents an acute and documented risk to transgender visitors, and travel there should be avoided. In April 2024 the authorities widened the legal definition of pornography to cover depictions of same-sex relationships and of transgender people, grouping these alongside necrophilia and paedophilia as "non-traditional relationships". Production and distribution carry up to four years' imprisonment, rising to thirteen years for material involving children. Human Rights Watch described the change as an explicit attack on LGBT dignity, and it hands prosecutors a charge that can attach to a trans person's visibility rather than to any conduct.

Enforcement followed quickly. In September 2024 the organisation TG House Belarus recorded more than fifteen LGBTQ+ people detained within a single month, at least eight of them transgender; most were charged with hooliganism and two with pornography. Detainees reported physical and psychological abuse in custody, several were beaten and pressured into statements circulated on pro-government channels, and some left the country rather than face further proceedings. Reporting by the Associated Press documents police beating LGBTQ+ people during arrest, laying coerced charges against them, and an expanding campaign of "LGBT propaganda" repression.

Official hostility is carried through state media and policy as well as through the courts. State television has equated LGBTI identities with paedophilia and called them a weapon in the hands of the West, and TG House recorded a rise in hate speech across state propaganda during 2024. The Prosecutor General's Office has announced plans for an administrative-penalty law against "LGBTI propaganda", which had not been tabled as of the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025, and a new National Security Concept places "traditional values" at the centre of state policy. At least ten transgender people left Belarus within a year because of discrimination and repression.

Protection machinery is effectively absent. Belarus has not reported hate-crime data to the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights since 2015 and maintains no National Point of Contact, so the only 2024 incident reporting comes from civil-society monitors such as Human Constanta. The constitutional guarantee of equality in Article 22 is unenforced in practice: analyses of the legal climate record clampdowns on civil society, harassment of activists, arbitrary detentions, and retention of the death penalty.

The administrative-penalty law on "LGBTI propaganda" announced by the Prosecutor General's Office had not been tabled at the time of the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025, and its current legislative status is unresolved in the sources held.

The sources do not address legal gender recognition, identity-document markers, entry or visa screening, border or airport questioning, bathroom and facility rules, access to hormone therapy or other healthcare, hate-crime sentencing enhancement, or recognition of partners and marriages. Whether a transgender visitor's documents are checked against gender presentation at the border is not established by anything in the inventory.

The 1999 US State Department report is a historical baseline and does not describe current conditions. The UN Treaty Body case digest cited here is a general compilation; the specific decisions it treats as relevant to Belarus are not identified in the sources held.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Persecution on the basis of sexual orientation is not explicitly recognized in Belarusian law as a ground for granting refugee status, and same-sex partners are not recognized for the purposes of immigration law. Despite this, after the fall of the communist regime many Belarusians requested and were granted political asylum abroad — most often citing formal or informal police harassment — with Amnesty International and AILGBT-Belarus documenting individuals granted asylum in the Czech Republic, France, the Netherlands and Sweden. Belarus is not a member of the Council of Europe, so activists cannot appeal to the European Court of Human Rights. In 2004, when an international gay and lesbian festival was targeted, authorities made threatening phone calls saying foreigners attending workshops and discussions 'would be immediately expelled from the country' under the article on intervention in domestic affairs. Wikipedia country coverage: The source gives no direct account of trans-specific facilities, but notes that qualified psychological help generally is not available in Belarus, and that the three Minsk universities offering full psychology courses (Belarus State University, Belarus Pedagogical University, European Humanities University) do not address the problems of sexual minorities. LGBTQ venues have been shut or raided: the gay club Oskar was closed by authorities in February 2000 (its owner Ivan Suchinski was later killed), riot police raided a 1999 pride party, and police have conducted unprovoked actions in bars frequented by homosexuals in Gomel and Minsk. In prisons and correctional facilities, homosexuality is subject to speculation, blackmail and extortion, and gays and lesbians are largely unprotected, with turnkeys often encouraging prisoners to abuse homosexuals. Wikipedia country coverage: A high percentage of suicide is observed amongst gays, lesbians, bisexuals and transgender people, while qualified psychological help generally is not available; the Minsk universities with psychology programs do not cover sexual minority issues. Police do not register brutality cases against sexual minorities or investigate homophobic motives, and officers instead collect personal data, passport details and mugshots of gay people at known cruising areas, as reported by Vstrecha in Brest and Gomel. In September 2008, two transgender men raped in Minsk did not report to police because they were unsure police would help; the text notes no youth-specific access-to-care findings beyond the general pattern of concealment and unavailable support. Blood donation carries no particular limitations for gay and bisexual men — all procedures and requirements are the same for all donors. Wikipedia country coverage: In May 2003, the administration of the European Humanities University in Minsk banned a screening of the documentary Outlawed about discrimination of gays and lesbians, with staff saying the ban came under pressure of the Russian Orthodox Church; the same university's psychology courses do not address sexual minority problems. Youth-specific politics are prominent: the April 2026 law bans 'propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness and pedophilia', the July 2001 Organising Committee of the 1st Belarusian Youth Congress voted against admitting Lambda Belarus delegates, and in March 2002 the youth organization Young Front published homophobic statements, with leader Paval Sieviaryniec calling homosexuality 'a death-worthy sin and perversion'. Opinion among the young is comparatively less hostile but still largely negative: Pew's May 2017 poll found 22% of younger Belarusians favor legal gay marriage vs 14% of elders, while a 2007 vote of Gomel region youth found 47.6% had negative feelings toward sexual and gender minorities and 10% wanted to criminalize homosexual relations. Wikipedia country coverage: Homosexuality remains highly stigmatized: a May 2017 Pew Research Center survey found 84% of Belarusians believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society, and 81% opposed same-sex marriage with only 16% in favor; a 2002 Lambda Belarus survey found 47% of Belarusians think gays should be imprisoned, and many believe homosexuality is a psychiatric illness. Gay life is largely underground — most LGBTQ people hide their orientation in public, and those who are 'out' face harassment, violence and physical abuse. State hostility is codified: the April 2026 law prohibits 'propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness and pedophilia' (compared by critics to Russia's 2013 law), and a 2024 Ministry of Culture decree categorized 'homosexualism' alongside pedophilia and necrophilia as pornography, enabling prosecution under Article 343 of the Criminal Code with up to four years in prison. Visibility through assembly is suppressed — pride events from 1999 to 2010 were repeatedly banned, raided or forcibly prevented, and no official organization represents gays and lesbians in Belarus, with other initiatives working outside the legal framework; there is also no anti-discrimination protection and no prohibition of hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity.

UKR.name: Ukraine
UKR.summary:
Nothing about being trans is criminalised in Ukraine, and legal gender recognition exists, but the procedure is medicalised: the 2016 protocol requires a "transsexualism" diagnosis and psychiatric observation before documents are amended. A Ukrainian court has ordered changes to passports and all other documents for two trans people without requiring sterilisation, which stands as a concrete gain on document amendment.

Obtaining the diagnosis that unlocks those documents has become harder. ZMINA reported on 28 July 2026 that trans women in Ukraine now face stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers when seeking a diagnosis, and that the difficulty is documentary as much as medical, affecting both transition procedure and border crossing.

Wartime procedure carries the sharpest visitor-facing risk. Gender Stream documents that since martial law began, holders of male gender markers have been stopped at the border by the State Border Guard Service. A foreign passport is not subject to conscription rules, so border crossing follows standard wartime entry rules, but wartime document checks can out a traveller, and Gender Stream advises and accompanies LGBTQI+ people and families evacuating from frontline regions while helping process and reissue documents for transgender people planning to cross the border legally.

Human Rights Watch reported on 15 May 2024 that cross-border networks became critical support for trans women in Ukraine, arranging assessments, diagnoses and the often-humiliating confirmation by the Military Medical Commission. A Ukrainian activist described the commission's 8am-to-8pm hours and the gatekeeping logic behind them: if a doctor says a person is a woman, the state can decline to decide.

Civil society operates openly despite the war. Gender Stream and Insight provide support and consultations, and Kyiv hosted a three-day Trans Forum in early June 2026, where participants examined the draft Civil Code's effect on the transition procedure and whether being trans grounds exemption from mobilisation.

There is no SOGI-specific hate-crime law, and societal attitudes lag the regional average. Amnesty International reported on 16 May 2013 a pervasive climate of homophobia in which violent attacks went unpunished and were routinely used as a pretext to deny LGBTI people the right to expression and peaceful public events, while lawmakers were urged to vote down proposals to criminalise. Human Rights Watch recorded on 26 June 2012 that LGBT activist Taras Karasiichuk was attacked near his Kyiv apartment, suffering a diagnosed concussion and broken jaw after threats had already forced the cancellation of a pride parade, and that police did not respond immediately despite medical referral.

The situation of transgender people amid the Russian invasion drew formal international attention in June 2022 through European Parliament written question E-002018/2022, filed in the context of Parliament's resolution on the war's impact on women, and was reported the same month by France24 as Ukraine's trans community caught in the crosshairs of war.
UKR.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources do not state whether the draft Civil Code discussed in June 2026 has been adopted, and no text of its transition-procedure provisions is available here.

Unresolved: whether the 2016 court ruling against compulsory sterilisation established a binding nationwide precedent or resolved only the two cases reported is not sourced; no later appellate or supreme-court authority is included in the inventory.

Unresolved: no sourced figure exists for how many people have been stopped at the border under martial law, and the inventory does not indicate whether those stops resulted in refusals of exit, delays, or referral to the Military Medical Commission.

Unresolved: the inventory contains no case-level evidence on whether the absence of a SOGI-specific hate-crime law has been tested in court since the 2013 Amnesty International reporting, and no data on prosecution outcomes for attacks on trans people.

Unresolved: whether exemption from mobilisation on grounds of being trans is available in practice, and on what legal basis, is left open by the sources, which record only that the question was debated.

Not sourced: the France24 and European Parliament items are brief and do not add procedural detail beyond establishing that the situation of trans Ukrainians was reported and raised internationally in 2022.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Ukraine's first LGBTQ rights group, Our World (Nash Svit), was created in 1998 as a community center and human rights advocacy organization. In 2008, LGBTQ organizations formed the Union of Gay Organizations of Ukraine coalition, and the Gay Alliance of Ukraine was founded in 2009. The source text does not describe trans-specific facilities or shelters. Wikipedia country coverage: Clause 211 of the Family Code of Ukraine explicitly bans same-sex couples from adopting children, while single Ukrainian citizens of any sexual orientation are permitted to adopt. Lesbian couples have greater parenting access than gay male couples because IVF and assisted insemination treatments are legal. A revised Civil Code draft submitted to Parliament on 22 January 2026 would automatically annul marriages if one spouse undergoes legal sex reassignment, directly targeting trans people's family recognition. Foreign adopters must be married in a registered different-sex marriage. Wikipedia country coverage: Ukraine's path to partner recognition has been long and uneven: a 2015 government action plan promised a civil partnership bill by 2017, but the Ministry of Justice declared in 2018 it could not proceed due to pressure from religious organizations. A civil unions bill was introduced in Parliament in March 2023, and on 14 May 2025 the government's EU accession roadmap (p. 3.11) set a Q3 2025 deadline for a registered partnerships law. On 10 June 2025, the Desnianskyi District Court recognized actual marital relations between two Ukrainian men (a first for Ukraine), and on 22 January 2026 the Supreme Court in Kyiv rejected a challenge to a lower-court ruling recognizing same-sex couples as de facto family. Meanwhile, a January 2023 NDI/KIIS poll found 56% of Ukrainians supported civil partnership registration for same-sex couples, while a June 2024 KIIS poll found only 28.7% supported civil partnerships without adoption (35.7% opposed, 25.6% indifferent). Wikipedia country coverage: A summer 2015 British Council survey found one in five Ukrainian youth would be uncomfortable having lesbian and gay people as friends. Most Ukrainians grew up with little or no comprehensive, fact-based public education about human sexuality, sexual orientation, or gender identity — a gap the source says promotes viewing homosexuals as dangerous and as sources of HIV/AIDS. The Ukrainian Council of Churches opposed the Istanbul Convention partly on grounds it could "distort" younger generations' sexual identity, framing anti-LGBTQ policy as youth protection. A source anecdote describes a 19-year-old confined indoors for over a year by parents after they discovered messages to his boyfriend. A 14 November 2024 meeting with the Ukrainian Students Association saw a student representative directly ask President Zelenskyy if he would sign registered partnerships legislation, to which he replied "Yes!"

Rights organisation report (16 May 2013): the government must legislate against discrimination and violent attacks on a sexual-orientation and gender-identity basis amid a pervasive climate of homophobia; lawmakers urged to reject criminalisation proposals; attacks routinely used as pretext to deny LGBTI people rights to expression and peaceful public events.
Rights blog (30 Aug 2016): a court ordered the passport and all other document changes requested by two trans people without requiring sterilisation — a concrete data point for document amendment.

Human-rights organisation (26 Jun 2012): an activist attacked near his home — the second violent attack in six weeks after threats forced cancellation of a pride parade; diagnosed concussion and broken jaw; police did not immediately respond despite a medical referral; the organisation urged an investigation into a homophobic motive.
UKR.blindLocalsOnly:
Legal gender recognition for residents runs through the 2016 protocol, which requires a diagnosis of "transsexualism" and psychiatric observation before civil documents are amended. A 2016 court order granted two trans people changes to their passports and all other documents without sterilisation, giving residents a documented precedent to cite when a clinic or registry demands one.

Since martial law, holders of male gender markers have been stopped at the border by the national border guard service, and residents with male markers face mobilisation rules that a foreign passport holder does not. a national support organisation provides consultations and support, advises and accompanies LGBTQI+ people and families evacuating from frontline areas to other parts of the country and abroad, and helps process or reissue documents for transgender people, including those planning to cross the border legally.

Diagnosis has become harder to obtain for residents since the full-scale invasion, with a national human-rights organisation identifying stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers in July 2026. Confirmation by the Military Medical Commission remains part of the gauntlet for people seeking exemption or document changes tied to gender, with commission hours running from 8am to 8pm and cross-border networks arranging assessments and diagnoses for trans women who cannot get them locally.

The draft Civil Code under discussion as of June 2026 would alter the transition procedure, and whether being trans grounds exemption from mobilisation was debated at the Trans Forum held in the capital in early June 2026. Residents also operate support organisations openly and hold public events such as that forum despite wartime conditions.
UKR.tangentialFactors:
The trans-specific risk assessment sits inside a general war-zone risk that is scored separately: shelling, martial law, curfew and displacement affect every traveller in Ukraine regardless of gender identity, and the sources on this record address the second layer only.

Ukraine's legal position on gender recognition is ahead of several neighbours in one respect, since a court has ordered document changes without sterilisation, while its protection machinery lags the regional average on hate-crime coverage, since no SOGI-specific hate-crime statute exists to charge an attack on that basis.

Amnesty International's 2013 reporting framed discrimination and violent attacks as pervasive rather than exceptional, and noted that lawmakers had to be urged to vote down proposals to criminalise conduct, which indicates an active legislative hostility alongside the absence of criminalisation today.

The European Parliament's written question was lodged in the context of a resolution on the war's impact on women, so international advocacy on trans Ukrainians has been routed through gender-based and displacement framings rather than through a dedicated trans-rights instrument.

MDA.name: Moldova
MDA.summary:
Moldova's legal framework is comparatively strong for the region. Since 2022, anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes have been criminal offences with sexual orientation and gender identity named explicitly, and the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover both grounds. A 2024 legislative analysis by ECOM, benchmarked against international standards and built on a survey of local partner organisations, still identifies gaps affecting LGBT people and people living with HIV in access to justice and in the operation of hate-crime and discrimination provisions.

Enforcement lags the statute. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 records hate speech as a serious problem with no meaningful state response, a finding echoed in the European Commission's country report, and notes that political hate speech rose during the election period. Amnesty International's 2025 reporting states that discrimination against LGBTI people remained commonplace and that freedom of expression and assembly was arbitrarily restricted, with impunity persisting for past violations.

One documented case shows how this lands on a trans person in an ordinary commercial setting: a trans woman was refused bank service because her documents did not match her presentation, and the Equality Council confirmed the discrimination and recommended preventive measures.

Public visibility is nonetheless real. Chisinau's Pride march proceeds through the city centre under police protection, and participants in the 2024 festivities came from a range of ages and backgrounds. In 2018 police deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters who tried to disrupt the solidarity march. Courts have also pushed back on local restrictions: on 28 February 2013 the Balti Court of Appeals ruled the northern city's local "gay propaganda" ban unconstitutional and a violation of human rights, striking down church-led prohibitions imposed after protests against the EU-backed anti-discrimination law.

Social hostility remains the counterweight. The Equality Council's study "Prejudices and Marginalization in Moldova 2022", published in January 2023, found acceptance of LGBT+ people extremely low: 79% of respondents would not accept LGBT+ neighbours and 60% would not accept them as work colleagues, with marginalisation increasing over the year. The predominant Orthodox Church and senior politicians, including the mayor of the capital, issue homophobic statements that colour the climate.

No accessible legal gender recognition exists. A medicalised procedure is described on paper but is reported not to function in practice, so a trans visitor should expect documents to reflect birth registration.

Detention is the sharpest documented risk. Igor Brumarețchi, a transgender man registered female at birth in 1972 whose documents were changed to male in 2007, was held for roughly four years in the Moldovan penitentiary system, most of it at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca. Reporting by Ziarul de Gardă in June 2024 and Observatorul de Nord in April 2025 describes him kept alone for long periods in unsanitary, rat-infested cells in the disciplinary isolation unit, ostensibly for his own safety, after his request to be placed in the protection unit was refused. He reports forced strip searches, gynaecology calls made over the intercom, staff opening his bathroom door, being addressed by a female name at roll-call, and says only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The National Penitentiary Administration replied that he was held alone at his own written request, that no rights were violated and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed. The case amounts to placement of a trans detainee by birth sex in the men's system, prolonged solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement and no special-unit option; he intends to sue in Moldovan courts and before the European Court of Human Rights.

The breakaway region of Transnistria, controlled by the neighbouring power Russia, stands outside this framework and has its own anti-LGBT legislation, including new rules prohibiting the promotion of "non-traditional sexual relations".

sources.title: Trăind de gardă/ Deținut transgender – dublu condamnat în închisoare de către „oamenii cu epoleți”
sources.summary: Ziarul de Gardă (15 June 2024) documents the four-year detention of Igor Brumarețchi, a transgender man registered female at birth in 1972 whose documents were changed to male in 2007. He served his sentence in Moldova's penitentiary system, mostly at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, held alone in unsanitary, rat-infested cells for long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit ('izolator disciplinar'), supposedly for his own safety, while his request for sector 12, the unit for detainees requiring protection, was refused. He describes forced strip body searches, 'go to the gynaecologist' calls over the intercom, staff opening his bathroom door, and being called 'Natașa' at roll-call, and says only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The National Penitentiary Administration (ANP) replied that he was detained alone 'at his own written request' with no rights violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed. Brumarețchi says he will sue in Moldovan courts and the ECtHR, and ZdG has notified the Ombudsman and GENDERDOC-M. The case amounts to de facto placement of a trans detainee by birth sex in the men's system, prolonged solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, and no special-unit option.

sources.title: Deținuți ai prejudecăților în instituțiile de stat. Persoane LGBT+, la un pas de suicid. Povestea tragică a unui locuitor al satului Dubna
sources.summary: Observatorul de Nord (7 April 2025) corroborates the same case: Igor Brumarețchi from Dubna village (Soroca district) spent three years locked alone in a cell at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, fully isolated from other detainees and humiliated by prison staff on grounds of sexual orientation, which brought him to the edge of suicide. The piece states the authorities admit homophobia still persists in state institutions and say they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment; the full investigation appeared on anticoruptie.md. Confirms the solitary-style isolation placement practice for a trans detainee in Moldovan prison No. 6 as of 2025.

MDA.localsOnly:
Residents have a working discrimination complaint route. The Equality Council examined a case of a trans woman refused bank service, confirmed discrimination and recommended preventive measures, which indicates a body that receives and decides SOGI complaints rather than one that only issues guidance.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable in practice. A medicalised process exists in legislation but is reported not to function, so trans Moldovans generally cannot correct identity documents; the practical consequence is persistent mismatch between documents and presentation in banking, employment and any identity check.

Prison conditions for trans detainees are the most severe documented resident-facing issue. The Brumarețchi case establishes that a trans detainee can be held in the men's system by birth sex, placed in disciplinary isolation rather than the protection unit, and denied a special-unit option, with the penitentiary administration disputing the discrimination claims. Authorities have acknowledged that homophobia persists in state institutions and say they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment; the extent to which these measures have been implemented is not established in the sources.

Everyday social exposure is high. The Equality Council's 2022 study records 79% rejection of LGBT neighbours and 60% rejection as colleagues, and reports that marginalisation increased over the year, which bears directly on housing and employment rather than on tourism.

Public speech by the Orthodox Church and by senior politicians, including the capital's mayor, remains a routine source of homophobic statements, and hate speech during election periods rises. The state response to this speech is described as not meaningful.

In Transnistria, residents live under a separate legal order that includes a prohibition on promoting "non-traditional sexual relations", with no access to the Moldovan equality-law protections described above.

LUX.name: Luxembourg
LUX.summary:
Luxembourg is among the strongest jurisdictions in its region for trans visitors. Legal gender recognition rests on self-determination: the Act of 10 August 2018 replaced the previous long and costly judicial procedure with a declaration-based route, and the process is administered through the official government portal (Guichet.lu) as an application to change gender status and first name(s) in the civil register. The reform was presented in May 2017 by Justice Minister Félix Braz and approved by the Chamber of Deputies in July 2018. The procedure is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited across employment, goods and services, education and health, with the CET equality body handling complaints. A national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018, and in July 2025 the government unveiled a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ Action Plan, which LGBTIQ+ organisations criticised for omitting depathologisation and other key elements.

The protection machinery has a documented gap on hate crime. As of June 2019 reporting, Luxembourg law contained no LGBTphobic aggravating circumstance for assaults, victims under-reported, and the justice minister signalled that the law would evolve following the 2017 intervention by a Council of Europe monitoring body.

Entry raises no trans-specific issue: travel falls under the common border-free travel zone, and there are no bathroom or facilities laws targeting trans people. No pattern of anti-trans violence against visitors is documented in the sources.

Detention is handled protectively. Prison authorities place detainees who disclose or openly show an LGBT or trans identity so that they are shielded from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners, with trans situations assessed case by case on the information available; such placements are described as exceptional, requests by LGBT detainees to be moved to an ordinary section are generally granted, and no codified birth-sex rule or special custody unit applies.

Standing gaps are narrow but real: no nonbinary marker is available, gender expression and sex characteristics are not explicitly named in anti-discrimination law, and no measures exist on conversion practices or intersex interventions. None of these gaps has a documented visitor-specific impact in the sources.

Not sourced: no trans-specific violence statistics, conviction rates for LGBTphobic assaults, or visitor-incident data for Luxembourg appear in the inventory, so the absence of a documented violence pattern rests on the absence of reporting rather than on recorded low incidence.

Not sourced: the inventory does not state whether gender expression or sex characteristics are covered indirectly through other legal instruments, only that they are not explicitly named in the anti-discrimination framework.

sources.title: Prisons luxembourgeoises : Les détenus gays et transgenres sont protégés
sources.summary: L'essentiel (26 August 2015), reporting Justice Minister Félix Braz's parliamentary answer to LSAP MP Cécile Hemmen, documents that Luxembourg prisons place inmates who disclose or openly show LGBT/trans identity so they are sheltered from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners, with trans-detainee situations handled case by case (the administration gathers all available information on the prisoner); such cases are described as 'exceptional'. Requests by LGBT detainees to be placed in an ordinary section are generally granted, and the minister warned against solutions that would stigmatise or isolate these detainees. A 1989 grand-ducal regulation requires staff to address detainees by surname, and penitentiary staff honour a detainee's chosen 'Monsieur'/'Madame' form of address. The Justice Ministry kept no statistics on LGBT prisoners (disclosure cannot be compelled without illegal privacy interference), and the planned Uerschterhaff prison (Sanem) was designed with multiple sections so detainees could be separated by sex, personality, grounds of detention and, among these, sexual orientation. Outcome: placement follows disclosed identity/need on a case-by-case basis with no codified birth-sex rule and no documented special custody unit or solitary/administrative-segregation practice for trans prisoners in Luxembourg.

AND.name: Andorra
AND.summary:
Andorra's legal framework for trans people rests on the 2022 Law of the Person and Family, which introduced legal gender recognition provisions alongside unified civil marriage. The Ministry of Equality obliges companies operating in the country to maintain protocols against sexual and gender-based harassment.

Andorran police recorded an average of two to three bias-motivated incidents each month during 2025, according to ILGA-Europe's most recent annual review. DiversAnd, the country's principal LGBTI organisation, flagged incidents around the June Pride celebrations of that year and reported them publicly.

No formal system exists to register and classify bias-motivated violence. DiversAnd has called for one so that such incidents can be recognised as hate crime, which indicates that the generic hate-crime provisions of the Penal Code are not routinely applied to bias against trans people.

Entry and movement carry no documented trans-specific obstacle. Andorra sits between Spain and France with open land borders, and it lies outside the Schengen area, where no document-gender checks are applied to arriving visitors. No facility or bathroom law restricts where trans visitors may use restrooms.

The media climate is not uniformly benign. A transphobic opinion piece published in El Periòdic d'Andorra on 27 September was pulled from the website with a public apology after DiversAnd requested its removal, although the article had already run in print.

Practical tolerance remains high in a small, tourism-dependent country with a conservative Catholic history, and the Ministry of Equality implemented equality measures during 2025.

GayLawNet's Andorra page carries a 'limited information' marking, and its index entries on civil unions, discrimination, hate crimes, marriage, sodomy and trans legal status have not been verified against the underlying statutes in this pass.

The procedure, documentary requirements and waiting periods for legal gender recognition under the 2022 Law of the Person and Family are not sourced here. The existence of recognition provisions is established; the process a visitor or resident would follow is not.

The two-to-three monthly figure is a police recording average for 2025. Its breakdown by type of bias, and in particular how much of it concerns gender identity rather than sexual orientation, is not sourced.

The relationship between the generic hate-crime provisions of the Penal Code and the absence of a bias-incident registration system is presented here as reported by DiversAnd; no court or prosecutorial data on how such cases are actually charged is available in the inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6, D7.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Public LGBT expression is protected and has a visible history in Andorra: the country's first LGBT demonstration was held on 6 September 2002, and the first gay pride parade followed on 23 June 2003 at Plaça del Poble in Andorra la Vella, organised by the association Som Com Som. The LGBT group DiversAnd was formed in 2019 (after Som Com Som ended its work in 2018) and organised a pride parade in June 2019; on 17 May 2019 the Department of Equality launched the short film "#lovingdiversity" to raise online awareness. Expression-related bias is penalised: hate crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation carry additional legal penalties, and Law 13/2019 (15 February 2019) bars discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity or expression across employment, education, health care, social services, housing and public establishments. In September 2023 Prime Minister Xavier Espot Zamora publicly came out as homosexual. Wikipedia country coverage: Trans and LGBT minors have explicit statutory protection: Law 14/2019 of 15 February on the rights of children and adolescents establishes that transgender children must be respected in their gender identity, and Law 13/2019 extends non-discrimination protection (including gender identity and expression) to education settings. The age of consent is 16 for both same-sex and heterosexual relationships under Articles 162 and 163 of the Penal Code, and same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the prohibiting law was abolished in 1791. Anti-bullying work in schools is a stated focus of the LGBT group DiversAnd, formed in 2019. Risks to LGBT youth are documented: in 2000 a 17-year-old gay man, Nuno Ribeiro, was murdered in the country because of his sexual orientation, prompting public outcry, and the source notes a few cases of parents expelling their children from home over their sexual orientation. Since the 2014 civil union law, adoption has been open to same-sex couples, and the Family Law passed 21 July 2022 lets trans people update name and gender on legal documents via a simple process without medical intervention. Wikipedia country coverage: Law 14/2019 of 15 February on the rights of children and adolescents establishes that transgender children must be respected in their gender identity, and Law 13/2019 extends non-discrimination protection to education, covering gender identity and expression. The LGBT group DiversAnd, formed in 2019, focuses specifically on preventing and addressing bullying and discrimination in schools. The age of consent is 16 for both same-sex and heterosexual relationships (Penal Code Articles 162-163), and the source notes the 2000 murder of 17-year-old Nuno Ribeiro, a gay teenager, which prompted public outcry; it also reports cases of parents expelling children from home over sexual orientation.

AND.tangentialFactors:
Anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity is recent and shallower than the equivalent coverage in Spain, the neighbouring state whose law most closely resembles Andorra's. Visitors crossing the border should not assume Andorran protections match Spanish ones.

Andorra's head of government, Xavier Espot Zamora, has served as prime minister since 2019 and came out publicly in September 2023, stating that he had never hidden his orientation. A serving head of government who is open about being gay is a direct signal about the standing of the country's political climate, though it says less about trans-specific attitudes than about LGB ones.

The evidence base for any assessment is thin because the population is very small. Absolute incident counts are low in a way that reflects scale as much as safety, and monthly averages of two to three recorded incidents are the more informative figure for a country of this size.
AND.localsOnly:

Gender-affirming care for minors is an active advocacy file rather than an established entitlement. In August, DiversAnd met the Ministry of Health to press for protocols covering puberty blockers and hormone therapy for 16-year-olds, and in some cases for 14-year-olds, following the regulatory changes made in 2022.

Residents who experience bias-motivated violence have no official channel for having it recorded as such. DiversAnd's campaign for a formal registration and classification system is directed at that gap, and the organisation has asked the authorities to recognise the incidents it documents as hate crime.

The Ministry of Equality implemented equality measures during 2025, which is the resident-facing expression of the same policy layer that produces the harassment-protocol obligation on employers.

MCO.name: Monaco
MCO.summary:
Monaco's legal framework on sexual orientation has deep roots: homosexuality has been legal since the 18th century, and hate crimes and hate speech motivated by sexual orientation are penalised. Reported discrimination is described as rare. The sources disagree on the broader point: Outright International states that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned, while Queer In The World describes prohibitions on SOGI discrimination as existing only in certain contexts.

A trans visitor faces no documented legal exposure in Monaco. There are no bathroom or facility restrictions on record, no reported anti-trans incidents, and no border friction: entry is normally made across the short land frontier with France under the common border-free travel zone. The principality is roughly 200 hectares in extent, heavily policed, and a low-crime luxury destination where street violence of any kind is unusual.

The US State Department's 2023 Human Rights Report found no significant changes in Monaco and recorded no torture, arbitrary detention or similar abuses; the only significant issues it identified were the criminal libel and lèse-majesté provisions, which it reports are not enforced. The human-rights machinery applicable to a visitor is therefore benign in practice rather than protective in design.

The assessment rests on that gap. Practical safety is very high and anti-trans hostility is not documented, but the principality offers little explicit trans protection: no functioning legal gender recognition process is described anywhere in the source material, and couple- and family-level recognition for same-sex partners stops short of equality. Visitors are advised to check current local law and customs before travelling.
MCO.outOfScopeNotes:
The two accessible sources conflict on whether SOGI discrimination is prohibited. Outright International's country overview, last updated 12 March 2026, says it is not banned; Queer In The World, updated 3 December 2023, says it is illegal only in certain contexts. The conflict is unresolved here and the stricter reading should not be relied on without checking current Monegasque statute text.

No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, sex-and-gender marker changes on identity documents, or what happens to a trans visitor's passport at the frontier. The absence of a documented process should be treated as not sourced rather than as confirmed absence.

The enforcement record behind the hate-crime and hate-speech provisions for sexual orientation is likewise not documented in the inventory, and no source applies those provisions to gender identity specifically.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D8.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Expression is partly protected by specific hate-speech law: Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression bans hate speech, incitement to hatred and violence based on sexual orientation. Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016 (technological crime law), punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2–5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months–3 years. In July 2010 a Monegasque court jailed a man for 5 days and fined him €5,000 for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 added 'sexual orientation' to Civil Code articles 238-1 (6 months–1 year for violent acts not causing total incapacity), 239 (10 years for attacking a partner or co-resident) and 421 (5 years' probation for unprovoked attacks on a person or group). Wikipedia country coverage: The source states Monaco does not recognize same-sex marriage, and ILGA-Europe's 2019 ranking (45th of 49 European countries) notes transgender people cannot alter their legal gender. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a cohabitation agreement (contrat de vie commune), introduced in Parliament on 16 April 2018, unanimously approved by the National Council on 4 December 2019 and in force six months after publication in the Journal de Monaco; it is signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry. Cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax, not like married couples, and the arrangement is also open to siblings and parents/children. Same-sex couples have no right to adopt children. Wikipedia country coverage: The source reports the LGBT community supports some gay-friendly establishments inside Monaco, but there are no official gay bars, clubs or events in the country, unlike nearby French cities Marseille, Nice and Lyon. Monaco is not an EU member (so EU LGBT-rights protections do not bind it) though it has strong cultural and economic ties with France. Monaco has no armed forces, only a National Guard; France handles defence and allows openly gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people to serve. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth-relevant findings are limited: the age of consent is 15 for both same-sex and opposite-sex relationships. The 2011 anti-discrimination bill's article 44 would have required a school programme every year of primary and secondary cycles to sensitise against racism and all article 1 discriminations (including sexual orientation), but the Council of Government did not approve the bill and its 18 December 2012 replacement dropped the sexual-orientation provisions. Same-sex couples' inability to adopt children directly affects family formation for youth, and most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which the source describes as viewing homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral.

Same-sex couples have no access to marriage or joint adoption in Monaco. The Nice-Matin account carried by the Haut Commissariat adds that there is no equal inheritance or succession rights, no survivor pension, and no parental leave for same-sex partners.

Residents live with very limited visibility: about 10 people are reported to be openly out, no Pride event exists locally, and there is no established community scene to congregate in. Outright International characterises LGBTIQ visibility in the principality as limited and reports discrimination as rare, though it records no legal ban on discrimination by ground of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Residents live with very limited visibility: about 10 people are reported to be openly out, no Pride event exists locally, and there is no established community scene to congregate in. One international overview characterises LGBTIQ visibility in the country as limited and reports discrimination as rare, though it records no legal ban on discrimination by ground of sexual orientation or gender identity.
MCO.tangentialFactors:
LGBT visibility in Monaco is exceptionally low. No gay Pride is held anywhere in the principality, and travel guides direct visitors to events across the border in France or Italy. There is no discernible local scene, and a local newspaper account reports that roughly 10 people are willing to be openly out.

A Council of Europe rapporteur, Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo, summarised the principality's standing as "C'est le triste bilan de Monaco", and Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings despite the long history of decriminalisation. International guidance for visitors recommends staying current with local laws and customs.

Adjacent legal risk for any traveller, not specific to trans people, comes from the criminal libel and lèse-majesté provisions, which the State Department describes as on the books but unenforced. The territory also markets itself with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory, which speaks to visitor hospitality rather than to legal status.

SMR.name: San Marino
SMR.summary:
San Marino is workable for trans visitors: safe in practice, thin in law. Consensual same-sex relations were decriminalised in 2004, no legal penalty attaches to gender identity, and no statute regulates which bathrooms or facilities a person may use. No pattern of anti-trans violence is documented in this small, tourism-dependent country, and entry carries no documented friction — the border with Italy is open, with no recorded identity screening that risks outing an arriving visitor.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. The 2026 edition of the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map lists San Marino among the countries with no functioning legal or administrative process for changing gender markers. The consequence falls on residents rather than travellers: a visitor's foreign documents govern throughout, and there is no domestic procedure that could alter them during a stay.

Constitutional anti-discrimination protection is anchored in sexual orientation. In a referendum held on 4 June 2019, Sammarinese voters approved inserting a clause prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation into the constitution. The sources assembled here do not record a parallel clause covering gender identity or gender expression.

Relationship recognition is in place. The legislature approved a civil-unes union law in November 2018, reported at the time as leaner than Italy's Cirinnà statute, and legal recognition of gay couples is dated to 2016 in other reporting. Partner recognition therefore exists, though it is framed for same-sex couples rather than as a trans-specific protection.

San Marino has engaged international protection machinery. It was one of twelve states examined at the 34th session of the Universal Periodic Review Working Group in November 2019, and ILGA has compiled the SOGIESC recommendations put to each state examined in that round, including San Marino, together with the responses. The individual recommendations are not reproduced in the material available here.

The overall picture for a visitor is very high de facto safety with minimal explicit legal infrastructure for trans people. No legal exposure is documented for a traveller, and the gaps identified — the absent gender-recognition process and the orientation-only constitutional clause — are resident-facing rather than border-facing.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: In 2008 the Grand and General Council amended the Penal Code to outlaw discrimination and hate speech based on sexual orientation, effective 3 May 2008, with penalty enhancements for hate crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation. Article 274 of the Criminal Code, which had punished 'habitual' homosexual acts causing public scandal with 3 months to 1 year imprisonment, was repealed in September 2004 (it was never reported as applied). Homosexuality was decriminalised in 1864. Wikipedia country coverage: Civil unions, in force 5 December 2018 and fully operational from 11 February 2019, grant same-sex and opposite-sex couples rights with respect to residency and citizenship as well as pensions, healthcare, succession and stepchild adoption. In December 2017 the Grand and General Council approved a budget-law amendment allowing foreign same-sex couples to marry in San Marino to encourage tourism, but Sammarinese same-sex couples remain barred from marrying and, as of 2024, the implementing legislation does not appear to have been drafted. Wikipedia country coverage: The 2018 civil union law gives couples certain rights including stepchild adoption, but households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and Sammarinese same-sex couples are still banned from marrying. No other custody-specific provisions appear in the source. Wikipedia country coverage: Civil unions confer healthcare rights on same-sex couples, and gay and bisexual men are allowed to donate blood in San Marino. Discrimination based on sexual orientation is banned under 2019 constitutional amendments, and the Penal Code provides penalty enhancements for hate crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation; there are occasionally reports of violence and hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. The age of consent is 14 for both opposite-sex and same-sex acts, and it is an offence to incite a minor under 18 to sexual corruption. Wikipedia country coverage: San Marino's sex education programme, together with emotional education programmes, expressly provides for knowledge of LGBTQ rights, and the 'Curriculum of education to citizenship' also covers LGBTQ matters. The age of consent is 14 for both opposite-sex and same-sex sexual acts, with a separate offence for inciting a minor under 18 to sexual corruption. Civil unions extend stepchild adoption rights to same-sex couples, though same-sex households otherwise lack equal legal protections. Wikipedia country coverage: Until recently LGBTQ people in San Marino went unnoticed, with very few public debates in media, society or politics, and in the early 2000s the government rejected LGBTQ groups' request to recognise 17 May as the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation was added to Article 4 of the Declaration of Citizens' Rights after a 2 June 2019 referendum passed with 71.46% in favour (the March 2019 council vote fell short at 35 for, 8 against, 1 abstention, needing 39). In 2022 Paolo Rondelli's election as Captain Regent made San Marino the first country in modern history with an openly homosexual head of state, and in November 2019 San Marino accepted UPR recommendations to outlaw gender identity discrimination.
