LIE.name: Liechtenstein
LIE.summary:
Liechtenstein is workable for trans visitors: safe in practice, thin in law. Same-sex relations are legal and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation is prohibited, but gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are absent from every anti-discrimination statute in force, and no procedure exists for changing a legal gender marker. Those gaps bind residents, employers and public bodies; a visitor entering for a short stay faces no legal exposure from them.

Entry falls under the common border-free travel zone operated with Switzerland and Austria, and no source reports friction at that border for trans travellers. There is no statute restricting access to sex-segregated facilities, and no documented pattern of anti-trans violence. The jurisdiction is very small, has very low crime, and is closely integrated with both neighbouring states.

Social attitudes are conservative without being mobilised against trans people. Writing in 2012, GlobalGayz described a population of roughly 35,000 with no organised gay scene at all, because friendship networks perform that role, and reported few organised enemies: no religious extremists, no far-right groups, no political figures demanding homophobic legislation, and gay people living comfortably with little interference. The first Pride was held in 2022.

Hostility has come from the top of the state. In his New Year interview of January 2016, Prince Hans-Adam II called rainbow families “irresponsible”, asserted that children have “a right to a normal family”, and suggested that Liechtenstein could disregard an adverse ruling of the European Court of Human Rights; the LGBT organisation Flay said it was shocked, and the Freie Liste called the remarks contrary to the Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights. Roman Catholicism is the state religion, and the archbishop publicly opposed marriage equality.

Civil marriage and joint adoption have been open to same-sex couples since January 2025. The Landtag moved in September 2022 to open civil marriage regardless of gender and sexual orientation and to remove the remaining legal differences, observing that registered partnerships were regarded as a second-class marriage; the Prince had said in 2021 that he had nothing against marriage equality other than adoption.
LIE.outOfScopeNotes:
The Reuters feature on small European states and LGBT equality returned HTTP 401 at research time and could not be read; any claim it carries about Liechtenstein is unresolved and none is used here.

The inventory sources are weighted towards sexual orientation and relationship recognition. No source addresses trans-specific access rules for sex-segregated facilities, or hate-crime provisions that enhance penalties for offences motivated by gender identity; the presence or absence of such provisions is unresolved on this evidence rather than confirmed.

The statement that there is no documented pattern of anti-trans violence reflects an absence of reported incidents in the sources consulted, not a verified absence of incidents. No source in the inventory records a trans-specific violent attack, its date or its outcome.

The GlobalGayz account dates from March 2012 and its population figure of roughly 35,000 is approximate and dated; its description of social tolerance reflects that period.

VAT.name: Vatican City
VAT.summary:
Vatican City presents essentially no criminal-law exposure to a trans visitor. Consensual homosexual conduct has not been subject to criminal prosecution in the territory in modern times, and decriminalisation has nineteenth-century roots; no documented criminal-law persecution of consensual same-sex conduct exists in Vatican City itself. Nothing about being trans is criminalised. There are no bathroom inspections, no morality police, and the gendarmerie and Swiss Guards do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of visitors of every presentation pass through each year without incident, and entry is made through the neighbouring city of Rome with no border formality or gender-related screening.

No legal recognition of gender exists in Vatican City, and no anti-discrimination protection, facilities rule, or document-amendment mechanism covers a visitor or a resident. The absence cuts both ways: there is no machinery that could confirm a trans person's status, and equally no statutory protection to invoke if a dispute arises.

The doctrinal climate is openly hostile. The Congregation for Catholic Education's 2019 document "Male and Female He Created Them" opposes what it calls gender theory, stating that it "denies the difference and reciprocity in nature of a man and a woman" and "eliminates the anthropological basis of the family." The 2024 declaration "Infinite Dignity" condemned gender-affirming surgery and "gender theory" as violations of human dignity. These are statements of institutional position issued by Vatican dicasteries; they are not enforced against tourists and carry no visitor-facing penalty.

The realistic worst case for a visitor is a dress-code refusal at the basilica or the Vatican Museums, where shoulders and knees must be covered. That is a garment rule applied to everyone regardless of gender identity, and it is resolved by covering up. There is no scenario in the sourced record in which a trans visitor is detained, screened, or turned back on the basis of gender expression.

Vatican City operates no prison system. It holds only a few cells for pre-trial detention, and anyone sentenced to imprisonment serves the term in an Italian prison with the costs borne by Vatican City. Because no domestic custodial system exists, there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, no designated custody facility, and no documented case of trans prisoner placement in this jurisdiction.
VAT.outOfScopeNotes:
No separate United States State Department Holy See chapter for 2023 or 2024 was available in the source set, so the assessment of visitor-facing enforcement rests on the criminal-law baseline and the encyclopedic entries on crime in Vatican City rather than on a current government travel advisory.

Rules governing gender markers on Vatican-issued travel documents, and any screening applied to them at foreign borders, are not sourced here and remain unresolved. The territory's extremely small resident population makes such provisions unlikely to exist in developed form, but that is inference, not a sourced finding.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare, hormone prescriptions, or recognition of foreign prescriptions within Vatican City is not addressed by any source in the inventory and is unresolved. In practice care would be sought in Rome, but no sourced statement confirms how Italian pharmacies or clinics treat a foreign trans patient.

The dress-code refusal described as the realistic worst case is drawn from general visitor guidance rather than from a documented incident involving a trans person; no sourced case of a trans visitor being refused entry on gender-expression grounds in Vatican City was located.

VAT.blindSummary:

Consensual homosexual conduct has not been subject to criminal prosecution in the state in modern times, and decriminalisation has nineteenth-century roots; no documented criminal-law persecution of consensual same-sex conduct exists here. Nothing about being trans is criminalised. There are no bathroom inspections, no morality police, and the gendarmerie and guards do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of visitors of every presentation pass through each year without incident, and entry is made through the adjoining national state/province with no border formality or gender-related screening.

No legal recognition of gender exists in the state, and no anti-discrimination protection, facilities rule, or document-amendment mechanism covers a visitor or a resident. There is no machinery that could confirm a trans person's status, and equally no statutory protection to invoke if a dispute arises.

The state operates no prison system. It holds only a few cells for pre-trial detention, and anyone sentenced to imprisonment serves the term in a national prison with the costs borne by the state. Because no domestic custodial system exists, there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, no designated custody facility, and no documented case of trans prisoner placement in this jurisdiction.

CYP.name: Cyprus
CYP.summary:
Cyprus is a workable destination for trans visitors. There is no legal restriction on gender presentation, no facility or bathroom law of the kind enacted elsewhere in the region, and no border obstacle beyond the standard entry rules that apply to any European Union member state. Tourist infrastructure is Western-standard and accustomed to international visitors.

The statutory framework contains explicit gender-identity protections in criminal law. Law 87(I)/2015 makes public incitement to violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity a criminal offence; the underlying penal code amendment dates from October 2013 and carries up to three years' imprisonment and/or a fine of €5,000. Law 31(I)/2017 provides that prejudice-based motivation is an aggravating factor in sentencing for hate crimes. Law 39(I)/2023 bans and criminalises conversion practices.

Legal gender recognition remains the principal gap. A self-determination bill was approved by the Council of Ministers in September 2022 and received its first parliamentary reading in November 2022; it was still pending as of 2024. Until it is enacted, change of registered sex is governed by the 2002 Civil Registry Law and requires surgery, an arrangement that binds residents rather than visitors.

Gender identity is not yet an explicit ground in the country's equal-treatment framework, and no national anti-homophobia action plan exists. The country's division is relevant to routing: the northern part of Cyprus operates under a de facto Turkish-controlled administration with its own, separate arrangements and a weaker protection framework, so the statutory guarantees described above should not be assumed to apply there.
CYP.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the legal gender recognition bill advanced beyond its first parliamentary reading after early 2024 is unresolved in the available inventory; the most recent sourced status is pending as of 2024.

The dating of the hate-speech offence is not fully consistent across sources: one account places the penal code amendment in October 2013, while the UPR material attributes the offence to Law 87(I)/2015. The penalty figures of up to three years' imprisonment and a €5,000 fine come from the 2013 account and are not independently corroborated here.

No enforcement record is sourced: conviction numbers under the incitement offence, or sentencing practice under the 2017 aggravating-factor provision, are not documented in the inventory.

The two European Commission Network of Legal Experts country reports are cited for scope only; their detailed findings on how gender-identity aspects of European Union directives are transposed were not extracted and remain unverified here.

Conditions facing trans people under the northern administration are described only in general terms; the inventory contains no legal analysis of that administration's framework beyond the existence of its own recognition process.

KHM.name: Cambodia
KHM.summary:
Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex sexual activity, dating from the French protectorate period through independence in 1953, and gender expression is not criminalised. The statutory framework nonetheless contains no SOGI non-discrimination provisions, and no legal gender recognition procedure is in force.

The state's posture toward sexual orientation and gender identity is formally cooperative. At its 2019 Universal Periodic Review Cambodia accepted recommendations to legalise same-sex marriage, and at the 2024 review it accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations, covering marriage equality, legal gender recognition based on self-defined identity, and anti-discrimination measures. Acceptance is a stated commitment; the inventory contains no evidence that implementing legislation has been enacted. Cambodia also hosted the visit of the UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, whose report identifies good practices, remaining challenges and recommendations to strengthen protection against violence and discrimination, and was circulated to national stakeholders in an unofficial Khmer translation.

The operative risks are street-level and detention-level rather than statutory. A Cambodian Centre for Human Rights study documents more than 135 cases of harassment and abuse against transgender women on city streets, describing the treatment as shocking, and records a police practice in Siem Reap in which transgender sex workers were targeted and forced to bathe in dirty, stagnant river water. Comparable abuse is reported across urban centres, including extortion attributed to police.

Violence also originates inside the household. A Rainbow Community Kampuchea study reported in 2019 found that 81% of queer women and transgender people under 35 had suffered emotional abuse from a family member, and that 35% of participants in that age group had considered suicide as a result of family rejection; one case involved a 27-year-old trans man sent by his mother to a rehabilitation facility to correct his gender.

Placement in detention is decided case by case rather than by published rule. In February 2025 the president of the Cambodian Human Rights Committee, Keo Remy, stated at a ceremony at Correctional Centre 2 in Prey Sar prison, Phnom Penh, that transgender offenders who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from the men's facility, Correctional Centre 1, to the women's facility, Correctional Centre 2. The remarks praised the centre and cited no statute or formal policy text. The same report notes that prison overcrowding has worsened amid arrests from a gang crackdown.

Phnom Penh and Siem Reap, the two principal cities, have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors, and international guidebooks carry dedicated sections for LGBT travellers. That infrastructure sits alongside the documented street and policing risks rather than displacing them.
KHM.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 12 Universal Periodic Review recommendations accepted in 2024, including the seven on marriage equality, have been translated into legislation is unresolved in this inventory; no implementing bill, statute or court judgment is cited.

The prison transfer practice described in February 2025 rests on a ministerial-level statement at an event, not on a published regulation. No statute or formal policy text is available to confirm its scope, its criteria or whether it binds the prison administration.

Hate-crime law, entry and visa rules for transgender travellers, document screening at ports of entry, and access to gender-affirming healthcare are not addressed by any source in this inventory and remain unsourced here.

The CCHR figures on street harassment and the Siem Reap policing practice are reported through press coverage of the study; the underlying report's methodology, sample and time period are not reproduced in the sources available for this pass.

The UN Independent Expert visit report is referenced through the UN Cambodia page, which summarises its scope; the recommendations themselves were not available for review in this pass.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Phnom Penh and Siem Reap have a visible LGBT scene with many bars, clubs and other venues catering to the community, and Pride parades have run annually since 2003 (first Siem Reap Pride in 2018). In February 2011 Cambodian tourism businesses launched a global 'Adore Cambodia!' campaign to signal welcome to LGBT tourists, which the Ministry of Tourism endorsed ('We have no policy to discriminate... We really support them'). A 2010 report described a concentration of poor and working-class LGBT people in Beoung Kak 2, dubbed 'Cambodia's first gay town'. Access to services is uneven: Cambodian law does not allow gender marker changes or gender-affirming surgeries, and trans sex workers in Siem Reap reported being forced to bathe in dirty river water, sometimes naked, and to leave the area while cisgender sex workers were not documented as receiving the same treatment. Wikipedia country coverage: State posture is officially non-hostile: the Ministry of Information sent a 2015 letter to media outlets asking them to stop mocking the LGBT community, citing the Constitution's protection of LGBT honour and rights, and in 2015 a Council of Ministers spokesman claimed existing law already protected LGBT people (a claim the Cambodian Center for Human Rights disputed). However, hostility persists at official and societal level: Prime Minister Hun Sen publicly disowned and disinherited his adopted daughter in 2007 because she is a lesbian, and a 2016 CCHR report found about 38% of surveyed transgender women had been arrested, with over 90% saying it was because they were transgender. The 2017 US State Department report listed violence against LGBTI persons among Cambodia's most significant human rights issues, noting LGBTI people were frequently harassed and bullied over their appearance and their work in entertainment and commercial sex sectors, with more than 100 incidents of violence or abuse reported by a local LGBTI organization. The same report noted increased government restrictions on speech, assembly and press freedom generally, while finding no official discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, citizenship, education or health care. Wikipedia country coverage: In June 2017 the Khmer Government announced new life-skills courses covering sexual health, gender-based violence, gender identity and combating discrimination against the LGBT population; these became part of the curriculum in all Cambodian schools in 2018, following advocacy that persuaded the government to introduce LGBT-inclusive classes nationwide. Before that rollout, LGBT activists working with the Ministry of Education trained more than 3,000 teachers in 20 schools across nine Cambodian provinces on including LGBT issues in their classes. Youth-specific harms remain documented: many LGBT Cambodians report bullying at school, and in January 2019 Cambodia received UN recommendations from Iceland, Mexico, Sweden and Uruguay to establish educational programmes and campaigns raising awareness of LGBT people and discrimination. The age of consent is 15 regardless of gender identity or sexual orientation, and in 2019 the director of the Cambodia Human Rights Committee reported rising HIV infections within the LGBT community, especially among people under 30.

KHM.localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition based on self-defined identity was accepted as a recommendation at the 2024 Universal Periodic Review but no implementing statute is recorded, so residents still have no established route to amend gender markers on official documents.

Legislation contains no SOGI non-discrimination provisions, leaving employment, housing, health and education complaints without a statutory basis, despite anti-discrimination measures being among the accepted 2024 recommendations.

Family violence against queer and transgender young people is widespread in the available data: 81% of queer women and transgender people under 35 reported emotional abuse by a family member, and 35% of that group had considered suicide because of family rejection.

Transgender prisoners who have undergone sex-change surgery are moved from Correctional Centre 1 to Correctional Centre 2 at Prey Sar, according to Keo Remy of the Cambodian Human Rights Committee in February 2025. The transfer practice was announced publicly rather than published as regulation, so it offers no enforceable entitlement, and it is unclear how it applies to detainees who have not had surgery.

Civil-society organisations including Rainbow Community Kampuchea and the Cambodian Centre for Human Rights produce the substantive documentation on LGBT conditions, and submitted jointly to the 4th-cycle Universal Periodic Review in December 2023.
KHM.comparisons: Pairwise: below Vietnam (0.63 — LGR legislation progressing, stronger state capacity), above India (0.58).
KHM.blindSummary:
The state has never criminalised same-sex sexual activity, dating from the historic period through independence in 1953, and gender expression is not criminalised. The statutory framework nonetheless contains no sexual orientation and gender identity non-discrimination provisions, and no legal gender recognition procedure is in force.

The national authorities' posture is formally cooperative. At the 2019 universal periodic review the state accepted recommendations to legalise same-sex marriage, and at the 2024 review it accepted all 12 recommendations on sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics, covering marriage equality, legal gender recognition based on self-defined identity, and anti-discrimination measures. Acceptance is a stated commitment; the inventory contains no evidence that implementing legislation has been enacted. The state also hosted the visit of the UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, whose report identifies good practices, remaining challenges and recommendations to strengthen protection against violence and discrimination, and was circulated to national stakeholders in an unofficial translation of the national language.

The operative risks are street-level and detention-level rather than statutory. a national human-rights centre documents more than 135 cases of harassment and abuse against transgender women on city streets, describing the treatment as shocking, and records a police practice in one provincial city in which transgender sex workers were targeted and forced to bathe in dirty, stagnant river water. Comparable abuse is reported across urban centres, including extortion attributed to police.

Violence also originates inside the household. a community-organisation study reported in 2019 found that 81% of queer women and transgender people under 35 had suffered emotional abuse from a family member, and that 35% of participants in that age group had considered suicide as a result of family rejection; one case involved a 27-year-old trans man sent by his mother to a rehabilitation facility to correct his gender.

Placement in detention is decided case by case rather than by published rule. In February 2025 the president of the national human rights committee stated at a ceremony at the women's correctional facility in the national capital's prison complex that transgender offenders who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from the men's facility to the women's facility. The remarks praised the facility and cited no statute or formal policy text. The same report notes that prison overcrowding has worsened amid arrests from a gang crackdown.

The two principal cities have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors, and international guidebooks carry dedicated sections for LGBT travellers. That infrastructure sits alongside the documented street and policing risks rather than displacing them.
KHM.blindOutOfScope:
Whether the 12 universal periodic review recommendations accepted in 2024, including the seven on marriage equality, have been translated into legislation is unresolved in this inventory; no implementing bill, statute or court judgment is cited.

The prison transfer practice described in February 2025 rests on an official statement at an event, not on a published regulation. No statute or formal policy text is available to confirm its scope, its criteria or whether it binds the prison administration.

Hate-crime law, entry and visa rules for transgender travellers, document screening at ports of entry, and access to gender-affirming healthcare are not addressed by any source in this inventory and remain unsourced here.

The figures on street harassment and the policing practice in one provincial city are reported through press coverage of the study; the underlying report's methodology, sample and time period are not reproduced in the sources available for this pass.

The UN Independent Expert visit report is referenced through the UN country page, which summarises its scope; the recommendations themselves were not available for review in this pass.

KHM.tangentialFactors:
Cambodia's non-criminalisation is long-standing rather than recent: same-sex activity was never prohibited under the French protectorate administration or after independence in 1953, which distinguishes it from neighbouring jurisdictions that retained or introduced such offences.

The trajectory of official engagement runs through the Universal Periodic Review process, with marriage-equality recommendations accepted in 2019 and a full set of 12 SOGIESC recommendations accepted in 2024, alongside the visit of the UN Independent Expert. The gap between accepted recommendations and enacted law is the central unresolved question for anyone assessing legal certainty on arrival.

The documented evidence base is uneven in age. The UNDP and USAID country report, Being LGBT in Asia: Cambodia, dates from 2014 and rests on a national LGBT community dialogue held in Phnom Penh in January 2013, participant interviews, an NGO and CBO survey and a literature review; it describes the legal and social environment as it stood a decade ago and should not be read as current law.

Family-level rejection is a documented driver of harm for younger Cambodians, with the RoCK findings concentrated on people under 35, which points to a risk profile that differs between visitors, who are largely outside family structures, and residents.

NPL.name: Nepal
NPL.summary:
Nepal criminalises nothing on the basis of gender identity or gender expression. Its Supreme Court has protected gender identity since a 2007 ruling that recognised the right to self-determined name and gender markers, and a third-gender category has been available on official documents by self-declaration.

In August 2024 the Supreme Court ruled that trans law student Rukshana Kapali must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification. Kapali had filed more than 50 lawsuits since 2021. Before that ruling, changing a marker to female or male had usually required surgery outside the country followed by in-country medical evaluations, including intrusive post-operative genital examinations.

The documentary pathway remained unclear at the level of ordinary administration. In February 2024 Human Rights Watch reported that no straightforward document-change procedure existed and called on the government to urgently create a clear, simple and rights-respecting process. A photograph accompanying that report shows a Kathmandu trans woman holding her 2023 citizenship certificate, which lists her gender as female.

Implementation trails doctrine. Government officials had limited marker changes to people identifying as third gender, while applications for female or male markers lagged behind. Reporting by The Diplomat in February 2024 concluded that the country's progressive reputation outruns actual policy.

Conditions on the ground differ sharply from the rulings. A Kathmandu Post feature published in November 2024 on life in the provincial city of Janakpur found that trans people face discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions, and are often subjected to physical and sexual harassment. Kathmandu has an established activist community; elsewhere, visibly trans people report harassment with little effective recourse from police.

For a visitor, the practical position is favourable: nothing in Nepalese law exposes a foreign passport holder to gender-identity criminalisation, and no legal step requires a trans visitor to disclose transition status at the border or at immigration.
NPL.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved and not sourced in this inventory: entry and visa rules for transgender travellers, including whether border or immigration officers cross-check gender markers against a visitor's appearance, are not addressed by any of the sources used here.

Unresolved and not sourced: the status of bathroom and facility access, of hate-crime protection specific to gender identity, and of marriage or partner recognition for transgender people in Nepal.

Unresolved and not sourced: whether the government has since issued a general document-change procedure following the February 2024 Human Rights Watch appeal, and whether the 2021 civil-society draft bill has entered the formal legislative process.

Dated material used here: the 2015 study-abroad research project describes social conditions in a period before the constitutional and judicial developments cited above and should be read as historical background.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D5, D7.

For this record: official-observer statement on the documentary-recognition gap.

JURIST (Aug 2024): Nepal's Supreme Court ruled that trans law student Rukshana Kapali must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed 50+ lawsuits since 2021; changing markers to 'female'/'male' has usually required surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations including intrusive post-operative genital exams. The Diplomat (Feb 2024): Nepal's 2007 ruling allowing self-identified legal gender was novel at the time and later cases reinforced it, but government officials limited changes to people identifying as 'third gender' while male/female marker changes lagged — the country's progressive reputation outruns policy. For this record: documented doctrine-versus-implementation gap.

Kathmandu Post feature (Nov 2024) on trans life in Janakpur: trans people face discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions and are often subjected to physical and sexual harassment. sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual acts have been legal in Nepal since a December 2007 Supreme Court ruling (Sunil Babu Pant v. Nepal Government) that homosexuality is not 'unnatural.' However, the Criminal Codes Act (2017), which replaced the 1963 Muluki Ain, still criminalizes 'unnatural sex' — it must be read in light of the court ruling. Prior to 2007, the Muluki Ain criminalized 'unnatural sexual intercourse' with up to 1 year imprisonment, and many Nepalese LGBTQI+ people were arrested under it. The age of consent is 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Wikipedia country coverage: Media representation of LGBT people in Nepal has historically been negative or comic relief, with caricatures of transgender people, gay people, and lesbians, though some positive depictions have emerged (e.g., Highway 2012, Soongava 2012). Some observers accused media and activists of pinkwashing and spreading disinformation about same-sex marriage and LGBT rights. Nepali media has been called out for forcefully using the term 'third gender' to describe trans men and trans women. Pride events including Nepal Pride Parade (since 2019), Queer Womxn Pride, and Trans Pride Parade (since 2020) are held annually. Wikipedia country coverage: Judicial cases have recognized foreign same-sex marriages between Nepali citizens and foreigners for immigration and residency purposes. Suman Pant's Supreme Court case established a precedent for same-sex spousal visas. Many Nepali LGBT people seek employment in countries that criminalize same-sex relationships (Malaysia, Brunei, Kuwait, Qatar), and Sunil Babu Pant has urged the government to inform sexual and gender minority workers about legal risks in these countries. Wikipedia country coverage: A drop-in centre with free HIV testing exists in Kathmandu through the Blue Diamond Society, which has more than 50 branches across the country. UNDP has recommended that Nepal provide all students, including transgender and intersex students, with access to safe toilets and bathroom facilities. Other organizations such as Mitini Nepal, Parichaya Samaj, and Sahaayam Nepal also provide resources. Wikipedia country coverage: As of June 2025, gender-affirming surgeries are available in Nepal — the first gender reassignment surgery was performed in June 2025 at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, which has since established a Gender Affirming Clinic. However, hormone replacement therapy and sex reassignment surgery are not widely accessible due to expense (4,500 rupees per six-month supply) and lack of providers; many trans Nepalis take hormones without medical supervision due to stigma. Various forms of conversion therapy are practiced in Nepal, including treatment in rehabilitation centres and traditional exorcism by family members. Lesbian couples are denied access to IVF, and there is a severe lack of comprehensive healthcare and research on LGBT Nepalis' needs. Some transgender people are forced to travel to India and Thailand for expensive surgeries due to the lack of a legal framework for gender-affirming care. Wikipedia country coverage: In April 2026, newly elected Prime Minister Balen Shah faced LGBTQ community criticism over a YouTube rap video containing derogatory and homophobic hate speech; following demands for apology, there was a significant increase in derogatory comments, hate speech, and death threats against the LGBTQ community by his supporters. On 30 October 2024, Aamul Paribartan Nagarik Party held a protest rally opposing homosexuality and LGBTQ rights, with Mitini Nepal's executive director noting anti-LGBTQ sentiments are gaining momentum in Nepal and South Asia. Some observers accused media and activists of pinkwashing and spreading disinformation about LGBT rights. The Communist Party of Nepal-Maoist made homophobic statements during the Civil War, describing homosexuality as 'a production of capitalism' and LGBT people as 'social pollutants.' Wikipedia country coverage: On 28 June 2023, Justice Til Prasad Shrestha issued an interim order directing the government to 'temporarily register' marriages of non-traditional couples and sexual minorities; the full Supreme Court bench has yet to deliver a final verdict. In April 2024, the National ID and Civil Registration Department instructed local authorities to enter same-sex marriages into a separate register, but temporary registration does not grant the same legal rights as opposite-sex couples — same-sex couples cannot inherit property, receive tax subsidies, make spousal medical decisions, or adopt children, and are labeled 'groom and bride' on certificates. The first marriage of a trans woman and a cisgender man occurred in November 2023, and as of June 2025 there were at least 17 documented queer marriages per Blue Diamond Society. Implementation is inconsistent: the Kathmandu District Court rejected a marriage registration in July 2023 despite the ruling, and it is unknown if all local governments comply. Wikipedia country coverage: Nepal's Education Board has implemented information about sexual and gender diversity in the curriculum for grades 7–9 (ages 13–15), making Nepal the second Asian country after Mongolia to do so, and universities offer courses on LGBT issues. However, many LGBT children still face discrimination and are unable to complete their education due to threats, bullying, and neglect from fellow students and teachers, and transgender Nepalis face severe gender-based violence and are unable to receive proper education, especially in rural areas. Queer Youth Group, a youth-focused organization, has filed writ petitions at the Supreme Court demanding legal recognition of gender identity and advocated for the citizenship bill. During the 2011 census, some census enumerators demanded a child be stripped when parents listed them as 'third gender.'

Recognition for residents runs through the citizenship certificate and the citizenship certificate alone in practice, and that pathway has historically been slow, discretionary and humiliating for applicants.

Marker changes to female or male, as distinct from third gender, were the contested category before the 2024 Supreme Court ruling, and remained the category where most rejections and delays were recorded.

Residents in provincial cities report discrimination when dealing with government institutions, and report physical and sexual harassment in public spaces, with police responses that residents describe as inadequate.

The bureaucratic burden documented by Human Rights Watch falls on Nepalese citizens navigating domestic document procedures. It does not attach to foreign visitors holding their own passports.

Scholarly observation reaches the same conclusion. A 2015 study-abroad research project on sexual and gender minorities in Nepal found that despite changing legislation, stigma and obstacles persisted in virtually every arena of life, amid a clash between patriarchal tradition and modernisation. LKA.name: Sri Lanka
LKA.summary:
Sri Lanka is a high-risk destination for transgender visitors. Sections 365 and 365A of the Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity, with penalties of up to ten years' imprisonment. Section 365 addresses "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and was applied to men; Section 365A, covering "gross indecency", was amended in 1995 to reach women as well, and Outright International records both provisions as applying to men and women.

Formal prosecutions are limited. The Canada Immigration and Refugee Board's 2012 country research recorded no convictions under the articles, yet the provisions structure everyday policing: Outright International reports that harassment, violence, extortion, arbitrary arrests and denial of services remain frequent. The US State Department's country report documents police harassment of LGBT persons alongside the penal-code provisions.

Authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence of same-sex conduct, a practice widely condemned as torture. The International Commission of Jurists identifies the Sri Lanka Police as the foremost perpetrators of human rights violations against LGBTI individuals, and recorded in August 2023 that both the Police and the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka had acknowledged this in the preceding months.

The Canadian board's research states that criminalisation "paves the way for police and anti-gay groups to brand all lesbian, bisexual, transgendered persons as perverts and criminals" — the route by which the same-sex provisions reach trans people. Human Dignity Trust's country profile further records that police use vagrancy and "cheating by personation" provisions against trans people, and lists Sri Lanka as criminalising trans gender expression.

There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination protection and no hate-crime statute. Legal gender recognition operates through an administrative certification process introduced by a circular issued in June 2016, which entitles holders to an identity card reflecting their gender; it is not legislation. The International Commission of Jurists argues that rule by circular is insufficient without legal reform, leaving recognition discretionary and revocable by policy.

Detention carries specific risk. Sri Lanka's Prisons Department has no dedicated transgender housing: Commissioner Gamini Dissanayake stated in October 2024 that current facilities make separate space impossible and that such accommodation is only planned for prisons built in the future. Placement is decided case by case. Detainees holding the recognised identity card are accommodated according to preferred gender "where possible"; those without it undergo a doctor's assessment of whether they can be considered transgender, after which inmate preference feeds the decision. Officials cited concern about people accused of sex offences identifying as transgender to enter female housing as a reason for resisting gender-based placement. The practical result is placement by birth sex as the default within the male and female ward system, with a medicalised, discretionary exception and no statutory placement rule.

The UK Home Office's country information package on sexual orientation and gender identity or expression (version 6.0, September 2024) assesses risk from both state and non-state actors and sets out protection, internal relocation and certification routes for LGBT+ asylum claims, indicating documented risk that is recognised by a foreign government. A joint stakeholder report submitted for Sri Lanka's third Universal Periodic Review cycle by EQUAL GROUND, Northwestern CIHR and GIHR documents human rights violations against LGBTIQ individuals.

Colombo has a small organised community, including EQUAL GROUND, and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners. That moderates day-to-day exposure but does not remove the legal and police risk.
LKA.outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile returned HTTP 403 at research time and could not be retrieved directly. The claim that police use vagrancy and "cheating by personation" provisions against trans people, and that Sri Lanka criminalises trans gender expression, is carried from the record's citation of that profile and remains unverified against the primary source in this pass.

Sources differ on whether legal gender recognition exists. Outright International states that recognition is possible through a certification process, while the position recorded here is that the June 2016 circular is administrative and not law. Both descriptions refer to the same circular; whether it constitutes legal gender recognition is unresolved.

Nothing in the inventory addresses whether a foreign-issued gender marker, passport annotation or overseas gender-recognition decision is recognised for entry, visa processing or detention in Sri Lanka. Entry screening on that point is not sourced.

No data is available on hate-crime prosecutions, on outcomes for trans detainees who are foreign nationals, or on whether the Prisons Department's October 2024 position has since changed. The prison account reflects statements made in October 2024.

The Human Dignity Trust profile, the US State Department report and the UK Home Office package were cited in the record but not read in full in this pass; their content is summarised at the level of the claims already carried.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D6, D8, D12, D13, D14.

Legal gender recognition is possible (via a certification process).

US State Department country report for Sri Lanka (custom URL): official human-rights assessment including the SOGI section - criminalisation under the penal code and police harassment of LGBT persons.

sources.title: Future prison constructions: Transgender inmates to receive separate accommodation
sources.summary: Sri Lanka's Prisons Department has no dedicated transgender housing today: Media Spokesperson/Commissioner Gamini Dissanayake (Oct 2024) said current prison facilities make giving transgender prisoners their own space impossible, and separate accommodation is only planned for prisons built in the future. Placement is decided case-by-case: trans detainees holding the recognised identity card (issued since the June 2016 gender-recognition-certificate circular) are accommodated per their preferred gender 'where possible', while those without it go through a doctor's assessment of whether they 'can be considered a transgender' before placement, weighing inmate preference. Officials explicitly worry about people accused of sex offences 'identifying as transgender' to enter female housing with born-male offenders, a stated reason for resisting gender-based placement. Outcome: placement by birth sex is the practical default in the current male/female ward system, with a medicalised, discretionary exception process and no statutory placement rule.

sources.title: Future prison constructions: Transgender inmates to receive separate accommodation
sources.summary: The Morning (original Daily Morning reporting, 4 Oct 2024) of the same Prisons Department statement: Commissioner Dissanayake said 'we always try to accommodate transgender prisoners who have the official identity card', and absent the ID a doctor assesses whether the inmate can be considered transgender, after which 'the preference of the particular inmate' feeds the accommodation decision. The piece also reports the Committee for Protecting Rights of Prisoners (CPRP) asking that future prisons give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space (including possible space within prison hospitals), citing that 'developed countries have recognised transgender rights'. Confirms the absence of a codified placement policy and the official preference-assessment route as of Oct 2024.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Gender-affirming surgery is relatively inaccessible in Sri Lanka because many hospitals lack the highly specialised surgical units and staff required; a physician interviewed for Human Rights Watch's 2016 'All Five Fingers are Not the Same' report said Sri Lankan doctors were often unfamiliar with surgical treatments for transgender patients. The National Blood Transfusion Service also bars men who have anal sex with men from donating blood, classifying male same-sex intercourse as 'risky behaviour' alongside drug use and having multiple partners. Wikipedia country coverage: Patients report meeting ignorance, curiosity and even ridicule from medical staff when seeking gender-confirming care, and some avoid public hospitals and clinics as a result, raising treatment costs; obtaining hormone therapy is described as similarly fraught. Legal gender recognition since 2016 requires bureaucratic certification that may be onerous to achieve, though no surgical intervention is legally required. Advocacy groups report police routinely ignore complaints from LGBTQ victims, especially involving sexual violence or blackmail, citing Article 365 as justification, and human rights organisations have documented police using the threat of arrest to assault, harass and extort LGBTQIA individuals. No youth-specific care-access findings appear in the source text. Wikipedia country coverage: Sri Lankan family law does not recognise same-sex marriages, same-sex civil unions, or provide equal rights to same-sex live-in couples; the marriage law dates from colonial times and is based on European law. The Catholic Church in Sri Lanka does not recognise same-sex marriages, with Cardinal Malcolm Ranjith stating that same-sex marriages 'are not a human right'. A 2023 report found 69% of the population opposed legalising same-sex unions, with 60% strongly opposed. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2016 the Ministry of Health issued a circular to health services and education institutions about issuing gender recognition certificates to transgender people, following a March 2015 complaint facilitated by the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka. In August 2021 a video of a homophobic counsellor caused controversy; the College of Psychiatrists clarified that modern medicine does not consider homosexuality an illness and called for decriminalisation, noting that unlike psychiatrists, counsellors are not regulated and do not require degrees. In March 2022 SJB MP Rohini Kumari Wijerathna tabled a bill to ban conversion therapy, which she said the government failed to support as of July 2024; despite professional college ethics, doctors are reportedly still regularly sought by families to administer 'treatment' to LGBTQ members. Sections 365 and 365A carry aggravated penalties of 10–20 years' rigorous imprisonment where an offence is committed by a person over 18 against a person under 16. Wikipedia country coverage: Sri Lankan society is described as generally tolerant of homosexuality, with politicians from both major parties and across the spectrum expressing support for LGBTQ rights, and the influential Asgiriya Buddhist chapter backing rights extension and constitutional amendment. In March 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa tweeted that he was determined to secure everybody's right to live with dignity regardless of sexuality and gender, which the Financial Times called the first such public acknowledgement by a South Asian head of state. A 2021 Social Scientists Association poll found 72.5% believed LGBT people should not be punished for their sexual identity, 65% said an LGBT person can do a job as well as anyone else, and 51.4% would support rights legislation; a 2018 Equality Fund survey found 12% of respondents were LGBTQI. Community organisations include Companions on a Journey (1994, Sri Lanka's first LGBTQ support group), the Women's Support Group (1999) and Equal Ground, though Article 365 remains cited to justify police harassment and moral policing of LGBTQ people in public and private settings.

LKA.tangentialFactors:
The protections that exist for trans people in Sri Lanka rest on administrative circulars rather than statute, so recognition and prison placement can change with a policy revision and carry no right of appeal. The gap between the June 2016 certification circular and the absence of a gender-recognition law is the specific deficiency the International Commission of Jurists addresses.

Risk is assessed by foreign governments as coming from both state and non-state actors, and the UK Home Office's framework treats internal relocation as a protection measure. That implies exposure varies by location and that moving within the country is treated as a meaningful change in risk rather than a guarantee of safety.

The criminal provisions and the police conduct they enable are longstanding rather than recent: Section 365A was extended to women in 1995, the Canadian board assessed the regime in 2012, the International Commission of Jurists published its assessment in August 2023, the Prisons Department spoke in October 2024, and Outright International's overview was updated in March 2026. The pattern is consistent across more than a decade of reporting.

Sri Lanka's treatment of LGBTIQ people is under active international scrutiny through the Universal Periodic Review, with civil society submitting documentation for the third cycle. Complaints and documentation channels therefore exist, but they operate at the level of advocacy and international review rather than domestic remedy.
LKA.localsOnly:
Residents live under the same Sections 365 and 365A as visitors, but the consequences are structural rather than episodic: police harassment, arbitrary detention, extortion and denial of services are recorded as frequent for LGBT people who are Sri Lankan residents, and the International Commission of Jurists names the Sri Lanka Police as the foremost perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals in the country.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity or expression, and no hate-crime provision applies to violence motivated by that status. Redress, where it exists, runs through non-governmental organisations and international mechanisms rather than domestic courts.

The June 2016 gender-recognition certification circular is a resident-facing route: a person who obtains the certificate is issued an identity card in their recognised gender, and Prisons Department officials said in October 2024 that they try to accommodate transgender prisoners who hold that card. Residents without the certificate are subject to a doctor's assessment before any gender-based placement decision.

Prison placement for residents is governed by no codified policy. Birth-sex placement in the existing male and female wards is the default, with a discretionary, medicalised exception process, and the Prisons Department has stated that separate transgender accommodation is only planned for prisons yet to be built. The Committee for Protecting Rights of Prisoners has asked that future prisons provide transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space, including within prison hospitals.

Residents at risk can pursue internal relocation and certification as part of an asylum or protection claim abroad, as set out in the UK Home Office's country information package, and can contribute to Universal Periodic Review documentation through organisations such as EQUAL GROUND.
LKA.comparisons: Pairwise: above Malaysia (0.28 — adds state-level Sharia “posing” laws with caning) and below Kenya (0.38 — criminalisation but stronger courts and civil society). The police-as-perpetrator documentation keeps Sri Lanka in High Risk rather than Elevated.

MNG.name: Mongolia
MNG.summary:
Mongolia decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 1993. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, but the protections are fragmented and no comprehensive equality law is in place. The constitution bars marriage equality, and no form of union recognition is available to same-sex couples.

The Criminal Code in force from 2017 carries hate-crime provisions covering bias motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. A residual offence addressing "satisfaction of immoral sexual needs" remains in the statute book and can be invoked as a pretext against gender-nonconforming people, even though no provision specifically criminalises homosexuality.

Enforcement practice works in the visitor's favour. After a police officer was charged in 2019 for assaulting a detained transgender woman, the LGBT Centre trained more than 500 police officers, prosecutors and judges on the hate-crime provisions, and the force issued guidelines requiring officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of what their identification documents state.

Entry and document handling raise no friction on foreign passports, there are no bathroom or facilities restrictions, and no documented pattern of police targeting exists. The realistic exposure for a visitor is street harassment when visibly trans, concentrated at night and outside the central districts of Ulaanbaatar, where social acceptance remains low.
MNG.outOfScopeNotes:
The Asian Development Bank source recorded no usable finding for this jurisdiction, so nothing in the record rests on it. The specific statutes in which Mongolia's fragmented anti-discrimination protections sit are not enumerated in the available sources, and the practical route to bringing a complaint is unresolved.

Only one enforcement episode is documented: the 2019 assault case and the training and guidance that followed it. Whether hate-crime provisions are charged consistently, and what outcomes those charges produce, is not sourced. Nor is there data on the frequency of street harassment against trans people, or on conditions outside Ulaanbaatar.

Whether the residual "satisfaction of immoral sexual needs" offence has been applied against trans or gender-nonconforming people in practice is not sourced. The record also does not establish what document or gender-marker rules apply to Mongolian passports, which matters only for residents and not for entry on a foreign document.

MMR.name: Myanmar
MMR.summary:
Myanmar criminalises consensual same-sex intimacy under Section 377 of the Penal Code, a colonial-era provision reported as carrying life imprisonment or up to 10 years, and police enforce it alongside vague public-decency provisions. Since the coup of 1 February 2021 the risk environment has intensified. The National Unity Government recorded 17 LGBT people killed and two critically injured, while Human Rights Myanmar's June 2024 submission to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial killings counted 5 to 12 killings of LGBTIQ+ people in military-controlled areas and identified intensified Section 377 enforcement as an aggravating factor in deaths.

Detention powers reach past Section 377. Section 35(c) of the 1945 Police Act criminalises face covering with up to three months' imprisonment and is applied specifically against transgender people, and authorities also hold people who cannot "satisfactorily account" for their presence. Outright International's overview reports torture and sexual violence in detention after the coup, and rights groups document arrest, torture and sexual abuse of LGBT people by junta authorities. Compulsory military service announced in February 2024 and the 2024 Conscription Law have driven queer people into fear and displacement.

Institutional recourse is effectively absent. The "Rainbow Amid the Storm" research found that 50% of LGBT respondents have no confidence in the legal system and more than 68% fear repercussions from abusers. Violence by police against trans women is documented in individual cases: a trans woman describing a 2016 arrest recounted stripping, a beating and 14 days of detention after walking home at night while accused of sex work, and 2013 arrests in Mandalay saw trans women forced to strip and parade naked while photographed, which police called a "public service."

Cultural control runs alongside the criminal law. In January 2025 the junta banned seven named LGBTQ-themed books as obscene and announced prosecutions against their publishers. Section 377 was in active use before the coup as well, illustrated by the 2018 charging of an outspoken HIV-positive LGBTI advocate and Yangon restaurant owner over an allegation involving an employee.

Outright International's assessment, updated March 2026, is that trans and LGBT visitors should avoid Myanmar entirely.
MMR.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not address legal gender recognition, marker or document changes, marriage or partner recognition, hate-crime provisions, or access to gender-affirming care in Myanmar; the current state of these questions is unresolved here.

No source in the inventory describes entry, visa or border-screening procedures as they affect trans travellers, so any screening risk at the point of entry is not sourced.

The treatment of LGBT people in areas outside military control is not covered by the inventory and remains unresolved; the resistance-controlled areas referenced in earlier framing are not substantiated by any source provided.

The precise penalty range under Section 377, and whether the 2018 charge against the advocate proceeded to conviction, are not resolved by the material supplied.

The scope of the two kill counts differs and neither source defines its verification method, so the true figure for LGBT deaths since February 2021 is not established.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Myanmar does not allow transgender people to change the gender assigned to them at birth, so the state does not recognise their gender identity. Transgender people are consequently subject to police harassment, sexual assault, mistreatment and extortion, and are frequently targeted using the 'shadow law' in section 35(c) of the Police Act (1945), which lets police detain anyone they consider behaving suspiciously after sunset. The source text describes no legal gender recognition procedure or documentary process for trans people in Myanmar. Wikipedia country coverage: LGBTQ access to care is shaped by criminalisation and stigma: Section 377 of the Penal Code (up to 10 years' imprisonment for same-sex acts) was called out by Aung San Suu Kyi in 2013 as hampering the country's efforts to combat HIV, and gay men are stigmatised, especially if living with HIV/AIDS. The 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights includes LGBTQ individuals as a vulnerable group in healthcare delivery, but it is a planning document rather than an enforceable law. On the youth side, the 2019 Child Rights Law contains a non-discrimination clause referencing sexual orientation, but it applies only to children and lacks enforcement mechanisms. Wikipedia country coverage: Myanmar has no enforceable legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Existing measures are symbolic or non-binding: the 2019 Child Rights Law's non-discrimination clause covers sexual orientation but only for children and has no enforcement mechanisms; the 2020 MRTV Broadcasting Guidelines discourage discriminatory media portrayals but carry no legal penalties; and the 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights is a planning document, not law. Following the June 2019 death by suicide of young gay librarian Kyaw Zin Win after workplace harassment, the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission called for enactment of anti-discrimination provisions, and the same year's events prompted a national conversation on LGBT issues. Wikipedia country coverage: Myanmar does not recognise same-sex marriages or civil unions. In 2014 a Burmese same-sex couple drew widespread media attention by holding an unofficial wedding ceremony after 10 years together, triggering a backlash from social conservatives who questioned why anti-homosexuality laws were not enforced against them. Same-sex couples can cohabit freely in Yangon and Mandalay and celebrate ceremonial marriages without legal persecution, but these carry no legal standing. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth-specific findings centre on the June 2019 death by suicide of Kyaw Zin Win, a young gay man working as a librarian at Myanmar Imperial University in Yangon, after continuous harassment and bullying from colleagues; more than 600 people attended his funeral and a rainbow flag was wrapped around his coffin. The university opened an investigation and suspended three staff members, and the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission launched a separate investigation and called for anti-discrimination provisions. Legally, the 2019 Child Rights Law includes a non-discrimination clause referencing sexual orientation, but it applies only to children and lacks enforcement mechanisms; meanwhile same-sex conduct remains criminalised under Section 377 with up to 10 years' imprisonment regardless of consent or privacy.

Penalties under Section 377 are reported inconsistently across sources, as life imprisonment or up to 10 years, and the exact sentencing range in current practice is not resolved by the available material.

Censorship of LGBTQ-themed publishing in 2025 indicates that the state's reach extends to representation and documentation, not only to conduct, which affects what material a visitor or researcher can obtain locally.

Visibility of gender-diverse people predates the current regime: nat kadaws, spirit mediums who are culturally visible transgender women, have long been part of public life, so visibility and criminalisation have coexisted for decades.

MMR.blindSummary:
The country criminalises consensual same-sex intimacy under Section 377 of the Penal Code, a historic-era provision reported as carrying life imprisonment or up to 10 years, and police enforce it alongside vague public-decency provisions. The parallel government recorded 17 LGBT people killed and two critically injured, while a June 2024 submission to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial killings counted 5 to 12 killings of LGBTIQ+ people in military-controlled areas and identified intensified Section 377 enforcement as an aggravating factor in deaths.

Torture and sexual violence in detention are reported after the coup, and rights groups document arrest, torture and sexual abuse of LGBT people by junta authorities. Compulsory military service announced in February 2024 and the 2024 Conscription Law have driven queer people into fear and displacement.

CUB.name: Cuba
CUB.summary:
Cuba's legal framework for trans people rests on the 2019 Constitution, whose Article 42 names sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories, the first constitution to do so. The 2022 Family Code, approved by referendum on 25 September 2022 with 66.87% support, legalised same-sex marriage and adoption and permits legal gender change without surgery. Consensual same-sex relations were removed from the Penal Code in 1979.

Legal gender recognition is administrative rather than surgical or judicial. The July 2025 civil-registry reform removed the remaining bureaucratic hurdles to name changes, and the Family Code already established that surgery is not a precondition.

Employment protection is narrower than the constitutional text. The Labor Code (Law 116) bars discrimination on grounds that include sexual orientation, but its article 2(b) covers orientation and does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground. A 2013 parliamentary amendment banning employment discrimination on sexual orientation passed after intense debate; Mariela Castro's proposal to extend the ban to gender identity, disability and HIV status drew support from some Christian and intellectual legislators, but only the sexual-orientation ban is confirmed as enacted.

Healthcare access has an explicit official basis. Resolution 126 (2008) brought trans healthcare into the public system, and CENESEX, the state sex-education centre, runs an official trans-care programme alongside a trans-rights campaign, working with the police and the supreme court on sexual-diversity education. In practice the economic crisis has degraded healthcare and hormone availability is reported as unreliable.

The equality settlement is contested rather than state-enforced. Opponents of the Family Code cited religious objections and feared that child-welfare provisions could be used against dissidents, while some government opponents planned to vote No purely to deny the Díaz-Canel administration a win amid the post-July-2021 crackdown, which produced more than 1,400 arrestees, and record emigration. The 25 September 2022 vote was only the fourth national election since 1959.

The counterweights are systemic rather than trans-specific. Cuba is a one-party state with no independent civil society, arbitrary-detention powers are broad, and police discretion is wide. There is no documented pattern of police targeting people for gender expression; the documented state hostility runs toward emigration and asylum claims rather than toward gender presentation.
CUB.outOfScopeNotes:

sources.summary: LegalClarity overview (30 May 2026): documents Cuba's arc from the UMAP forced-labour camps for gay men (1965-68, ~60 hrs/week cutting cane in Camagüey, electric-shock and injection 'curing' experiments) to today's progressive framework — 1979 Penal Code removal of consensual same-sex acts, Castro's public acceptance of blame (La Jornada, 2010), Resolution 126 (2008) trans healthcare in the public system, the 2019 Constitution (Art 42, first to name sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories), and the 2022 Family Code (same-sex marriage/adoption, legal gender change without surgery). Notes the gap between law and daily life: Labor Code Law 116 bars SOGI discrimination but does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground, and the Labor Code's article 2(b) covers orientation, not identity.

Americas Quarterly (15 Sept 2022): previews Cuba's 25 Sept 2022 Family Code referendum — only the 4th national vote since 1959 — which would guarantee marriage equality, surrogacy, codified domestic-violence penalties and shared parental rights; opponents cite religious objections and fear child-welfare provisions could be used against dissidents, while some government opponents planned to vote No purely to deny the Díaz-Canel administration a win amid the post-July-2021 crackdown (1,400+ arrestees) and record emigration. Useful context for how contested (rather than state-enforced) the equality settlement is.

Links International Journal of Socialist Renewal (23 Dec 2011): sympathetic first-person account 'Rainbow Cuba' disputing claims of systematic state homophobia — documents the UMAP camps (conscripts paid seven pesos a day), the 1975 declaration-era turning point, and CENESEX's state-backed programme: a trans-rights campaign, work with the police and the supreme court, and sexual-diversity education. Historical baseline (pre-2019 constitution) showing official institutions campaigning for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s.

Washington Blade (21 Dec 2013): Cuban lawmakers approved a labor-law amendment banning employment discrimination on sexual orientation after intense parliamentary debate. Mariela Castro of CENESEX proposed extending the ban to gender identity, disability and HIV status; the trans-specific amendment drew support from some Christian and intellectual legislators, while passage of the sexual-orientation ban was the confirmed outcome. The measure predates the 2019 Constitution and the 2022 Family Code.

Washington Blade (26 May 2018): documents Cuba's use of 'treason'/'treason against the homeland' charges against LGBTI citizens who flee to seek asylum — Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to 8 years in prison if they returned after filing Dutch asylum claims (Jan 2018); a woman deported from the Netherlands was detained (19 May 2018), and LGBTI activists (incl. Nelson Gandulla, Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation) remained monitored. Relevant to visitors: Cuba's hostility toward emigration/asylum, not toward gender expression as such.

CUB.tangentialFactors:
The historical baseline is severe and well documented. Between 1965 and 1968 the UMAP forced-labour camps held gay men, who cut cane in Camagüey roughly 60 hours a week for seven pesos a day and were subjected to electric-shock and injection experiments presented as cures. Consensual same-sex acts left the Penal Code in 1979, and Fidel Castro publicly accepted blame for the UMAP era in 2010.

Official institutions have campaigned for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s, with CENESEX running trans-rights work and engaging the police and the supreme court, a baseline that predates the 2019 Constitution.

Cuba's hostility toward departure is documented and distinct from its stance on gender expression. In January 2018 Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to eight years in prison for treason against the homeland after filing asylum claims in the Netherlands, a woman deported from the Netherlands was detained on 19 May 2018, and LGBTI activists including Nelson Gandulla of the Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation remained under monitoring. A trans visitor who sought asylum or fled could meet this machinery; a visitor who does not is unlikely to encounter it.

Compared with neighbouring jurisdictions, Cuba's constitutional and family-law settlement is among the most transformed in Latin America, though the employment-law gap on gender identity places it behind the standard its own constitution sets.
CUB.localsOnly:
Cuban workers are covered by Labor Code Law 116, which bars discrimination including on sexual orientation, but gender identity is not listed as a separate protected ground and article 2(b) addresses orientation only. Residents seeking redress therefore have a weaker statutory hook for identity-based workplace claims than for orientation-based ones.

Residents access trans healthcare through the public system under Resolution 126 (2008) and through CENESEX's official programme, which also conducts sexual-diversity education and works with police and courts. Supply-side reliability is constrained by the economic crisis.

The Family Code governs resident families directly, covering marriage, adoption, shared parental rights and codified domestic-violence penalties, and the July 2025 civil-registry reform governs name changes for people registered in Cuban civil records.

Citizens face the treason provisions if they leave to seek asylum, and independent LGBTI activists have been monitored. The absence of independent civil society means there is no organisation outside the state to which a resident can appeal.
CUB.comparisons: Pairwise: below Argentina (0.73 — democracy, independent NGOs, stronger recourse) and above Lithuania (0.66) and Vietnam (0.63 — Cuba's constitutional GI protection and official trans programme edge it).

ECU.name: Ecuador
ECU.summary:
Ecuador's legal framework on gender identity is among the strongest in the region. Legal gender recognition has been available since 2016, and the December 2023 reforms to the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data, regulated by a decree issued by President Daniel Noboa on 11 June 2024, allow adults to change name and sex or gender marker directly at the civil registry, once, without surgery. Constitutional Court rulings in 2024 and 2025 extended document changes to trans adolescents and publicly rebuked the National Assembly for stalling implementation of trans-rights legislation; an April 2026 report describes the adolescent ruling as opening a path for others seeking legal recognition.

The constitutional footing is explicit. Article 11 of the 2008 Constitution binds the state to respect differences of ethnicity, nationality, social and generational standing and gender, and names sexual orientation and gender identity among the principles that underpin non-discrimination in a secular, multinational state.

Violence remains the dominant visitor-facing risk. A monitoring group documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023 with inadequate state response, and reporting from January 2024 recorded rising violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians as the government's declared internal armed conflict against gangs got under way; two further LGBTQ people were killed in the conflict's first weeks. Quito and Guayaquil, the two largest cities, carry real street risk, and police capacity is absorbed by the security crisis, which weakens the practical value of the formal protection machinery.

Detention is a serious exposure. Ecuador's prisons are almost universally male, and trans detainees are placed according to birth sex or legal sex rather than gender identity, with protective placement applied unevenly. Trans women held in male pavilions have reported rape, torture directed at their gender identity, beatings, forced head-shaving and denial of medical care. A visitor who is arrested should expect placement in a male facility.

Family and partner recognition is partial. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2019, but a constitutional ban bars same-sex couples from adoption. In May 2018 the Constitutional Court ordered the Civil Registry to register the daughter of a same-sex couple, a precedent for state recognition of same-sex families. Conversion practices involving torture are explicitly criminalised.
ECU.outOfScopeNotes:
Availability of legal gender recognition for under-18s is unresolved across the sources. Outright International's overview, updated 12 March 2026, states that recognition is not available to people under 18, while an April 2026 AP report describes Constitutional Court rulings allowing trans adolescents to change name and sex on official records. The statutory route and the judicial route may differ; the inventory does not settle which governs a routine application today.

The January 2024 Los Angeles Blade page on rising violence returned HTTP 403, so the claim rests on the underlying article as cited rather than on a retrieved page. The specific figure of two LGBTQ people killed in the opening weeks of the internal armed conflict is carried in the same reporting and is not independently corroborated in this inventory.

The prison census total of 73 trans women is a single point-in-time count with no date given, and the counter-organisation's assertion that the true number is much higher is unsourced here. No figure in the inventory quantifies violence against trans visitors specifically, as distinct from Ecuadorian LGBTQ residents.

No source in the inventory addresses airport or border screening of transgender travellers, entry-decision practice on gender markers, or how Ecuadorian consulates abroad handle document corrections.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6, D8.
