The reglamento streamlines civil-registry gender-marker changes, which is the operative procedure for legal gender recognition.
The cited page returned HTTP 403. The underlying Los Angeles Blade piece (Jan 2024) reports that violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians is increasing amid the internal armed conflict.

AP (Apr 2026) reports that Constitutional Court rulings in Ecuador let trans adolescents change name and sex on official records, in a case described as opening a path for others seeking legal recognition.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex marriage legalised in 2019 but same-sex couples barred from adoption by constitutional ban; legal gender recognition possible since 2016 (not available to under-18s); conversion practices involving torture are explicitly criminalised.

The US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Ecuador documents discrimination based on sexual orientation among societal problems in Ecuador, alongside excessive police force, media restrictions and corruption.

The 2008 Constitution of Ecuador (Georgetown/PDBA text): Article 11 principles bind the state to respect ethnic, national, social, generational and gender differences as well as sexual orientation and identity, forming the constitutional non-discrimination foundation for LGBTI rights in a secular, multinational state.

PinkNews (31 May 2018): the Constitutional Court ordered the Civil Registry to register the daughter of the same-sex couple Helen Bicknell and Nicola Rothon, the child Satya Amani Bicknell Rothon. Lawyer Jose Luis Guerra said the refusal violated the child's rights, in a precedent ordering state recognition of same-sex families.

sources.title: Trans Women in Ecuador's Prisons | PrisioTrans Human Rights Program
sources.summary: Silueta X (leading Ecuadorian trans-rights organisation), PrisioTrans program, documents 2011-2026: trans women in Ecuador's almost universally male prisons are held in male spaces and face gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and health-care barriers. Key cases: trans woman Helen Maldonado died during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male prison space; 2022 complaint over cruel/inhuman/degrading treatment of trans women in Lago Agrio; 2024 allegations of forced head-shaving, beatings and violence targeting breast/body implants; 2026 death in State custody of a 23-year-old trans woman drew calls for an independent investigation at the El Encuentro maximum-security prison. The program explicitly does NOT push a one-size placement rule, instead advocating individualised housing decisions per Inter-American standards considering gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, and cites the July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty.

sources.title: Trans Women Report Being Punished for Their Identity in Ecuador Prisons (Spanish)
sources.summary: Pulitzer Center investigation: Ecuador's prisons are 'almost always male' - the last prison census counted 73 trans women across all Ecuadorian prisons (organisation Fundacion Vivir Libre says there are many more), and trans women are placed in male pavilions. Case: Venezuelan trans woman Alexa (27) detained Aug 2023 at Penitenciaria del Litoral was initially sent to male pavilion 9 with three other trans women rather than the 'prioritaria' pavilion reserved for vulnerable populations (where many sexo-gender-diverse inmates are held); she received no medical exams or HIV treatment there. The story documents rapes and torture reported to be directed at prisoners' gender identity, showing placement practice operates by birth sex/legal sex with protective 'prioritaria' placement used unevenly.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1997 (Constitutional Tribunal Case No. 111-97-TC, striking Article 516 of the Penal Code), and the 1998 Constitution made Ecuador the first country in the Americas to bar discrimination based on sexual orientation. The 2016 Gender Identity Law lets people change legal gender and birth name on ID cards solely by self-determination, without surgery. Conversion therapy was criminalised in 2014 under Article 151 of the Penal Code as equivalent to torture, punishable by 7–10 years' imprisonment, yet as of 2023 hundreds of clinics still promote it. The first gay pride march was held in Quito in 1998. Wikipedia country coverage: The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Adoption is constitutionally limited to different-sex couples (Article 68), and on 14 August 2026 new adoption legislation passed 118–0 explicitly prohibiting single and same-sex couples from adopting, though the 2018 Constitutional Court had ordered the Civil Registry to register a girl as the daughter of a lesbian couple (5–3, one abstention). The U.S. State Department's 2011 report found LGBT community members' right to equal access to formal education was frequently violated, and clinics have confined young people against their will, including the daughter of parents who unsuccessfully sought her release. Wikipedia country coverage: Despite a conservative, macho culture in which homosexuality tends to be viewed negatively, pride marches have been authorised in all major cities with police protection and official participation — the 2011 Guayaquil march included a vice prefect, a city councillor and a National Assembly member. Attendance reached about 20,000 in Guayaquil in 2017 (with the Bolívar and San Martín monument lit in rainbow colours) and over 18,000 in Quito in 2018, and the Presidential House was lit in rainbow colours in June 2017. Presidential candidate Nelson Zavala was fined over $3,000 and barred from office for a year in 2013 for calling gay people 'sinners' and 'immoral', and Diane Marie Rodríguez Zambrano became the first openly transgender candidate in 2013 and the first transgender lawmaker in 2017. Conversely, the 2011 State Department report said gay, lesbian and transgender people still suffered discrimination from public and private bodies, and LGBT groups claimed police and prosecutors did not thoroughly investigate deaths of LGBT individuals.

ECU.localsOnly:
Silueta X, Ecuador's leading trans-rights organisation, runs the PrisioTrans programme documenting conditions for trans detainees from 2011 to 2026. Its findings are that trans women are held in male spaces across a prison system that is almost universally male, and face gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and barriers to health care. Documented cases include the death of trans woman Helen Maldonado during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral, where she was held in a male prison space; a 2022 complaint over cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment of trans women in Lago Agrio; 2024 allegations of forced head-shaving, beatings and violence targeting breast and body implants; and the 2026 death in state custody of a 23-year-old trans woman at the El Encuentro maximum-security prison, which prompted calls for an independent investigation.

PrisioTrans does not press a single placement rule. It advocates individualised housing decisions under Inter-American standards that weigh gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, and it cites a July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty.

The Pulitzer Center's investigation found that the last prison census counted 73 trans women across all Ecuadorian prisons, a figure the organisation Fundación Vivir Libre considers a substantial undercount. Its case study is Alexa, a 27-year-old trans woman detained in August 2023 at Penitenciaria del Litoral and sent to male pavilion 9 with three other trans women rather than to the prioritaria pavilion reserved for vulnerable populations, where many sex- and gender-diverse inmates are held; she received no medical examinations or HIV treatment there.

For residents, the practical route to a corrected identity document runs through the civil registry under the June 2024 regulation, with the constitutional non-discrimination provisions available as a basis for complaints. Same-sex couples remain barred from adoption despite marriage equality.
ECU.comparisons: Pairwise: above Colombia (0.55 — Ecuador's LGR is now simpler) and below India (0.58 — comparable; Ecuador has far better law, India lower targeted-murder rate).
ECU.blindSummary:
The country legal framework on gender identity is among the strongest in the region. Legal gender recognition has been available since 2016, and the December 2023 reforms to the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data, regulated by a decree issued by the head of government on 11 June 2024, allow adults to change name and sex or gender marker directly at the civil registry, once, without surgery. Constitutional Court rulings in 2024 and 2025 extended document changes to trans adolescents and publicly rebuked the national legislature for stalling implementation of trans-rights legislation; an April 2026 report describes the adolescent ruling as opening a path for others seeking legal recognition.

The constitutional footing is explicit. Article 11 of the 2008 Constitution binds the state to respect differences of ethnicity, nationality, social and generational standing and gender, and names sexual orientation and gender identity among the principles that underpin non-discrimination in a secular, multinational state.

Violence remains the dominant visitor-facing risk. a monitoring group documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023 with inadequate state/province response, and reporting from January 2024 recorded rising violence against LGBTQ residents as the government's declared internal armed conflict against gangs got under way; two further LGBTQ people were killed in the conflict's first weeks. The two largest cities carry real street risk, and police capacity is absorbed by the security crisis, which weakens the practical value of the formal protection machinery.

Detention is a serious exposure. The country prisons are almost universally male, and trans detainees are placed according to birth sex or legal sex rather than gender identity, with protective placement applied unevenly. Trans women held in male pavilions have reported rape, torture directed at their gender identity, beatings, forced head-shaving and denial of medical care. a visitor who is arrested should expect placement in a male facility.

Family and partner recognition is partial. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2019, but a constitutional ban bars same-sex couples from adoption. In May 2018 the Constitutional Court ordered the Civil Registry to register the daughter of a same-sex couple, a precedent for state/province recognition of same-sex families. Conversion practices involving torture are explicitly criminalised.
ECU.blindOutOfScope:
Availability of legal gender recognition for under-18s is unresolved across the sources. an international organisation's overview, updated 12 March 2026, states that recognition is not available to people under 18, while an April 2026 wire-service report describes Constitutional Court rulings allowing trans adolescents to change name and sex on official records. The statutory route and the judicial route may differ; the inventory does not settle which governs a routine application today.

The January 2024 trade-press page on rising violence returned HTTP 403, so the claim rests on the underlying article as cited rather than on a retrieved page. The specific figure of two LGBTQ people killed in the opening weeks of the internal armed conflict is carried in the same reporting and is not independently corroborated in this inventory.

The prison census total of 73 trans women is a single point-in-time count with no date given, and the counter-organisation's assertion that the true number is much higher is unsourced here. No figure in the inventory quantifies violence against trans visitors specifically, as distinct from resident LGBTQ people.

No source in the inventory addresses airport or border screening of transgender travellers, entry-decision practice on gender markers, or how the country consulates abroad handle document corrections.

ECU.tangentialFactors:
Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation is documented in Ecuador's societal record well before the current framework: the United States State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report listed it among the country's societal problems, alongside excessive police force, media restrictions and corruption. The excessive-force finding matters indirectly, since it predates and helps explain the low trust between LGBT people and police that persists today.

The pattern sits inside a wider regional contrast. Ecuador's combination of constitutional non-discrimination language, statutory gender recognition and marriage equality places it ahead of most neighbouring jurisdictions on paper, while its prison and homicide record places it behind. The gap between the written framework and enforcement is the defining feature of the country for an LGBT traveller.

Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records the same-sex marriage legalisation of 2019, the constitutional adoption ban, recognition available since 2016, and the criminalisation of conversion practices involving torture.

JAM.name: Jamaica
JAM.summary:
Jamaica criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. The Offences Against the Person Act punishes buggery with up to 10 years' hard labour, and the US State Department's 2023 country report confirms the provision remains in force. No law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and individuals are not legally permitted to register a change of gender, so a trans visitor has no domestic legal recognition to rely on.

The defining case is Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed and shot to death by a mob at a street party in 2013 after being outed. Police did not investigate the killing. The case is now before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights as Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica, and an amicus brief filed in February 2024 argues that continued criminalisation and systemic discrimination leave transgender Jamaicans exposed to housing, educational and employment insecurity.

Police protection is unreliable. The US Department of Justice country packet records that LGBT victims do not report attacks because police leak incident details, fail to investigate violence including murder, and do not intervene during attacks. The Inter-American Commission's 2012 report on Jamaica describes the violent persecution and fear to which gay and lesbian people are subject as deplorable. Human Rights Watch documented police harassment of gay men and of HIV/AIDS outreach workers alongside community and family violence carried out with impunity and official indifference. Amnesty International's 4 June 2006 urgent appeal reported police ill-treatment and torture of LGBT people as well as vigilante attacks.

Vigilante violence remains a live risk. Amnesty documented gay men and lesbians beaten, cut, burned, raped and shot once their orientation became known, and lesbians raped and driven into exile abroad. Community members report that beatings and stonings of trans people are common but rarely reported because reporting achieves nothing.

Detention carries a specific and documented danger. The State Department reports that prisoner-on-prisoner violence is common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for perceived LGBTQI+ identity, in facilities operating far beyond capacity; a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by other inmates accusing him of being gay. No gender-recognition framework exists to inform how a trans detainee would be housed.

sources.summary: Amicus brief in Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica before the Inter-American Commission (filed Feb 2024): argues Jamaica's continued criminalisation of LGBTQ persons and systemic discrimination make transgender persons especially vulnerable — sections document housing insecurity, educational and employment insecurity for transgender Jamaicans under the discrimination regime.

UNDP 'Being LGBT in Jamaica' National Survey (March 2023): national survey of LGBT Jamaicans with dedicated chapters on violence due to prejudice and discrimination and on transgender access to health care; quantifies lived experience of violence and service exclusion under the criminalisation backdrop.

US DOJ/EOIR Jamaica country packet (2013): Offences Against the Person Act makes 'buggery' punishable by up to 10 years' hard labour; LGBT victims are reluctant to report because police leak incident details, fail to investigate LGBT violence including murder, and do not intervene during attacks (documented via the CVC and local organisations).

IACHR Report on the Situation of Human Rights in Jamaica (10 Aug 2012): finds 'the violent persecution and fear to which gays and lesbians are subject in Jamaica to be deplorable'; covers citizen security, police killings including the May 2010 operation, and justice administration, with civil-society input from Jamaicans for Justice and the Jamaica Forum for Lesbians, All-Sexuals and Gays (J-FLAG).

HRW letter (30 Nov 2004) citing its report 'Hated to Death: Homophobia, Violence, and Jamaica's HIV/AIDS Epidemic': documents police harassment of gay men and HIV/AIDS outreach workers, community and family violence carried out with impunity, and official indifference; five Jamaican human-rights organisations backed the report's 16 Nov 2004 Kingston launch.

Amnesty International urgent appeal (4 Jun 2006): reports vigilante violence and police ill-treatment or torture of LGBT people in Jamaica — gay men and lesbians beaten, cut, burned, raped and shot once orientation known; lesbians raped and driven into asylum abroad; concern that prominent musicians promote homophobia.

sources.title: Gays ostracised in prison – study
sources.summary: Jamaica Gleaner reporting (5 Feb 2019) on UWI lecturer Carla Moore's 2018 study (Apr-Nov 2018, funded by the Inter-American Institute of Human Rights, the IBA and the UN Latin American Institute for the Prevention of Crime): Jamaicans perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender 'are isolated' in Jamaica's penal institutions and rehabilitation opportunities for them are 'basically non-existent'. Inmates' movement inside facilities is severely curtailed and access to resources often limited because of entrenched homophobia/transphobia - other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners. The study estimated that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at Tower Street Adult Correctional Centre belong to sexual or gender minorities and reported that lesbians face prevalent 'corrective rape'. Evidence that LGB/trans prisoners are socially ostracised and isolated rather than integrated, with no specialised housing policy documented.

sources.title: Jamaica 2023 Human Rights Report (US Department of State)
sources.summary: US State Dept country report: 'Prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity'; correctional facilities were significantly overcrowded (Tower Street maximum-security cells at three times capacity), with harsh, life-threatening conditions, and a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay. The report also records that Jamaica barred legal gender registration ('Individuals were not legally allowed to register a change of gender'), that the buggery law (up to 10 years' hard labour) criminalised consensual same-sex conduct, and that no anti-discrimination law protected SOGI. Official-state confirmation that trans prisoners face identity-targeted violence in Jamaican prisons with no gender-recognition framework for accommodation decisions.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: In 2012 LGBT activist Maurice Tomlinson sued Jamaican TV stations (TVJ, PBCJ, CVM) for refusing to air a 30-second ad, "Love and Respect," promoting recognition of LGBT people's humanity; the Constitutional Court ruled against him in November 2013, and the Court of Appeal heard the appeal in February 2016 with judgment reserved. The UN Human Rights Committee's 2011 review regretted "virulent lyrics by musicians and entertainers that incite violence against homosexuals" and urged Jamaica to investigate and sanction those responsible. Dancehall artists including Buju Banton, Beenie Man, Bounty Killer, Elephant Man, Sizzla and Shabba Ranks have written or performed songs advocating attacking or killing gay and lesbian people, and a 2005 agreement between dancehall labels and groups like OutRage! and the Stop Murder Music Coalition sought to end anti-gay lyrics in live performance. Wikipedia country coverage: In January 2018 Jamaica banned entry to Steven Anderson, a Holocaust-denying anti-gay pastor from Arizona, after an outcry from activists; he said he was told at the airport he would not be allowed into the country. LGBT Jamaicans have fled abroad for safety — Maurice Tomlinson moved to Toronto in 2011 after death threats, Gareth Henry sought asylum in Canada in 2008, and Simone Edwards was granted asylum in the Netherlands in 2008 — and Tomlinson's July 2019 IACHR petition asks that Jamaica allow naturalization of same-sex spouses of Jamaican citizens on the same terms as heterosexual spouses. In January 2019 the Director of Tourism, Donovan White, said gay tourists are welcome and that Jamaicans harboured no open hostility toward gay visitors. Wikipedia country coverage: In September 2019 Montego Bay Mayor Omar Davis and Councilor Charles Sinclair blocked the local cultural center's use by the local LGBT group to protect the building's "sacredness," and other venues then cancelled reservations over fear of backlash, forcing cancellation of the October 2019 Pride events; police said they could not provide protection to LGBT Jamaicans given the whipped-up hysteria. J-FLAG reported in 2012 harassment of gay and lesbian patients by hospital and prison staff, and numerous reports of violence against gay inmates by wardens and other inmates, with few seeking recourse through the prison system. Quality of Citizenship Jamaica, founded in 2013, worked to create safe spaces for LGBT women, youth and transgender people before ending operations in 2018. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2011 Parliament passed the Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms (Constitutional Amendment) Act, explicitly banning same-sex marriage and any other kind of union from being recognized in Jamaica. In 2019 both Prime Minister Andrew Holness and Opposition Leader Peter Phillips announced opposition to legalizing same-sex marriage, and in July 2019 Maurice Tomlinson petitioned the IACHR to rule that Section 18(2) of the Constitution contravenes the American Convention on Human Rights, seeking repeal and recognition of his Canadian marriage. Although lesbian civil ceremonies have taken place — including the 2012 celebration in Jamaica of Jamaican-born Nicole Y. Dennis-Benn and Emma Benn, legally married in New York — Jamaica recognizes no legal basis for partnerships between women. Wikipedia country coverage: J-FLAG data showed that young people aged 18 to 29 bore the brunt of violence based on sexual orientation, including 68 reports of sexually motivated harassment or abuse in 2012 with 53 assault cases and at least two killings. In July 2013 a mob in St. James stabbed to death Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old, and the case remained unsolved with no arrests as of 2022. University campuses have been sites of anti-LGBT violence: students at UWI's Mona campus rioted in April 2006 while police protected a man chased across campus, and in November 2012 two campus security guards beat a reportedly gay student seeking refuge from a mob, after which the University of Technology established a working group on intolerance and bullying. Dr. J. Carolyn Gomes resigned as head of Jamaicans for Justice in 2013 after nationwide pushback on sexual-education leaflets for adolescents that mentioned anal sex. Wikipedia country coverage: Polls show deep hostility: 96% opposed legalizing homosexual relations in 2001; 70% said in 2008 that homosexuals are not entitled to the same basic rights; 85.2% opposed legalizing homosexuality among consenting adults in a 2010 survey; 88% disapproved of homosexuality in a 2016 J-Flag poll; and 2023 polling indicates at least 60% oppose acceptance of homosexuality. Time magazine labelled Jamaica "the most homophobic place on Earth" in 2006, and in 2013 the majority of LGBTQ people in the country said they faced homophobic violence in public. J-FLAG, founded December 1998, operates underground and anonymously as Jamaica's first LGBT human rights organization, and co-founder Brian Williamson was stabbed to death in June 2004 with a crowd outside his home celebrating and chanting slurs. In 2012 about a third of the population — over 900,000 Jamaicans — believed the government was not doing enough to protect LGBT people from violence and discrimination.

JAM.tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Commission's report of 10 August 2012 places LGBT persecution inside a wider pattern of citizen security failures in Jamaica, covering police killings including the May 2010 operation and the administration of justice, with input from Jamaicans for Justice and the Jamaica Forum for Lesbians, All-Sexuals and Gays.

Human Rights Watch's documentation was launched in Kingston on 16 November 2004 with the backing of five Jamaican human-rights organisations, and the Inter-American Commission likewise drew on local civil society, indicating an established domestic advocacy infrastructure that a visitor may encounter as a source of assistance.

Amnesty International's 2006 urgent appeal also raised concern that prominent Jamaican musicians promote homophobia, a cultural influence that operates alongside the legal regime rather than within it.

The UNDP national survey published in March 2023 supplies quantified baseline data on violence and service exclusion among LGBT Jamaicans, against which the older qualitative accounts can be read.
JAM.comparisons: Pairwise: above Malaysia (0.28 — adds Sharia caning statutes) and below Sri Lanka (0.33 — police-as-perpetrator but less mob-killing culture). Jamaica's mob-violence pattern plus failed investigation of the Dwayne Jones killing keeps it in High Risk.

TTO.name: Trinidad and Tobago
TTO.summary:
Trinidad and Tobago demands real caution from trans visitors: the criminal law has moved, the protective framework has not. The High Court struck down the colonial same-sex criminal provisions in Jones v Attorney General (2018), a challenge brought after activist Jason Jones stated publicly that he faced up to 25 years' imprisonment for consensual sex with an adult male partner; the ruling was upheld on appeal. Decriminalisation removed exposure to prosecution, but it did not produce legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, or any mechanism for changing documents.

Recognition remains absent in practice as well as in law. The director of the TT Transgender Coalition, Rae Alibey, stated in July 2024 that the trans community is the most marginalised group in the country and is not recognised at all, that gender identity is not treated as distinct from sexual orientation, and that institutional forms carry no gender-identity marker. A visitor whose documents do not match presentation has no statutory route to alignment and no statutory claim if a mismatch is raised at a bank, hotel, clinic or government counter.

Parliamentary and constitutional channels have been closed repeatedly. The ruling party's Constitution Review Committee decided against adding sexual-orientation protections to the constitution, announced at a special convention in August 2024; CAISO's Dr Angelique Nixon said the community had been waiting far too long for equal rights and protection. The refusal follows a longer pattern: in June 2016 Prime Minister Keith Rowley told Parliament that the state must protect all citizens regardless of whom they sleep with, while declining to repeal the same-sex criminal laws.

Violence risk is documented and specific. Police warned in November 2024 that cyber criminals were creating fake dating profiles to lure LGBT victims into meetings ending in armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault, with cars, cash and phones stolen; two separate incidents were reported in a single week. A Newsday editorial in June 2024 recorded almost half a dozen Grindr-related attacks in recent months and quoted Supt Claire Guy-Alleyne identifying the legislative gap behind them: there is no specific hate crime category in Trinidad and Tobago legislation. Community advocates separately report trans people being beaten, stoned and chopped, with most incidents never reported to police.

Custody is an elevated-risk setting. The Justice through a Gender Lens Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers, launched in November 2018, states plainly that there are no special facilities in the Trinidad and Tobago penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities. Placement therefore depends on a sentencing judge's recommendation to prison authorities, with no dedicated facility behind it.
TTO.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory establishes whether any bill for legal gender recognition or SOGI anti-discrimination protection has been introduced, tabled or defeated in the Parliament of Trinidad and Tobago; the record establishes only that the 2024 constitutional review declined to include sexual-orientation protections.

Enforcement outcomes for the documented Grindr-related robberies and assaults are unresolved: the inventory carries police warnings and incident counts through November 2024 but no information on arrests, charges or convictions in those cases.

Whether the 2018 protocol's sentencing recommendations have ever been acted on by the prison service, and whether any trans inmate has been housed accordingly, is not sourced here.

The claim that most incidents of violence against trans people go unreported rests on community advocate accounts rather than on police or health statistics; no official incidence data for anti-trans violence in Trinidad and Tobago appears in the inventory.

The current status of the Jones v Attorney General decriminalisation ruling after appeal is not re-verified by any source in this inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2, D5, D6, D8.

sources.title: Protect transgender inmates'
sources.summary: Trinidad Express (Camille Hunte, 28 Nov 2018) on the official 'Justice through a Gender Lens' Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers (launched Nov 2018 by the CCJ, CAJO, UN Women, JURIST Project, TTAWJ and the Judicial Institute of TT): the Protocol states plainly that 'in Trinidad and Tobago, there are no special facilities in our penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities'. It directs judicial officers sentencing a person whose gender identity does not accord with their birth certificate to use recommendations to prison authorities to ensure provisions are in place for the inmate's physical safety, and instructs courts to refer to intersex/transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and permit court access irrespective of dress. Official acknowledgment that housing placement for trans prisoners is discretionary, unsafe, and mediated only through sentencing recommendations - with no facility of its own.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Under Section 8 of the Immigration Act, homosexual men and women who are not citizens are prohibited from entering Trinidad and Tobago, though this law is not known to have been enforced. In 2016, the Caribbean Court of Justice ruled that neither Trinidad nor Belize violated Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson's freedom of movement, but clarified that neither state can ban homosexuals from CARICOM countries from entering due to treaty obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas, notwithstanding their laws that ban the entry of gays. Wikipedia country coverage: Trinidad and Tobago does not recognize same-sex marriage or civil unions, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same rights and benefits as opposite-sex couples. In July 2018, Justice Frank Seepersad approved a property dispute resolution between two gay partners, noting unequal treatment under current law and warning that without agreement the court would have had to rely on innovative applications of trust law to determine property division after dissolution of a same-sex union. Same-sex couples are unable to legally adopt in Trinidad and Tobago. Wikipedia country coverage: The Silver Lining Foundation is an LGBTQ group that seeks to end bullying against LGBTQ youth. A 2009 University of the West Indies study for the Ministry of Social Development found that four of every five Trinbagonians believed in denying someone rights or equality based on sexual orientation, prompting the founding of CAISO to encourage public discussion and legislative protections.

TTO.tangentialFactors:
The absence of a hate-crime category is the single structural gap that connects the street incidents to the courts: prosecutors and police have no offence to charge that records bias motivation, so attacks on trans and LGBT people are processed as ordinary assault or robbery. Supt Claire Guy-Alleyne's June 2024 acknowledgement of the gap came from within the police service itself, not from advocacy commentary.

Official rhetoric and official law have diverged for at least a decade. Keith Rowley's 2016 undertaking to protect all citizens regardless of sexual conduct was paired with an explicit refusal to repeal, and the 2024 constitutional review repeated the exclusion. Reform has been blocked through political channels rather than defeated in court.

Older travel and culture profiles of the country, including a GlobalGayz profile from August 2012, state that homosexuality is illegal and that the laws are mostly ignored in practice. That description predates the 2018 decriminalisation ruling and does not reflect current law; visitors relying on pre-2018 material will misstate both the criminal position and the enforcement picture.

The 2018 protocol was a joint launch involving the Caribbean Court of Justice, the Caribbean Association of Judicial Officers, UN Women, the JURIST Project, the Trinidad and Tobago Association of Women Judges and the Judicial Institute of Trinidad and Tobago, which gives its pronouncements institutional weight even though they bind no facility.

The TT Transgender Coalition has called for national discussions and attitudinal research as prerequisites to recognition, indicating that no such process is currently under way.

GHA.name: Ghana
GHA.summary:
Trans visitors in Ghana face a legal framework that, in its current form, criminalises identity itself. The Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill passed by Ghana's Parliament on 29 May 2026 provides for up to three years' imprisonment for identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer, with total prison terms of three to ten years and longer terms for promotion or advocacy. Presidential assent by President John Mahama was still outstanding at the time of the most recent reporting, and Mahama had previously signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill after the earlier version failed to reach him.

The 2026 bill adds a reporting obligation: it establishes a duty on persons who become aware of prohibited acts to report them to the police. For a visitor, that converts acquaintances, colleagues, landlords and hotel staff into potential informants, and it removes the discretion that previously shielded people from formal complaint.

The 2026 law is not an isolated event. Parliament unanimously passed the Promotion of Proper Human Sexual Rights and Ghanaian Family Values Bill in February 2024, carrying up to three years for identifying as LGBTQ+ and up to five years for forming or funding LGBTQ+ groups. President Nana Akufo-Addo declined to assent while legal challenges were pending; the Supreme Court of Ghana unanimously dismissed two of those challenges, with Justice Avril Lovelace-Johnson observing that until there is presidential assent there is no act and deferring review until signature. The bill then lapsed unsigned when the 8th Parliament dissolved before the 2024 election. Its unanimous passage, and its reintroduction, indicate the direction of travel rather than a stray piece of legislation.

Criminalisation predates both bills. Section 104(1)(b) of Ghana's Criminal Offences Act, a colonial-era provision on 'unnatural carnal knowledge', remains on the books, though Human Rights Watch reported in 2018 that it is rarely enforced through prosecution. That low formal enforcement rate did not make Ghana safe. Human Rights Watch documented mob violence against LGBT people, police abuse and extortion of suspected LGBT individuals, including victim interviews conducted in Kumasi and Tamale in 2017, and published a report titled 'No Choice but to Deny Who I Am: Violence and Discrimination against LGBT People in Ghana' in January 2018.

The new bill enumerates transgender people explicitly alongside lesbian, gay, bisexual and queer people. It therefore supplies the state pathway by which a trans person in Ghana can be imprisoned for identity alone, with no requirement of any act. The bill contains no provision on how such prisoners would be housed, and there is no publicly documented policy in Ghana on the housing of trans prisoners, leaving placement to correctional discretion.

Community organisations describe the effect of the 2026 bill's passage in advance of assent. One Love Sisters Ghana reports panic among LGBT people, risk of eviction and widespread self-censorship. A 2017 survey of 113 Ghanaians living in Finland, conducted for a Diaconia University of Applied Sciences thesis, found that most respondents opposed decriminalisation or legalisation on religious and cultural grounds and concerns about effects on children, while most supported families loving and accepting LGBT relatives but not blessing their marriages. That diaspora sample is not representative of Ghana's population, but it is consistent with the political support the bill received.
GHA.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether President John Mahama has assented to the 29 May 2026 bill is unresolved in the source inventory. The most recent reporting states that ratification was still required and that the bill was expected to be signed. The legal status of the bill at the time a visitor reads this record should be verified against Ghanaian official sources before travel.

Nothing in the inventory addresses gender-marker or identity-document rules for trans people in Ghana, the treatment of foreign passports bearing conflicting markers at ports of entry, asylum or non-refoulement claims, or access to gender-affirming healthcare. These are not sourced and remain unaddressed here rather than assumed either way.

The Reuters report of the February 2024 parliamentary passage returned HTTP 401 at research time and could not be read directly; the passage itself is corroborated by JURIST and Human Rights Watch.

The inventory does not document any instance of a trans person actually being prosecuted or imprisoned for identity under section 104(1)(b) of the Criminal Offences Act, nor any data on the current population of LGBT detainees in Ghanaian prisons. The claim that the 2026 bill creates a pathway to imprisonment for identity alone is a statement about the statute's terms, not about documented enforcement.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5.

sources.title: Ghana parliament passes bill criminalising gay acts
sources.summary: BBC (30 May 2026): Ghana's parliament approved a new bill criminalising homosexuality and the promotion of LGBTQ+ activities. Identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer carries up to three years' imprisonment, and the bill adds a duty to report prohibited acts to police. sources.title: People 'panicking' as Ghana passes sweeping law criminalising LGBTQ+ activity
sources.summary: The Guardian (1 Jun 2026): the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill, passed by Ghana's parliament on 29 May 2026 and expected to be signed by President Mahama, mandates prison terms of three to 10 years, with up to three years for identifying as LGBTQ+ and longer terms for promotion or advocacy. Community groups such as One Love Sisters Ghana report panic, eviction risk and self-censorship. No publicly documented policy exists in Ghana on housing trans prisoners.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of speech, expression and assembly, but the source states these rights are actively denied to LGBTQ people, and pro-LGBTQ activism is repeatedly thwarted by the government. In 2006 the government banned an LGBTQ rights conference at the Accra International Conference Centre, and in March 2020 President Akufo-Addo banned the Pan Africa ILGA conference planned for Accra as illegal. The Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill passed by Parliament in February 2024 (reintroduced in March 2025 and passed again in May 2026) criminalises identifying as LGBTQ (up to three years), funding or forming an LGBTQ-related group (up to five years), advocacy or intentional support of LGBTQ activities (three to five years, with some proposals at 5–10 years), public displays of same-sex affection, crossdressing, and disseminating information perceived as supporting LGBTQ people. Those identifying as an 'ally' of LGBTQ people may also face prison. Wikipedia country coverage: The source contains no finding on legal gender recognition procedures or document-change rules for transgender Ghanaians. The closest grounded items are that the 1992 Constitution defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman (Article 39 emphasises traditional values), that a 2017 ILGA poll found 55% of Ghanaians believe transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender, and that the pending anti-LGBTQ bill would criminalise crossdressing and identifying as transgender. Wikipedia country coverage: Facilities for LGBTQ people in Ghana have been shut down rather than provided: in February 2021 religious and political leaders forced an LGBTQ Centre in Accra to close, and LGBT+ Rights Ghana's Accra office, opened in January 2021, was raided and closed by National Security in late February 2021 after opposition from locals, religious institutions and politicians. Most LGBTQ groups operate secretly or online, with FOTHA-Ghana members using the dark web for safety. There is no supported housing or shelter provision in the source; instead young LGBTQ people are disowned and evicted from family homes, and the Solomon-supported Solace Initiative provides human-rights-trained paralegals to defend LGBTQ people in court. Wikipedia country coverage: Mental health and healthcare access are severely constrained: mental health professionals in Ghana are often not trained to work with LGBTQ populations and may hold prejudiced views, and the Ghana Mental Health Authority has not fully implemented inclusive policies under its 2012 Mental Health Act. Due to fear of persecution many LGBTQ people avoid seeking healthcare altogether, creating barriers to mental and sexual health support, and the source reports high rates of anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation and some deaths by suicide linked to forced evictions, blackmail and violence. Conversion therapy, which families often seek from religious groups when a young person discloses same-sex orientation or non-conforming gender identity, is described as commonly administered in abusive and inhumane settings; an August 2018 report documented conversion therapy programmes run by religious leaders, and a 2018 conference claimed about 400 people had registered for such programmes. Youth-specific: a study found LGBTQ+ adolescents in Ghana are at significantly higher risk of suicidal ideation and self-harm than their heterosexual peers, and government HIV/AIDS campaigns present the disease as an issue for straight people, leaving gay men unaware that HIV can be transmitted through anal sex even though the country receives HIV funding. Wikipedia country coverage: The source states plainly that no broad legal protections exist for LGBT people against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in areas such as education, health, housing and employment. Enforcement of the 'unnatural carnal knowledge' law (Section 104, Criminal Code 1960, a misdemeanour carrying up to three years under Article 296(4)) overwhelmingly targets LGBTQ people while heterosexual couples doing the same acts are rarely or never prosecuted, a disparity CDD-Ghana describes as moral policing rather than criminal justice. In a 2017 ILGA poll 59% of Ghanaians agreed LGBTQ people should be protected from workplace discrimination (62% for transgender people), while 89% reported disliking LGBTQ individuals and nearly 90% said they would report a relative or co-worker to police. The UN Human Rights Committee's October 2012 recommendation to eliminate 'unnatural sexual relations' and eradicate discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity was rejected by Ghana along with all other recommendations. Wikipedia country coverage: Ghana does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions: the 1992 Constitution defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, and no provision of Ghanaian law allows legal recognition of same-sex relationships, leaving LGBTQ people in vulnerable legal positions around long-term relationships and shared property. Same-sex couples are explicitly excluded from the adoption process, since the system does not support joint applications from non-heterosexual partnerships. The pending Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill would additionally ban same-sex marriage and adoption by same-sex couples outright. Wikipedia country coverage: Young LGBTQ Ghanaians are disowned by families and communities and evicted from their homes, and families often seek conversion therapy from religious groups when a same-sex orientation or non-conforming gender identity is disclosed — reported to be commonly administered in abusive and inhumane settings, with medical bodies warning conversion therapy is ineffective and potentially harmful. A study found LGBTQ+ adolescents in Ghana face significantly higher risk of suicidal ideation and self-harm than heterosexual peers. On education policy, in January 2025 President John Mahama said he prefers teaching traditional family values through Ghana's school curriculum rather than passing anti-LGBTQ laws, and the National Coalition for Proper Human Sexual Rights and Family Values has actively opposed comprehensive sex education. The pending bill targets youth directly by criminalising identification as LGBTQ (three years), with Pan Africa ILGA's banned March 2020 Accra conference intended partly to protect queer youth in Africa.

GHA.tangentialFactors:
Ghana illustrates how a legislative instrument can matter without ever being law. The 2024 bill passed unanimously and was defeated only by the absence of presidential assent and the dissolution of Parliament, not by court judgment or popular rejection. A visitor assessing Ghana should therefore treat the 2026 bill's pending status as a question of timing rather than of outcome, given the President's stated willingness to sign.

The Supreme Court's dismissal of the challenges to the 2024 bill did not clear the statute. Justice Avril Lovelace-Johnson's reasoning was procedural: there was no act to challenge because no assent had been given, and review was deferred until the President signed. The petitioners' lawyers said they would explore further options. This sequencing means that constitutional challenge in Ghana has so far operated at the threshold rather than on the merits of criminalisation.

The gap between the colonial-era offence and the new statutory scheme is a gap in evidence rather than in law. Section 104(1)(b) survived unchanged for decades with little reported prosecution, while the violence documented by Human Rights Watch in 2018 came largely from police and vigilante actors rather than from courts. The 2026 bill's reporting duty is designed to shift the enforcement burden toward third parties and formal complaint, which may change that pattern.

Human Rights Watch has been the principal external documentation of LGBT conditions in Ghana since its 2018 report, and has consistently urged the President to veto the 2024 bill and, by extension, opposes the 2026 legislation. Its reporting on Ghana forms part of its wider work on criminalisation in West Africa, though the source inventory for this record does not extend to comparative data on other states in the region.
GHA.comparisons: Pairwise: above Nigeria (0.19 — SSMPA in force with mob lynching culture) and below Kenya (0.38 — criminalisation but stronger courts). Ghana's near-passage of an identity-criminalising bill is what separates it from Elevated band: the legal floor is currently the old 3-year statute, but the demonstrated legislative intent is far harsher.

Community organisations describe the effect of the 2026 bill's passage in advance of assent. One community group reports panic among LGBT people, risk of eviction and widespread self-censorship. A 2017 survey of 113 diaspora nationals found that most respondents opposed decriminalisation or legalisation on religious and cultural grounds and concerns about effects on children, while most supported families loving and accepting LGBT relatives but not blessing their marriages. That diaspora sample is not representative of the population, but it is consistent with the political support the bill received.
GHA.blindOutOfScope:
Whether the national President has assented to the 29 May 2026 bill is unresolved in the source inventory. The most recent reporting states that ratification was still required and that the bill was expected to be signed. The legal status of the bill at the time a visitor reads this record should be verified against official national sources before travel.

Nothing in the inventory addresses gender-marker or identity-document rules for trans people, the treatment of foreign identity documents bearing conflicting markers at ports of entry, asylum or non-refoulement claims, or access to gender-affirming healthcare. These are not sourced and remain unaddressed here rather than assumed either way.

The Reuters report of the February 2024 parliamentary passage returned HTTP 401 at research time and could not be read directly; the passage itself is corroborated by two other outlets in the inventory.

The inventory does not document any instance of a trans person actually being prosecuted or imprisoned for identity under section 104(1)(b) of the national criminal code, nor any data on the current population of LGBT detainees. The claim that the 2026 bill creates a pathway to imprisonment for identity alone is a statement about the statute's terms, not about documented enforcement.
blindSourceSummaries: In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed a bill on human sexual rights and family values (up to 3 years for simply identifying as LGBT, 5 years for 'promotion'); the president refused to assent pending legal challenges, the top court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when parliament dissolved.

In late May 2026 parliament passed a new bill on human sexual rights and family values: up to three years' imprisonment for identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer, longer terms for promotion/advocacy, and a 'duty to report' prohibited acts to police; the current president's ratification was still required and widely expected as of the reporting.

Under existing law, 'unnatural carnal knowledge' carries up to 3 years; mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection; the capital has a resilient underground community whose 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks.

Neither the 2024 nor the 2026 bill text, as reported, contains any provision on how trans prisoners would be housed; no national prison placement rule, trans special unit, or solitary/segregation practice is documented in any source in this record; the 2026 reports also describe panic, eviction risk and self-censorship among community groups.
GHA.blindTangential:
The country illustrates how a legislative instrument can matter without ever being law. The 2024 bill passed unanimously and was defeated only by the absence of presidential assent and the dissolution of the parliament, not by court judgment or popular rejection. a visitor assessing the country should therefore treat the 2026 bill's pending status as a question of timing rather than of outcome, given the President's stated willingness to sign.

The national Supreme Court's dismissal of the challenges to the 2024 bill did not clear the statute. The justice's reasoning was procedural: there was no act to challenge because no assent had been given, and review was deferred until the President signed. The petitioners' lawyers said they would explore further options. This sequencing means that constitutional challenge has so far operated at the threshold rather than on the merits of criminalisation.

The gap between the historic-era offence and the new statutory scheme is a gap in evidence rather than in law. Section 104(1)(b) survived unchanged for decades with little reported prosecution, while the violence documented in 2018 came largely from police and vigilante actors rather than from courts. The 2026 bill's reporting duty is designed to shift the enforcement burden toward third parties and formal complaint, which may change that pattern.

a human rights organisation has been the principal external documentation of LGBT conditions in the country since its 2018 report, and has consistently urged the President to veto the 2024 bill and opposes the 2026 legislation. Its reporting on the country forms part of its wider work on criminalisation in the wider national area, though the source inventory for this record does not extend to comparative data on other states in that area.
GHA.localsOnly:
Residents, not only visitors, are caught by the reporting duty introduced in the 2026 bill. Members of households, landlords, employers and community members who learn of prohibited acts become obliged to report them to the police, which places LGBT Ghanaians in conflict with their own families and neighbours rather than only with the state.

Organisations working with LGBT people have been operating in a climate of documented police and vigilante violence well before the 2026 bill. Human Rights Watch's 2018 report recorded police abuse and extortion of suspected LGBT individuals alongside mob attacks, and its endnotes document interviews conducted in Kumasi and Tamale in 2017. Residents of those areas have reported to such organisations that the principal threats come from vigilantes and from police, not from prosecution.

One Love Sisters Ghana reports that LGBT Ghanaians are experiencing panic, risk of eviction from housing and self-censorship following the 2026 bill's passage. Housing insecurity is a direct consequence where a landlord can report a tenant under the new duty to report.

Public opinion research touching on the Ghanaians' own attitudes is limited to a small 2017 survey of 113 Ghanaians living in Finland, which found majority opposition to decriminalisation but majority support for familial acceptance of LGBT relatives short of marriage. No national polling data on attitudes to transgender people is available in this record.

MAR.name: Morocco
MAR.summary:
Morocco criminalises same-sex conduct under Article 489 of the penal code, which punishes "indecent acts" between persons of the same sex with six months to three years of imprisonment. Outright International reports that the provision is applied with wide police discretion and that arrests are arbitrary; 170 people were charged with same-sex relations in 2018. Human Rights Watch recorded Article 489 in its April 2018 report "Audacity in Adversity" among the statutes used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across the wider region.

Trans visitors face a further layer of exposure that the statute does not name. Cairo 52's country review finds no specific legal provisions governing transition, yet documents de facto criminalisation under Article 498, where morality charges follow gender-expression discrepancies and arrest produces involuntary outing. The Cairo 52 report "A Web of Violence: The Systemic Erasure of Transgender People in Morocco" (January 2026, by Hamzawya and Nora Noralla), drawn from interviews with 17 trans and non-binary Moroccans, describes an interlocking system of legal, medical, social and economic hostility and finds that Article 489 is weaponised to arrest trans people on the basis of gender expression alone.

No legal gender recognition pathway exists for trans people. A recognition process introduced in 2021 is open to intersex people only. Gender-affirming healthcare operates without any regulatory framework, a gap that pushes some residents into self-medication, and the Grand Mufti opposes transition. Morocco once pioneered gender-affirming surgery for foreign patients while enforcing what the 2026 report characterises as a de facto prohibition on the same care for its own citizens.

Two documented cases show how gender expression is policed in practice. In November 2024 Brazilian influencer Liziane Gutierrez was arrested in Marrakesh on suspicion of being transgender and alleges that police forced her to display her genitals; she spent about a month in jail. In January 2019 El País reported that after a minor traffic accident in Marrakesh, a cross-dressing man identified as Chafiq was handcuffed, filmed by bystanders and by police officers, and had his identity documents photographed and posted online. He subsequently sought asylum in Europe.

Public identification as LGBTIQ carries significant risk of violence and harassment, and the authorities block LGBTIQ organisations. Human Rights Watch documented a 2020 campaign of online harassment directed at presumed gay and bisexual men. Police retain wide discretion throughout the country, and the documented incidents occurred in a major tourist centre rather than in any marginalised quarter.
MAR.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Article 489 has been charged against foreign visitors on gender-expression grounds, as distinct from the two documented police incidents, is not resolved in the available sources.

The current operation and eligibility scope of the 2021 intersex recognition process is stated only in the Cairo 52 review and has not been independently verified here.

Practical effect of the 2014 UN Human Rights Council resolution on Moroccan enforcement is not sourced; its existence as a scrutiny framework is the only established point.

The ILGA "State-Sponsored Homophobia" survey of May 2008 predates the documented cases and its figures have not been checked against current statute, so it is treated as background rather than current law.

Differences in policing between tourist centres and other cities are not established by the sources; both documented incidents occurred in Marrakesh, which is a single data point rather than a measured pattern.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The source text contains no information on current transgender-specific healthcare access, identity-document procedures, or housing/shelter provisions for trans visitors. The only medical-related reference is historical: in the 1950s, publicity around French entertainer Coccinelle helped establish Casablanca as a place where certain doctors were willing to perform sex change operations 'albeit in clandestine circumstances' — indicating a legacy of unregulated, non-official gender-affirming care rather than any documented public facility. Separately, during the April 2020 outing campaign, some landlords ejected tenants who were targeted, pointing to housing insecurity as a documented risk but not to any supportive facility. Wikipedia country coverage: Morocco has no law against discrimination or harassment on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no LGBTQ rights legislation has been enacted by any political party. In 2017, following the UN Universal Periodic Review, former Minister of Justice and Liberties Mustafa Ramid called homosexuals 'trash' in an interview, prompting local human rights associations to sign a petition to Prime Minister Othmani demanding an investigation into what they termed his 'discriminatory and unconstitutional statements towards sexual minorities'. Police disproportionately target perceived LGBTQ people, and arrested individuals' names are publicised before trial. Wikipedia country coverage: The source text states plainly that there is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Morocco. Enforcement is punitive rather than protective: in December 2007 a court in Ksar el-Kebir convicted six men under Article 489 after an online video of a private party — reported in the press as a 'gay marriage' — circulated, with defendants' lawyers saying no evidence of prohibited conduct was presented; the men were sentenced on 17 December 2007 to varying terms. Following the arrests, dozens of people marched through the streets of Ksar el-Kebir calling for the men's punishment. Wikipedia country coverage: The state actively shapes youth attitudes: the government has banned books on homosexuality and required schools to teach a curriculum that 'emphasises ... the danger and depravity of "unnatural acts"'. Minors face direct criminal-adjacent exposure — in 2016, two girls in Marrakesh were arrested after a cousin photographed them kissing and their mother complained to police; their case was postponed to December 2016, when both were acquitted, provoking the #freethegirls outcry. In the April 2020 outing campaign, sociologist Khalid Mouna noted that transgender influencer Sofia Talouni sought to 'isolate young Moroccan homosexuals by breaking up their family unit', and journalist Hicham Tahir reported receiving 'a hundred testimonies' from victims or witnesses; one person allegedly committed suicide. A trans woman was also violently beaten in Tangier in November 2022, with three minors and an adult arrested over the assault, while only 21% of Moroccan respondents in the 2018–19 Arab Barometer survey said homosexuality is acceptable.

MAR.tangentialFactors:

The country hosted pioneering gender-affirming surgery for foreign patients, yet residents are now denied that care under an unwritten prohibition, so a visitor's nationality may shape access in ways the law does not state.

Regional legal patterns shape enforcement. The Human Rights Watch annex covering laws used against same-sex conduct and gender expression places Morocco within a broader statutory cluster, and the 170 charges recorded in 2018 indicate sustained use of the penal code rather than isolated prosecutions.

The UN Human Rights Council adopted the sexual orientation and gender identity resolution in September 2014, establishing an international scrutiny framework that formally applies to Morocco. Whether that scrutiny has altered policing practice is not evidenced in the sources.

The 2019 humiliation case ended in a claim for asylum in Europe, an outcome that indicates the perceived absence of domestic remedy for a person targeted over gender expression.

DZA.name: Algeria
DZA.summary:
Algeria is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the Penal Code of 1966 (Ordinance 66-156 of 8 June 1966), which ILGA records as covering both male/male and female/female relations with 2 months' to 2 years' imprisonment and fines of 500-2000 Algerian dinars. The US State Department's 2023 country report gives the same range, 2 months' to 2 years' plus fines, for undefined "homosexual acts". The UK Home Office country-of-origin information report of 26 July 2026 confirms that this 1966 Penal Code remains the operative framework.

Gender transition is not addressed by a dedicated statute, but it is blocked in practice. Cairo 52 reports that Algeria has no legal framework for gender-affirming healthcare, that Penal Code articles 274 and 264 could be used against providers, and that the absence of any legal gender-recognition route means civil-status gender-marker changes are theoretically unavailable. Cairo 52 also documents arrests within the LGBT+ community under indecency provisions (articles 333, 338 and 333 bis), with little information recorded on whether those arrested were trans. Snopes rated TRUE, on 5 August 2024, the claim that Algeria prohibits medical and surgical gender-affirming care and prohibits being transgender; that rating was published alongside the debunking of a false rumour about a boxer, and the debunked rumour does not affect the legal finding.

Enforcement is documented. On 24 July 2020 police raided a private home in el-Kharoub, Constantine Province, over an alleged gay wedding and arrested 44 people, 9 women and 35 men, mostly university students; on 3 September 2020 a court sentenced 2 to prison and gave 42 suspended terms, treating party decorations and "gay appearance" as evidence. A visibly trans person is exposed to the same indecency provisions, and the evidentiary standard used in that case indicates how little conduct is required for a charge to stand.

Detention offers no trans-specific protection. The US State Department reports that prison authorities separate vulnerable persons but that LGBTQI+ detainees have no specific legal protections, and that civil society notes compounded discrimination for LGBTQI+ persons. There is no anti-discrimination protection in law, no legal gender recognition, and no visible community infrastructure; activism operates almost entirely underground.

The UK Home Office assessment is that internal relocation within Algeria is viable for gay males, but that lesbians and trans females face societal difficulties, and that refusals of asylum are rarely certifiable as clearly unfounded. Unlike Tunisia or Morocco, Algeria has no documented trans-visitor incident on record, partly because very few tourists visit and researchers have limited access; the legal exposure for a visibly trans visitor is real, but the recorded enforcement pattern is thinner than Egypt's entrapment machinery or Tunisia's 2024-25 arrest wave.
DZA.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: Cairo 52 records arrests under indecency articles 333, 338 and 333 bis but states that little information is available on the trans identity of those arrested, so the share of trans defendants in these cases is not sourced.

Unresolved: whether Penal Code articles 274 and 264 have actually been applied against providers of gender-affirming care is not evidenced in the inventory; Cairo 52 frames their use as a possibility rather than a documented prosecution.

Unresolved: the Snopes formulation that Algeria "prohibits being transgender" is a fact-check rating of a compound claim and is not traced in the inventory to a specific statutory provision; the underlying provisions identified elsewhere are the 1966 Penal Code's same-sex and indecency articles.

The ILGA figures are from the 2008 State-Sponsored Homophobia survey and are dated, though the same Penal Code is confirmed in force by the July 2026 UK Home Office report. No trans-specific visitor incident, sentence, or enforcement case for Algeria is sourced in this inventory.

An Arab Barometer survey published by the BBC on 23 June 2019, with 25,000 respondents across 10 countries plus the Palestinian territories, found Algeria was the exception in which fewer than 50% accepted a woman as head of state; the same polling recorded region-wide identification as "not religious" rising from 8% to 13% since 2013.

The legal architecture is shared with neighbouring states: the same Penal Code model that ILGA recorded in 2008 is the one the 2026 UK Home Office report confirms is still in force, so the age of the statute does not indicate repeal. What distinguishes Algeria from Egypt and Tunisia is documentation volume rather than a more permissive law.

Very low tourist arrivals and restricted researcher access mean incident reporting is sparse, so an absence of recorded trans-specific cases should not be read as an absence of risk.

TUN.name: Tunisia
TUN.summary:
Tunisia is a country in active legal and police hostility toward trans people, and trans visitors should treat it as a destination to avoid. Penal Code Article 230 punishes same-sex conduct with up to three years' imprisonment, and Article 226 bis on public indecency is applied to gender expression; enforcement falls disproportionately on transgender women. In October 2021 two transgender women were arrested under morality and debauchery provisions.

The scale of enforcement is documented by Amnesty International on 11 February 2025: at least 84 people, mainly gay men and transgender women, were arrested, arbitrarily detained and prosecuted between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025 on public indecency and morality charges. The arrests took place in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef, and the sweep is national in character rather than confined to any one city. A mass conviction on 31 October 2024 imposed prison terms of up to four and a half years; the convictions were upheld on appeal on 5 February 2025, with four people released after their sentences were reduced.

Custody itself is a site of specific harm for trans women. The Intersection Association reports that transgender women in Tunisian prisons are processed under their former names and birth gender in detention records, arrest processes and court hearings, a systemic refusal of identity that begins at arrest and continues through sentencing. Local documentation describes severe abuse for trans women held in men's facilities.

Legal gender recognition is not available as a reliable route. In April 2023 the Tunis Court of First Instance refused recognition to a transgender man, and recognition remains unsettled below the Court of Cassation, decided case by case and frequently denied.
TUN.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether forced anal examinations have in fact stopped since the 2017 pledge to the United Nations is unresolved in these sources; the inventory records the commitment and the retention of the statute, not compliance in practice.

The outcome of any appeal of the April 2023 gender-recognition refusal to the Court of Cassation is not sourced here, as is the current state of any consolidated precedent on recognition.

The grounds for the sentence reductions that led to the release of four people on 5 February 2025 are not stated in the inventory.

No source in this inventory addresses visa or border screening, identity-document checks at entry, healthcare access, or facilities rules for trans visitors in Tunisia; these are not sourced rather than established as safe or absent.

CMR.name: Cameroon
CMR.summary:
Cameroon criminalises same-sex conduct under Article 347-1 of the penal code, which carries a sentence of up to five years' imprisonment. The 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations, and Cameroon is one of 31 African countries that criminalise them; reporting places Cameroon among the states in Africa with the highest prosecution rates. There is no legal gender recognition procedure and no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation.

Appearance alone has served as the basis for prosecution. In November 2011 a Cameroonian court jailed Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome for five years after they were seen wearing women's clothes and ordering Baileys, with the original judge citing their dress, speech and the drink as proof that they were gay. An appeals court acquitted both men on 9 January 2013. Defence lawyer Alice Nkom said the conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts, and Amnesty International welcomed the acquittal. Arrests made on grounds of effeminacy or appearance under the colonial-era sodomy law have carried sentences of six months to five years.

The February 2021 prosecution of the trans woman Shakiro (born 29 July 1997 in Douala, a YouTuber and activist with a substantial online following) is the clearest documentation of how the law reaches visibly gender-nonconforming people. She and her friend Patricia were arrested in a Douala restaurant for the clothes they were wearing and were convicted of attempted homosexuality, indecent dressing and identity-document irregularities. A Douala court sentenced each to five years, the maximum statutory term, plus a fine of 200,000 CFA francs (about $370), on 12 May 2021 reporting, with an appeal filed. Lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu called the judgment a political decision made with no proof of any acts. Shakiro described five months of what she called hell in Douala's central prison, held initially in leg chains, before release pending appeal; she subsequently left Cameroon to claim asylum abroad, and has since been granted asylum in Belgium. Her case and exile form part of Cameroon's record of criminalisation prosecutions.

Human Rights Watch reported on 11 May 2022 that violence against LGBTI people had risen sharply: from 9 March 2022 onward, security forces arbitrarily arrested at least six people and detained eleven, all of them victims of group attacks, over alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity, and gendarmes beat two of them in detention. HRW senior researcher Ilaria Allegrozzi framed the pattern as a consequence of the statute itself, which lets both civilians and security forces abuse LGBTI people without consequence. Police violence and mob violence against perceived LGBT people are both documented, and beatings of gay and trans people in public are reported as common. US State Department reporting as far back as 2010 recorded discrimination against gays and lesbians among societal abuses alongside security-force killings, torture, harsh prison conditions and arbitrary arrests, describing the criminalisation context of Article 347.

For a visitor: visible trans expression in a public place is treated in practice as a prosecutable offence, arrests have been made on the strength of clothing, speech and drink orders rather than any observed act, and detention carries a real risk of beatings. No legal mechanism exists in Cameroon to recognise a trans person's gender, and no protection machinery covers anti-trans violence.
CMR.outOfScopeNotes:
Several points remain unresolved or unsourced. The outcome of the appeal against the Shakiro and Patricia sentence is not stated in the sources; only that an appeal was filed and Shakiro was released pending it. Her asylum grant in Belgium is not independently corroborated within this inventory beyond the record carried forward here.

Whether the at least six people arrested and eleven detained by security forces in the period Human Rights Watch described from 9 March 2022 were charged, convicted or released is not sourced. Nor is the number of prosecutions brought annually under Article 347-1: the claim that Cameroon has among Africa's highest prosecution rates is carried without a figure.

The exact current wording and full penalty range of Article 347-1 are not reproduced in the sources; only the five-year maximum is documented. The six-month-to-five-year range for arrests on effeminacy or appearance grounds comes from 2013 reporting and may reflect the colonial-era statute rather than the 2016 penal code. It is unresolved whether the 2013 acquittal established any binding precedent.

Nothing in this inventory addresses passport or visa screening of gender markers at Cameroonian entry points, availability of healthcare for trans visitors, or which specific facilities are accessible; these are not sourced and should not be inferred from the legal findings above.
