sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Documents: In February 2021, two Cameroonian transgender women (Shakiro and Patricia) were arrested in Douala for 'wearing women's clothing in a restaurant' and were later convicted of 'attempted homosexuality, public indecency, and failing to carry identification.' Identification failure was therefore used as a charge alongside anti-homosexuality counts, and the women were sentenced to five years. Separately, Jean-Claude Roger Mbede was arrested in 2011 for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance. No content on legal gender recognition, name change, or ID/marker procedures appears in the source. Wikipedia country coverage: Entry/visa: The source provides no visa policy, entry-refusal, or border-admission procedure text. The closest material is outbound asylum-related: in July 2010 the UK granted a gay Cameroonian man the right to claim asylum, prompting Cameroon's Minister of Communication, Issa Tchiroma Bakary, to argue that homosexuals are not prosecuted for private activities and that 'he is not the only gay person in Cameroon.' An external link to UK government travel advice for Cameroon on local laws and customs is listed, but no Cameroonian visa or entry rule for LGBTQ travelers is described. Wikipedia country coverage: Border/carriage screening: In August 2011, a gay Cameroonian man was granted temporary immigration bail from the UK Border Agency after Air France refused to carry him to Yaoundé. In May 2012, the UK Border Agency sought to return asylum-seeker Ediage Valerie Ekwedde, finding 'no credible evidence' that he was gay, but was forced to keep him in custody after he threatened to 'make a fuss' on the return flight. In May 2005, the government threatened to conduct medical examinations to 'prove' the homosexual activity of 11 men arrested at a nightclub on suspicion of sodomy. No text on Cameroonian border screening procedures exists. Wikipedia country coverage: Facilities: Jean-Claude Roger Mbede served a three-year sentence at Kondengui Central Prison for the SMS messages. Douala's main prison is described as 'hell' by prisoners accused of homosexuality, and Shakiro and Patricia spent five months in prison before being released pending appeal in 2021. Alternatives-Cameroon, an LGBTQ organization, is listed as forced to shutdown after a police raid, eliminating a service base. In November 2011, three young men were sentenced to five years for oral sex in a parked car, and two men were sentenced to five years based on appearance, women's clothing and ordering a cream-based liquor. Wikipedia country coverage: Care access: The source does not describe healthcare, HIV, or medication access for transgender visitors. The nearest service-access finding is institutional: Alternatives-Cameroon, an LGBTQ organization, was forced to shutdown after a police raid, and few lawyers are willing to defend the accused in homosexuality cases. The 2005 government threat of medical examinations to 'prove' homosexual activity of detained men represents coercive, not care, contact with health services. Wikipedia country coverage: State & media hostility: In 2006, tabloids published the names of at least 50 prominent people claimed to be homosexual, boosting circulation and prompting criticism from the state communication council for privacy invasion; President Paul Biya publicly urged respect for privacy while simultaneously prosecuting people accused of homosexual activity. The Law on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime (Law No. 2010/012, Article 83(1)) criminalizes online same-sex sexual propositions with 1–2 years' imprisonment and 500,000–1,000,000 CFA francs fines, doubled where intercourse followed. Cameroon was described in 2020 as prosecuting consensual same-sex conduct 'more aggressively than almost any country in the world'; the US Department of State's 2010 report noted harassment and extortion of gays and lesbians by law enforcement and false allegations used to harass or extort. On 30 June 2024, President Biya's daughter Brenda Biya came out as a lesbian on Instagram, sparking national backlash and hope among LGBTQ Cameroonians. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth & education: No contemporary youth, school, or minor-specific legal policy appears in the source. The only youth-adjacent material is historical ethnography: in 1921 Günther Teonmann documented a same-sex custom among the Bafia people, where the 'kiembe' stage begins around age 15 and involves close male sexual friendships with a 'lexan,' with consent symbolized by sharing earthnuts from a basketry plate, and where a father might later name his newborn after the lexan regardless of gender. Two young men were sentenced to five years in 2011 for oral sex in a parked car, and Bakary dismissed asylum claims by asserting homosexuals are not prosecuted for private acts. Nothing on trans-youth travel, medication, or education targets is documented.

CMR.tangentialFactors:
The prohibition is colonial in origin: reporting on the 2013 acquittals describes the underlying sodomy law as colonial-era, and the 2016 penal code carried the ban forward in explicit statutory language rather than replacing it. Cameroon's position is comparable to that of the 30 other African states that criminalise same-sex relations, though its prosecution rate is at the high end of that group.

Outcomes are not uniform. The 2013 appeals-court acquittal of Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome, welcomed by Amnesty International, shows that convictions resting on appearance and stereotype can be reversed, while the Shakiro judgment shows the same evidence base producing the maximum statutory term. The involvement of lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu, and of Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, indicates an active but narrow defence and monitoring presence.

Shakiro's public profile matters to her case: she is a Cameroonian trans activist who built a Facebook and YouTube following discussing trans life before her 2021 arrest, and her subsequent exile is part of the same documented pattern. Adjacent background from US State Department reporting lists killings, torture, harsh prisons and arbitrary abuses by security forces alongside anti-gay discrimination, situating LGBTI mistreatment within a broader record of abuse rather than a distinct regime.

Nothing in the sources indicates that general street crime, transport, entry formalities or other travel logistics differ for trans visitors from what applies to any traveller; those are outside this assessment.

Conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts. Establishes the pattern: arrests on appearance grounds under a historic-era sodomy law with six-month-to-five-year sentences.
CMR.blindTangential:
The prohibition is historic in origin: reporting on the 2013 acquittals describes the underlying statute as historic-era, and the 2016 penal code carried the ban forward in explicit statutory language rather than replacing it. The jurisdiction's position is comparable to that of the 30 other states that criminalise same-sex relations, though its prosecution rate is at the high end of that group.

Outcomes are not uniform. The 2013 appeals-court acquittal, welcomed by an international human rights organisation, shows that convictions resting on appearance and stereotype can be reversed, while the 2021 judgment shows the same evidence base producing the maximum statutory term. The involvement of defence counsel and of two international monitoring organisations indicates an active but narrow defence and monitoring presence.

The trans woman at the centre of the 2021 case had a public profile: she built a large social media and video-platform following discussing trans life before her arrest, and her subsequent exile is part of the same documented pattern. Adjacent official reporting from 2010 lists killings, torture, harsh prisons and arbitrary abuses by security forces alongside anti-gay discrimination, situating LGBTI mistreatment within a broader record of abuse rather than a distinct regime.

Nothing in the sources indicates that general street crime, transport, entry formalities or other travel logistics differ for trans visitors from what applies to any traveller; those are outside this assessment.
CMR.localsOnly:
Cameroonian residents live under the same Article 347-1 exposure as visitors, but with no exit route: gender-nonconforming residents have been arrested in their own neighbourhoods and restaurants, and the Shakiro judgment demonstrates that a residence in Douala offers no protection against a five-year term for how a person dresses.

Residents face abuse from both sides of the enforcement line. HRW documented that in the period from 9 March 2022 security forces arrested and detained LGBTI people who were themselves victims of group attacks, rather than investigating the attackers, and that gendarmes beat two detainees. The researcher's assessment is that the statute licenses civilians and security forces alike to act with impunity.

No procedure exists for a Cameroonian to change legal gender markers on national documents, and no anti-discrimination or hate-crime law protects residents on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. Detention itself is a documented hazard: held in Douala's central prison for five months, Shakiro was kept initially in leg chains and described the period as hell, conditions consistent with the harsh-prison and arbitrary-arrest findings in US State Department reporting from 2010. Residents convicted under the statute carry a criminal record that constrains them indefinitely, and those who fled, as Shakiro did, do so by claiming asylum abroad.

TZA.name: Tanzania
TZA.summary:
Tanzania's Penal Code criminalises same-sex activity, with imprisonment of up to life available as a penalty. The semi-autonomous island jurisdiction of Zanzibar operates a separate criminal statute, the Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004, enacted by Zanzibar's House of Representatives, so a visitor may face two overlapping criminal-law regimes depending on where they are.

Amnesty International's January 2024 report, "We Are Facing Extinction," documents escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment in Tanzania and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people. Proposed legislation on same-sex relations was deferred after protests, within a documented climate of discrimination that limits how far rights can be enjoyed in practice.

In June 2024 the UN Human Rights Office condemned as "horrendous" the attack on Mauzinde, a Tanzanian transgender activist from Rahaleo. She was abducted by 12 men and found beaten in a forest with her ears cut off. The Office called for bold action to combat discrimination against LGBTIQ people and flagged possible violations of ICCPR Article 20 and the equality guarantees of Article 13 of Tanzania's Constitution.

OONI's 2024 report on a surge in online LGBTIQ censorship records state-directed blocking of LGBTIQ websites, social networks and rights sites, based on measurement data. Access to information, support networks and rights documentation is constrained online as well as in public.

Reporting from the ground matches the legal picture. A 2020 interview with three pseudonymised Tanzanian LGBT activists described substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence, denial of basic rights, and homophobia and transphobia driving the urgency of their advocacy. A trans visitor therefore faces exposure to criminal liability, documented societal violence, and an official environment in which hostility has been expressed at the highest levels.
TZA.outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Tanzania returned HTTP 403 at research time and could not be retrieved. The criminalisation finding, including the availability of life imprisonment, rests on that profile's underlying documentation as cited in the inventory and was not independently verified against the statute text in this pass.

No sourced material was available on legal gender recognition, identity-document or marker rules, visa and entry screening that could disclose a person's gender history, healthcare access, restroom or facility rules, hate-crime provisions, or recognition of partners. These questions remain unresolved rather than assessed, and the absence of sourced restriction should not be read as an absence of restriction.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D3, D13.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Government respect for freedom of speech and freedom of assembly is described as declining, and UN human rights defenders in Tanzania may not make public statements supporting tolerance for fear of reprisals. Broadcast content regulations of 2018 bar inciting hatred on grounds of sexual preference, and online content regulations issued the same year banned such hate speech but were completely repealed by the 2020 online content regulations. The Media Council of Tanzania's 2020 Code of Ethics for Media Professionals still bars hate speech, stereotypes and discrimination based on sexual orientation. Named activists — Maria Sarungi Tsehai, Fatma Karume, Mwanahamisi Singano, Carol Ndosi, Zara Kay, Khalifa Said, Goodluck Haule — have openly backed LGBTQ rights against officials such as Magufuli, Paul Makonda, Ally Hapi and Hamisi Kigwangalla who pushed persecution. Wikipedia country coverage: In October 2017 the government deported staff of several HIV/AIDS groups on the basis of 'promoting homosexuality'. The source otherwise contains no visa, entry permit or border-crossing rules for travelers; the only related reference is an external link to UK government travel advice for Tanzania on local laws and customs. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2018 a 'witch hunt' against gay people was declared in Dar es Salaam, where gay men were forced to undergo anal examinations and torture. Also in 2018 Dar es Salaam Regional Commissioner Paul Makonda announced a 17-strong committee of police, lawyers and doctors to identify and punish homosexuals, scouring the internet for videos of supposedly LGBTQ people; the Foreign Ministry said the crackdown lacked government support and Denmark withheld 65 million kr (about US$9.8 million) in aid. A 2013 Human Rights Watch and Wake Up and Step Forward Coalition report documented torture of LGBT people in police custody, including a 19-year-old gay man arrested after leaving a nightclub in Mbeya who said police raped him and beat the soles of his feet with canes, electric wires and water pipes. Tanzania's human rights record is described as poor, with police custody abuse detailed in the US State Department's 2013 report. Wikipedia country coverage: There are no gay bars in Tanzania, although some places exist where gay men meet; lesbians are less visible than gay men. No other facility, shelter, or safe-space information appears in the source text. Wikipedia country coverage: Tanzania has a high HIV/AIDS rate with reportedly one million people infected, and in October 2017 the government deported HIV/AIDS group staff for 'promoting homosexuality', directly disrupting services. Gay men were subjected to anal examinations and torture during the 2018 Dar es Salaam witch hunt, and 2013 reports documented rape and beatings in police custody. On the policy side, the 2013 National Family Planning Guidelines and Standards commit to services 'regardless of age, parity, marital status, creed, race, color, or sexual preference', counselling 'any woman, man, couple, or young person regardless of age'; the Nursing and Midwifery (practice) Regulations 2010 bar withholding nursing care based on sexual orientation, and the 2017 National Guidelines for Respectful and Compassionate Nursing and Midwifery Care require non-discriminatory care. No youth-specific healthcare provision beyond the age-inclusive family planning counselling language is stated. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples have no legal recognition anywhere in Tanzania, so no partner can be sponsored, inherited from, or recognized as next of kin through relationship status. Adoption requires a married couple, so a same-sex couple cannot adopt jointly. Same-sex sexual acts between men carry a maximum penalty of life imprisonment under the Penal Code as revised by the Sexual Offences Special Provisions Act 1998 (section 138A 'gross indecency', 1–5 years or fines of TSh 100,000–300,000 for the general offence), and Zanzibar's Penal Code of 1934 (as amended 2004) outlaws sex between women with up to five years' imprisonment or a TSh 500,000 fine. Heterosexual oral and anal sex is also illegal.

TZA.tangentialFactors:
The US State Department's 2013 Human Rights Report for Tanzania named excessive force by security forces, gender-based violence including female genital mutilation/cutting, and lack of access to justice as the three most widespread problems in the country, alongside discrimination based on sexual orientation and societal violence against persons with albinism. Sexual-orientation discrimination sits inside a broader pattern of state and societal abuse rather than standing alone, which shapes what a complaint is likely to achieve.

The UN Human Rights Office grounded its June 2024 statement in ICCPR Article 20 and Article 13 of the Tanzanian Constitution, indicating that equality and non-discrimination guarantees exist in binding instruments the state has accepted. The gap between those guarantees and the documented attack on Mauzinde is the practical measure of protection available to a visitor.

OONI's findings show the censorship reaching LGBTIQ social networks and rights organisations, not only explicit content, which narrows the channels through which a visitor could obtain local guidance or contact support.

ETH.name: Ethiopia
ETH.summary:
Same-sex conduct is a criminal offence in Ethiopia under Article 629 of the 2004 Criminal Code, which covers conduct between men and between women. Enforcement is rare, but the provision underpins pervasive stigma, harassment and violence against LGBTIQ+ people. Stakeholder submissions to Ethiopia's Universal Periodic Review report penalties of up to one year, with harsher terms under aggravating provisions; a 2009 academic study of the same legal framework reports a maximum of three years for male homosexuality.

Ethiopia has no legal gender recognition, by either surgical or psychiatric pathway. A stakeholder submission to the 47th session of the UPR states the practical consequence directly: trans men are legally women and trans women are legally men. A trans visitor in a different-gender relationship can therefore be characterised as engaging in same-sex conduct under the criminal code.

The same UPR stakeholder material documents discrimination, violence, stigma in access to services and an absence of police protection for LGBTQ+ people, and identifies transgender people as particularly at risk within the criminalisation framework. The Advocates for Human Rights and House of Guramayle reached the same findings in their April 2024 submission on SOGIE in Ethiopia.

The US State Department's 2023 human rights report describes near-total concealment of identity as the practical result of criminalisation: individuals generally do not publicly identify as LGBTQI+, activists report surveillance, entrapment and fear for their safety, and harassment and violence increased toward the end of 2023. Societal discrimination is reported at high levels nationwide across education, employment and healthcare, and being outed carries a risk of physical violence and ostracism.

Enforcement and incitement have converged in documented episodes. In August 2023 security forces carried out a crackdown on 'homosexuality', while non-state actors ran an online incitement wave that ended in physical attacks. Christian and Muslim groups campaign publicly for harsher penalties, and the Orthodox Church declared its stance in June 2024.

There is no hate-speech or hate-crime legislation covering gender identity, no protection from arbitrary arrest based on gender identity or expression, and no workplace or fair-housing discrimination protection including gender identity. LGBTI organisations cannot register, and Pride events are not allowed with participants unprotected. The Charities & Societies Proclamation, Article 69, blocks registration of LGBTI groups as contrary to public morality.

US State Department reports from 2008, 2010 and 2011 record the same criminalisation and societal stigma, indicating a legal regime that has persisted across the period covered by the sources. The F&M Global Barometers time series scores Ethiopia 'no' on every protection axis in every year from 2011 to 2024.
ETH.outOfScopeNotes:
The maximum penalty for same-sex conduct is stated inconsistently across the sources: UPR stakeholder material gives up to one year with harsher terms under aggravating provisions, while the 2009 Lund University thesis gives up to three years for male homosexuality. The current operative figure under Article 629 of the 2004 Criminal Code is not resolved by the inventory.

No source in the inventory documents a prosecution of a trans person under the same-sex conduct provision on the basis of their birth-sex legal status, so the mechanism described in the UPR submission remains a legal-structure finding rather than a case-based one.

The inventory contains no material on entry or visa rules, border or airport screening, document checks at the point of entry, or whether gender markers on foreign passports are inspected. Nothing is sourced on how Ethiopian authorities treat a visitor whose passport marker differs from their presentation.

There is no source on access to gender-affirming care, medication continuity or health facilities for visitors, beyond the general finding of discrimination in healthcare. Nor is there sourced material on recognition of foreign marriages or partnerships.

Source dates range from 2008 to March 2026, and several key documents are stakeholder submissions rather than government statements; enforcement practice in the current period is described mainly through the 2023 report and the August 2023 crackdown, with no later enforcement data in the inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D5.

sources.summary: Stakeholder submission to Ethiopia's UPR (47th session): same-sex activity criminalised, leaving LGBTQ+ people at serious risk of harm and systematic exclusion; discrimination, violence, lack of police protection and stigma in services; no legal gender change - trans men are legally women and trans women legally men, so trans people in different-gender relationships can fall foul of the same-sex conduct law.

Stakeholder UPR report by The Advocates for Human Rights and House of Guramayle (April 2024) on SOGIE in Ethiopia: documents discrimination, violence, and lack of protection; notes transgender people are particularly at risk given the criminalisation framework.

F&M Global Barometers country profile, time series 2011-2024 (all years scored 'no' on every protection axis): no legal gender recognition (neither surgical nor psychiatric pathway exists), no hate-speech or hate-crime legislation covering gender identity, no freedom from arbitrary arrest based on gender identity/expression, LGBTI organisations cannot register, Pride events not allowed and participants unprotected, no workplace or fair-housing discrimination protections including gender identity. National LGBTI organisations exist despite the ban on registration.
US State Department 2008 Human Rights Report for Ethiopia (archived): documents the criminalisation of same-sex conduct and societal stigma.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Ethiopia (archived): the LGBT section notes criminalisation and societal discrimination. The report also documents arrests of opposition figures and CSO-law restrictions on civil society.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Ethiopia: the LGBT section notes criminalisation. The report also documents anti-terrorism prosecutions, CSO-law restrictions on civil society, torture and harsh prison conditions.

Lund University master's thesis (2009) by Daniel Iddo Balcha: 'Homosexuality in Ethiopia' - analyses the construction of homosexuality in relation to gender and feminism; male homosexuality criminalised (up to 3 years); media and elite create homophobia in discourse; the church effectively campaigns hatred; female homosexuality simply overlooked; attitudes shifting under globalisation.

sources.title: Ethiopia — Outright International country overview

Charities & Societies Proclamation Art 69 blocks registration of LGBTI groups as 'contrary to public morality'. sources.title: US State Dept 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices — Ethiopia
sources.summary: US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report, Ethiopia §6.7: criminalization of consensual same-sex conduct drives near-total concealment of identity. Individuals generally do not publicly identify as LGBTQI+; activists report surveillance, entrapment and fear for their safety, with harassment and violence increasing toward end of 2023. High levels of societal discrimination nationwide in education, employment and healthcare; being outed risks physical violence and ostracism.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: In the early 2010s some Ethiopian media outlets, cooperating with the government, imposed restrictions on discussion of "LGBTQ ideology," though these censorship policies have not been enacted into law. Internet censorship has limited the ability of LGBTQ people and allies to organize campaigns and petitions, and in 2008 a petition for equal rights signed by hundreds of homosexuals was blocked en route to Prime Minister Meles Zenawi's office. A pro-gay conference scheduled for Addis Ababa in 2012 was cancelled after fundamentalist Christian and religious groups protested and called organizers "missionaries of evil." In 2023 the House of Guramayle reported that self-identified gay, lesbian and transgender people face online harassment on platforms such as TikTok, including an August 2 TikTok user calling for gay men to be stabbed and a young man threatened with "We should find them and kill them." Wikipedia country coverage: In July 2021 German authorities issued a deportation order for a trans woman of Qatari origin holding Ethiopian citizenship. She testified that after someone discovered she was registered as male in her passport and attempted extortion, she was reported to Ethiopian authorities, held in an Ethiopian men's prison for about a year, and subjected to physical and sexual abuse by staff and inmates. German officials argued she would be safe in Ethiopia because she could "pass" as cisgender, citing the absence of explicit laws regarding gender identity as justification for deportation. The UK government publishes travel advice for Ethiopia covering local laws and customs. Wikipedia country coverage: On 10 August 2023 the Ethiopian government raided hospitality venues in Addis Ababa to crack down on alleged homosexual activity; security forces shut down guest houses and arrested managers, and the Addis Ababa Peace and Security Administration Bureau announced measures "against hotels, restaurants, guest houses, and other entertainment venues suspected of involvement in homosexual acts," calling on the public to report such incidents. Detention conditions are documented as abusive: ILGA World recorded police residential searches without warrants following neighbor complaints, physical abuse during detention, and a 2014 case in which a gay man was denied legal counsel and assaulted by other inmates, with no trial records found. In January 2021 two people released from detention had their sexual orientation disclosed to their families by police; one subsequently died by suicide. Wikipedia country coverage: The AIDS Resource Center in Addis Ababa reported that the majority of self-identified gay and lesbian callers, mostly male, requested help changing their behavior to avoid discrimination, and many gay men reported anxiety, confusion, identity crises, depression, self-ostracism, religious conflict and suicide attempts. In early December 2011 Christian and Muslim religious leaders tried to derail a sexual health seminar targeted at men who have sex with men; the government intervened and the seminar went ahead at a different location. Stigma and discrimination toward people living with HIV/AIDS affected residents' ability to receive an education, find employment and integrate into the community. Youth-specific: the 2014 anti-gay rally organizers and religious figures publicly blamed gay people for the rape of children and young men, and an anonymous LGBTQ activist told the AP in 2019 of concern about wide misconceptions that gay people may be culpable for rising rape incidence — a climate that deters young people from seeking services. The DANA Social Club (founded 2013 by Beki Abiy) campaigns for transgender people's rights to sex reassignment surgery. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2008 an unofficial gay marriage took place at the Sheraton Addis in Addis Ababa. In Nuer society, researcher Brian MacDermot encountered a transgender woman — formerly a man who dressed as a woman — who received spiritual approval to change status and marry a husband, suggesting precolonial acceptance of gender fluidity. Same-sex marriage has no legal recognition: in December 2008 nearly a dozen Ethiopian religious figures, including the leader of Ethiopian Muslims and heads of the Orthodox, Protestant and Catholic churches, adopted a resolution urging lawmakers to ban homosexual activity in the constitution. In March 2014 the Council of Ministers endorsed a bill that would have made homosexuality a 'non-pardonable' offence, but the government later cancelled both that bill and a planned April 2014 anti-gay rally, with spokesman Redwan Hussien saying the current jail term was deemed sufficient. Wikipedia country coverage: In early April 2014 the Addis Ababa Youth Forum, together with a church group linked to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, planned an anti-gay rally for 26 April in Addis Ababa alongside debate on the proposed anti-gay bill; group chairman Dereje Negash claimed "Children are being raped by gay people in this country," though the government later cancelled the rally. Religious figures in December 2008 held homosexuality responsible for a rise in sexual attacks on children and young men. On education, the US Department of State's 2011 Human Rights Report found that stigma and discrimination toward people living with HIV/AIDS impacted residents' ability to receive an education. Historically, David F. Greenberg reported that shepherd boys of the Amhara and Qemant developed homosexual relationships with one another until marriage.

ETH.tangentialFactors:
Documented trans-specific enforcement in Ethiopia is thinner than in jurisdictions where gender-identity offences are charged directly; the risk here is structural rather than case-based, arising from criminalisation combined with the absence of legal gender recognition rather than from a documented pattern of trans-targeted prosecutions.

The wider civil-society environment constrains any protection machinery a visitor might hope to reach. US State Department reports for 2010 and 2011 document restrictions on civil society under the Charities & Societies Proclamation, alongside anti-terrorism prosecutions, arrests of opposition figures, torture and harsh prison conditions; the 2023 report records activists describing surveillance and entrapment.

A 2009 Lund University thesis analysing Ethiopian discourse finds that media and elite actors construct homophobia, that the church campaigns effectively in that direction, and that female homosexuality is largely overlooked in public discussion. The same study notes attitudes shifting under globalisation, while recording that national LGBTI organisations exist despite the registration ban.

Historical continuity is the pattern across the source set: the 2008, 2010, 2011 and 2023 US State Department reports and the 2011–2024 barometer series all describe the same criminalisation and the same absence of protective law, so a visitor should not expect a materially different legal position from the one described in older material.
ETH.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Ghana (0.24 — Ghana's near-passed bill signals worse trajectory; Ethiopia's steady-state is worse today), above Tanzania (0.18) and below Kenya (0.38 — criminalisation but stronger courts, visible community, and a 2023 Supreme Court NGO-registration win).

Stakeholder submissions to the national Universal Periodic Review report penalties of up to one year, with harsher terms under aggravating provisions; a 2009 academic study of the same legal framework reports a maximum of three years for male homosexuality.

The state has no legal gender recognition, by either surgical or psychiatric pathway. a stakeholder submission to the 47th session of the review states the practical consequence directly: trans men are legally women and trans women are legally men. a trans visitor in a different-gender relationship can therefore be characterised as engaging in same-sex conduct under the criminal code.

The same review stakeholder material documents discrimination, violence, stigma in access to services and an absence of police protection for LGBTQ+ people, and identifies transgender people as particularly at risk within the criminalisation framework. an international human rights organisation and a national community group reached the same findings in an April 2024 submission on SOGIE.

a foreign government's 2023 human rights report describes near-total concealment of identity as the practical result of criminalisation: individuals generally do not publicly identify as LGBTQI+, activists report surveillance, entrapment and fear for their safety, and harassment and violence increased toward the end of 2023. Societal discrimination is reported at high levels nationwide across education, employment and healthcare, and being outed carries a risk of physical violence and ostracism.

Enforcement and incitement have converged in documented episodes. In August 2023 security forces carried out a crackdown on 'homosexuality', while non-state actors ran an online incitement wave that ended in physical attacks. Major Christian and Muslim groups campaign publicly for harsher penalties, and the national Orthodox Church declared its stance in June 2024.

There is no hate-speech or hate-crime legislation covering gender identity, no protection from arbitrary arrest based on gender identity or expression, and no workplace or fair-housing discrimination protection including gender identity. LGBTI organisations cannot register, and Pride events are not allowed with participants unprotected. The Charities & Societies Proclamation, Article 69, blocks registration of LGBTI groups as contrary to public morality.

Foreign government human rights reports from 2008, 2010 and 2011 record the same criminalisation and societal stigma, indicating a legal regime that has persisted across the period covered by the sources. a global barometer time series scores the state 'no' on every protection axis in every year from 2011 to 2024.

The inventory contains no material on entry or visa rules, border or airport screening, document checks at the point of entry, or whether gender markers on foreign passports are inspected. Nothing is sourced on how authorities treat a visitor whose passport marker differs from their presentation.

LBN.name: Lebanon
LBN.summary:
Lebanon is dangerous for trans visitors — the Arab world's most socially open country layered over one of its most explicitly anti-trans statutes. Article 521 of the Penal Code prescribes up to six years' imprisonment for “men disguising themselves as women” — a direct criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Article 534 (“intercourse contrary to the order of nature,” up to 1 year) remains in force though several courts have ruled it inapplicable to same-sex relations. Courts have granted legal gender recognition in some post-surgery cases since 1987, but inconsistently.

Legal gender recognition runs through the civil registry code of 1951, and the judiciary has a long record of reviewing plaintiffs' name and gender-marker changes, with the earliest recorded instance dating to an 1887-era precedent entered as Lebanese Civil Decision 1987. Medical and religious authorities hold heavy roles in that process, so approval depends on documentation and institutional discretion rather than a settled entitlement; a judge approved a plaintiff's gender-marker change on identity documents in 2015, and Human Rights Watch reports that trans people in Lebanon face policing and documentation barriers and calls on the state to ensure access to legal gender recognition.

Enforcement against gender non-conformity extends beyond the statute. In May 2018 security forces arrested a prominent LGBT rights activist and pressured him to cancel Beirut Pride, nine days of LGBT-identity activities, in a crackdown Human Rights Watch called a violation of freedom of assembly. Cairo 52 records both de facto and explicit criminalisation targeting transgender women and documents a rise in prejudice and violence in Beirut, including incidents respondinging to a decriminalisation bill tabled in parliament.

Beirut's queer scene is the region's most visible — bars, NGOs (Helem, Proud Lebanon), and a documented court history — but the climate deteriorated sharply since 2022: state-affiliated militia groups attacked queer venues after an anti-discrimination bill was introduced.
LBN.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on legal gender recognition and the conflict is unresolved here. Outright International's country overview, updated March 2026, states that legal gender recognition is not possible in Lebanon, while Cairo 52 and Manara Magazine document approvals, including a 2015 marker change and a case law line reaching back to an 1887-era precedent. Whether Outright is describing a de facto bar rather than a formal prohibition is not sourced either way.

Outright also records that same-sex relations for men and for women are not legal throughout the country; the interaction between that statement and the 2009 and 2017 court rulings on Article 534 is not reconciled in the inventory.

The EUAA Lebanon country focus carries a dedicated section on LGBTIQ persons, including activists, as a distinct risk category with defined terms of reference and a stated source methodology. That is a country-of-origin assessment framework for protection claims, not guidance on entry screening or visitor status, and no visitor-facing consequence is sourced from it.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D5, D6, D8, D12, D13.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Article 534 of the Lebanese Penal Code still stands, prohibiting sexual relations 'contradicting the laws of nature' with up to a year in prison, and has been used to harass and persecute LGBT people through police arrests, including intrusive anal examinations ordered by prosecutors (e.g., 36 people arrested in a 2012 cinema raid). Although multiple courts from 2007 to 2023 declined to apply Article 534 to same-sex conduct — including an August 2023 district court of appeal ruling that consensual same-sex sex is not unlawful — the law remains on the books. LBN.tangentialFactors:

The decriminalisation line matters for how Article 534 is applied. A 2009 precedent held that consensual same-sex conduct is not a criminal offence, and a February 2017 ruling by another judge questioning the legal basis for prosecuting homosexuality moved Lebanon further from enforcement of the provision, though the article itself remains on the books.

Advocacy infrastructure is established and regional in reach: Georges Azzi co-founded Helem in 2004, the first LGBT advocacy group in the Arab world, and later led the Arab Foundation for Freedoms and Equality, campaigning for LGBT equality across hostile neighbouring countries.
LBN.localsOnly:

JOR.name: Jordan
JOR.summary:
Jordan does not criminalise same-sex relations: the colonial-era ban was abolished in 1951, and no statute on the books criminalises gender expression as such. That baseline does not translate into safety. Human Rights Watch reported in June 2024 that authorities in Jordan, Egypt and Kuwait substitute public-morality and debauchery provisions for formal criminalisation, using them to harass LGBT people legally.

Legal gender recognition has no clear pathway. Intersex people can change official gender markers, transgender people cannot. The Court of Cassation's ruling in Case No. 2092/2014 allowed a plaintiff born in 1977 to change name and gender from male to female in official records after hormone therapy and surgery undertaken in Australia, since such procedures are unavailable domestically; the court justified the change by reclassifying the plaintiff as intersex rather than recognising a trans identity.

Gender-affirming surgery is permitted for intersex people and criminalised for transgender people under Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law No. 25 of 2018, with penalties reaching ten years' imprisonment; providers face liability under the same medical-liability framework. Care that cannot be obtained at home must therefore be sought abroad.

The operating environment has tightened. A cybercrime law enacted in 2023 criminalises online speech on grounds of inciting immorality and undermines free speech and privacy, and Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 records the arrest and harassment of peaceful dissidents and journalists under vague laws alongside intrusive digital surveillance. In December 2023 Human Rights Watch documented a coordinated crackdown in which authorities targeted LGBT rights activists, officials smeared activists online by sexual orientation, social-media users circulated their photographs with messages inciting violence, and directors of two LGBT organisations described official intimidation.

CAIRO 52's Jordan profile reports a notable rise in the targeting of transgender individuals and spaces by both security forces and civilians, working through Ottoman- and British-era morality provisions, and states that security forces coerced queer community spaces into complete cessation of activity, pushing transgender and queer people to leave. New legislation further curtails LGBTQ+ speech and digital access, and intersex people can change legal gender markers while transgender people cannot.
JOR.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory attributes a ten-year maximum penalty for sex reassignment to Jordanian legislation in the context of the 2014 case analysis, while the statutory citation supplied for the current ban is Article 8 of the 2018 Medical and Health Liability Law. Whether the ten-year figure derives from the earlier statute, from the 2018 law, or from both is unresolved in these sources.

OutRight International's profile, updated 12 March 2026, states that marker changes are allowed 'in some cases' without specifying the criteria, which sits uneasily with the intersex-only reading given by CAIRO 52. The scope of any exception beyond intersex classification is not sourced here.

Enforcement frequency is not established: the sources document a 2023 crackdown, coerced closures and a reported rise in targeting, but give no figures on arrests, prosecutions or convictions under morality provisions, and no data on violence against trans visitors specifically. Whether the 2014 Court of Cassation ruling binds lower courts as precedent is also not addressed.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D7, D12.

HRW World Report 2024 Jordan chapter (11 Jan 2024): authorities limited civic space in 2023 and enacted a new cybercrime law undermining free speech and privacy online. Peaceful dissidents and journalists were arrested and harassed under vague, abusive laws, with intrusive digital surveillance, conditions that shape online expression for visitors and residents alike.

Officials smeared activists online by sexual orientation, social-media users posted their photos with messages inciting violence, and two LGBT organisation directors cited official intimidation.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The Jordanian government tolerates a few cafés in Amman that are widely considered gay-friendly. Books@Cafe opened in 1997 and remains a popular bookstore and cafe for patrons supportive of "creativity, diversity and tolerance." No other facility types (shelters, detention, health) are described in the source. Wikipedia country coverage: Homosexuality has not been criminal in Jordan since the 1951 penal code, which legalised private, adult, non-commercial, consensual same-sex acts with an age of consent of 18 regardless of gender or orientation, but the source states there is an "absence of legal protection" combined with vague morality laws that give security forces and private individuals license to target LGBTQ people with impunity. The 2023 Human Rights Watch report found Jordan's "cybercrime" and "morality" laws used to persecute LGBTQ people, and in August 2023 authorities promulgated a new cybercrime law that could target digital content on gender and sexuality and activists advocating LGBTQ rights; security forces intimidated activists with threats of violence, arrest and prosecution, forcing several to shut down organisations, stop activities or flee. The Press and Publication Law (amended 1998, 2004) replaced a ban on depicting "sexual perversion" with a requirement that the press respect "the values of ... the Arab and Islamic nation," and the 2018 Medical Responsibility Law vagely outlawed "changing of sex" while legalising "correction of sex," potentially criminalising doctors performing gender-affirming surgery. Honor killings as a legal justification for murder were made illegal under the 2013 revised Penal Code, and a 2019 Arab Barometer survey found 93% of Jordanians said society should not accept homosexuality. Wikipedia country coverage: The age of consent for sexual activity in Jordan is 18 regardless of gender and/or sexual orientation, set by the 1951 penal code revision. The source includes a youth-angled account from Jordanian model Khalid Abdel-Hadi: "Growing up, it was hard for me to find topics, subjects and publications that I could relate to! In my country, most magazines rejected me and my ideas due to my young age at the time, and I felt like an outcast in my own society!" The 2007 launch of My.Kali, the first LGBTQ publication in the MENA region (online from 2008), is the only youth/education-adjacent media access finding; no school, curriculum or bullying findings appear in the source.

JOR.localsOnly:
Residents have no administrative route to change a gender marker on the basis of a transgender identity; the available route runs through intersex classification, as in Case No. 2092/2014. People who have transitioned abroad remain unable to reflect that status in Jordanian records.

Providers of gender-affirming surgery face criminal liability under Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law No. 25 of 2018 where the patient is transgender, which effectively removes domestic surgical care from residents as well as visitors.

Community organisations have been coerced into closing, and LGBT activists have been targeted by officials through online smears and intimidation of organisational directors. Residents operating in this space carry exposure that does not fall away when they are at home.

IRQ.name: Iraq
IRQ.summary:
Iraq is among the most dangerous countries in the world for a trans visitor. On 27 April 2024 the Council of Representatives passed an amendment to the 1988 Law on Combatting Prostitution that explicitly criminalises consensual same-sex relations, gender-affirming healthcare and diverse gender expression; the President signed it on 29 June 2024 and it has been in force since 1 July 2024. The Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor and ILGA Asia both record it as the operative legal baseline.

The penalties are severe. Same-sex relations carry 10 to 15 years' imprisonment. Undergoing or performing gender-affirming procedures carries 1 to 3 years, which places transition itself beyond the law. The statute also penalises the 'promotion of homosexuality'. Human Rights Watch called for outright repeal on 20 May 2024; the BBC recorded that supporters framed the law as upholding religious values while rights groups condemned it.

State violence is not the only hazard. The US State Department's 2012 human rights report for Iraq documented sectarian violence, torture and impunity alongside what it called societal discrimination and violence against individuals based on perceived sexual orientation and gender identity. A BBC investigation found that dozens, possibly hundreds, of gay people have been killed in recent years while authorities turned a blind eye, and reported a UN assessment that state neglect makes Iraq a perpetrator of the violence rather than a protector of those targeted.

Targeted killings of visible figures have occurred. In October 2023 a prominent Iraqi TikToker was fatally shot in Baghdad amid a crackdown on the LGBTQ community, an attack that coincided with a hardening anti-LGBT climate. The UK Home Office's July 2025 country policy and information note assesses risk from both state and hybrid actors and from non-state actors as substantial enough to underpin LGBT+ asylum claims, including on internal relocation and certification grounds.
IRQ.outOfScopeNotes:
The exact passage date is recorded inconsistently across sources: Human Rights Watch gives 27 April 2024 and ILGA Asia gives 28 April 2024. Both agree on presidential signature on 29 June 2024.

The precise penalty attached to the 'promotion of homosexuality' offence is not stated in the available sources and remains unresolved here.

Whether the amended statute applies uniformly across the Kurdistan Region, and how regional authorities enforce it, is not sourced in this inventory and is unresolved.

Enforcement statistics for the 2024 offences are not available in these sources; the violence documented by the BBC and the US State Department predates the statute and is largely non-state in origin.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D5.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: No legal gender recognition framework appears in the source; instead, the April 27, 2024 parliamentary vote criminalizes "biological sex changes based on personal desires and inclination" with up to three years in prison for both the transgender person and the doctor (court-ordered procedures on intersex people excluded), effectively closing off legal sex-change documentation. On documents generally, the Iraqi Kurdistan Personal Status Law (1992) Article 7 requires couples seeking to marry to produce medical documents proving they are not infected with AIDS, while the Iraqi Personal Status Law (1959) Article 3 defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman to create children. Wikipedia country coverage: The 2024 law on homosexual relations carries penalties of up to 15 years in prison with fines and deportation, making removal a stated consequence of criminalized status. Asylum and relocation are handled largely by NGOs: Iraqi LGBT (established September 2005) focuses on relocating LGBTQ people to safer countries and providing legal help for those seeking asylum, and the International Railroad for Queer Refugees (founded 2008) provides financial and resettlement assistance to LGBTQ asylum seekers fleeing prosecution for sexual orientation or gender identity. Wikipedia country coverage: Iraqi LGBT's main goal is the creation and maintenance of several "safe houses" in Iraq where people fleeing prosecution can find protection and safety. Separately, OWFI led over 40 local organizations to change Iraq's Anti-Shelter Policy, which had allowed only government-run shelters to exist, expanding basic civil liberties in the region. Historically, Saddam Hussein ordered all Iraqis with AIDS to be relocated to a special prison facility after the disease reached Iraq in 1986. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex marriage and civil unions are illegal in Iraq, and both personal status laws define marriage as a union between a man and a woman (Iraqi Personal Status Law 1959, Article 3; Iraqi Kurdistan Personal Status Law 1992, Article 1). The Personal Status Law was amended in 1981 to allow a wife to divorce her husband where the husband is guilty of a homosexual relationship, treated as infidelity. On the organizational side, Rasan implemented larger projects from 2016 as partners of COC Nederland in a project called "Pride Program" (locally "Crossing Iraqi Rainbow"). Wikipedia country coverage: In early 2012, a large wave of killings targeted "emo" teenagers accused of homosexuality on the basis of their clothing — the "Emo Killings" — carried out by Shi'a death squads of the Mahdi Army and condemned by human rights groups outside Iraq. Media reported harassment at school for not adopting conventional clothing or hairstyles, and flyers appeared in Baghdad naming people and threatening them unless they cut their hair, stopped wearing nonconformist clothing, and gave up their "alternative" lifestyles. Compulsory religious education was introduced into Iraqi schools in summer 1993, and Iraqueer (formed March 2015) runs education work including published guides on security and health safety, YouTube videos, and workshops teaching about gender and sexuality, advocacy, and safety in crisis.

IRQ.tangentialFactors:
The 2024 amendment sits within a longer documented pattern rather than standing alone: the US State Department was recording anti-LGBT violence and official impunity in Iraq as early as its 2012 report, and the BBC's later investigation describes the same impunity continuing across the intervening decade.

Official framing matters for how a visitor is likely to be treated on the street and at checkpoints. Supporters of the law presented it as a defence of religious values, which gives hostile actors a public mandate that predates and outlasts any single incident.

The UK Home Office's decision to publish a dedicated Iraq note on sexual orientation, gender identity and expression in July 2025 indicates that foreign governments treat the risk as ongoing and country-wide, and that the assessment covers both official and non-official perpetrators.
IRQ.comparisons: Pairwise: below Oman (0.09 — similar explicit statute but no militia murder campaigns) and Iran (0.09), above Brunei (0.07) and Saudi Arabia (0.05).

VEN.name: Venezuela
VEN.summary:
Venezuela presents a mixed and unstable picture for trans visitors. Gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised, and the country has produced visible trans political figures, but there is no legal gender recognition procedure, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute. Trans people therefore have no route to amend identity documents, and conduct targeting them carries no dedicated legal penalty.

The European Union Asylum Agency maintains a dedicated LGBTIQ+ country profile for Venezuela as part of its reference material for international protection decisions, and the AFS Vance Center published an LGBTQ guide covering Venezuela in October 2024. The existence of these dedicated reference documents reflects a shared assessment among international bodies that LGBTIQ+ people in the country face conditions serious enough to underpin protection claims, even though the underlying conduct is not formally criminalised.

Since the disputed presidential election of July 2024, LGBTQ Venezuelans have faced persecution documented by rights observers as unprecedented, tied directly to the political crisis; the opposition presidential candidate left the country on 7 September 2024. The persecution is not framed as gender-based in isolation, but the broader repression wave has swept in LGBTQ people, and arbitrary detention powers are applied broadly against perceived dissidents.

State targeting of LGBT politicians is documented. In December 2015, Amnesty International declared Rosmit Mantilla, a Voluntad Popular deputy and the country's first openly gay parliamentarian, a prisoner of conscience held in the custody of the national intelligence service, SEBIN. He marked his 33rd birthday in his cell. That case establishes that openly LGBT political participation can attract direct state retaliation rather than institutional protection.

Trans political participation has nonetheless had precedents. In August 2015, Tamara Adán became Venezuela's first transgender candidate for the National Assembly. Her candidacy was possible because candidacy rules did not require the document amendments that trans people cannot obtain in the absence of a legal gender recognition process; the visibility did not translate into a recognition framework.

On marriage and partnership, the record shows a legislative push without enactment. In January 2014 an equal-marriage bill was reported as set to be presented to the National Assembly within the week, and no later enactment of that measure is recorded in the sources.

Public opinion data points in a comparatively supportive direction. A poll conducted in early March 2023 found that a majority of Venezuelans agree the LGBTIQ+ population should hold the same rights as other citizens; 82% recognised the term LGBTIQ+, and 36% considered gay, lesbian and bisexual orientation to be innate. Societal tolerance, where documented, is not matched by any statutory protection.

For a trans visitor, the practical risk is less a matter of targeted gender-based enforcement than of a collapsed institutional environment: no anti-discrimination remedy, no hate-crime mechanism, degraded healthcare including access to hormone therapy, and predatory policing that applies to everyone regardless of identity. There is no institutional recourse when things go wrong.
VEN.outOfScopeNotes:
The contents of the AFS Vance Center guide and of the EUAA LGBTIQ+ country profile are cited here only as reference documents; their specific findings on risk factors, safe regions, or protective actors are not detailed in the available inventory and remain unresolved.

Whether any sub-national authority in Venezuela has adopted anti-discrimination or gender-recognition measures of its own is not addressed by the sources. The national absence of such laws is established; the local position is not.

The outcome of Tamara Adán's 2015 candidacy, and whether she or any later trans candidate subsequently won office, is not sourced here. Only the candidacy itself is documented.

The legal procedure, if any, by which a resident could obtain a foreign gender recognition or rely on consular action from another country is not addressed in the sources and is treated as unresolved.

The exact legal basis on which SEBIN held Rosmit Mantilla, and whether his case remained active after December 2015, are not covered by the inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: LGBTQ expression has both official recognition and documented suppression: the International Day Against Homophobia has been marked since 2000, the government has recently begun participating in Pride events, and in May 2016 the National Assembly unanimously passed a resolution establishing 17 May as the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia — but the Supreme Court suspended that resolution in August 2016. Openly gay and transgender activists Tamara Adrián and Rosmit Mantilla were elected as Alternate Deputies in the 2015 parliamentary election, the first LGBT members of Venezuela's legislature. Police harassment remains a serious problem: in May 2026, NGOs including the Observatorio Venezolano de Violencias LGBTIQ+, Caleidoscopio Humano and Movimiento SOMOS denounced the detention of around 30 people in a police raid on an LGBTQ+ venue in Barquisimeto, Lara state, where officers allegedly entered without proper warrants, extorted detainees and accused them of 'committing the crime of homosexuality' despite homosexuality being legal. Wikipedia country coverage: The source text contains no general healthcare or transition-care provisions, but it does note that lesbian couples are allowed to access IVF, while same-sex couples cannot legally adopt children. For legal gender recognition, a 2017 constitutional action before the Supreme Justice Tribunal requires each case to be individually assessed with certified birth certificates and a psychiatric and psychological report from a specialist demonstrating the veracity of the intended sexual identity — and the Tribunal still has not granted the requested name and gender changes. Trans people also remain unable to actually change identity-card information: although SAIME announced in September 2016 that transgender people may request a new identity card matching their gender identity, there is currently no administrative procedure or mechanism to enact the relevant article. Wikipedia country coverage: The universal age of consent is 16, with no differential age for same-sex conduct. Children of same-sex parents gain specific legal standing: on 15 December 2016 the Supreme Tribunal of Justice ruled that a baby may be registered in the Civil Registry with both mothers' surnames, basing the decision on Article 75 of the Constitution, and declared that the state must protect all families without distinction, so that children and teenagers born into same-sex families enjoy all the rights and guarantees of children born into opposite-sex families. Same-sex couples are still unable to legally adopt, though a 2023 Equilibrium CenDE poll found 48% of Venezuelans supported adoption by same-sex couples (34% totally, 14% somewhat) versus 39% opposed. On acceptance generally, a 2013 Pew survey found 57% of 18–29-year-olds believed homosexuality should be accepted by society, compared with 51% of 30–49-year-olds and 45% of those over 50; no education-specific findings appear in the text.

VEN.localsOnly:
Resident trans people have no legal route to obtain gender recognition, which means identity documents remain mismatched for the duration of a person's life unless they leave the country or find a foreign procedure that applies. The same absence affects marriage, employment formalities, and any interaction requiring a consistent legal identity.

No anti-discrimination statute protects gender identity in employment, housing, healthcare or public services, and there is no hate-crime legislation against which targeted violence could be prosecuted as a distinct offence. Recourse, where it exists at all, runs through general criminal law with all of its evidentiary and institutional weaknesses.

Openly LGBT political activity has produced documented state retaliation. The case of Rosmit Mantilla, imprisoned under SEBIN custody after being declared a prisoner of conscience by Amnesty International, shows that visibility in public life can lead to detention rather than to any form of official protection.

Healthcare access has deteriorated to the point where hormone therapy and other trans-specific care are unreliable, and the collapse of public services removes the possibility of complaining about denial of care through any functioning channel. Trans women have historically been visible in urban life, but that visibility coexists with policing that is predatory toward the population at large and with no institutional mechanism for redress.
VEN.comparisons: Pairwise: above Trinidad & Tobago (0.42 — court-decriminalised with dating-app ambush pattern) and below Peru (0.48 — LGR exists). Venezuela's distinguishing factor is the absence of any legal floor whatsoever plus active regime persecution.

Trans women have historically been visible in urban life, but that visibility coexists with policing that is predatory toward the population at large and with no institutional mechanism for redress.
VEN.tangentialFactors:
The legal environment must be read against the political crisis rather than against a trans-specific statute, since the persecution documented after July 2024 operates through general powers of detention and intimidation applied to perceived dissidents. LGBTQ people are affected as part of that wave rather than through a named LGBTIQ+ offence.

The 2023 polling data shows that documented public attitudes are more supportive than the legal framework would suggest. A majority backed equal rights for the LGBTIQ+ population, and familiarity with the term was high at 82%. The gap between that recorded opinion and the absence of any anti-discrimination or gender-recognition law is a point of contrast for anyone comparing Venezuela with neighbouring jurisdictions.

The record contains no evidence that Venezuela follows the regional trend toward same-sex marriage legislation. The 2014 equal-marriage bill is the only legislative milestone noted, and no enactment follows it in the sources, which is consistent with the country's broader pattern of stalled rights legislation during the period of economic and political crisis.

The AFS Vance Center LGBTQ guide of October 2024 and the EUAA country profile are comparative reference points rather than evidence of conditions in their own right. They indicate how international practitioners assess the country, and they are the kind of documentation a visitor could consult alongside their own planning.

BOL.name: Bolivia
BOL.summary:
Bolivia's 2016 Gender Identity Law grants legal recognition on the basis of self-declared identity through an administrative procedure, permitting a change of name and gender marker without surgery or a medical diagnosis. Gender identity is a protected ground in the country's anti-discrimination legislation.

The 2009 Constitution prohibits discrimination, and the US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report on Bolivia documented that constitutional guarantee alongside persistent societal discrimination against LGBT people.

The 2016 statute was enacted despite low public support for trans rights. Trans activists secured access to legislators of the ruling party, and heteronormative provisions were adopted in the same period because organised religion and LGBT organisations were both constituencies of the party in government. Contradictory laws therefore stand side by side, so a visitor who relies on the gender-identity statute may still encounter provisions built on a heterosexual, cisgender presumption.

Partner recognition followed later: the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an opinion in January 2018, and in December 2020 Bolivia's civil registry recognised free unions between same-sex couples.

Formal protection has not produced equal treatment in practice. Agencia Presentes reported in December 2024 that Bolivia's first virtual survey of LGBTI people documented what it called the great exclusion of LGBTI people in the country.

Official institutions show the same gap. Reporting from August 2014 described homosexuality as taboo in Bolivia's armed forces, with gay soldiers testifying anonymously to discrimination and sanctions.
BOL.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no sourced material on entry or visa rules for trans travellers, on airport or border screening that could disclose gender history, on which gender markers Bolivian authorities accept in foreign passports, on bathroom or facility access rules, on hate-crime sentencing, or on access to legal and medical care while visiting. Those questions remain unresolved on this record.

Whether the administrative recognition process under the 2016 law is available to non-residents or holders of foreign documents is not stated in any source here.

Whether the discrimination documented in Bolivia's armed forces in 2014 persists in its 2014 form is not sourced by the inventory; the reporting is dated and its current status unresolved.

The December 2024 survey source does not give its sample size, method, or whether trans respondents were identified separately from LGBTI respondents as a whole, so the strength of that finding cannot be assessed from this inventory.

A Newsweek article of July 2017 counting 18 countries believed to fully legalise LGBT military service after the US trans military ban does not single out Bolivia and cannot be used to characterise Bolivian policy.

The US State Department's 2011 report also covers arbitrary deprivation of life, prison conditions and corruption; that material is outside the scope of trans visitor risk and has not been carried into the record.

Unsourced dimensions after this research pass: D1, D2, D4, D5, D6, D8, D13.

PRY.name: Paraguay
PRY.summary:
Paraguay demands real caution from trans visitors and remains the most conservative country in its region. There is no legal gender recognition procedure in force: the judiciary has yet to issue final rulings on ten lawsuits filed by trans people seeking recognition of their legal names, among them cases brought by Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepúlveda that have been pending since 2016. Both plaintiffs have taken communications to the UN Human Rights Committee under the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and are awaiting a decision. Amnesty International's 2025-26 reporting records two trans migrants who were denied identity documents.

The protection framework is empty. No anti-discrimination law covers gender identity and there is no hate-crime statute. Amnesty documents persistent structural discrimination, and AP reported in September 2025 that discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of their hometowns and into migration and sex work. The same reporting period records 37 registered feminicides in 2025.

Hostility reaches official institutions. Asunción's city council banned an event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March, and an April bill would merge the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family. Elite-level rhetoric is on record: ruling-party figure Horacio Cartes made a violent remark in 2017 about his son marrying a man, later apologising to those offended, within a political climate that included calls to burn books not promoting 'traditional gender ideology'.

Nothing criminalises being trans, and there is no documented pattern of police targeting trans people. Asunción has a small organised community. Tourist traffic is low and the inventory contains no documented incidents involving trans visitors, so the operative risk is social hostility and the absence of any protection machinery rather than state persecution.

Partner recognition is also absent. Paraguay recognises neither same-sex marriage nor civil unions. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights' advisory opinion that OAS signatories must permit same-sex marriage binds Paraguay as a party, but domestic law has not been adapted, and commentators inside the country describe the legislative work still required to extend marriage to everyone.
PRY.outOfScopeNotes:
The outcomes of the ten name-recognition lawsuits and of the UN Human Rights Committee communications are unresolved in the inventory; no source records a final ruling or Committee decision, so the current status of those cases is not sourced.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa screening, passport or ID gender-marker rules for foreign travellers, or access to healthcare for visitors. Whether a trans visitor's documents are examined at the border, and on what basis, is not sourced here.

The claim that there is no documented pattern of police targeting rests on the absence of such reports in the available sources rather than on an affirmative official finding; the inventory contains no dedicated study of police conduct toward trans people.

Whether the April bill merging the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family has been enacted is unresolved in the inventory, which records the bill but not its passage.

Adoption practice is described from a 2017 legal analysis; whether courts or child-welfare agencies apply the statutory gap in current cases is not sourced.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: During the Stroessner dictatorship (1954–1989), LGBT people faced heavy persecution; in the 1959 'Case 108' (Caso 108), police arrested and tortured 108 gay men in Asunción and made their names public, with the government publicly encouraging hatred and violence against LGBT people. Reports of violence and discrimination against LGBT community members are frequent in Paraguay today and are often ignored by the police. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Paraguay since 1990, though the age of consent is 16 for homosexuals and 14 for heterosexuals. There is no broad anti-discrimination law, and a November 2015 bill to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has not advanced since introduction. Wikipedia country coverage: In October 2017, the Government of Paraguay implemented a ban on discussion of LGBT issues within public schools, and the Minister of Education said it might consider burning books that raise awareness about transgender people. Transgender people are not allowed to legally change their name and gender on official documents, though in December 2016 two transgender women filed a lawsuit to change their names citing constitutional free expression and identity provisions. Wikipedia country coverage: In October 2016, the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare approved Resolution 695 requiring that all transgender people may use their social name on medical records, medical history and forms, and that health service officials must treat transgender patients using their identified social name. Law 7018 on Mental Health (enacted 15 November 2022) states that a mental health diagnosis cannot be made on the exclusive basis of sexual choice or identity. Wikipedia country coverage: There is no broad legal protection against LGBTI discrimination through an anti-discrimination law in Paraguay, though specific laws and decrees prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in limited contexts: Law 5162/2014 (adolescent dormitory placement must consider sexual orientation), Decree 6973 under Law 577/2016 (protection of women from violence without discrimination based on sexual orientation), Law 6149/2018 (non-discrimination for stateless persons based on sexual orientation and gender identity), Law 6534/2020 (sexual orientation data as sensitive personal data), and Article 28 of the Ministry of Public Defense internal rules (prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation against employees). A bill to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity introduced in November 2015 has not advanced. Wikipedia country coverage: In October 2017, the Government of Paraguay implemented a ban on discussion of LGBT issues within public schools, and the Minister of Education added that it might consider burning books that raise awareness about transgender people. Law 5162/2014's Criminal Enforcement Code requires that collective dormitory placement for adolescents take into account age, sexual orientation, and degree of psychic development.

Adoption law does not explicitly bar same-sex couples or single men and women: Law 1136/97 restricts adopters only on grounds of infectious disease, mental disorders or child-abuse records, a statutory gap that permits same-sex adoption in practice while social barriers remain.

Trans Paraguayans who leave their hometowns commonly relocate to the capital or abroad, and AP reporting links that internal displacement directly to discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence, with sex work a frequent survival strategy after migration.
