GTM.name: Guatemala
GTM.summary:
Guatemala demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: Asociación Lambda's observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022, with 35 victims saying they intended to flee the country. Guatemalan officials have explicitly excluded trans women from femicide-law protection on the grounds that they are not "biological women," an exclusion that Central American governments have long maintained and that underpins the documented violence context.

There is no legal gender recognition in Guatemalan law. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights' 2017 Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 urged Guatemala and neighbouring states to deliver gender recognition and marriage equality, but compliance remains uncertain; reporting in January 2018 recorded the region's states as urged rather than bound. The Arcus Foundation reported in May 2024 that an organised opposition defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash against recognition in Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras and Mexico.

No SOGI hate-crime statute protects trans people. A 2022 law instead increased penalties for "aggravated" LGBT visibility before being struck down, and Human Rights Watch warned in January 2022 that a bill before Congress threatened to erase gender-identity protections and restrict legal recognition of trans people. Congress has repeatedly advanced anti-LGBT initiatives, including Law 5276 and the 2022 "Life and Family Protection" bill, shelved after protests.

Detention carries documented physical danger. Human Rights Watch reported in October 2020 that trans women held in Guatemala's men's prisons on the basis of birth sex are exposed to sexual assault; Bárbara Herrarte of Redmmutrans described being raped by cellmates at night. The report found no gender-identity-based placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice, and no court ruling on the custody of trans detainees.

The community is organised, with groups such as Asociación Lambda and Redmmutrans documenting violence and advocating for recognition.
GTM.outOfScopeNotes:
Compliance with Inter-American Court Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 in Guatemala is unresolved in the source material: the inventory records the 2018 urging of states to abide by it and a 2024 assessment that backlash persists, but does not establish whether Guatemala enacted a gender-recognition statute afterwards.

Whether Guatemala's prison authorities adopted a gender-identity placement policy, a trans unit or a segregation practice after the October 2020 Human Rights Watch report is not sourced here and should be treated as unresolved.

The fate of the January 2022 anti-trans bill documented by Human Rights Watch (whether enacted, amended or stalled) is not stated in the inventory; only that it was introduced and threatened gender-identity protections.

sources.summary: Wikipedia article on transfemicide: documents killings of trans women; for Guatemala it records that Central American governments have long excluded trans women from femicide protections, and that Guatemalan officials justified this exclusion by stating that transgender women are not 'biological women'. The exclusion is official and underpins the documented violence context for Guatemala.

Arcus Foundation report (May 2024): the Inter-American Court's 2017 gender-identity opinion (Advisory Opinion OC-24/17) advanced legal gender recognition in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, but a vociferous opposition movement defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash in all four countries.

HRW (Jan 2022): 'Guatemala: Anti-Trans Bill Threatens Rights' — documents legislative attacks on trans people, including bills that would erase gender identity protections and restrict legal recognition.

GTM.localsOnly:
Trans Guatemalans convicted or detained are assigned to prisons on the basis of birth sex, with no policy providing gender-identity-based placement, no trans-specific unit and no segregation practice on record as of the October 2020 Human Rights Watch reporting, and no court ruling has ordered alternative custody arrangements. Bárbara Herrarte of the Red Multicultural de Mujeres Trans (Redmmutrans) described forced sex at night from cellmates during her time in a men's prison.

Asociación Lambda's observatory flags forced internal displacement among LGBT Guatemalans driven by violence, meaning residents rather than visitors are the population that relocates within or out of the country under threat.

Residents seeking legal recognition of gender have no statutory route in Guatemalan law, and the 2022 legislative package that would have tightened restrictions on gender identity and family recognition was withdrawn after public protest.
GTM.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Honduras (0.39) and below Trinidad & Tobago (0.42). Guatemala's distinguishing factor is the documented murder count plus explicit official exclusion of trans women from protective law.
GTM.blindSummary:
The jurisdiction demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: a local observatory run by Asociación Lambda recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022, with 35 victims saying they intended to leave the country. National officials have explicitly excluded trans women from femicide-law protection on the grounds that they are not "biological women," an exclusion that neighbouring states have long maintained and that underpins the documented violence context.

There is no legal gender recognition in national law. The supranational human rights court's 2017 advisory opinion OC-24/17 urged the jurisdiction and neighbouring states to deliver gender recognition and marriage equality, but compliance remains uncertain; reporting in January 2018 recorded states as urged rather than bound. The Arcus Foundation reported in May 2024 that an organised opposition defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash against recognition in four neighbouring jurisdictions.

No SOGI hate-crime statute protects trans people. A 2022 law instead increased penalties for "aggravated" LGBT visibility before being struck down, and Human Rights Watch warned in January 2022 that a bill before the national legislature threatened to erase gender-identity protections and restrict legal recognition of trans people. The legislature has repeatedly advanced anti-LGBT initiatives, including Law 5276 and the 2022 "Life and Family Protection" bill, shelved after protests.

Detention carries documented physical danger. Human Rights Watch reported in October 2020 that trans women held in the national prison system on the basis of birth sex are exposed to sexual assault; Bárbara Herrarte of Redmmutrans described being raped by cellmates at night. The report found no gender-identity-based placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice, and no court ruling on the custody of trans detainees.

The community is organised, with groups such as Asociación Lambda and Redmmutrans documenting violence and advocating for recognition.
GTM.blindOutOfScope:
Compliance with advisory opinion OC-24/17 is unresolved in the source material: the inventory records the 2018 urging of states to abide by it and a 2024 assessment that backlash persists, but does not establish whether a gender-recognition statute was enacted afterwards.

Whether prison authorities adopted a gender-identity placement policy, a trans unit or a segregation practice after the October 2020 Human Rights Watch report is not sourced here and should be treated as unresolved.

The fate of the January 2022 anti-trans bill documented by Human Rights Watch (whether enacted, amended or stalled) is not stated in the inventory; only that it was introduced and threatened gender-identity protections.

HND.name: Honduras
HND.summary:
Honduras is among the most dangerous countries in the Americas for trans women. Human Rights Watch finds that states in the region exclude transgender women from their femicide legal frameworks, and Vicky Hernández v. Honduras, heard by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, is the leading transfemicide case worldwide. The Court's 2021 judgment held the Honduran state responsible for the 2009 killing of trans activist Vicky Hernández and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime, and ordered reforms including legal gender recognition; Honduras has partially implemented them.

Nothing in Honduran law criminalises being trans, and a legal name-change process exists. Against that, Human Rights Watch's 2009 report "Not Worth a Penny" documents police rape, assault and extortion of trans people, and the US State Department's 2021 Human Rights Report lists violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture and lack of accountability for gender-based violence among the country's significant human-rights problems.

The Lawg Education Fund places Honduras among the world's highest rates of violence against women and LGBTI persons, with trans women facing the sharpest obstacles to justice. Its conclusion is that institutions "fail to effectively investigate and prosecute" these crimes; it attributes the resulting impunity to under-reporting, lack of police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources and intentional mishandling of cases.

Detention is a specific and acute hazard. Human Rights Watch reports that Honduras places transgender women in men's prisons, which exposes them to physical and sexual abuse. A Honduran judge told the organisation of a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards, and said she had informed prosecutors, who did not investigate: "There's no way to protect trans women in men's prisons."

For a visitor, the practical position is that formal legality and formal protection coexist with near-total impunity and with documented abuse by security forces. Arrest, detention or police contact carries the risk of placement in the men's system and of extortion or violence by officers. Coverage of the country's legal framework records bans on same-sex marriage and adoption, so a partner carries no recognition in law.

The prison evidence is dated 2017 and 2020, so current conditions in the penitentiaries are not confirmed by these sources. sources.summary: Corresponsales Clave (trans activist Kendra Jordany, 6 Sep 2017), drawing on the torture-prevention centre CPTRT: trans women in Honduras' national penitentiaries are held in the MEN'S system. At Penitenciaria de Marcala authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after CPTRT intervention was she isolated from the men and her feminine belongings returned. sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The Constitution grants citizens the right to establish and associate with political parties and interest groups, but initial efforts to register an LGBTQ rights group in the 1980s met with government opposition or extended delays; the first organizations arose anyway, often in response to the HIV/AIDS pandemic, had no legal standing, and were essentially ignored by the Government except for police harassment. In 2004 the Government extended formal recognition to three LGBTQ rights interest groups despite organized protests from the Catholic Church, Pentecostals and conservative legislators. Public expression continued despite risk: about 400 people marched in a pride parade in July 2017 in San Pedro Sula, considered one of the world's most dangerous cities. Penal Code Article 321-A (Decree No. 23-2013) punishes public or media incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence against a person or group on listed grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity with three to five years' imprisonment and fines of L.50,000 to L.300,000. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex unions are not legally recognized in Honduras; the 2005 constitutional amendment expressly bans same-sex marriage and de facto unions, refuses to recognize same-sex marriages or unions performed legally in other countries (Article 112), and prohibits same-sex couples from adopting (Article 116). Same-sex couples and same-sex-headed households are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. The source also references an approved 'name change to LGBTI' — described by the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association as an 'aberration in God's eyes' — indicating a legal name-change mechanism for LGBTI persons exists, though the text gives no procedure details. Wikipedia country coverage: The Government offers medical care to all citizens and has been increasingly working with non-governmental organizations to raise awareness on HIV/AIDS, but the socially conservative influence of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestants has made it difficult for any comprehensive public program to be implemented. Female prostitutes and men who have sex with men are identified as the highest-risk groups. Separately, the 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs gives police permission to raid city streets, entrap sex workers under 'sanitation control' and arrest anyone who 'goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals' — a provision LGBTQ organizations say police use to harass and detain transgender women, restricting their access to public space. No youth-specific care or medication findings appear in the source text. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2013 the National Congress adopted amendments to the Penal Code via Decree No. 23-2013. Article 27 makes hatred or contempt based on sexual orientation or gender identity an aggravating circumstance in criminal responsibility. Article 321 punishes with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages anyone who arbitrarily blocks, restricts or denies the exercise of individual and collective rights or refuses a professional service on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity. In March 2017 the newly enacted Penal Code took effect; LGBTQ rights groups met with Congress to dispel doubts about wording and ensure Articles 321 and 321-A remained, and the anti-discrimination articles were ultimately kept. Wikipedia country coverage: The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs lets police raid streets and arrest anyone who 'goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals'; LGBTQ rights organizations have documented numerous instances of police using it as a pretext to harass and detain transgender women. International human rights organizations state the military Government has targeted LGBTQ people for harassment, abuse and murder, and early LGBTQ organizations faced police harassment. Political hostility is also visible: the two major parties have mostly ignored LGBTQ rights, only a handful of dissident members of the Democratic Unification Party expressed interest in working with the LGBT community, and three candidates who backed same-sex marriage before the November 2017 elections all failed to win National Congress seats. President Juan Orlando Hernández said on 12 October 2018 that personally as a Christian he is against same-sex marriage, and the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association urged President Xiomara Castro to stop 'immoral laws'.

SLV.name: El Salvador
SLV.summary:
El Salvador presents a specific and documented risk profile for trans visitors. The country has no Gender Identity Law and no legal recognition of gender identity, so trans visitors have no domestic mechanism to correct or align documents with their gender. The penal code does contain an enhanced penalty for bias-motivated killing: in September 2015 the National Assembly approved reforms under which homicides motivated by sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, political affiliation or gender carry 30 to 60 years under Article 129.

The limits of that framework are illustrated by the killing of Camila Díaz Córdova, a trans Salvadoran woman who had been deported from the United States and was killed in January 2019. In July 2020 a San Salvador judge found three police officers guilty of her murder and sentenced each to 20 years. The judgment was the first homicide conviction in El Salvador for killing a transgender person, and Human Rights Watch treated it as significant for transgender Salvadorans' rights while documenting that violence and discrimination against LGBT people continued.

Human Rights Watch reports of October 2020 and January 2021 record that El Salvador, with Guatemala and Honduras, fails to effectively address violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people, and that the resulting insecurity drives asylum claims to the United States. The reports document concrete obstacles victims encounter when attempting to obtain police and judicial protection.

The peer-reviewed record on the lethal violence is longitudinal: a 2024 study in the journal Dilemas, produced at Fundação Oswaldo Cruz, profiles the crimes, victims and perpetrators of homicides against LGBTI+ people in El Salvador across 2000 to 2020, giving the documented baseline for anti-LGBTI+ killings in the country over two decades.

Since the state of exception began in March 2022, trans women have been among those swept up in mass raids and held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. A February 2024 investigation by GatoEncerrado records the case of Jennifer, arrested in San Salvador on 14 April 2022 and held first at the El Penalito police lockups and then in prison. Custodians forcibly shaved her hair, singled her out along with another trans woman named Rosa for outdoor punishment drills while handcuffed and forced to squat in the sun, and denied her access to the HIV clinic. A judge freed her after roughly four months, finding that her arrest had no basis; Rosa remained imprisoned at the time of reporting.

Socorro Jurídico Humanista and Cristosal link this treatment to the absence of a Gender Identity Law. The prison system assigns placement by birth sex, contains no special custody provision for trans detainees, and trans detainees are exposed to targeted abuse inside it, with no effective recourse while the state of exception runs.
SLV.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in this inventory: whether Article 129's enhanced penalties have been applied to any trans victim other than Camila Díaz Córdova, and how often the provision is charged in practice.

Unresolved: the status of Rosa after February 2024, when the GatoEncerrado report recorded her still imprisoned; no later reporting is provided.

Not sourced here: entry and visa rules for El Salvador, border or airport screening practices, any document gender-marker requirement applied at entry, or the treatment of foreign gender markers by Salvadoran authorities. The dossier carries no finding on these points from the present inventory.

Not sourced here: whether the state of exception remains in force beyond early 2024, the current national homicide rate, and any provision on marriage or partner recognition for transgender visitors or residents.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: A 2022 ruling by the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court ordered El Salvador's Name Law to be reformed so that individuals can change their names to match their gender identity, holding the existing laws unconstitutional because they discriminated on the basis of gender; the case originated in a 2016 lawsuit by a transgender activist. Despite this order, the Legislative Assembly had taken no action to guarantee changes of name and gender in legal documents as of 2023, so transgender Salvadorans still cannot update official papers. Same-sex marriage is not recognized: the Family Code's Article 11 defines marriage as a heterosexual union, individuals may adopt but same-sex couples cannot adopt as a couple, and the Law on Family Violence does not apply to same-sex couples. Wikipedia country coverage: Prison conditions are explicitly hostile: homosexual inmates are strictly forbidden from dressing or behaving in an effeminate manner, and men are targeted by police officers, soldiers, and prison guards for effeminate behavior or dress through unwarranted searches, theft of property, sexual assault, and other physical violence. The justice system itself fails to recognize trans people: in the 1999 investigation of Doris and Maricela, the two transvestites were forced to wear men's clothing for their hearing. Health facilities also fail trans patients — hospital specialists frequently dismiss their problems as a side effect of being transgender, and patients are sometimes made to wait longer or denied care, though this can be done discreetly. Wikipedia country coverage: Transgender health care access is severely restricted: there is a lack of protocols and programs for hormone therapy and sex reassignment surgery, and one study found that many trans women did not seek medical help after suffering side effects from surgeries, having learned not to trust the system. For LGBT people in general, even when individuals reach out for psychological care they feel insecure and report prejudice, and such care often arrives in the form of conversion therapies — frequently deployed by parents attempting to change a child's sexual orientation; LGBT community members experience suicide ideation and attempts at higher rates than the general population. Policy has partly addressed this: in April 2009 the Ministry of Public Health and Social Assistance published guidelines banning discrimination against LGBT and HIV-positive people in health services, a 2009 national HIV/AIDS health plan included a prohibition on sexual orientation-based discrimination in health care, and since 2005 a national HIV/AIDS policy has developed with the first National HIV testing day established in 2007. Gay and bisexual men are allowed to donate blood, though policy prohibits those who 'engage in risky behaviours' from donating. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex relationships are not recognized: same-sex marriage is not legal, and since 2006 there have been proposals to amend the Constitution to restrict recognition even of same-sex couples married legally abroad. Two legal challenges to the ban were dismissed by the courts on technical and procedural grounds (20 December 2016 and 17 January 2019), although the Constitutional Court declared a proposed marriage ban unlawful in January 2018 and admitted a lawsuit for recognition of same-sex marriage for a hearing in August 2019, following a January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion holding same-sex marriage to be a human right. Beyond marriage, same-sex couples cannot adopt as a couple, and the Law on Family Violence (Ley contra la Violencia Intrafamiliar) does not extend to same-sex couples, leaving same-sex households without the legal benefits available to heterosexual married couples. Public backing is low: a 2010 poll showed only 10% support for legalizing same-sex marriage, and the 2017 AmericasBarometer recorded 19% support. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth-specific education findings: sexuality is absent from school curriculum, in line with societal expectations, which leads many LGBT students to remain invisible in school to avoid discrimination; LGBT students, particularly those whose gender expression does not match that assigned at birth, drop out of school at high rates, and some LGBT students have been expelled outright for their sexuality and identity. The gap continues in higher education, where no known universities or graduate programs offer Sexuality Studies programs; academic publications exist — most from the University of El Salvador, often from psychological or legal science perspectives — but with varying levels of support within them. Family-level harms hit minors directly: where LGBT children do come out, families may subject them to conversion therapy or family prayers to convert them to heterosexuality, and when these methods fail, families sometimes expel the child from the home and sever all connections. A broader community-level finding is that young Salvadoran homosexuals now encourage older homosexuals to come out, and globalization is slowly changing the young LGBT community, though it still faces heavy unacceptance. Wikipedia country coverage: Public opinion is deeply hostile: a 2013 study showed that 62% of Salvadorans do not accept homosexuality and 85% believe it acceptable to attack a transgender individual on the basis of their identity, and El Salvador is described as one of the most socially-homophobic countries in Latin America. The climate is shaped by religious teaching (over 50% identify as actively practicing Catholics, many of the rest attend evangelical churches, and church leaders have organized opposition to LGBT rights legislation) and by an embedded machismo culture in which being Salvadoran means being virile; heterosexuals are described as afraid of defending or befriending gay people for fear of stigma and of being accused of being gay themselves, and being 'gay friendly' is seen as against nature, anti-religious, and anti-masculine. Violence is pervasive: about 500 hate crimes against LGBTQ people were reported between 1998 and 2015 (with many unreported), police have shown blatant refusal to cooperate in LGBT death investigations, and gang violence includes targeting of LGBT people through physical and sexual assault, forced recruitment, and 'taxing' for safety; on 28 July 2020 a San Salvador judge convicted three police officers of killing transgender woman Camila Díaz Córdova, sentencing them to 20 years each. Visibility is nonetheless growing: Entre Amigos organized El Salvador's first Gay Pride Parade in June 1997 to commemorate the massacre of trans women in the 1980s and it continues today, San Salvador authorized permanent rainbow paintings at several crossroads in July 2017, a 2015 hate crime law added sexual orientation and gender identity provisions to the Criminal Code (three to six years imprisonment), and a 2018 Institutional Policy for the Care of the LGBT Population allows LGBT people to file legal complaints against discrimination.

SLV.localsOnly:
Residents live without any form of legal gender recognition. No Gender Identity Law exists, so Salvadorans cannot obtain documents matching their gender, and the prison system continues to place people by birth sex.

The absence of a Gender Identity Law is treated by Socorro Jurídico Humanista, Cristosal and other organisations as the structural cause of the abuse documented inside the prison system, and trans Salvadorans detained under the state of exception remain exposed to forced shaving, punitive drill, isolation and denial of medical care, including HIV treatment.

Discrimination and violence have been persistent enough over the 2000 to 2020 period to sustain regular outward migration and asylum claims, and Salvadoran LGBT people continue to cite obstacles to obtaining police and judicial protection as a reason for leaving.
SLV.comparisons: Pairwise: above Guatemala (0.40 — the homicide collapse is real and large) and Honduras (0.39), below Trinidad & Tobago (0.42). El Salvador's profile is unique: street-violence probability way down, arbitrary-state-power probability way up.
SLV.blindSummary:
The state presents a specific and documented risk profile for trans visitors. It has no Gender Identity Law and no legal recognition of gender identity, so visitors have no domestic mechanism to align documents with their gender. The penal code does contain an enhanced penalty for bias-motivated killing: in September 2015 the national legislature approved reforms under which homicides motivated by sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, political affiliation or gender carry 30 to 60 years under Article 129.

The limits of that framework are illustrated by the killing of a trans woman who had been deported to the destination country where asylum claims are lodged and was killed in January 2019. In July 2020 a judge in the national capital found three police officers guilty of her murder and sentenced each to 20 years. The judgment was the first homicide conviction in the state for killing a transgender person, and an international human rights organisation treated it as significant for transgender residents' rights while documenting that violence and discrimination against LGBT people continued.

Two reports by that international human rights organisation, published in October 2020 and January 2021, record that the state and two neighbouring jurisdictions fail to effectively address violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people, and that the resulting insecurity drives asylum claims to the destination country. The reports document concrete obstacles victims encounter when attempting to obtain police and judicial protection.

The peer-reviewed record on the lethal violence is longitudinal: a 2024 study in a journal published at a Brazilian public health foundation profiles the crimes, victims and perpetrators of homicides against LGBTI+ people in the state across 2000 to 2020, giving the documented baseline for anti-LGBTI+ killings over two decades.

Since the state of exception began in March 2022, trans women have been among those swept up in mass raids and held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. a February 2024 investigation by a domestic news outlet records the case of a trans woman arrested in the national capital on 14 April 2022 and held first at police lockups and then in prison. Custodians forcibly shaved her hair, singled her out along with another trans woman for outdoor punishment drills while handcuffed and forced to squat in the sun, and denied her access to the HIV clinic. a judge freed her after roughly four months, finding that her arrest had no basis; the second trans woman remained imprisoned at the time of reporting.

Two domestic human rights organisations link this treatment to the absence of a Gender Identity Law. The prison system assigns placement by birth sex, contains no special custody provision for trans detainees, and trans detainees are exposed to targeted abuse inside it, with no effective recourse while the state of exception runs.
SLV.blindOutOfScope:
Unresolved in this inventory: whether Article 129's enhanced penalties have been applied to any trans victim other than the January 2019 case, and how often the provision is charged in practice.

Unresolved: the status of the second trans woman after February 2024, when a domestic news report recorded her still imprisoned; no later reporting is provided.

Not sourced here: entry and visa rules for the state, border or airport screening practices, any document gender-marker requirement applied at entry, or the treatment of foreign gender markers by national authorities. No finding on these points is carried from the present inventory.

Not sourced here: whether the state of exception remains in force beyond early 2024, the current national homicide rate, and any provision on marriage or partner recognition for transgender visitors or residents.

The regional picture matters for expectation-setting. Human Rights Watch groups El Salvador with Guatemala and Honduras as three neighbouring countries where violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people go inadequately addressed, and where the failures of police and judicial protection push LGBT Salvadorans, Guatemalans and Hondurans into asylum claims in the United States.

A tension runs through the evidence base. CRI.name: Costa Rica
CRI.summary:
Costa Rica decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1971 and, in 2020, became the first Central American country to adopt marriage equality. For a trans visitor this is the region's most permissive legal setting, backed by institutions that operate rather than merely exist.

Legal gender recognition is administrative. Executive Decree 41173-MP, in force since 2018, allows a change of gender marker on identity documents without surgery and without a court order. The state health system funds gender-affirming care.

The UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, reporting on her July 2023 visit (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024), praised near-universal health coverage and specific protective legislation while recording her concern about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups. She recommended intersectional data collection as a basis for addressing it.

Policy headwinds are real. A conversion-therapy prohibition bill has been stalled in committee since its 2019 report. In 2025 authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education programme and the 2022 anti-LGBT bullying protocol, withdrawing two of the main preventive frameworks in schools.

Detention is the clearest gap between policy and practice. In June 2017 the Justice Ministry, then under Vice-Minister Marco Feoli, announced that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual could choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility, with relocation decided case-by-case alongside prison social workers and psychologists; a circular ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners and an exclusive module was under consideration, with Spain's model cited. Reporting in June 2019 found a trans woman, Stephanie, held at CAI Orosi de Cartago, a men's facility where staff said only men are held, and she described identity-targeted abuse including a rape with a broomstick-handle at La Reforma in Alajuela witnessed by a custodian. The Justice Ministry told the outlet there were 23 transgender people in the national prison system at the time.

Official posture has generally been supportive and has drawn organised opposition. The government officially recognised the International Day Against Homophobia in 2008, when President Óscar Arias and Health Minister María Luisa Avila directed public institutions to facilitate and support activities directed at the eradication of homophobia. In May 2014 President Luis Guillermo Solís flew the rainbow flag at the Casa Presidencial on equal mast with the national flag for 17 May, prompting lawmakers from PASE, National Restoration and other conservative parties to call it a provocation while a same-sex civil union bill was pending.

Partner protections extend into social security: survivor's pensions were extended to same-sex partners under all national-budget pension plans (Ministry of Labor announcement of 25 June 2016, first individual survivor benefit approved 29 June 2018), with the teachers' separate budget excluded.
CRI.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the post-2018 document process also alters the sex marker on all identity documents, or only the name and photograph, is not resolved by the sources held here; Outright International states only that gender change on documents is possible without surgery or court order.

The practical implementation of the 2017 prison placement policy after 2019 is not sourced beyond the CRHoy reporting of that year, which documented a trans woman held in a men's facility. The 23 transgender prisoners cited by the Justice Ministry is a June 2019 figure and has not been refreshed.

The ILGA World Database entry for Costa Rica is held as a reference link but its individual indicators are not itemised in the inventory, so no claim here rests on it.

Enforcement of anti-discrimination law against trans people, and any screening of gender markers at ports of entry, are not documented in the sources supplied; the UN Special Rapporteur's discrimination findings are stated at the level of marginalised groups generally.

The current status of the stalled conversion-therapy bill beyond its 2019 committee report, and the legal instrument used to scrap the 2025 sex-education programme and anti-bullying protocol, remain unresolved.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D5.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Costa Rica has demonstrated supportive expression rights for LGBTQ people. President Luis Guillermo Solis placed a rainbow flag in the Presidential House on 15 May 2014, and President Carlos Alvarado Quesada became the first Costa Rican President to march at the annual gay pride parade in San José in June 2019, an event that drew about 100,000 participants. In 2018, President Alvarado issued a public apology to the LGBT community for past state persecution. The President also designating 17 May as the National Day Against Homophobia by executive order in 2008. Wikipedia country coverage: No explicit visa or entry policy targeting LGBTQ travelers is described in current law, but the text notes that in December 2018, President Alvarado signed executive decrees covering immigration rights for binational same-sex couples, extending rights to immigrants as well. The most relevant historical finding concerns the 1990 incident when the Minister of the Interior instructed Costa Rican consulates not to grant visas to women travelling unaccompanied by men, warning all such women would be stopped at the airport, in an attempt to block foreign lesbians from attending an international meeting — this policy is decades old and not described as current. Wikipedia country coverage: The Supreme Court ruled in 2000 that a gay sauna must remain open, holding that "subjective criteria of morality and proper behaviour have no legal basis" and violate constitutional rights. In 2011, the Supreme Court reversed its 2008 ruling and now allows same-sex couples equal access to conjugal visits in prison. These are the only facility-related findings present in the source text. Wikipedia country coverage: The source text confirms that the Costa Rican state historically engaged in persecution of LGBTQ people — President Alvarado's July 2018 apology cited state "promoted and executed persecutions, raids, arbitrary arrests and beatings." Police harassment and raids of LGBTQ people and private establishments were "formerly commonplace" while homosexuality was technically legal. In 2020, the Legislative Assembly strengthened hate crime penalties: up to 20–35 years' imprisonment for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation (amending article 112 of the Penal Code), 1–3 years for exclusion or segregation based on sexual orientation (article 380), and 3–10 years for inflicting physical or mental pain, intimidation, coercion, or blackmail based on sexual orientation (article 386bis). Wikipedia country coverage: In 1993, Universidad Internacional de las Américas was found to have a policy of expelling LGBTQ students and firing LGBTQ faculty and staff; when the Ministry of Education was informed, it said the policy would likely violate constitutional articles 20, 33, and 70 if enforced. Comprehensive sex education campaigns are described as "almost nonexistent" in Costa Rican public high schools due to opposition from the Catholic Church and other religious groups. LGBTQ rights remain a major political flashpoint affecting young people — the 2018 general election was sharply divisive over same-sex marriage, and a 2012 poll found 60% of 18–34-year-olds supported equal rights for same-sex couples. A 2016 bill to allow transgender people to change name and gender without surgery or judicial permission was unsuccessful; since 2013 transgender people can change legal name with a judicial order, and since May 2018 name changes on official IDs are permitted through a simple, free procedure by the TSE.

CRI.tangentialFactors:
Opposition to LGBT equality is organised and parliamentary rather than street-level. Conservative lawmakers from PASE, National Restoration and allied parties attacked the presidential rainbow flag in 2014 as a provocation, and the conversion-therapy bill has been held in committee since 2019 — a legislature that contains a durable blocking bloc even where the executive and courts move ahead.

The 2025 repeal of the comprehensive sex-education programme and of the 2022 anti-LGBT bullying protocol sits alongside the stalled conversion-therapy bill as the main indicators of rollback pressure. These affect school environments rather than visitors directly, but they signal the direction of domestic policy debate.

The UN Special Rapporteur's 2023 country visit placed Costa Rica among states praised for near-universal coverage, and her concern about discrimination was framed for marginalised groups generally rather than as a finding specific to trans people.

A 2000 Supreme Court ruling held IVF unconstitutional; GayLawNet records it in the context of partnership benefits rather than as a trans-specific rule.

The survivor's-pension extension for same-sex partners, announced in 2016 and applied from 2018, shows benefits machinery reaching same-sex couples, but the teachers' pension budget was excluded, so coverage is not uniform across public schemes.

The state health system funds gender-affirming care for residents. The UN Special Rapporteur recommended that the authorities collect intersectional data to measure and address discrimination against LGBT and gender-diverse people in access to services.

The Justice Ministry's 2017 circular allows trans prisoners to request placement in a facility matching their gender identity, decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists, and ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners; an exclusive trans module was under consideration, modelled on Spain's protocols for vulnerable prison populations developed with CEJIL since 2016.

Residents with same-sex partners are entitled to survivor's pensions under all national-budget pension plans, following the Ministry of Labor announcement of 25 June 2016 and approval of the first individual survivor benefit on 29 June 2018; the teachers' separate budget remains outside the scheme.

PAN.name: Panama
PAN.summary:
Panama is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 2008 by presidential decree on constitutional nondiscrimination grounds. No traveller-facing restrictions are in force: there are no bathroom or facilities laws, no documented inspection of gender markers at the border, and no recorded pattern of police targeting trans visitors.

Legal gender recognition exists but requires surgery, and no nonbinary recognition is available. A visitor whose passport carries a marker inconsistent with presentation has no documented record of friction at Panamanian entry points, though the surgery requirement shapes which documents residents are able to obtain in the first place.

No statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. The National Assembly blocked an amendment to the general anti-discrimination law in 2024, and no acts are formally recognised as hate crimes. At the 2025 Universal Periodic Review multiple states urged Panama to adopt explicit anti-discrimination protections, reform gender recognition and strengthen safeguards against violence. Those reforms remain stalled, leaving the country behind much of the wider hemisphere.

Same-sex marriage is not available. The Supreme Court ruled in March 2023 that marriage equality is not a constitutional right, following a 2017 draft ruling by Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega that found the family code's bars on same-sex marriage not unconstitutional while leaving the National Assembly to legislate civil unions. The government signalled in 2018 that it would comply with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights decision of 9 January 2018, but no implementing legislation followed.

Social hostility is moderate. Machista culture persists and trans women face documented employment exclusion, yet violent targeting remains well below Northern Triangle levels. Public approval of same-sex marriage stands at 12 percent, ranked 18th of 22 in the Americas by the AmericasBarometer 2023. Panama City has a visible, established trans community and hosts regional LGBT organising.

Whether the government's 2018 signal of compliance with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights decision produced any bill before the National Assembly is unresolved in the inventory, as is whether any civil-union mechanism currently exists in practice.

Equaldex records marriage as banned while the Supreme Court's March 2023 ruling is reported separately; the two are consistent on outcome but the inventory does not establish whether further litigation is pending.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The Panamanian state has repeatedly acted against LGBT legal equality: the Code of Private International Law approved 8 May 2014 (Article 40) states that same-sex marriages are strictly prohibited and foreign same-sex marriages will not be recognized; the Supreme Court ruled on 27 March 2023 (after a seven-year delay) that there is no positive right to same-sex marriage under the constitution; and a constitutional amendment defining marriage as between a man and a woman was approved by the National Assembly on 29 October 2019 but withdrawn before the referendum after public protests. No laws protect LGBT people from discrimination, and Article 39 of the Constitution, which bars associations contrary to moral or legal order, has been used to refuse registration of gay organizations (as with the first gay group, AHMNP, founded 1996, which only gained legal recognition in 2005 after a three-year battle). Religious and political hostility is documented: the Roman Catholic Church defeated a 2004 civil-union proposal, condemned the 2018 Inter-American Court advisory opinion, and one deputy labelled that opinion "a danger to the human race"; a 2015 bill to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has not advanced. Gay and bisexual men are barred from donating blood, and a 2017 public survey found 78% of Panamanians opposed to same-sex marriage.

PAN.tangentialFactors:
Gender diversity is received unevenly across the country. In the Guna Yala indigenous territory a flourishing third-gender community, the Omeggid, is accepted as completely normal, and strong matriarchal figures elevate the status of women. Visitors moving between that territory and the capital should expect markedly different local attitudes to gender nonconformity.

The marriage litigation of 2017 and 2018 shows how organised the opposition remains. Two lawsuits, a suit seeking recognition of a foreign same-sex marriage and a direct challenge to the family code, were combined after oral arguments in the summer of 2017, with amicus briefs from regional marriage-equality advocates and public support from the First Lady, while Catholic and evangelical groups spearheaded opposition. A subsequent civil-union proposal came under attack from the Catholic Church.

Public opinion is a real constraint on reform. Only 12 percent of respondents approve of same-sex marriage, placing Panama 18th of 22 in the Americas on the AmericasBarometer 2023, and Outright International assesses the country as lagging much of Latin America on legal protections.

Blood donation carries an indefinite deferral for men who have sex with men, a rule that applies to visitors as well as residents.

DOM.name: Dominican Republic
DOM.summary:
The Dominican Republic does not criminalise same-sex relations. The Constitutional Court's 2024 review of the surviving sodomy-law articles resolved that the current criminal code contains no prohibition on same-sex conduct; those articles had reached only police officers and members of the armed forces, with no equivalent provision for heterosexual acts, and Human Rights Watch filed an amicus brief arguing that they violated equality and privacy. The outcome settles the criminal-law question but leaves the wider framework untouched: there is no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and no recognition of same-sex partnerships or marriage.

There is no legal gender recognition. A trans visitor has no route to have a chosen name or gender marker reflected in documents, and the Dominican authorities recognise no domestic process for it.

The Dominican Republic accepted recommendations at its Universal Periodic Review on discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and on the rights of intersex persons. The review record shows the commitments being accepted without any accompanying detail on domestic implementation, so no statute, regulation or complaint mechanism follows from them in the sources available.

Documented violence against trans women in the Dominican Republic is high and falls hardest on the most marginalised, in particular trans sex workers. The country's longest-standing trans-led organisation, the Community of Dominican Trans and Transvestite Sex Workers (COTRAVETD), co-founded in 2004, has recorded the community's conditions first-hand for two decades.

Tourist enclaves such as Punta Cana and Puerto Plata operate as insulated resort environments under international scrutiny, and Santo Domingo has a visible trans community and an annual Pride caravan. Beyond those settings, machista culture shapes daily life and police harassment of trans people is a documented feature of enforcement practice, so visibility carries risk that varies sharply by place and by who is present.

Unresolved: the source inventory for this pass contains nothing on entry or visa screening, on document or marker rules applied to travellers at the border, on hate-crime sentencing enhancements, or on access to gender-affirming care. The material on the Brewster ambassadorship and the 2017 Santo Domingo conference is LGB-focused. It is used here only as evidence of the hostility and polarisation a trans visitor would be entering, not as direct documentation of trans-specific incidents.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: A former law criminalising acts violating "decorum and good behaviour" in public was used by police to harass, fine or jail same-sex couples for public displays of affection; it was repealed by a 1997 amendment to the Criminal Code. In 2006 several gay clubs and bars in Santo Domingo were shut down as part of a police harassment programme, and in 2012 police crashed the Santo Domingo LGBT Pride Parade and arrested marchers on the ground they were improperly using the national flag. Reports indicate that visible, politically active LGBTQ community signs are often targets of government crackdowns, sometimes with support of religious leaders. Wikipedia country coverage: Transgender people in the Dominican Republic are not allowed to change their legal gender and name to reflect their gender identity. In June 2018 President Danilo Medina issued an executive decree granting 35 transgender Dominicans the possibility to change their legal name to match their gender identity; television journalist Mía Cepeda was one of the 35 and subsequently changed her name. A 2017 ILGA poll found only a plurality of 5% of Dominicans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender. Family law statutes recognise no legal status between same-sex persons, neither marriage nor marriage-like relationships. Wikipedia country coverage: Citizens of the Dominican Republic have a constitutional right to access health care services, but health care programs for the LGBTQ community have generally focused on HIV/AIDS education, often run by non-governmental organizations such as Amigos Siempre Amigos. Discrimination on account of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal in areas including health care, employment, education, housing, banking, transportation, government services and public accommodations, so many LGBTQ people feel the need to remain in the closet. Since 2011, Law 135/2011 on HIV/AIDS has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. No youth-specific or medication-related care findings appear in the source text. Wikipedia country coverage: The socially conservative mores of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestant denominations hold significant sway in both public policy and prevailing attitudes surrounding LGBTQ rights, and reports suggest visible LGBTQ community signs are often targets of government crackdowns often with the support of religious leaders. Because most residents hold conservative views, the major political parties have not expressed much public support for LGBTQ rights legislation. Former openly gay U.S. Ambassador Wally Brewster (2013–2017) was regularly insulted by religious leaders and some politicians, and evangelical groups started an unsuccessful petition asking the government to expel him, telling him to "go home and cook since he's married to a man." A 2017 ILGA poll found 69% of Dominicans said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals. Wikipedia country coverage: The family law statutes recognise no legal status between persons of the same sex — neither marriage nor civil or domestic partnerships — and the 2010 constitutional amendment added Article 55 stating the State shall promote and protect family organization based on marriage between a man and a woman; same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned. Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for any of the rights given to opposite-sex married couples. Article 41 of Law 544-14 (Private International Law) could justify recognition, since marriage is valid if considered such by the law of the place of celebration, national law or domicile of at least one spouse. On 9 January 2018 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an advisory opinion that parties to the American Convention should grant same-sex couples accession to all existing domestic family registration systems including marriage, and several Dominican legal experts have said the country must implement it.

CAN.name: Canada
CAN.summary:
Canada is among the safest large destinations for trans visitors. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, and no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration. Most provinces allow the gender marker on official documents to be changed by declaring one's identified gender, and Prince Edward Island's 2016 amendment to its Vital Statistics Act removed the prior surgery requirement, replacing it with a declaration supported by a letter from a doctor. Federally, identity documents can carry an X marker. Entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.

Healthcare coverage is universal. Discrimination complaints have a defined route as well: the Ontario Human Rights Code expressly covers gender identity and gender expression, and the Ontario Human Rights Commission publishes guidance setting out how such complaints are handled under the Ontario Human Rights Code.

Detention is the weakest part of the framework. Since Bill C-16, federal correctional policy requires transgender prisoners to be placed according to their gender identity, and prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Both placement and gender-affirming treatment have been contested in court, including litigation in which lawyer Barbara findlay represented a trans prisoner challenging her placement in a women's institution and the withholding of gender-affirming medical care.

The counterweight is a rising hate-crime climate. Statistics Canada recorded 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, up 1% after a 34% jump the year before; incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, ending three consecutive years of increases from a 2023 peak of 889. Across the longer arc, police-reported hate crime has risen for six consecutive years and is up 169% since 2018, with offences motivated by gender identity and gender expression among the fastest-growing categories, and Egale Canada documents an increasingly organised anti-trans movement.

Two provinces have moved against residents. Alberta and Saskatchewan have enacted policy rollbacks affecting trans people living there, including school-facing measures on names, pronouns and notification of parents. These rules govern residents rather than visitors, but they mark the direction of provincial politics running alongside the human-rights statutes.
CAN.outOfScopeNotes:
Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report covering 2SLGBTQI people could not be retrieved for verification; its findings are unresolved here and no claim rests on them.

The federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan survey findings page could not be retrieved either; the content of those quick stats is unresolved.

The inventory provides no gender-identity or gender-expression hate-crime counts for 2024. Only the sexual-orientation category is quantified, so the trans-specific figure for that year is not sourced.

No source in the inventory gives processing times, fees or turnaround for legal gender recognition, for the federal X marker, or for updating passports and identity documents. Those practical timelines are unresolved.

Whether the federal correctional placement rule is applied uniformly across provincial institutions is not sourced; the correctional evidence here comes from one province's officers and from reporting, not from a national audit.

AUS.name: Australia
AUS.summary:
Australia treats gender identity as a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, in force since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that gender-identity discrimination protection extends to trans women as women, and awarded compensation against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member.

State law has moved the same way. Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections for gender-diverse people in April 2024, and New South Wales passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024.

Visitors encounter none of the restrictive machinery found elsewhere: there are no laws confining bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held since 2017, which matters to same-sex couples arriving together.

Counterweights are documented. The Tickle case itself grew out of organised exclusionary activism, and ANROWS research maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender diverse rights in Australia, naming organised exclusionary campaigns, disputes over access to facilities and to records, and pressure to roll back existing rights. The same body of research documents systemic discrimination and harassment experienced by trans people.

Detention carries the sharpest residual risk. Queensland's 2009 corrective services procedure on transgender prisoners was assessed as largely ineffective; oversight passed to the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, fully in force from 2023, and inspection standards issued in August 2023 for Queensland prisons and youth detention centres direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender. Queensland placement is therefore identity-based, with a discretionary admission caveat and an exception tied to sexual reassignment surgery.
AUS.outOfScopeNotes:
Two sources in the inventory were not retrievable at research time: the Queensland Human Rights Commission page on strengthened protections for gender-diverse people returned HTTP 404, and the New South Wales Parliament bill document returned HTTP 400. The claims drawn from them rest on the inventory's own descriptions of the underlying items and remain unverified against the primary documents.

Entry and visa screening is not directly sourced. The absence of border friction for trans travellers rests on no contrary reporting in the inventory rather than on a rule or official statement, and the treatment of a foreign passport carrying a changed gender marker is unresolved here.

The wording of the Queensland surgery exception is ambiguous in the source: it states that only transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from the identity-based admission process, and the direction of that exclusion is not resolved.

The assessment that Queensland's 2009 procedure was largely ineffective comes from a 2009 Queensland Law Student Review article rather than an official evaluation, and no source in the inventory reports on how the 2023 standards have been applied in practice.

The historical account of state-by-state decriminalisation of homosexual conduct was set aside as general LGB legal history with no trans-specific bearing. No source in the inventory addresses hate-crime statutes, public-accommodation rules outside the facilities disputes ANROWS maps, or healthcare access for visitors.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Public expression is protected and visible: Sydney hosts an annual Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras and has been named one of the most gay-friendly cities in the world. Federal hate crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025, effective immediately) explicitly covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status with up to 7 years' imprisonment, and Victoria's Anti-vilification Act 2025 (effective 30 June 2026) covers the same grounds. Some states cover only sexual orientation in their own vilification laws (NSW, ACT, VIC), others also gender identity (SA, TAS, QLD), while NT and WA cover neither. Wikipedia country coverage: Medicare covers many major sex reassignment surgeries, but there is often a gap of thousands of dollars between the Medicare benefit and the surgeon's fee; private hospital policies that include SRS typically carry a waiting period of about 12 months. Since November 2017 a transgender child can access puberty blockers and hormone treatment without court approval where child, parents and doctors agree. Youth-specific: in January 2025 the Queensland government paused new prescriptions of puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for under-18s in public health services (existing patients exempted); the Queensland Supreme Court ruled the directive unlawful on 27 October 2025, but a new ministerial directive reinstated substantially the same restrictions on 28 October 2025, with a legal challenge filed in December 2025. A NSW independent review released September 2024 found puberty blockers 'safe, effective and reversible' but called for more long-term research, and from April 2025 Medicare IVF rebates were extended to single individuals and same-sex couples (not surrogacy). Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex marriage was legalized on 9 December 2017 (Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017, following a 61.6% 'Yes' postal survey result), making Australia the last of the Five Eyes countries to do so. States and territories began granting domestic partnership benefits from 2003 onwards, and federal law has recognized same-sex couples as de facto relationships since 2009, with civil unions, domestic partnerships and registered relationships available in most jurisdictions (except WA and the Northern Territory, where couples often need judicial approval to prove a de facto relationship). De facto partners face a higher burden of proof than married couples — requiring proof of relationship before a court for benefits, differing eligibility timeframes under Centrelink, migration and family law, which can impede arranging a partner's funeral and is poorly understood by some government departments. Wikipedia country coverage: Australia's Medicare covers many sex reassignment surgeries, but a gap between the benefit and the surgeon's fee can run to thousands of dollars, with private insurers typically imposing roughly a 12 months waiting period before claims. Since November 2017 a transgender child can access puberty blockers and hormone treatment without court approval where child, parents and treating doctors agree; puberty blockers are Stage 1 (from around age 10, reversible) and hormone therapy Stage 2 (usually from 16, irreversible), with sex reassignment surgery generally unavailable until 18. In January 2025 Queensland Health paused puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for new under-18 public patients, a directive ruled unlawful by the Queensland Supreme Court on 27 October 2025 but reinstated by ministerial discretion on 28 October 2025 pending reviews. From 1 August 2013 religious aged care providers receiving Commonwealth funding can no longer exclude people based on LGBTI status or same-sex relationships; in April 2025 Medicare rebates for IVF were extended to single individuals and same-sex couples (not surrogacy). Wikipedia country coverage: Australia legalized same-sex marriage on 9 December 2017 after a postal survey returning 61.6% 'Yes'; overseas same-sex marriages are automatically recognized and couples could no longer be barred from divorcing. Federal law has recognized same-sex couples as de facto since 2009, with reforms amending 85 federal laws across taxation, superannuation, health, social security, aged care, child support, immigration, citizenship and veterans' affairs, and Centrelink recognizing same-sex de facto partners from 1 July 2009. States and territories have offered domestic partnership or relationship recognition from 2003 onwards (civil partnerships in the ACT and Queensland; registered partnerships in NSW, Tasmania, Victoria and South Australia), while Western Australia and the Northern Territory lack such schemes, so couples often need judicial approval to prove a de facto relationship. De facto partners face higher eligibility periods and a burden of proof that married couples do not, which can affect funeral arrangements and is poorly understood by government departments. Wikipedia country coverage: Since 2016 every jurisdiction has an equal age of consent of 16 for all sexual acts, except Tasmania and South Australia where it is 17; Queensland was the last to equalise in 2016, dropping anal intercourse from 18 to 16. Religious educational institutions may still discriminate against LGBT students and teachers under sections 37 and 38 of the Sex Discrimination Act 1984, though discrimination against LGBT students is barred in Queensland, the Northern Territory and Tasmania, and Tasmania has the fewest exemptions overall. The Safe Schools Coalition Australia, begun in Victoria in 2010 and national from 2014, was curtailed under the Turnbull government (restricted to high schools, role plays removed, parental consent required) and lost federal funding after mid-2017, though Victoria, the ACT and South Australia fund it themselves; earlier, GaLTaS lobbied for LGBT students from 1991 to 1998. Trans youth are directly targeted: Tasmania's 2019 law lets a person change legal gender at 16 without parental permission and recognises non-binary genders, and the 2021 Census counted 13,554 (17.3%) children in same-sex couple families, up from 6,915 (14.8%) in 2016.

NZL.name: New Zealand
NZL.summary:
New Zealand's legal framework for trans people rests on statutory self-declaration: the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act 2021 eased correction of sex markers on identity documents, and the Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2022 outlaws conversion practices. The Human Rights Act 1993, however, is the subject of an open review rather than settled protection: the New Zealand Law Commission's Issues Paper 53, 'Ia Tangata' (June 2024), examines the Act's coverage of transgender people, non-binary people and people with innate variations of sex characteristics.

Reported anti-trans hostility rose sharply. Data released under the Official Information Act and reported by RNZ on 17 April 2024 shows 229 gender-identity-motivated hate incidents reported to police in 2023, against 161 in 2022, a 42% increase. Police themselves say the figure likely understates the true level of anti-trans hate, and the reports clustered in March 2023, the month the anti-trans campaigner Posie Parker visited.

Population-level survey data points the same way. The Counting Ourselves survey, reported by RNZ on 27 February 2025, found that almost one in five trans and non-binary New Zealanders were threatened with physical violence because of their gender identity in the preceding four years, and 8% experienced deliberate physical violence. It is described as the first clear population picture of violence against these communities.

Community assessment as of mid-2024 describes a worsening street climate alongside the statutory gains. Writing in The Spinoff on 2 July 2024, Jennifer Shields records a spate of rainbow event cancellations and the security demands that followed the 2023 Posie Parker protest, with advocates arguing that police are failing rainbow communities even as the 2021 registration Act and the 2022 conversion-practices Act took effect.
NZL.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses restroom or facility access, visa and border screening, or identity-document checks at entry for New Zealand, so those questions remain unresolved here rather than confirmed as unproblematic.

Prison housing placement is unresolved: the sources describe no rule on birth-sex versus identity-based placement, no dedicated unit, and no segregation or solitary practice for New Zealand.

Whether the Law Commission's 2024 recommendations have been enacted, and what scope of protection the Human Rights Act ultimately carries for trans, non-binary and intersex people, is not sourced in this inventory.

The 42% rise is a count of incidents reported to police, not of charges laid or convictions recorded, and police state that the count understates true incidence. The Counting Ourselves figures are self-reported survey prevalence over a four-year window, not police-recorded crime.

New Zealand's rating in the Spartacus Gay Travel Index 2026 is not stated in the inventory and has not been verified.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5.

sources.title: LGBTQ people in prison (Wikipedia; New Zealand section)
sources.summary: New Zealand: citing Dalzell, Pang & Broemdal 2024 (Australian & New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry, 'Gender affirmation and mental health in prison'), the article reports that trans people in New Zealand prisons are more likely to have prior experience of abuse and show a higher rate of incarceration, and that the NZ government has declared support for gender-affirming healthcare and gender-affirming clothing for incarcerated persons. No placement rule (birth-sex vs identity housing), special unit, or solitary/segregation practice for New Zealand is described.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Public LGBTQ expression is legal and visible: pride events have been held since the 1970s, Auckland's Hero Parade ran annually 1992–2001 drawing over 100,000 and at its height 200,000 attendees, and Pride marches run every February alongside the family-oriented Big Gay Out, which draws appearances from the Prime Minister, the Opposition Leader and politicians from both centre-left and centre-right parties. Open expression is also protected in law: discrimination on sexual orientation has been banned since the Human Rights Act 1993, gay, lesbian and bisexual people have served openly in the military since 1993, and passports have carried an "X" sex descriptor since November 2011. After the 2020 election, 10% of MPs (12 members) were openly LGBT+, the highest proportion of out elected representatives in the world, falling to 5 after 2023. Wikipedia country coverage: New Zealand has a visible LGBT scene with multiple gay bars, restaurants, clubs, festivals and venues in Auckland and smaller scenes in Wellington, Tauranga, Christchurch, Dunedin and Hamilton, plus several organisations and publications catering to LGBT people. Gender-affirming surgical capacity is thin: surgeries are done largely in private hospitals or overseas, the country's only specialist surgeon retired in 2014, and publicly funded operations were limited to four every two years (three male-to-female, one female-to-male), leaving 111 people on the waiting list by October 2018 with some waits projected at up to 50 years. Publicly funded fertility treatment is available to women on a scored eligibility basis, but only men without sperm qualify for public assisted-reproduction funding, so most male same-sex couples must pay privately. Wikipedia country coverage: State hostility toward trans people has intensified under the coalition of New Zealand First and the ACT Party: in September 2022 the Ministry of Health removed advice stating puberty blockers were safe and fully reversible from its website after backlash from anti-trans campaigners, with senior advisers conceding the information was "no doubt true" but removing it anyway to reduce queries. In July 2025 Sport and Recreation Minister Mitchell ordered Sport NZ to scrap its transgender-inclusive sports guidelines after lobbying by the anti-trans group Save Women's Sport Australasia, and on 19 November 2025 Health Minister Simeon Brown announced a ban on puberty blockers for minors with gender dysphoria (effective 19 December 2025), citing the Cass Review; it was condemned by RANZCP, PATHA and multiple NZ doctors, welcomed by the ruling parties and criticised by Labour and the Greens, and blocked by a Wellington High Court injunction on 17 December 2025 pending judicial review. Historically the state criminalised male homosexuality from 1858/1893 with penalties including life imprisonment and flogging until the Homosexual Law Reform Act 1986, though Parliament unanimously apologised in 2017 for those convictions and passed expungement in 2018. Earlier hostility included a 1968 petition for decriminalisation being rejected by Parliament. Wikipedia country coverage: Transgender youth are the sharpest political target: New Zealand prescribed up to seven times more puberty blockers to trans youth than England, Wales, Denmark and the Netherlands from 2014–2022 (400 children), after 48 children received them in the first recorded year of use in 2011, and the November 2025 government ban applies specifically to minors with gender dysphoria (existing patients may continue, and the drug stays available for early-onset puberty). Health safeguards for young people also went backwards: the Ministry of Health scrubbed its puberty-blockers safety page in September 2022, declined in April 2024 to say whether it would follow Britain's restrictions, and in November 2024 issued a brief recommending a "more precautionary approach" while conceding available evidence "all indicates the use of pubertal blockers is safe". Youth drove the conversion-therapy ban: Youth MP Shaneel Lal co-founded the Conversion Therapy Action Group in 2018, delivered a 150,000-signature petition, and his online campaign generated over 100,000 submissions (a record) before the ban passed on 15 February 2022, with Prime Minister Ardern citing vulnerable youth while the Justice Select Committee had initially refused a ban in 2019 to protect religious expression; the National Party's youth wing broke from its own party to back the bill. Intersex children are also affected: New Zealand law permits "normalising" genital surgery on intersex infants (regional outlier data showed interventions on girls under 6 months), drawing UN Committee on the Rights of the Child recommendations in October 2016, and the proposed registration bill would let 16- and 17-year-olds change legal sex with guardian consent plus health-professional confirmation.

A substantial community archive exists for residents and researchers: PrideNZ.com holds over 1,000 audio recordings of interviews and events from Aotearoa New Zealand's LGBTQIA+ communities, a rainbow timeline, more than 18,000 GayNZ.com articles from 2001 to 2017, and Homosexual Law Reform 40th-anniversary resources including Hansard transcripts of the parliamentary debates.

NZL.comparisons: Pairwise: below Australia (0.85 — comparable law, but NZ's documented 2023 hate-crime spike and police-failure pattern are worse) and above Germany (0.83).
NZL.blindSummary:
The country legal framework for trans people rests on statutory self-declaration: a 2021 registration Act eased correction of sex markers on identity documents, and a 2022 Act outlaws conversion practices. The Human Rights Act 1993 remains the subject of an open review rather than settled protection: the national law-reform commission's Issues Paper 53, 'Ia Tangata' (June 2024), examines the Act's coverage of transgender people, non-binary people and people with innate variations of sex characteristics.

Reported anti-trans hostility rose sharply. Data released under official-information legislation and reported by the national broadcaster on 17 April 2024 shows 229 gender-identity-motivated hate incidents reported to police in 2023, against 161 in 2022, a 42% increase. Police themselves say the figure likely understates the true level of anti-trans hate, and the reports clustered in March 2023, the month an anti-trans campaigner visited.

Population-level survey data points the same way. a national community survey, reported on 27 February 2025, found that almost one in five trans and non-binary residents were threatened with physical violence because of their gender identity in the preceding four years, and 8% experienced deliberate physical violence. It is described as the first clear population picture of violence against these communities.

Community assessment as of mid-2024 describes a worsening street climate alongside the statutory gains. A 2 July 2024 commentary records a spate of rainbow event cancellations and the security demands that followed the March 2023 protest, with advocates arguing that police are failing rainbow communities even as the 2021 registration Act and the 2022 conversion-practices Act took effect.

Prison housing placement is unresolved: the sources describe no rule on birth-sex versus identity-based placement, no dedicated unit, and no segregation or solitary practice for this jurisdiction.

Whether the law-reform commission's 2024 recommendations have been enacted, and what scope of protection the Human Rights Act ultimately carries for trans, non-binary and intersex people, is not sourced in this inventory.

The 42% rise is a count of incidents reported to police, not of charges laid or convictions recorded, and police state/province that the count understates true incidence. The survey figures are self-reported prevalence over a four-year window, not police-recorded crime.

This jurisdiction's rating in the February 2026 international travel index is not stated in the inventory and has not been verified.
