ALB.name: Albania
ALB.summary:
Albania does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or gender expression. Homosexuality carried a ten-year prison sentence until 1995; the operative instrument since 2010 is an anti-discrimination law that covers sexual orientation but provides no basis for same-sex marriage. A National LGBTI Action Plan runs from 2021 to 2027, and observers record that implementation falls short of its commitments.

Nothing in the record indicates trans-specific screening at the border or on arrival, and no restriction on facilities or bathrooms is on record. Police targeting of trans visitors is not documented in any source here. The realistic exposure is social rather than legal: Rainbowphilia logged ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people in 2023, and hostility is sharper outside Tirana and in more conservative rural areas. Tirana hosts an annual Pride.

International scrutiny is unusually open for the region. Graeme Reid, the UN Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, carried out a country visit from 1 to 12 July 2024, issued an end-of-mission statement on 12 July 2024, and presented report A/HRC/59/43/Add.1 on 17 June 2025 assessing Albania's adherence to national and international human-rights standards. EU candidate status is the stated driver of slow alignment with those standards.

Protection machinery exists and has been used. An Anti-Discrimination Commissioner receives and mediates complaints, and has ruled against public figures who made hostile statements about LGBT people.
ALB.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no sourced information on legal gender recognition in Albania, on rules for changing name or sex markers on identity documents, or on whether such changes affect passport presentation at entry. This is unresolved here, not established either way.

No source addresses visa or border screening procedures that could disclose a visitor's trans status, nor any restriction or requirement affecting access to hormone therapy or other trans-specific healthcare while in the country.

Sentencing outcomes and enforcement results for the ten bias-motivated violence cases logged in 2023 are not stated, so the effectiveness of criminal-law responses to that violence cannot be assessed from these sources.

The two Koha Jonё items carry 2018 URLs but 2021 publication dates; the discrepancy is unresolved. Whether the implementation deficits identified in the National LGBTI Action Plan have been remedied following the July 2024 visit and the June 2025 report is likewise not sourced.

Unsourced dimensions after this research pass: D4, D5, D6, D7.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: On 4 May 2013 the Albanian Parliament amended the criminal code to put hate crimes against sexual orientation and gender identity on par with race, ethnicity, religion and disability offences, and simultaneously passed a law punishing dissemination of homophobic information through any means, including the internet, by a fine and up to two years imprisonment. Public expression of LGBT identity is discouraged by social attitudes: 56.1% of Albanians told Gallup's Balkan Monitor (2010) that homosexuals should not show their preferences in public, and 56.2% said they should not hold public posts such as teacher. Visibility efforts exist nonetheless, e.g. the first Miss Trans Albania pageant in Tirana in 2014 and the news portal historiaime.al launched by Pro LGBT in 2012. Wikipedia country coverage: The source confirms that same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised in Albania in any form, and that households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex couples. In April 2018 People's Advocate Erinda Ballanca pledged to support the right to legally change one's gender, but the text does not state whether a legal gender recognition procedure exists or how documents are handled. In 2016, under pressure from faith-based leaders, members of parliament removed sexual orientation and gender identity from Article 18 of the Constitution at the last moment, contrary to promises; PINK Embassy condemned this on 20 July 2016. Wikipedia country coverage: The 2010 comprehensive anti-discrimination law (in force from 4 February 2010) applies to health care as well as employment, goods and services, education and housing, and in October 2020 it was expanded to prohibit discrimination on the grounds of sex characteristics and HIV status. In practice access is weak: in December 2010 Deputy Commissioner for Labour, Social Affairs and Health Tritan Shehu said homosexuality should be treated by medical staff as a hormonal and psychological disorder; the Commissioner for Protection from Discrimination reprimanded him only on 30 September 2011 after a lengthy delay, and LGBT groups had already lost trust in the body over slow, bureaucratically impeded investigations (only 1 of 9 LGBT-linked cases concluded by December 2012). A 2022 nationwide questionnaire found only 9.3% of Albanians would accept an LGBT person as a family doctor, and youth-specific data show 55% of Albanians aged 16–27 (2015) would not want homosexual neighbours, with a 2016 study finding homophobia among Albanian university students associated with being male, politically conservative and religious. In June 2016 the government passed a National Action Plan for LGBTI addressing bullying and discrimination in primary and secondary education, which drew strong political opposition.

ALB.tangentialFactors:
Parliamentary rhetoric has at times been openly hostile to LGBT work. In July 2021 Democratic Party MP Luçiano Boçi attacked LGBT campaigning in high schools as extra-curricular groups with a suspicious, revolting agenda, and MP Nard Ndoka used Facebook to brand the government LGBT and accuse it of pushing LGBT values in schools. Both episodes fall under the Berisha-led opposition and illustrate the political environment in which domestic advocacy operates.

The Anti-Discrimination Commissioner reprimanded ruling Democratic Party MP Tritian Shehu in October 2011 after he told parliament that homosexuality is a disease and should be treated with hormones, warning him to avoid remarks that create an atmosphere of tension toward the LGBT community. Ten years later the same office mediated complaints about screenings of the film 'Strange World', ruling in favour of the complainant in one case.

Prime Minister Sali Berisha voiced support for same-sex marriage in July 2009, framing the anti-discrimination law as an EU-integration measure. That posture, combined with the 2024 UN country visit, marks Albania as more institutionally receptive than several neighbouring jurisdictions, though the gap between policy and practice remains the recurring finding of the international reviews.
ALB.localsOnly:

Community organisations run material support schemes for the most exposed residents, including food packages distributed to trans sex workers and to people living with HIV. Rainbowphilia's casework recorded ten bias-motivated violence incidents against trans people in 2023.

Anti-LGBT messaging from elected officials has repeatedly surfaced around school-based education campaigns, shaping the environment for teachers and student groups.

MKD.name: North Macedonia
MKD.summary:
North Macedonia carries no criminal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct or for being transgender, and its anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation and gender identity following the 2019 amendments. The practical baseline for a trans visitor is therefore legal tolerance paired with weak protection, rather than legal exposure.

Public trans organising proceeds openly. TransFormA's March for Visibility of Trans People in Skopje marked Transgender Day of Visibility on 30 March 2024 under the words "we march bravely", and the capital's Pride and trans march events have taken place without serious incident.

The protective machinery around such events is thin. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 records hate speech as a serious and continuing problem with countless reports and no meaningful state response, a reading the European Commission's country report shares, alongside routine social-media death threats. The US State Department's 2019 human rights report separately documents societal violence and discrimination against LGBT people.

Enforcement is not entirely absent. In September 2023 the Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentenced a man to two years in prison for assaulting an LGBTI activist, applying the sexual orientation and gender identity aggravating grounds of the Criminal Code.

Global Voices reported a worrisome trend of mobilising religious institutions to scapegoat this small vulnerable group, a factor that raises the chance of confrontation around visible trans presence even where authorities permit demonstrations.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. The government withdrew the Draft Law on Civil Registry containing the legal gender recognition chapter one day before Parliamentary Committee review, leaving no domestic procedure for changing a gender marker in force. Documents issued abroad remain the ones a visitor travels on.

No relationship recognition is available: a 2014 government motion defined marriage strictly as a union of one man and one woman, ruling out same-sex marriage and adoption, and required two-thirds of members of parliament. A partner travelling as a couple should expect no legal acknowledgement of the relationship.

ECRI has called for a ban on nonconsensual intersex surgeries, a care-protection gap relevant to intersex visitors considering medical treatment while in the country.
MKD.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the 2014 motion defining marriage passed the two-thirds parliamentary threshold is not stated in the sourced material, only that the conservative DPA was expected to supply the additional votes.

Unresolved: no source addresses whether foreign identity documents carrying a changed gender marker, or an X marker, are accepted at entry, in hotels, or by medical providers; nothing in the inventory covers airport or border screening of trans travellers.

Unresolved: the 2023 Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentence is the only enforcement outcome in the inventory; the general rate of investigation and prosecution of anti-trans violence, and how often the SOGI aggravating grounds are applied, is not sourced.

Unresolved: ECRI's call for a ban on nonconsensual intersex surgeries is a recommendation in the record; its implementation status, and any separate consent protections for intersex persons in law, are not sourced here.

Unresolved: whether North Macedonia recognises marriages or partnerships concluded abroad is not addressed by any source in the inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6, D7.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The source documents ongoing legal and social restrictions on expression for LGBTQ people: homosexuality was criminalized until 1996 (decriminalization was a Council of Europe accession condition), and same-sex relationships remain unrecognized — family law defines marriage as "a union between a man and a woman," and a 2015 constitutional amendment attempt (passed 72-4 in committee, approved in Parliament 20 January 2015) would have barred any legal recognition absent a two-thirds majority. In 2019 the Criminal Code amendments explicitly listed sexual orientation and gender identity under the hate speech provisions. Expression of gender identity via official documents remained restricted until the ECHR ruled (January 2019) that requiring sex reassignment surgery before changing a gender marker violated human rights; the court awarded €9,000 in damages, but NGOs report the government still failed to recognize gender identity changes in ID documents. Wikipedia country coverage: Constitution and law prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation in access to government services such as health care, and the government enforced such laws according to the 2019 US Country Report. Health-adjacent support exists through EGAL (described as the oldest organization working on gay/lesbian health issues) and the LGBTI Support Center in Skopje, a subsidiary of the Helsinki Committee for Human Rights that offers free legal aid. However, trans people seeking lawful gender recognition face a documented hurdle: despite the January 2019 ECHR ruling, NGOs complain the government has failed to implement gender identity changes in identification documents. Wikipedia country coverage: Harassment comes from multiple directions — the 2019 US Country Report found the LGBTQ community is "still prejudiced and harassed by the society, media and the authorities," with hate speech on social media following the first Pride Parade (June 2019) and the Skopje public prosecutor deemed ineffective in processing hate speech cases. State hostility is also legislative and administrative: Strumica Mayor Kostadin Kostadinov nullified all memoranda with LGBTQ organizations in June 2023 and vowed to veto future ones; a 2025 Pride Parade drew less attendance after organizers declared it a protest, prompting foreign embassies to pull funding. Public opinion polling (Center for Civil and Human Rights, 2002) found over 80% of respondents viewed homosexuality as "a psychiatric disorder that endangered families" and about 65% considered it a crime warranting jail. North Macedonia ranked 10th worst European country for LGBTQ tourists in 2019. Wikipedia country coverage: Young LGBTQ people face direct physical harm: a 2019 US Country Report details fellow students verbally and physically attacking a gay high school student, breaking his nose; the student reported the incident to the principal but chose not to report it to police. The same report cites CSO Coalition Margini documenting 70 cases of violence against LGBTI individuals in 2019 (five discrimination cases, one verbal assault by a police officer), and notes most such violence goes unreported to police or institutions. More broadly, "there are many reports about public humiliations, worker firings and even casting homosexual teenagers onto the streets due to revelation of their sexual orientations." On the protective side, the Law on Primary Education adopted in July 2019 introduced anti-discrimination language covering sexual orientation and gender identity.

Residents face a documented pattern of hate speech with no meaningful state response, as recorded in ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 and the European Commission country report, with social-media death threats reported as routine.

Domestic LGBTI organisations have begun quantifying the economic cost of discrimination in the national economy, alongside the case for legal protection.

The 2014 marriage-definition motion entrenched marriage as a union of one man and one woman in constitutional terms, foreclosing both same-sex marriage and adoption for couples formed in the country.

MKD.blindSummary:
The country carries no criminal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct or for being transgender, and its anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation and gender identity following the 2019 amendments. The practical baseline for a trans visitor is legal tolerance paired with weak protection, rather than legal exposure.

Public trans organising proceeds openly. a local advocacy group's March for Visibility of Trans People in the capital marked Transgender Day of Visibility on 30 March 2024 under the words "we march bravely", and the capital's Pride and trans march events have taken place without serious incident.

The protective machinery around such events is thin. The 2024 annual review of legal conditions records hate speech as a serious and continuing problem with countless reports and no meaningful state/province response, a reading the national human-rights reporting body shares, alongside routine social-media death threats. The 2019 human rights report of the national rights department of the parent country separately documents societal violence and discrimination against LGBT people.

Enforcement is not entirely absent. In September 2023 the jurisdictional criminal court of the capital sentenced a man to two years in prison for assaulting a LGBTI activist, applying the sexual orientation and gender identity aggravating grounds of the Criminal Code.

Reporting describes a worrisome trend of mobilising religious institutions to scapegoat this small vulnerable group, a factor that raises the chance of confrontation around visible trans presence even where authorities permit demonstrations.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. The government withdrew the Draft Law on Civil Registry containing the legal gender recognition chapter one day before Parliamentary Committee review, leaving no domestic procedure for changing a gender marker in force. Documents issued abroad remain the ones a visitor travels on.

No relationship recognition is available: a 2014 government motion defined marriage strictly as a union of one man and one woman, ruling out same-sex marriage and adoption, and required two-thirds of members of the national legislature. a partner travelling as a couple should expect no legal acknowledgement of the relationship.

The national human-rights monitoring body has called for a ban on nonconsensual intersex surgeries, a care-protection gap relevant to intersex visitors considering medical treatment while in the country.

MNE.name: Montenegro
MNE.summary:
Montenegro decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1977, in the same year as Croatia and Slovenia, and the prohibition has not returned. The current framework comprises an anti-discrimination law that expressly covers gender identity, hate-crime provisions that list sexual orientation and gender identity as motives, and a same-sex partnership law adopted in 2020 after parliament rejected an earlier version on 31 July 2019. A visitor has no legal exposure for being trans or for presenting gender non-conformingly in public.

Two gaps shape what that framework delivers. There is no legal gender recognition statute, so change of gender markers is handled through inconsistent administrative practice rather than a defined procedure. The European Commission has also found that prosecutors overuse misdemeanour charges in place of proper hate-crime proceedings, which blunts the sentencing uplift the hate-crime provisions were written to provide.

Organised hostility is documented and recurrent. The first Podgorica Pride, planned for May 2011, was cancelled after two attacks on gay people in the capital; the march that eventually went ahead in October 2013 drew roughly 150 marchers behind some 2,000 police, with rock-throwing opponents held back by tear gas. ILGA-Europe's 2024 review records anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech continuing in political rhetoric, more than 222 reported online hate-speech incidents, and a psychologist who wears non-gender-conforming clothes on television targeted by abusive comments, threats and several physical attacks, with the police response under monitoring. Gender non-conformity in visible public settings is the specific trigger in that case.

For a visitor the assessment is favourable on paper and uneven on the ground: functioning institutions, police protection at Pride events, an annual Podgorica Pride that now proceeds, and a small tolerant coastal tourist scene, set against hate speech in political discourse and a social climate in which visibility outside tolerant settings invites harassment. Standard caution applies in the more conservative north.
MNE.outOfScopeNotes:
The absence of a legal gender recognition statute is stated in the review material available here, but the specific documents, medical requirements or fees demanded by individual administrative bodies are not sourced in the inventory and remain unresolved.

Whether the 2020 partnership law retains the parenting, foster care and adoption exclusions set out in the December 2018 draft is not confirmed by the sources in hand; the exclusion is documented for the draft, not verified against the enacted text.

Several social-climate sources are dated. The account of entrenched anti-gay opinion and harassment when visible comes from March 2012, and the cancelled 2011 Pride is reported in the same material; both are concrete but predate the partnership law and the annual marches, so their present weight is not independently verified here.

The physical attacks on the psychologist reported in the 2024 review are described as having a monitored police response, but no outcome of any investigation or charge is stated in the source.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Montenegro: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech and political rhetoric continued; a psychologist wearing non-gender-conforming clothes on TV was targeted by hate comments, threats and several physical attacks (police response monitored); a groundbreaking study found only 28.1% of companies' anti-discrimination policies explicitly mention sexual orientation; a new Action Plan for the 2019-2023 LGBTI Strategy was adopted with €45,000; over 222 online hate-speech incidents reported.
Human Dignity Trust records Montenegro's decriminalisation of same-sex conduct in 1977, grouped with Croatia and Slovenia as a European cohort of that year (page updated 18 June 2026).

GlobalGayz (March 2012): decriminalised in 1977; small gay scene with deeply entrenched anti-gay opinion, discrimination and harassment when visible; the first Podgorica Pride was cancelled in May 2011 after two attacks on gay people in the capital. Dated but concrete on social climate.

Al Jazeera (Oct 2013): Montenegro's first Pride marched through Podgorica — roughly 150 marchers guarded by some 2,000 police, rock-throwing opponents stopped by tear gas; Queer Montenegro's Danijel Kalezic: 'From this day we are no longer invisible.' Shows both state protection and organised hostility.

PinkNews (2 Aug 2019): MPs blocked the same-sex partnership law on 31 July 2019 despite government backing — ERA's Western Balkans office: LGBT people 'forced to live as second-class citizens' (no hospital visitation or shared-benefit rights); a 2018 ERA study found 51% of LGBT+ Montenegrins were closeted.

CDM (Dec 2018): the Government adopted the Draft Law on Same-Sex Partnership granting couples near marriage-equivalent rights via registrar ceremony — explicitly excluding parenting, foster care and adoption; shows the reform trajectory before the 2019 parliamentary block.

MNE.tangentialFactors:
Montenegro sits at the front of its regional cohort on legal reform, and the gap between statute and enforcement is the recurring theme in external monitoring. The supranational Commission's finding on misdemeanour substitution is the clearest expression of it: the offences exist, the charging practice does not match them.

A 2018 study by the European Region of the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association found that 51% of LGBT+ Montenegrins lived closeted, and its Western Balkans office described LGBT people as forced to live as second-class citizens without rights such as hospital visitation and shared benefits at the time the partnership bill was blocked. A subsequent survey found that only 28.1% of companies' anti-discrimination policies explicitly mention sexual orientation, an indicator of how far workplace protection reaches in practice.

The pattern of Pride events shows both sides of the picture at once: the 2011 cancellation after attacks, the 2013 march escorted by 2,000 police against stone-throwing crowds, and the annual marches held since. State protection has been reliable; the hostility it protects against has not disappeared.
MNE.localsOnly:
Residents face a partnership regime with defined limits. The draft adopted by the Government in December 2018 granted couples near-marriage-equivalent rights through a registrar ceremony and explicitly excluded parenting, foster care and adoption; that exclusion is the resident-facing boundary of the relationship recognition now in force.

Workplace and service discrimination remain under-documented in employer policy: only 28.1% of companies' anti-discrimination policies name sexual orientation explicitly, according to the study cited in ILGA-Europe's 2024 review. The same review notes a new Action Plan for the 2019-2023 LGBTI Strategy adopted with €45,000 in funding, and records more than 222 reported online hate-speech incidents during the period.

Legal gender recognition has no statutory basis. Applications are handled administratively, and practice between offices is inconsistent, so Montenegrins seeking a marker change face an unpredictable process rather than an appealable decision.

BIH.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
BIH.summary:
Bosnia and Herzegovina does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina removed it from its criminal code in 1996 and Republika Srpska followed in 1998, each through its own entity-level code, so a trans visitor carries no legal exposure on that basis.

Statutory protection at state level is explicit. The amended Anti-Discrimination Law, adopted in 2016 after public consultations in autumn 2015, covers sexual orientation and gender identity in the terminology used locally; the Sarajevo Open Centre presented the amendments together with the Agency for Gender Equality. Bias-motivated violence is treated as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, where the hate-crime regulation names sexual orientation and gender identity directly.

Institutional practice has moved as well. Sarajevo Pride has proceeded annually since 2019 under heavy police protection, and most cantons have appointed prosecutors specifically for anti-LGBTI hate crimes.

The counterweight is documented hostility. The Sarajevo Open Centre's Pink Report 2024, the annual monitor of LGBTI human rights in the country, records a year in which a number of negative events had significant impact and concludes that the worsening trend visible for some time is becoming increasingly evident. Organised anti-LGBTI violence has occurred even where security was arranged in advance: in February 2014 attackers assaulted Sarajevo Pride organisers after the Sarajevo Open Centre had coordinated security with police roughly three weeks earlier, and Human Rights Watch called for the attackers to be prosecuted.

For a visitor the assessment is that there is no legal exposure, that Sarajevo and established tourist areas are workable, and that visible trans presentation carries elevated risk in Republika Srpska and in rural areas, where the monitoring trend is unfavourable and the protection machinery is thinner than in the capital.
BIH.outOfScopeNotes:
Marriage and partner recognition for trans visitors and residents is not addressed by the sources assembled for this record and remains unresolved here.

The content of Republika Srpska's separate hate-crime regime, as distinct from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina's, is not sourced in this inventory; only the fact that the two regimes differ is established.

Whether the attackers who assaulted Sarajevo Pride organisers in February 2014 were prosecuted is not stated in the available material, despite Human Rights Watch's public demand that they be.

The Pink Report 2024 is cited here for its overall assessment of the year and the direction of the trend; the specific incidents it catalogues are not reproduced in this record.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6, D7.

For this record: current national climate assessment from the leading local monitor.

Balkan Diskurs (25 Oct 2024): legal gender recognition is formally accessible but vague and ineffective in practice — the Council of Ministers' 2022 action plan conditions document changes on 'completed' medical transition, constraints described as discriminatory and degrading. For this record: the documentation pathway a trans person navigating the system faces — resident-facing, not a border issue.

Human Rights Watch (4 Feb 2014): violent attack on Sarajevo Pride organisers — Sarajevo Open Centre staff said they had arranged security with police about three weeks earlier; HRW's Lydia Gall demanded prosecution of attackers. For this record: precedent that organised anti-LGBT violence occurs even WITH prior police coordination (dated 2014, context for later attacks).

GlobalGayz (2012): same-sex conduct decriminalised in the Federation of BiH (1996) and Republika Srpska (1998) via the two entities' own criminal codes; the 2009 Law Against Discrimination prohibits discrimination on sexual orientation but omitted gender identity as originally intended. For this record: entity-level legal baseline plus the pre-2016 gender-identity protection gap.

Sarajevo Open Centre (Jul 2016): BiH's amended Anti-Discrimination Law explicitly covers sexual orientation and gender identity with correct local terminology — SOC co-presented the amendments with the Agency for Gender Equality after fall-2015 public consultations. For this record: the statutory protection now on the books at state level.

For this record: entity-level sentencing enhancement for bias attacks in FBiH (RS runs its own separate regime).

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Anti-discrimination law adopted in 2016 explicitly bans discrimination on sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics, and the 2009 Law Against Discrimination covers 'gender expression'. In April 2016 the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina amended its Criminal Code to outlaw hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity (published 15 June 2016), with similar bans already in Republika Srpska and Brčko District. Public expression has nonetheless been met with violence: the Queer Sarajevo Festival 2008 was stormed by football fans and religious extremists shouting death threats, and in 2014 the Constitutional Court ruled authorities had failed to protect festival participants' freedom of assembly. The first BIH Pride March was held in Sarajevo on 9 September 2019 with an estimated 2,000 marchers, but in March 2023 police cancelled LGBTQ film screenings in Banja Luka for 'security concerns' and activists were chased and attacked afterwards. Wikipedia country coverage: The source's further-reading list cites a 2017 PLOS ONE qualitative study documenting stigma and discrimination that men who have sex with men experience from healthcare professionals and the general community in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Legal gender change is available only after sex reassignment surgery and other medical treatments. Public attitudes also bear on care: a 2015 survey found 48% of Bosnians would try to 'cure' their child if the child came out as gay, and another 16% would stop communicating with that child. Wikipedia country coverage: There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples at national or subnational level: the Constitution is silent on gender eligibility for marriage, while both entities' family codes limit marriage to opposite-sex couples, and same-sex couple households are not eligible for the same legal protections as opposite-sex couples. On 19 October 2018 the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted a request to legalise civil unions; a working group was established in January 2020 but its start was postponed due to the COVID-19 pandemic. A 2015 survey found 19% of the population supported granting same-sex couples some marriage-associated rights, and a 2017 Pew poll found 13% support for same-sex marriage with 84% opposed. Wikipedia country coverage: The age of consent is set equally at 14 years regardless of gender and sexual orientation, with sex below 14 treated as statutory rape. Youth are directly targeted in family attitudes: a 2015 survey found 48% of Bosnians would try to 'cure' a child who came out as gay and 16% would cut off contact with that child. LGBTQ youth face violence around public events — at the 2008 Queer Sarajevo Festival eight people including a policeman were injured — and the 2021 study found the 2019 Sarajevo Pride parade increased support for LGBT activism only in Sarajevo, not nationwide.

BIH.localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition is formally accessible in Bosnia and Herzegovina but is vague and ineffective in practice. The Council of Ministers' 2022 action plan conditions changes to identity documents on completed medical transition, and the constraints imposed through that pathway are described by local researchers as discriminatory and degrading.

Trans residents also face restricted access to healthcare and institutional suspicion when dealing with the authorities, a position the Balkan Diskurs reporting of October 2024 characterises as precarious. These are documentation and care-access problems that arise inside the system rather than at the border.

Residents bringing a bias-motivated incident forward can draw on the state Anti-Discrimination Law and, in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on hate-crime aggravation at sentencing; most cantons have designated prosecutors for anti-LGBTI hate crimes, which affects how such complaints are handled locally.
BIH.comparisons: Pairwise: below North Macedonia (0.62 — MKD's anti-discrimination law is stronger) and above Cambodia (0.61, tie — different profiles).

The counterweight is documented hostility. The 2024 annual monitor of LGBTI human rights in the state records a year in which a number of negative events had significant impact and concludes that the worsening trend visible for some time is becoming increasingly evident. Organised anti-LGBTI violence has occurred even where security was arranged in advance: in February 2014 attackers assaulted Pride organisers after the monitoring organisation had coordinated security with police roughly three weeks earlier, and an international human rights organisation called for the attackers to be prosecuted.

For a visitor the assessment is that there is no legal exposure, that the main city and established tourist areas are workable, and that visible trans presentation carries elevated risk in the second entity and in rural areas, where the monitoring trend is unfavourable and the protection machinery is thinner than in the main city.

GEO.name: Georgia
GEO.summary:
Georgia is dangerous for trans visitors, and the position has deteriorated sharply. In September 2024 the Parliament of Georgia adopted the law "On the Protection of Family Values and Minors", which bans legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, public LGBT assembly and the dissemination of "LGBT information". It is the harshest such legislative package in the region, and it removed the two routes by which a trans visitor or resident would ordinarily deal with documents and care.

One day after the law passed, Kesaria Abramidze, a trans model and influencer and one of Georgia's best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her apartment in Tbilisi. German foreign-affairs committee chair Michael Roth and EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell condemned the law as further derailing Georgia's EU path. AP reported in October 2024 that the killing, together with Russia-style "gay propaganda" provisions, had raised fears of hate crimes against LGBT people in the conservative South Caucasus nation.

The refusal of protection by the security apparatus predates the 2024 law. In June 2019 the Interior Ministry declared the country's first-ever Tbilisi Pride "impossible" in the planned city-centre locations, citing safety risks; organisers reported a week of pressure from an unidentified government official to cancel the march, and far-right groups had vowed to thwart it. In 2021 the Pride office was ransacked by far-right mobs while police stood by, and investigators have documented police failure to protect demonstrators.

The machinery of protection is itself under strain. The foreign-agents law is choking local rights groups and LGBT organisations, which refuse to register as "foreign agents" and consequently face fines or bankruptcy. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records that the anti-LGBTI law has eroded trust in institutions, that applications to LGBTI services have fallen as a result, that large numbers of LGBTI people are fleeing Georgia and seeking asylum documentation, and that misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is spreading.

Trans-specific legal barriers are older than the 2024 package. Legal activists told IWPR in May 2012 that the law needed changing to allow gender recognition, and that job applications become difficult when a person's gender identity does not match official paperwork. In August 2024 WISG and partner organisations reported to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers calling for urgent action: effective investigations into anti-LGBTI violence, withdrawal of the proposed anti-LGBTI legislation, improved hate-crime data collection, and protection of LGBTI assembly and expression. Those requests describe protections that are not currently in force.
GEO.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the killing of Kesaria Abramidze has resulted in arrests, charges or convictions is not sourced in the available inventory; the reporting establishes the death and its timing against the law, not the criminal outcome.

The quality and completeness of hate-crime data collection is not resolved here. The August 2024 report to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers recommends improved collection, which implies gaps, but no figures on recorded anti-trans offences or prosecution rates are available in the inventory.

The enforcement posture of the 2024 law against visitors specifically is not documented. The inventory establishes the statutory bans and a documented pattern of police non-protection of demonstrators, but contains no reported case of a foreign visitor prosecuted under the package.

The status of the 2019 and 2021 incidents as to any legal liability of the Interior Ministry or of the mobs remains unresolved; no sourced outcome of investigations or litigation is available.

The 2012 employment-material is more than a decade old and predates both the 2024 statute and subsequent administrative changes, so its precise current application to residents is undated rather than confirmed.

The extent to which the foreign-agents law's registration requirements fall on a foreign visitor's own advocacy, as distinct on resident organisations, is not sourced and should be verified with a Georgian legal adviser before relying on it.

ARM.name: Armenia
ARM.summary:
Armenia carries no criminal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct; the provision was repealed in 2003, and the country has no statute of the restrictive type applied to LGBT people in neighbouring Azerbaijan. Trans visitors face no legal exposure for being trans, but the legal framework offers them little affirmative protection: there is no discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the anti-discrimination bill tabled in 2018 did not pass.

Legal gender recognition exists as an administrative practice and is medicalised. Equaldex records that a legal gender change has been available since 2006 but requires surgery, that gender-affirming care is restricted, and that no non-binary recognition is available. Hate-crime protection covering bias-motivated violence is characterised as ambiguous since 2022, and same-sex marriage is prohibited.

Pink Human Rights Defender NGO's annual report on the human rights situation of LGBT+ people in Armenia during 2024 documents discrimination, torture and inhuman or degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion, violations of private and family life, and discrimination in education and work. It records hate speech as a persistent feature of public discourse and devotes a chapter to the pressure directed at a transgender individual who participated in a beauty pageant.

Trans people in positions of visibility have drawn extreme political hostility. In April 2019 Lilit Martirosyan, Armenia's first registered trans woman, received death threats after delivering a speech on LGBTI discrimination in the national assembly; members of parliament called for her to be burned alive.

Enforcement of violence against LGBT spaces is unreliable. In May 2012 a Molotov cocktail was thrown at the gay-friendly DIY bar in Yerevan and a fire set; police took twelve hours to respond, though two suspects were later detained through CCTV footage. Equaldex's public-opinion measure puts acceptance at 5 out of 100, indicating a social environment where visible trans presence draws hostility well beyond central Yerevan.

The capital has an organised community, with Pink Armenia and the trans-led organisation Right Side operating locally. Visibility outside those networks remains a source of risk rather than protection.
ARM.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory addresses Armenian border control, visa issuance or document-screening practice as it affects trans travellers, including what happens if a passport gender marker does not match presentation. That question remains unresolved here.

The requirement that legal gender change be preceded by surgery is sourced to Equaldex, a comparison aggregator, rather than to the text of the Armenian legislation itself; the governing statute was not supplied for verification. The same applies to the characterisation of hate-crime protection as 'ambiguous since 2022' and to the restricted status of gender-affirming care.

The 5/100 public-acceptance figure comes from Equaldex's methodology and has not been corroborated against an Armenian polling source. The ILGA-Europe/COC mission report dates from 2009 and describes conditions at that time rather than the present.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D5.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Armenian authorities and private actors have repeatedly restricted LGBT expression and media. In 2013, police proposed a bill criminalizing 'non-traditional sexual relationships' and LGBT 'propaganda' to youth modeled on Russian law; it failed to pass after Pink Armenia argued it was a distraction tactic. In 2017, organizers of the Yerevan International Film Festival canceled the screening of two LGBT-themed films following negative public reaction. In November 2018, a Christian LGBT group was forced to cancel planned forums and events due to 'constant threats' and 'organized intimidation' from political and religious leaders and what it described as insufficient police readiness to protect them. Public expression carries social cost: a 2012 study found 55% of Armenians would end a relationship with a friend or relative who came out, and 70% find LGBT people 'strange'; in 2014 the Iravunk newspaper published a list of dozens of Armenian LGBT Facebook accounts calling them 'zombies', and the Court of Appeals ruled the newspaper had not offended anyone, ordering plaintiffs to pay 50,000 dram (~US$120) to the newspaper. Transgender activist Lilit Martirosyan, who in April 2019 became the first transgender person to speak at Armenia's National Assembly, received numerous death threats via Facebook and email, and in February 2020 a nationalist party member attempted to 'clean up' the same lectern by burning incense over it, denouncing her speech as a desecration. Wikipedia country coverage: The source text does not describe Armenian visa, passport, or entry screening rules for transgender travelers. It does document one asylum case relevant to entry and status: on 30 January 2024, the administrative court of Yerevan granted asylum and refugee status to Salman Mukayev, a Russian citizen from Chechnya who had applied for protection fearing persecution for homosexuality, with the ruling grounded in concerns about repressive treatment of the LGBT community in both Chechnya and Russia. The text also notes that following the 2022 Russo-Ukrainian war there has been an influx of LGBTQ Russians into Yerevan. Wikipedia country coverage: Facilities and spaces serving LGBT people are concentrated and fragile. Most LGBTQ-friendly spaces in Armenia are in central Yerevan, particularly near the opera house and the Cascade, and after the 2018 revolution a nascent underground clubbing culture developed at venues such as Relokant and the now-closed Poligraf, a nightclub known as a safe space for the LGBTQ+ community. In the military, conscripted gay men have reported being given a separate set of tableware, being forced to live in restrooms, and being forced to clean restrooms, with some subjected to physical violence or sexual assault by other soldiers; since 2001 homosexuality has been treated as an illness making gay men unfit for service, and since 2018 a health ministry decree exempting those with a 'personality disorder' has frequently been applied to LGBTQ individuals, with gay men who disclose their sexuality facing additional invasive psychiatric examinations during conscription. Wikipedia country coverage: Police custody and treatment of LGBT detainees are documented as abusive and declining in trust. In April 2023, police raided Poligraf in Yerevan, detaining over forty individuals; Pink Armenia's chairperson Lilit Avetisyan stated that officers 'laid all those present on the ground, used violence, took everyone to the police department, and started mocking them, mainly based on their clothing and sexual orientation.' A 2025 Pink Armenia report highlights the LGBT+ community's declining trust in law enforcement. Earlier, in 2004 after the killing of openly gay American Joshua Haglund, police briefly jailed several of his local gay acquaintances while trying to present the killing as a crime of passion, and his family's attorneys said law enforcement badly mistreated gay men and ignored key facts. A 2017 US State Department report cited arbitrary arrest and detention and failure to protect LGBT+ individuals from violence; in 2010 Yerevan's mayor ordered police to use force against suspected homosexuals and 'transvestites', and in both the 2018 Shurnukh mob attack (nine activists injured, two hospitalized) and the 2023 vigil for the murdered trans woman Adriana (eggs, bottles and stones thrown at over 100 mourners), attackers were released or police present did not intervene. As of 2025 the Council of Europe is providing training to Armenian police officers, prosecutors and investigators to identify and investigate hate-motivated incidents on SOGIESC grounds. Wikipedia country coverage: Asylum cases exist: on 30 January 2024 the administrative court of Yerevan granted asylum and refugee status to Salman Mukayev, a Russian citizen from Chechnya who feared persecution for homosexuality in Chechnya and Russia. Since the 2022 Russo-Ukrainian war Armenia's capital Yerevan has also seen an influx of LGBTQ Russians. Entry-related protection appears limited, however, since the source reports no legal framework protecting LGBT individuals from discrimination and notes declining community trust in law enforcement. Wikipedia country coverage: Most LGBTQ-friendly spaces in Armenia are concentrated in central Yerevan, particularly near the opera house and the Cascade, and a nascent underground queer clubbing culture developed after the 2018 Armenian Revolution at venues such as Relokant and Poligraf. Poligraf, a nightclub known as a safe space for the LGBTQ community, was raided by police in April 2023, with over forty people detained, and the venue is now closed. Ballroom and drag communities have also developed in the capital. No LGBT-specific health or shelter facilities are described, though a 2018 health ministry decree exempting people with a "personality disorder" from conscription has frequently been applied to LGBTQ individuals. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth is an explicit policy target: in 2013 Armenian police proposed a bill to outlaw "non-traditional sexual relationships" and the promotion of LGBT "propaganda" to youth, modeled on the Russian law; NGOs including Pink Armenia condemned it and the bill failed to pass. The age of consent in Armenia is 16, regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Attitudes shaping youth exposure are strongly negative: a 2012 study found 70% of Armenians view LGBT people as "strange," and 55% said they would end a relationship with a friend or relative who came out as gay. Diaspora youth context is also documented, with conservative Armenian-Americans staging large anti-LGBT+ protests in Glendale, California in June 2023 after a child brought rainbow stickers home from school.

In May 2012 a Molotov cocktail was thrown at a gay-friendly bar in the capital and a fire set; police took twelve hours to respond, though two suspects were later detained through CCTV footage. The public-opinion measure puts acceptance at 5 out of 100, indicating a social environment where visible trans presence draws hostility well beyond central areas of the capital.

The capital has an organised community, with a national human rights NGO and a trans-led rights organisation operating locally. Visibility outside those networks remains a source of risk rather than protection.
ARM.blindOutOfScope:
No source in the current inventory addresses border control, visa issuance or document-screening practice as it affects trans travellers, including what happens if a passport gender marker does not match presentation. That question remains unresolved here.

The requirement that legal gender change be preceded by surgery is sourced to a comparison aggregator rather than to the text of the national legislation itself; the governing statute was not supplied for verification. The same applies to the characterisation of hate-crime protection as 'ambiguous since 2022' and to the restricted status of gender-affirming care.

The 5/100 public-acceptance figure comes from the aggregator's methodology and has not been corroborated against a domestic polling source. The international mission report dates from 2009 and describes conditions at that time rather than the present.
blindSourceSummaries: Local rights organisation’s annual report on the human-rights situation of LGBT+ people in this nation during 2024: documents discrimination, torture and inhuman/degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion targeting LGBT people, violations of private and family life, education and work rights, and hate speech — including a chapter on pressure around a trans individual participating in a beauty pageant.

Comparison service covering this nation and two neighbours: this nation decriminalised in 2003; legal gender change is legal but requires surgery (since 2006); gender-affirming care is restricted; no nonbinary recognition; hate-crime protections ‘ambiguous’ since 2022; no protection statute; same-sex marriage banned. Public-opinion acceptance scores are very low.

Regional monitors’ fact-finding mission report (Feb 2009): comprehensive mission report covering visibility, coming out, societal and institutional hostility, media coverage, discrimination, harassment and violence, community organising, and legislation affecting LGBT people in this nation.

Community blog (May 2012): arson attack on the gay-friendly community bar in the capital — Molotov cocktail thrown, fire set; police took 12 hours to respond; two suspects detained via security cameras — documents anti-LGBT hate violence in this nation.

News report (April 2019): this nation’s first registered trans woman received death threats (including legislators calling for her to be burned alive) after a historic speech in the national assembly on LGBTI discrimination — documents extreme political hostility toward trans people.
ARM.blindLocalsOnly:
Residents seeking legal gender recognition must complete a medicalised administrative procedure, and the change is conditioned on surgery. Gender-affirming care is restricted in availability, and there is no legal category for non-binary people.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, education, housing or services, since the 2018 anti-discrimination bill failed. Hate-crime treatment of bias-motivated attacks is ambiguous, which affects the recourse available after violence.

LGBT residents documented in the 2024 annual report continue to face inhuman or degrading treatment, including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion, alongside violations of private and family life. A national human rights NGO and a trans-led organisation provide the principal organised support and advocacy in the capital.
ARM.tangentialFactors:
Regional comparison matters for expectation-setting: Equaldex's three-way comparison of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia places Armenia at the decriminalised end of the spectrum, while Azerbaijan retains criminalisation. A visitor crossing the border should not read Armenia's domestic tolerance as a regional norm.

The institutional picture has been documented for a long period. The ILGA-Europe and COC fact-finding mission report 'Forced Out: LGBT People in Armenia' (February 2009) covers societal and institutional homophobia, media coverage, discrimination, harassment and violence, and the state of legislation affecting LGBT people; the 2024 findings above indicate that several of those patterns persist fifteen years on.

Public hostility is not confined to informal settings. The 2019 threats against Lilit Martirosyan originated from serving members of parliament, and the 2024 report records organised pressure around a trans person's participation in a public event.

AZE.name: Azerbaijan
AZE.summary:
Police conduct is the clearest documented danger. In September 2017, national police in the capital detained dozens of LGBT people on dubious charges and beatings were documented; at least 60 people were imprisoned or fined, and the raids formed part of a wave of arrests ahead of an international sporting event. In July 2023, officers raided a private birthday party at which queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats of being outed.

A trans woman was murdered in the capital in March 2024, and the police investigation into the killing was inadequate. The response of the authorities is as significant as the violence itself: nothing in the record indicates that the state treats the killing of a trans woman as a matter requiring a serious investigation.

In April 2024 the European Court of Human Rights issued a ruling on the September 2017 arrests and mistreatment of LGBTI people, a matter the Azerbaijani government had acknowledged in 2019. The judgment addresses state conduct that the authorities themselves conceded had occurred.

Hostile messaging originates in official and state-affiliated media. State-affiliated Real TV aired discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people after a Women's Day march demanding access to trans healthcare. Media monitoring by QueeRadar found 77% of 428 analysed pieces hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people, and an activist was told to remove a rainbow flag from a cafe in Baku.

For a visitor, the practical reading is that contact with police carries a risk of mistreatment rather than an expectation of protection, and that visible signs of LGBTI affiliation can attract hostile attention from media and officials in both public and semi-public settings.
AZE.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources reviewed here do not address whether gender expression or gender identity is criminalised in Azerbaijan, what penalties might apply, or whether any statute regulates public order in ways used against trans people. That question is unresolved on this inventory.

Entry and visa rules, gender markers on passports and other travel documents, and border screening practices are not covered by these sources and remain unsourced.

The outcome of the investigation into the March 2024 murder of a trans woman is not stated in the material reviewed, and whether charges were brought is unresolved.

Access to healthcare, including hormone therapy or gender-affirming care, appears only as the subject of a Women's Day march demand; no source here describes the availability of such care to a visitor.

Hate-crime legislation and its application to anti-trans violence are not addressed in this inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The Gender Resource Center (Gender Resurs Mərkəzi), established in 2020, is described as a queer-feminist platform created in direct response to the lack of safe space and resources for people of different genders and sexual orientations in Azerbaijan. AZAD LGBT also ran in-person programming in Baku, including LGBTQ movie nights attended by a local psychologist who joined post-film Q&As. Wikipedia country coverage: Forced medical examinations were among the abuses inflicted on at least 100 members of Baku's LGBTQIA+ community arrested in September 2017. Transgender people cannot change their gender on official documents (though they may change their name to match their gender identity), and LGBTQIA+ military conscripts can be declared unfit for service under Articles 18/b (personality disorders) and 17/b (reactive psychoses and neurotic disorders) of the Regulation on Military Medical Examinations. Gender and Development, created in 2007, runs local projects in collaboration with the Ministry of Health. Youth-specific: 14-year-old Elina Hajiyeva died in April 2019 after a suicide attempt linked to unaddressed homophobic bullying at her school in Baku, where the principal failed to call an ambulance; the Ministry of Education launched a bullying action plan on 13 May 2019 and established a hotline. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples are not legally recognised in Azerbaijan; same-sex marriage and civil unions are neither recognized nor performed, and same-sex couples are not allowed to adopt children. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned. ILGA-Europe has ranked Azerbaijan last (49 of 49) in Europe every year since 2015, citing 'a near total absence of legal protection.' Wikipedia country coverage: In April 2019, 14-year-old Elina Hajiyeva of Baku died two days after a suicide attempt driven by homophobic bullying her school ignored; the principal was convicted on 24 October 2019 by the Sabail District Court of negligence resulting in death and sentenced to 2 years and 2.5 months of restriction of liberty plus 18,500 AZN ($10,882) compensation, while the school director, deputy director and psychologist were dismissed. The case triggered a nationwide social-media anti-bullying campaign and a Ministry of Education action plan announced 13 May 2019 to ensure a healthy environment in general education institutions, improve school-family relations and protect students from abuse, alongside a new hotline. On the education-resource side, AZAD LGBT launched a website in 2015 providing free online LGBTQ education tools, and Minority Magazine covers education topics. The age of consent is 16 for both heterosexual and homosexual sex. Wikipedia country coverage: Azerbaijan's constitution guarantees freedom of expression for everyone by all forms of expression, and the Azerbaijan Press Council (founded 2003) handles complaints under a Press Code of Conduct, though it is unknown whether it has assessed complaints of state-controlled media using homosexuality to discredit government critics. Media has been criticized for spreading fear and hate toward queer people through discriminatory language and negative portrayals, with politicians and officials using it to shape public perception; Vahid Aliyev of the Minority Azerbaijan webpage criticized this unprofessionalism. The 2017 US State Department report listed interference in the freedoms of expression, assembly and association through intimidation, incarceration on questionable charges and blocking of websites. LGBTQIA+ expression nonetheless exists: gay.az, the first news website for LGBTQIA+ people, launched 25 May 2011 (Ruslan Balukhin), and Minority Magazine, the first LGBTQIA+ online magazine, was founded by Samad Ismayilov in December 2015, becoming an NGO in August 2017; Ismayilov's documentary about a trans man premiered in Baku on 25 November 2017 with Dutch embassy support, drawing about 80 people. Wikipedia country coverage: The source describes medical and safe-space facility issues rather than visitor facilities: in September 2017 at least 100 members of Baku's LGBTQIA+ community were arrested in a crackdown ostensibly on prostitution, and detainees were subjected to beatings, interrogation, forced medical examinations and blackmail; the 2017 US State Department report added that police threatened rape and used electric shocks on detainees. By law, no groups are excluded from blood donation apart from people infected with HIV/AIDS, but it is unknown whether men who have sex with men are de facto permitted to donate. The Gender Resource Center, established in 2020, was created specifically in response to a lack of safe space and resources for people of different genders and sexual orientations. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples are not legally recognised in Azerbaijan: same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognized or performed, and same-sex couples are not allowed to adopt children. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned. On the international side, Nafas LGBTI Azerbaijan Alliance regularly holds talks with the EU Delegation to Azerbaijan and other European embassies about the difficulties LGBTQ people face, and the Dutch embassy supported the 2017 Baku screening of a documentary about a trans man. Critics have argued Azerbaijan should not be allowed to host international events because of its discrimination against LGBTQIA+ people, a controversy that flared around Eurovision 2012. Wikipedia country coverage: In April 2019, 14-year-old Elina Hajiyeva of Baku attempted suicide after homophobic bullying at her school; the principal took no action, tried to attribute the attempt to family difficulties, did not call an ambulance, and Hajiyeva died in hospital two days later. The school director, deputy director and psychologist were dismissed, and on 24 October 2019 the Sabail District Court of Baku sentenced the principal to 2 years and 2.5 months of restricted liberty plus 18,500 AZN ($10,882) compensation. The case sparked a nationwide social media campaign, a video by 2011 Eurovision winner Nigar Jamal to President Ilham Aliyev, and a Ministry of Education anti-bullying action plan launched 13 May 2019 with a new hotline. The age of consent is equal for heterosexual and homosexual sex at 16; AZAD LGBT concentrates on education and in 2015 launched a website with free online LGBTQ education tools, and Minority Magazine covers education issues. Azerbaijan also mandates military conscription for able-bodied men aged 18 to 35, under which LGBTQIA+ enlistees can be deemed unfit under Articles 18/b and 17/b of the Regulation on Military Medical Examinations, and queer conscripts often conceal their orientation to avoid dedovshchina hazing.

KAZ.name: Kazakhstan
KAZ.summary:
Kazakhstan carries no direct legal exposure for a trans visitor. Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, no statute restricts changing clothes according to gender presentation, no bathroom or facilities restriction applies, and no propaganda law is in force. Police conduct toward trans people is described as unhelpful rather than predatory, with no recorded pattern of police targeting.

A propaganda ban is nonetheless under active consideration. In June 2024 the Ministry of Culture and Information confirmed it was reviewing the petition 'We Are against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda in Kazakhstan!', filed by the Union of Parents, which met the threshold for government consideration. Human Rights Watch warned on 10 July 2024 that the proposed ban would violate rights nationwide. A visitor should treat the current absence of a propaganda statute as the state of the law today, not as a settled position.

Legal gender recognition exists but is heavily medicalised. Psychiatric board assessment and surgery requirements are applied in practice, so a visitor whose documents do not match presentation should expect no administrative route to reconcile them while in the country.

The documentation of bias violence is weak. The OSCE/ODIHR hate crime reporting summary for 2024 records that Kazakhstan has not reported hate-crime data since its 2018 report and has no nominated National Point of Contact for hate crimes, with victim-support and awareness measures identified as lacking. A visitor who experiences bias violence would encounter a reporting machinery with no designated entry point.

Recorded incidents remain real. An international monitoring body recorded 62 anti-LGBTI bias incidents in Kazakhstan in 2024. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review covering January to December 2023 documents an LGBTQI activist almost run over in a bias-motivated attack that drew no investigation, and an LGBTQI+ education NGO refused registration of its employment site after listing its focus as its stated activity.

Trans-specific movement into the country is documented: ILGA-Europe records a wave of transgender people arriving from Russia since 2022, indicating cross-border entry by trans people without a legal barrier to arrival.

Social risk operates alongside a functioning legal remedy. Kazakhstan's Supreme Court ordered compensation in September 2019 from a Facebook user who posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments, rejecting a 'moral foundations' defence in favour of privacy rights. The two women fled Kazakhstan for eight months fearing for their safety before the ruling, which measures the gap between what the courts will protect and what daily life imposes.

For a visitor the assessment is: no legal exposure, low visibility for anyone who does not disclose, main cities presenting no practical difficulty, and social hostility rather than the state as the operative risk.
KAZ.outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the Union of Parents propaganda petition after June 2024 is unresolved in the available sources; no source confirms whether it advanced to drafting, was shelved, or produced legislation.

Whether the 62 anti-LGBTI bias incidents recorded in 2024 are disaggregated for trans victims is not sourced, so the trans-specific share of that count cannot be stated.

Whether the psychiatric board and surgery requirements for legal gender recognition are codified in subordinate regulation or applied as administrative practice is not sourced here; the inventory supports 'applied in practice' only.

Whether Kazakhstan has since resumed hate-crime reporting to ODIHR or nominated a National Point of Contact after the 2024 summary is unresolved.

No source in this inventory documents a trans-specific physical assault with a named victim and a dated outcome, so the violence findings rest on the activist incident recorded for 2023 and the aggregate 2024 count.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6, D13.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review covering Jan–Dec 2023 (Kazakhstan): documents access-to-services bias (an LGBTQI+ education NGO denied employment-site registration after listing its focus), bias-motivated violence (an LGBTQI activist almost run over with no investigation), and a wave of transgender people arriving from Russia since 2022.

OSCE/ODIHR Hate Crime Reporting 2024 summary for Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan has not reported hate-crime data to ODIHR since the 2018 report, has no nominated National Point of Contact for hate crimes, and would benefit from victim-support and awareness measures — an institutional-gap finding on documentation of bias violence.

HRW (10 Jul 2024): in June 2024 the Ministry of Culture and Information said it was reviewing a 'We Are against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda in Kazakhstan!' petition (Union of Parents) that met the threshold for government consideration; HRW warns the proposed ban would violate rights nationwide — a live, dated legislative threat.

ECOM (2024): ECOM has monitored and documented rights violations against LGBT people since 2017. Its analysis identifies health-right barriers across the EECA region and in individual countries including Kazakhstan, alongside informal behavioural practices that policy analysis misses.

HRW (24 Sep 2019): Kazakhstan's Supreme Court ordered compensation from a Facebook user who posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments — privacy rights upheld over a 'moral foundations' defence; the women fled Kazakhstan for eight months fearing for safety, illustrating both the privacy remedy and the social risk.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults has been legal since late 1997 (de jure 1998), when Article 104 of the Penal Code criminalising 'buggery' was repealed and a common age of consent of 16 was introduced; lesbianism was never a criminal offence. However, on 30 December 2025 President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a law banning 'information containing propaganda of pedophilia and/or non-traditional sexual orientation' in public spaces and media, with violations punishable by a 10-day arrest and a fine. The Mäjilis had approved a harsher version on 12 November 2025, and Kazakhstan now sits alongside Russia, Hungary and Georgia in prohibiting 'LGBTQ propaganda' by law. Wikipedia country coverage: Since 2003 transgender people in Kazakhstan may change legal gender on identity documents, but only after a diagnosis of 'gender identity disorder' involving medical tests and a 30-day psychiatric evaluation by a medical commission. Applicants must pay around ₸100,000 tenge, and although since 2023 commissions can in principle be assembled in every region, in practice the only functioning one is in Almaty because of requirements for separate specialist rooms. A positive decision yields a certificate valid for six months to start medical transition, and since 2011 document changes require gender-affirming surgery, hormone therapy and sterilisation; people under 21 cannot change gender on documents at all. Wikipedia country coverage: As of 2020 same-sex couples cannot legally adopt children in Kazakhstan, and in February 2024 President Tokayev signed a law prohibiting adoption of orphans by same-sex couples. Deputy Minister of Education Natalya Jumadildaeva stated that a parent's sexual orientation would play a 'key role' in approval, assessed through a 'special psychological test'. Critics, including independent media, noted the law was modelled on Russian legislation. Wikipedia country coverage: Kazakhstan does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. No laws exist protecting LGBTQ people from discrimination in employment, education, housing, health care, public accommodations or credit, and 89% of people opposed same-sex marriage in a 2015-16 Pew survey.

Legal gender recognition for residents is medicalised rather than administrative. Psychiatric board assessment and surgery requirements are applied in practice, which sets the document conditions residents live under and shapes what identification a trans resident can present.

Health-right barriers affecting LGBT people in Kazakhstan are documented in ECOM's regional analysis, which has monitored and recorded rights violations against LGBT people since 2017. The analysis identifies both formal barriers and informal behavioural practices that routine policy assessment misses.

Access to services is biased at the registration level: an LGBTQI+ education NGO was refused employment-site registration in 2023 after listing its focus, which constrains how organisations serving LGBT residents can operate openly.

Residents reporting bias violence have no designated National Point of Contact and no hate-crime data channel to ODIHR, so there is no institutional route through which patterned violence enters official statistics or triggers victim support.

The 2019 Supreme Court privacy ruling gives residents a civil remedy against exposure and organised harassment, established against a 'moral foundations' defence. Its practical value sits beside the fact that the two women in that case had already left the country for eight months by the time it was decided.
KAZ.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Peru (0.48) and just below the USA/Mexico (0.50) — Kazakhstan has no institutional hostility machinery but a far weaker protection floor — and above Armenia (0.46) and Turkey (0.47).

For a visitor the assessment is: no legal exposure, low visibility for anyone who does not disclose, main population centres presenting no practical difficulty, and social hostility rather than the state as the operative risk.

KAZ.tangentialFactors:
Within its region Kazakhstan stands as the most liveable country in Central Asia for trans people, a relative statement that does not lift it to the standard of European jurisdictions. The comparison matters mainly for expectation-setting: the floor is low, and the ceiling here is not high.

The June 2024 propaganda petition is the principal source of legal turbulence. It has not produced legislation in the sources available, but it is a dated, documented and government-acknowledged attempt that would, if enacted, restrict public expression about LGBT people nationwide.

Documentation capacity is a variable worth holding alongside incident counts. Kazakhstan's silence toward ODIHR since 2018 means official statistics understate bias violence, so the 62 incidents recorded by civil-society monitoring in 2024 should be read as a floor rather than a total.

Regional displacement affects the picture. Transgender people have been arriving from Russia since 2022, and the presence of a documented inflow suggests Kazakhstan is being used as a destination by people leaving a worse regime, not as a transit hazard.

A civil-society layer exists and is visible in the record: monitoring and litigation by Feminita and ECOM, and a Supreme Court privacy precedent that a visitor could in principle invoke.

UZB.name: Uzbekistan
UZB.summary:
Article 120 of Uzbekistan's 1994 Criminal Code criminalises consensual same-sex conduct between men and carries a penalty of up to three years' imprisonment. Human Dignity Trust and the UK Home Office's country-policy note of July 2024 both record the offence as in force, and the Home Office documents Article 120 cases prosecuted between 2009 and 2023, so the provision is applied rather than dormant.

Trans visitors fall inside this exposure. There is no legal gender recognition in Uzbekistan, so a trans person remains legally their sex assigned at birth, and Human Dignity Trust notes that transgender people may be prosecuted under Article 120 on that basis. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 states that police target gay and bisexual men and trans women with arbitrary detention, prosecution and imprisonment.

Enforcement is entangled with extortion. The US State Department's 2023 human rights report records that LGBTQI+ people are arrested and then released, or threatened with arrest unless they pay bribes, and that police coerce LGBTQI+ people into informing on others under threat of prison. Human Rights Watch reported in March 2021 that gay and bisexual men face discrimination, violence, blackmail and extortion from both state and non-state actors with almost no effective protections.

Custodial abuse is documented and unpunished. The 2021 US State Department report records torture and ill-treatment, arbitrary detention in custody, and social stigma and violence against LGBT people under the criminalised framework. Human Rights Watch's 2024 chapter reports that forced examinations, which the WHO treats as torture, are used against detainees, and that impunity for police ill-treatment persists.

Because the conduct is a criminal offence, the framework itself blocks recourse: a person accused under Article 120 cannot safely approach the authorities about violence committed against them. Human Rights Watch's 2021 assessment of near-total absence of protection is consistent with the State Department's findings of stigma and abuse in custody.

Community infrastructure cannot operate in the open. The UK Home Office notes that LGBTI organisations cannot register and work unofficially, and that rural taboos drive discrimination outside the capital. The US State Department reports that websites and bloggers self-censor on LGBTQI+ issues and that societal harassment continued through 2023.

ECOM's 2024 national report on Uzbekistan examines the legislative framework, anti-discrimination provisions, criminalisation of HIV transmission, legal gender recognition, access to human rights, and the rights to health and to work, indicating that medical and employment settings are additional sites of exposure alongside the criminal law.
UZB.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents a specific case of a trans visitor being prosecuted under Article 120; the risk assessment rests on the legal mechanism of birth-sex status combined with police targeting of trans women, which is sourced but not tied to a named visitor case.

The inventory does not state whether Uzbek identity-document or visa rules restrict entry on gender-identity grounds, or whether any screening at the border risks disclosure; that question remains unsourced here.

Whether Article 120 has been applied to trans women through the birth-sex theory specifically, as distinct from general police targeting, is not resolved by these sources.

The US State Department's 2021 findings are now dated relative to the 2023 and 2024 reports, and the ECOM 2024 report's individual findings are known only by scope in this inventory, not by content.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6, D12, D13.
