NIC.name: Nicaragua
NIC.summary:
Nicaragua does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or trans identity. The penal code that took effect in March 2008 repealed the 1992 sodomy provision, which had carried one to three years' imprisonment and whose vague wording had also been usable against LGBT-rights campaigning and sexual-health work.

Formal legality does not translate into protection. The US State Department's 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices in Nicaragua documents a police and parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived opponents of the government that authorities did not investigate or prosecute, and lists violence or threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex persons among the year's significant human rights violations. The official US assessment places anti-LGBTI abuse inside a broader climate of state impunity.

Amnesty International's May 2019 reporting on the crackdown that followed the April 2018 protests records at least 325 people killed and more than 2,000 injured, according to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights. The same reporting describes journalist Miguel Mora being beaten by a pro-government mob and states that he was targeted in part for being gay, an instance of homophobia operating inside the political repression rather than beside it.

For a visitor, the practical consequence is that no effective domestic recourse is visible in these sources: they document non-investigation and non-prosecution of state-linked violence, and Amnesty International describes a continuing government crackdown on independent media after the 2018 protests. Nothing in the source set identifies a functioning domestic complaint mechanism or civil-society channel through which a trans visitor harmed in Nicaragua could obtain redress.
NIC.outOfScopeNotes:
The Franklin & Marshall Global Barometers entry for Nicaragua records no documented finding for this jurisdiction, so survey-based evidence on public attitudes toward LGBT people remains unresolved here.

Recent trans-specific figures, including counts of trans women killed over the past two and a half years and NGO tallies of violence against LGBTIQ+ people in 2024, are not carried in the current source set and are unverified for this record.

The sources assembled do not address legal gender recognition or marker changes on Nicaraguan passports, entry or visa screening of trans travellers, restroom and facility access rules, restrictions on gender-affirming healthcare, hate-crime sentencing provisions, or recognition of same-sex partners. None of these can be stated either way from this inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D3, D4, D5, D6, D13.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: A 1992 law (Article 204 of the Criminal Code), added by social Christians to a bill originally meant to protect women from rape, made it an offence punishable by up to three years' prison to "induce, promote, propagandize, or practice sex among persons of the same sex in a scandalous manner"; it was signed by President Violeta Chamorro in July 1992, the Supreme Court rejected an unconstitutionality appeal in March 1994, and the language was dropped when a new Penal Code took effect on 1 March 2008. Separately, the source notes that media reporting is largely suppressed in Nicaragua as much of the media has been since the 2018 protests, which limits coverage of LGBT issues. Wikipedia country coverage: In June 2014 the Nicaraguan Congress approved a revised Family Code limiting marriage, partnerships and adoption to heterosexual couples; it took effect on 8 April 2015, and several organizations filed an action of unconstitutionality against it. Same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal benefits and protections available to opposite-sex married couples. Wikipedia country coverage: Discrimination based on sexual orientation is banned in access to health services: Article 3(l) of Law N° 820 (promotion, protection and defence of human rights in the face of HIV and AIDS) prohibits discrimination on sexual orientation grounds, and Article 1 of Ministerial Resolution 671-2014 prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression in access to health services. No youth-specific care-access findings appear in the source text. Wikipedia country coverage: Article 315 of the Penal Code (offences against labour rights) makes discrimination based on "sexual option" punishable by up to one year in prison, covering employment. Article 3(l) of Law N° 820 prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation in the HIV/AIDS context, Ministerial Resolution 671-2014 bars it in health services, and Article 36(5) of the Penal Code makes discrimination based on sexual orientation an aggravating circumstance when committing any criminal offence. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples receive no equal legal benefits or protections. The June 2014 Family Code (effective 8 April 2015) limits marriage, partnerships and adoption to heterosexual couples, and Article 72 of the Constitution defines marriage and stable unions as resting on voluntary agreement between a man and a woman. On 9 January 2018 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an advisory opinion that parties to the American Convention on Human Rights must grant same-sex couples access to all domestic family-registration figures including marriage; the source does not record any Nicaraguan implementation of it. Wikipedia country coverage: Violence against the LGBTQ community is described as generally culturally accepted and legally unenforced, with attacks largely unreported out of fear of retaliation and poor legal outcomes; a 2012 Center for Justice and International Law survey counted 53 aggressions between 1999 and 2011, including 15 murders (10 gay men, 4 transgender people, 1 lesbian), with the true figure expected to be higher. NGO Programa Feminista La Corriente reported 67 assaults, 1 hate crime/murder and 2 suicides in 2021; 39 assaults, 3 hate crimes and 1 suicide in 2022; 35 assaults, 2 hate crimes, 1 murder, 1 suicide, 2 sexual assaults and 1 extortion in 2023; and 13 assaults, 5 hate crimes and 1 missing person in the first two quarters of 2024 — with trans women the most targeted group and state police among the aggressors (tied with family members in 2022). Public opinion is largely opposed: a Pew survey of 9 November–13 December 2013 found 77% opposed same-sex marriage, 16% in favour, 7% unsure, while the 2017 AmericasBarometer showed 24.5% support. Visibility is uneven — gay men are generally more visible in public than lesbians, who often socialise privately — and an annual Gay Pride celebration has been held in Managua around 28 June since the country's first public pride festival in 1991.

GUY.name: Guyana
GUY.summary:
Guyana is one of five countries in the Western Hemisphere that still criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Sections 352 to 354 of the Criminal Law Act create offences of gross indecency and attempted buggery, and buggery carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment. Prosecutions are rare, but the provisions anchor stigma against LGBT people and give police a vocabulary of threat.

No legal gender recognition exists. The direct anti-cross-dressing offence, section 153(1)(xlvii) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act, derived from an 1893 statute, was struck down by the Caribbean Court of Justice in November 2018 in McEwan v Attorney General, which held it unconstitutionally vague and a violation of freedom of expression. The challenge was filed in 2010 with SASOD after trans women were arrested in 2009 and held for three nights under the same provision.

Violence against trans women is documented and persistent. At the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights' 191st session in Washington in November 2024, a hearing requested by the Guyana Equality Forum heard testimony from Blossom Inc., SASOD and the Guyana Sex Work Coalition on the impact of gender-based violence on migrant women, sex workers and trans women; Commission chair Roberta Clarke called on Guyana to take urgent action. The record carries 69 documented cases of violence against trans women between 2018 and 2022.

The justice system has failed trans complainants directly. In January 2017 trans woman Petronella Trotman was stabbed in Georgetown with scissors, sustaining a neck wound, and pelted with glass bottles. When the matter came before magistrate Dylon Bess on 2 March 2017, she was told to "dress like a man," refused entry to the courtroom, and the case was dismissed; the prosecution had rested on the 1893 cross-dressing offence, whose "improper purpose" test left the outcome to the magistrate's discretion.

Policing remains a risk in its own right. SASOD documented in May 2019 that officers use residual clauses of the Summary Jurisdiction Act to extort LGBT people, threatening men found in "compromising positions" with arrest to extract bribes, harassing same-sex couples at seawalls and parks, and leaving complainants who file formal reports to face secondary discrimination at stations and give watered-down accounts. Loitering and vagrancy provisions remain usable against LGBT populations, particularly sex workers.

Public attitudes have shifted measurably: a 2022 poll recorded 72% acceptance, with hostility 13 percentage points lower than in 2013. Five of six parties in the 2025 general election, including the ruling party, backed decriminalisation, though no repeal has followed. There is no anti-discrimination legislation; the UN Human Rights Committee called for such legislation in April 2024. A small organised community operates in Georgetown through SASOD and allied groups.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Guyana retains colonial-era criminal provisions — Section 351 (gross indecency, up to 2 years' imprisonment) and Section 353 (buggery, life imprisonment) of the Criminal Law (Offences) Act 1893 — kept in force after independence, and a constitutional 'savings clause' blocks judicial review of such inherited laws even where they undermine human rights. Cross-dressing was decriminalized only on 13 November 2018, when the Caribbean Court of Justice struck Section 153(1)(XLVII) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act as unconstitutional, archaic and vague. No legal gender recognition procedure is described in the source. Document access is illustrated by a trans woman who on 2 March 2017 was denied entry to the Georgetown Magistrates Court because she was not 'dressed like a man', after which her case against her attacker was dismissed. Wikipedia country coverage: SASOD managing director Joel Simpson stated in May 2019 that discriminatory laws have enabled law enforcement to extort LGBTQ people, with recorded cases of victims blackmailed by police who threatened arrest under the sodomy laws; hate crimes often go unreported. SASOD has been working with health professionals to improve their knowledge of LGBTQ people, and with the University of Guyana and nursing schools across the country. Discrimination and violence at the hands of law enforcement, religious leaders and others are described as widespread, leading most LGBTQ people to hide their orientation. No youth-specific or minor-specific care findings appear in the source. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex marriage and civil unions do not exist in Guyana. On adoption, the U.S. Department of State reports that LGBTQ people are not disqualified from adopting, and both married and single people may adopt; in December 2015 the Director of Guyana's Childcare and Protection Agency stated the CPA does not discriminate, as no laws bar LGBTQ individuals or same-sex couples from adopting, fostering or serving as guardians, and encouraged LGBTQ people to become adoptive parents. Public support is low but shifting: 14% backed legalizing same-sex marriage in the 2013 CADRES survey, while LAPOP's AmericasBarometer score for support of same-sex marriage rose from 7.2 (2010) to 20.6 (2017) on a 0–100 scale, against an Americas average of 26.8.

Decriminalisation has cross-party political cover rather than opponents: five of the six parties contesting the 2025 election, the ruling party among them, campaigned in favour of repealing the same-sex conduct provisions, which places the barrier to reform in legislative scheduling rather than declared policy.

Public opinion is no longer the obstacle it was a decade ago. The 2022 acceptance figure of 72% and the 13-point fall in hostility since 2013 suggest a social climate more permissive than the statute book implies, which bears on how much risk a visibly trans visitor attracts in public space.

The 2018 Caribbean Court of Justice judgment is the template for challenging vague morality offences in the region, and it removed the single provision most likely to be used against a trans person in the street or a public building. Sustained legal advocacy exists and is well connected internationally: SASOD brought the McEwan challenge, its officers testify before the Inter-American Commission, and Guyana Equality Forum secured the November 2024 hearing. Allied groups including Blossom Inc. and the Guyana Sex Work Coalition work on violence against trans women specifically.

SUR.name: Suriname
SUR.summary:
Suriname has not criminalised consensual same-sex conduct since 1869. In March 2015 the Penal Code was amended so that Articles 175, 175a and 176 reach discrimination and hate speech grounded in sexual orientation, and a revision carried out after the 2011 Universal Periodic Review equalised the age of consent for same-sex and opposite-sex relations.

Protection rests on an implied reading rather than an explicit statute. Article 8.2 of the Surinamese Constitution lists 'any other status' among prohibited grounds, and the government treats that clause as extending to sexual orientation and gender identity. No statutory instrument enumerates sexual orientation or gender identity as protected grounds, and the LGBT Platform Suriname has repeatedly called for a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability.

Legal gender recognition is not available in Suriname. A trans visitor holding documents in a name or sex marker that does not match their presentation has no domestic procedure through which those documents can be aligned.

Formal guarantees have not removed daily exposure. A joint submission by LGBT Platform Suriname, Heartland Alliance and Akahata to the UN Human Rights Committee records that LGBTI people face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatization despite constitutional protection, and the US State Department's 2015 human rights report on Suriname documents discrimination against LGBTI persons and other minorities.

Before the Human Rights Committee in July 2024, Suriname's delegation asserted that national laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, citing monitoring bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission. Committee experts pressed the delegation on implementation of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' judgment concerning transgender identity, and that implementation remains open.

Civil society space exists on paper: LGBTI organisations can register in Suriname, and the LGBT Platform Suriname was founded on 29 August 2011.
SUR.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no entry, visa or border-screening procedure specific to trans travellers entering Suriname, and no information on whether documents are inspected against presentation at airports or land crossings. This is unresolved rather than cleared.

No data is sourced on trans-specific killings or assaults in Suriname with dates, perpetrators or outcomes, so the pattern of lethal violence cannot be assessed from this inventory.

Facilities law, access to hormones and transition-related healthcare, and any hate-crime sentencing enhancement beyond the March 2015 Penal Code discrimination and hate-speech provisions are not sourced here. Whether those Penal Code articles have been used in prosecutions is not recorded.

The content of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' judgment on transgender identity, the precise measures the Human Rights Committee experts asked Suriname to implement in July 2024, and the current status of that implementation are unresolved on this record.

The enforceability of the 'any other status' clause before Surinamese courts, and whether a trans litigant could rely on it in practice, are not sourced.

KGZ.name: Kyrgyzstan
KGZ.summary:
Kyrgyzstan presents a high-risk environment for trans visitors. Consensual same-sex conduct has been legal since 1998, with the age of consent equal at 16, but the legal machinery around gender has moved in the opposite direction: a 2020 amendment to the Law on Civil Status removed the provision allowing trans people to change their legal gender markers, and ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records that since 2021 trans people cannot obtain legal recognition at all under amendments to the law on civil acts.

Legal gender recognition is now unavailable in practice. TGEU's Trans Rights Index Map 2024 places Kyrgyzstan alongside Hungary, Bulgaria and Russia as states that removed the right to legal gender recognition, and scores Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan at only the bare minimum of not banning recognition, the floor of trans legal status in their wider grouping.

There is no relationship recognition to rely on: Kyrgyzstan has no same-sex marriage and no civil unions, and a 2016 constitutional amendment explicitly bans same-sex marriage.

Law enforcement is the sharpest day-to-day exposure. ECOM data cited by ILGA-Europe shows high levels of stigma and discrimination against trans people, particularly from police, and an extortion culture directed at LGBT people has been documented in the country.

An active anti-LGBT political campaign is running. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records legislative pushes against LGBT people accompanied by a media campaign of homophobic and transphobic statements from members of parliament, and two discriminatory laws targeting the LGBTI community and restricting LGBTI organisations were adopted in 2023-2024.

Organised public LGBT life in the capital has contracted to nothing. Reporting on the closure of Bishkek's only LGBT club, a car-wash venue at Asanbay, describes patrons entering furtively through a derelict yard and confirms that no other gay venue remained in the city; The Guardian's 19 October 2017 account of the same closure attributes the change to a ban on 'LGBT propaganda' and records patrons saying that all of them would be victims at some point.

Access to transition-related care is documented as a regional problem rather than a solved one: an ECOM study from 2024 examines trans people's access to medical services including HIV prevention and hormone replacement therapy across the eastern Europe and central Asia region, with country-level coordination covering Kyrgyzstan, and it includes information relevant to trans migrants.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The source states that reports of discrimination and violence against LGBTQ people in Kyrgyzstan are frequent, and that after the government launched legal reforms including an "anti-gay propaganda law" in 2014, there was a near 300% increase in attacks against LGBTQ people. Police officials were reported in 2018 to be blackmailing LGBTQ people on social media and dating sites, demanding between 5,000 and 30,000 soms (roughly 70 to 500 US dollars). In March 2019, after a march of about 400 people in Bishkek that was dubbed Kyrgyzstan's "first gay pride march," MP Jyldyz Musabekova publicly called for participants to be beaten, though other deputies condemned her remarks. The source also notes that LGBTQ people fear social ostracism from friends and family, especially in rural areas, and that Bishkek's only gay bar, London, closed in 2017. Wikipedia country coverage: The source documents a patchwork rather than protective framework: same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1998, with an age of consent of 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, but the constitution has explicitly banned same-sex marriage since 2016 and no same-sex unions are recognised. A 2014 bill criminalising expression creating a "positive attitude toward non-traditional sexual relations" via media or networks passed first reading 79–7 in October but ultimately expired without a final vote. On 14 August 2023 the president signed amendments to the child protection law (Article 2-1) expanding information deemed harmful to children to include content that "promotes non-traditional sexual relations," though the law does not define key terms or mention sexual orientation explicitly. No non-discrimination statute protecting LGBTQ people is described in the source. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth are a specific target: the August 2023 child protection law restricts children's access to information that "promotes non-traditional sexual relations," and the 2014 anti-propaganda-style bill was framed around media accessible to minors, echoing Russia's 2013 law on "propaganda...to minors." On transition care, Clause 47 of the Law on the Protection of the Health of Citizens was amended (from 2024) to bar trans people from accessing transition-related care before age 25, where previously the process could start at 18 — directly affecting trans youth and young adults. A draft law proposed on 30 January 2026 and passed first reading on 4 June 2026 would prohibit transgender individuals from changing gender markers and accessing gender-affirming care and surgeries, affecting minors as well. The age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

TJK.name: Tajikistan
TJK.summary:
Consensual same-sex relations have been legal in Tajikistan since 1998 and are legal throughout the country. The statutory position offers little practical protection: there is no protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity in Tajikistan's legislation, and a 2020 ECOM legislative analysis built from questionnaires completed by local partners identifies legal barriers and gaps affecting gay men, men who have sex with men and trans people, documenting cases where the written law protects but practice does not.

Authorities maintain a register of LGBTIQ people, introduced by police in 2016 and described by Outright International as a 2017 government registry of "proven" LGBT persons. ILGA-Europe's annual review for 2024 reports that police lure LGBT people into fake meetings in order to register them in a database, harvest their social-media contacts and extort money, with more than ten such cases recorded in Sughd province.

Raids conducted in 2022 and 2023 in several cities brought forced HIV testing and arbitrary criminal charges. The IPHR report documents ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion by police. In 2024 ECOM recorded 27 human-rights violation cases against LGBT people, involving arbitrary arrest by police, blackmail and extortion.

Forced or sham marriages are imposed on LGBT people, and police decline to intervene. The 2022 anti-discrimination law does not address discrimination on these grounds and only partially aligns with United Nations standards.

Access to care is a live concern: a 2024 ECOM study examines trans people's access to medical services, including HIV prevention and treatment and hormone replacement therapy, across the wider region, with a Tajikistan country coordinator contributing and guidance included for trans migrants.

For a visitor: there is no expression statute, but registry practices, police entrapment and the absence of any recourse make discovery dangerous. People who disclose their orientation or gender identity become targets of physical and psychological abuse, including abuse by police.
TJK.outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Rights Watch World Report 2025 chapter on Tajikistan contains no material on transgender prisoners or prison housing. Its detention references concern opposition figures and deportees rather than the placement or conditions of trans detainees, so the treatment of trans people in Tajikistani custody is unresolved on this inventory and should not be inferred either way.

Legal gender recognition, including whether a trans visitor or resident can change identity documents or gender markers, is not addressed by any source in this inventory. That question remains unresolved here rather than answered in the negative.

Entry, visa and border-screening rules for Tajikistan, including any document inspection that could disclose a traveller's trans status, are not covered by these sources and are unresolved.

The exact provisions of the 2022 anti-discrimination law are described only in general terms by the sources available; the specific articles, penalties and complaint mechanisms have not been verified.

Whether the police registry distinguishes trans people from lesbian, gay and bisexual registrants, and how many people it currently holds, is not stated in the inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Public expression of support for LGBTQ people is effectively suppressed: the country's public attitude toward LGBTQ people has been described as "entirely negative," with a state of "hypervisibility" in which homophobic and transphobic remarks from politicians have become part of everyday politics. The Supreme Mufti, Saidmukarram Abdulkodirzoda, has publicly called same-sex relations a "disaster," condemned countries legalising same-sex marriage, and spoken against human-rights activists and anti-discrimination laws. LGBTQ groups themselves operate anonymously — one NGO focuses solely on trans issues, another on general LGBTQ issues — and activists have no access to the Ministry of Health or other state authorities, making state-level advocacy impossible. Wikipedia country coverage: Medical facilities for trans people are effectively absent: gender-affirming medical services are not available in Tajikistan, so trans individuals must go abroad to medically transition, and most doctors have no expertise in treatments trans people need. Legal gender change is blocked in practice because although Tajik law allows reassignment on some documents, medical institutions issue no official documents for the purpose; a diagnosis of transsexualism is required, surgeries are required for transgender women but not men, evaluation is by commissions of three psychiatrists on an unregulated case-by-case basis, and activists say bribes are often necessary — only three to six people have successfully changed legal gender. A trans-focused NGO has drafted a hormone-replacement-therapy protocol used to educate endocrinologists. More broadly, LGBTQ patients report disrespectful treatment by medical staff, and some Tajik psychologists and doctors offer pseudoscientific "cure methods" treating homosexuality as an addiction like alcoholism or drug addiction. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to married heterosexual couples. Same-sex sexual activity itself has been legal since May 1998 (consensual sex between women was never criminalised), and the age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation — but no relationship-recognition framework exists. The country's first anti-discrimination law, adopted in July 2022, dropped sexual orientation and gender identity as protected grounds, leaving only "sex." Wikipedia country coverage: The only youth-relevant legal finding is that the age of consent is 16 in Tajikistan regardless of gender or sexual orientation; the source text contains no findings on LGBTQ minors, education-sector policies, or school environments.

TKM.name: Turkmenistan
TKM.summary:
Turkmenistan criminalises consensual sex between men, and the penalty framework has hardened rather than loosened. Article 135 of the Criminal Code identifies consensual same-sex acts between adult men as an offence, and the Criminal Code adopted in April 2022 retained the 'sodomy' provisions while increasing both the severity and the scope of the punishments attached to them. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report on Turkmenistan lists the criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct among the country's significant human rights issues, together with abuses committed by security-service officials who operate with impunity.

The exposure a visitor faces is not limited to a court date. Attorneys who brought off asylum claims for Turkmen clients describe suspects subjected to interrogation, torture and confinement to mental hospitals, and warn that women fleeing the country are vulnerable to sexual violence and so-called honor killings. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records torture and inhumane treatment as present throughout Turkmenistan, with relatives reporting LGBTI people subjected to them.

Legal recourse inside the country is effectively closed. A 2020 stakeholder submission to the UN Universal Periodic Review states that LGBT persons and people living with HIV in Turkmenistan have no effective legislative means of enjoying their fundamental human rights, and identifies Article 135 as the core foundation of profound systemic discrimination against them. The same submission records increasing flight abroad.

Flight has produced results at the asylum stage. In May 2007 the Sexuality and Gender Law Clinic at Columbia Law School secured US asylum for an anonymous Turkmen woman persecuted because she is a lesbian and for her political opinions, an award believed to be the first ever granted to a lesbian from Turkmenistan, and it documents the persecution grounds cited by people leaving the country. In September 2019 attorneys at Goldberg Kohn secured asylum for a lesbian couple from Turkmenistan who feared imprisonment and torture on return.

The surrounding conditions raise the cost of any exposure. The state maintains strict control of media and heavy monitoring of communications, and no independent research on LGBTI issues has been possible in the country since 2019. There is no legal gender recognition, no organised community to appeal to and no protection machinery a visitor could reach. Any discoverable online history or visible nonconformity is dangerous under that degree of surveillance, and total concealment of both identity and online presence is the only defensible posture while in the country.

Entry and visa rules for transgender visitors, including any screening or questioning at the border and the treatment of passports bearing markers that differ from presentation, are not addressed in the sources reviewed here. sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Media in Turkmenistan is entirely owned by the state and no civil society exists, which the source identifies as the reason surveillance data on LGBTQ rights and allied issues is scarce. The government has justified its discriminatory frameworks in UN dialogue by arguing that any deviations pose a potential threat to the fabric of Turkmen traditions and society. Wikipedia country coverage: Transsexual people are described as an unacknowledged category in Turkmen law, alongside homosexual women, for whom no penal provisions exist. Turkmenistan has consistently rejected pleas to implement anti-discrimination legislation despite requests by multiple nations via three Universal Periodic Reviews, though in February 2021 it told the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights it intended to 'study the option of introducing anti-discrimination legislation'. Wikipedia country coverage: Repeat prosecutions under Article 135 can incur compulsory admission to psychiatric clinics, where internees may be subjected to involuntary conversion therapy. Homosexuality is institutionally perceived as a form of mental disorder within these facilities. Wikipedia country coverage: Investigations into offences under Article 135 are grossly humiliating and may involve torture by state and non-state actors, and repeat convictions can lead to compulsory psychiatric admission with involuntary conversion therapy. In October 2019 a gay doctor was tortured by the state apparatus over a long span before temporarily disappearing. No youth- or minor-specific care access findings appear in the source. Wikipedia country coverage: Male homosexuality is explicitly illegal under Criminal Code Chapter 3, Article 135 section (1), punishable by up to 2 years in prison with additional terms of 2 to 5 years in a labor camp possible; Article 19 allows increased penalties for repeat convictions, and a 2019 amendment raised the prior 1997 maximum of 2 years. Enforcement was rare before Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow became president in 2006, and reported consequences now include state-sponsored violence and torture during criminal investigation, plus vigilante attacks especially in prison. In May 2020 multiple well-known figures from the modelling industry were arrested on charges of homosexuality, and media is entirely state-owned. Wikipedia country coverage: LGBTQ people in Turkmenistan face active discrimination and stigmatization compared to non-LGBTQ residents, and homosexuality is institutionally perceived as a form of mental disorder. Reported extrajudicial consequences of being gay include state-sponsored violence and vigilante attacks, especially in prison. Turkmenistan is one of only two post-Soviet states where male homosexual activity remains criminalized, alongside Uzbekistan, and the absence of civil society plus state-only media renders data on these issues scarce.

TKM.tangentialFactors:
The criminal provision sits within a wider pattern of state abuse rather than standing alone. The 2021 human rights report places the same-sex conduct law next to security-service violence and official corruption committed with impunity, which means an arrest initiated under Article 135 would unfold inside an investigative system that the international monitoring bodies already regard as abusive.

Torture risk is the most consistently reported feature of detention, documented both in ILGA-Europe's 2025 review and in the account of the 2019 asylum case. Detention in a psychiatric facility appears in the same account as an alternative to criminal proceedings, a route that would be difficult for a foreign visitor to detect or challenge from outside the country.

Turkmenistan's position in the international system contrasts sharply with neighbouring and comparable post-Soviet jurisdictions where decriminalisation has already occurred or where legal gender recognition procedures exist. Nothing comparable is available here, and the increasing flight abroad noted in the 2020 UPR submission indicates that people with the means to leave generally do so.

The country's informational closure compounds every other risk: with state control of media, heavy internet monitoring and no independent research permitted since 2019, outside assessments rest on the older documentary record and on testimony from those who have already fled.
TKM.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Qatar (0.12 — different profiles: TKM's opacity prevents even documenting abuse; QAT's abuse is documented), below Uzbekistan (0.22 — UZB has enforcement data and some civil society) and Russia (0.12, tie).
TKM.blindSummary:
this country criminalises consensual sex between men, and the penalty framework has hardened rather than loosened. Article 135 of the Criminal Code identifies consensual same-sex acts between adult men as an offence, and the Criminal Code adopted in April 2022 retained the 'sodomy' provisions while increasing both the severity and the scope of the punishments attached to them. a foreign government's 2021 human rights report on the country lists the criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct among the significant human rights issues, together with abuses committed by security-service officials who operate with impunity.

The exposure a visitor faces is not limited to a court date. Attorneys who brought off asylum claims for local clients describe suspects subjected to interrogation, torture and confinement to mental hospitals, and warn that women fleeing the country are vulnerable to sexual violence and so-called honor killings. an international LGBTI rights organization's annual review records torture and inhumane treatment as present throughout the country, with relatives reporting LGBTI people subjected to them.

Legal recourse inside the country is effectively closed. A 2020 stakeholder submission to an UN review procedure states that LGBT persons and people living with HIV have no effective legislative means of enjoying their fundamental human rights, and identifies Article 135 as the core foundation of profound systemic discrimination against them. The same submission records increasing flight abroad.

Flight has produced results at the asylum stage. In May 2007 a law school clinic secured foreign asylum for an anonymous local woman persecuted because she is a lesbian and for her political opinions, an award believed to be the first ever granted to a lesbian from this country, and it documents the persecution grounds cited by people leaving. In September 2019 attorneys at a law firm secured asylum for a lesbian couple from the country who feared imprisonment and torture on return.

The surrounding conditions raise the cost of any exposure. The state maintains strict control of media and heavy monitoring of communications, and no independent research on LGBTI issues has been possible in the country since 2019. There is no legal gender recognition, no organised community to appeal to and no protection machinery a visitor could reach. Any discoverable online history or visible nonconformity is dangerous under that degree of surveillance, and total concealment of both identity and online presence is the only defensible posture while in the country.

SYR.name: Syria
SYR.summary:
Syria is a country trans visitors should not enter. The Penal Code remains the operative framework after the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024: Article 520 criminalises "sexual acts against nature" and Article 517 criminalises public indecency, and both are applied to women as well as men. There is no legal gender recognition procedure, and LGBTI organisations cannot register.

The security position for trans people has deteriorated since December 2024. The Guardians of Equality Movement documented waves of violence against Syrian transgender women over the first two months of 2025, with non-state armed groups and security forces implicated across several cities, and circulated video footage from February 2025 showing authorities detaining trans women. Any state actor or armed group operating today can act against a trans visitor under the existing criminal provisions, and there is no complaints mechanism or protective machinery that a foreign trans person could use.

Documented patterns of digital targeting persist: entrapment through dating and social applications and extortion of alleged homosexuality have been recorded throughout the conflict period, and a visitor using those channels in Syria carries the same exposure.

Nothing in the sources indicates screening, detention or placement rules specific to trans detainees, visa treatment of trans applicants, or access to gender-affirming care. Absence of those findings is not evidence of safety; the sourced picture is criminalisation without remedy alongside active trans-targeted violence.
SYR.outOfScopeNotes:
The European UNHCR-affiliated EUAA country focus entry on treatment by state, non-state and societal actors recorded no usable finding for Syria in this inventory, so its assessment of actor behaviour remains unexamined here.

Whether Articles 520 and 517 survive in amended form under post-2024 governance is unresolved in these sources; the most recent country overview, updated 12 March 2026, still describes the Penal Code provisions as operative, but no legislative text from the transitional authorities was available to confirm amendment or repeal.

No sourced material covers entry or visa decisions affecting trans applicants, airport or border screening that could expose a visitor's gender history, detention classification by gender, or availability and legality of gender-affirming medical care.

The February 2025 detention footage and the reported arrests are described in monitoring reports without case outcomes, charges, or subsequent judicial proceedings, which remain unverified.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D12.

No usable finding recorded for Syria.

Country overview updated 12 March 2026: Syria's legal landscape remains highly restrictive - Penal Code Articles 520 ('acts against nature') and 517 (public indecency) criminalise same-sex conduct for both men and women; legal gender recognition impossible; LGBTI organisations cannot register.

HRW report 'Audacity in Adversity' of 16 April 2018 (updated 30 August 2021): documents LGBT activism across the Middle East and North Africa including Syria, with tallies that ISIS claimed at least 16 killings in Syria for alleged sodomy as of June 2016 (23 in Iraq, 3 in Libya). Activists worked to draw attention to the killings including at the UN Security Council.

Syria Direct feature of 11 October 2020 (Will Christou, Alicia Medina): LGBT Syrians describe life at home and abroad - in Damascus homosexuality and 'public decency' offences are illegal, and a 36-year-old (Amira al-Tabbaa) describes living 'only in whispers' when meeting friends in gay-friendly cafes.

Newsweek, 2015: two gay refugees from Syria and Iraq testified at the first-ever meeting on LGBT rights at the UN Security Council - a closed session co-sponsored by the US and Chile - about the constant fear of violence and death under authoritarian governments, militant groups and ISIS.

PinkNews, 23 June 2010: Syrian authorities raided several private gay parties over preceding weeks, arresting more than 25 men in the latest swoop - most charged with 'homosexual acts', others with dealing or buying drugs, per gaymiddleeast.com.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Expression is criminalised and chilled: Article 520 of the 1949 penal code prohibits "carnal relations against the order of nature" with up to three years' imprisonment, and a 2010 police crackdown arrested over 25 men on charges including homosexual acts, encouraging homosexual behaviour and organising obscene parties. Public cultural expression has been squeezed since the civil war — the region's only gay tour (Damascus and Aleppo, run by Bertho) stopped operating in Syria, and the underground LGBTQ hubs of Damascus, previously the only places such a scene could exist, have been eradicated. Digital expression persists but anonymously: the "One of you" movement began on Facebook in March 2020 (later moving to Twitter), with university students painting LGBTQ flag colours on their fingers and posting photos under #oneofyou, most using fake accounts for fear of being identified; it drew reactions ranging from defence to threats of blood before dying out amid COVID-19. Earlier literary expression includes Nizar Qabbani's 1971 poem "The Evil Poem" describing a relationship between two women. Wikipedia country coverage: The government has established voluntary clinics that can test for HIV/AIDS and distribute some educational pamphlets, alongside tolerating the work of some NGOs. Hammams in Aleppo and Damascus were the main venues of the pre-2011 gay tour, described by its organiser as "a paradise for gay people" where "we never had any problems," but the civil war ended that activity and wiped out the underground LGBTQ venues of Damascus. Wikipedia country coverage: Health care access is shaped by official stigma and under-provision: in 2005 the Deputy Minister of Religious Endowments publicly called HIV/AIDS "divine punishment" for fornication and homosexuality, while the Health Ministry claimed only 369 people were infected and offered free medicines — NGOs estimated at least five times that number and the UN chastised the government for ineffective prevention. Comprehensive public education, especially for LGBTQ people, does not exist; the government offers only voluntary HIV testing clinics, pamphlets, and a limited HIV/AIDS educational program for youth in secondary schooling (the youth-specific element). Prevalence is low — under 2 per 100,000 in the general population and under 1% among most-at-risk populations in 2018, with 1,013 reported cases through Q3 2019 since the first reported infections in 1987. Physical safety is also a care barrier: beatings and torture of LGBTQ people occur frequently, including attacks by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham and the Islamic State, which reported executing at least 30 people for "sodomy" in its areas. Wikipedia country coverage: There is no anti-discrimination protection; instead the state criminalises same-sex conduct via Article 520 of the 1949 penal code (up to three years' prison), and enforcement has included the 2010 arrest of over 25 men. Violence is carried out by non-state armed actors too — Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham and the Islamic State beat and torture LGBTQ people, and ISIS claimed at least 30 executions for "sodomy," reported to the UN Security Council in August 2015 in the Council's first-ever discussion of LGBTQ concerns. Political actors openly endorse harsher treatment: Free Syrian Army member Nasradeen Ahme said he would enforce tougher laws and would not object to stoning homosexuals, while secular leader Miral Bioredda said Syrian society would say "no way" to gays claiming rights. In the diaspora, Syrian LGBTQ+ refugees face discrimination and exclusion in host countries based on race, language, skin colour and religious background. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth are both a target and an organising force: the "One of you" movement launched around March 2020 on Facebook was started by university students painting LGBTQ flag colours on their fingers and photographing themselves by a faculty building, most hiding behind fake accounts out of fear of recognition, and it drew hostile reactions including promises of blood before fading amid COVID-19. On health education, the government runs only a limited HIV/AIDS educational program for youth in secondary schooling, with no comprehensive public education for LGBTQ people. Young Syrians also feature as refugees and activists — Abdulrahman Akkad, a Syrian young man in Germany, came out publicly on Facebook in July 2017 while under family pressure to marry against his will, and his case was raised in the German Parliament's 2020 human rights session; the 2017 film Mr. Gay Syria follows two gay Syrian refugees rebuilding their lives.

SYR.tangentialFactors:
The violence recorded since December 2024 is not solely a state phenomenon. The Guardians of Equality Movement's April 2025 field investigation also worked to correct reporting that LGBTQIA+ individuals were being hunted in Homs, finding through its on-the-ground reporter network that the claim was inaccurate, an effort aimed at preventing incitement against the community. Verified and unverified claims circulate together in this environment, and a visitor cannot rely on public reporting to establish where threat is concentrated.

Lethal non-state violence has an extended record. Human Rights Watch's "Audacity in Adversity" tallied at least 16 killings in Syria claimed by ISIS for alleged sodomy as of June 2016, alongside 23 in Iraq and 3 in Libya, with activists including these cases in representations to the UN Security Council.

State enforcement predates the current transition. In June 2010 Syrian authorities raided a series of private parties over preceding weeks, arresting more than 25 men in the latest operation, most charged with homosexual acts and others with drug offences.

International attention has not translated into protection on the ground. In 2015 two gay refugees from Syria and Iraq addressed the first UN Security Council session dedicated to LGBT rights, a closed session co-sponsored by the United States and Chile, describing exposure to violence under authoritarian governments, militant groups and ISIS.
SYR.comparisons: Pairwise: above Saudi Arabia (0.05 — SYR's chaos vs SAU's systematic state machinery) and below Iraq (0.08 — IRQ now has a codified anti-trans statute; SYR has codified indecency + active violence waves).

LBY.name: Libya
LBY.summary:
Libya's Penal Code criminalises "illicit sexual intercourse" and "indecent acts", with the indecent-acts provisions carrying up to five years' imprisonment; same-sex relations are not legal for men or women, and where no specific statute reaches conduct, other provisions are used instead. The Guardian's regional guide lists Libya among states where imprisonment is the penalty for homosexuality, with terms varying by country.

Cairo 52's country review finds de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and of the transition process itself, whether social, medical or surgical, enforced through those same indecent-acts and illicit-intercourse provisions. Recent religious rulings have designated gender-affirming medical steps as impermissible, which narrows the ground on which a trans person can seek care or be seen in public.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable: official identity documents cannot be changed. Same-sex relationships carry no legal recognition, there are no legal protections against discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTI organisations cannot register.

Extrajudicial violence is documented where armed groups hold territory. In Derna, Islamist extremists executed three young men accused of homosexual acts in April 2015, and a young man there was targeted by local Islamists from November 2014 for effeminate dress and "contemporary" clothing. In November 2012, twelve men accused of being gay were tortured and threatened with death by a Libyan militia. D+C reported in June 2015 that information in Derna flows only through the mosque and that the situation for LGBT people was worsening as militias controlled territory.

For a visitor, the modal bad outcome is detention by one of several armed authorities rather than a court process, with torture and threatened killing documented in militia custody.
LBY.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not resolve whether gender nonconformity or transition attracts a penalty distinct from the five-year maximum attached to the indecent-acts provisions; Cairo 52 documents de-facto criminalisation through those provisions but does not state a separate statutory term.

Enforcement frequency, arrest statistics and the identity of the authorities currently holding territory are not sourced in this inventory, so the relative weight of militia detention versus state prosecution remains unresolved.

Consular access for foreign nationals detained outside the capital is not addressed by any source here and should be verified independently before travel.

Descriptions of the religious rulings vary in scope: the sourced claim concerns gender-affirming medical steps, and any broader prohibition on the use of the term "gender" in media or institutions is not established by these sources.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6.

YEM.name: Yemen
YEM.summary:
Yemen's Penal Code 1994 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Article 264 defines homosexuality between men as anal penetration and punishes unmarried participants with 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment, with a different penalty prescribed where the participants are married. Readings of the statute that treat the conduct as a capital offence circulate alongside the codified sentence, and a visitor should treat execution as a live risk rather than a remote theoretical maximum.

The statute's reach is territorial. Cairo 52's country review records that the penal provisions apply only in government-controlled regions, while the rest of the country sits under competing faction authorities, so legal exposure shifts at front lines and checkpoints. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2026 makes the same finding for events of 2025, describing Houthi and government factional control as determining where the law applies at all.

Where Houthi-run courts have applied the provisions, the sentences have been severe. Amnesty International documented more than 40 people sentenced to death, flogging or prison over same-sex conduct in January and February 2024: the Dhamar criminal court on 23 January sentenced nine to death, seven by stoning and two by crucifixion, with 23 others receiving six months to ten years for "homosexuality" or "spreading immorality", and an Ibb court on 1 February handed further death sentences. Amnesty demanded an immediate halt to the executions.

Formal law is only part of the exposure. Cairo 52 reports that the erosion of the rule of law, the humanitarian crisis and the growing power of militias have produced de facto criminalisation that is rarely enforced by any court but is used to justify civilians taking matters into their own hands. Vigilante violence therefore operates outside any judicial process, and in neither setting does a visitor have a safe authority to appeal to.

Expression is constrained as well. Human Rights Watch's 2018 regional report identifies "breach of modesty" laws used against sexual and gender expression, and could find no activists in Yemen willing to speak about their work, a documented gap in whatever protection machinery the country retains.
YEM.outOfScopeNotes:
How the death-penalty readings of Article 264 relate to the codified sentence of 100 lashes and one year's imprisonment is unresolved in the sources available here; the statute text cited by GayLawNet does not itself specify a capital penalty, while Cairo 52 and IPS both report death as a possible outcome. The provision applicable where participants are married is likewise stated only as "differently prescribed" and has not been sourced in full.

No sourced material in this inventory addresses entry or visa screening, gender markers on passports or identity documents, recognition of a visitor's stated gender, or access to gender-affirming care in Yemen. These remain not sourced rather than cleared.

The frequency of enforcement outside the documented court cases and the current status of the 2024 death sentences, including whether any were carried out, are not established by the inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D3, D4, D5, D6, D7, D12, D13.

Same-sex sexual activity is criminalized under Article 264 (men: 100 lashes and up to a year in prison for unmarried men, death for married men) and Article 268 (women: up to three years for premeditated lesbianism), and a provincial court sentenced several people to death for homosexual acts in 2024, with Houthi-administered courts in 2024 sentencing dozens accused of homosexuality to death, imprisonment and flogging.

BTN.name: Bhutan
BTN.summary:
Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021. Penal Code Sections 213 and 214, the 'unnatural sex' provisions carrying one month to one year of imprisonment, were voted down by the lower house 43-1 in June 2019; the upper house reinserted the ban, and a December 2020 joint sitting resolved that homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex. The Penal Code Amendment Act entered into force on 17 February 2021, and no reversal has followed. The provisions had gone unenforced for at least 15 years before repeal.

The repeal did not create a protective framework. Bhutan has no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit protections on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and sex characteristics. Discrimination and stigma persist, with health-care access singled out as a domain where trans and LGBTIQ people are turned away or poorly served.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable. Administrative changes to gender markers on identity documents are suspended because standardised guidelines do not exist, leaving trans people with documents that do not match their presentation.

That document mismatch has direct consequences for reporting crime. Trans people are more than four times as likely to experience assault. A 49-year-old trans woman interviewed by Bhutan Broadcasting Service in November 2024 described having nowhere to report violence: police dismiss her cases on the reasoning that her identity card reads male, so 'both parties are men'. Families pressure victims to accept what has happened as fate, and assistance routed through the national LGBTQIA+ committee is slow. The result is practical impunity for anti-trans violence despite formal decriminalisation.

LGBTIQ organisations may register and operate legally, including Rainbow Bhutan, though activists describe the registration process as lengthy and burdensome.

Official engagement exists at institutional level. UNFPA Bhutan's 2024 Free & Equal campaign trained the Royal Court of Justice, the Attorney General's Office and the Cabinet Secretariat, and secured the first direct dialogue between Bhutan's LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians. Two consultation workshops brought community members together with UN representatives and the National Commission for Women and Children.

Public trans visibility remains exceptional. Dechen, described as one of only two trans women living publicly in Bhutan, fought at 16 to wear the female school uniform kira, a first in Bhutanese society. The LGBT Bhutan Facebook page, started around 2013-2014, produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population. LGBTIQ Bhutanese otherwise report near-total social invisibility rather than overt persecution: there is no shared language for gay or trans identities, and lesbianism is under-recognised.
BTN.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources give two different start dates for the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page, one around 2014 and one in 2013; the discrepancy is unresolved in the inventory.

Whether the suspension of administrative gender-marker changes has a stated review date, or which ministry holds the file, is not sourced here.

No source in the inventory records police guidance, training or disciplinary outcomes addressing the refusal to take reports from trans complainants, so the practical impunity finding rests on victim testimony rather than on documented institutional response.

Whether the 2024 Free & Equal training produced any change in Royal Court of Justice or Attorney General's Office practice is not stated in the sources.

The claim that trans people are more than four times as likely to experience assault is reported without a stated methodology or baseline population in the inventory.

Entry, visa and document requirements for visitors are not covered by any source in this inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6, D7.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Health-sector provisions are documented but trans-specific care access is not directly covered. The Code of Professional Fidelity issued in 2021 by the Bhutan Medical and Health Council protects sexual orientation, and the 2020 Standard Operating Procedure for Gender Based Violence Prevention and Response requires healthcare providers to ensure age-appropriate, culturally, and sexual orientation and gender identity sensitive care, and requires case managers to provide tailored care for people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities. Legal gender recognition also runs through the health system: transgender people may change their gender marker in legal identification documents only after submitting a medical note plus a supporting letter from a civil society organisation. Youth-specific: the National Strategic Framework on Comprehensive Sexuality Education (2021) covers LGBTI issues, yet Rainbow Bhutan's director states most LGBTQ youths drop out of school, and of the 316 people registered as LGBTQ in 2019, 10 were below age 19. Wikipedia country coverage: Bhutan provides no legal recognition of same-sex relationships: 'Bhutan does not provide any form of legal recognition for same-sex couples.' A marriage bill using gender-neutral pronouns was discussed during the 2018 summer parliamentary session but was deferred due to the 2018 parliamentary election; the director of Rainbow Bhutan said the community believed the conversation would be revived under the newly elected progressive government. As of the source, there is no form of legal recognition, meaning partners of trans and other LGBTQ people cannot be recognised in any legal proceeding.

BTN.tangentialFactors:
Bhutan's repeal lowered the global tally of states criminalising consensual same-sex conduct from 72 to 71 in March 2021, placing it among a small group of jurisdictions that have legislated out of criminalisation rather than been compelled to by a court.

The legislative path was contested rather than smooth: the upper house moved to restore the ban after the lower house vote, and the final position was settled by a joint sitting clarification rather than a clean amendment. The trajectory since has been stable, with no post-2021 reversal recorded in the sources.

The gap between institutional engagement and street-level outcomes is the defining pattern. Training of justice-sector bodies and first parliamentary dialogue coexist with police refusal to take reports from trans complainants, so formal decriminalisation has not yet translated into enforceable protection.

Social conditions lean toward invisibility rather than confrontation. Reporting describes little persecution or violence in everyday life alongside near-total lack of public recognition, no shared vocabulary for trans and gay identities, and under-recognised lesbianism. Public figures such as Dechen and activists including Rainbow Bhutan director Tashi Tsheten are exceptions that mark how narrow the space for open visibility remains.

Trans residents cannot obtain legal gender recognition, and administrative changes to gender markers on identity documents are suspended pending standardised guidelines. Until those guidelines exist, documents will continue to contradict presentation for anyone who has transitioned socially.

Reporting anti-trans violence is obstructed at the first step. Police decline cases where the complainant's identity card records a male sex marker, reasoning that both parties are men. Where a case is accepted and routed through the national LGBTQIA+ committee, response is slow, and families commonly press the victim to accept the assault as fate.

Health-care access is the domain where discrimination and stigma are most consistently reported, and no anti-discrimination statute gives a remedy when a facility refuses service.

Community organising has a documented history: the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page, founded by Karma Dupchen in 2013, produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population, and the first direct dialogue between LGBTIQ+ community members and parliamentarians took place in 2024.

blindSourceSummaries: An international LGBTI-rights organisation's overview of this nation (updated 12 March 2026): consensual same-sex intimacy decriminalised in 2021, but there is no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit protections on sexual orientation or gender identity; LGBTIQ organisations may register, though activists call the process lengthy and burdensome. Legal gender recognition is unavailable — earlier administrative gender-marker changes are suspended for lack of standardised guidelines. Discrimination and stigma persist, especially in health-care access.

A national broadcaster (November 2024): trans people are over four times more likely to experience assault; a 49-year-old trans woman describes having nowhere to report violence — police dismiss her cases because her identity card reads male ('both parties are men'), families pressure victims to accept it as fate, and help routed through the LGBTQIA+ committee is slow. Practical impunity for anti-trans violence despite formal decriminalisation.

A United Nations agency's report (31 March 2025, 37 pages): the 2024 equality campaign trained the highest court, the office of the top government lawyer and the cabinet secretariat, and secured the first-ever direct dialogue between this nation's LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians; two consultation workshops convened community members with United Nations and national children-and-women commission representatives.

A news site (10 June 2019): this nation's lower house voted 43-1 to repeal Penal Code Sections 213-214 'unnatural sex' provisions (1 month to 1 year, unenforced for at least 15 years); upper-house ratification still pending at that point.

A news site (11 March 2021): the Penal Code Amendment Act came into force 17 February 2021 — after the upper house reinserted the ban, a December 2020 joint sitting clarified that 'homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex', completing decriminalisation (the global count of criminalising nations fell from 72 to 71). A later freshness review confirms this stands with no post-2021 reversal.

A national broadcaster's feature: an online community page (from around 2014) produced this nation's first public affirmation of a gay population; profiles the page's admins and one of only two trans women living publicly, who at 16 fought to wear the female school uniform — a first in this nation's society. Public trans visibility exists but remains exceptional.

A news outlet (28 October 2015): this nation's LGBT people report very little persecution or violence but near-total social invisibility — growing up gay was described as a very alienating experience, with no shared language for gay or trans identities and lesbianism under-recognised. A prominent public LGBT figure founded the online community page in 2013.

Trans residents cannot obtain legal gender recognition, and administrative changes to gender markers on identity documents are suspended pending standardised guidelines. Until those guidelines exist, documents will continue to contradict presentation for anyone who has transitioned socially.

Reporting anti-trans violence is obstructed at the first step. Police decline cases where the complainant's identity card records a male sex marker, reasoning that both parties are recorded as men. Where a case is accepted and routed through the national LGBTIQ+ committee, response is slow, and families commonly press the victim to accept the assault as fate.

Health-care access is the domain where discrimination and stigma are most consistently reported, and no anti-discrimination statute gives a remedy when a facility refuses service.

Community organising has a documented history: a community social-media page founded in 2013 produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population, and the first direct dialogue between LGBTIQ+ community members and national legislators took place in 2024.
BTN.blindTangential:
The 2021 repeal lowered the global tally of states criminalising consensual same-sex conduct from 72 to 71, placing this country among a small group of jurisdictions that legislated out of criminalisation rather than being compelled by a court.

The legislative path was contested rather than smooth: the national upper chamber moved to restore the ban after the lower chamber vote, and the final position was settled by a joint sitting clarification rather than a clean amendment. The trajectory since has been stable, with no post-2021 reversal recorded in the sources.

The gap between institutional engagement and street-level outcomes is the defining pattern. Training of justice-sector bodies and first legislator dialogue coexist with police refusal to take reports from trans complainants, so formal decriminalisation has not yet translated into enforceable protection.

Social conditions lean toward invisibility rather than confrontation. Reporting describes little persecution or violence in everyday life alongside near-total lack of public recognition, no shared vocabulary for trans and gay identities, and under-recognised lesbianism. Publicly visible trans residents and rights-group directors are exceptions that mark how narrow the space for open visibility remains.

LAO.name: Laos
LAO.summary:
Laos does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. The penal code, modelled on the French system after independence in the 1950s, contains no sodomy offence, distinguishing the country from neighbours that retained colonial-era prohibitions.

Trans visitors nonetheless have no legal footing. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, and no documented recourse when officials withhold documents or services; the one-party political system leaves no independent civil society to appeal to.

Social visibility is real. Trans-feminine people are a recognised presence, and the LGBT scene is small, discreet and social rather than public or institutional. Tourist cities are accustomed to visitors, so the dominant risk is administrative — an opaque system in which a passport that does not match presentation can stall a traveller — rather than violent.
LAO.outOfScopeNotes:
The registration status of 'Proud to be us Laos' is unresolved. Al Jazeera names it as the country's only LGBT advocacy group, while the record treats no LGBT organisation as registered in Laos; the sources do not settle which is correct.

No source in the inventory documents a procedure, timeline or refusal rate for legal gender recognition, and none records a trans traveller denied entry, detained, or refused a document. Absence of such reports is not evidence that these events do not occur.

Two inventory sources, the UNAIDS joint analysis and the Asian Development Bank legal-status review, yielded no usable finding for Laos. Hate-crime protection, partner recognition and access to gender-affirming care therefore remain not sourced in this record.

The description of the social scene rests on a single first-person account from 2000 and may not reflect present conditions.

TLS.name: Timor-Leste
TLS.summary:
Timor-Leste does not criminalise same-sex sexual conduct, a position the country has held since 1975. No source in the current inventory records anti-trans legislation, arrest patterns, or police targeting, and no law is documented restricting trans people from public facilities, health care, or employment.

No legal gender recognition procedure exists. The practical consequence for a visitor is that a foreign identity document, including a passport marker changed in a home jurisdiction, is the operative document, and there is no domestic route by which a foreign trans person could alter or regularise a marker while in Timor-Leste. Domestic services are thin and the community is small, so support networks exist rather than institutional infrastructure.

Annual Pride marches take place in Dili. The first parade was held in 2017, drew international attention, and was endorsed on television by the Prime Minister. A second parade followed in July 2018, and the third, the Marsa Diversidade Pride March on 12 July 2019, drew an estimated 3,000 participants, roughly six times the turnout of the 2017 march. President Francisco Guterres backed the 2019 event publicly, stating that he was a President for all people.

Political endorsement does not translate into uniform public acceptance. Reporting on the 2017 parade records day-to-day rejection, including hostile messages sent to the parade organiser's family. A visitor should expect visible public openness in the capital alongside social disapproval that is more likely to surface in family, church, and community settings than in encounters with authorities.

Timor-Leste is a young, Catholic-majority democracy whose political leadership has repeatedly aligned the country with international human rights framing on sexual orientation and gender identity. The government endorsed the 2011 joint statement on sexual orientation and gender identity at the UN Human Rights Council and voted in favour of the 2013 UN resolution on vulnerability and discrimination. This positioning stands in contrast to neighbouring states where pride events and LGBT advocacy have met official hostility.
TLS.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Timor-Leste's courts or the Timor-Leste Police (PNTL) have applied any provision of the penal code to transgender people specifically is unresolved in the inventory. No source documents arrests or enforcement targeting trans people, but no source documents the absence of such enforcement either.

No source in the inventory addresses trans-specific violence, assault, or homicide with dates or outcomes. The report of hostile messages to a parade organiser's family is the only documented incident, and it is recorded as social rejection rather than as physical violence or police conduct.

Entry and visa rules, including any screening of travel documents at Dili's Nicolau Lobato International Airport, are not sourced here. The claim that Timor-Leste presents an open environment for visitors is drawn from reporting on pride events and is not a documented finding about border practice.

Whether the constitutional equality provisions have been read to cover gender identity specifically in any judicial ruling is unresolved. The inventory does not cite a Timorese court decision to that effect, and the claim rests on general reporting about the constitution rather than on a specific judgment.

PNG.name: Papua New Guinea
PNG.summary:
Papua New Guinea is dangerous for trans visitors. Sex between men is criminalised, with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment, and the regime of stigma and violence around it applies visibly to transgender people. The Asian Development Bank's 2024 assessment of the legal status of sexual and gender minorities across 17 countries in Asia and the Pacific includes Papua New Guinea, with decriminalisation among the topics examined, confirming that the criminal-law position remains a live legal question rather than a settled matter.

Reporting on trans and gender-diverse people in Port Moresby documents direct targeting. ABC News reported in October 2014 that gay and transgender people in the capital are commonly raped or beaten, in some cases by police officers. A 24-year-old gay man recounted being pelted with stones and bottles. Transgender people who present as women face the same street-level exposure. The Hanuabada village on the capital's outskirts is described as a pocket of tolerance where residents live openly, including transgender people wearing women's clothing in the street without retaliation, which indicates both that open life is possible in PNG and that it is confined to specific, self-protecting communities.

The violence risk sits inside a wider accountability failure. Human Rights Watch's 2009 assessment recorded provincial commanders documenting more than 50 sorcery-related killings in two highland provinces in a single year, with perpetrators rarely brought to justice, and a mob stripping, beating with hot iron rods and burning a woman accused of sorcery within yards of a police station. Police routinely take no action, and sorcery accusations, including those linked to HIV deaths, are used to conceal murder and mitigate sentences. Human Rights Watch's 2017 world report recorded that police abuse, including of children, continues to be reported with little accountability even for fatalities or egregious physical abuse.

For a visitor, the trans-specific risk is inseparable from the general security situation and from sorcery-accusation violence, which operates through the same social mechanics of accusation, mob action and impunity that surround anti-LGBT violence. There is no legal gender recognition and no LGBT organisation operating openly at a national level.
PNG.outOfScopeNotes:
The specific statutory penalty for consensual male same-sex conduct in Papua New Guinea is not stated in the source inventory provided for this pass; the figure carried in this record should be verified against the Criminal Code before publication. The source inventory carries no provision on legal gender recognition, birth-certificate amendment or driver's licence markers for trans people, and none on entry, visa or immigration screening procedures that could expose a traveller's trans status.

No source in this inventory addresses hate-crime legislation, official protection orders, or any enforcement action taken under the sodomy provisions in the period covered by the sources. Enforcement of the criminal law is therefore unresolved rather than evidenced either way.

The reporting on sorcery-accusation killings and police behaviour derives from 2008 to 2017 material. Present-day enforcement patterns, and whether police conduct has changed under the current government, are not sourced here and remain unresolved.

sources.summary: The ADB publication 'Assessment of the Legal Status of Sexual and Gender Minorities in 17 Countries in Asia and the Pacific', content dated 17 May 2024, lists Papua New Guinea among the 17 assessed countries. Its keywords include decriminalization and SOGIESC inclusion.
