AGO.name: Angola
AGO.summary:
Angola's decriminalisation of same-sex conduct took effect on 11 February 2021. The statute adopted in 2019 overturned the colonial-era provision describing same-sex relationships as a 'vice against nature' and, in the same instrument, made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation punishable by imprisonment. A continental survey published in October 2019 rated Angola as having gone furthest among African reforms of that period, both by removing the colonial offence and by attaching penalty to orientation-based discrimination in employment and services.

The constitutional layer is thinner than the statutory one. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre's chapter on transgender rights in Angola records that Article 23 of the Constitution does not list gender or sexual orientation among the prohibited grounds of discrimination, while the rights of identity, privacy, liberty, protection from torture and freedom of expression sit across Title II. Sexual-orientation discrimination is therefore addressed in the Penal Code rather than anchored in the equality article, and gender identity does not appear as a protected ground in either place.

Formal international-review channels are active. A shadow report on Angola's compliance with the African Charter was submitted for the African Commission's 81st session in Banjul in October and November 2024 by Angolan organisations including Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, I am Trans Movement, ASTA and Diversidade Masculina, with support from ILGA and Synergia; it documents human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people. Separately, Angolan LGBTQI+ organisations lodged a submission with the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights ahead of the Committee's 74th pre-session review of the state, foregrounding discrimination and health-access issues for lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer people.

Trans visibility in Angolan public life has a documented history. In April 2012 the kuduro singer Titica, born male and presenting female, became a mainstream star at 25, in a Catholic country where the article records homosexuality was then illegal and punishable by hard labour. The trajectory from that period to the 2021 reform is one of open presence preceding and outlasting the legal change.
AGO.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved on this inventory: whether Angola provides legal gender recognition, and on what documentary or medical terms. None of the six sources addresses a recognition procedure, so no statement about changing gender markers on identity documents can be sourced here.

Unresolved: entry and visa screening practice, including any questioning of trans travellers at border or airport, and the gender-affirming care available to a visitor. The CESCR submission raises health access in a resident context; no source describes care access for non-residents.

Unresolved: enforcement data for the sexual-orientation discrimination offence, including whether any conviction has been recorded since the 2021 commencement, and any recorded case of violence against a trans person with date and outcome. The sources establish the existence of the provision and of documented violations generally, not case-level results.

Unresolved: how trans detainees or prisoners are housed, the constitutional standing of gender identity as such, and whether the anti-discrimination provision is read as covering gender identity rather than sexual orientation alone. The SALC chapter maps the Article 23 gap but the inventory carries no litigation outcome on the point.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6, D13.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Two specific LGBT groups operate in Angola, but only one, Iris Angola Association, has received official and legal recognition by the Angolan Justice Ministry in June 2018. At that time Iris Angola had about 200 members, based in Luanda with offices in Benguela and Lubango. The three major political parties have not formally addressed LGBT issues in their platforms, and in 2010 the government refused to receive openly gay Israeli ambassador Isi Yanouka allegedly due to his sexual orientation. Wikipedia country coverage: There is no specific law allowing transgender people in Angola to change their gender marker on official documents and passports. Section 78 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 states that, in general, there should be no alteration of details entered into registration records, but section 87 gives the Civil Registrar general authority to make changes, including changes of name and where a change of facts alters a person's legal identity and status — meaning transgender people could possibly use this section to change their legal gender. A 2017 ILGA poll found 49% of Angolans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender. Wikipedia country coverage: The source text contains no substantive entry or visa provisions; the only entry-adjacent items are external reference links listing 'Asylumlaw.org: Sexual Minorities & HIV Status (Angola) – various information packets used for asylum purposes' and 'Angola travel advice: Local laws and customs' from the UK Foreign & Commonwealth Office. Separately, in 2010 the Angolan Government refused to receive openly gay Isi Yanouka as the new Israeli ambassador, allegedly due to his sexual orientation — a diplomatic reception decision rather than a visa rule. Wikipedia country coverage: Legally, people living with HIV/AIDS in Angola are entitled to health care services and protection from employment discrimination. Beyond this statutory health-care entitlement, the source text provides no information on shelters, safe houses, gender-neutral facilities or other dedicated facilities for LGBTQ people. Wikipedia country coverage: Two specific LGBT groups operate in Angola, and only one — Iris Angola Association — has received official and legal recognition, granted by the Angolan Justice Ministry in June 2018; at that time it had about 200 members and was based in Luanda with offices in Benguela and Lubango. The government does allow non-governmental organizations to exist, and some charities have begun working with LGBT community members on HIV/AIDS education. On relationship recognition, there is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Angola, and social pressure to marry a partner of the opposite sex is significant — in 2005 an unofficial same-sex commitment ceremony was reported as 'shameless' and 'abominable' in national news magazines. Wikipedia country coverage: Education-focused work for LGBTQ Angolans is nascent and underfunded: the first association, Acção Humana (Human Action), launched in 2006 but has been unable to receive funding, and efforts to develop educational programs specifically for LGBT people have struggled to get NGO funding. An HIV/AIDS educational program for LGBT people is only just beginning to develop through NGOs such as Population Services International, and a 2007 study estimated roughly five percent of HIV infections were among men who have sex with men. The source text contains no youth- or minor-specific findings on travel, medication or education targeting.

AGO.tangentialFactors:
Angola's reform is regularly cited comparatively as an outlier on the continent: a 2019 overview framed its drafting strategy, removing the colonial offence while adding an anti-discrimination penalty in one statute, as the most advanced of the African reforms of that cycle. Visitors reading continental coverage should expect commentary that describes Angola in favourable terms relative to neighbouring jurisdictions.

Two formal review mechanisms carry country-specific findings that may change between sessions: the African Charter shadow-report process at the African Commission (the Angola submission was filed for the 81st session, October–November 2024) and the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights pre-session channel (submission ahead of the 74th session). Both are routes through which documentation of violations reaches an international body, and both depend on Angolan civil-society filing.

Cultural context recorded in the sources describes a predominantly Catholic country, a setting that shaped both the earlier criminalisation and the visibility of trans public figures within it.

COD.name: DR Congo
COD.summary:
The Democratic Republic of Congo does not criminalise same-sex conduct. Same-sex activity has never been outlawed, including under Belgian colonial rule, and the age of consent is equal for all partners. A stakeholder submission to the country's 5th-cycle Universal Periodic Review (Savie asbl and co-signatories, March 2024) states that the state neither protects nor promotes LGBTIQ+ rights, leaving the absence of a ban without any accompanying legal safeguard.

Public same-sex affection can be prosecuted under Article 176 of the Penal Code, which punishes anyone who publicly outrages morals by actions, and local ordinances are also applied against LGBTQ people. Queer In The World reports that LGBT expression is censored and can carry exposure to imprisonment. Enforcement is discretionary rather than statutory, which means the exposure arises from police and administrative action rather than a specific offence of identity or orientation.

There is no legal gender recognition and no procedure for legal gender change, so a trans visitor's documents will stand as issued and cannot be aligned locally. Same-sex marriage has been constitutionally banned since 2006, and no other relationship recognition exists, so a visitor's partner has no legal standing in the country.

Violence against LGBT people is documented as involving the police, the security forces and the armed forces, including reports of harassment and torture. Armed groups in the provinces have committed extreme violence against LGBTQ people with near-total impunity, and the collapse of state authority in parts of the country makes formal legal protections theoretical in practice. ZMB.name: Zambia
ZMB.summary:
Zambia criminalises consensual same-sex conduct and the prohibition is actively enforced. Amnesty International's campaign of 26 November 2024, "Madalitso's story", follows a 36-year-old Zambian medical professional who had served three years of his sentence by November 2024 for consensual same-sex acts; his imprisonment removed a trained clinician from a health system already short of workers. The case is presented by Amnesty as illustrative of the persecution of LGBTI people in the country.

Police are a documented source of risk rather than protection. The US State Department's 2021 country report records police perpetrating violence and verbal and physical harassment against people on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation, and advocacy groups reported that police routinely solicit bribes after arresting LGBTI individuals, with on-the-spot fines reportedly raised from 500 to 15,000 kwacha (about $30 to $900). The 2022 report adds that detained LGBTI people are frequently threatened with charges under unrelated laws as leverage to extort payment for release. For a trans visitor, this means visible trans presentation can draw police attention, harassment and a demand for money, with gender identity named as an explicit basis of that treatment.

Investigative practice has included intrusive forensic procedures. Human Rights Watch's 2016 report "Dignity Debased" documents forced anal examinations in at least eight countries, Zambia among them. The practice was less frequent there than in Egypt or Tunisia, but prosecutors have placed medical reports derived from anal examinations into evidence in sodomy prosecutions, including a mass trial of roughly 20 men. Victims described the examinations as painful, degrading sexual violence, and the report recommends a worldwide ban.

Societal violence is fuelled by prevailing prejudice and misperceptions of the law, which place LGBTI people at risk of attack by members of the public. The State Department's 2022 report links a specific escalation to official statements: President Hakainde Hichilema's remarks of 30 May 2022 opposing basic LGBTQI+ protections and same-sex marriage were followed by a spike in public hate speech, threats and assaults. The same report found no credible evidence of government agents condoning violence.

The government's formal position is refusal of recognition. The 2021 report states that the authorities continued to reject recognition and protection of LGBTQI+ rights, and the 2022 report found no credible efforts to rescind discriminatory laws targeting LGBTQI+ persons. Discrimination in employment, housing, education and health care continued through both reporting years.
ZMB.outOfScopeNotes:
Legal gender recognition for trans people is not addressed anywhere in the source inventory; whether Zambian authorities permit a change of name or gender marker on official documents remains unresolved here and is not sourced.

The specific statutory penalty for consensual same-sex conduct, and the section of the Penal Code relied on, are not stated in these sources; only the fact of criminalisation and the serving of a prison sentence is documented.

The current frequency of forced anal examinations is unresolved. Human Rights Watch's evidence dates from 2016 and describes the practice as less frequent in Zambia than in Egypt and Tunisia at that time; no later source confirms whether it continues.

Whether President Hichilema's 30 May 2022 statement still represents government policy, and whether the spike in hate speech and assaults it preceded has since subsided, is not sourced.

Enforcement data after 2022 is thin: the inventory supplies a 2024 imprisonment case and 2024 advocacy framing, but no figures on arrest rates, sentence lengths or court outcomes across the period.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D3, D4, D5.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Freedom of expression on LGBTQ matters is effectively barred: the Zambian government does not permit advocacy of LGBTQ rights, and the U.S. Department of State's 2021 report concluded that 'Freedom of expression or peaceful assembly on LGBTQI+ matters remained nonexistent.' In 1998 Vice President Christon Tembo called for the arrest of people promoting gay rights, and the Registrar of Societies stated he would refuse to register any LGBTQ organisation. In The People v. Paul Kasonkomona (2013), an activist arrested after calling for decriminalization on a TV talk show was cleared: the Magistrate Court and then the High Court ruled he was reasonably exercising his right to freedom of expression, with the High Court rejecting the 'soliciting', 'public place' and 'immoral purposes' charges — though the government contested the decision. Wikipedia country coverage: LGBTQ people are subjected to human rights violations by police, are subject to arbitrary arrest and detention, and suffer violence and abuse in custody; police are reported to threaten and extort LGBTQ persons. The U.S. State Department's 2021 report states police perpetrated violence and verbal and physical harassment based on gender identity and sexual orientation, and that LGBTQI+ persons faced 'prolonged detentions'. Those prosecuted for same-sex conduct are subjected to forced anal examinations for evidence-gathering — described by Amnesty International in a 2014 case as 'tantamount to torture and scientifically invalid' and condemned by the WHO and medical authorities. Wikipedia country coverage: There are no broad legal protections against discrimination in health care, but limited standards exist: the Health Professions Council of Zambia's 2014 Code of Ethics bars practitioners from discriminating in patient management based on sexuality, and the Ministry of Health's 2022 Zambia Consolidated HIV Guidelines require facilities to serve all adolescents regardless of sexual orientation or sexual behaviour. However, as of July 2007 no public or private programmes provided HIV-related counselling to homosexual men (adult HIV prevalence about 17 percent), the government National AIDS Control Program does not address same-sex relationships, and the 2021 State Department report notes LGBTQI+ persons faced 'inability to access healthcare services'. Societal discrimination in access to health care is documented (US State Dept 2010; Global Rights/IGLHRC). Youth angle: the National Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health Policy (2015) recognises sexual orientation and gender identities as central aspects of being human, and Section 158(3) of the penal code subjects only same-sex conduct between minors to court-determined community service or counselling — with no equivalent provision for opposite-sex minors. The source contains no text on trans-specific healthcare or medication. Wikipedia country coverage: Section 158(3) of the penal code, amended in 2005, targets children who commit 'gross indecency' with another child of the same sex (in public or private), or who attempt to procure such acts, making them liable to 'such community service or counseling as the court may determine in the best interests of the child' — with no parallel offence for minors of opposite sex. Societal discrimination is reported in access to education for LGBTQ people (US State Dept 2010; Global Rights/IGLHRC). On the attitudinal side, the source reports that younger generations are beginning to show slightly more positive, open-minded attitudes toward LGBTQ peers, driven by the internet and the country's fast digitization exposing people to more stories from different facets of life. Wikipedia country coverage: Social attitudes are described as mostly negative, coloured by perceptions that homosexuality is immoral and a form of insanity, reflecting evangelical religious influence and colonial-era attitudes; a 2010 survey found only 2 percent of Zambians find homosexuality morally acceptable, nine points below Uganda's 11 percent. Anti-LGBTQ mobilisation is organised — the NGO Zambia Against People with Abnormal Sexual Acts (ZAPASA) formed in 1999 'to combat homosexuality'. Violence is frequent and communal: threats, stalking, vandalism, hate crimes including murders, with little recourse from police; in May 2014 residents of Marapodi, Lusaka apprehended two suspected lesbians and demanded their arrest, and in January 2015 an openly gay man was attacked by a mob that reportedly included three police officers. Most LGBTQ people in Zambia are closeted due to fear of targeting, with lesbians especially vulnerable in the patriarchal structure; meanwhile the internet and digitization are credited with reducing prejudice among growing youth, and in 2013 Christine Kaseba, wife of then-President Michael Sata, said silence around men who have sex with men should end and no one should be discriminated against on the basis of sexual orientation.

ZMB.tangentialFactors:
Official hostility and official restraint appear side by side in the record. The 2022 report found no credible reports of government agents condoning violence, yet the head of state's own intervention in May 2022 preceded a measurable rise in hate speech, threats and assaults, indicating that political rhetoric, not state force, drove that wave of violence.

Zambia's use of forced anal examinations as prosecutorial evidence places it in a documented group of at least eight countries, though Human Rights Watch assessed the practice as less frequent there than in Egypt and Tunisia. The recommendation on the table is a worldwide ban, which no source in this inventory reports Zambia to have adopted.

Extortion converts the criminal law into a recurring financial exposure: reported on-the-spot fines moved from 500 to 15,000 kwacha, and charges under unrelated statutes are used as the threat. A visitor stopped by police should expect a demand for payment rather than a routine procedure.

The loss of Madalitso's medical labour illustrates a secondary consequence of enforcement in a country whose health system is already short of workers, a point Amnesty uses to show the reach of the persecution beyond the individual sentence.
ZMB.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Ghana (0.24 — both criminalisation-plus-mobilised-hostility), above Zimbabwe (0.27, actually below — ZMB's documented 15-year serving sentence and current campaign edge it below ZWE) and below Morocco (0.25).

ZWE.name: Zimbabwe
ZWE.summary:
Zimbabwe criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. The offence covers sodomy and, per the Human Dignity Trust country profile, acts involving contact between males that would be regarded by a reasonable person as indecent, so conduct short of intercourse can still fall within the criminal law.

Amnesty International's report of 9 January 2024 (index AFR 01/7533/2024), 'We are facing extinction — escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponisation of law and their human rights implications in select African countries', documents rising anti-LGBTI sentiment and the use of law against LGBTI people in the countries it examines, including Zimbabwe. The report's finding of law being used as an instrument of hostility is the operative risk context for a visitor, alongside the statutory exposure itself.

Healthcare access is formally protected. In July 2018 Zimbabwe's health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gay people, sex workers and transgender and gender-non-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states that care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty, noting that nowhere in policy or law does it say it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups. It was issued precisely because patients had avoided clinics for fear of mistreatment or of staff tipping off police. A trans visitor can therefore expect public facilities to be formally obliged to treat them, while day-to-day treatment still depends on staff trained under a 2018 handbook.

Support infrastructure exists despite criminalisation. GALZ (Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe), a voluntary membership organisation established in 1990, reports more than 4,000 community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups and 4 resource centres. Its services include legal support explicitly covering 'sodomy' arrests, counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes. Legal aid and counselling are reachable for a traveller who needs assistance.

Social hostility, rather than routine prosecution, is the more likely pressure a visitor encounters. Academic work on Zimbabwean social work describes homosexuals living secluded lives because of prejudice, which points to concealment as the ordinary survival strategy and to exposure in public as the trigger for trouble.
ZWE.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state the penalties attached to the sodomy and indecency offences, so the severity of exposure on conviction is unresolved here.

Whether Zimbabwe provides legal gender recognition, and on what terms a trans person can change identity documents, is not sourced in this inventory and remains unresolved.

The frequency and pattern of prosecutions under the sodomy provisions, and whether the 2024 Amnesty International findings have produced specific enforcement actions in Zimbabwe, are not established by these sources.

It is unresolved whether the 2018 health ministry handbook remains in force, has been revised, or is applied uniformly across public facilities; only its July 2018 release is documented.

The report examines anti-LGBTI sentiment and the use of law against LGBTI people in select African countries.

GALZ (Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe) official site: voluntary membership organisation established 1990, now 4,000+ community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups, 4 resource centres. For the record: documented local support infrastructure — legal aid and counselling reachable despite criminalisation, useful for an LGBTI traveller needing assistance.

(International Journal of Humanities and Social Science, July 2012) arguing that homosexuality is 'as African as the baobab tree and as Zimbabwean as the Great Zimbabwe Ruins' and tracing same-sex relations in pre-colonial and post-colonial Zimbabwe. ZWE.blindSummary:
The state criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. The offence covers sodomy and, per the Human Dignity Trust country profile, acts involving contact between males that would be regarded by a reasonable person as indecent, so conduct short of intercourse can still fall within the criminal law.

Amnesty International's report of 9 January 2024 (index AFR 01/7533/2024), 'We are facing extinction — escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponisation of law and their human rights implications in select countries', documents rising anti-LGBTI sentiment and the use of law against LGBTI people in the countries it examines, including this country. The report's finding of law being used as an instrument of hostility is the operative risk context for a visitor, alongside the statutory exposure itself.

Healthcare access is formally protected. In July 2018 the national health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gay people, sex workers and transgender and gender-non-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states that care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty, noting that nowhere in policy or law does it say it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups. It was issued precisely because patients had avoided clinics for fear of mistreatment or of staff tipping off police. a trans visitor can therefore expect public facilities to be formally obliged to treat them, while day-to-day treatment still depends on staff trained under a 2018 handbook.

Its services include legal support explicitly covering 'sodomy' arrests, counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes. Legal aid and counselling are reachable for a traveller who needs assistance.

Social hostility, rather than routine prosecution, is the more likely pressure a visitor encounters. Academic work on national social work describes homosexuals living secluded lives because of prejudice, which points to concealment as the ordinary survival strategy and to exposure in public as the trigger for trouble.

It is unresolved whether the 2018 national health ministry handbook remains in force, has been revised, or is applied uniformly across public facilities; only its July 2018 release is documented.

MWI.name: Malawi
MWI.summary:
Malawi is dangerous for trans visitors. On 28 June 2024 a three-member panel of the Constitutional Court rejected the challenge to Penal Code sections 153, 154 and 156, which carry up to fourteen years' imprisonment, and left any reform to parliament. Human Rights Watch called the decision a dark day and warned of heightened risks of arbitrary arrest and violence against LGBT people.

The application was brought by Dutch national Jan Willen Akster and Jana Gonani, a trans woman who had received an eight-year sentence in a men's prison in December 2021. Faith-based groups filed briefs in the proceedings, and religious leaders led nationwide protests claiming that the case sought to legalise same-sex marriage.

Human Rights Watch reported in October 2018, in the 61-page report 'Let Posterity Judge' based on interviews with 45 LGBT people in Lilongwe and Blantyre alongside lawyers, activists and officials, that police arbitrarily arrested and detained transgender people and at times assaulted them in custody. The report found that people whose gender expression differs from expectations are the most likely to be targeted.

Medical services are refused on gender-expression grounds. The same report documented a trans man who was beaten and then denied treatment, and nurses who mocked people presenting for HIV tests.

Sections 153 and 156 carry up to fourteen years for men and five years for women. A 2012 moratorium on arrests issued by the justice minister was reaffirmed in December 2015 but suspended by the Mzuzu High Court in 2016 following litigation by religious leaders, leaving its legality contested. In April 2018 police in Mzuzu arrested Limbani Sibande, 24, and charged him under section 156 rather than section 153, apparently to circumvent the six-year moratorium while both provisions faced a constitutional challenge; police spokespersons confirmed his custody.

Arrests have been accompanied by community violence. Two men arrested on 7 December 2015 had their house ransacked, were assaulted by neighbours and threatened with being burned alive, and faced attempted extortion and humiliation by community police, including forced stripping, forced medical and HIV/STD examinations, and photographs distributed on social media.

The United States State Department's 2011 human rights report for Malawi documented discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people, harsh prison conditions, and twenty people killed in the protest killings of July 2011.
MWI.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory addresses legal gender recognition or the rules governing sex and gender markers on passports and identity documents, so that question is unresolved here.

Entry, visa and border-screening procedures for trans travellers are not sourced, including whether presentation at immigration raises any risk of refusal or referral.

Whether the moratorium on arrests is currently operative in practice after the June 2024 Constitutional Court ruling is unresolved; the inventory contains no enforcement statistics or arrest data for the period after the judgment.

Hate-crime provisions, facilities and bathroom rules, access to transition-related healthcare, and recognition of partners or marriages beyond the dismissed application are not covered by the available sources.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D13.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Malawi's Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law, in force from 17 April 2015, bans all same-sex marriages and unions and states that gender is assigned at birth; it does not allow a person who has undergone gender reassignment surgery to marry someone of that person's prior gender. The source describes no process for legal gender recognition, and notes there are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Since 2019, limited protection exists only against hate speech, via the Communications (Broadcasting) Regulations 2019 (sections 22(1-d) and 30(2-d)), which bar broadcast content likely to incite hatred on account of gender identity or sexual preference. Wikipedia country coverage: In September 2009 Mary Shawa, secretary for nutrition, HIV and AIDS in the president's office, argued Malawi must give gay people access to HIV and AIDS services, saying a human rights approach was needed for risk groups such as men who have sex with men. The June 2021 Lilongwe pride petition to city officials demanded better access to healthcare for LGBTQ people. An October 2018 Human Rights Watch report found LGBTQ community members vulnerable to arbitrary arrest, physical violence and discrimination. Wikipedia country coverage: State hostility is documented at the highest levels: in April 2010 President Bingu wa Mutharika called same-sex marriage "evil and bad before the eyes of God," and in July 2011 he threatened activists Undule Mwakasungula and Gift Trapence, saying he would "hunt you in your homes... smoke you out," forcing them into hiding amid treason threats. The 2011 U.S. State Department report found senior officials created a discriminatory environment, citing tourism minister Daniel Liwimbi calling same-sex activity "very un-Malawian." In January 2016 People's Party spokesperson Ken Msonda posted on Facebook that gays "are worse than dogs" and should be killed; the Malawi Law Society filed charges, but the director of public prosecution took over and discontinued the case on 21 January. In February 2014 the Muslim Association of Malawi called for the death penalty for gay people, and on 4 January 2017 thousands across 28 districts protested against legalizing homosexuality in marches led by the Episcopal Conference of Malawi and the Evangelical Association of Malawi. Media hostility includes the 2010 arrest and 60-day sentence of Peter Sawali for posting "Gay rights are human rights" posters in Blantyre, and international outlets' failure to report trans woman Tiwonge Chimbalanga's gender identity during her trial. Wikipedia country coverage: Malawi does not recognize same-sex unions: the 2015 Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law explicitly bans them, and at the 2011 Universal Periodic Review the government rejected every recommendation to decriminalize same-sex relations, stating it "had no plans to legalize homosexuality" and that it "should not be unduly singled out and unnecessarily pressured." Recommendations came from Sweden, Mexico, France, Canada, Germany, Australia, the UK, Italy, Austria, Ireland, Luxembourg, the United States ("Decriminalize homosexual activity"), Spain, Switzerland and Norway. The UN Human Rights Committee's June 2012 provisional concluding observations urged Malawi to amend the Penal Code and protect same-sex couples from violence, and Malawi failed to file its ICCPR report for over 17 years. Donor pressure has been contested domestically: the Malawi Council of Churches urged international organizations to "refrain from using aid as a means of forcing the country to legalise sinful acts like homosexuality," and Justice Minister George Chaponda blamed civil society leaders for withdrawn foreign aid. Wikipedia country coverage: Malawi is described as "a highly conservative country" where, in the government's own 2012 UN report, "the vast majority of society has not accepted homosexuality and homosexuality is not practiced in the open." Community visibility is emerging but fragile: the country's first pride parade was held in Lilongwe on 26 June 2021, organised by the Nyasa Rainbow Alliance with 50+ attendees delivering a petition for marriage equality and healthcare. Public hostility is documented — bail was denied to Chimbalanga and Monjeza in 2009 because "the public out there is angry with them," and the magistrate said he sentenced them to protect society — while a January 2016 interview in which gay man Eric Sambisa said "Kill us or give us our rights" led to his brief police detention and time in hiding. The 2018 Human Rights Watch report found arbitrary arrest, physical violence and discrimination against LGBTQ community members.

MWI.tangentialFactors:
Religious mobilisation is the principal force shaping the legal environment. Faith-based organisations filed briefs defending the penal provisions, and religious leaders organised nationwide protests in 2023 and litigation in 2016 that produced the suspension of the moratorium on arrests.

Reform now runs only through parliament, which the Constitutional Court expressly designated as the body to consider any change to sections 153, 154 and 156. No legislative movement is sourced in the material.

Prison conditions form part of the risk picture: a trans woman was held for eight years in a men's prison, and a foreign government's 2011 reporting described Malawi's prisons as harsh.

External monitoring continues through foreign government human rights reporting and international human rights organisations, both of which have published detailed findings on Malawi's treatment of LGBT people.
MWI.comparisons: Pairwise: above Zambia (0.24 — ZMB has an active 15-year serving case; MWI's moratorium holds) and below Zimbabwe (0.27, comparable). The gender-expression criminalisation listing is what places MWI in the mid-0.2s rather than higher.

SDN.name: Sudan
SDN.summary:
Sudan is a jurisdiction where gender nonconformity is itself a criminal offence. Article 152 of the Penal Code prohibits wearing clothing of the opposite sex, and the provision is framed around gender presentation rather than sexual conduct alone. A trans visitor whose appearance is read as incongruent with the sex on their documents is exposed to this provision directly, independent of any other behaviour.

Same-sex sexual activity between men and between women is also criminalised. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, with the death penalty historically available for a third offence. The 2010 US State Department human rights report for Sudan documents the then-applicable Article 148 provisions, which carried flogging and the death penalty, alongside extrajudicial killings, torture and other abuses under the Bashir government.

The Sovereign Council amended the criminal code in July 2020. The death penalty for homosexuality was removed, the maximum penalty for a third offence was set at life imprisonment, the punishment of 100 lashes for same-sex intimacy was abolished, and a first offence was made punishable by up to five years' imprisonment. The 2020 reform did not touch Article 152, and the current maximum for same-sex activity remains life imprisonment.

There is no legal gender recognition in Sudan. Gender-affirming healthcare is legally constrained, and the state's reliance on Sunni fatwas blocks transition; the ongoing conflict further restricts what care remains reachable. Cairo 52's Sudan profile also documents state violence against LGBTQIA+ people, including extrajudicial killings, though it records no arrest statistics specific to trans people.

For a visitor, the assessment is straightforward: statutory criminalisation of gender nonconformity, a life-imprisonment ceiling for same-sex conduct, no legal recognition of a trans person's status, and documented state violence with no dependable recourse while the conflict continues.
SDN.outOfScopeNotes:
No arrest or prosecution statistics specific to trans people are available in this inventory; Cairo 52 records their absence. Whether Article 152 is in practice enforced against foreign visitors, and on what evidentiary basis, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The inventory does not state whether the 2020 amendment altered Article 152 in any way, nor does it give the current penalty attached to Article 152 itself. The relationship between the 2020 five-year first-offence provision and the cross-dressing offence is unresolved on these sources.

Enforcement data for the 2020 amendments, the number of prosecutions brought under them, and any consular or judicial recourse available to a detained foreign national are not covered by the sources reviewed. The scale of state violence against LGBTQIA+ people is documented qualitatively but not quantified.

Gender-nonconformity framing for visitor risk.

Human Dignity Trust country profile: Sudan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, with sentences including a maximum of life imprisonment and, historically, the death penalty for a third offence.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Sudan: its LGBT section notes criminalisation under Article 148, with flogging and death penalty provisions. The report also documents extrajudicial killings, torture and abuses of the Bashir regime.

Berkouwer, Sultan & Yehia (2014): 'Homosexuality in Sudan and Egypt: Stories of the Struggle for Survival', produced with activists of Bedayaa, the LGBTQI organisation for the Nile Valley. The work records daily struggles, discrimination and violence rooted in societal gender and sexual norms.

Rainbow Sudan — Sudan's community magazine: runs sections on LGBTI rights in Sudan, including history and analysis, and profiles Sudanese LGBTI organisations, documenting an organised local community presence.

76crimes (15 Jul 2020): Sudan's Sovereign Council removed the death penalty for homosexuality — maximum now life imprisonment for a third offence — abolished the 100 lashes for same-sex intimacy, and set up to five years' imprisonment for a first offence in the criminal-code amendment.

SDN.tangentialFactors:
The penalty regime has moved in one direction only. The 2020 amendment removed corporal and capital punishment for same-sex conduct but left the underlying offence intact and retained life imprisonment at the top of the scale, so the change reduces the severity of the worst outcomes without altering the fact of criminalisation.

Documentation of the environment predates the current period and comes from several independent directions. A 2014 study produced with activists from Bedayaa, the LGBTQI organisation for the Nile Valley, records daily struggles, discrimination and violence rooted in societal gender and sexual norms, indicating that the risk is social as well as statutory. The 2010 US State Department report places the LGBT provisions within a broader pattern of extrajudicial killing and torture under the Bashir regime.

Regional comparison is not available from this inventory: no neighbouring jurisdiction's trans-specific penalty regime is sourced here, and the record cannot support statements about whether Sudan is more or less severe than adjacent states.
SDN.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Iraq (0.08 — IRQ has a codified anti-trans statute; SDN has Art 152 + active civil war) and above Syria/Yemen (0.06 — SDN's legal system, though hostile, nominally exists where SAF controls territory).

SSD.name: South Sudan
SSD.summary:
South Sudan carries a statute that reaches gender presentation on its face: the law criminalises a male person who "dresses or is attired in the fashion of a woman". For a trans visitor presenting female, that provision is the operative exposure, and it does not depend on any sexual conduct or on any disclosure of identity.

The same law treats consensual same-sex sexual conduct as "unnatural offenses", defined as "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", punishable by up to 10 years' imprisonment. Where the conduct is nonconsensual, the term rises to up to 14 years.

United States State Department country reports on human rights practices for 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022 each record that there were no reports of authorities enforcing the same-sex conduct provision. The reports describe no repeal, moratorium or prosecutorial policy accompanying that non-enforcement, so the offences remain in force and available to an enforcement authority.

The dress offence is drafted in terms of sex and attire rather than identity or diagnosis. A visitor therefore faces it as a matter of visible presentation, with no threshold of behaviour, documentation or intent to cross first.
SSD.outOfScopeNotes:
The current source set does not address legal gender recognition, identity-document or passport marker rules, visa and entry screening, airport or border procedures, healthcare access, facilities, hate-crime protection, or recognition of partners. These questions remain unresolved for South Sudan on the present inventory.

The reports identify the offences only by their statutory wording. The name and year of the enacting instrument are not established by this source set, and no claim about a specific Penal Code or enactment year should be read as sourced here.

No source in the inventory documents violence against trans people, community or advocacy organisations, or official statements on gender identity in South Sudan. The absence of such material in this pass is not a finding that no such incidents or organisations exist.

The enforcement finding rests on the reporting method of a single government's annual country reports. Independent monitoring or court-record verification of non-enforcement is not present in the inventory.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: LGBTQI+ persons reported that security forces routinely harassed and sometimes arrested, detained, tortured and beat them, according to US State Department reports covering 2018 to 2022. Staff of the LGBTQ-supportive organisation Access for All were detained for several months after a security force raid in 2017, and were released without charge. A 2017 ministerial statement threatened to order security forces to arrest LGBTQ persons and detain them until they procreate, though no such arrests were reported by year's end. Wikipedia country coverage: LGBTQ persons in South Sudan face abuse and discrimination from government agents and widespread stigmatisation among the broader population. Security forces were reported to beat and torture LGBTQI+ persons between 2018 and 2022, and the 2011 State Department report found 'widespread' societal discrimination against gay men and lesbians. There is no hate crime legislation protecting LGBTQ persons from harassment or abuse based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Wikipedia country coverage: South Sudan has no anti-discrimination or hate crime legislation protecting LGBTQ persons from harassment or abuse on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. The only exception noted is that, as of 2020, harassment of employees based on sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited for all oil and gas companies operating in the country. The Non-Governmental Organisations Act (2016) bars organisations from contravening the country's 'sovereignty, ... its institutions and laws', which may prevent LGBTQ-supportive civic groups from operating given that same-sex activity is illegal. Wikipedia country coverage: In September 2017 the minister for Labour, Public Service and Human Resource Development, Gathoth Gatkuoth Hothnyang, said the government would order security forces to arrest LGBTQ persons and detain them until they procreate. In July 2010 then-President Salva Kiir Mayardit said homosexuality is not in the 'character' of Southern Sudanese people and would never gain support, and in 2006 bishop Abraham Mayom Athiaan split from the Episcopal Church of Sudan over insufficient condemnation of homosexuality. The US State Department's 2022 report found most openly LGBTQI+ citizens had fled South Sudan because of 'actively hostile government rhetoric and action'. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in South Sudan, and same-sex marriage has been constitutionally banned since the country adopted its Constitution in 2011. Wikipedia country coverage: LGBTQ people face widespread stigmatisation among the broader population, and the country has no known LGBTQ-support organisations. A community-based LGBTQ-rights group, Access for All, was intimidated into closing in 2017 after a security force raid and staff detentions, and its executive director later left the country. Visibility is further constrained by Section 379 of the Penal Code, which criminalises 'any male person who dresses or is attired in the fashion of a woman' with up to three months' imprisonment, and by the fact that most openly LGBTQI+ citizens have fled the country.

SSD.tangentialFactors:

Five consecutive annual reports reproduce the same offence wording and the same penalty tiers, which indicates a settled legal position across the 2018 to 2022 reporting period rather than a recent legislative change.

The consistent finding of no reported enforcement sits uneasily with the breadth of the dress offence, and the reports do not explain the gap. Whether that reflects non-prosecution, unrecorded proceedings, or a limitation of the reporting method is unresolved in the current source set.

The penalty structure is asymmetric: the nonconsensual tier carries a longer term than the consensual tier, which means the reports do not treat the provision as operating only against coercive conduct.

SOM.name: Somalia
SOM.summary:
Somalia carries criminal penalties for same-sex conduct under the 1964 penal code. Sources differ on the statutory maximum: the Human Dignity Trust records life imprisonment, while US State Department reporting for 2021 and 2022 gives a range of three months to three years. The 2022 reporting notes no official reports of enforcement of that provision, with impunity the norm for sexual-minority violence.

The greater danger lies in territory not administered by the federal authorities. In areas held by Al-Shabaab, local interpretations of sharia apply, and homosexuality is punishable by death there; documented executions are reported under that authority. Al-Shabaab's leadership has publicly stated an intent to enforce harsh punishments, and senior figures have described a 'death chamber' for gay and lesbian people. The 2010 US State Department human rights reporting already recorded the death penalty being imposed under Islamic law in insurgent-controlled areas, so this is a long-standing practice rather than an emerging one.

Even where the federal state is absent from the process, clan-based justice and mob violence against gender nonconformity remain pervasive. The US State Department's assessment describes an environment of pervasive violence and statelessness in which no effective protection exists. No mechanism for legal gender recognition exists anywhere in the country.

The practical consequence for a trans visitor is that exposure carries lethal risk, and no part of the country is safe for visible gender nonconformity. That assessment is shared with the asylum system: a 2016 report by Benjamin Christman, summarised in Erasing 76 Crimes in February of that year, concluded that gay persons should not be returned to Somalia owing to persecution risk, and that finding has served as a non-refoulement basis for LGBT asylum seekers. Al Jazeera's 2013 reporting on Somali refugees in Kenya records the same pattern of persecution driving displacement, with Al-Shabaab figures threatening those returned.
SOM.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on the maximum statutory sentence under the 1964 penal code, giving either life imprisonment or three years. This dossier records both figures rather than resolving the discrepancy, which may reflect a distinction between the general criminal statute and specific provisions.

No source in the inventory addresses document or marker rules, entry and visa procedures, access to gender-affirming care, or hate-crime legislation for Somalia, and no conclusion is drawn on any of those points. Al-Shabaab's exact territorial control figures are not quantified in the supplied material, so the scale of the sharia-based regime is stated qualitatively only.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2, D4, D6.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Under Article 409 of the Somali Penal Code (1973), sexual intercourse with a person of the same sex is punishable by imprisonment from three months to three years, and an 'act of lust' other than intercourse is punishable by two months to two years. Article 410 allows an additional security measure, usually police surveillance, to prevent 're-offending'. The Marriage Law of 1974 defines marriage as a contract between a man and a woman. Wikipedia country coverage: In al-Shabaab-controlled areas and Jubaland, capital punishment is imposed for consensual same-sex sexual activity, with punishment at a judge's discretion. ILGA reported in 2021 killings by al-Shabaab or other non-state armed groups of alleged homosexual activity, including two male teenagers aged 15 and 18 with a man aged 20 in 2017, and a young man in 2018; in 2024 two men were executed by Al-Shabaab. In government-controlled areas, civil law specifies prison sentences of up to three years, and LGBTQ people are regularly prosecuted. Wikipedia country coverage: Family planning services are hard to access, as is fact-based information on human sexuality, and Islamic social mores often make it difficult to publicly discuss HIV transmission. Since 1999, much AIDS/HIV education and care has come from international organizations such as the United Nations. Somalia has one of the lowest HIV infection rates on the continent, with adult prevalence estimated at 0.5% in 2007. Wikipedia country coverage: The law does not prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, as reported by the U.S. Department of State in 2022. Consensual same-sex sexual activity is illegal for both men and women, with prison sentences of up to three years under civil law and capital punishment in al-Shabaab-controlled areas and Jubaland. Wikipedia country coverage: There is pervasive social stigma against same-sex relationships, and sexual orientation is considered a taboo topic with no public discussion in any region of the country, per U.S. Department of State reports from 2010 and 2022. Stigmatization and criminalisation occur in a context where 99% of the population follows Islam and the country has experienced decades of civil war and unstable government. A number of human rights and LGBTQ activists and those accused of homosexuality have been forced to flee the country for fear of execution or assassination. Wikipedia country coverage: The Marriage Law of 1974 defines marriage as 'a contract between a man and a woman having equal rights and duties with the object of creating a family,' effectively excluding same-sex unions from legal recognition. Wikipedia country coverage: ILGA reported in 2021 that al-Shabaab or other non-state armed groups killed individuals for alleged homosexual activity, including two male teenagers aged 15 and 18 (together with a man aged 20) in 2017, indicating youth-specific lethal risk. As of 2004, one group reportedly existed for LGBTQ people in Somalia, and by 2022 there were few, very discreet, and mostly online-based LGBTQI+ organizations holding events. Wikipedia country coverage: Sexual orientation is considered a taboo topic with no public discussion in any region of the country, per the U.S. Department of State's 2010 Human Rights Report, and severe societal stigma prevents LGBTQI+ individuals from making their sexual orientation or gender identity known publicly as of 2022. As of 2004, one group reportedly existed for LGBTQ people in Somalia, and by 2022 organizations were few, discreet, and mostly online-based. Many Somali immigrants have formed majority Somali or solely Somali LGBTQ organizations in Canada.

Where refugees are pushed back toward Somalia, they enter precisely the environment described above, and the threat comes from Al-Shabaab rather than from the destination country itself.

ERI.name: Eritrea
ERI.summary:
Article 310(1) of Eritrea's 2015 Penal Code criminalises "homosexual conduct" and carries up to seven years' imprisonment. The provision descends from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code, which Eritrea retained after independence with a longer sentence. The UK Foreign Office records same-sex activity as a crime and confirms that no anti-discrimination legislation protects lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender people.

Exposure is not limited to prosecution. The US State Department's 2023 reporting states that openly LGBTQI+ persons risk imprisonment and for that reason did not participate in the political process, and that societal discrimination against them continues. A 2011 State Department report relayed by Asmarino records societal abuse and discrimination against gay men and lesbians, and documents the government labelling disloyal individuals as "gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles" — a state practice that makes the accusation itself a tool of official pressure.

The 2010 State Department report combines the criminalisation and stigma findings with torture, arbitrary detention and indefinite national service, which define what detention in Eritrea would mean for a person suspected of same-sex conduct. The UK raised these concerns with Eritrea bilaterally and through the EU; the US, UK and Outright International all maintain current reporting on the situation.

Nothing in the sources addresses trans people specifically. No data exists on how gender non-conformity is treated, whether identity documents can be changed, or what screening a traveller would undergo. The informational closure recorded in the reporting — no independent media and no civil society to document conditions — is itself the reason the risk for a trans visitor cannot be bounded.
ERI.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved and not sourced: whether Eritrea's laws address gender identity or gender expression separately from same-sex conduct, and whether any penalty regime applies to trans people as such. The inventory contains no trans-specific provision.

Unresolved and not sourced: rules on gender markers in passports or identity documents, entry or visa screening that could disclose a traveller's gender history, recognition of partners or marriages, access to gender-affirming healthcare, and facility access. No source in the inventory addresses these.

Unresolved and not sourced: prosecutions under Article 310(1), sentencing practice, or any recorded case involving a foreign visitor. The reporting establishes the law and the societal and official hostility around it, not enforcement outcomes.

Unresolved: the absence of trans-specific findings is attributed in the sources to informational control rather than to a finding that no harm occurs.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The Eritrean government restricts freedom of expression and sponsors censorship of LGBTQ issues. A 2023 US State Department report found Eritrea has no public LGBTQ organizations and tightly restricts expression on sexual orientation and gender identity, so LGBTQI+ people cannot freely assemble, associate or express themselves publicly for fear of identification, arrest, discrimination or violence. State censorship is compounded by heavy social stigma, and in the early 2000s state-run radio and television aired programs detailing the alleged dangers of homosexuality. Wikipedia country coverage: Foreign LGBTQ nationals have been removed from Eritrea on the basis of local law. In 2013 Paolo Mannina, a gay Italian citizen teaching literature at a technical school in Asmara, was dismissed and deported; the government called him a 'dangerous individual who is potentially destabilizing to the moral order and public of the country' and justified the expulsion under Article 7 of the Agreement on Italian Technical Schools, which requires compliance with local laws including Article 600 of the Penal Code. In 2004 three hotel workers from Western countries were expelled for homosexual activity, at least one described as openly homosexual. The Eritrean ambassador to Italy stated that any foreigner must respect local customs and the provisions of law prohibiting homosexual relations; Italian diplomats condemned the action. Wikipedia country coverage: Detention facilities are used against people suspected of same-sex conduct. In 2003 six gay men arrested in a public bathroom in Asmara were transferred to the Adi Abeyto prison facility, known for housing political prisoners and journalists. The source reports that abuse, torture and beating of prisoners is commonplace and that some prisoners have been illegally executed, though the UK Foreign and Commonwealth Office reported the death penalty was not used in 2013. Gays and lesbians serving in the Eritrean military are reported to have been subjected to severe abuse, including physical and verbal abuse and threats from superiors and fellow soldiers (a 2002 UK refugee claimant account, unconfirmed). Wikipedia country coverage: Criminalization under Article 600 undermines health and care access: ILGA and some HIV/AIDS prevention groups have condemned the law, arguing it makes prevention programs directed at men who have sex with men extremely difficult, and the US State Department lists societal discrimination against people with HIV/AIDS as an 'area of concern'. There are no laws banning conversion therapy, and OutRight Action International found conversion therapy and attempts to forcibly change sexual orientation or gender identity are widespread due to social stigma; LGBTQ people have reportedly been offered conversion therapy in lieu of jail time. No youth-specific care findings appear in the source text. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Eritrea, and same-sex couples cannot adopt. There is no protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and the government has rejected a UN Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review appeal to legalize same-sex sexual activity as 'in direct contradiction with the values and traditions of the Eritrean people', with no major efforts to change or rescind existing laws. In 2010 Eritrea, with other African states, rejected the Yogyakarta Principles.

ERI.tangentialFactors:
Eritrea's penal provision is an inheritance rather than a local invention: the 1957 Ethiopian penal code supplied the text, and the post-independence code adopted in 2015 kept it with an enhanced penalty. Comparable documentation from the US State Department spans 2010, 2011 and 2023, and from the UK Foreign Office in its Country of Concern reporting, so the finding is consistent across more than a decade of external observation.

The 2023 State Department reporting notes that Eritrea's assault law makes no gender distinction, which leaves assault protections formally gender-neutral while same-sex conduct remains separately criminalised.

Conditions outside the criminal code shape any detention: torture and arbitrary detention are recorded, alongside indefinite national service. Openly LGBTQI+ persons are excluded from political participation in practice because of imprisonment risk.
ERI.comparisons: Pairwise: level with South Sudan (0.10 — different profiles: ERI is a functioning totalitarian state; SSD is a failing one) and below Turkmenistan (0.12, comparable opacity but lower penalties) and above Somalia (0.04).
ERI.blindSummary:
Article 310(1) of the 2015 Penal Code criminalises "homosexual conduct" and carries up to seven years' imprisonment. The provision descends from the 1957 penal code of the parent nation, retained after independence with a longer sentence. The national foreign office records same-sex activity as a crime and confirms that no anti-discrimination legislation protects lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender people.

Exposure is not limited to prosecution. National reporting from 2023 states that openly LGBTQI+ persons risk imprisonment and for that reason did not participate in the political process, and that societal discrimination continues. A 2011 report records societal abuse and discrimination against gay men and lesbians, and documents the government labelling disloyal individuals as "gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles", a state practice that makes the accusation itself a tool of official pressure.

Reporting from 2010 combines the criminalisation and stigma findings with torture, arbitrary detention and indefinite national service, which define what detention would mean for a person suspected of same-sex conduct. The national foreign office raised these concerns with the government bilaterally and through an international union; national authorities and an international monitoring organisation maintain current reporting on the situation.

Nothing in the sources addresses trans people specifically. No data exists on how gender non-conformity is treated, whether identity documents can be changed, or what screening a traveller would undergo. The informational closure recorded in the reporting — no independent media and no civil society to document conditions — is itself the reason the risk for a trans visitor cannot be bounded.
ERI.blindOutOfScope:
Unresolved and not sourced: whether the penal code addresses gender identity or gender expression separately from same-sex conduct, and whether any penalty regime applies to trans people as such. The inventory contains no trans-specific provision.

Unresolved and not sourced: rules on gender markers in passports or identity documents, entry or visa screening that could disclose a traveller's gender history, recognition of partners or marriages, access to gender-affirming healthcare, and facility access. No source in the inventory addresses these.

Unresolved and not sourced: prosecutions under Article 310(1), sentencing practice, or any recorded case involving a foreign visitor. The reporting establishes the law and the societal and official hostility around it, not enforcement outcomes.

Unresolved: the absence of trans-specific findings is attributed in the sources to informational control rather than to a finding that no harm occurs.

ATG.name: Antigua and Barbuda
ATG.summary:
Antigua and Barbuda requires real caution. In July 2022 the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court struck down Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995, decriminalising sodomy and gross indecency between adults, and read the constitutional prohibition on sex discrimination to cover sexual orientation and gender identity as well.

That ruling does not amount to a statutory protection regime. No explicit anti-discrimination protection on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity exists in Antiguan and Barbudan law, and same-sex unions are not recognised. A visitor who is refused service, housing or transport on these grounds has no statute to invoke, only the constitutional argument the court opened in 2022.

There is no mechanism to change a legal gender marker. Only name changes are available, and Outright International records that transgender people are particularly vulnerable in Antigua and Barbuda precisely because no legal gender recognition process exists. A visitor whose passport marker does not match their presentation should expect that mismatch to be visible at every point where documents are checked.

Social hostility remains a live factor. Orden David, the Antiguan activist who brought the challenge that produced the 2022 judgment, was bullied and physically attacked before his case succeeded, including being struck in the head and knocked out in daylight. Tourist resort areas are comparatively insulated, but that insulation is a matter of circumstance rather than legal protection.

The protection machinery is unfinished. A January 2025 submission from The Advocates for Human Rights to the UN Human Rights Committee, filed ahead of its review of Antigua and Barbuda, sets out the SOGI-protection questions the state still faces after decriminalisation, indicating that the post-2022 legal position remains under international scrutiny rather than settled.
ATG.outOfScopeNotes:
The consequence axis of an arrest is undocumented. The Outright International country profile (page states 'Last Update: March 12, 2026') contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement: no birth-sex versus identity rule, no trans-specific units, no solitary or segregation practice. In a jurisdiction with no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination statute, a detained trans visitor would enter a prison system whose treatment of them is not described in any source held here.

Entry and visa screening are not covered by this inventory. Whether immigration or security screening asks about gender marker, sex or transition status, and what happens on a mismatch between a passport marker and presentation at the border, is unresolved and not sourced.

Facility access rules, including restroom and changing-room use in hotels, airports and public buildings, are not sourced. Nor is access to gender-affirming healthcare, its availability locally, or whether a visitor could obtain it.

It is also unresolved whether the 2022 constitutional reading of 'sex' has been applied in any decided case since the judgment, or how a court would handle a discrimination claim brought by a transgender complainant specifically rather than a sexual-orientation claim.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2, D3, D4, D5, D6, D7, D8, D13.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (Jul 2022): 'Antigua and Barbuda: High Court Decriminalizes Gay Sex' — the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court strikes down the 'sodomy' and 'gross indecency' provisions.

However, no explicit antidiscrimination protections exist, same-sex unions are not recognised, and trans people are particularly vulnerable because there is no mechanism to change legal gender markers - only name changes.

El País/AP (June 2023): profile of Orden David, the Antiguan LGBTQ activist who challenged the country's anti-sodomy law and won in 2022 - he had been bullied and physically attacked (struck in the head, knocked out in daylight); the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court ruled the law unconstitutional; six Caribbean countries still criminalise.

St Lucia Star (Dec 2019): ECADE announced court challenges to buggery and indecency laws in Barbados, St Kitts-Nevis, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and Saint Lucia, arguing the laws stigmatise and legitimise hate speech, discrimination and violence.

The Advocates for Human Rights (January 2025): submission to the UN Human Rights Committee for Antigua and Barbuda listing LGBTQ+ rights issues ahead of its review — documents the open SOGI-protection questions the state still faces post-2022 decriminalisation.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: State hostility is documented through official positions rather than media reporting: at the May 2016 UN Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review, six governments (Argentina, Australia, France, Germany, the Netherlands and Nicaragua) advised Antigua and Barbuda to repeal its sodomy ban and guarantee full human rights to LGBTQ people. The Minister of Social Transformation, Samantha Marshall, called the ban antiquated and said it should be repealed, while Parliamentary Secretary Maureen Payne-Hyman assured the Council that the LGBTQ community is not persecuted in the country. On 24 August 2016 the government then announced it had no intention of repealing the sodomy ban, while acknowledging that a lawsuit would most certainly strike it down given identical jurisprudence with Belize. The Eastern Caribbean Alliance for Diversity and Equality announced on 1 November 2019 it planned to file a legal challenge by end of 2019, which culminated in the 5 July 2022 Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court ruling (Orden David et al v The Attorney General) voiding the criminal provisions as unconstitutional. Wikipedia country coverage: Before the 5 July 2022 ruling, Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995 criminalized consensual same-sex intimacy with imprisonment of up to fifteen years for adult-on-adult buggery, five years where a minor committed the act, and life where an adult committed it on a minor; 'serious indecency' carried up to ten years where the target was a child under sixteen. People convicted as 'repeat offenders' of buggery were placed on the Sex Offenders Register for the remainder of their life. The Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court (Orden David et al v The Attorney General of Antigua and Barbuda) declared those provisions unconstitutional and void on 5 July 2022. Wikipedia country coverage: The law does not address discrimination or harassment on account of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not recognize same-sex unions in any form (marriage or partnerships), and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same rights given to opposite-sex married couples. In May 2016 at the UN Human Rights Council's Universal Periodic Review, Argentina, Australia, France, Germany, the Netherlands and Nicaragua urged repeal of the sodomy ban; Minister of Social Transformation Samantha Marshall called the ban antiquated and Parliamentary Secretary Maureen Payne-Hyman assured the Council that LGBTQ people are not persecuted. On 24 August 2016 the government said it had no intention of repealing the ban (while acknowledging a lawsuit would likely succeed given Belize's identical jurisprudence), and on 1 November 2019 the Eastern Caribbean Alliance for Diversity and Equality announced a planned legal challenge.

ATG.tangentialFactors:
Antigua and Barbuda sits inside a wider regional pattern rather than standing apart from it. Six Caribbean countries still criminalise same-sex conduct, and the 2022 judgment came out of a coordinated legal strategy: in December 2019 the Eastern Caribbean Alliance for Diversity and Equality (ECADE) announced court challenges to buggery and indecency laws in Barbados, St Kitts-Nevis, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and Saint Lucia, arguing that those laws stigmatise and legitimise hate speech, discrimination and violence against LGBT people.

The direction of travel across the Eastern Caribbean is therefore toward decriminalisation, but the pace is uneven and the accompanying protections have not followed the penalties out of the statute book. Comparable states that retain the offences provide a reference point for what a reversal would look like, and litigation of this kind remains subject to appeal and to legislative change.
ATG.localsOnly:
Residents can change a name but cannot change a legal gender marker, so the identity documents a resident carries will continue to show the sex assigned at birth indefinitely. There is no process, administrative or judicial, that produces a corrected marker.

Same-sex unions are not recognised, which affects inheritance, hospital visitation, next-of-kin decisions and immigration sponsorship for Antiguan and Barbudan couples. No anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, housing, education or public accommodation, so residents must rely on the constitutional reading established in the 2022 judgment, case by case.

Orden David's litigation is the origin of the current constitutional position, and his experience of bullying and physical assault before the ruling reflects the environment local LGBT people navigated in the absence of legal protection. The pending review by the UN Human Rights Committee, with the January 2025 Advocates for Human Rights submission on the record, keeps the outstanding SOGI-protection questions formally before an international body.

BRB.name: Barbados
BRB.summary:
Barbados decriminalised same-sex conduct in December 2022, on the strength of a constitutional challenge filed in June 2018 with trans activist Alexa Hoffmann as claimant, supported by the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network and the University of Toronto's international human-rights program. The Human Dignity Trust records the Barbados case as one of a series of constitutional challenges to colonial-era anti-gay statutes across the Eastern Caribbean.

Impunity for anti-trans violence is documented and recent enough to matter. In April 2019 a Barbadian court imposed no jail time for the violent meat-cleaver attack on Alexa Hoffmann, an outcome reported through Maurice Tomlinson and the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network. A visibly trans visitor who is assaulted should not expect a custodial sentence against the attacker.

Trans people on the island are visible and exposed at once. A second Trans Day of Remembrance vigil was held in Barbados in November 2018, organised with a national women's organisation, a local ally and veteran trans advocates, and Hoffmann has given first-person accounts of what visibility and danger look like there in daily life.

Employment offers no shield. Trans Barbadians are reported to be frequently fired or refused work for dressing in a way employers object to, and the Employment (Protection from Discrimination) Bill does not cover them, according to an August 2020 commentary on the island's labour rules.

The Welcome Stamp remote-work visa is marketed to outsiders on a promise of openness, while the employment regime that trans residents face gives them no protection against dismissal. Entry on that visa says nothing about how a trans worker or visitor will be treated once on the ground.
BRB.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in this inventory: whether Barbados provides legal gender recognition or allows a trans person to amend gender markers on passport, birth certificate or national ID. No source here addresses it, and the summary makes no claim either way.

Not sourced in this material: hate-crime or aggravated-offence provisions covering anti-trans violence, rules on access to sex-segregated facilities, recognition of trans marriages or partners, and any entry or immigration screening that could disclose a traveller's trans status. Each would need separate verification.

The status of the Employment (Protection from Discrimination) Bill is unresolved here: the inventory reports what the bill excludes, not whether it was enacted or amended after 2020, so current statutory coverage for trans workers is unconfirmed.

The account of frequent dismissals of trans workers comes from an August 2020 commentary rather than official or survey data, and no enforcement record for employment complaints is available in this inventory.

The December 2022 decriminalisation is documented through the Human Dignity Trust's case page rather than through the text of the court judgment or the state's response to it; the precise scope of the ruling is not set out here.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D6.
