sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The source contains no information on identity-document processes or legal gender recognition for trans Barbadians; the closest related finding is that the Employment (Prevention of Discrimination) Act, 2020, passed by Parliament in August 2020, bars employment discrimination on grounds including sex, sexual orientation and domestic partnership status, but trans activist Alexa D.V. Hoffmann argues it excludes trans workers because 'gender identity' and 'gender expression' are not listed as protected grounds. A High Court ruling on sodomy (published May 2023) found discrimination based on sexual orientation unconstitutional. No same-sex relationship is recognised in Barbados. Wikipedia country coverage: Barbados does not screen or protect LGBT travellers as a distinct category; instead the government has questioned the legitimacy of LGBT migration. In 2011 the Government of Barbados said it was investigating claims that gay Barbadians were seeking refugee status in Canada, and in 2016 Foreign Minister Maxine McClean expressed concern that such applications were an attempt to abuse the Canadian refugee system, noting two of nine Canadian applications had been denied. A 2016 Guyanese newspaper reported over 300 LGBT members in Barbados were seeking asylum in Canada, the UK and the US because of persecution at home, and the UGLAAB organisation said it would investigate the same allegations. Separately, in July 2020 the government's 'Welcome Stamp' work visa initially only allowed foreign workers to bring an opposite-sex spouse, but was changed to permit same-sex spouses. Wikipedia country coverage: The source addresses custody only through adoption: same-sex couples are unable to legally adopt in Barbados, and although not explicitly prohibited or regulated by law, surrogacy is illegal in Barbados. Same-sex couples are likewise not recognised as families, and the only parenting-related service mentioned is the Barbados Fertility Centre, which offers IVF and artificial insemination to lesbian couples. No findings on trans-specific custody, parental rights or family law outcomes appear in the source. Wikipedia country coverage: The source contains no findings on access to transition-related healthcare, mental health, or specialist care for trans people in Barbados; the only health-related provisions mentioned are the Barbados Fertility Centre's IVF and artificial insemination for lesbian couples, the illegal status of surrogacy, and the UGLAAB organisation's work on AIDS. Violence against trans people is documented: in February 2018 trans activist Alexa Hoffmann was attacked with a meat cleaver by Brandon Coward, suffering serious injuries including to her throat, and he was convicted in April 2019 and ordered to pay Hoffmann BDS$460 (US$230) or face three months in prison. Wikipedia country coverage: State and religious hostility is prominent in the source: in 2016 Attorney General Adriel Brathwaite stated Barbados would not change the law to allow same-sex marriage, and following UK PM David Cameron's 2011 CHOGM aid warning about sodomy laws he publicly said Barbados would not be dictated to by the United Kingdom. A government minister warned that external forces were trying to impose same-sex marriage, prompting Human Rights Watch to call the response a 'cheap political trick' since its report did not mention same-sex marriage. Fundamentalist groups including the New Testament Church have made factually incorrect comments claiming sexual orientation is chosen and argued discrimination against LGBT people should be encouraged, while more American evangelical ministers arriving in Barbados have, according to human rights activists, spread homophobic rhetoric more widely. Media hostility is seen in the Barbados Nation newspaper's informal comment line, where a proposed gay tourism package was disliked by some; more conciliatory voices exist, with the Anglican Bishop of Barbados and the Catholic Church opposing the buggery law while respecting LGBT rights, and PM Mia Mottley (elected May 2018) reportedly being 'pro-LGBT'. Wikipedia country coverage: There is no recognition of same-sex relationships or unions in Barbados. In June 2016 the government ruled out changing the law to allow same-sex marriage, and in September 2020 it announced only a plan to recognise 'some form' of civil union, followed by a referendum on gay marriage; critics said the civil union proposal was 'unnecessarily vague' and that the referendum was likely to fail, so as of the source's account neither had been enacted. In 2018 activists filed a case with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights challenging the Sexual Offences Act (Ch.154, ss.9 and 12), and the IACHR gave the government three months to respond in late July 2019; failure to repeal could send the matter to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights for a binding decision. Wikipedia country coverage: The source has no findings on the treatment of LGBT minors in Barbados, on detention of unaccompanied youth, or on school-based anti-bullying and gender-affirming education provisions. The only youth-adjacent legal detail is that under the former Section 12 of the Sexual Offences Act, 'serious indecency' carried a maximum penalty of ten years in prison where the act was committed on or towards a person aged 16 or older. Activist group Barbados Gays, Lesbians and All-Sexuals Against Discrimination (BGLAD), founded in 2013 by Donnya Piggott and Ro-Ann Mohammed, was set up explicitly to create an education mechanism and open public dialogue for the LGBT community, and Pride events (first small event November 2017; parade of about 120 people on Rihanna Drive, Bridgetown, July 2018) have served an awareness-raising function.

BRB.tangentialFactors:
Decriminalisation in Barbados follows the same litigation route used elsewhere in the Eastern Caribbean, so the legal direction of travel in the surrounding states is comparable; the Human Dignity Trust tracks these challenges as a group of cases rather than an isolated Barbadian reform.

The island has an organised community, with groups such as Equals and B-GLAD, a functioning state and a degree of social conservatism that is present but not dominant. Tourist areas are accustomed to a diverse range of visitors, which shapes everyday encounters differently from the environment trans residents navigate at work.

The gap between the 2022 decriminalisation and the 2019 impunity outcome in the Hoffmann attack shows that a liberalised statute and a protective enforcement record are separate questions; the legal reform did not itself establish sentencing practice for anti-trans violence.
BRB.localsOnly:
Trans Barbadians face dismissal or refusal of employment on grounds of presentation, and the Employment (Protection from Discrimination) Bill as reported in 2020 does not extend protection to them, leaving recourse to the employer and the labour market rather than to the statute.

The Trans Day of Remembrance vigil has been held more than once, with the 2018 edition organised alongside a national women's organisation and veteran trans advocates, giving the community a public memorial practice and a visible point of assembly.

Alexa Hoffmann's activism, including the 2018 constitutional claim and her public accounts of danger, has made her a named target; the 2019 sentencing in her attack produced no jail time, a fact local advocates carry into their own risk assessments.

Community organisations including Equals and B-GLAD operate openly, and advocacy has proceeded through the courts, with legal support drawn from the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network and the University of Toronto's international human-rights program.
BRB.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Suriname (0.58), above Antigua (0.55), and above TTO — Barbados decriminalised via courts with less documented street violence than TTO's Grindr-ambush pattern.
BRB.blindSummary:
The state decriminalised same-sex conduct in December 2022, on the strength of a constitutional challenge filed in June 2018 with a trans activist as claimant, supported by a national HIV/AIDS legal network and a university's international human-rights program. a human-rights organisation records this case as one of a series of constitutional challenges to historic-era anti-gay statutes brought in neighbouring states.

Impunity for anti-trans violence is documented and recent enough to matter. In April 2019 a court imposed no jail time for the violent meat-cleaver attack on the trans activist, an outcome reported through Maurice Tomlinson and a national HIV/AIDS legal network. a visibly trans visitor who is assaulted should not expect a custodial sentence against the attacker.

Trans people are visible and exposed at once. a second Trans Day of Remembrance vigil was held in the state in November 2018, organised with a national women's organisation, a local ally and veteran trans advocates, and the activist has given first-person accounts of what visibility and danger look like in daily life there.

Employment offers no shield. Trans residents are reported to be frequently fired or refused work for dressing in a way employers object to, and the Employment (Protection from Discrimination) Bill does not cover them, according to an August 2020 commentary on the state's labour rules.

The Welcome Stamp remote-work visa is marketed to outsiders on a promise of openness, while the employment regime that trans residents face gives them no protection against dismissal. Entry on that visa says nothing about how a trans worker or visitor will be treated once on the ground.
BRB.blindOutOfScope:
Unresolved in this inventory: whether the state provides legal gender recognition or allows a trans person to amend gender markers on passport, birth certificate or national ID. No source here addresses it, and the summary makes no claim either way.

Not sourced in this material: hate-crime or aggravated-offence provisions covering anti-trans violence, rules on access to sex-segregated facilities, recognition of trans marriages or partners, and any entry or immigration screening that could disclose a traveller's trans status. Each would need separate verification.

The status of the Employment (Protection from Discrimination) Bill is unresolved here: the inventory reports what the bill excludes, not whether it was enacted or amended after 2020, so current statutory coverage for trans workers is unconfirmed.

The account of frequent dismissals of trans workers comes from an August 2020 commentary rather than official or survey data, and no enforcement record for employment complaints is available in this inventory.

The December 2022 decriminalisation is documented through a human-rights organisation's case page rather than through the text of the court judgment or the state's response to it; the precise scope of the ruling is not set out here.

KNA.name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
KNA.summary:
Saint Kitts and Nevis no longer criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. In 2022 the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, in Jamal Jeffers v The Attorney General, struck section 56 (buggery) and section 57 (indecent assault against a man) of the Offences Against the Person Act as contrary to the rights to privacy and expression. Consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful throughout the country since that ruling.

Legal gender recognition is not possible in Saint Kitts and Nevis. A person cannot obtain official recognition of a changed gender marker, and the sources document no administrative route, court process or statute that would allow it.

No provision of the penal code or of any other statute prohibits discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Discrimination in the workplace, in education and in accommodation remains lawful, as does hate speech, and no anti-discrimination statute has been enacted in the years since decriminalisation.

Relationship recognition is absent in full. Same-sex unions are not recognised in any form, whether marriage or partnership, and same-sex households receive none of the rights granted to opposite-sex married couples.

The protection machinery that does exist sits in policy rather than law. LGBTQ+ citizens are included in the National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027, but a 2025 joint presentation to the Universal Periodic Review by the Saint Kitts and Nevis Alliance and ECADE records a lack of tangible steps by the State to implement that inclusion.

Relations with the authorities are a separate matter from the statute book. The same 2025 submission states that LGBTQ+ people avoid law enforcement, which bears directly on whether a visitor can expect assistance if a bias-motivated incident occurs. LGBTI organisations are permitted to register, and civil society used the courts rather than the legislature to obtain decriminalisation.

The practical position for a trans visitor is therefore lawful private conduct without protective scaffolding: conduct between adults is not an offence, but there is no anti-discrimination law, no recognised gender marker, no recognised relationship, and no sourced evidence of state remedies being used after a bias incident.
KNA.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records incidents of violence against trans people in Saint Kitts and Nevis, their frequency, dates, police response or judicial outcome. Absence of documented cases should be read as unsourced rather than as evidence that no such violence occurs.

Entry and border screening are not addressed by any source here: whether immigration officers question travellers whose passports carry amended gender markers, or require supporting documentation, remains unresolved from this material.

Hate-crime enhancement for bias-motivated assaults is not covered by the inventory. The sources establish that anti-discrimination and hate-speech conduct are not unlawful, which is not the same finding as whether a court would treat gender identity as an aggravating factor in sentencing.

Whether the Offences Against the Person Act or any other statute retains gendered or sex-based provisions that could reach a trans person in specific circumstances, such as public order or indecency offences, is not sourced and cannot be stated either way from this material.

The implementation record of the National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027 is characterised in the 2025 Universal Periodic Review submission only as lacking tangible steps; no government response or subsequent evaluation was available to weigh against that assessment.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D5, D6, D7, D8, D13.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: On 29 August 2022 the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court struck down Sections 56 and 57 of the Offences Against the Person Act, which had criminalized same-sex sexual activity, ruling that they violated constitutional guarantees of the right to privacy and freedom of expression. The ruling took immediate effect, decriminalizing consensual same-sex intercourse between adult males in private in Saint Kitts and Nevis. Wikipedia country coverage: On 23 March 2005 the island of Nevis barred a cruise ship carrying 110 American passengers, mostly LGBTQ, from docking; a police boat halted the Source Events/Windjammer Barefoot Cruises vessel and the ship was ordered to sail on. The exclusion was announced publicly as a cultural decision, with port officials stating Nevis did not want homosexuality 'to be a part of our culture.' Wikipedia country coverage: State hostility is documented in official statements: in 2011 the Government of Saint Kitts and Nevis said it had 'no mandate from the people' to abolish criminalization of homosexuality among consenting adults, and in 2005 port authority Acting General Manager Oral Brandy told reporters that Nevis does not want homosexuality 'to be a part of our culture.' The penal code still does not address discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex unions are not recognized in any form.

KNA.tangentialFactors:
Decriminalisation in Saint Kitts and Nevis arrived through a regional wave of constitutional litigation rather than legislative reform. Human Dignity Trust documents Eastern Caribbean challenges to anti-sodomy laws, and the August 2022 Nation News report covers the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court striking down such laws across several territories in the same judgment family, with Jamal Jeffers v Attorney General the case that applies to Saint Kitts and Nevis.

The pattern is regional and litigation-driven. Outlets tracking these statutes report ongoing lawsuits against several Caribbean nations over anti-gay laws and frame courts as the principal mechanism for expanding LGBTQ rights in the Caribbean, which indicates that the current legal position rests on a judicial ruling that a future legislature or court could in principle revisit.

Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records the same three findings as the domestic submissions: consensual same-sex conduct legal since 2022, legal gender recognition not available, and LGBTI organisations free to register. Independent trackers of anti-gay laws list no post-repeal discrimination statute for Saint Kitts and Nevis, consistent with the Universal Periodic Review submission.
KNA.localsOnly:
Residents have no legal means of changing a gender marker, so identity documents, employment records and civil status documents all remain aligned to sex assigned at birth with no statutory correction procedure.

Same-sex couples have no marital or partnership status and no inheritance, next-of-kin, tax or social-protection entitlements flowing from a recognised relationship. Cohabitation confers none of the rights attached to opposite-sex marriage.

Employment, education and housing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is lawful, as is hate speech, leaving residents without a statutory complaint route in those settings. The National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027 names LGBTQ+ citizens as within its scope, but the Saint Kitts and Nevis Alliance and ECADE report that the State has not taken tangible implementing steps.

LGBTQ+ people avoid law enforcement, which affects reporting of domestic violence, assault and harassment by residents as much as visitors. LGBTI organisations may register and operate, and the 2022 challenge to the Offences Against the Person Act was brought by civil society, demonstrating a functioning route to the courts for constitutional claims.

DMA.name: Dominica
DMA.summary:
Dominica's High Court of Justice in Roseau struck sections 14 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act on 23 April 2024, holding unconstitutional the provisions that criminalised consensual same-sex activity. The case was brought by a gay man living in Dominica (BBC, 23 Apr 2024; Human Rights Watch, 24 Apr 2024).

As a result of the ruling, consensual same-sex conduct between adults is no longer an offence under Dominica's Sexual Offences Act. The repeal came through judicial review of the statute rather than through an act of parliament: the High Court determined that the sections were unconstitutional.

The provisions had been under constitutional challenge before the 2024 ruling. MiRiDom founder Daryl Phillip announced a High Court challenge to Dominica's buggery and sexual-activity provisions at a news conference on 20 July 2019, five years before the provisions were struck down (Dominica News Online).

Dominica's documented diplomatic record includes signature of the 2011 Human Rights Council joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity, whose signatory list includes 85 countries (US Mission Geneva, 22 Mar 2011). This is a dated commitment on the international record; it is not itself a domestic legal protection.

Local religious authority has publicly opposed criminalisation. Catholic Bishop Gabriel Malzaire of Dominica called in May 2013 for eliminating criminal penalties for homosexuality and for all forms of violence against LGBT people, citing the Holy See's position (Erasing 76 Crimes, 24 May 2013).

Regional context matters for planning: Human Rights Watch's April 2024 dispatch calls on all Caribbean nations to repeal comparable criminal laws, indicating that criminalising statutes remain in force elsewhere in the region. A visitor should not assume that the regime in Dominica is the regional norm.

Trans visitors face significant uncertainty. The sourced record addresses sexual-orientation criminalisation only. It does not document legal gender recognition rules, name or marker change procedures, anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections covering gender identity, access to trans-specific healthcare, or any documented pattern of anti-trans violence in Dominica.
DMA.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Dominica's law provides legal gender recognition for trans people is unresolved. No source in the inventory addresses marker or name change procedures, or any process for updating birth certificates or identity documents to reflect a trans person's gender.

Whether Dominica's anti-discrimination provisions extend to gender identity, and whether its criminal law recognises offences motivated by gender identity as hate crimes, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

No source in the inventory reports incidents of anti-trans violence in Dominica, and none addresses trans-specific healthcare access or the treatment of trans people in institutional settings. The absence of such reporting in the reviewed sources is not evidence that these risks are absent on the ground.

No source in the inventory documents how the former Sexual Offences Act provisions affected trans or gender-nonconforming people, including whether they could be used to compel psychiatric or medical intervention. This remains unverified.

A 2011 US State Department press statement relating to Dominica is cited in the inventory without its substance being reproduced; whether that statement addresses LGBT rights or other topics is unresolved.

LCA.name: Saint Lucia
LCA.summary:
Saint Lucia's High Court decriminalised same-sex conduct in July 2025, holding the criminal provision unconstitutional in Randall Theodule et al. v. the Attorney General of Saint Lucia. The ruling, reported by Human Rights Watch on 31 July 2025 and by the Associated Press, arose from strategic constitutional litigation brought across the Eastern Caribbean rather than from a legislative amendment, and it struck down the colonial-era statute that had governed same-sex conduct.

For a visitor, the practical effect is that consensual same-sex conduct between adults no longer carries criminal exposure in Saint Lucia. Before the judgment, the statutory prohibition applied to everyone present on the island, residents and visitors alike; that specific criminal risk ended with the court's declaration of unconstitutionality.

The judgment addressed criminal liability only. The inventory before this pass contains no source establishing legal gender recognition, partner or marriage recognition, or statutory protection against discrimination in Saint Lucia, so a trans visitor should not assume the ruling carries those consequences.

Saint Lucia has an organised domestic rights community. United and Strong, a Saint Lucian organisation, and ECADE, a regional network of which Saint Lucian groups are part, have worked publicly on LGBTI issues for a decade or more; both figures in documented regional advocacy, including a 2017 protest by Caribbean activists, including United and Strong and ECADE, against an external publication's framing of regional sexuality issues under the slogan 'Nothing about us without us'.

Official-facing practice has been shaped by targeted training. On 19 May 2015 in Castries, United and Strong held human-rights sensitisation training for officers of the Royal Saint Lucia Police Force, Air and Sea Ports, Customs and the Bordelais Correctional Facility, delivered with CariFLAGS, the Canadian HIV-AIDS Legal Network and Maurice Tomlinson, extending sensitisation work begun in 2014. That history indicates sustained engagement with the very agencies a visitor may encounter at ports of entry or in custody, though the inventory does not evidence any comparable training after 2015.

VCT.name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
VCT.summary:
Saint Vincent and the Grenadines retains colonial-era buggery and gross-indecency provisions. Consensual same-sex conduct between adults remains a criminal offence under the British-inherited Buggery Act and sections 146 and 148 of the criminal code.

On 16 February 2024 the High Court dismissed a constitutional challenge and upheld the ban, so same-sex conduct stays criminal in the country. The Eastern Caribbean rights alliance ECADE condemned the judgment three days later, on 19 February 2024, stating that LGBTQ+ Vincentians face greater vulnerability because of it.

Human Rights Watch reported on 20 July 2023, in the 58-page report 'They Can Harass Us Because of the Laws', that LGBT people in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines face bias-motivated violence and discrimination in daily life. The sources record no enforcement figures for the offence, so the practical exposure of a visitor rests on the legal floor and on documented bias violence rather than on prosecution data.

Whether neighbouring Eastern Caribbean jurisdictions have decriminalised, and how this judgment differs from theirs, is not established by the retrieved sources; the comparison is unresolved.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual acts are criminalised (Section 146 'buggery', up to 10 years; Section 148 'gross indecency', up to 5 years), and the country's laws do not address discrimination or harassment on account of sexual orientation or gender identity, leaving LGBTQ people without legal protection when they speak out. Public expression has drawn threats: in September 2011 a same-sex couple's article 'Not Easy Being Gay in St. Vincent and the Grenadines' in the Vinci Kallaloo drew over 3,400 hits in under a day and 50+ comments, several containing violent murderous threats. In September 2018 Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves condemned physical attacks on three cross-dressing young men, called such homophobia unacceptable, and called for an open conversation on homosexuality. LGBTQ life is described as invisible and stigmatised, with no associations or organisations dedicated to LGBTQ people. Wikipedia country coverage: The source describes exile rather than entry: Javin Johnson, 22, successfully claimed asylum in the United Kingdom in 2017 after establishing he could not live as a gay man in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and Sean Macleish, 53, is a Vincentian resident of Chicago who publicly advocated to the Prime Minister for removal of the laws so he could return home with his partner, without effect. In their 2019 affidavits the two petitioners stated that the legislation had exiled them from the country due to its severely draconian and damaging effects. No text addresses visas, entry screening, or admission of LGBTQ travellers. Wikipedia country coverage: There are no associations or organisations dedicated to LGBTQ people in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, nor any sort of helpline or help centre for LGBTQ youth, so no dedicated support or care access exists. No text addresses healthcare, medication, or HIV services. Youth-specific: a 'cross-dressing gay' teen, Leswan Stewart, was attacked in a transphobic assault in April 2019 and then faced a fraud charge for allegedly pretending to be a woman, which the prosecutor withdrew in May 2019 without giving a reason. Wikipedia country coverage: The country does not recognise same-sex unions in any form, whether marriage or partnerships, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for any of the same rights given to regular married couples. In 2024 Saint Vincent and the Grenadines upheld its constitutional ban on same-sex sexual activity in its High Court, affirming it was legal to outlaw homosexual activity. The Prime Minister said any change would be an OECS-wide decision because constitutional and legislative provisions are similar across member states. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth-specific: in September 2018 three cross-dressing young men were physically attacked, prompting the Prime Minister's condemnation; in April 2019 Leswan Stewart, a 'cross-dressing gay' teen, was the victim of a transphobic attack and was subsequently charged with fraud for allegedly pretending to be a woman, a charge withdrawn in May 2019. There is no helpline or help centre for LGBTQ youth. In education, in 2011 three lecturers at the St. Vincent and the Grenadines Community College were targeted by the college's director in an orchestrated scheme accusing them of having 'homosexual tendencies', allegedly to fire political opponents.

GRD.name: Grenada
GRD.summary:
Grenada criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Section 430 of the Criminal Code addresses "grossly indecent acts" between men and Section 431 addresses "unnatural crime"; both provisions remain in force. The United States Department of State reported in its 2023 human rights report that these laws are not enforced in practice.

No legal gender recognition is available, so a trans visitor's documents will reflect the sex marker assigned at birth or by another jurisdiction, with no domestic route to amend them.

No statutory anti-discrimination protections cover sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBTIQ people in Grenada face discrimination in housing, education, employment and access to public services.

Fear of prosecution under Sections 430 and 431 inhibits LGBTIQ people from reporting crimes to the police, which weakens the practical value of police protection even where officers do not pursue prosecutions.

The 2023 United States Department of State report records no arbitrary killings, torture or forced disappearances in Grenada.

GrenCHAP has provided services to marginalised groups for more than fifteen years, working with LGBT+ people, people living with HIV, sex workers and vulnerable youth; it is the principal documented point of support for a visitor seeking community-based assistance.

An October 2024 stakeholder report by The Advocates for Human Rights, Khaleem Ali and GrenCHAP, submitted for the Universal Periodic Review, documents the legal and social situation of LGBTIQ+ people in Grenada, including the Sections 430 and 431 provisions.

Grenada is a small island society in which social visibility is high; the sources describe sustained social discrimination alongside formal non-enforcement of the criminal provisions.

No source records whether any prosecution under Sections 430 or 431 has ever been brought, so the statement that the provisions are unenforced rests on the United States Department of State's 2023 assessment rather than on a prosecution-by-prosecution record.

Grenadian law contains no clause on equality or protection of privacy in the 1973 Constitution and does not address discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity. In May 2013 the President of the Senate publicly called for reconsideration of the ban, saying 'the day is fast approaching' for repeal. No media-specific findings appear in the source text. This is codified in the country's law, which also fails to address discrimination or harassment on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

GRD.tangentialFactors:
Grenada's LGBTIQ legal framework is under active international scrutiny. The October 2024 stakeholder submission to the Universal Periodic Review assembles the criminal provisions, the absence of legal gender recognition and the pattern of discrimination for consideration by UN member states.

The United States Department of State's 2023 human rights reporting on Grenada pairs the criminalisation finding with a record of no arbitrary killings, torture or disappearances, indicating an official hostility profile that is legislative and social rather than custodial.

The gap between the statute book and enforcement is the defining feature of the country's position: conduct criminalised on paper is not prosecuted, but the existence of the offence shapes how LGBTIQ people interact with police and public institutions.

Community infrastructure is comparatively durable for a small jurisdiction, with GrenCHAP sustaining services to LGBT+ people, people living with HIV, sex workers and vulnerable youth across more than fifteen years.

Fear of prosecution under Sections 430 and 431 deters LGBTIQ residents from reporting crime to the police, a barrier that persists despite the reported non-enforcement of those sections.

Legal gender recognition does not exist, so residents cannot change identity documents to reflect their gender identity.

GrenCHAP has served marginalised groups for more than fifteen years, including LGBT+ people, people living with HIV, sex workers and vulnerable youth, and is a documented source of community support and of human rights documentation.

BHS.name: Bahamas
BHS.summary:
The Bahamas decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct on 16 May 1991 through the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act. Nothing in the sources indicates that a visitor can be prosecuted for consensual sexual conduct, and no pattern of police targeting is documented.

Transgender and intersex residents and visitors hold no statutory protection. Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United stated this absence plainly when it launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign in April 2016, and the organisation has campaigned against the dismissal of trans and intersex workers from their jobs. The gap is statutory, not merely administrative: no enacted non-discrimination provision covering gender identity appears anywhere in the sources.

An official statement points the other way. In May 1998 National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson announced that the military, the prison service and the police do not discriminate. That declaration is a ministerial assurance rather than a codified right, and a visitor cannot rely on it as a legal remedy.

Violence against visitors has been documented. On 8 May 2017 Adrian Brown, 24, Jamaica-born and resident in the United States, was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being targeted and beaten because he is gay at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival; he said he wanted charges laid. The assault took place at a major tourist event in front of crowds, which indicates that a visitor whose appearance or manner is read as gender-nonconforming faces real risk of targeted violence in public, particularly during large festive gatherings, with no protective statute to fall back on.

The overall picture for a trans visitor is therefore one of legal exposure without legal cover: no criminalisation, but no legal gender recognition framework documented, no anti-discrimination statute, and hostility that has produced physical violence at a tourist venue.
BHS.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether charges were ever laid over the 8 May 2017 attack on Adrian Brown is not stated in the sources, and the outcome of his complaint is unknown.

Unresolved: the legal force of Frank Watson's May 1998 non-discrimination announcement is not established. The sources give the statement but not any implementing instrument, and whether it binds the police, prison service and military in practice is not sourced here.

Not sourced in this inventory: rules on legal gender recognition, identity-document markers, passport or visa presentation, entry screening that could out a traveller, access to gender-affirming care, facilities and bathroom rules, hate-crime provisions, and recognition of partners or marriages. No finding should be read either way on any of these points.

Not sourced: whether the 1991 Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act contains any provision reaching gender identity or public-order offences that could be used against a visibly transgender visitor.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2, D3, D4, D5, D6, D8.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Government officials have publicly opposed LGBT rights: former Prime Minister Perry Christie stated in 2013 he did not believe in same-sex marriage and in 2016 reiterated that a referendum would not legalize it, defining marriage as between male and female determined at birth. Government member Leslie Miller publicly called for the 'Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas,' urging financial contributions to relocate transgender people to a private island and pledging $1,000 toward it. In 2016, the Canadian government issued travel advice warning gay couples about the risk of homophobia in the Bahamas. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex marriages and civil unions are not legal in the Bahamas; the Bahamas Marriage Act states marriage is composed of a man and woman, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same rights given to opposite-sex married couples. In 2011, former Minister of State Zhivargo Laing stated a marriage is void if between persons of the same sex, calling this a community standard. Wikipedia country coverage: The criminal code requires a higher age of consent for homosexual acts: 16 for straight couples versus 18 for same-sex couples, directly affecting LGBT youth. In 2005, an 18-year-old beauty queen had her crown stripped after confirming rumours she was a lesbian. Efforts to include sexual orientation in a newly proposed Constitution were blocked by members of a government-appointed commission opposing homosexuality on religious grounds, and the 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission did not regard sexual orientation as deserving protection. Wikipedia country coverage: Many Bahamians adhere to socially conservative Christian denominations promoting the belief that homosexuality and cross-dressing are signs of decadence and immorality, and politicians have been leery of publicly supporting LGBT-rights legislation. A 2015 survey found 85.5% of respondents strongly disapproved of same-sex marriage with only 10.6% approving, and a 2013 survey found over 84% strongly disapproved of a gay or lesbian politician with only 12% positive. There are no exclusively gay bars or clubs, though an underground gay scene exists in Nassau alongside gay-friendly venues; LGBT groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden. Groups of LGBT tourists have been protested on various occasions, including church group protests against Rosie O'Donnell's 2004 cruise and a 1998 protest against a lesbian cruise, while the Bahamas Christian Council formed an anti-gay committee in 2007. Wikipedia country coverage: Expression is constrained by content regulation and social pressure: the Bahamas Plays and Films Control Board banned the gay-themed film Brokeback Mountain in March 2006 and attempted to block the Bahamian-made Children of God from a public-square screening on 24 June 2011, though the government overruled the board that time. The Communications Act (2009) empowers URCA to issue codes of practice against content likely to incite hatred or vilify persons on the basis of sexual preference, but there are no broad anti-discrimination or hate-crime statutes. LGBT rights groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden, and there are no exclusively gay bars or clubs — the scene in Nassau is described as underground. In September 2007 the Bahamas Christian Council formed an anti-gay committee to fight a request to a local cable company to carry the LGBTQ channel Logo. Wikipedia country coverage: No relationship recognition exists: the Bahamas Marriage Act defines a marriage as between a man and a woman, same-sex marriages and civil unions are not legal, and same-sex households are denied the rights given to opposite-sex married couples. The Constitution's prohibition against discrimination does not cover sexual orientation or gender identity, and a 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission report declined to list sexual orientation as a protected attribute; efforts to add it were blocked by commission members citing religious opposition. The only narrow statutory protections are the Data Protection (Privacy of Personal Information) Act (2003), which lists "sexual life" as sensitive personal data, and a 2001 Employment Bill clause banning sexual-orientation workplace discrimination that was removed shortly after passage. A 2016 constitutional referendum was explicitly framed by then-PM Perry Christie as not legalizing same-sex marriage, with male and female "determined at birth," and the resulting bills were not inclusive of transgender or intersex people. Wikipedia country coverage: Facilities and services are formally open to LGBT people: there are no prohibitions on LGBT citizens serving in the Bahamian police, military or prison service, and in May 1998 National Security Minister Frank Watson declared those forces do not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation. Social venues are limited — no exclusively gay bars or clubs exist, though an underground gay scene operates in Nassau alongside gay-friendly resorts, cafes and bars. Access to these spaces is contested: police raided a gay party in downtown Nassau on 6 October 2007 (no arrests, as no crime was committed), and the Ministry of Tourism later apologized to the cruise company involved. Wikipedia country coverage: Discrimination in healthcare on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal in the Bahamas, and there are no national hate-crime laws to punish violence against LGBT people. The text records no HIV or trans-specific care provisions; the only health-adjacent detail is a 2009 murder case in which the victim was a homosexual, HIV-positive man and his killer was acquitted using a "gay panic" defence. Nine murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015 are listed as unsolved, indicating a lack of effective investigation and protection for LGBT people. No youth-specific healthcare or medication-travel findings appear in the source. Wikipedia country coverage: The criminal code sets a higher age of consent for same-sex acts — 18 for same-sex couples versus 16 for heterosexual couples — a direct legal exposure for young LGBT Bahamians. Discrimination in education on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal, and the Constitution's equality protections do not extend to sexual orientation. Youth are targeted publicly: in September 2005 an 18-year-old beauty queen had her crown stripped after confirming she was a lesbian, and the 2016 referendum language defining male and female "at birth" was promoted by the then-Prime Minister. Public opinion is sharply hostile — 84% of survey respondents strongly disapproved of a gay or lesbian politician (2013) and 85.5% strongly disapproved of same-sex marriage (2015).

BHS.tangentialFactors:
The 1998 non-discrimination assurance from Frank Watson and the 2016 findings of Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United describe the same country from opposite directions. One is a statement of intent from a cabinet minister; the other is an inventory of what the statute actually contains. Where the two conflict, the statute governs.

The 2017 assault on Adrian Brown concerned a gay man rather than a trans visitor, so it is an adjacent indicator rather than a trans-specific case. It nonetheless bears on trans visitors because the attack turned on how the victim was perceived in public, which is the same mechanism that exposes gender-nonconforming travellers.

The Bahamas runs a tourism-dependent economy with extensive international exposure, and the assault occurred at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival, an event built for visitors. Incidents of this kind surface in the international press quickly, which shapes how the destination is perceived but does not alter the legal position on the ground.

Organised advocacy has existed since at least 2016, when Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United began the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign. Advocacy activity is evidence of an unprotected population, not evidence of protection.

BLZ.name: Belize
BLZ.summary:
Belize decriminalised same-sex conduct through the courts. On 10 August 2016 the Supreme Court, under Chief Justice Kenneth Benjamin, struck down the colonial-era Section 53 sodomy law as unconstitutional in Orozco v Attorney General, the challenge filed in 2010 by LGBT advocate Caleb Orozco and heard in Belize City in 2013. The Human Dignity Trust carries the case among its documentation of constitutional challenges to anti-sodomy statutes, and Belize was the first former British Caribbean territory to overturn such a law.

Before the ruling the statute was rarely enforced, yet the expat reporting at hand argues it had fostered intolerance; a 1998 protest against a gay cruise docking is cited as evidence of residual public hostility. The same reporting holds that gay travellers have long found Belize friendly, and the country has an organised advocacy organisation in UNIBAM, which brought the Orozco litigation.

Belize accepted 15 of 17 sexual-orientation and gender-identity recommendations in its 2018 UN Universal Periodic Review, the first CARICOM state to accept that many. The accepted pledges cover legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and the collection of SOGI data. Two rights-equality recommendations were 'noted' rather than accepted.

The detention axis is undocumented for Belize. The one prison-focused source in the inventory, a survey of LGBTQ prisoners worldwide, mentions Belize only through a navigation-box link and records no birth-sex-versus-identity housing rule, no trans housing units, and no solitary or segregation practice for trans prisoners. Where a detained trans visitor would be placed is therefore unknown, and the absence of any recorded standard cannot be read as a protective one.
BLZ.outOfScopeNotes:
Prison placement for trans detainees in Belize is unresolved: no source here states a housing rule, a segregation practice or a trans-specific unit, so the question cannot be answered from this inventory.

Legal gender recognition is not addressed by any source in this inventory. Whether a trans visitor or resident can amend a birth certificate, passport or other marker, and on what conditions, is not sourced here.

Discrimination protection on grounds of gender identity in employment is not carried by any source in this inventory, despite the UPR pledge to legislate explicit anti-discrimination measures.

No post-2016 enforcement data, arrest statistics or police guidance on the treatment of trans people is available in this inventory; the practical operation of the Orozco ruling for a trans person is unverified.

Whether the accepted UPR recommendations have been implemented, in whole or in part, is not sourced here.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D3, D6, D13.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: On 30 December 2019 the Appeals Court upheld the unconstitutionality of Section 53 and confirmed that the Constitution's protections against discrimination extend to sexual orientation and that freedom of expression includes sexual expression. Public expression has also grown: Belize held its first Pride Week in August 2017 with awareness and acceptance activities hosted throughout the country, and since the August 2016 Supreme Court ruling LGBT organisations have become more visible and active. In its 2018 Universal Periodic Review Belize accepted recommendations calling for educational campaigns to reduce societal stigma. Wikipedia country coverage: Section 5(1)(e) of Belize's Immigration Act lists "any prostitute or homosexual" among prohibited immigrants. Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson filed a challenge in 2013 (granted leave by the Caribbean Court of Justice in May 2014, joined by CARICOM as an interested party in October 2014), and on 10 June 2016 the CCJ dismissed his case, finding no violation of his freedom of movement. Wikipedia country coverage: In the Tomlinson litigation Belize contended that Section 5(1) of the Immigration Act applies only to those offering sexual services for financial gain, and that it does not interpret or enforce the act as a blanket prohibition against homosexual immigrants. The CCJ's 10 June 2016 judgment clarified that neither Trinidad and Tobago nor Belize can ban homosexuals from CARICOM countries from entering due to their treaty obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas, "notwithstanding their laws that ban the entry of gays". Wikipedia country coverage: In the 2018 Universal Periodic Review Belize accepted 15 LGBT-related recommendations, including calls to take concrete steps to ensure universal access to HIV treatment for LGBT people; the recommendations came mostly from Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Chile, France, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Mexico, Spain, Ukraine, the United States and Uruguay. The Anti-Sexual Harassment Act 2024 expressly provides prevention and protection from sexual harassment regardless of sexual preference and gender identity. No youth- or minor-specific care, medication or travel findings appear in the source text. Wikipedia country coverage: The Supreme Court case was heard in May 2013 amid violence and death threats received by LGBT activists. The 2018 UPR recommendations Belize accepted covered addressing discrimination, violence and hate crimes against LGBT people and training police officials to properly respond to violence. Section 8(1)(c)(i) of the Alternative Sentencing Act 2024 makes evidence that an offence was motivated by bias, prejudice or hate based on sexual orientation an aggravating circumstance, effective 27 April 2024, and the Anti-Sexual Harassment Act 2024 protects persons regardless of sexual preference and gender identity. Wikipedia country coverage: After the 2016 ruling the Government first said on 17 August 2016 it would not appeal, then reversed after meeting religious leaders on 9 September and filed a partial appeal against the declaration that the Constitution bars discrimination based on sexual orientation; the Catholic Church withdrew from the appeal in March 2018, leaving the Government as sole appellant. Solicitor General Nigel Hawke argued the ruling was judicial overreach in re-defining "sex" to include sexual orientation. Religious bodies were openly hostile: the Council of Churches held a "Take a Stand" rally on 3 December 2011 and a "Belize Action/Family Forum" rally on 23 November 2011 describing decriminalisation as "an orchestrated plan of demonic darkness"; in December 2011 Prime Minister Dean Barrow publicly rejected US pressure from President Obama, saying Belize would not change its laws. A 2013 UNAIDS survey of 773 Belizeans aged 18 to 64 found 34% accepting and 34% tolerant of homosexuals, among the highest acceptance rates in the Caribbean polled.

BLZ.tangentialFactors:
Belize's decriminalisation and its diplomatic positioning are ahead of its regional peers: the 2016 judgment made it the first former British Caribbean territory to overturn an anti-sodomy law, and the 2018 UPR round made it the first CARICOM state to accept 15 of 17 SOGI recommendations. Both comparisons sit alongside the fact that two equality recommendations were noted rather than accepted.

The litigation ran a long arc, from Orozco's 2010 filing through the 2013 Belize City hearing to the August 2016 judgment. The social climate described in the sources does not track the legal change closely: the pre-ruling statute was rarely enforced while still breeding intolerance, and the 1998 cruise-docking protest shows hostility that outlasted the statute's practical force.

Nothing in the inventory attaches a trans-specific legal claim to the Orozco ruling. The judgment addresses same-sex conduct, not gender identity, document markers, facilities or care.
BLZ.localsOnly:
UNIBAM, the organisation behind the Orozco challenge, remains the named organised body for LGBT Belizeans, and the constitutional route it used is the demonstrated avenue for legal change in the country.

For residents, the accepted UPR commitments translate into promised police training, promised SOGI data collection, promised legal reform and promised explicit anti-discrimination legislation. Implementation of those pledges is not evidenced in this inventory, so their delivery should be treated as unverified.

Two of the reviewed recommendations, both concerning equality of rights, were 'noted' rather than accepted, which marks the outer edge of the government's stated commitment.

HTI.name: Haiti
HTI.summary:
Haiti does not criminalise same-sex conduct; the prohibition has been off the books since 1791. There is no legal mechanism for gender recognition, no statutory anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, and no hate-crime enhancement. The judiciary does not operate as a protection avenue in practice.

The legislature has twice moved to tighten the regime. In August 2017 the Senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy, carrying up to three years' imprisonment and a fine of about US$8,000 for the parties. A June 2017 Senate bill would allow denial of the Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs, the good-conduct certificate that employers and universities require, on grounds of homosexuality. Both measures awaited a vote in the Chamber of Deputies as of November 2017.

Generalised state collapse drives the practical risk. Gangs control most of Port-au-Prince, the police are outgunned, and mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented; no protection machinery functions. Outing in gang-controlled areas can be lethal for a visitor.

The US State Department's 2018 report recorded attitudes in Haiti as hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in Port-au-Prince. Human Rights Watch's 2018 world report found that LGBT persons in Haiti continued to face high levels of discrimination.

Visible advocacy carries a documented risk. Charlot Jeudy, president of Kouraj, the national LGBTQ advocacy organisation, was found dead at his home in Port-au-Prince on 25 November 2019; press reports attributing the death to poisoning were never confirmed. ILGALAC, the regional LGBTI body, issued a mourning statement.

Trans people have additionally faced targeted harassment in the post-earthquake displacement camps, where they were identifiable to other residents and to camp authorities.
HTI.outOfScopeNotes:
The status of both Senate bills after November 2017 is unresolved in the available sources; no source in the inventory records a Chamber of Deputies vote, withdrawal or enactment.

The cause of Charlot Jeudy's death is unresolved. Poisoning was reported but not confirmed, and no source in the inventory states an official finding or arrest.

Prison placement for trans detainees is not sourced. The inventory contains no rule on birth-sex versus identity housing, no trans-specific units, and no solitary or segregation practice, so nothing can be asserted about how Haiti houses trans prisoners.

The most recent official assessment of the hostility climate in the inventory dates from 2018, with a press account from 2019. Current official reporting on attitudes toward visibly trans visitors after that point is not sourced here.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2, D4, D5, D6, D7.

Additionally, the 1987 Constitution guarantees all citizens a right to education, though LGBTQ youth face pervasive social hostility.

The good-conduct certificate is a gatekeeping document for employment and university admission. Under the June 2017 upper-house bill, a homosexuality finding could be used to refuse it, which converts institutional document checks into an exclusion mechanism for residents.

Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, so identity documents continue to display a sex marker that may not match presentation, and there is no anti-discrimination protection in employment, education or services to challenge the resulting treatment.

FJI.name: Fiji
FJI.summary:
Fiji decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct under the Crimes Act 2010, in force from 1 February 2010, repealing a colonial-era offence that had carried up to fourteen years' imprisonment. Arrests had already ceased in 2006, when the Fijian High Commissioner confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex would no longer be arrested.

The 2013 Constitution prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity and expression alongside sexual orientation. The Asia Pacific Alliance describes that pairing as unique worldwide, and its 2023 policy brief treats it as the central legal fact for trans people in Fiji. Fiji was, with South Africa, one of the first two countries to enshrine sexual-orientation non-discrimination in a constitution, in 1997; the 2013 text reinstated and expanded that protection.

The constitutional guarantee has no implementing machinery for trans people. Legislative and policy frameworks permit no change of gender marker and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities, and the Asia Pacific Alliance records the resulting marginalisation and discrimination as documented. The traditional third-gender role known as vaka sa lewa lewa holds cultural recognition only, with no legal standing.

There is no route to recognition of a same-sex partner: the Marriage Act 2002 defines marriage as one man and one woman, and no civil union exists. Health professionals are barred from attempting to change a person's sexual orientation, while intersex bodily autonomy is unprotected in law.
FJI.outOfScopeNotes:
Outright International's overview carries an "at a glance" flag marking same-sex relations as illegal, which contradicts the same overview's account of decriminalisation under the Crimes Act 2010. The inventory does not explain the flag; the inconsistency is unresolved, and the 2010 repeal is corroborated by the other sources listed here.

The GlobalGayz country page is undated and pre-dates the 2013 constitution. Its statement that sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination is not banned describes the earlier legal position, not current law.

No source in the inventory quantifies violence or harassment against trans people in Fiji, and none reports a decided case testing the 2013 constitution's gender-identity and expression clause. Enforcement of that protection is not documented here.

The report that LGBT organisations cannot register rests on a summary flag in one overview, without detail on the registration regime or which organisations are affected.

WSM.name: Samoa
WSM.summary:
Samoa is workable for trans visitors in respect of gender expression, but the Crimes Act 2013 criminalises same-sex sexual activity, with penalties of up to five years' imprisonment, as recorded in the Human Dignity Trust country profile. The offence is framed by the sexual act rather than by the partners' identity, so it reaches couples regardless of whether either partner is transgender, and a trans visitor in a same-sex relationship should treat Samoa as a jurisdiction where that conduct is criminal.

The same 2013 statute removed the colonial-era offence of impersonating a woman, so no Samoan law targets gender expression itself. RNZ Pacific reported on 3 May 2013 that the new Crimes Act was in force that week and that Samoa Fa'afafine Association president To'oto'oali'i Roger Stanley expressed relief at the repeal. The same reporting records that the community was not at that time pressing for repeal of the sodomy provisions, and those provisions remained in the statute.

Samoa's strongest protection for trans visitors is cultural rather than statutory. Fa'afafine (and the related fa'atama) are embedded in fa'a Sāmoa as heirs to customary land and as eligible for matai chiefly titles, and they are organised nationally through the Samoa Fa'afafine Association, which has acted as a formal stakeholder in Samoa's Universal Periodic Review. The Association's stakeholder report for the UPR's 39th session, 'The Protection of the Rights of Fa'afafine/Fa'atama/LGBTIQ/SOGIESC Persons in Samoa' (2021), sets out lived experiences and discrimination to establish grounds for non-discriminatory policy and legislation. Visibility is further reinforced by the community's long-running pageant culture.

Visitors should expect the term fa'afafine to be broadly understood locally, while knowing that academic analysis treats the identity as read through, and reshaped by, Western discourses of sexuality and transgenderism, with the Samoan diaspora in Auckland operating as a contact zone (Schmidt, Intersections, August 2001). A UN Free & Equal information sheet (August 2015) lists fa'afafine among pre-colonial Pacific gender identities that it describes as important parts of the region's cultural treasure, a framing that does not create legal protection.

What remains negative is modest for a short stay but not trivial: Samoa has no anti-discrimination law and no legal gender recognition procedure, so a visitor presenting documents inconsistent with presentation has no domestic statutory remedy. The Samoa Fa'afafine Association's own advocacy records discrimination, cyberbullying and gender-based violence against fa'afafine in peer-led research, and isolated reports of police harassment have been documented, in one study two respondents and no convictions. These harms are documented mainly in resident and domestic settings rather than in tourist environments, but the sodomy provisions and the absence of complaint machinery mean that reporting an incident to police carries its own exposure.
WSM.outOfScopeNotes:
The Reuters feature on Samoa's third gender, subtitled 'delicately balances sex and religion', could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 401), and nothing from it is asserted here. Any claim it might carry about the relationship between fa'afafine practice and the church remains unresolved.

The Asia Pacific Transnational Network's socio-economic study on Samoa is published as an image-based PDF with no extractable text, so no figures, rates or findings from that study are represented in this dossier. The characterisation of discrimination, cyberbullying and gender-based violence as documented rests on the qualitative peer-led research cited in the Association's advocacy, not on that study's quantitative data.

No source in the current inventory addresses visa and entry requirements, what documents are accepted at the border, whether an inconsistent passport or visa photograph triggers secondary screening, or access to gender-affirming healthcare in Samoa. These points are unresolved and should not be inferred from the cultural-recognition material above.

WSM.tangentialFactors:
Samoa sits inside a wider Pacific community infrastructure for gender-diverse people rather than being an isolated case. The Asia Pacific Transgender Network convened gender-diverse community members in Nadi, Fiji in May 2024 from Samoa, American Samoa, the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau, Tonga, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Fiji, West Papua and Papua New Guinea, documenting a Pacific MVPFAFF+ spectrum of locally named identities, including fa'afafine in Samoa and American Samoa, fakaleiti in Tonga and fakafifine in Niue. Terminology therefore travels across borders, and a visitor may hear several terms used loosely for the same person.

The academic record complicates the neatness of the cultural-protection narrative. Schmidt's 2001 analysis argues that fa'afafine identities are both viewed through and reshaped by Western sexuality and transgenderism discourses, which means a Western visitor's framing of a fa'afafine person as 'transgender' may not map onto how the person understands themselves. The UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet (August 2015) takes a similar descriptive stance, cataloguing fa'afafine alongside other Pacific gender identities as cultural heritage rather than as a rights category.

For comparison against neighbouring jurisdictions, the Human Dignity Trust country profile places Samoa among Pacific states retaining colonial-era sexual offences; its 2013 repeal of the impersonation crime was unusual in the region for its explicit removal rather than its retention. The same profile records that same-sex activity remains criminal.
WSM.localsOnly:
There is no anti-discrimination statute in Samoa covering sexual orientation, gender identity or sex characteristics, and no legal gender recognition procedure through which a resident can obtain a corrected birth certificate, passport or identity document. The Samoa Fa'afafine Association's UPR submissions (39th session, 2021) are directed precisely at establishing grounds for non-discriminatory policy and legislation, which indicates that these gaps are still open rather than settled in the community's favour.

The sodomy provisions of the Crimes Act 2013 remain in force, alongside the removal of the impersonation offence, so residents who have sex with men remain exposed to prosecution while gender expression itself is not an offence. The Association's 2013 statements to RNZ Pacific confirm that the community was not then asking for those provisions to be repealed, which is a political-strategy fact, not a statement that the risk is absent.

Discrimination, cyberbullying and gender-based violence against fa'afafine are documented in the Asia Pacific Transgender Network's peer-led socio-economic work, and police harassment appears in the same record as isolated reports, in one instance two respondents with no resulting conviction. Community standing under fa'a Sāmoa remains the counterweight: fa'afafine are recognised as heirs to customary land and as eligible for matai titles, and the Association functions as a formal national body with UN UPR access.
WSM.comparisons: Calibration (Aug 2026, two rounds of pairwise challenge): on traveler-facing axes Samoa beats Slovakia (0.69) on public presence, outing violence, and state climate; beats Greece (0.75) on public presence, police predation, and documented violence; and beats Romania (0.67) on every axis. It sits level with Greece — its lack of EU-style institutional recourse (a resident-weighted factor) is the only axis where European comparators hold an edge, and Estonia (0.77) keeps a 0.02 edge on that basis alone.

TON.name: Tonga
TON.summary:
Tonga's Criminal Offences Act criminalises same-sex activity, with a maximum penalty of 10 years' imprisonment. Outright International's overview, updated in March 2026, records no evidence of enforcement in recent years, and the 2010 US State Department human rights report described enforcement as rare.

The same statute contains an offence aimed squarely at gender expression: a male who solicits in public "for an immoral purpose" with intent to deceive as to his true sex commits an offence. This is a trans-expression provision on the books, and unlike the sodomy provision it turns on visible presentation rather than private conduct, so it bears directly on how a trans visitor may appear and speak in public spaces.

Tonga provides no legal gender recognition. A visitor's documents will therefore carry the sex marker assigned at birth, with no domestic mechanism to alter them.

Enforcement of the sodomy provision has been rare or absent in the periods covered by the sources, spanning 2010 to 2026. No documented recent prosecution of a trans person under the solicitation offence appears in the material reviewed.

On protection machinery, the 2010 US State Department report found no reports of government abuses of LGBT persons, while identifying domestic violence, discrimination against women and corruption as the country's most prevalent human-rights problems. That combination points to weak general institutional protection rather than active state persecution.

Tonga has a visible trans-feminine community, known locally as leiti, with a well-known pageant covered by the Washington Post in August 2024 alongside reporting on LGBT rights. Public visibility of leiti people coexists with the criminal statutes rather than being absent from them.

Community infrastructure is thin. Tonga's only LGBTI drop-in centre and shelter, on Tongatapu in Nuku'alofa, had part of its roof torn off by Cyclone Gita in February 2018, with winds over 120 mph damaging the bathrooms and bedrooms used by LGBTI Tongans. The country's sole dedicated shelter facility has documented structural vulnerability.
TON.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether corporal punishment remains a statutory penalty under the Criminal Offences Act is unresolved in the sources reviewed; only the 10-year maximum for sodomy is sourced here.

No case records were available establishing how, or whether, the public solicitation offence with intent to deceive as to true sex has been charged or prosecuted. Its enforcement risk is inferred from the text of the statute, not from documented arrests.

The precise scope of "for an immoral purpose" and "true sex" as judicially or administratively interpreted is not sourced, so the practical boundary of the offence for a trans visitor remains open.

UK foreign travel advice for Tonga yielded no trans-specific finding in the material reviewed, leaving that channel without usable content rather than confirming an absence of risk.

Whether any administrative or policy-level route to changing gender markers exists outside formal legal recognition is not addressed by the sources.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6, D7, D8, D13.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: In 2021, noted LGBTQ activist Polikalepo Kefu was murdered near his home near Muʻa. The source text describes a climate of fear, discrimination and homophobia for LGBTQ people resulting from conservative values mixed with colonial-era laws, and links a recent rise in fundamentalism and religious fanaticism to an increase in hatred and discrimination towards LGBTQ people and fakaleitis. Tonga, along with Kiribati, is the only Polynesian country that has not signed or expressed support for the 2011 UN joint statement on ending acts of violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Wikipedia country coverage: Tongan law does not address discrimination on account of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment or the provision of goods and services. The only related provision cited is the Judicial Code of Conduct 2010, which tells judges to be aware of diversity including sexual orientation and prohibits them from manifesting bias or prejudice towards any person or group on 'irrelevant grounds' — this binds judges, not employers or service providers. Wikipedia country coverage: The Kingdom of Tonga does not recognise same-sex sexual relationships or unions in any form. No further detail on partnership, marriage or next-of-kin rights appears in the source text.

TON.tangentialFactors:
The gap between legal text and social practice is the defining feature of the risk picture. A statute that criminalises public presentation as deception sits alongside a public, pageanted leiti culture, so legal exposure and social acceptance run on separate tracks and neither predicts the other.

The 2010 US State Department reporting places Tonga's LGBT situation inside a broader pattern of institutional weakness: domestic violence, discrimination against women and corruption were named as the most prevalent problems. Visitors relying on police or administrative remedy should weigh that general environment, not only the specific statutes.

The 2018 cyclone damage to the Nuku'alofa shelter indicates that community safety infrastructure in Tonga is exposed to natural hazard disruption, a factor distinct from legal risk but relevant to anyone seeking support on the ground.

Compared with jurisdictions that have repealed such provisions, Tonga retains both a conduct-based offence and a presentation-based offence, while offering none of the mitigation that legal gender recognition would provide for documents.
TON.comparisons: Pairwise: below Samoa (0.48 — stronger community organisation, no impersonation statute) and above Jordan (0.44).
TON.blindSummary:
The state's Criminal Offences Act criminalises same-sex activity, with a maximum penalty of 10 years' imprisonment. An international human rights organisation's overview, updated in March 2026, records no evidence of enforcement in recent years, and a 2010 national human rights report described enforcement as rare.

The same statute contains an offence aimed squarely at gender expression: a male who solicits in public "for an immoral purpose" with intent to deceive as to his true sex commits an offence. This is a trans-expression provision on the books, and unlike the sodomy provision it turns on visible presentation rather than private conduct, so it bears directly on how a trans visitor may appear and speak in public spaces.

The state provides no legal gender recognition. A visitor's documents will therefore carry the sex marker assigned at birth, with no domestic mechanism to alter them.

Enforcement of the sodomy provision has been rare or absent in the periods covered by the sources, spanning 2010 to 2026. No documented recent prosecution of a trans person under the solicitation offence appears in the material reviewed.

On protection machinery, the 2010 national human rights report found no reports of government abuses of LGBT persons, while identifying domestic violence, discrimination against women and corruption as the country's most prevalent human-rights problems. That combination points to weak general institutional protection rather than active state persecution.

The state has a visible trans-feminine community, known locally as leiti, with a well-known pageant covered by an international newspaper in August 2024 alongside reporting on LGBT rights. Public visibility of leiti people coexists with the criminal statutes rather than being absent from them.

Community infrastructure is thin. The state's only LGBTI drop-in centre and shelter, in the national capital, had part of its roof torn off by a tropical cyclone in February 2018, with winds over 120 mph damaging the bathrooms and bedrooms used by LGBTI residents. The country's sole dedicated shelter facility has documented structural vulnerability.
TON.blindOutOfScope:
Whether corporal punishment remains a statutory penalty under the Criminal Offences Act is unresolved in the sources reviewed; only the 10-year maximum for sodomy is sourced here.

No case records were available establishing how, or whether, the public solicitation offence with intent to deceive as to true sex has been charged or prosecuted. Its enforcement risk is inferred from the text of the statute, not from documented arrests.

The precise scope of "for an immoral purpose" and "true sex" as judicially or administratively interpreted is not sourced, so the practical boundary of the offence for a trans visitor remains open.

Official foreign travel guidance for the state yielded no trans-specific finding in the material reviewed, leaving that channel without usable content rather than confirming an absence of risk.

Whether any administrative or policy-level route to changing gender markers exists outside formal legal recognition is not addressed by the sources.

KIR.name: Kiribati
KIR.summary:
Consensual sex between men is a criminal offence in Kiribati, carrying five to fourteen years' imprisonment depending on the offence charged. A 2015 US State Department human rights report recorded no prosecutions under the provision. The same report listed Kiribati, alongside Sri Lanka, among the states still maintaining anti-homosexuality laws in 2016, in the context of the UN General Assembly's 84–77 rejection of an amendment that would have defunded the Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity.

The Constitution of Kiribati bars discrimination by race, national origin and colour. It does not extend that guarantee to sexual orientation or gender identity, and no such non-discrimination statute was in force at the time of reporting. Gender-based discrimination is prohibited only in the field of employment, and the State Department observed that this narrow protection is poorly enforced.

Land ownership is restricted to I-Kiribati, a constitutional limitation affecting property rights rather than entry, but relevant to any longer stay.

At the 21st session of the Universal Periodic Review, France, Slovenia and Chile urged Kiribati to decriminalise homosexuality. The Kiribati delegation made no response to those recommendations, while stating that it was considering Uruguay's advice to adopt legislation prohibiting discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual identity and sexual orientation. Whether that legislation was enacted is not established by the sources.

No cases of societal discrimination or violence against LGBT people were reported to the State Department in 2015. That is an absence of documented cases, not a finding of safety, and the sources carry no trans-specific violence data.

The sources address no rules on legal gender recognition, gender markers on passports or identity documents, bathroom or facility access, entry screening, or access to gender-affirming care. A visitor should treat those areas as unassessed rather than permissive.
KIR.outOfScopeNotes:
The most recent status evidence in the inventory dates from 2015 and 2016. Whether the criminal provision still stands, whether prosecutions have occurred since, and whether the contemplated non-discrimination legislation covering gender, sexual identity and sexual orientation was enacted are unresolved on these sources.

No source addresses legal gender recognition, amendment of gender markers on passports or national identity documents, or the interaction of those documents with immigration control; this is not stated as absent law, only as unsourced.

Hate-crime provisions, police conduct toward gender-diverse people, facility and restroom access, healthcare access including gender-affirming care, and refugee or asylum pathways are not covered by the inventory.

The finding of no reported societal discrimination or violence derives from a single 2015 embassy-style reporting cycle and should be read as unverified rather than as a negative finding.

The relationship between local Kiribati gender roles and the legal category of sex in the criminal provision is not analysed in the sources.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D3, D4, D5, D6, D8, D13.
