sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Sections 153–155 of the Penal Code make male homosexuality and related acts felonies: anal intercourse (buggery) carries up to 14 years' imprisonment, attempts or assault with intent up to 7 years, and acts of gross indecency between males up to 5 years. The text states the law is not enforced and that there are no reports of prosecutions directed against LGBTQ people under these provisions. Female homosexuality is legal. Wikipedia country coverage: Lesbians may face violence and discrimination despite female homosexuality being legal. In November 2016 Kiribati voted at the UN General Assembly to keep the Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity (the amendment to block the anti-LGBTQ proposal failed 84–77); Kiribati and Sri Lanka were the only countries criminalising homosexuality that voted this way. Employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been prohibited since 2015 under Article 107(2)(b) of the Employment and Industrial Relations Code 2015. Wikipedia country coverage: The Marriage Act (Cap 54) does not expressly forbid recognition of same-sex marriages, but generally assumes the partners are of the opposite sex; its restrictions on marriage cover family relatives, parties below age 16, and bigamy. The Magistrate's Court (Bowi Inano) has legal power to void and dissolve marriages. The Constitution's Article 15(3) anti-discrimination protection lists race, place of origin, political opinions, colour and creed, and does not expressly address sexual orientation or gender identity.

KIR.tangentialFactors:
Ethnographic literature documents a locally grounded gender-diverse role, the Pinapinaaine or Binabinaaine, shared with Tuvalu and discussed in Besnier's 2014 study “Gender on the edge”. The University of Hawai'i at Manoa research guide on gender identity and sexual identity in the Pacific notes that such Pacific identity expressions are rendered as homosexual or transgender only through Western vocabulary, so imported categories of trans identity may not map onto local ones.

Kiribati's position in 2016 was set against sustained external pressure: three states pressed for decriminalisation at the Universal Periodic Review, and the state was singled out in a UN General Assembly report for retaining anti-homosexuality laws. Delegation silence on the decriminalisation recommendations, paired with openness on a non-discrimination statute, indicates the direction of official engagement without indicating change in the criminal law.

The 2015 observation that no societal discrimination or violence was reported contrasts with the criminal statute itself, which remains a standing legal exposure for men who have sex with men and for anyone perceived to fall within it.

TUV.name: Tuvalu
TUV.summary:
Tuvalu's Penal Code criminalises male same-sex conduct, and the provisions carry a colonial-era origin. ILGA World's jurisdiction database records the offence as in force, and the US State Department's 2013 human rights report for Tuvalu describes the same criminalisation under the Penal Code without documenting any prosecution.

No government abuse of LGBT people was reported in that 2013 assessment. The picture the inventory supplies is of a statute that exists in law rather than one applied in court, but the evidence ends in 2013 and nothing more recent on enforcement is available here.

Discrimination is described as customary and religious in origin rather than state-imposed. The 2013 State Department report states that traditional customs perpetuate religious and social discrimination, including against women, and the GlobalGayz archive of historical material on Tuvalu places the sodomy law within that colonial legacy.

Tuvalu's recorded diplomatic position is a 2011 one. A US Mission Geneva release dated 22 March 2011 lists Tuvalu among roughly 80 signatory states of the UN joint statement on human rights, sexual orientation and gender identity. No later foreign-policy position appears in the inventory.

Transgender Tuvaluans appear in the national response to HIV but not in any legal framework. The 2017 Global AIDS Progress Report from the Tuvalu Ministry of Health, submitted for UNAIDS, states that the national response draws on a Pacific Multi-Country Mapping and Behavioural Study on HIV and STI risk and vulnerability among key populations, including men who have sex with men and transgender Tuvaluans. The inventory contains no legal gender recognition provision, no gender-identity discrimination statute, and no trans-specific violence record for Tuvalu.
TUV.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved from this inventory: the penalty attached to the criminalisation offence is not stated in any source available here, and neither is the age of consent or the statutory definition. The 2013 report documents absence of prosecution but supplies no enforcement statistics and no information on police practice.

Not sourced: legal gender recognition or any administrative route for changing gender markers; the gender-entry rules applied to passports and national identity documents; entry, visa, or border treatment of transgender travellers; anti-discrimination or hate-crime legislation covering gender identity; access to gender-affirming healthcare and any restriction on it; bathroom and facilities access; marriage and partner recognition; and documented incidents of violence against transgender people.

Also unresolved: whether the colonial-era provisions have been amended, repealed, or re-enacted since the 2017 source, and whether Tuvalu's 2011 diplomatic endorsement of the UN joint statement remains its current position. The absence of recent reporting in the inventory is not evidence that nothing has changed.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2, D3, D4, D5, D6.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Sections 153, 154 and 155 of the Penal Code make male homosexual intercourse, attempts and gross indecency between males felonies punishable by up to 14, 7 and 5 years' imprisonment respectively, creating a theoretical custody exposure for trans women perceived as male. In practice the source reports the law is not enforced, with the US Department of State noting no prosecutions of consenting adults under these provisions as of 2013. No detention-conditions, strip-search or specific custody-treatment findings for transgender detainees appear in the text. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2011 Tuvalu signed the UN "joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity," condemning violence and discrimination against LGBTQ people. The source does not document any specific hate-crime incidents, statistics or hate-crime legislation for Tuvalu. Wikipedia country coverage: The Labour and Employment Relations Act 2017 bans workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation, covering a broad list of protected grounds including gender, sex, pregnancy, marital status, HIV/AIDS status and disability. Constitutional protection is weaker: the freedom from discrimination in section 27 of the Constitution (as amended in 2023) lists sex among protected attributes but does not refer to sexual orientation. No gender-identity or gender-expression protection is described anywhere in the text. Wikipedia country coverage: Tuvalu does not recognize same-sex marriage or civil unions; the 2023 constitutional amendments banned same-sex marriage, and the Charter of Duties and Responsibilities in section 43(2)(b) defines a family unit as "a marriage as between a man and a woman to the exclusion of all others." The Marriage Act (Cap 29) does not expressly prohibit recognition of same-sex unions but generally assumes the parties are male and female, and same-sex marriages do not appear in its "restrictions on marriage" section. No partner-visa, next-of-kin, or foreign-union recognition provisions are discussed. Wikipedia country coverage: A 2005 study found about 14% of young Tuvaluan men aged 15 to 24 had had sex with a male partner at some point in their lives. The age of consent is 15 for heterosexual vaginal sex and lesbian sex, while the Penal Code's male homosexual provisions carry separate felony penalties (14, 7 and 5 years), an asymmetry that affects young men who have sex with men. 2017 UNAIDS estimates put the population at about 300 MSM and about 40 pinapinaaine nationwide; no education-policy, school-bullying or youth-service findings are given.

TUV.tangentialFactors:
Decriminalisation advocacy is documented in international fora rather than in Tuvaluan legal change. The GlobalGayz archive includes an OHCHR Human Rights Day op-ed urging states to decriminalise consensual same-sex relations, and the 2011 Geneva release names regional human rights forums and an intergovernmental monitoring council among the channels used to press the issue.

The signatory count is itself a datapoint. Roughly 80 states had endorsed the UN joint statement by March 2011, which places Tuvalu's position then as an endorsement of the statement's language rather than a rejection of it, even while the colonial-era offence remained on the books.

All sourcing on Tuvalu is short and old. The five available items span 2011 to 2017, and the newest legal or enforcement account is the 2013 State Department report. Anything about the current state of Tuvaluan law, enforcement practice, or public attitudes after 2017 is not established by this inventory.
TUV.comparisons: Pairwise: above Kiribati (0.38 — comparable law, slightly less isolation-driven vulnerability) and below Tonga (0.46).
TUV.blindSummary: Male same-sex conduct is criminalised here (14 years, unenforced), there is no legal gender recognition, and the society is very small, tight-knit and church-centred; there is no specifically documented anti-trans violence. Assessment caveat: very small jurisdiction with limited data. Single incidents and absent documentation carry correspondingly little evidential weight; do not over-interpret sparse data in either direction.
TUV.blindOutOfScope: The criminalisation is unenforced; the evidence base is very thin.
blindSourceSummaries: A country page on an international legal-rights database: documents this country's legal status — male same-sex conduct criminalised under historic provisions.

A foreign government's 2013 human-rights report on this country: traditional customs perpetuate religious and social discrimination including against women; no government abuses; the LGBT section notes criminalisation under the penal code but no prosecutions.

The health ministry's 2017 global AIDS progress report (UNAIDS): the national HIV response, drawing on a regional multi-country mapping and behavioural study on HIV and STI risk vulnerability among key populations (including MSM and transgender residents).
A foreign mission's post (March 2011) on LGBT rights in the UN context - this country was among the states of its region signing a joint statement of support for decriminalisation and SOGI rights.

LGBT travel-news archive: includes a UN human-rights office opinion piece on decriminalising homosexuality as a first step toward equality (Oct 2011), noting this country among regional states supporting the UN call.
TUV.blindTangential: Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (14 years, unenforced) — a formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
TUV.localsOnly:
Discrimination against LGBT Tuvaluans is described as socially and religiously generated. The 2013 State Department report attributes the pattern to traditional customs that perpetuate religious and social discrimination, a finding that also reaches women and that is not tied to official policy.

No prosecution for male same-sex conduct was documented in the 2013 assessment, and no government abuses against LGBT people were recorded at that point. The country's HIV programme nevertheless treats MSM and transgender Tuvaluans as key populations for outreach, drawing on a multi-country mapping and behavioural study of risk and vulnerability.

SLB.name: Solomon Islands
SLB.summary:
Solomon Islands criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity between men and between women under colonial-era Penal Code provisions, carrying a maximum penalty of 14 years' imprisonment. ILGA World and the Human Dignity Trust both record the offence and the same statutory maximum.

US State Department human rights reporting for 2013 found no prosecutions under the provisions, and the Human Dignity Trust profile records no prosecutions in recent years. The offence nonetheless remains in force, so exposure is a matter of the statute standing rather than of an active prosecution campaign.

Monitoring bodies record no LGBT-specific abuses and no abuses by security forces in the reporting years covered, which indicates that the practical risk to a visitor sits in the criminal provision itself, in social responses, and in the absence of any protective framework rather than in routine police action against LGBT people.

No relationship recognition of any kind exists. Parliament has not legislated same-sex marriage, and there is no legal recognition of same-sex partnerships. No non-discrimination shield covering sexual orientation or gender identity is recorded in the sources.

Senior office has carried official hostility toward same-sex relationships. On 8 June 2018 Governor General Sir Frank Kabui used his Queen's Birthday address to warn that 'same sex marriage cannot populate the world'.

The legal framework addresses same-sex conduct only. No source in the inventory records a trans-specific offence, a trans-specific protection, or any provision governing gender identity, so a trans visitor has no statutory footing in either direction.
SLB.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not address legal gender recognition, changes to gender markers on passports or national identity documents, or whether entry and exit screening asks about gender identity. These are unresolved: no source either grants or denies such procedures.

No source covers hate-crime provisions for trans victims, access to gender-affirming health care, rules on sex-segregated facilities, or asylum and refugee screening on gender-identity grounds. Their status is not sourced here and should not be read as either present or absent.

Whether foreign nationals are in practice prosecuted under the Penal Code provisions, or whether visitors are exposed to them differently from residents, is not stated by any source in the inventory.

The human-rights reporting in the inventory dates from 2010 to 2013, with one official statement from 2018 and secondary summaries of undated currency. Current enforcement practice after that window is unresolved, and the Wikipedia entry is a tertiary source.

No source documents violence directed specifically at trans people, community infrastructure, or housing and employment outcomes for trans residents, so claims about the level of social hostility toward trans visitors are unsupported by this inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2, D3, D4, D5, D6, D8, D13.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The climate is defined by decriminalization since the 1880s and repeated official rejection of reform: the Law Reform Commission proposed legalizing gay and lesbian sexual activity in December 2008, but the move was strongly opposed, and the government told the United Nations in 2011 it had no intention of decriminalising homosexuality. Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare publicly opposed same-sex marriage in a 2017 speech to a local church group, and in June 2018 Governor General Frank Kabui acknowledged that being gay or lesbian 'is said to be biological and is beyond individual control' while still condemning any legal change, citing both the criminal code and the Bible. Enforcement is nonetheless absent: the U.S. Department of State reported no arrests or prosecutions directed at LGBTQ people in 2010, 2011, 2012 or 2013, and the source notes the law is not enforced. Constitutional reform has narrowed visibility of the issue — a 2009 draft constitution listed 'sexual orientation' as a prohibited ground of discrimination, but the 2011, 2013 and 2014 drafts dropped it, with reform still ongoing as of 2019.

VUT.name: Vanuatu
VUT.summary:
Vanuatu never criminalised same-sex conduct, and there is no documented pattern of anti-trans violence against visitors. That baseline sits alongside an official posture moving sharply against LGBT people: in November 2024 the Ministry of Justice and Community Services was directed to appoint a committee drafting a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion. National Human Rights coordinator Albert Nalpini said a Council of Ministers decision earlier in 2024 had targeted LGBTQIA+ activities, with V-Pride framed as contrary to constitutional, Christian and Melanesian values. For a visibly trans or gender-nonconforming visitor, that framing is the operative risk signal, since it invites suspicion of advocacy or promotion rather than merely of private conduct.

Parliament amended the Marriage Act in November 2024 to define marriage as the union of a male and a female. Internal Affairs Minister Andrew Napuat confirmed that same-sex marriages cannot be registered and that pastors must not perform ceremonies against the law. Couples travelling together should therefore expect no recognition of an existing marriage.

Legal gender recognition does not exist, so a visitor's documents will reflect the gender assigned at birth. There is no mechanism to alter markers before or during travel.

Protection machinery offers thin cover. A 2016 joint workshop by VPride Foundation and the Vanuatu Women's Centre established that same-sex partners receive no protection under the Family Protection Act 2008 and must instead rely on penal-code routes. University of the South Pacific law lecturer Anita Jowitt documented a single prosecuted case of violence against lesbians and an LGBTI court presence that was near-invisible. VPride, founded in 2014, met opposition from church leaders, officials and chiefs at its founding, and a small community remains based in Port Vila.
VUT.outOfScopeNotes:
The national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy was at the committee-drafting stage when last sourced, in November 2024; its final text, whether it has been adopted, and what penalties or enforcement mechanisms attach are unresolved and not stated in the available material.

No source in the inventory reports prosecutions, detentions or violence against trans people under the 2024 measures, so the practical enforcement picture for a trans visitor is unresolved rather than established as either active or dormant.

Whether the Family Protection Act 2008 exclusion has since been addressed, and whether any legal gender recognition process has opened, are not sourced either way. Port Vila is the only location where community presence is documented; conditions elsewhere are not covered.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D3, D4, D5, D6, D7, D8, D13.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Vanuatu is described as socially conservative: gay and lesbian travellers and citizens are advised to avoid public displays of affection, and there is no active gay scene. Section 2(2)(j) of the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2024 bars digital communications that denigrate a person by reason of, among other grounds, sexual orientation. The Ni-Vanuatu group VPride Foundation (founded 2009) advocates LGBTQ rights and freedom of speech, has organised awareness events, and first marked the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia in Vanuatu in 2016. Wikipedia country coverage: There is no legal protection against all forms of discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no general prohibition of employment discrimination on that basis. Narrow exceptions exist: Section 18.2(f) of the Teaching Service Act 2013 bars the Vanuatu Teaching Service Commission from discriminating on "sexual preference" in recruitment, promotion, professional development, transfer and staff management; the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2024 (s.2(2)(j)) bars denigrating digital communications by sexual orientation. The Office of the Public Prosecutor's Prosecution Policy 2003, Prosecutors Code (Gazette no. 13 of 2017) and its General Principles on vulnerable witnesses in sexual and gender-based violence cases require prosecutors to disregard sexual preference and to treat discrimination or hostility based on sexual orientation or gender identity as factors weighing toward prosecution. Vanuatu signed the UN joint statement on ending violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2011.

NRU.name: Nauru
NRU.summary:
Nauru decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2016, repealing provisions of a criminal code inherited from Queensland in 1899, together with the attempted-suicide offences that sat alongside them. Visitors should not expect prosecution for consensual same-sex intimacy under Nauruan law.

Trans visitors have no legal standing to rely on. Kaleidoscope Trust's country assessment records that intersex and transgender people in Nauru have no explicit legal recognition or protection, and that same-sex marriages and unions remain illegal. No source in this inventory documents how Nauru handles gender markers on passports or other identity documents, so a visitor cannot assume that documents will reflect a stated identity.

The one gender-identity provision found for Nauru applies inside immigration detention. The Nauru Regional Processing Centre Rules 2014, made under the Asylum Seekers (Regional Processing Centre) Act 2012, prohibit discrimination against any person on grounds of sex or gender, sexual preference or gender identity within that facility. The rule is a non-discrimination guarantee, not a placement rule: it does not address housing by birth sex versus identity, special units, or solitary confinement, and it covers immigration detention rather than Nauru's criminal-justice prison system.

No documented case of anti-trans violence, and no trans-prisoner case or court ruling, was found for Nauru in these sources. Nauru's diplomacy has pointed the other way: it was among the 84 countries joining the 2011 joint statement on ending violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity, delivered by Colombia on behalf of the group, alongside Fiji, the Marshall Islands and Micronesia.

The evidence base is thin. Nauru has roughly 12,000 residents, and the sources available here carry little first-hand reporting on day-to-day conditions for trans people, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

Unresolved: no hate-crime provision protecting trans people was found, and the inventory does not state whether Nauruan law provides any aggravated-penalty or sentencing protection on gender-identity grounds. The 2016 decriminalisation event is well sourced; the surrounding criminal-law architecture is not.

Unresolved: the absence of documented anti-trans violence reflects an absence of reporting in these sources, not a demonstrated absence of incidents. With a population near 12,000 and no dedicated monitoring body identified, the record should be read as unverified rather than as confirmation that no harm occurs.

Unresolved: the Regional Processing Centre Rules' practical application, including any complaint mechanism and any enforcement outcome, is not described, and the boundary between that facility's rules and Nauru's domestic prison regulations remains unstated beyond the fact that the two are separate regimes.

Nothing in these sources documents where transgender prisoners are housed, whether special units or separation orders exist, or how solitary confinement is applied, and no trans-prisoner case or ruling was located. Residents held in the criminal-justice system therefore cannot be described as covered by the Regional Processing Centre Rules.

The country's small size cuts both ways. Roughly 12,000 people means limited institutional capacity and few specialised services, and any trans resident is likely to be visible within a small community.

PLW.name: Palau
PLW.summary:
Palau decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2014. The Penal Code signed by the President in April 2014 dropped the sodomy offence formerly at section 2803 of Chapter 28, "Sex Crimes", Title 17, which carried up to ten years' imprisonment; Palau's Attorney General confirmed the repeal. No offence against consensual same-sex conduct is currently in force.

Palau's government has a dated record of opposing anti-LGBT violence and discrimination. At its 2011 Universal Periodic Review, Palau accepted recommendations to repeal criminalisation and to combat discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. In March 2011, Palau was among the 84 countries on whose behalf Colombia delivered a joint statement to the Human Rights Council calling for an end to violence and human-rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

No legal gender recognition pathway is available: the sources document no procedure by which a trans person can amend the gender marker on Palau identity or travel documents, so visitors should expect documents to reflect the marker assigned at issuance.

No anti-trans violence is documented in the available record for Palau. The absence of incidents should not be read as a finding of safety. Palau's population is very small and the evidence base correspondingly thin, which gives this assessment greater-than-usual uncertainty.

Unresolved: there is no sourced record of anti-trans violence in either direction. No incident reports, police statistics or victim accounts appear in the inventory, so the absence of documented cases cannot be treated as evidence that none occur.

FSM.name: Micronesia (FSM)
FSM.summary:
The Federated States of Micronesia carries no documented legal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct. US State Department human rights reporting in 2010 and again in 2015 recorded no laws criminalising homosexuality in the country, and current legal overviews likewise describe no criminalisation. Earlier provisions of this kind existed in some constituent states, but none remain in force.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been illegal since a 2018 constitutional equality reform, adopted by the national Congress. The archived US State Department reports from 2010 and 2015 predate that reform and describe only limited protection against such discrimination, so they should not be read as the current position.

No legal gender recognition procedure is documented for the Federated States of Micronesia, and no source in the current record describes the availability of marker or document amendment for transgender visitors or residents. Equally, nothing in the record establishes entry or visa screening that could expose a visitor's trans status, nor any provision governing single-sex facilities, transition-related healthcare, or hate-crime treatment of anti-trans violence.

The evidence base is thin in exactly the direction that matters for transgender visitors. Absence of criminalisation is documented; absence of anti-trans discrimination, violence, or official hostility is not. Where the record is silent, the map treats that as unresolved rather than as reassurance.
FSM.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current record addresses entry, visa, or customs screening procedures for transgender travellers to the Federated States of Micronesia, including whether document markers are inspected or questioned. This is unresolved and should be verified with the FSM Immigration Office before travel.

The availability of transition-related healthcare, of doctors willing to prescribe hormones, and of competent, non-discriminatory medical care is not sourced. It should be checked with the FSM Department of Health and Social Services or a clinician in Pohnpei directly.

There is no documented hate-crime statute covering gender identity or expression, and no documented guidance for law enforcement or the FSM National Police on handling anti-transgender incidents. Whether the 2018 equality amendment has been interpreted to cover gender identity, and by which court or authority, is unresolved on the present evidence.

No sources address single-sex facilities, public-order laws affecting gender presentation, or the treatment of transgender people in detention or police custody. Claims about violence risk, partner recognition, or official protection cannot be supported from the inventory and remain unverified.

MHL.name: Marshall Islands
MHL.summary:
The Marshall Islands has no criminalisation regime covering same-sex conduct. Human Dignity Trust's global record of criminalisation history dates the country's decriminalisation to 2005, in the same period as repeals recorded for the United States in 2003 and for Cape Verde and San Marino in 2004. A visitor therefore faces no statutory offence for consensual same-sex relations.

No procedure for legal gender recognition is documented for the Marshall Islands. A traveller whose passport carries a gender marker changed in another country has no local route to amend documentation, and the marker on the document presented at entry is what border and screening officials will work from.

The most recent official country reporting in the inventory is the 2015 United States State Department Human Rights Report for the Marshall Islands. It identifies prison conditions, corruption and domestic violence as the significant problems under review, records no reports of torture, arbitrary killing or enforced disappearance, and reports no LGBT-specific abuses.

The Pacific Sexual and Gender Diversity Network profiles Anfernee Nenol Kaminaga, a 25-year-old pansexual genderqueer Marshallese who co-created and led Brighten the Rainbow, described as the first openly LGBTIQ initiative in the Marshall Islands. Openly LGBTIQ organising at that level exists, which bears on how visible a visitor's own presentation is likely to be received.

The population is very small and the evidence base thin. The absence of documented anti-trans or LGBT-specific abuse in official reporting is an absence of records rather than a demonstration of protection, and this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.
MHL.outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and visa requirements for the Marshall Islands, including any screening question touching on gender identity or sexuality, are not covered by the sources in this inventory and remain unresolved.

The statement that no legal gender recognition exists is carried in the record without a primary statutory or government source in the current inventory; it should be verified against Marshallese legislation before being relied on as a finding.

The inventory contains no material on hate-crime or anti-discrimination provisions, on recognition of same-sex partners or marriages, or on access to gender-affirming healthcare. Whether such provisions exist is unresolved rather than confirmed absent.

Official human-rights reporting stops at 2015. Conditions after that date, including any change in the treatment of trans visitors, are not sourced here.

BEN.name: Benin
BEN.summary:
Benin does not criminalise same-sex relations anywhere in the country. Outright International's country overview records that, alongside this legality, SOGIESC discrimination is not prohibited by law, legal gender recognition is impossible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. The statutory position is therefore legal but entirely unshielded: there is no recognition pathway and no statutory protection to invoke.

The US State Department's 2023 country report on human rights practices found that Benin's law does not explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of SOGIESC, and that LGBTQI+ couples and families are not recognised. The report describes hostility toward the community that is most pronounced outside major urban areas, and records LGBTQI+ persons being routinely refused medical care, including hormone treatment, as well as social services. A trans visitor needing routine or hormone-related care should expect refusal, particularly outside Cotonou and Porto-Novo.

Social violence is the sharper risk. Erasing 76 Crimes reported in April 2024 that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace in Benin. The same report describes the Hirondelles Club at the Rehoboth Friendship Centre, which has housed LGBT+ youth since about 2020: a 20-place temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed. Its existence indicates both that displacement and family violence are common enough to require such a shelter and that survivor-support infrastructure remains very small relative to need.
BEN.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved and not sourced in this inventory: whether Benin's passport or identity-card authorities will amend a gender marker for trans citizens, and whether entry screening or immigration interview questions ask about gender history. No source addresses bathroom or facilities access, hate-crime sentencing enhancement, or whether gender-based rather than sexuality-based violence is recorded separately by Benin's police.

The claim that lynchings are commonplace rests on a single outlet's April 2024 framing rather than on police or court statistics, and no case-level incidents with dates and outcomes are available here. Whether the Hirondelles Club currently has capacity, and whether comparable shelters operate in other cities, is likewise not established. Any trans-specific violence figures distinct from anti-LGBT violence generally remain not sourced.

For this record: current social-violence risk (lynchings) plus the existence of small survivor-support infrastructure.

Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are NOT criminalised anywhere in Benin, but SOGIESC discrimination is not prohibited, legal gender recognition is impossible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. For this record: the current statutory baseline — legal but entirely unshielded, no recognition pathway.

US State Department 2023 Country Report (Benin): the law does not explicitly prohibit SOGIESC discrimination; LGBTQI+ couples and families are not recognised; the community — especially outside major urban areas — faces hostility, with LGBTQI+ persons routinely refused medical care (including hormone treatment) and social services. For this record: official US assessment of on-the-ground hostility and service denial, with an urban/rural split visitors should weigh.

Washington Blade (31 Aug 2015), commissioned by the European Forum of LGBT Christian Groups: LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria describe discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments. For this record: regional religious-institution hostility including Benin — dated 2015, treat as context not current-state evidence.

Erasing 76 Crimes (8 May 2012): interview with anthropologist Patrick Awondo (political sociology/medical anthropology, EHESS Paris) citing evidence of same-sex relationships in Benin alongside Cameroon, Zimbabwe and Burkina Faso, and Melville Herskovits' record of women-women marriages in the ancient Dahomey kingdom (modern Benin); frames same-sex practice as indigenous rather than a colonial import. For this record: historical baseline supporting the localsOnly framing that today's statutory legality sits on pre-colonial practice, not recent liberalisation.

BEN.tangentialFactors:
Reporting commissioned by the European Forum of LGBT Christian Groups and published by the Washington Blade on 31 August 2015 describes LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria facing discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments. The account is a decade old and is offered as regional context on religious-institution hostility rather than as evidence of current conditions in Benin.

Source currency varies across the record: Outright International's overview was updated on 12 March 2026, the State Department report covers calendar year 2023, and the shelter and lynching reporting dates from April 2024. The hostility and service-denial findings are drawn from a US government human-rights assessment rather than from Benin's own authorities.
BEN.localsOnly:
Same-sex practice in the territory now called Benin has a documented pre-colonial history. Anthropologist Patrick Awondo of EHESS Paris cites evidence of same-sex relationships in Benin alongside Cameroon, Zimbabwe and Burkina Faso, and Melville Herskovits recorded women-women marriages in the ancient Dahomey kingdom. On this record, today's statutory legality sits on indigenous practice rather than on recent liberalisation.

For residents, the practical constraints are structural. LGBTI organisations cannot register as legal entities, which limits how organised advocacy, shelter funding and complaint handling can be conducted. There is no legal gender recognition procedure, so Beninese trans people have no domestic route to align official documents with their gender, and no anti-discrimination law to which they can appeal in employment, housing, health care or education.

The report describes hostility toward the community that is most pronounced outside major metropolitan areas, and records LGBTI persons being routinely refused medical care, including hormone treatment, as well as social services. a trans visitor needing routine or hormone-related care should expect refusal, particularly outside the largest cities.

The same report describes a friendship-centre shelter for LGBT+ youth operating since about 2020: a 20-place temporary accommodation facility through which almost 380 young people have passed. Its existence indicates both that displacement and family violence are common enough to require such a shelter and that survivor-support infrastructure remains very small relative to need.
BEN.blindOutOfScope:
Unresolved and not sourced in this inventory: whether the state's passport or identity-card authorities will amend a gender marker for trans residents, and whether entry screening or immigration interview questions ask about gender history. No source addresses bathroom or facilities access, hate-crime sentencing enhancement, or whether gender-based rather than sexuality-based violence is recorded separately by national police.

The claim that lynchings are commonplace rests on a single outlet's April 2024 framing rather than on police or court statistics, and no case-level incidents with dates and outcomes are available here. Whether the shelter currently has capacity, and whether comparable shelters operate in other cities, is likewise not established. Any trans-specific violence figures distinct from anti-LGBT violence generally remain not sourced.
blindSourceSummaries: A monitoring organisation (9 Apr 2024): a local safe-housing club has housed LGBT+ youth since about 2020 — a temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people from the country and the sub-region have passed; the framing is that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace. Current social-violence risk (lynchings) plus the existence of small survivor-support infrastructure.

An organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are NOT criminalised anywhere in the country, but sexual-orientation-and-gender discrimination is not prohibited, legal gender recognition is impossible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register.

A government annual human-rights report: the law does not explicitly prohibit sexual-orientation-and-gender discrimination; LGBTQI+ couples and families are not recognised; the community — especially outside major urban areas — faces hostility, with LGBTQI+ persons routinely refused medical care (including hormone treatment) and social services. Official assessment of on-the-ground hostility and service denial, with an urban/rural split visitors should weigh.

A news outlet (31 Aug 2015): LGBT people in several countries of the region describe discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments. Regional religious-institution hostility relevant to this country — dated 2015, treat as context not current-evidence.

A monitoring organisation (8 May 2012): an interview with a researcher citing evidence of same-sex relationships in this country alongside several regional countries, and an anthropologist's record of women-women marriages in ancient times in the same country; frames same-sex practice as indigenous rather than a historic-era import. Historical baseline supporting the framing that today's statutory legality sits on long-standing practice, not recent liberalisation.
BEN.blindLocalsOnly:
Same-sex practice in the country has a documented pre-historic history. an anthropologist based at a national research institute in a neighbouring national jurisdiction cites evidence of same-sex relationships in the state alongside three other national jurisdictions, and a mid-twentieth-century researcher recorded women-women marriages in the pre-historic nation that occupied the modern state/province. On this record, today's statutory legality sits on indigenous practice rather than on recent liberalisation.

For residents, the practical constraints are structural. LGBTI organisations cannot register as legal entities, which limits how organised advocacy, shelter funding and complaint handling can be conducted. There is no legal gender recognition procedure, so trans residents have no domestic route to align official documents with their gender, and no anti-discrimination law to which they can appeal in employment, housing, health care or education.
BEN.blindTangential:
A 2015 report commissioned by a faith-community forum describes LGBT Christians in several national jurisdictions of the wider area facing discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments. The account is a decade old and is offered as regional context on religious-institution hostility rather than as evidence of current conditions in the state.

Source currency varies across the record: the regional human-rights overview was updated in March 2026, the national assessment covers calendar year 2023, and the shelter and lynching reporting dates from April 2024. The hostility and service-denial findings are drawn from an external government human-rights assessment rather than from the state's own authorities.

TGO.name: Togo
TGO.summary:
Togo criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. The provision is the Penal Code offence of "acts against nature committed with an individual of one's sex", carrying a maximum of three years' imprisonment and a fine (Human Dignity Trust).

The United States Department of State's 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices records that this provision was enforced during the reporting period. The same report states that the law also reaches "promotion of same-sex conduct" and that the clause extends to advocacy and to gender identity expression. Because the statute's language is defined in terms of sexual acts rather than identity, a trans visitor's exposure is not self-evident from the code alone; the practical risk attaches to conduct, visibility and advocacy, and the sources do not delimit where the promotion clause ends.

Violence against LGBT people is documented as an ongoing state-level concern rather than an isolated pattern. The 2022 and 2023 State Department reports each list crimes involving violence or threats of violence targeting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons among the significant human rights issues in the country.

State officials have been recorded as part of the problem. The State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report documented security-force torture, impunity, and official and societal discrimination against members of the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender community. The combination of criminalisation, enforced provisions and documented official hostility means a trans visitor who encounters police cannot assume the state machinery is neutral.

Law enforcement in the capital is described in firsthand reporting as actively hostile. A Washington Blade account published on 31 August 2015, based on interviews conducted between 14 and 31 March 2015 in Lomé and neighbouring countries, states that Lomé's police are "particularly merciless when dealing with LGBT locals and tourists". The same account returns to the site of a 2008 attack on the author in the capital, and explicitly frames tourist exposure in Lomé as a live risk rather than a theoretical one.

Conditions of detention compound the exposure created by arrest. The State Department's 2022 report lists cruel treatment, harsh prison conditions and arbitrary detention among significant human rights issues, alongside criminal libel enforcement. A visitor detained under the sodomy or promotion provisions faces a custodial system already assessed as abusive.

Documentation and assistance exist, but at civil-society level. In an alternative report to the United Nations Human Rights Committee submitted in June 2021, the Togolese association Synergia together with AAEC describes work on HIV within MSM and trans populations under the National Strategic Plan 2016–2020, documentation of LGBT rights violations across the country and neighbouring francophone West African states, and the provision of legal and judicial support to victims. This is the only documented channel in the source inventory through which a trans visitor reporting mistreatment could seek assistance.

The sources do not establish that the three-year maximum has been applied to transgender persons specifically, and they contain no dated record of recent prosecutions. Enforcement of the law is documented; the frequency, the demographics of those charged and the sentences imposed are not.

NER.name: Niger
NER.summary:
Niger is among the most dangerous countries in the region for a trans visitor, and the legal position hardened sharply in 2025 and 2026. In March 2025 the ruling junta's Charter of Refoundation banned “LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior” in Article 25, the first explicit statutory-level outlawing of same-sex conduct in the country's history. The ban operates alongside the five-year transition declared after the July 2023 coup.

The prohibition is now carried in the penal code. A February 2026 revision of the penal code criminalises “indecent, unnatural, and LGBTQIA+ acts” under article 390, punishable by five to ten years' imprisonment and fines; same-sex marriage under article 391 carries ten to twenty years; article 392 targets LGBTQIA+ associations. Article 390 also reaches anyone who “artificially changes sex at birth”, a clause that on its face exposes trans and intersex people to imprisonment for transition-related procedures. The state news agency confirmed on 1 June 2026 that LGBTQIA+ practice is criminalised under the 2026 revision.

The drafting is broad enough that reporting on the law reads asexuality as among the sanctionable conducts, so the exposure is not confined to sexual acts between people of the same sex. An earlier 2023 draft penal code, which did not take effect in that form, proposed up to five years for same-sex conduct, twenty years for conducting, officiating or witnessing a same-sex marriage, and five years for participating in or financing “homosexual” organisations; it also fixed age of consent at 21 for same-sex acts against 13 for different-sex acts, a distinction that would expose adult same-sex partners to prosecution.

Enforcement under junta rule has been immediate and public. By 1 July 2026 at least 40 people had been arrested for homosexuality and 16 men, including high-ranking military officials, were imprisoned following the new penal code. Campaigners describe a witch-hunt atmosphere. Arrest under these provisions carries the risk of outing anyone travelling with a partner or documented history, and detention by security forces under a military government offers no meaningful avenue of complaint.

Earlier precedent points the same way. In 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under public-indecency article 276, which carries up to three years; the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them, showing the cost of delivering an acquittal. In December 2022 the national legislature backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, weeks after a subnational court had acquitted two young women precisely because no statute criminalised same-sex conduct.

Access to HIV prevention has deteriorated alongside criminalisation: sources report that PrEP drug access has collapsed, with campaigners warning of an AIDS resurgence among men who have sex with men. No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, document markers, entry screening, or facilities access; those must be treated as unassessed rather than safe.
NER.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source in the inventory states whether the 2023 draft penal code's specific penalties took independent effect or were wholly absorbed into the February 2026 revision; the two sets of figures (five years, twenty years, five years in the draft versus 5–10, 10–20 in the 2026 code) may describe the same instruments or different ones.

Unresolved: the claim that asexuality falls within the sanctionable conduct rests on a single newspaper reading of the drafting, not on judicial interpretation or official comment; no court ruling applying article 390 to asexual or aromantic persons is sourced here.

Unresolved: the Charter of Refoundation's Article 25 is reported as setting no specific penalties itself, and the relationship between charter provisions and penal code articles in enforcement practice is not documented in the inventory.

Not sourced in this inventory: legal gender recognition and document-marker rules, entry and visa screening procedures that could expose a trans traveller's status, public facilities or bathroom restrictions, and any hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection. Silence in these sources should not be read as a permissive position.

Unresolved: the exact status of the 40 arrests and 16 imprisonments reported on 1 July 2026, including charges, convictions and sentences, is not detailed beyond the campaigner account.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Creating, managing, financing or participating in LGBTQIA+ organizations, clubs and social venues — directly or indirectly — is punishable under the February 2026 penal code by 10 to 20 years in prison and fines up to 500 million CFA francs (about €762,244 / US$882,829). Two gay rights organizations reportedly operated in secret in Niger, partly because they were not formally registered. Following the 2026 law, organizations providing HIV prevention services to men who have sex with men stopped working, with a representative warning that people no longer have access to condoms, HIV testing or PrEP. Wikipedia country coverage: The U.S. State Department's 2013 Human Rights Report found no reports of violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity and no documented cases of discrimination, though it noted stigma or intimidation probably prevented incidents from being reported; the same report recorded two men caught naked in a parked car arrested for 'public indecency' and fined. Asylum seekers who staged Niger's first LGBTQ public demonstration in Niamey in 2022 — from Cameroon, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire — faced societal discrimination including shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers. After the 2026 penal code, local media reported dozens of people arrested across the country, some imprisoned, including military officials. Wikipedia country coverage: There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in Niger. Article 95 of Law 2022-59 on the Protection of Personal Data prohibits collecting or processing data revealing sexual orientation, punishable by three months to five years imprisonment and fines of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs (published by the Ministry of Communication and New Information Technologies in June 2025). The only other protection, in Law 2015-36 on Illicit Trafficking of Migrants (Art. 4), was repealed in 2023 by decree of President Abdourahamane Tiani, with prior convictions and their effects expunged. Wikipedia country coverage: Young people are directly hit: in Maradi in 2022 two young women were prosecuted over lesbianism (acquitted because no legislation then existed) but were imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos on social media allegedly portraying a lesbian act. In Niamey in 2025, two young women reported by a third person were prosecuted for 'public indecency' and acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere, sparking widespread debate; the judge was allegedly sanctioned for being too lenient. The 2013 U.S. State Department report found no documented cases of discrimination in education based on sexual orientation, though it cautioned that stigma suppressed reporting. Under the pre-2025 rules the age of consent was unequal: 13 for heterosexual acts versus 21 for homosexual acts. Wikipedia country coverage: LGBTQIA people in Niger face stigmatization among the broader population. Since March 2025, Article 25 of the military junta's 'Charte de la Refondation' has criminalized all LGBTQIA+ acts or practices, and the February 2026 penal code adds 5 to 10 years' imprisonment and fines up to 100 million CFA francs for same-sex relations, public announcement of a same-sex relationship, and changing or attempting to change one's birth sex, with mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences unavailable. Justice Minister Alio Daouda said 'all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be' are 'not in line with our social and cultural values', and President Mohamed Bazoum's 2023 proposals focused public discourse on 'social contagion'. After the 2026 law, LGBTQ people went into hiding; historically many led socially acceptable public lives while keeping relationships private, and Niger's authorities refused to recognise the 2022 protesters' refugee status.

NER.tangentialFactors:
Niger's 2025–2026 measures sit within a wider pattern of states across the continent hardening anti-LGBTQIA+ statutes, so the country is not an isolated case in the region and visitors crossing borders should expect comparable or worse exposure in neighbouring jurisdictions.

The security context compounds the legal risk: rule by a military junta since the July 2023 coup means the enforcement apparatus is a military one, and the imprissonment of senior military officials for homosexuality indicates that the campaign reaches into institutions that would ordinarily be considered insulated.

Campaigners' framing of a witch-hunt and the reported collapse of PrEP supply suggest the surrounding public-health and social climate is deteriorating, which raises the risk of community violence and denunciation independent of formal charges.

A February 2026 revision criminalises “indecent, unnatural, and LGBTQIA+ acts” under article 390, punishable by five to ten years' imprisonment and fines; same-sex marriage under article 391 carries ten to twenty years; article 392 targets LGBTQIA+ associations. Article 390 also reaches anyone who “artificially changes sex at birth”, a clause that on its face exposes trans and intersex people to imprisonment for transition-related procedures. The national news agency confirmed on 1 June 2026 that LGBTQIA+ practice is criminalised under the 2026 revision.

The drafting is broad enough that reporting on the law reads asexuality as among the sanctionable conducts, so exposure is not confined to sexual acts between people of the same sex. An earlier 2023 draft penal code, which did not take effect in that form, proposed up to five years for same-sex conduct, twenty years for conducting, officiating or witnessing a same-sex marriage, and five years for participating in or financing “homosexual” organisations; it also fixed age of consent at 21 for same-sex acts against 13 for different-sex acts.

Enforcement has been immediate and public. By 1 July 2026 at least 40 people had been arrested for homosexuality and 16 men, including high-ranking military officials, were imprisoned under the new code. Campaigners describe a witch-hunt atmosphere. Arrest carries the risk of outing anyone travelling with a partner or documented history, and detention by security forces under a military government offers no meaningful avenue of complaint.

Earlier precedent points the same way. In 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under public-indecency article 276, which carries up to three years; the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them. In December 2022 the national legislature backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, weeks after a subnational court had acquitted two young women precisely because no statute criminalised same-sex conduct.

Access to HIV prevention has deteriorated alongside criminalisation: sources report PrEP supply collapsing, with campaigners warning of an AIDS resurgence. No source addresses legal gender recognition, document markers, entry screening, or facilities access; these are unassessed rather than safe.

TCD.name: Chad
TCD.summary:
Chad carries formal criminal exposure for a trans visitor, not merely social hostility. The national penal framework criminalises consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults, with punishments ranging from three months to two years' imprisonment; the most recent current-law baseline is the US State Department's 2023 Human Rights Practices report on Chad. A trans person whose conduct or relationships are read as same-sex falls under that provision, and a visitor travelling with a partner is exposed in the same way as a resident.

The pre-criminalisation legal climate was undefined rather than permissive. The 2010 US State Department report on Chad recorded that the law prohibited but did not define 'unnatural acts', and found no evidence that year that the provision had been used against LGBT persons. The same report documented no known LGBT organisations and few reports of violence, with most persons living discreetly because of social strictures. The direction of travel since then has been toward codified punishment: further criminalisation efforts that failed in Ethiopia and Rwanda succeeded in Chad and Nigeria, according to a HuffPost and GroundTruth Project analysis.

No source in this inventory documents enforcement in either direction. There are no recorded arrests, prosecutions or acquittals of trans or LGBT persons in Chad in the reporting years covered here. That silence is an evidentiary gap, not a finding of safety. In a state that criminalises consensual same-sex conduct, that documents no legal gender recognition, and that has no documented community organisations or protective institutional channels, the structural signals resolve toward danger, and the penal provision remains usable against a visibly trans visitor at any time: arrest, prosecution and imprisonment are all within the state's reach.
TCD.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: this inventory contains no enforcement data for Chad — no documented arrests, prosecutions, convictions or acquittals of trans or LGBT persons in the years covered by the sources. Enforcement levels are unknown, and the absence of cases in the reporting must not be read as evidence that the law is not applied.

Not sourced in this inventory: Chad's rules on legal gender recognition and identity documents; entry, visa and border-screening treatment of trans travellers; access to gender-affirming healthcare; hate-crime or non-discrimination provisions covering gender identity; and marriage or partner recognition. Any claim about these areas would require verification against Chad's current civil status law, passport and immigration regulations, and health ministry guidance, none of which appear here.

The 2023 US State Department report is the most recent current-law baseline used; the 2010 report describes a pre-2017 legal climate in which 'unnatural acts' was undefined and undocumented in its use. The 2006 report on the Déby period covers general state abuses and contains no trans-specific finding, and is cited only as background on enforcement capacity. The HuffPost and GroundTruth Project piece is advocacy analysis rather than a legal text, used here for the regional trajectory of criminalisation efforts only.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: There are no laws formally restricting LGBTQ+ people's freedom of expression, association, or peaceful assembly, but discrimination and marginalization effectively limit these rights in practice. Chadian activists say social and familial pressure has been used to coerce LGBTQ+ people into changing their sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression. LGBTQ+ people continue to hide their identity to protect their safety, per the U.S. State Department's 2023 report. Wikipedia country coverage: There is no legal gender recognition in Chad, so transgender people have no pathway to amend official documents. The 2017 penal code (in force 1 August 2017) criminalizes same-sex sexual activity under Article 354, with imprisonment of three months to two years and fines of 50,000 to 500,000 CFA francs (about 89 to 885 USD). Wikipedia country coverage: There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Chad, so same-sex couples cannot adopt children together. Single people may adopt, but this requires a social services investigation that includes an inquiry into the applicant's moral standing, which can be used as grounds to deny adoption — a route that can be weaponized against LGBTQ+ applicants. Wikipedia country coverage: Men who have sex with men (MSM) are unlikely to be able to donate blood, not because of a formal ban but due to discrimination and hostility when accessing healthcare. Because homosexuality is criminalized, authorities refuse to investigate or prosecute crimes committed against LGBTQ+ people, and local civil society members say dozens of LGBTQ+ people are imprisoned under the pretext of other charges. LGBTQ+ Chadians also have difficulty obtaining housing, employment, and government services. Wikipedia country coverage: There is no legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in Chad. The one exception is Article 350(i) of the Penal Code, which imposes ten to twenty years' imprisonment when rape is committed because of the victim's sexual orientation. Despite constitutional universal suffrage, LGBTQ+ people are often denied voter registration by local authorities. Wikipedia country coverage: Former Prime Minister Delwa Kassiré Coumakoye defended the 2017 criminalization law on religious grounds, saying homosexuality is condemned by all religions. The National Assembly passed the penal code on 12 December 2016 by 111 votes to 1 with 4 abstentions, and after the 2013 arrest of two gay men in Abéché for celebrating their wedding, religious groups, women's groups, and youth associations petitioned the government to punish the men. LGBTQ+ people are societally viewed as threats to family, procreation, and marriage, homosexuality is perceived as a Western invention, and in a 2024 survey only 15 percent of Chadians felt their local area would be a good place for gay and lesbian people to live. Wikipedia country coverage: There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Chad. In 2013, two gay men were arrested in Abéché for celebrating their wedding — before the penal code formally outlawed homosexuality — the bar was ordered closed for two years, and both men were fined and initially given two-year prison sentences, with community outcry following their suspended sentences on appeal. Wikipedia country coverage: Article 360 of the Penal Code, Chapter III on sexual offenses against minors, punishes anyone who, without violence, maintains a sexual relationship or practices sexual touching on a person of the same sex under eighteen years of age with one to three years' imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 500,000 francs (about 177 to 885 USD). Youth associations were among the groups that petitioned the government after the 2013 Abéché wedding arrests, and Chadian activists report social and familial pressure used to coerce people into changing their sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression.

TCD.tangentialFactors:
Chad's criminalisation law sits within a documented wave of conservative anti-LGBT advocacy in the region. Attempts at further criminalisation that failed in Ethiopia and Rwanda succeeded in Chad and in Nigeria, a trajectory that marks Chad's law as the product of an active campaign rather than a static legal inheritance.

Chad's broader human rights record shapes the enforcement risk facing a trans visitor. US State Department reporting on the Déby era documented extrajudicial killings and torture by the state, and the withdrawal of the MINURCAT mission; those reports carry no trans-specific finding, but they describe a security apparatus with a documented capacity for violence against individuals.

Social conditions documented before the 2017 criminalisation are still the least-sourced layer of the picture. The 2010 report described discretion as the prevailing survival strategy and no organised LGBT presence; it also recorded few reports of violence, which in that year reflected both genuine social discretion and the absence of any reporting channel.

GAB.name: Gabon
GAB.summary:
Gabon has no law criminalising same-sex intimacy. The same conduct was nonetheless prohibited between July 2019 and July 2020, and that episode is the best guide to how quickly the position can move. Gabon gained independence in 1960 with no inherited colonial-era sodomy statute, and same-sex conduct was not an offence until the new penal code, Law 042/2018, entered into force on 5 July 2019.

The 2019 code did not name homosexuality. Article 402 listed "les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe" within "atteintes aux mœurs", exposing those convicted to up to six months' imprisonment and a fine of five million CFA francs, roughly US$8,500. Enforcement was not theoretical: two men were arrested within months of enactment and released only after paying police bribes, a pattern the US Department of State documented in its 2019 country report alongside societal discrimination.

The National Assembly overturned the ban in July 2020, restoring the pre-2019 position in which same-sex relations between men and women were lawful nationwide. The reversal divided public opinion sharply, and Gabon's current decriminalised status rests on ordinary legislation rather than an entrenched constitutional settlement.

That settlement arrived at referendum on 16 November 2024, when the constitution adopted by the military government that took power in the August 2023 coup ending 56 years of Bongo-family rule was approved by more than 90% of voters on turnout of about 55%. Civil society had demanded the re-criminalisation of homosexuality during the drafting; that demand lost. The adopted text instead protects privacy under Article 18 in terms read as protective of LGBTI people. Article 16, however, defines marriage in a way that excludes same-sex couples, so the constitution blocks criminalisation while also blocking marriage equality.

There is no legal gender recognition in Gabon, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. A visitor presenting documents in a gender inconsistent with the marker on their passport should expect no domestic legal remedy for discrepancies, and there is no registered community machinery that would receive or advise a trans traveller. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records both absences, as well as the same-sex relations position as legal nationwide since the 2020 repeal.

Nothing in the sources documents arrests, prosecutions or detentions of LGBTI people since the 2020 repeal, but the 2019–2020 period shows what can happen within weeks of a change in the law, including arrests settled by police bribes rather than charges. Conservative social attitudes remain widely held, and discrimination is documented rather than hypothetical. Discretion in public life remains prudent, and the constitutional privacy protection is a legal guarantee, not a guarantee of social tolerance.
GAB.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents whether Article 18 of the 2024 constitution has been invoked in any court proceeding, and no case law on privacy-based LGBTI claims is available. Its practical effect on enforcement is therefore unresolved.

Nothing here addresses hate-crime sentencing, police training, or any official protection mechanism for LGBTI people beyond the constitutional privacy text; the inventory contains no data on such provisions, and their absence should not be inferred as proof that none exists.

Access to gender-affirming care, HIV services and other trans-specific health provision is not covered by any source provided, so the map carries no assessment of it.

No post-2020 arrest, detention or prosecution data appears in the inventory. The 2019 arrests are the only enforcement incidents sourced here, and they are reported by a single outlet whose account of the two men's release through police bribes is not independently corroborated in the inventory.

Visa, entry and border-screening treatment of transgender travellers is not sourced for Gabon. The fine figures for the 2019 offence vary slightly between sources, given as 5,000,000 CFA francs, about US$8,500 and about US$8,561, reflecting exchange-rate timing rather than a difference in the statute.

Unsourced dimensions after this research pass: D2, D4, D5, D6, D8, D13.

The November 2024 referendum places sexual-minority legal status inside a wider constitutional overhaul driven by a military government that ended a 56-year family dynasty. High turnout and an overwhelming yes vote indicate broad acceptance of the document as a whole, not necessarily broad support for its privacy protections, which is why the re-criminalisation demand that failed during drafting cannot be treated as a measure of public opinion.

The marriage article is the clearest instance in the sources of a jurisdiction where decriminalisation and the exclusion of same-sex couples from marriage coexist within a single constitutional text. The registration ban on sexual-minority groups removes the institutional base that would otherwise press for the partner-recognition and gender-recognition law that does not exist.
GAB.localsOnly:
Residents of Gabon face no criminal penalty for same-sex relations. The repeal by the National Assembly in July 2020 restored the position that prevailed from independence until July 2019, when Law 042/2018 took effect and Article 402 filed same-sex relations under offences against public morals, carrying up to six months in prison and a five million CFA franc fine.

Same-sex marriage is unavailable. Article 16 of the constitution adopted at the 16 November 2024 referendum defines marriage in terms that exclude same-sex couples, and Article 18's privacy guarantee does not alter that definition.

No procedure for legal gender recognition exists, and no domestic legal mechanism is available for correcting the gender marker on identity documents.

LGBTI organisations cannot register. Community advocacy, support networks and any formally constituted protection machinery operate without legal standing, which leaves residents without institutional recourse in cases of discrimination or police mistreatment.

Discrimination against LGBTI people is documented in official reporting, including the US Department of State's 2019 human rights report, and the period of criminalisation saw arrests settled by police bribes. Social conservatism and the absence of anti-discrimination legislation shape daily life regardless of the repeal.

COG.name: Republic of the Congo
COG.summary:
The Republic of the Congo does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct between adults. A systematic review of the country's legislation carried out for the EUAA's May 2024 COI Query Response found no law that prohibits such conduct, and the US State Department's 2022 and 2023 human rights reports record no prosecutions of LGBTQI+ persons under the ambiguity surrounding that conduct.

Penal Code Article 331 sets the age of consent at 21 for same-sex acts, against 18 for different-sex acts. The same provision criminalises 'shameless acts or acts against nature' with a person of the same sex under the age of 21, punishable by six months to three years' imprisonment and a fine. The EUAA review describes the provision's scope as applied to same-sex conduct as ambiguous, and reports that sources treat it as a basis for discriminatory treatment.

The provision is not a dormant text. The State Department's 2022 reporting states that police cite it to extract bribes from gay men, and its 2023 reporting confirms that the 'act against nature' law continued to be used as a pretext for soliciting payments from men. No arrests or prosecutions of LGBTQI+ persons under the provision were known during 2023.

For a trans visitor, the practical exposure lies less in a prosecution risk than in routine contact with police. Document checks, identity controls and any interaction that reveals or is assumed to reveal a person's gender history can bring a person into contact with the same officers who use the provision for extortion. The reported pattern is that the ambiguity is operationalised as leverage.

Reported violence against LGBTQI+ persons comes from both state and nonstate actors. Local NGOs told the State Department that LGBTQI+ people in the Republic of the Congo face psychological and physical harassment, violence and financial extortion, and that this pattern continued through 2023. The law offers no protection against any of it: the country has no anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation or gender identity.
COG.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not address trans-specific matters: legal gender recognition, requirements for changing sex markers on identity or travel documents, entry and visa screening procedures applied to transgender travellers, or whether immigration officers consult gender history in the course of border control. These are unresolved here, not absent from the jurisdiction's practice.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare, the legal status of facilities arrangements (bathrooms, detention, shelters), and any hate-crime or hate-speech provisions touching gender identity are not covered by the sources assessed, and no finding is made on them.

Whether the EUAA or State Department reporting captures the situation outside the capital, or the treatment of trans persons distinct from gay men, is not established in the inventory. The documented policing practice is described in terms of gay men specifically.

Nonstate violence sits alongside official conduct in the reporting, which suggests hostility is not confined to state institutions. Physical and psychological harassment, including financial extortion, are documented for LGBTQI+ persons in the country generally, with no dated pattern of effective state response recorded in the sources available.

BDI.name: Burundi
BDI.summary:
Burundi criminalises same-sex conduct. The prohibition dates from the 2009 penal code, and US State Department human rights reports covering 2009, 2010, 2012 and 2015 document discrimination against gays and lesbians under that framework, together with arrests and harassment of LGBT people. No source in this inventory identifies any protection, exemption or decriminalisation measure.

The risk posture escalated in December 2023, when President Évariste Ndayishimiye publicly called for homosexuals to be "stoned", adding "that's what they deserve". Human Rights Watch, reporting in January 2024, condemned the remarks as stoking fear among LGBT people and urged the ruling party to renounce persecution. The Iteka League, the Burundian LGBTQ rights organisation operating in exile, characterised the speech as "a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people".

Burundians living under the criminalisation regime reported terror in the weeks that followed. SOS Médias Burundi, writing in January 2024, quoted members of two LGBTQ associations speaking anonymously, who described the presidential remarks as "a real license to kill (us)". The same reporting restates that same-sex relations are criminalised in Burundi.
BDI.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition, identity-document markers, visa or entry screening that could disclose a person's status, hate-crime sentencing enhancement, same-sex partnership or marriage recognition, restroom or facility access rules, or restrictions on gender-affirming care. Whether any of these exist, and in what form, remains unresolved on the available material.

The inventory does not state the specific article or penalty range of the 2009 penal code provision criminalising same-sex conduct, nor does it record a prosecution, conviction or acquittal under that provision with a date and outcome. It also does not establish whether the presidential remarks of December 2023 were followed by any formal enforcement directive or arrests.
