CAF.name: Central African Republic
CAF.summary:
The Central African Republic is dangerous for trans visitors.

Nothing in national law protects a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor. The constitution defines marriage as a union between one man and one woman and same-sex marriage is banned, so a visitor travelling with a partner has no recognition of that relationship, and affection between same-sex partners in public can be prosecuted under the public-morals provisions.

Consensual same-sex relations between adults are not explicitly criminalised in the penal code. Article 85 instead criminalises attacks on public morals, and same-sex conduct in public draws harsher penalties than other offences covered by the same moral-offence provisions. The practical effect for a visitor is that any visible same-sex or gender-nonconforming conduct in public exposes them to arrest on morals grounds.

The United States State Department's 2023 human rights report states that same-sex activity in public is criminalised in practice and that this treatment has pushed the affected community underground. The same report records that there were no known organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights in the country, so a visitor who faces trouble has no established local support network to turn to.

Legal gender recognition is not permitted in the Central African Republic. A visitor whose passport or identity marker does not match their presentation has no local legal route to align those documents, and should expect identity screening to proceed on the marker as issued.

Detention carries serious physical risk. Documentation from 2012 recorded extrajudicial killings, torture and rape by security forces and by Seleka rebels, together with harsh prison conditions. That reporting is more than a decade old and contains little trans-specific material, but it describes the conditions a visitor would enter if arrested on public-morals grounds.

The social climate compounds the legal exposure. Attitudes toward sexual orientation and gender identity issues are treated as taboo and characterised as imported from Europe or contrary to African values, which raises the likelihood of hostility from the public as well as from officials.
CAF.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on the criminalisation question and this is unresolved. The 2019 overview states that same-sex relations between consenting adults are not explicitly criminalised, relying on Article 85's public-morals offence, whereas the 2023 United States State Department report describes same-sex activity in public as criminalised. The distinction between a specific offence and enforcement through the morals provision is not settled by the available material.

No source in the inventory documents arrests, prosecutions or sentences under Article 85, so the frequency and severity of enforcement are not sourced. Likewise there is no sourced information on hate-crime sentencing, on access to healthcare for trans visitors, or on airport and border screening practices directed at gender-nonconforming travellers.

The 2012 documentation of killings, torture, rape and prison conditions derives from a period of armed conflict and is not trans-specific; its current applicability to detention of a trans visitor is not verified. The 2024 Universal Periodic Review stakeholder submissions and the two earlier recommendations are recorded as inputs to the review process only, with no sourced outcome as to implementation.

sources.summary: ILGA World report 'Our Identities Under Arrest' (2023): global survey of laws criminalising LGBT people, including the Central African Republic.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report, Central African Republic: no legal anti-discrimination provisions for LGBTQI+ persons; marriage constitutionally defined as a 'union between one man and one woman' with same-sex marriage banned; legal gender recognition not permitted; LGBTQI+ persons cannot serve openly in the military; criminalisation of same-sex activity in public pushed the community underground, and there were no known organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for the Central African Republic: documents extrajudicial killings, torture and rape by security forces and Seleka rebels, and harsh prison conditions, with limited LGBT-specific content.

Erasing 76 Crimes / ILGA overview (20 May 2019): in the Central African Republic same-sex relations between consenting adults are not explicitly criminalised, but Article 85 of the criminal code criminalises 'attacks on public morals' — public same-sex acts carry harsher penalties than other moral offences. SOGI issues remain taboo and seen as 'imported from Europe'/'contrary to African values'; CAR received two UPR recommendations (SOGI non-discrimination, improving the situation of sexual minorities).
UN OHCHR summary of stakeholders' submissions for the Central African Republic's UPR (45th session, January 2024): includes SOGI-related stakeholder recommendations.

CAF.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Malawi (0.26), above Zambia (0.24), below Senegal (0.27).

CAF.tangentialFactors:
The country has engaged with the international review mechanism on these questions. It received two Universal Periodic Review recommendations concerning non-discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and improving the situation of sexual minorities, and the January 2024 United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights summary of stakeholder submissions for the country's 45th-session review again contains SOGI-related recommendations. Whether any of these recommendations have been implemented is not sourced here.

The Central African Republic appears in ILGA World's 2023 survey of laws criminalising LGBT people, but the underlying national position is narrower than that inclusion suggests: consensual same-sex relations are not expressly prohibited, while exposure arises from the public-morals offence rather than a specific sodomy statute.

The 2012 human rights reporting that documents state violence also covers armed-group violence during the Seleka period, an environment of general instability in which a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner has no special status or protection.
CAF.localsOnly:
Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity; the United States State Department's 2023 report confirms the absence of legal anti-discrimination provisions for LGBTQI+ persons.

LGBTQI+ persons cannot serve openly in the Central African Republic's armed forces.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable, so residents have no administrative procedure to change the sex marker on identity documents.

There were no known organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights operating in the country as of the 2023 reporting, and the affected community is described as having been driven underground by enforcement of the public-morals offence.

Residents seeking change must work through the Universal Periodic Review process, where two earlier recommendations on SOGI non-discrimination and the situation of sexual minorities, and further stakeholder recommendations in the January 2024 submissions, form the documented record of external pressure.

GIN.name: Guinea
GIN.summary:
Guinea is a high-risk destination for transgender visitors. Article 274 of the 2016 Penal Code punishes consensual same-sex conduct with six months to three years' imprisonment, a fine of GNF 500,000 to 1,000,000, or both; the US State Department's 2023 Human Rights Report records the same criminalisation under the code's indecency provisions and documents violence and discrimination against LGBT persons alongside police harassment.

Enforcement is not confined to conduct. Arrests are made on the basis of clothing and appearance, and the statute operates as a basis for extortion, with releases commonly secured through payment to police. The Advocates for Human Rights and Khaleem Ali's joint stakeholder report to the Universal Periodic Review in October 2024 records arbitrary arrest, harassment and extortion by police, deepening stigma and fear among LGBT people.

The same 2024 reporting describes an environment that is hostile and at times lethal, with threats of physical violence and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. Widespread stigmatisation deters victims from reporting violence, so documented incidents understate the actual level of harm.

There is no legal gender recognition procedure in Guinea. A visitor whose passport or other documents do not match their presentation has no domestic mechanism to align them, which leaves identity checks, including at entry and in any contact with police, as a point of exposure.

Detention carries additional risk. US State Department reporting has documented torture and abuse by security forces and mistreatment in prisons, conditions that apply to anyone arrested under the criminalising provisions. Governance has been under military rule since the 2021 coup, and the 2024 stakeholder submissions address both state and non-state actors as sources of violence and discrimination.
GIN.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether Article 274 or the indecency provisions have been applied against foreign nationals or visitors, or whether entry and visa processing includes any screening of transgender documents. No sourced material addresses access to healthcare, hormone treatment or HIV services for trans people in Guinea, nor any hate-crime enhancement, anti-discrimination statute, or recognition of partners or marriages.

Rules on restroom or facility access, and any guidance issued to accommodation providers or tour operators, are not covered by these sources. The scope of the military government's directives on LGBT matters since 2021 is likewise not established here beyond the fact of junta rule. The 2011 State Department material is more than a decade old and its specific findings on prison conditions should be treated as historical context rather than current measurement.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Guinea: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised (Article 325, 'indecency' provisions); documents violence and discrimination against LGBT persons and police harassment.

The Advocates for Human Rights + Khaleem Ali joint UPR stakeholder report (Oct 2024) on LGBT+ rights in Guinea: criminalisation of consensual same-sex activity; police arbitrary arrests, harassment and extortion; a hostile and 'sometimes deadly' environment; widespread stigmatisation hinders reporting of violence.
US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Guinea: documents security-force torture, prison abuse, FGM, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and societal discrimination.

Wikipedia country coverage: Section 9.9.30(b) of the Guinea Aeronautical Regulations (2022), issued by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, bars competent government agencies from using Passenger Name Record data that reveals an individual's sex life or sexual orientation, alongside racial, ethnic, political, religious, trade-union or health data. The text gives no further detail on entry screening, visa rules, or border checks for trans or LGBTQ travelers. Wikipedia country coverage: LGBTQ people in custody are frequently abused, and transgender women are arrested and imprisoned under the stated pretext of protecting them from community violence, then held in male prisons where they often experience sexual violence. A 2024 Universal Periodic Review stakeholder submission reports LGBTQ people held for up to five days despite the 48-hour legal limit, with most released only after paying bribes or fines. Wikipedia country coverage: LGBTQ people in Guinea face discrimination when seeking healthcare, alongside housing, education and employment. Law L/2024/001/CNT/SGG of January 12, 2024 on HIV Prevention, Care, and Protection defines 'members of sexual minorities' to include gays, lesbians, bisexuals, intersex and transgender people whether or not they self-identify, and Ordinance No. 056/2009/PRG/SGG on HIV/AIDS lists sexual minorities as a vulnerable and marginalized group; there are no laws protecting LGBTQ people from discrimination in health services. Wikipedia country coverage: Both the 1998 Penal Code (Article 325) and the 2016 revision (Article 274) criminalize same-sex sexual conduct, carrying six months to three years in prison and fines of 500,000 to 1,000,000 Guinean francs under the 2016 text — a higher minimum fine than before — with violence or attempted violence raising sentences to five to ten years, and acts with a minor under 21 triggering the maximum. Police use the law for extortion, judging potential LGBTQ status from clothing and appearance; in 2016-2017 the organization Afrique Arc-en-Ciel Conakry reported gay men jailed and fined for release, and in 2023 the Office for the Protection of Women, Children, and Morals added a unit to investigate same-sex conduct. Security forces have arrested, harassed and been violent toward LGBTQ people accused of disrupting social order; in 2010 Prime Minister Lansana Kouyate said consensual same-sex activity was wrong and should be illegal and that sexual orientation should not be a human right. Wikipedia country coverage: There is no recognition of same-sex unions in Guinea. Adoption is open to a couple married at least five years or an unmarried person aged at least 30 with a 15-year age gap, and Guinean law does not specifically bar LGBTQ persons from adopting. Wikipedia country coverage: The penal code treats same-sex acts involving a minor under 21 as warranting the maximum sentence, a broad youth-linked age threshold. LGBTQ people face discrimination when seeking education, and families arrange forced heterosexual marriages, with religious, cultural and familial pressure used to attempt to convert LGBTQ people — a pressure that falls heavily on younger people. Wikipedia country coverage: A survey spanning 2021 to 2023 found 87 percent of Guineans would dislike or strongly dislike having a gay neighbor, and the U.S. State Department's 2011 report described homosexuality as socially, religiously and culturally taboo with no LGBTQ organizations in the country. The 2023 report found LGBTQ groups do exist but could not obtain legal recognition despite no law barring it; most LGBTQ Guineans do not disclose publicly, there is no substantial political presence of openly LGBTQ people, and LGBTQ people are cast as part of a Western imperialist agenda attributed to the United States and France. Some LGBTQ Guineans have been internally displaced to escape areas whose religious and cultural norms endanger them.

GIN.tangentialFactors:
US State Department human rights reporting on Guinea has covered the same core facts across more than a decade: the 2011 report already noted criminalisation and societal discrimination against LGBT people, and the 2023 report repeats criminalisation, violence, discrimination and police harassment. The pattern is persistent rather than episodic, and a visitor should not read any single year's reporting as evidence of a change in conditions.

The 2011 reporting also covers security-force torture, prison abuse and other forms of violence by state agents, which situates LGBT-specific mistreatment within a broader record of conduct by the same institutions. The 2024 stakeholder submissions extend the assessment beyond state actors, describing threats and violence from non-state actors as well.

Guinea's criminalising regime sits alongside a broader West African pattern of penal provisions covering same-sex conduct, but the specific combination here of appearance-based arrest, routine extortion at the point of release, and absent gender recognition raises the practical exposure of a visibly transgender visitor above what the statutory penalty alone would suggest.
GIN.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Senegal/Zimbabwe (0.27), below Sierra Leone-region peers.
GIN.blindSummary:
The state is a high-risk destination for transgender visitors. Article 274 of the 2016 Penal Code punishes consensual same-sex conduct with six months to three years' imprisonment, a fine of GNF 500,000 to 1,000,000, or both; the national human rights reporting for 2023 records the same criminalisation under the code's indecency provisions and documents violence and discrimination against LGBT persons alongside police harassment.

Enforcement is not confined to conduct. Arrests are made on the basis of clothing and appearance, and the statute operates as a basis for extortion, with releases commonly secured through payment to police. a joint stakeholder report to the Universal Periodic Review in October 2024 records arbitrary arrest, harassment and extortion by police, deepening stigma and fear among LGBT people.

The same 2024 reporting describes an environment that is hostile and at times lethal, with threats of physical violence and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. Widespread stigmatisation deters victims from reporting violence, so documented incidents understate the actual level of harm.

There is no legal gender recognition procedure in the state. a visitor whose passport or other documents do not match their presentation has no domestic mechanism to align them, which leaves identity checks, including at entry and in any contact with police, as a point of exposure.

Detention carries additional risk. National human rights reporting has documented torture and abuse by security forces and mistreatment in prisons, conditions that apply to anyone arrested under the criminalising provisions. Governance has been under military rule since the 2021 coup, and the 2024 stakeholder submissions address both state/province and non-state actors as sources of violence and discrimination.
GIN.blindOutOfScope:
The inventory does not resolve whether Article 274 or the indecency provisions have been applied against foreign nationals or visitors, or whether entry and visa processing includes any screening of transgender documents. No sourced material addresses access to healthcare, hormone treatment or HIV services for trans people in the state, nor any hate-crime enhancement, anti-discrimination statute, or recognition of partners or marriages.

Rules on restroom or facility access, and any guidance issued to accommodation providers or tour operators, are not covered by these sources. The scope of the military government's directives on LGBT matters since 2021 is likewise not established here beyond the fact of junta rule. The 2011 reporting is more than a decade old and its specific findings on prison conditions should be treated as historical context rather than current measurement.

Residents live under the same Article 274 penalty as visitors, with the added exposure of being identifiable within their own communities. Arrest on the basis of clothing or appearance is a documented practice, and the fine of GNF 500,000 to 1,000,000 represents a substantial sum locally, which makes payment to police an ordinary route out of detention and a standing instrument of extortion.

LBR.name: Liberia
LBR.summary:
Liberia criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. The offence of sodomy is punishable by one year of imprisonment, and applies to women as well as men. This is a domestic-origin provision rather than a colonial import, meaning there is no external legal framework pressing toward repeal.

There is no legal gender recognition. No process exists for a trans person to amend the name or gender marker on a Liberian identity document, so a visitor whose documents do not match their presentation carries documentation that cannot be brought into consistency by any administrative route.

Legislative pressure is active and hostile. On 16 October 2024, Rep. Johnson N. Williams was reported to be seeking other lawmakers' support for a harsh anti-homosexuality bill filed that summer, with related proposals that would imprison children as young as ten years old for gay sex. The existing one-year penalty therefore understates what the legislature has been considering.

Proposals to raise penalties have surfaced before. Reporting from Monrovia in April 2012 recorded anti-gay sentiment growing after the United States announced plans to promote LGBT rights overseas, new Liberian legislation proposed to impose longer jail time for homosexuality, and a group distributed fliers targeting supporters of gay rights. The pattern is one of measurable legislative escalation combined with mobilised public hostility toward LGBT advocates.

Senior political leadership has publicly defended the criminal law. In a joint interview published on 19 March 2012, Nobel Peace Prize laureate President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf defended laws criminalising homosexuality in Liberia. Her remarks drew international comment on the country's stance. Nothing in the current record indicates that this position has been displaced at the top of government.

Mob violence against LGBT people is documented, which places trans visitors at physical risk that operates independently of whether they are ever charged. The trans-specific hazard is compounded: a trans visitor may be perceived as engaging in same-sex conduct, or may be targeted for appearance rather than proven conduct, and the criminal law provides no defence against either.

The most detailed country-level assessment available is the UNDP/OHCHR country report on sexual orientation, gender identity and expression in Liberia, published in April 2020, which reviews the legal, social and human-rights environment for people of diverse sexual orientation and gender identity through a participatory process.
LBR.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the anti-homosexuality bill filed in the summer of 2024 has advanced in committee or on the floor since the report of 16 October 2024. The record documents Rep. Johnson N. Williams seeking support, not enactment.

Unresolved: whether the provisions allowing imprisonment of children as young as ten years old form part of the same bill as the one Rep. Johnson N. Williams was promoting, or belong to related but separate proposals.

Unresolved: the precise statutory text, section number and gender-specific wording of the one-year sodomy penalty. The inventory states the penalty and that it covers both sexes but does not cite the Liberian criminal statute directly.

Not sourced in the inventory: any account of mob violence incidents against trans people in Liberia with specific dates, locations or judicial outcomes. Mob violence is asserted as documented but not itemised, so the severity and frequency cannot be quantified here.

Not sourced in the inventory: Liberian entry or visa rules, airport or border screening practice, whether travellers are asked questions bearing on gender identity or sexual orientation, or the treatment of mismatched name and gender markers at immigration. No assessment of document screening at entry can be made from the current record.

Not sourced in the inventory: hate-crime or anti-discrimination legislation covering gender identity, the scope of protection extended to visitors, or any complaint mechanism available to foreign nationals. The 2020 UNDP/OHCHR report is cited as a source but its specific findings on protection machinery are not reproduced in the inventory.

Not sourced in the inventory: access to gender-affirming healthcare, hormone therapy or HIV-related services for visitors, and whether such services are available to non-residents. No statement on care access should be read as evidence that care exists or does not exist.

Not sourced in the inventory: same-sex marriage or civil union status, which is distinct from the criminalisation of sodomy and remains unaddressed by the current record.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D3, D4, D5, D7.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Gender-affirming hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgery are not available in Liberia, so trans people have no domestic clinical facility for transition-related care. Beyond health facilities, the source notes that some private spaces exist where LGBTQ people can be their authentic selves, often sponsored by advocacy organizations such as Stop AIDS in Liberia (SAIL) or the Transgender Network of Liberia (TNOL), or created by private individuals, since LGBTQ Liberians often have to hide their identities in public. Wikipedia country coverage: Care access is shaped by criminalization: enforcement of the sodomy law is uncommon, but its existence deters LGBTQ crime victims from reporting to police, and some LGBTQ people have been arrested on the basis of their sexuality or gender identity after attackers used their LGBTQ status as an excuse. Health-wise, a 2013 UN-AIDS survey put HIV/AIDS prevalence among Liberian men who have sex with men at 19.8%, and Stop AIDS in Liberia (SAIL) — the first NGO founded by LGBTQ Liberians for LGBTQ people — was set up to educate MSM about HIV/AIDS, test them, and counsel those testing positive, later expanding services to all LGBTQ people since 2012. Gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery are unavailable domestically. No youth-specific (minors' medication, travel, or targeting) findings appear in this source text. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex marriage is not recognized in Liberia. In 2012 then-Senator Jewel Howard Taylor introduced a bill that would have made same-sex marriage a first-degree felony carrying up to ten years; it passed the Senate but not the House, so it never became law, and President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf had threatened to veto either 2012 anti-LGBTQ bill. By contrast, Section 2.4(b)(iii) of Liberia's Decent Work Act (2015) entitles all who seek to work in Liberia to do so regardless of sex, gender identity or sexual orientation.

LBR.tangentialFactors:
The April 2020 UNDP/OHCHR country report is the principal multi-topic reference for the broader human-rights environment for people of diverse sexual orientation and gender identity in Liberia. Its participatory methodology means it captures lived experience alongside statute, and it remains the benchmark against which the 2024 legislative activity should be read.

The 2012 escalation was externally catalysed: reporting linked the growth in anti-gay sentiment, the proposed longer sentences and the distribution of fliers directly to a US announcement of plans to promote LGBT rights overseas. This suggests that perceived foreign advocacy for LGBT rights can trigger domestic legislative and extra-legal backlash in Liberia, a dynamic trans visitors should anticipate.

Commentary on the 2012 remarks by President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf focused on the contradiction between her Nobel Peace Prize, awarded for work in women's rights and reconciliation, and her defence of criminalising homosexuality. That contradiction was international in nature and did not translate into domestic legal reform in the period covered by the record.

The 2024 bill has not been shown to have passed. The available reporting documents Rep. Johnson N. Williams seeking support rather than the bill's enactment, so the operative law remains the existing one-year sodomy offence. The distinction matters for assessing exposure: the current exposure is one year plus documented mob violence, while the proposed exposure is substantially higher.

The related proposals to imprison children as young as ten years old for gay sex mark the direction of travel in Liberian legislative debate. Even where such provisions are unsuccessful, their presence in the bill text signals that age of consent and child protection framing are being used to argue for the criminalisation of homosexuality.
LBR.comparisons: Pairwise: below Sri Lanka (0.33) and above Azerbaijan (0.30).

MDG.name: Madagascar
MDG.summary:
Same-sex conduct between adults is legal in Madagascar, but only from age 21. Penal Code Article 331 treats same-sex acts involving a person under 21 as indecent assault, carrying five to ten years' imprisonment, so the age of consent is unequal and a visitor whose partner or counterparty is under 21 faces a serious criminal exposure that a heterosexual visitor does not.

Status on arrival is thin. There is no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions, no anti-discrimination law, and no legal gender recognition, so a trans traveller holds no locally recognised identity, no partner status and no named protection under Malagasy law.

The social environment is the dominant practical factor. Homosexuality is not illegal, yet it is widely considered socially unacceptable, and LGBT Malagasy people conceal their lives in order to keep jobs and live in peace, relying on private networks and coded language. A trans visitor is read through that same expectation of concealment, and visible gender non-conformity carries the social cost that local LGBT people manage by hiding.

Official posture is hostile to protection. At Madagascar's fourth universal periodic review in January 2025, the government rejected United Nations recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent. Six Malagasy organisations — Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers' Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage and Madagascar LGBT+ — stated that refusing to act endorses impunity and condones violence.

Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are documented rather than hypothetical: the United States State Department's 2011 human rights report recorded societal discrimination and violence against the LGBT community in Madagascar alongside unlawful killings under the post-coup regime.
MDG.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory for this pass contains no material on legal gender recognition or on the existence or absence of an anti-discrimination statute. Those elements are carried forward from the standing record and remain unverified against a source here.

No source in the inventory documents how Article 331 has been enforced: there is no case, charge or conviction cited, and Rights in Exile's reference to case law is not specified. Whether the under-21 provision is used against adults in practice is unresolved.

No source addresses police treatment of trans visitors specifically, entry or visa screening that could disclose gender history, or access to gender-affirming care. The absence of documented police targeting in these materials is not evidence that none occurs.

Dating is inconsistent for one source: the France 24 'Focus' report is labelled August 2024 in the inventory while its URL indicates April 2024. The most recent item overall is dated 17 July 2025, so conditions after that date are not covered.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6.

sources.summary: France 24 'Focus' report (Aug 2024): 'LGBT people in Madagascar forced to hide their sexuality' — although homosexuality is not illegal, it is widely considered socially unacceptable; many hide to keep jobs and live in peace, developing their own networks and coded language.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Madagascar: documents the post-coup regime, unlawful killings, and 'societal discrimination and violence against women, persons with disabilities, and the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) community'.

BBC News Pidgin overview of decriminalisation in Africa (July 2020): Madagascar entry — same-sex activity legal only from age 21 under the Penal Code (under-21 same-sex acts remain offences); no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions; regional context as ~22 of 53 African states had moved to decriminalise.

Queer In The World Madagascar guide (updated 3 December 2023): same-sex activity legal for over-21s but LGBT people face discrimination and lack civic rights such as marriage and adoption; the legal framework is limited in progress compared with other countries.

Erasing 76 Crimes (17 July 2025): in Madagascar’s fourth UPR (January 2025, 235 recommendations) the government rejected UN recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent; six Malagasy organisations (Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers’ Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage, Madagascar LGBT+) protested that "Refusing to act is to endorse impunity and condone violence."

Rights in Exile (AsyLex) Madagascar resources: Penal Code Article 331 sets a different age of consent for same-sex acts (indecent-assault band of five to ten years’ imprisonment); documents general societal discrimination against LGBTQI+ people plus state-protection capacity, case law and supporting organisations.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Public expression by LGBTQ people is constrained: in early July 2021 the Malagasy government cancelled an LGBTQ party held at a bar in Antananarivo on the grounds of "incitement to debauchery". The U.S. State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report recorded general societal discrimination, with public attitudes ranging from tacit acceptance to violent rejection, particularly of transgender sex workers, who were frequent targets of verbal abuse, stone throwing and even murder. Supporters of a same-sex couple were subjected to insults and death threats on social media, and religious leaders publicly accused them of "promising homosexuality". Wikipedia country coverage: Madagascar does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions: Article 2 of Law No. 2007-022 on Marriage and Matrimonial Regimes prohibits marriage between two persons of the same sex whether before the Civil Registrar or under traditional ceremonies. Article 39 of the same law names "gender identity" as a cause for absolute nullity of marriage, a direct legal exposure for trans people. Law No. 2014-038 on the Protection of Personal Data (Article 18) bars processing of sensitive data including data on health or sexual life, and Law No. 2017-045 on Credit Information Bureaus (Article 2) likewise protects sexual orientation as sensitive data. Wikipedia country coverage: Family custody/adoption is restricted to heterosexual married couples: Article 33 of Law No. 2005-014 on Adoption states that "Full adoption is only permitted to heterosexual spouses." The source also notes that most civic liberties, including the rights to marry and adopt children, are not afforded to LGBTQ individuals. In a 2020 case, a 33-year-old woman was arrested for the statutory rape of a 19-year-old woman after the younger woman's mother filed a complaint, with the mother allegedly acting to cover up an incest and rape accusation against the father. Wikipedia country coverage: Access to care and health protection is addressed mainly through HIV policy: Act No. 2005-040 on the Fight against HIV/AIDS requires information, education and communication programs adapted to the sexual orientation of target groups, and Article 26 mandates special provisions to protect vulnerable groups — expressly including young people, sex workers, men who have sex with men and mobile populations — against HIV transmission. Youth-specific: minors under 21 are the class protected by the Penal Code's two-to-five-year penalty for "indecent or against nature" acts, and in the 2020 case a 19-year-old woman was the subject of such a charge. Care access is further complicated by religious leaders offering the young woman conversion therapy, and by the 2011 finding that transgender sex workers faced violent rejection.

MDG.comparisons: Pairwise: above KEN (0.38 — Madagascar has no criminalisation; Kenya does). Level with Turkey (0.47).

Same-sex conduct between adults is legal in the country, but only from age 21. The Penal Code treats same-sex acts involving a person under 21 as indecent assault, carrying five to ten years' imprisonment, so the age of consent is unequal and a visitor whose partner or counterparty is under 21 faces a serious criminal exposure that a heterosexual visitor does not.

Status on arrival is thin. There is no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions, no anti-discrimination law, and no legal gender recognition, so a trans traveller holds no locally recognised identity, no partner status and no named protection under local law.

The social environment is the dominant practical factor. Homosexuality is not illegal, yet it is widely considered socially unacceptable, and LGBT residents conceal their lives in order to keep jobs and live in peace, relying on private networks and coded language. a trans visitor is read through that same expectation of concealment, and visible gender non-conformity carries the social cost that local LGBT people manage by hiding.

Official posture is hostile to protection. At the country fourth universal periodic review in January 2025, the national government rejected United Nations recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent. Six local organisations — Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers' Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage and the country LGBT+ organisation — stated that refusing to act endorses impunity and condones violence.

Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are documented rather than hypothetical: the 2011 human rights report of the national government's principal foreign affairs department recorded societal discrimination and violence against the LGBT community alongside unlawful killings under the post-coup regime.

COM.name: Comoros
COM.summary:
Comoros criminalises same-sex sexual activity under its penal code, and the provision has been used against people whose conduct became known to authorities. Reported penalties differ between sources: Outright International gives Article 300 of the 2020 penal code as six months to two years' imprisonment plus a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 francs (US$240 to 720), the Human Dignity Trust states a maximum of three years, and a December 2024 Washington Blade report cites Article 318 carrying up to five years.

Enforcement is documented. Two women were arrested in June 2024 after asking an imam to marry them, and on 12 December 2024 a Comorian court sentenced them to five and six months respectively for homosexuality before releasing them with the terms served. It was the first conviction of this kind, and the Human Dignity Trust called it a human-rights violation. The first imprisonment for same-sex intimacy followed a leaked video in 2022.

Application is uneven rather than absent. The US State Department's 2023 human rights report records no arrests or prosecutions during that year and states that authorities did not actively enforce the law. The statute itself remains in force, and the government has repeatedly refused United Nations recommendations to decriminalise.

No non-discrimination law protects LGBTQI+ persons. Police reported that they do not incite or tolerate violence against them and no such violence was reported in 2023, yet widespread impunity is listed among the country's major human-rights problems.

Detention carries additional exposure: the State Department's 2010 report records poor prison conditions, alongside restrictions on movement, press and religion and discrimination against women.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable, so a trans visitor arriving with documents in a retained name or marker has no domestic route to a matching record. No hate-crime provision or partner recognition for same-sex couples is recorded in these sources.
COM.outOfScopeNotes:
The applicable penalty is unresolved in these sources: three years, two years plus a fine, and five years are each reported, and the discrepancy is not reconciled by any source in the inventory.

The enforcement position after the December 2024 conviction is not sourced. The inventory contains no reporting on arrests, prosecutions or police practice in 2025 or 2026, so the current enforcement posture beyond that date is not established here.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa screening of transgender documents, airport or border treatment, access to healthcare, restroom or facility rules, hate-crime charging, or recognition of same-sex partners. These are not sourced rather than confirmed absent.

The 2010 prison-conditions findings are more than a decade old and have not been refreshed in the inventory.

DJI.name: Djibouti
DJI.summary:
Djibouti does not explicitly criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Articles 353 and 354 of the penal code refer vaguely to "good morals" and to obscene or public-morality offences without naming same-sex relations, and no statute states the position either way. Authorities retain the power to prosecute public same-sex conduct under these provisions, and the country's at-a-glance legal assessment marks same-sex relations as not lawful throughout the territory. The practical result is that same-sex conduct is treated as de facto illegal even though no explicit offence exists on the books.

Public-morality and "obscene acts" provisions are used against people, so a trans visitor who is visible or who engages in any same-sex conduct in public faces exposure to prosecution on that basis. There is no reported case law defining the limits of these articles, and no guarantee of how they are applied to a foreign national.

No legal gender recognition procedure exists. A trans visitor cannot obtain or amend an identity document reflecting their gender under Djibouti law, and there is no statutory route by which a passport or other document issued by another country would be recognised as consistent with a presented gender marker.

LGBTI organisations cannot register in Djibouti. There is consequently no community infrastructure, no support or outreach services, and no organisation to contact in an emergency. The absence of any such body also means there is no domestic monitoring of how the public-morality provisions are enforced.

No legal prohibition of discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity exists in general law. The only protection reported is in the employment field, and it is not accompanied by any wider equality framework, hate-crime provision, or anti-violence mechanism.

Societal conditions are hostile. Sexual orientation and gender identity are treated as taboo, public societal discussion of homosexuality is not tolerated, and social and religious intolerance is pervasive. People fear family and community shunning if they are disclosed, which makes reporting to authorities unlikely and self-concealment the ordinary strategy.

The state does operate a complaint route: allegations can be filed with the police or with the national human-rights commission (CNDH). No cases of official violence against LGBTI people are citable in the reporting period, which reflects the absence of documentation rather than a demonstrated record of protection.
DJI.outOfScopeNotes:
Two sourced statements on discrimination protection do not align: one describes protection as existing in employment only, while the United States State Department's 2023 report states that there is no legal prohibition of discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Whether an employment-level protection exists in practice, and whether it covers gender identity, is unresolved on this inventory.

No cases of official violence against LGBTI people are citable from the available reporting, and the inventory contains no documented instance of the public-morality provisions being applied to a trans person specifically. Whether articles 353 and 354 have been used against trans individuals, and with what outcome, is not sourced here.

The most recent detailed human-rights reporting in this inventory is from 2023. Whether the penal code articles have been amended, whether any registration decision on LGBTI organisations has changed, and whether any gender-recognition procedure has been introduced since then is unresolved.

Documentation of the treatment of sexual minorities in Djibouti has been scarce across independent research sources for well over a decade, so the absence of adverse findings should not be read as evidence of safety.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Djibouti: limited LGBT-specific content, serving only as a historical baseline. The remainder of the report addresses general conditions, including suppression of the opposition, harsh prison conditions, FGM and trafficking.

Canadian IRB Response to Information Request DJI104070.E (research 2009–Mar 2012, via ecoi.net): documentation on treatment of sexual minorities in Djibouti was scarce across all consulted sources, leaning on the US 2010 country report — a dated historical baseline showing how little legal/protection framework and support services existed in that period.

DJI.tangentialFactors:
Djibouti's wider political environment shapes how any legal provision would be enforced. Reporting on the country documents suppression of the opposition and harsh prison conditions, alongside other serious rights concerns including female genital mutilation and trafficking. A state that treats political dissent this way offers no realistic expectation that a marginalised foreign national would obtain discretionary protection.

The evidence base for the country's treatment of sexual minorities has been thin for a long period. A Canadian Immigration and Refugee Board research response covering 2009 to March 2012 found documentation scarce across all consulted sources and relied on the 2010 United States country report as its principal reference, indicating how little legal, protective or support framework existed at that time. The 2015 United States State Department report contained only limited LGBT-specific content and served mainly as a historical baseline. The 2023 United States State Department report is the most recent detailed account available here.

Compared with jurisdictions that have explicit decriminalising statutes, a constitutional equality clause, or a functioning gender-recognition process, Djibouti offers none of these. The ambiguity of the penal code is itself a risk factor: conduct that is not named in law can still be prosecuted under a morality provision, and the visitor has no advance way to know where the line sits.

MRT.name: Mauritania
MRT.summary:
Mauritania presents one of the most severe legal environments for trans visitors. The Cairo 52 country review finds that transgender people are effectively criminalised through the Penal Code's debauchery provisions, and that Article 264, framed around public indecency and debauchery, is applied to gender nonconformity with penalties of one month to two years' imprisonment and fines of 5,000 to 150,000 ouguiya. Gender expression alone can therefore bring a person within the reach of the criminal law.

The wider sexual-conduct regime carries a far heavier ceiling. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that Mauritania criminalises same-sex sexual activity with a possible death penalty under Sharia law, and reporting from Erasing 76 Crimes states that the Penal Code retains a maximum sentence of death by stoning for men. The government confirmed a de facto moratorium on the death penalty in 2021, but the statute remains on the books and arrests and detentions under these provisions have continued in recent years.

Enforcement is inconsistent rather than absent. The US State Department's 2023 Human Rights Report on Mauritania states that consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised but that the penalties are not enforced, while also documenting reports of violence and threats against LGBT people, civil society objections to the scant number of indictments, and instances in which officials acted with impunity. A visitor should read that pattern as a landscape of under-protection rather than safety: prosecutions are rare, official protection is unreliable, and physical risk persists.

Official data on the trans community in Mauritania is gravely lacking, and the low visibility of LGBT people drives stigma, which in turn limits any practical ability to assess risk before arrival.

MRT.blindSummary:
The state presents an exceptionally severe legal environment for trans visitors. The national review finds that transgender people are effectively criminalised through the Penal Code's debauchery provisions, and that Article 264, framed around public indecency and debauchery, is applied to gender nonconformity with penalties of one month to two years' imprisonment and fines of 5,000 to 150,000 ouguiya. Gender expression alone can therefore bring a person within the reach of the criminal law.

The wider sexual-conduct regime carries a far heavier ceiling. The national profile records that the state criminalises same-sex sexual activity with a possible death penalty under religious law, and reporting from an LGBT crime-tracking publication states that the Penal Code retains a maximum sentence of death by stoning for men. The government confirmed a de facto moratorium on the death penalty in 2021, but the statute remains on the books and arrests and detentions under these provisions have continued in recent years.

Enforcement is inconsistent rather than absent. The national 2023 human rights reporting states that consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised but that the penalties are not enforced, while also documenting reports of violence and threats against LGBT people, civil society objections to the scant number of indictments, and instances in which officials acted with impunity. That pattern indicates under-protection rather than safety: prosecutions are rare, official protection is unreliable, and physical risk persists.

Official data on the trans community is gravely lacking, and low visibility drives stigma, which limits any practical ability to assess risk before arrival.

GNB.name: Guinea-Bissau
GNB.summary:
Same-sex conduct is legal in Guinea-Bissau. The 1993 penal code decree (4/93) omits same-sex offences entirely, and the country has never criminalised them. The Law on Prevention, Protection and Combating Domestic Violence (6/2014), Article 5, extends protection to victims regardless of sexual orientation. Guinea-Bissau signed the 2008 UN statement on sexual orientation and gender identity.

No legal gender recognition exists. There is no trans framework of any kind, no partnership or marriage recognition for same-sex couples, and no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity or sexual orientation in employment, services or public life. Nothing in the sourced record documents a document-amendment or border-screening pathway for trans travellers, and none can be assumed.

The dominant visitor risk is state capacity and enforcement rather than a specific statute. US State Department reporting for 2012 records a coup that year, arbitrary killings, torture, drug-trafficking-linked corruption and entrenched impunity within the security apparatus; the 2011 reporting records security-force torture and further impunity. These findings describe conditions a trans traveller would encounter regardless of the absence of anti-LGBT law.

Societal hostility is documented. The 2011 US State Department report notes stigma against LGBT people; the country guide records isolated violence cases in 2018 and no visible LGBT scene to orient visitors. The travel-safety assessment stands at 34/100, categorised Caution.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Social taboos against homosexuality sometimes restricted freedom to express sexual orientation, according to the U.S. Department of State's 2012 human rights report, even though the same report found society was relatively tolerant of consensual same-sex conduct. A 2010 Pew Research Center study of 19 African countries found Guinea-Bissau among the most tolerant: nine percent said homosexual behavior was morally acceptable and fifteen percent said it was not an issue. Wikipedia country coverage: Government guidelines for civil servants' housing allowances restricted facilities access: only heterosexual married couples were entitled to family-size (larger government) housing, while same-sex couples received the single-person allotment. The U.S. Department of State's 2011 Human Rights Report recorded the same rule, finding the law only recognized heterosexual married couples as entitled to larger government housing. Wikipedia country coverage: Article 5 (Principle of equality) of the Law against Domestic Violence (Law No. 6/2014) states that all victims, regardless of sexual orientation, enjoy the fundamental rights inherent to human dignity and are guaranteed equal opportunities to a life free from violence as well as physical and mental health. The U.S. Department of State's 2012 report found no official discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in access to health care, and no reported violent incidents or human rights abuses targeting people on that basis; antidiscrimination laws do not apply to LGBT individuals. In 2018 a local NGO director countered that there were some cases of violence targeting people based on sexual orientation or gender identity and that Guinea-Bissau lacks legal protections for LGBTI people. No youth-specific or minor-specific health access findings appear in the source text. Wikipedia country coverage: The U.S. Department of State's 2012 report found no official discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in employment or access to education. On family formation, a French government website states single and married people are eligible to adopt children but does not say whether LGBTQ people are disqualified, leaving youth placement status unclear. No findings specific to trans or LGBTQ minors, school students, or youth travelers appear in the source text.

GNQ.name: Equatorial Guinea
GNQ.summary:
Equatorial Guinea is high risk for trans visitors. The 2022 penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex intimacy or gender diversity, but that gap in the statute does not translate into safety: authorities continue to apply the 1954 Law on Vagrants and Criminals, which classifies homosexuality as an illness and normalises conversion practices, and a 2020 Draft Law titled 'Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals' would move conduct squarely into the criminal code if enacted; its current status is unclear.

Detention of LGBT people is documented. A Synergía IHR report on lesbophobia and police raids records police and military intervention in the assembly, expression and residential spaces of lesbian women, and in Bata the collective detention of women identified as lesbians on the stated grounds that 'lesbians are members of a sect', including collective punishment where a single individual is sought. The same reporting documents twelve women imprisoned between January and August 2024 in raids led by the Armed Forces and State Security, with detention used to extract bribes and sentences imposed indefinitely.

Three further instruments institutionalise discrimination against LGBT personnel and residents: the Military Justice Code, a ministerial order concerning 'immoral' activities, and a provincial regulation. The United States State Department's 2021 country report found no legal anti-discrimination protections and pervasive societal stigma toward LGBT persons. LGBT advocacy itself operates under the general repression of the country's government, one of the longest-ruling in Africa, which constrains freedom of expression, digital rights and journalist safety and leaves victims without meaningful recourse.
GNQ.outOfScopeNotes:
Several matters relevant to trans visitors could not be resolved from the available sources. Whether the 2020 Draft Law 'Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals' has advanced beyond draft status is unclear in the inventory. The sources do not address legal gender recognition, name or marker changes on identity and travel documents, entry or visa screening that could disclose gender history, or access to gender-affirming care; the current position on each of these is unsourced here.

No source in this inventory records a hate-crime statute, a complaint mechanism, or judicial remedy available to an LGBT victim of violence in Equatorial Guinea, and none records a documented case involving a trans foreign visitor specifically. The IRB-CISR country information record returned no usable finding for this pass.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The source describes the legal framework rather than document or legal-gender-recognition procedures: same-sex sexual activity is legal and the age of consent is 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Since 15 November 2022, Article 364(2) of the new Penal Code bars employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, the first provision explicitly protecting lesbian, gay and bisexual people, and Law 1/2016 on the Protection of Personal Data (Articles 10 and 41) protects personal data on "sexual life" where it entails discrimination. The criminal code in force is a revision of the Spanish Criminal Code dating to the Francoist era, said to carry anti-homophobic undertones. No text on legal gender recognition documents appears; same-sex couples simply have no legal recognition. Wikipedia country coverage: School officials have reportedly denied transgender students access to some facilities, and teachers have reportedly discriminated against and excluded LGBTQ+ girls. Transgender women have reported harassment and sexual violence while in police custody, and there are reports of security forces subjecting LGBTQ+ people to sexual violence and discrimination in the military, jails and prison. In 2014 four men were detained over a video found on a phone and made to explain their actions on national television; a lesbian couple in Añisok were tied up at the police station, paraded through town with banners calling them witchcraft-practicing lesbians, photographed and shamed. In August 2023 police illegally detained Trifonia Melibea Obono, founder of Somos Parte del Mundo, after her group submitted a report on torture and ill-treatment of LGBTQI+ people to the EU headquarters in Madrid; arrests and restrictions rose significantly afterward. Wikipedia country coverage: The source documents violence rather than clinical care: rape is sometimes used as a form of conversion therapy, and queer women are forcibly impregnated in an attempt to make them heterosexual. LGBTQ+ women and transgender men are described as vulnerable to sexual violence in the military and from family, while laws against rape are not effectively enforced because the crime is rarely reported, and police and judicial officials may decline to act where the perpetrator has political connections or is in the police or military. Transgender children are especially vulnerable to commercial sexual exploitation according to a local NGO, and minors generally are sexually exploited for commercial sex. No text on medication, hormone access or health services is present. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples have no legal recognition, and same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex couples. ILGA reports evidence that state intimidation of sexually diverse individuals persists, and although no law explicitly criminalizes homosexuality, LGBTQ+ people are still detained and punished through public shaming. Wikipedia country coverage: LGBTQ+ people face discrimination in education and employment: teachers have reportedly discriminated against and excluded LGBTQ+ girls, and school officials have reportedly denied transgender students access to some facilities. Family is an educational barrier because LGBTQ+ children are often forced out of their homes, which frequently causes them to drop out of school. Minors are sexually exploited for commercial sex, with transgender children especially vulnerable according to a local NGO, and academics and government employees can be ousted if perceived as not heterosexual. The age of consent is set at 18 regardless of gender and/or sexual orientation.

GNQ.tangentialFactors:
Equatorial Guinea's pattern of repressive governance shapes the risk environment for trans visitors. A UPR stakeholder submission by Small Media, EG Justice, IPI and Digital Rights in Equatorial Guinea, filed for the country's fourth Universal Periodic Review, documents restrictions on freedom of expression, digital rights and journalist safety; that environment also removes the public advocacy space in which LGBT complaints would otherwise be raised.

Scholarly analysis of Trifonia Melibea Obono's 2019 novel 'Yo no quería ser madre', published in Hispanic Studies Review in October 2025, reads the social climate as organised around compulsory heterosexuality and the invisibility of queer lives. This is cultural context rather than law, but it corroborates the societal stigma reported by the United States State Department in 2021.

SWZ.name: Eswatini
SWZ.summary:
Same-sex relations are illegal in Eswatini for men and women throughout the country, as recorded on 12 March 2026. Legal gender recognition is not available, so a trans visitor's documents will be read as issued, and no route exists to align them with lived gender.

LGBTI organisations cannot register in Eswatini. The registrar of companies refused registration to an LGBTI group in July 2019, and the government continues to deny such groups organisational status. A visitor should not expect to find a registered national advocacy body to contact for assistance.

Hostility from official figures is on the record. A 2021 United States State Department report found that some traditional, religious and government officials publicly criticised same-sex sexual conduct as neither locally nor Christian in character.

Public visibility nonetheless exists and has been tolerated in narrow form. The first Eswatini Pride was held in July 2018 and described as a success, and in June 2021 LGBTQI+ people held a virtual Pride celebration without incident. These events mark a small space of visibility in a state where the underlying conduct remains criminal.

The wider environment is an absolute monarchy with severely restricted civic space, which shapes how any incident involving a trans visitor would be handled by authorities.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Rock of Hope states that with no legislation recognising LGBTIs or protecting gender identity, LGBTQ people 'cannot be open about their orientation or gender identity for fear of rejection and discrimination', and most choose to remain in the closet or move to South Africa. In April 2022 the High Court, while upholding refusal to register Eswatini Sexual and Gender Minorities, accepted that the constitution protects LGBTQ persons' rights to freedom of association, privacy and expression. Advocacy groups have had trouble registering with the government — officials refused to register ESGM in June 2019 'on the grounds of morality'. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples are prohibited from adopting children in Eswatini, while prospective heterosexual adoptive parents may be single, married or divorced. There is no legal recognition of same-sex relationships, and in June 2012 Prime Minister Barnabas Sibusiso Dlamini said people of the same sex 'cannot even go to regional offices to get married' and that the country was 'not even ready to consider it'. Wikipedia country coverage: A 2019 survey found 59% of LGBTQ Swazis had been discriminated against or treated disrespectfully at public health facilities, with 30% denied healthcare services. In February 2012 public health officials ran a Valentine's Day campaign urging gay people to test for HIV, and Deputy Director of Health Simon Zwane said the Health Ministry was extending HIV counselling and testing to same-sex couples — a move LGBTQ groups welcomed. Section 4.3 of the 2013 National Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health requires the Ministry of Health to make family planning information and services available 'regardless of sex, gender, age, status, sexual orientation and religion'. Youth-specific: the National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health (2021) state that the right to equality includes freedom from discrimination because of one's sex or sexual orientation. Wikipedia country coverage: In March 2015 a 26-year-old lesbian woman from Nhlangano was murdered by a man who did not want to be in the presence of lesbians, and a few months earlier a gay man was murdered in the same town. The 2021 National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health name LGBT people as a key population at higher risk of gender-based violence, and the National Strategy to End Violence 2023-2027 lists sexual orientation or identity among its inclusivity principles. The 2017 Broadcasting Guidelines Services and the 2022 Broadcasting (Content) Guidelines bar licensees from broadcasting material that sanctions, glamorises or incites violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation. A 2013 survey found 43% of lesbian and transgender respondents had attempted suicide in the past year and 78% regularly used intoxicating substances to feel normal. Wikipedia country coverage: There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in areas such as education, health, housing and employment. Limited protections exist in policy: the 2021 National Social Security Policy defines equity as free from discrimination including sexual orientation, and the 2021 National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health include sexual orientation in the right to equality. In 2012 former Foreign Affairs Minister Mgwagwa Gamedze rejected a UN working group call for an LGBTQ protection law, saying so few gays lived in Eswatini that drafting one was not worth the effort; in May 2017 the UN Human Rights Committee pressed the government on measures to protect people from discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Wikipedia country coverage: There is no legal recognition of same-sex relationships in Eswatini. In June 2012 Prime Minister Barnabas Sibusiso Dlamini said same-sex couples cannot marry and that it would take time before the country allowed it in law; in 2014 Press Secretary Percy Simelane said the government was 'closely monitoring the situation with a view to take a legal position'. Same-sex couples are also prohibited from adopting children. Wikipedia country coverage: The National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health, issued in 2021, state that the right to Equality includes freedom from discrimination because of one's sex or sexual orientation, and define gender-based violence to include violence directed at a person based on gender identity or perceived adherence to norms of masculinity and femininity. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in education. The source contains no findings specific to transgender minors, school settings, or youth travel with medication.

LSO.name: Lesotho
LSO.summary:
Lesotho does not criminalise same-sex conduct. A common-law crime of sodomy was struck down in 2012, and the US State Department's 2016 human rights report for Lesotho records no criminalisation while documenting societal stigma against LGBT people.

There is no legal gender recognition in Lesotho. No law permits a change of the gender marker on official documents, and the Southern African Litigation Centre's 2017 constitutional analysis concludes that section 4(1), through the grounds of sex and other status, should be read to cover gender identity on the authority of the UN Human Rights Committee, an interpretation that has not been enacted in statute.

On that 2017 assessment, a trans traveller whose passport marker does not match their presentation or stated identity could face a charge, since no statutory route exists to have the document treated as consistent.

Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are documented rather than hypothetical. The joint stakeholder submission to the Universal Periodic Review filed in October 2024 by The Advocates for Human Rights, the Master of Healing Foundation and Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho records rape, assault and discrimination against LGBT people, barriers to health and education services, and SOGIESC discrimination at community level, and finds that same-sex conduct is not criminalised while no protections exist. Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho separately documents failures by state and non-state actors to prevent violence, harassment and discrimination.

The International Commission of Jurists' November 2024 submission to the same review names the rights of LGBTIQ+ persons to equality and non-discrimination as one of three key concerns it raises for Lesotho.

Employment protection rests on the Labour Code, whose non-discrimination clause omits gender and sexual orientation, alongside the Labour Act 3 of 2024, the current statutory framework covering unfair discrimination, unfair labour practices, freedom of association, and prohibitions on forced and child labour.
LSO.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in the sources: whether the Labour Act 3 of 2024 adds gender identity or sexual orientation to the non-discrimination grounds that the earlier Labour Code omitted. The Act's text is cited for unfair discrimination and related provisions, but the inventory does not state which grounds it enumerates.

Unresolved: whether any Lesotho court has applied the section 4(1) gender-identity interpretation argued in the 2017 constitutional analysis, and whether any of the concerns raised in the October and November 2024 Universal Periodic Review submissions produced recommendations that Lesotho accepted. No outcome is sourced.

The charge risk stated for a passport marker mismatch is an analytical legal conclusion in the 2017 briefing, not a documented arrest or border incident; no case of a trans traveller being stopped at entry on document grounds is sourced here.

The US State Department evidence on detainees, the Lesotho Defence Force mutiny and the killing of Lieutenant-General Mahao dates from 2016 and is not corroborated by a more recent source in this inventory.

Unsourced dimensions after this research pass: D4, D5, D6, D12.

LSO.tangentialFactors:
Lesotho's wider state-security record forms part of the environment a visitor enters. The US State Department's 2016 human rights report documents the Lesotho Defence Force mutiny arrests, the torture of detainees and the killing of Lieutenant-General Mahao, alongside its section on LGBT persons. Systemic mistreatment of detainees is not confined to any one group.

The International Commission of Jurists pairs its LGBTIQ+ equality concern with two further matters: inclusive education for children with disabilities and the revocation of practising certificates held by lawyers employed by non-governmental organisations. Restrictive action against NGO lawyers bears on the availability of legal assistance.

Lesotho's engagement with the Universal Periodic Review in late 2024 produced at least two independent stakeholder submissions on LGBTIQ+ rights, indicating an active but externally driven protection track rather than settled domestic reform.

Lesotho is a small state with a correspondingly small organising base: the People's Matrix Association, documented in the October 2020 briefing by the Southern African Litigation Centre, the Matrix and the Women and Law in Southern Africa Research and Education Project, is the only known LGBTI organisation in the country. Services, shelters and peer networks available to a trans traveller are therefore limited.

The Matrix briefing on legal gender recognition, researched by Professor Alex Müller with community consultations, measures Lesotho's law and policy against international best practice and records the gap between them.

CPV.name: Cabo Verde
CPV.summary:
Same-sex relations are not criminalised in Cabo Verde, and the country's employment discrimination prohibition covers sexual orientation. The protection does not extend to gender identity, leaving trans visitors and residents without an explicit statutory basis for workplace complaints (Outright International, updated 12 March 2026).

No legal gender recognition framework is on record. As of 2016 civil law blocked Tchinda Andrade, the first publicly self-outed trans woman in Cabo Verde, from changing her legal name to a female one; the source inventory contains no later statute or administrative route for legal gender change.

Same-sex unions are not recognised. Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva stated on 11 July 2017 that same-sex marriage was not on the government's agenda, following LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Public visibility is high by regional standards. Cabo Verde held its first public Pride in 2013, the second African country to do so. The 2018 Pride Week in Praia combined a parade with campaigns by the Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, the Associação LGBTI de Praia and the Associação Arco Iris, which petitioned the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law; the gender-equality institute ICIEG and UN Women took part. Polling in 2019–21 found 82% would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour.

Trans-specific violence is documented at individual level rather than as a recorded pattern. Tchinda Andrade, who came out in 1997 at age 19, described Cabo Verde as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other African countries and São Vicente as relaxed, but reported verbal violence and two physical attacks against her. The inventory contains no case series, prosecution record or official count of anti-trans violence.
CPV.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any administrative practice permits a gender or name marker change on identity documents is unresolved. The only sourced statement is Tchinda Andrade's 2016 account that civil law blocked her name change; no later legal or administrative status is in the inventory.

Enforcement of the employment discrimination protection is not sourced. The inventory states the prohibition exists and that it covers sexual orientation, but records no complaint outcomes, labour-inspectorate practice or court decisions.

Hate-crime or aggravated-penalty provisions covering anti-trans motivation are not sourced either way. The absence of such a provision in the inventory is not evidence that none exists.

The scale of anti-trans violence beyond Tchinda Andrade's reported verbal abuse and two physical attacks is not sourced. No police statistics, NGO incident counts or court records are available here, so the assessment of low documented risk rests on a single first-person account plus the absence of a recorded pattern.

Entry, visa and border-screening rules for trans travellers, including how gender markers on passports are treated at arrival, are not covered by any source in this inventory.

sources.summary: Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations not criminalised; employment discrimination protection covers sexual orientation (not gender identity); no same-sex union recognition; LGBTIQ orgs register freely; first public Pride 2013 (second African country); 2019–21 polls: 82% would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour; Cabo Verde one of two African UN LGBTI Core Group members, made 2024 UPR anti-discrimination commitments.

Equal Eyes (20 Jul 2018): 2018 Pride Week in Praia — parade plus NGO campaigns (Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, Associação LGBTI de Praia, Associação Arco Iris) petitioning the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law; state gender-equality institute ICIEG and UN Women engaged.

Observador/Lusa (11 Jul 2017): PM Ulisses Correia e Silva said same-sex marriage is not on the government's agenda, distancing himself from MpD secretary-general Miguel Monteiro's opposition, after LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Afrobarometer Dispatch No. 362 (May 2020): 'All in this together' - Africans are tolerant on ethnic, religious and national differences but not sexual differences; Cabo Verde, Namibia and São Tomé and Príncipe stand out as particularly tolerant countries; tolerance toward sexual minorities remains remarkably weak even among younger respondents.

Rede Angola interview (22 Jun 2016) with Tchinda Andrade, first publicly self-outed trans woman in Cabo Verde (came out 1997, age 19): describes Cabo Verde as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other African countries and São Vicente as relaxed, but reports verbal violence and two physical attacks; civil law blocked her legal change to a female name — no legal gender recognition as of 2016.

CPV.tangentialFactors:
Afrobarometer Dispatch No. 362 (May 2020) places Cabo Verde alongside Namibia and São Tomé and Príncipe as particularly tolerant African countries, while finding that tolerance toward sexual minorities remains remarkably weak across the continent even among younger respondents. The same survey frames tolerance on ethnic, religious and national differences as broadly high, which is not the same measure as acceptance of sexual difference.

Cabo Verde is one of two African members of the UN LGBTI Core Group and made anti-discrimination commitments under the Universal Periodic Review in 2024. LGBTIQ organisations register freely in the country. Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva's 2017 remark distancing himself from MpD secretary-general Miguel Monteiro's opposition to same-sex marriage indicates division within the governing party rather than a settled legislative position.
CPV.localsOnly:
Residents are covered by an employment discrimination prohibition that names sexual orientation, giving a domestic legal basis for workplace complaints on that ground. No equivalent gender-identity ground is stated in the sources.

Domestic partners have no route to legal recognition of a same-sex union, so inheritance, hospital visitation and next-of-kin questions are governed by default civil law rather than partnership status.

LGBTIQ organisations operate openly and register without restriction, and the national gender-equality institute ICIEG engages with Pride programming. Advocacy groups including the Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, the Associação LGBTI de Praia and the Associação Arco Iris petition the National Assembly directly.

Public acceptance is measurable: 82% of respondents in 2019–21 polling said they would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour, and the country has held public Pride events annually since 2013.
