CPV.blindSummary:
Same-sex relations are not criminalised in the state, and the country's employment discrimination prohibition covers sexual orientation. The protection does not extend to gender identity, leaving trans visitors and residents without an explicit statutory basis for workplace complaints (Outright International, updated 12 March 2026).

No legal gender recognition framework is on record. As of 2016 civil law blocked Tchinda Andrade, the first publicly self-outed trans woman in the state, from changing her legal name to a female one; the source inventory contains no later statute or administrative route for legal gender change.

Same-sex unions are not recognised. The head of government stated on 11 July 2017 that same-sex marriage was not on the government's agenda, following LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Public visibility is high by regional standards. The state held its first public Pride in 2013, the second state/province on the continent to do so. The 2018 Pride Week in the principal city combined a parade with campaigns by three national LGBT associations, which petitioned the national assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law; the national gender-equality institute and an international agency took part. Polling in 2019–21 found 82% would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour.

Trans-specific violence is documented at individual level rather than as a recorded pattern. Tchinda Andrade, who came out in 1997 at age 19, described the state as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other national settings and her home province as relaxed, but reported verbal violence and two physical attacks against her. The inventory contains no case series, prosecution record or official count of anti-trans violence.
CPV.blindOutOfScope:
Whether any administrative practice permits a gender or name marker change on identity documents is unresolved. The only sourced statement is Tchinda Andrade's 2016 account that civil law blocked her name change; no later legal or administrative status is in the inventory.

Enforcement of the employment discrimination protection is not sourced. The inventory states the prohibition exists and that it covers sexual orientation, but records no complaint outcomes, labour-inspectorate practice or court decisions.

Hate-crime or aggravated-penalty provisions covering anti-trans motivation are not sourced either way. The absence of such a provision in the inventory is not evidence that none exists.

The scale of anti-trans violence beyond Tchinda Andrade's reported verbal abuse and two physical attacks is not sourced. No police statistics, NGO incident counts or court records are available here, so the assessment of low documented risk rests on a single first-person account plus the absence of a recorded pattern.

Entry, visa and border-screening rules for trans travellers, including how gender markers on passports are treated at arrival, are not covered by any source in this inventory.

STP.name: São Tomé and Príncipe
STP.summary:
Same-sex conduct has been legal in São Tomé and Príncipe since the Penal Code entered into force in November 2012, and the age of consent is set equally at 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. One source states that Law 15/2021 raised the age of consent to 18 for everyone in 2021, which would apply to visitors as well as residents; the sources disagree on the current figure.

São Tomé and Príncipe has no legal framework for gender-identity recognition. There is no procedure for amending sex or gender markers on identity documents, so a traveller whose passport, visa or other papers do not match their presentation should expect the mismatch to be visible to border and hotel officials with no domestic remedy behind it.

No form of relationship recognition exists for same-sex couples. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised, and same-sex couples cannot adopt.

Protection against discrimination is narrow. Article 16.2 of the 2019 Labour Code prohibits discrimination in employment on grounds of sexual orientation, and no broader general anti-discrimination statute covers housing, services or public accommodation. Article 130(2)(d) of the Penal Code permits enhanced sentencing for crimes motivated by hatred of a person's sexual orientation, a provision that on its face addresses bias-motivated violence.

The state has signed the United Nations joint statement on sexual orientation and gender identity, placing its official position on record in favour of decriminalisation and non-discrimination.
STP.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents incidents of violence against transgender people in São Tomé and Príncipe, their dates, or any police or judicial outcome, so the level of such violence is unresolved rather than established as low.

Nothing in the sources addresses airport or border screening of gender markers, entry or visa rules that turn on gender presentation, access to gender-affirming healthcare, or restroom and facility rules. These remain not sourced.

The current age of consent is stated inconsistently across the sources (16 versus 18); the discrepancy is unresolved and should be checked against the text of Law 15/2021.

Enforcement of the Labour Code's sexual-orientation clause and of the Penal Code's bias-motivation sentencing enhancement is not evidenced by any case or complaint data in the inventory.

MDV.name: Maldives
MDV.summary:
The Maldives criminalises same-sex conduct under its 2014 Penal Code, which extended the offence beyond Muslims to everyone, and reporting on the statute notes that death-penalty provisions remain theoretically in reach. Enforcement is documented rather than theoretical: police on Dhaandhoo arrested two men, aged 56 and 27, on 29 August 2015 after they were found engaging in homosexual activity in a private home.

The Dhaandhoo case matters for what it shows about reach. Prosecution extended into a residence on a local island, so the exposure is not confined to conduct in public spaces or to Maldivian nationals. Rainbow Warriors warned after the arrests that tourists could face similar threats.

The state's international legal position constrains available protections. The Maldives holds reservations to the ICCPR, CEDAW and the CRC, and UN review of those reservations records concerns including sharia-based treatment of children born outside marriage. Within that framework the Human Rights Committee recommended anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and action against the stigmatisation of homosexuals.

Human-rights measurement points the same way. In HRMI's 2024 second expert survey, experts most commonly identified LGBTQIA+ people — alongside migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers — as at risk of violations of empowerment rights.
MDV.outOfScopeNotes:
Gender identity is not addressed by any source in this inventory. Document and marker rules, gender-recognition procedure, entry and visa screening that could disclose a visitor's gender history, and the treatment of gender-nonconforming travellers are unresolved here, as is the penalty structure for gender nonconformity as distinct from same-sex conduct.

Whether resort islands are treated differently from local islands is not sourced in this inventory. The single enforcement example available is a local island, and no source in the inventory states either that resorts are legally exempt or that visitors there face equivalent risk.

The national UPR report supplies acceptance and rejection counts for 126 first-cycle recommendations without identifying which recommendations were rejected. Whether the Human Rights Committee's recommendation on sexual-orientation anti-discrimination fell within the 20 rejected is unresolved.

Hate-crime provisions covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and rules governing access to gendered facilities, are not sourced in this inventory.

Maldives national UPR report (A/HRC/WG.6/22/MDV/1, April 2015): the government’s own submission — of 126 first-cycle recommendations it fully accepted 89, partially accepted 11, took note of 6 and rejected 20 with reasons; reports full implementation of 58 and partial implementation of 32 over four years.

MDV.tangentialFactors:
The 2024 HRMI survey scores political participation in the Maldives relatively better, at 6.4 out of 10, while other civil and political rights score considerably lower. Institutions that record citizen input therefore function better than the machinery that would deliver a remedy to a person facing prosecution or stigmatisation.

Groups identified alongside LGBTQIA+ people as at risk of empowerment-rights violations include migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers. The pattern across these categories is one in which several minority and advocacy-facing groups encounter the same weak protection, rather than a position specific to gender or sexuality alone.

In its second-cycle Universal Periodic Review the government's own submission accounted for 126 first-cycle recommendations: 89 fully accepted, 11 partially accepted, 6 noted and 20 rejected with reasons, alongside claimed full implementation of 58 and partial implementation of 32 over four years. The gap between acceptance and reported implementation is where the anti-discrimination recommendations sit.

The Rainbow Warriors warning issued in 2015 treats the Maldives as a threat environment for visitors, which places the Dhaandhoo arrests in a regional pattern of cross-border concern rather than an isolated domestic matter.

PRK.name: North Korea
PRK.summary:
North Korea exposes trans visitors to unbounded official discretion rather than a defined statute. The Criminal Code of 1950, revised in 2009, appears to contain no penalty for consensual same-sex acts, but Article 193 prohibits the import, possession and distribution of "decadent culture," including sexual recordings, and Article 262 punishes collective "obscene activities." Neither provision is defined in terms that constrain how the authorities apply it.

The US State Department's 2022 human rights report on North Korea reaches the same position: no specific law criminalises same-sex conduct, and the regime's total control leaves no space for LGBT life. Its 2020 report states that reliable information on LGBT persons is unavailable and that repression of all civil society is the dominant human-rights reality in the country.

Gender identity has no standing in public life. A sex-marker change on a birth certificate or citizen card is formally possible under "unavoidable circumstances," on application to the People's Security Agency together with a state forensic medical evaluation, and in practice requires surgical intervention. No law explicitly bans gender-affirming care, but the under-resourced health system makes hormones and surgery effectively inaccessible.

Official hostility toward homosexuality is on the record. In April 2014 the state news agency KCNA rejected the UN Commission of Inquiry's report on North Korean human rights as a political fabrication and dismissed commissioner Michael Kirby as "a disgusting old lecher with a 40-odd-year-long career of homosexuality," using his sexual orientation to discredit the inquiry. KCNA had stated earlier that same year that homosexuality does not exist in North Korea.

Controls tightened in the decade after that inquiry. Reporting by BBC Korean on 10 October 2024 identifies new legislation, including the Pyongyang Cultural Protection Act, as tightening state control, and describes a collective-over-individual order that forces sexual minorities into silent self-suppression and frames LGBT life as a human-rights abuse.

Defector testimony documents the consequences of that order. Jang Young-jin, a novelist who left North Korea in the late 1990s and was forcibly outed, is the first publicly known gay defector; an openly gay defector published an autobiography in 2017, and CNN carried his account of homosexuality's place in North Korean society and its punishment in April 2017.

Outright International's country page, updated 12 March 2026, records no documented state or non-state violence against LGBTIQ people in North Korea and no route by which an LGBTI organisation can register. The absence of documented violence sits alongside the absence of independent reporting capacity and of any registration or recognition machinery for gender identity.
PRK.outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and visa screening, including any inspection of devices or digital material at the border, is not addressed by the sources in this inventory and remains unresolved here.

Whether a foreign trans visitor's passport gender marker would be recognised on arrival, and how it interacts with North Korean identity documents, is not sourced and is unresolved.

Hate-crime protection, anti-discrimination enforcement, bathroom and facilities rules, and marriage or partner recognition are not covered by the inventory; no positive finding should be read from their absence in this record.

The claim of no documented violence against LGBTIQ people comes from a single advocacy source and is qualified by the US State Department's statement that reliable information on LGBT persons in North Korea is not available. The two findings are not fully reconcilable on the evidence given.

Conditions of travel escort and surveillance inside the country are described in general terms by the sources but not specified for trans visitors, and remain unresolved.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6, D13.

Wikipedia country coverage: As of 2026, there is no North Korean law that recognizes same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships. Article 8 of the Family Law of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea states that 'Marriage may be done only between one man and one woman'. Additionally, per the U.S. State Department's 2020 report, same-sex couples could not legally adopt children in North Korea.

PSE.name: Palestinian Territories
PSE.summary:
Trans visitors face a severe and split risk environment. Two separate criminal-law regimes apply across the territories, and the difference between them is decisive: consensual same-sex conduct is not an offence in the West Bank, while in Gaza the same conduct carries up to ten years under a statute that the de facto authorities there have enforced with lethal violence.

The West Bank operates under Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960. Jordan's 1951 revision of its own code deleted offences against consensual private sexual conduct, and the 1960 code carried that position forward, so no provision criminalises consensual same-sex acts there. Israel stopped applying the older Mandate code in 1977.

Gaza is governed by Criminal Code Ordinance No. 74 of 1936, which remains in force. Section 152(2) punishes consensual same-sex "carnal knowledge" with up to ten years' imprisonment, and Human Rights Watch has found the section's vague "unnatural offences" concepts incompatible with the rights to privacy and non-discrimination. Hamas has executed people for alleged homosexuality.

Trans identity is nowhere explicitly criminalised. The 1936 ordinance is silent on it, but its public-morality provisions can be turned against trans people, and periodic transphobic threats and attacks are reported across both territories.

The Palestinian Authority has not legislated any protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and it is a non-signatory to the key international treaties that would supply one. No hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection is in force anywhere in the territories.

Formal legality in the West Bank does not translate into safety. Social and family persecution makes the practical reality harsher than the written law, with family and clan hostility a persistent source of violence against queer and trans people. Palestinian Authority police banned LGBTQ activity by the organisation al-Qaws; rights groups condemned the action, and the organisation then received a wave of hate messages that activists said pose a serious threat to the community.

Gaza is in a catastrophic war. Gender-affirming healthcare there is essentially destroyed or unavailable, and a visitor who needs hormones or other routine trans-related care should assume no reliable supply exists.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Palestinian law is a patchwork of foreign-occupation legacies — Ottoman, British, Jordanian, Egyptian and Israeli — with the Palestinian Authority having legislated neither for nor against homosexuality. The British Mandate Criminal Code (1936), which criminalized sodomy and 'act against the law of nature' with prison terms up to 14 and 10 years respectively, remains disputed as to applicability: Human Dignity Trust and Human Rights Watch say it is still in force in Gaza, Amnesty does not report same-sex acts as illegal, and editor-in-chief Anis F. Kassim argues it could be read as permitting homosexuality. The 2003 draft Palestinian penal code contained provisions criminalizing adult consensual same-sex conduct (up to five years for male-male sodomy), but it is unknown whether it was implemented. Equaldex is cited as stating there are no broad legal protections from discrimination for LGBTIQ+ people in Palestine; no legal gender recognition provisions appear in the source text, and Palestinian queer organisations operate from within Israel, with statelessness cited as a structural condition of LGBTQ Palestinians. Wikipedia country coverage: HIV prevention and care are described as inadequate: HIV-positive queer individuals often do not receive continuous antiretroviral therapy because medication is limited and social stigma is high, and comprehensive epidemiological surveillance is lacking — only 98 HIV/AIDS cases were officially registered in Palestine between 1988 and 2017 (79 AIDS, 19 HIV-positive), with the true number likely far higher because taboos hinder data collection. In Gaza since October 2023, collapse of the healthcare system plus Israeli blockades has made access to life-saving HIV medication especially difficult. In Israel, LGBTQ Palestinian asylum seekers are routinely excluded from basic healthcare programs and shelter access available to other asylum seekers, and some have faced house arrest or deportation; only in June 2022 did Israel begin issuing work permits to gay Palestinian refugees granted asylum and those fleeing domestic violence. Wikipedia country coverage: The only youth-linked legal provision cited is Section 152(1)(c) of the British Mandate Criminal Code, under which sodomy with a child under sixteen carries up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Section 152(2)(b) criminalizing 'carnal knowledge' against the law of nature with up to 10 years. Islamist actors contest LGBTQ content in education and youth spaces: the Palestinian Mujahideen Movement and the Rightly-Guided Caliphs Assembly criticized UNRWA for promoting what they see as un-Islamic values including LGBTQ issues, and the Islamic Movement in Israel opposed Israel's conversion therapy ban (activist Maisan Hamdan noting the movement's sole stated aim is Palestine's liberation without LGBTQ inclusion). Public acceptance is ranked Palestine 130 on the Global Acceptance Index with very little change 2010–2020, and the source reports civil society groups protecting women and children are 'vulnerable to attack' in Gaza.

SLE.name: Sierra Leone
SLE.summary:
Sexual activity between men is a criminal offence in Sierra Leone under the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act, which carries a penalty of up to life imprisonment; The Human Dignity Trust country profile records the statute as the basis of the country's criminalisation regime. Consensual sexual relations between women are not explicitly outlawed, so the exposure of a trans woman to the sodomy provision depends on how the offence is applied to her, but the absence of an explicit prohibition does not translate into safety.

No legal protection on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is documented. Amnesty International's 2025 country report records no non-discrimination protection covering SOGI, which means a visitor who is discriminated against in a hotel, a clinic, a workplace interaction or a police station has no statutory complaint to make.

Violence against LGBT people has produced fatalities and a failed justice response. In November 2004 the lesbian activist FannyAnn Eddy was raped and murdered; her alleged killer was arrested in January 2005, police refused to classify the killing as a hate crime, and the accused was reported to have escaped from custody in July 2005. The case is the clearest documented instance of lethal violence against an LGBT activist in the country's records and of the state's failure to treat such violence as bias-motivated.

Discrimination is documented at both official and societal level. The US State Department's 2012 human rights report recorded official and societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender individuals, in a country context that also reported police killings and corruption. A joint civil-society shadow report to the UN Human Rights Committee in March 2014, 'Breaking the Silence on Human Rights Violations in Sierra Leone', documented discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity, hate speech issued by religious institutions, and hate crimes targeting LGBTI human-rights defenders, alongside discrimination in health services and education.

Lesbian women face significant social, cultural and economic barriers to living freely, including stigma, harassment and limited acceptance from families and communities, according to Amnesty International. A trans visitor should expect the same social environment to apply to her, compounded by the criminalisation regime where male same-sex conduct is concerned and by an official apparatus that has been recorded as discriminatory.
SLE.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not address legal gender recognition, the amendment of sex markers on passports or national identity documents, or any screening of travel documents at entry. Nothing in the inventory indicates whether a trans visitor's documents will be questioned on arrival, and no visa or entry rule specific to gender identity is documented here.

No source in the inventory states whether the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act has been used in a prosecution in recent years, or how frequently the penalty is imposed. The record of enforcement is unresolved on the available material.

Whether the 1861 Act's provisions reach conduct involving trans women, as opposed to cisgender men, is not addressed in the sources; the Amnesty International finding that sexual relations between women are not explicitly outlawed does not settle how the statute is applied to a trans person.

The inventory contains no hate-crime statute, no bias-motivated-offence sentencing provision, and no documented mechanism for reporting anti-trans violence to a dedicated unit. The 2014 shadow report's findings on hate crimes against LGBTI defenders are civil-society documentation, not a statement of enacted law.

Facilities, accommodation rules and access to gender-affirming care are not covered by any source listed, and no assessment of them is possible from this material.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2, D3, D4, D5, D6, D12.

The 2014 shadow report also records discrimination in health and education services on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, which bears on access to care for a trans visitor who needs a clinic, a hospital or a pharmacy interaction during her stay.

XKX.name: Kosovo
XKX.summary:
Article 24 of the Constitution of the Republic of Kosovo prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, and the 2015 Law on Protection from Discrimination extends that protection to gender identity. Outright International's March 2026 overview records that implementation of both provisions remains inconsistent in practice, so the formal guarantees a visitor can cite are stronger than what is reliably delivered.

Legal gender recognition exists but runs through a court-supervised route rather than an administrative one. In January 2019 Blert Morina's application concerning name and gender-marker change on Kosovo identity documents was before the Constitutional Court, and applicants in Kosovo followed closely the European Court of Human Rights ruling in X v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, which held that a surgical requirement for changing a gender marker violates private-life rights.

Same-sex partnership recognition has been blocked repeatedly. Kosovo's Assembly voted against same-sex-couple recognition amendments to the Civil Code in 2022 and rejected a law recognising same-sex civil unions in March 2022. Prime Minister Albin Kurti told attendees during Pride week that he would do his utmost to secure adoption of the Civil Code, and in April 2024 pledged to legalise same-sex civil unions, with a Ministry of Justice working group drafting the bill. As of February 2026 the Assembly had still not adopted the new Civil Code, amid fierce opposition that included members of the ruling party. IntelliNews reports that the draft Civil Code's gender-neutral marriage language would open the way to same-sex marriage if it entered into force.

Public hostility is documented and directed at individuals. The Center for Social Group Development's 2022 annual report found intolerance and hatred, with politicians' hate speech common during the Civil Code debates, and an artist received death threats over a painting. Kosovo is a Muslim-majority state, and Reuters reported in May 2024 that the same-sex union debate was proceeding amid fierce opposition.

LGBTI organising is visible and proceeds in public. The third annual Pride Parade was held in Pristina, accompanied by a week of exhibitions, parties, conferences and discussions organised by the Center for Equality and Liberty, and Kosovo Pride Week has run under the motto "I love you as you are!".
XKX.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the new Civil Code has been adopted after February 2026 is unresolved in the sources provided; the latest dated statement is the February 2026 record of continued non-adoption.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa screening of trans travellers, whether gender markers on foreign passports are inspected at Pristina International Airport, or whether documents can be flagged. Any statement on that question would be unsourced.

Penalties for hate-crime offences, the enforcement record of the 2015 Law on Protection from Discrimination, and the outcome of Blert Morina's Constitutional Court case are not sourced here.

Whether Kosovo itself imposes a surgical or medical requirement for legal gender recognition is not stated in the inventory; only the European Court of Human Rights ruling against such a requirement in the neighbouring case is documented. Access to gender-affirming healthcare, and rules on restroom and facility use, are likewise not sourced.

Unsourced dimensions after this research pass: D1, D2, D4, D5, D6, D7, D8, D9, D13.

GIB.name: Gibraltar
GIB.summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing territory whose own legislature and Supreme Court govern its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council. No such extension is on record in the sourced material.

The principal legal gap for a trans visitor is gender recognition. No route exists in Gibraltar to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore expects to travel on a document whose gender marker cannot be altered by any local process, and to be read in public under that marker.

Discrimination protection covering sexual orientation and gender reassignment has been in force since 2007. The sourced material does not set out what that protection covers in practice: whether it reaches service counters, single-sex facilities, health care, or employment in the visitor's own terms is not stated.

Same-sex activity has been legal since 1993, with an equal age of consent since 2012. Civil partnerships have existed since 2014, and same-sex marriage was passed unanimously in December 2016. A Supreme Court ruling in 2013 established a right of adoption by same-sex partners.

The 2016 marriage bill followed a public consultation opened in December 2015, which returned 3,490 replies from an electorate of 24,117. Reporting at the time described the population as divided over the change, while noting that an inter-ministerial committee chaired by a government minister had weighed the arguments and that the main parties supported the amendment; a draft bill amending the Civil Marriage Act was placed before Parliament in August 2016.

Official language on hostility has been directed at anti-gay abuse rather than at transgender persons. In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would 'urgently' consider legislation to tackle 'disgusting lurking homophobia' following an incident of anti-gay abuse. That statement evidences an enforcement intent against homophobic abuse; it does not establish trans-specific protection.
GIB.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the substantive scope of the 2007 protection for gender reassignment. The sourced material records that the term appears in the discrimination law but does not state what it covers in practice, including access to health care, single-sex facilities, or employment records.

Not sourced: whether any procedure, including a deed poll or statutory declaration, permits a Gibraltarian resident to obtain a corrected gender marker on a United Kingdom travel document, and whether United Kingdom gender recognition law applies to persons resident in Gibraltar. This is an open research question rather than a negative finding.

Not sourced: the existence, wording or enforcement of any hate-crime provision denigrating transgender persons, and any recorded incident of violence against a trans person in Gibraltar with a date and legal outcome.

Unresolved: whether the Ministry for Justice and Equality statement of July 2021, made in response to anti-gay abuse, resulted in enacted legislation, and whether any such legislation addresses abuse of transgender persons. The statement is the only enforcement-intent evidence on record here and it concerns homophobia.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Gibraltar's Parliament passed a bill on 19 September 2013 (royal assent 25 September, in force 10 October) amending the Crimes Act 2011 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation as a hate crime. In July 2021 the Justice Ministry began investigating a further proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence, prompted by what Chief Minister Fabian Picardo called 'disgusting lurking homophobia' on social media during Pride month. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for 'transgender identity.' Wikipedia country coverage: The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, de jure legalising LGBT adoption after a long-term lesbian couple — denied adoption for lack of legal recognition of their relationship — challenged the law; the government amended the law via the 2014 civil partnership legislation. The Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024, explicitly allowing same-sex couples to adopt children without discrimination. In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. Wikipedia country coverage: In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy allowing lesbian couples to access assisted reproductive technology. In February 2021 Gibraltar implemented a surrogacy law for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practice conversion therapy. Wikipedia country coverage: The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender was equalised at 16: the Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 8 April 2011 that the higher age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set an equal age of consent of 16, taking effect on 23 November 2012. Before this, gay male minors faced a discriminatory age of 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent had been defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009; the Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 enquiry into overseas territories recommended making discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status illegal in all overseas territories.

BMU.name: Bermuda
BMU.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Bermuda; local legislation governs, and the United Kingdom measures could be applied only by Order in Council.

Bermuda decriminalised consensual sex between adult men in 1994, when the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to strike two sections of the Criminal Code. In July 2013 the Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act, which outlawed discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and, in the same instrument, on grounds of age; same-sex marriage was not permitted at that time.

Same-sex couples married in Bermuda in 2017 lost that route the following year. The Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act in February 2018, replacing same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships available to same-sex and opposite-sex couples alike, which made Bermuda the first jurisdiction anywhere to revoke marriage equality. In March 2022 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council upheld that restoration of the opposite-sex definition of marriage, so a partnership rather than a marriage is the status available to same-sex couples.

For a transgender visitor the decisive fact is the protection gap. Bermuda has no legal recognition of transgender people and no gender-recognition framework, so there is no route to amend a gender marker on local documents and no recognition machinery a visitor could rely on at the border or in dealings with local authorities. The 2013 amendment's protected ground as enacted is sexual orientation; the inventory does not record gender identity as a protected ground, and no hate-crime provision covering gender identity is sourced here.
BMU.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether gender identity functions as a protected ground under Bermuda's human-rights legislation, whether any local gender-recognition statute exists, and whether hate-crime provisions reach conduct motivated by gender identity are all unresolved on the present inventory; none of these points is sourced here.

The enforcement record of the 2013 discrimination protections, including complaint volumes and outcomes, is not sourced. Whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 or its 2025 single-sex-services code has ever been proposed for extension to Bermuda by Order in Council is likewise unresolved.

CYM.name: Cayman Islands
CYM.summary:
Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in the Cayman Islands in 2001 by an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature declined to act, and the reform left an unequal age of consent in its wake.

London–local friction over the scope of protections is documented from 2009, when the United Kingdom's Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the draft Cayman Islands constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission deplorable and warning that the drafting could leave the territory's courts affording less protection than Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights requires. The Foreign and Commonwealth Office answered that the draft's list of discrimination grounds was open-ended.

The judiciary outran the legislature on relationship status. In March 2019 Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie struck down the prohibition on same-sex marriage; the Court of Appeal reversed that ruling in August 2019, so no same-sex marriages can be performed locally. In December 2020 the immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who had married in Ireland, with the Court of Appeal holding that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. The practical position for a visitor is therefore recognition of an existing foreign marriage for immigration effects, without any locally conferred marital status.

Public visibility carries official backing. The territory's first Pride parade, held on 7 August 2021 and organised by the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation, drew around 600 participants including the premier, the governor, ministers and members of the Legislative Assembly. Participants were asked by organisers to refrain from excessive displays of affection, a condition reflecting sensitivities about public space rather than a legal prohibition.
CYM.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the unequal age of consent identified after the 2001 decriminalisation has since been amended by the Legislative Assembly is unresolved in the available sources; no later legislative text is provided.

The scope of the December 2020 recognition beyond immigration effects is unresolved. Whether a foreign same-sex marriage is given general legal effect in the Cayman Islands, for purposes such as property, succession or next-of-kin status, is not sourced here.

No source in the inventory addresses whether the territory has enacted a civil partnership, domestic partnership or equivalent status scheme, or whether any such bill is pending.

Nothing in the inventory covers hate-crime provisions, their wording or their enforcement, or recorded incidents of violence against trans people in the Cayman Islands. Those questions remain unsourced rather than answered negatively.

Whether the Court of Appeal's equality reasoning in the recognition case has been applied to other areas of law, and whether any further appeal or legislative response followed, is not established by the available material.

VGB.name: British Virgin Islands
VGB.summary:
Same-sex intimacy has not been a criminal offence in the British Virgin Islands since January 2001, when the United Kingdom's Privy Council ordered the repeal of the sodomy laws in the British Virgin Islands and four other remaining British Caribbean territories after the local legislature declined to act. Local legislator Orlando Smith accepted the outcome publicly, stating that "there is nothing we can do."

The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010, including its 2025 single-sex-services code, does not automatically apply in the British Virgin Islands. Local law governs, and measures of the United Kingdom's Parliament extend to the territory only when brought into force by Order in Council. A trans visitor should not assume the Equality Act's discrimination and service-access protections are available there by default.

Family status remains contested rather than settled. In 2022 the Court of Appeal of the British Virgin Islands refused the BVI Christian Council's application for permission to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack in proceedings testing whether the same-sex marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome, celebrated in the United Kingdom, is valid under British Virgin Islands law. The appellate court found the proposed appeal had no realistic prospect of success. The trial court's finding had been in favour of the two women, and the litigation was also testing a declaration that the territorial prohibition on same-sex marriage is unconstitutional.

Opposition to same-sex marriage is organised locally through the BVI Christian Council, which pursued the appeal bid after losing in the court below. A trans visitor who is married, or who has a spouse, should expect the British Virgin Islands legislature and its courts to be the venues where recognition is decided, rather than the United Kingdom's Parliament, and should treat marriage recognition as unresolved rather than guaranteed.
VGB.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved and not established by these sources: the final outcome of the Forbes and Lettsome challenge on the validity of their marriage and on the constitutionality of the territorial marriage prohibition. The inventory records only the Court of Appeal's refusal of the BVI Christian Council's appeal bid against Justice Adrian Jack's case-management orders in July 2022.

Not sourced in this inventory: whether the British Virgin Islands has any gender-recognition regime, any process for changing sex markers on local identity documents or on the British passport issued to territorial residents, any hate-crime provision covering gender identity, or any general anti-discrimination statute. The Equality Act 2010's non-extension is stated, but the absence of a local equivalent is not documented here and should not be asserted beyond what these sources support.

The only social-behavioural account offered, the GlobalGayz piece, is dated August 2012 with later circulation in 2017, describes the local population generically, and addresses sexual orientation rather than gender identity directly. Its characterisation of homophobia as "silent and invisible" cannot be dated to present conditions or extended to trans people.

AIA.name: Anguilla
AIA.summary:
Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory whose law is local law: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the island, and they can be applied there only by Order in Council.

Sex between men in private is legal, but the repeal was imposed from London rather than enacted by Anguilla's own legislature. On 5 January 2001 the Privy Council ordered decriminalisation of private consensual same-sex conduct in five Caribbean territories — Anguilla, the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands — acting unilaterally after the local legislatures refused to repeal their statutes, and religious leaders protested the decision. Anguilla had never carried the prohibition in exactly the same statutory form as those other territories. A first-person account published in June 2023 dates the change to 2000 rather than January 2001.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised under Anguilla law. A commercial destination-wedding service states that plainly while marketing the island's venues to same-sex couples, which means a ceremony performed there carries symbolic status only.

Public LGBT life on the island is close to invisible: no community organisations, no venues, no Pride, and only a handful of hotels marketed to gay travellers. Anguilla's roughly 15,000 residents and 35 square miles are given as reasons the scene stays small, and the muted, not 'out and proud' atmosphere is attributed to the imposed colonial legacy rather than to local choice. A queer family visiting in June 2023 described the trip as uneventful.
AIA.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not contain the text of the instrument by which decriminalisation took effect in Anguilla, so the precise statutory mechanism and its current wording are unresolved here.

Sources disagree on the date of the change: a 2023 travel account gives 2000, while the contemporaneous Associated Press report of the Privy Council order is dated 5 January 2001. Both are reported as sourced; the discrepancy is unresolved.

Whether the Equality Act 2010 or the 2025 single-sex-services code has ever been the subject of an Order in Council extending it to Anguilla is not sourced in this inventory and remains unresolved.

No sourced material in this inventory addresses gender recognition, identity-document marker rules, hate-crime or hate-speech protection, access to gender-affirming care, or screening procedures at entry that could disclose a visitor's trans status. These are not established either way by the available sources.

The claim that Anguilla never had the prohibition in the same statutory form as the other territories rests on a single 2012 country report and is not corroborated against primary legal text in this inventory.

MSR.name: Montserrat
MSR.summary:
Same-sex conduct is legal in Montserrat. In January 2001 the British government scrapped the anti-gay statutes applying to Montserrat and four other Caribbean territories, stating that the laws violated signed international human rights agreements. The reform reached the island as an Order in Council from London, overriding the objections of local politicians and religious leaders rather than following their consent.

A trans visitor should expect a very small, widely dispersed population with almost no visible public LGBT life. Reporting from 2012 describes the local social scene as decimated, capturing the mood with the observation that gay people 'are everywhere but hardly here'.

That scarcity has physical causes. Hurricane Hugo in 1989 and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption wastelanded the south of the 104 km2 island and displaced more than half the population northward, scattering an already thin community across a reduced habitable area.

The 2001 reform was met by religious leaders who called it totally unacceptable, and the territory's politics at the time read as a cultural rift with London. Nothing in the available sources documents organised opposition, community organising, or visible hostility since.

TCA.name: Turks and Caicos Islands
TCA.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the Turks and Caicos Islands. Local law governs the territory, and the United Kingdom measures reach it only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 2001, decriminalised through the United Kingdom-led Caribbean reform programme, and the constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.

The Court of Appeal ordered the Director of Immigration to issue a residence permit to Timothy Haymon as the same-sex spouse of Richard Sankar. Reading "spouse" in the Immigration Ordinance to include a same-sex spouse lawfully married in another jurisdiction, the court held that a refusal on sexual-orientation grounds contravened the equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees, while leaving the constitution's male-female marriage definition untouched and treating it as controlling. Residence recognition is therefore available to same-sex partners of residents and visitors.

United Kingdom HM Passport Office operational guidance, current as of 2025, states that transgender citizens are recognised in the Turks and Caicos Islands and covers nationality, legitimacy, adoption, gender recognition, civil partnerships and marriage, and documents for the territory. Gender-recognised travel documents for this jurisdiction are handled by the United Kingdom passport authority.

A resident account from May 2009 describes a social environment with no visible scene, where privacy is the norm and little information about gay life circulates publicly. About two-thirds of residents are not originally from the islands.
TCA.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory establishes a local gender-recognition statute or procedure for the Turks and Caicos Islands. Whether a territory-level mechanism exists for amending gender markers on local documents, as distinct from the United Kingdom passport, is unresolved here.

The constitutional non-discrimination guarantee was applied on sexual-orientation grounds in the residence case. Its application to gender identity, and any court ruling on that basis, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

Hate-crime provisions, facilities and restroom rules, healthcare access, and any screening practice that risks disclosing a visitor's trans status are not covered by the available sources.

The HM Passport Office statements on adoption, civil partnerships, marriage and gender recognition are operational guidance from the United Kingdom passport authority; the underlying local statutory provisions they rest on are not sourced in this inventory.

FLK.name: Falkland Islands
FLK.summary:
The Falkland Islands, a British Overseas Territory with its own Legislative Assembly, legislate locally. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1989 and the age of consent has been equal since 2005. Same-sex marriage and civil partnerships have been available since 29 April 2017; the bill passed the Legislative Assembly in March 2017 by 7 votes to 1, and the registrar general subsequently confirmed that it is law. Civil partnerships are open to opposite-sex couples as well as same-sex couples.

The Constitution Order 2008 bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation at Article 16. The provision covers sexual orientation only; the sources do not identify a gender-identity ground in the Constitution.

UK frameworks do not reach the Islands. The UK Equality Act 2010 and the Gender Recognition Act 2004 do not extend to the Falkland Islands, and the territory's own ordinances govern instead. These include the Crimes Ordinance 2014, which makes sexual-orientation hate-stirring an offence; the Crime and Public Order (Equality) Ordinance 2014, which provides sexual orientation as an aggravating factor in sentencing and recognises acquired gender under a UK Gender Recognition Certificate; and the Prisons Ordinance 2017.

The Crime and Public Order (Equality) Ordinance 2014 has permitted legal gender change since 2014. Gender recognition is not available on a self-identification basis, and no non-binary status is recognised.

The registrar general also confirmed that same-sex marriage is not legal in the South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands, a separate dependency for which the UK is responsible; the equality reform applies to the Falkland Islands themselves.
FLK.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources state that the Crimes Ordinance 2014 criminalises sexual-orientation hate-stirring but do not give the penalty ranges, the elements of the offence, or any reported prosecution. Enforcement of the constitutional non-discrimination guarantee and the sentencing aggravating factor is likewise unsourced here; whether either has been invoked in a decided case is unresolved.

No source in this inventory addresses facilities or bathroom access, healthcare provision for trans residents or visitors, immigration or security screening, name and gender markers on travel documents presented at entry, or documented incidents of violence against trans people. Those points should be treated as not sourced rather than as absent risk.

The exact commencement procedure for the 2017 marriage legislation is not detailed: the bill passed in March 2017 and marriage has been available from 29 April 2017, with the registrar general's reply confirming the law in June 2017. Whether gender recognition under the 2014 ordinance is available to persons who are not settled residents is not covered by the sources.

[1] Rob Salerno blog (22 Jun 2017): the Falklands registrar general confirmed by reply that the same-sex marriage and civil partnership bill passed in March is law, resolving the outstanding question of its assent; the same registrar confirmed that same-sex marriage is not legal in the South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands dependency.

SHN.name: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
SHN.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha; local law governs, and the United Kingdom measures can be applied only by Order in Council.

Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful in the territory since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across all three island groups. The 2009 constitutional order imposed by the United Kingdom bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation territory-wide, and those protections have been in force since 2009.

Same-sex marriage was legislated island by island. The Ascension Island Council approved the marriage ordinance on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0, it was signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016, and it commenced on 1 January 2017. Tristan da Cunha followed on 4 August 2017 and Saint Helena on 20 December 2017. Adoption by same-sex couples became lawful the same year.

The sources in this inventory are aggregator and index pages covering LGBT rights generally; none addresses gender recognition, identity documents, entry screening, or healthcare access for trans visitors.
SHN.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition, the rules for changing sex or gender markers on passports or local identity documents, or what a trans visitor's documents must show on arrival. Those points remain unresolved here.

Enforcement of the 2009 anti-discrimination protections, any hate-crime provisions, complaints outcomes and the experience of trans people in policing, healthcare or single-sex facilities are not sourced. Nothing is stated about whether screening at entry could disclose a traveller's trans status.

The source base consists of aggregator pages: an Alchetron page updated 25 April 2026, Wikiwand mirrors of Wikipedia articles, and a GayLawNet index last accessed 23 June 2013 that cites ILGA's State-sponsored Homophobia. The GayLawNet entry may lag current law, and the aggregator pages are not primary legal texts; the ordinances and the 2009 constitutional order themselves were not consulted for this record.

PCN.name: Pitcairn Islands
PCN.summary:
The Pitcairn Islands stand under the United Kingdom's framework: defence and external affairs are reserved to the United Kingdom, and United Kingdom domestic measures such as the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not apply here of their own force. Local law governs, and those measures could reach Pitcairn only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001.

The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and that guarantee has been in force since 2010.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, and it recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn.

Adoption has been available to same-sex couples since 2015 and is open to married, unmarried and single people alike.

GGY.name: Guernsey
GGY.summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically. Local law governs, and United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

On 10 December 2015 the States approved same-sex marriage by 37 votes to 7. Two alternatives were put and rejected as insufficient: a civil-partnership-only scheme, and a single secular status called Union Civile that would have applied to all couples alike. The enabling legislation was left to a separate bill, which commenced in 2018.

Family recognition moved earlier the same year. A review of the Adoption Law recorded at page 1170 of the States of Guernsey Billet d'État of 24 June 2015 ended a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples adopting. The States agreed that same-sex couples may adopt, that civil partnerships are recognised for that purpose, and that both partners hold equal parental responsibility.

No source establishes legal gender recognition or trans-specific protection in force in Guernsey.
GGY.outOfScopeNotes:
No source establishes a legal gender-recognition mechanism in Guernsey, and none establishes trans-specific anti-discrimination protection in force. Whether local equality law covers gender identity on the same footing as sexual orientation is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The material reviewed on Les Nicolles contains no rule for housing trans prisoners by birth sex or identified gender, no trans-specific unit, and no stated solitary or segregation practice for trans prisoners. Nothing on the prison-housing axis can be verified from it.

No Order in Council extending the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 to Guernsey appears in the sources reviewed, so the Act and its 2025 single-sex-services code are treated as not applying. Confirming the absence of such an order is a research task still outstanding.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity is legal in Guernsey for both men and women; it was criminalised until decriminalisation prior to 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the UK. The male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences in its criminal law, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private, which can expose men to prosecution for private-life conduct that is lawful elsewhere. Wikipedia country coverage: Transgender people have been able to legally change their gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. However, Guernsey law only allows a new birth certificate to be issued and does not amend or remove records from existing birth certificates, so prior gender markers remain on the original record. Guernsey is also the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted civil partnership legislation, though UK civil partnerships were recognised for succession purposes from 2 April 2012. Wikipedia country coverage: A 2004 law enabled the States of Guernsey to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 banned discrimination based on gender identity. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had specifically outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity existed in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the Guernsey lawmaking body passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously (33-0) explicitly including sexual orientation, rejecting all amendments proposing exemptions for small businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations; it takes effect from 1 October 2023.

IMN.name: Isle of Man
IMN.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the Isle of Man. Local law governs, with United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency whose parliament, Tynwald, frames these questions through its own bills. The Legislative Council's proceedings of 26 April 2016 record the Third Reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016 alongside consideration of the Equality Bill 2016, which is the primary legislative record of the island's marriage-equality debate.

Employment protection preceded that debate by a decade. On 30 November 2005 the House of Keys adopted an amendment to the Employment Bill, tabled by Onchan MHK Peter Karran, barring dismissal of gay and lesbian employees on sexual-orientation grounds and aligning the island's employment law with United Kingdom human-rights law.

Political commitment at the top of the Manx government followed. On 9 June 2015 Chief Minister Allan Bell publicly backed same-sex marriage and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition.

The Marriage and Civil Partnership Act received Royal Assent and same-sex marriage took effect on the island in July 2016. The first conversion of a civil partnership to a marriage was completed within days of entry into force. Civil partnerships have been legal on the island since 2011 and are convertible to marriage without a second ceremony, and the registration process has run as a routine administrative matter.
IMN.outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the Equality Bill 2016 beyond its appearance on the Legislative Council's agenda of 26 April 2016 is not sourced in this inventory, and its final provisions remain unresolved here.

No source in this inventory addresses prison housing for trans detainees. The island's only functioning prison, the Isle of Man Prison at Jurby, operates remand, convicted, female, young-offender, vulnerable-prisoner and segregation units, but no birth-sex-versus-identity placement rule, trans-specific unit, or trans-specific segregation practice is documented; the point is unresolved rather than established either way.

Entry and visa screening that could disclose gender history, gender-marker rules on Manx documents, hate-crime protection, criminalisation, access to gender-affirming care, and facilities law are not covered by the sources assembled here and should be verified independently.

GUF.name: French Guiana
GUF.summary:
French Guiana stands under France's national framework as an overseas department: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France.

Legal gender recognition has been available on a simplified administrative basis since 2017, by declaration, with no requirement of surgery, sterilisation or psychiatric diagnosis. Anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity has been in force since 2012, and hate-crime sentence enhancement provisions were added in 2017. Nothing in French law criminalises trans status or gender expression.

Same-sex relations and same-sex marriage are legal under French law. Pride events are held, the scene is small and anchored in Cayenne, and a travel guide rates the territory "Very Safe for LGBTQ+".

The sharpest documented state machinery is custodial. Trans women incarcerated in France on the basis of their legal gender occupy a legal gray area, and that practice reaches French Guiana as a jurisdiction applying French prison law. The CGLPL, France's national preventive mechanism, reported on 25 May 2021 that serious violations in the treatment of transgender persons persist across French places of deprivation of liberty; its findings apply to detention facilities here.

The friction a trans visitor meets is practical rather than legal. Specialised gender-affirming healthcare is thin, remoteness pushes residents into metropolitan France for care, and local reporting describes transphobia and cultural taboos that discourage visibility and reporting of incidents.
GUF.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents an incident involving a trans visitor to French Guiana; the assessment rests on the general French legal framework and on national detention findings.

Whether French Guiana's detention facilities have received a CGLPL visit, and what was found there specifically, is unresolved in these sources.

The account of prison placement practice for trans women dates from January 2018; whether that practice has since changed is unresolved.

Entry and visa screening with respect to gender markers on travel documents is not sourced here, and neither is the enforcement record of the 2017 hate-crime provisions in French Guiana.

One country guide in the inventory returned no usable finding on the safety of trans visitors.

GLP.name: Guadeloupe
GLP.summary:
Guadeloupe stands under France's national framework: French criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules on identity documents apply here as they do in the metropole. Same-sex marriage is available, gender-identity discrimination is prohibited, and legal gender recognition follows the simplified French procedure. No legal penalty attaches to trans existence.

Custodial settings are the documented risk area. A BuzzFeed News report of January 2018 found that in French prisons, whose rules govern detention in Guadeloupe, the placement of trans women follows the legal gender recorded on the incarceration papers, which may not correspond to the person's presentation; in practice, assignment is said to weigh the individual's best interests, with individual cells or placement in more welcoming wings used where possible. The national preventive mechanism, the CGLPL, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, reporting serious violations of fundamental rights across French detention facilities and drawing on some forty referrals received since 2010.

Support infrastructure has expanded. Guadeloupe's first dedicated LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, offering reception, support and guidance for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities; it was driven by a federation of Guadeloupean associations. During the opening, the minister responsible for family affairs and diversity, Aurore Bergé, announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted to overseas territories.

Community organisation is visible and growing. A September 2023 interview with organisers of Secret's Out described community members increasingly reconciling their lives with their orientation, with activism advancing after Martinique, alongside the work of Amalgame Humani's. In 2025, Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe. A 2023 local mapping of anti-LGBT violence exists, and organisers describe a gap between legal protection and lived experience.
GLP.outOfScopeNotes:
The gap organisers describe between legal protection and lived experience is asserted in interview material without quantified evidence; the 2023 mapping's findings are not published in the sources available here, so the scale of anti-trans violence in Guadeloupe remains unresolved.

Whether trans detainees in Guadeloupe's own correctional facilities have been placed according to the criteria described in the 2018 reporting, and whether the CGLPL's findings apply to local facilities specifically, is not sourced.

The measures announced by Aurore Bergé in April 2024 are described as commitments; their implementation status in Guadeloupe is not documented in the inventory.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa screening, customs questions about hormone medication, or healthcare access for trans visitors in Guadeloupe.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: France decriminalised same-sex relations in the Penal Code of 1791, retaining this in the 1810 Code, but LGBTQ people still faced legal harassment under public morality laws; some in Alsace and Lorraine were interned in Nazi camps (1940 annexation) and persecuted under Vichy despite no sodomy law. Vichy's 6 August 1942 article 334 (later 331) set age of consent at 21 for homosexual vs 15 for heterosexual relations, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982 under Mitterrand. A 1960 'Mirguet amendment' ordonnance doubled penalties for indecent exposure in homosexual activity (art. 330, 2nd alinea), repealed in 1980. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 before 1980; the Senate has yet to vote. A bill banning conversion therapy passed the Senate 7 December 2020 and was published 1 February 2022, with penalties of two years' imprisonment and/or €30,000. Wikipedia country coverage: On 31 December 2004 the National Assembly made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; civil liberties groups including Reporters Without Borders called this a serious infringement on free speech. The law of December 2004 created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual orientation or disability. An MP from the ruling UMP party, Christian Vanneste, became the first person convicted under the law in January 2006, though that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Pride has been held in Paris since 4 April 1981 (Place Maubert, ~10,000 people), reaching 500,000 participants in 2019, with events held in dozens of other cities. Wikipedia country coverage: Transgender people have been allowed to change legal gender without surgery or medical diagnosis since 1 January 2017 (law signed 18 November 2016), but they must still go before a court to change the gender marker; a first name change can be done at the registry office. Self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were both dropped from the final bill. Until 2015 France refused to recognise surrogate children as French citizens, leaving many in legal limbo; the Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born to a surrogate abroad can be adopted by the partner of the biological father, the Court of Appeal of Paris held in May 2019 that a Canadian birth certificate must be recognised, and in December 2019 the Court of Cassation ruled that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France. In 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be considered the mother of the child she conceived before her sex change; a 2017 legal bid for 'neutral sex' classification was rejected by the Court of Cassation. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2010 France became the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness (gender identity disorder removed by decree), yet French trans rights organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale. Gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems in gender-affirming healthcare provision: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent, self-determination model. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned the Little Mermaid Observatory — a group opposed to all gender transition for minors — to report on youth gender care, which called transition a 'health scandal' and transness a 'social contagion'; a bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 (opposed by the Macron government, no update since 23 July 2024), while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. Blood donation deferrals for gay and bi men were cut to four months in April 2020 and abolished entirely on 16 March 2022. Wikipedia country coverage: The French Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'a primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access, though this did not change actual practice. In October 2018 President Macron denounced homophobic violence as 'unworthy of France' after a rise in attacks, and a report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims (about 1,380 in 2018). In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, France's interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of The Little Mermaid Observatory; one member resigned and the president stepped away. LGBTQ people in Mayotte face frequent family rejection, harassment and discrimination, and in 2006 Lifou Island proposed a 'family code' banning homosexuality with eviction or lynching as punishment (not approved). Wikipedia country coverage: In March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos announced a policy fighting all forms of discrimination including homophobia in schools as one of 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' to tackle anti-LGBTQ bullying, providing reporting services, a helpline for students and staff, and requiring all French schools to give guidance on LGBTQ issues, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms; in February 2019 the use of 'parent 1' and 'parent 2' on school enrolment forms caused widespread conservative outrage. Legislation to ban medical transition for under-18s passed the Senate in May 2024, prompting large-scale protests, making trans minors a direct legislative target.

MTQ.name: Martinique
MTQ.summary:
Martinique stands under France's national framework. Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department in full, so identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime operate here as in the metropole. Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1815, the 2013 marriage-equality law applies, and gender-marker change is available through the simplified judicial route introduced by the state's 2016-17 reforms.

Discrimination protection rests on several instruments that reach the island directly. Goods and services have been covered since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2), employment since Labour Code article L1132-1 in 2008, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, where the wording 'sexual identity' was replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. Nothing in the criminal law criminalises being trans.

Detention is the sharp exception. Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code requires that detainees be placed in facilities matching the gender marker on their identity documents, so placement follows the marker rather than anatomy. In practice most trans women are therefore held in all-male facilities, where other detainees threaten them; a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records detainees telling trans women 'we don't want any women here'. The French prison framework governs Martinique's establishments as French law, and this pattern of placement and threat reaches them.

The CGLPL, France's detention-places watchdog, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty. The finding rests on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on inspections at which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed, and it makes recommendations on placement, isolation, safety and staff training. Because the opinion addresses French establishments as a category, its findings bind the department's prisons too.

Community infrastructure on the island is real but small. JM Concept 972 is a Martinique lesbian, gay, bi and trans network providing information, meetings and services, and running private parties and garden parties supported by gay-friendly heterosexual supporters, with dated events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September 2025.

Unresolved: the sources give no inspection or incident data specific to Martinique's own prisons. The CGLPL opinion is national in scope and the sites it names for interviews are metropolitan, so its application to the island's establishments follows from their status as French places of deprivation of liberty rather than from a documented local inspection.

Unresolved: no source in the inventory records enforcement outcomes for gender-identity discrimination claims brought on the island, nor local court decisions on gender-marker change here.

Unresolved: the inventory does not state whether the CGLPL's recommendations on placement, isolation, safety and staff training have been implemented in Martinique's facilities.

Goods and services have been covered since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2), employment since Labour Code article L1132-1 in 2008, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, where the wording 'sexual identity' was replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. Nothing in the criminal law criminalises being trans.

Detention is the sharp exception. Article D248 of the national criminal procedure code requires that detainees be placed in facilities matching the gender marker on their identity documents, so placement follows the marker rather than anatomy. In practice most trans women are therefore held in all-male facilities, where other detainees threaten them; a national news feature of 12 January 2018 records detainees telling trans women 'we don't want any women here'. The national prison framework governs the state/province establishments as national law, and this pattern of placement and threat reaches them.

The national detention-places watchdog issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across all national places of deprivation of liberty. The finding rests on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on inspections at which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed, and it makes recommendations on placement, isolation, safety and staff training. Because the opinion addresses national establishments as a category, its findings bind the state/province prisons too.

Community infrastructure on the ground is real but small. a local lesbian, gay, bi and trans network provides information, meetings and services, and runs private parties and garden parties supported by gay-friendly heterosexual supporters, with dated events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September 2025.
