REU.name: Réunion
REU.summary:
Réunion is a department of France and stands under French national law without local variation: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France proper.

Same-sex marriage reached Réunion with the metropolitan statute adopted in 2013, following the bill announced by Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault in October 2012 for passage through the National Assembly and the Senate.

Discrimination on the ground of 'identité sexuelle' has been prosecutable in France since the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 in July 2012, which made transphobic harassment a criminal matter. The provision is in force in Réunion.

Legal gender change rests on the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282, adopted by the National Assembly on 19 May 2016 after being tabled by roughly forty Socialist deputies. Three government sub-amendments tabled alongside it could narrow its scope, and the sources do not establish the final wording.

Detention is the sharpest documented exposure. Under article D248 of the criminal procedure code, prisoners are placed according to the sex recorded on their identity documents, which leaves transgender women held in male prisons in a legal grey area. BuzzFeed News reported on 12 January 2018 that such women are punished for considerably more than their alleged crimes, following cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid threats from other inmates.

The French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL) issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding the persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities. Its findings rest on referrals received since 2010 covering some forty transgender people, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site and documentary inspections, and it issued recommendations to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. The opinion addresses the national custody framework that covers Réunion.

No local violence series, enforcement pattern or institutional hostility programme appears in the sources, and equally no documented local support infrastructure; a small, discreet community should be assumed but is not evidenced.

MYT.name: Mayotte
MYT.summary:
Mayotte stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as in France proper.

No law criminalises being trans or being in a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage has been available on the island since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975, and the National Assembly's vote simplifying legal gender change for trans people extends to the department.

Placement in custody follows the gender marker carried on the identity document under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Trans women are therefore typically held in all-male facilities, where other detainees threaten them; anatomy does not determine where a person is placed.

The national detention-places watchdog CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty. Its opinion rests on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people, and on inspections at which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. Those findings bind Mayotte's establishments as French establishments.

Formal rights and lived experience diverge. A 2023 account of Bruno Agar, a teacher at the university centre of Mayotte, and his Malagasy partner describes a long and complicated path before the two married at Sada Town Hall, on a predominantly Muslim island where same-sex marriage remains a rarity in Africa and the Islamic world.

Legal representation on the island is thin. A gay-friendly lawyer directory returns no referenced practitioner for Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi, Sada and other towns, while Maître Isabelle Zribi, a lawyer at the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation based in Paris, is listed as available to take instructions.
MYT.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports a trans person detained in Mayotte, the facility used, or any incident involving one; the prison material describes the French framework and metropolitan inspections, and its application to local establishments is an extension of law rather than a documented local case.

Whether the CGLPL's 2021 findings have been acted on in Mayotte, and whether any complaint by a trans detainee here has produced a remedy, is unresolved and not sourced.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare on the island, and whether the simplified gender-change procedure has in fact been completed by any resident, are not sourced.

The enforcement of the gender-identity anti-discrimination provisions locally, including any recorded complaint or hate-crime incident with an outcome, is not sourced.

The lawyer directory's coverage is self-described as incomplete, so the absence of a listed practitioner should be read as an absence of reference rather than a finding that none exists.

NCL.name: New Caledonia
NCL.summary:
New Caledonia is a French collectivity in which France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents and the justice system, while the territory legislates locally on many domestic matters. The result is a mixed record: the protections that visitors would rely on are national French provisions that apply here, and no source in this inventory records any local ordinance narrowing them.

Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's 2013 marriage-equality statute, which applies as French law; France's first wedding under that statute was reported on 29 May 2013, and the bill had been announced for introduction in Parliament in October 2012 as a campaign commitment. Nothing in the inventory criminalises trans people or same-sex relations.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual identity became prosecutable under the French Penal Code through the 2012 sexual-harassment legislation, and that provision was reworded to read gender identity in 2016. As a penal provision it extends to New Caledonia, so discriminatory conduct and transphobic motivation can be pursued as discrimination rather than as a distinct offence.

Detention is the sharpest documented risk. Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code places prisoners according to their legal gender marker, so trans women are ordinarily held in all-male facilities where assault by other detainees is reported, placement following the identity document rather than anatomy. The French detention-places watchdog CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on-site inspections at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. The French prison framework governs establishments in this collectivity, so the placement rule and the recorded pattern of violations apply here.

The overall assessment is therefore one of formal protection under an inherited national framework combined with a documented, unresolved vulnerability in custody. This record is evidence-thin on local conditions: it establishes what the law says and what the national machinery has found, and does not establish how those provisions are experienced on the ground in a small, close-knit society.

PYF.name: French Polynesia
PYF.summary:
French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France, and French law governs it in matters of justice and civil status. Trans visitors therefore enter a legal regime in which gender recognition, detention policy and the rights framework are set by Paris, while much of daily life is regulated by the territorial institutions in Papeete.

France's national treatment of trans detainees reaches French Polynesia. Detention follows the gender marked on an identity document, and Article D248 of the French Code of criminal procedure requires separate men's and women's establishments; a trans woman holding a male marker is consequently held with men. BuzzFeed News, reporting on the situation in France in January 2018, treated this as a legal grey area rather than a settled outcome.

The national preventive-mechanism for places of deprivation of liberty, the CGLPL, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding that France's Law 2016-1547 removed the requirement for medical transition or surgery when changing the gender on civil status, but that no norms were ever added governing how detainees should be housed in line with that change. Serious violations were documented across French detention, and the CGLPL's framework applies to French Polynesia's prisons. A trans visitor who is detained in the territory is therefore exposed to housing arrangements that national regulators themselves have found incompatible with the country's own gender-recognition law.

Gender-diverse healthcare in French Polynesia is limited by the small number of specialists available locally. Some trans residents, including rae-rae, face rejection from their families and leave for mainland France to obtain specialised services that the territory cannot provide. The gap between the law on paper and the care actually reachable in the archipelago is the most concrete material constraint for a trans person staying any length of time.

A reform effort to narrow that gap failed. Under Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua, the territorial government tabled a social-security bill that would have fully reimbursed hormonal treatment with progesterone and testosterone, matching mainland France. After heated debate in the Territorial Assembly the bill did not obtain sufficient support and lapsed.

The cultural setting is unusually documented. The mahu role, a traditional Polynesian recognition of gender diversity in which individuals embody both male and female qualities and hold recognised standing, predates colonisation, and mahu and rae-rae are visible across the islands in daily life. The territory hosted its first international LGBTQIA+ rights colloquium in 2023, bringing territorial government and church representatives together with the University of French Polynesia. Reporting from OutTraveler in July 2025 described this openness as ingrained in the culture rather than secured by law, noting that a visiting gay couple checked online whether the destination was safe before travelling and found mainstream inclusivity and acceptance operating without pride flags or organised protest. The 118-island territory has no Pride movement to speak of, which visitors read either as reassurance or as evidence that visibility is tolerated rather than defended.
PYF.outOfScopeNotes:
It is unresolved whether Article D248 and the gender-marker detention rule described in the 2018 BuzzFeed News report have been revised since that reporting; the inventory sources the position as it stood then and through the CGLPL's 2021 opinion, and does not document a later change.

The inventory does not state whether French Polynesia has any territory-specific anti-discrimination statute of its own, nor how the national protections are actually invoked in the territory. Travel-writer accounts of mainstream inclusivity are single-perspective and describe visitor experience rather than measured incidence; the absence of reported incidents in the sources is not evidence that none occur.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: All sodomy laws were repealed in 1791 with the Penal Code of the French Revolution, which made no mention of same-sex relations in private; this policy was retained in the Penal Code of 1810. However, an indecent-exposure clause (article 330, 2nd alinea) inserted into the Penal Code in 1960 doubled the penalty for indecent exposure carried out as homosexual activity, following the 'Mirguet amendment' which designated homosexuality a national scourge; it was repealed in 1980. Separately, a Vichy-era law of 6 August 1942 set the age of consent at 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual ones (lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 in 1982). LGBTQ people from Alsace and Lorraine were persecuted and interned in Nazi concentration camps after 1940, and the Vichy regime persecuted LGBTQ people despite no law criminalising homosexuality. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 before 1980; the Senate has yet to vote. Wikipedia country coverage: On 31 December 2004 the National Assembly amended anti-discrimination legislation to make homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment. Civil-liberty groups including Reporters Without Borders criticised this as a serious infringement of free speech, while the conservative Chirac government justified it by pointing to rising anti-gay violence. The same 2004 law amended the 1881 Law on Freedom of the Press to cover offences including injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence, and discrimination based on gender, sexual orientation or disability. Christian Vanneste of the UMP became the first person convicted under the law in January 2006, though that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Wikipedia country coverage: When a physical assault or murder is motivated by the sexual orientation of the victim, the law increases the penalties that would normally be applied. In 2017, transphobia became a cause of aggravation for all crimes punishable by prison. In October 2018, after a series of homophobic attacks, President Emmanuel Macron denounced the violence as 'unworthy of France' and promised 'concrete measures' without specifying their content. A report released on 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims of transphobic and homophobic attacks compared with roughly 1,380 in 2018. Conversion therapy, described by a French survivor as 'psychological rape', is believed to remain in practice to an unknown extent; Le Refuge estimated 3–4% of its helpline calls concerned the issue, and the ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and took effect on 1 February 2022. Overseas, Mayotte reports frequent family rejections, harassment and discrimination, and in 2014 only about 20% of overseas residents viewed homosexuality as a sexuality like any other, against 77% in metropolitan France. Wikipedia country coverage: National legislation enacted in 1985 prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, housing and other public and private provision of services and goods. In July 2012 Parliament added 'sexual identity' as a protected ground, a phrase criticised by ILGA-Europe because of its ambiguity, though still described by them as an important step; on 18 November 2016 a new law replaced 'sexual identity' with 'gender identity' in article 225-1 of the Penal Code. The Labour Code now bars exclusion from recruitment, internships, training or any disciplinary or discriminatory measure, direct or indirect, on account of sexual orientation or gender identity among many other grounds. The December 2004 law also created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité (High Authority against Discrimination and for Equality). Wikipedia country coverage: The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access to such treatments, though this change to guidelines has not altered actual practice. In March 2024, senators from the centre-right Republican Party commissioned The Little Mermaid Observatory — described as a group opposed to all forms of gender transition for minors — to produce a report on youth gender-affirming care, which called gender-affirming care a 'health scandal' and youth transness a 'social contagion' before being disputed by doctors and advocates. A 2022 DILCRAH controversy revealed that the president of the scientific committee of the government's interministerial delegation against anti-LGBT hatred was a member of The Little Mermaid Observatory, which had called gender-affirming healthcare 'mutilation'; one committee member resigned. Opposition votes were recorded in the National Assembly against same-sex marriage in 2011 and 2013, and conservative outrage followed the 2019 use of 'parent 1' and 'parent 2' on French school enrolment forms. Wikipedia country coverage: Civil solidarity pacts (PACS), registered domestic partnerships enacted in 1999, afford most of the legal protections of marriage but deny PACS partners the right to adoption and artificial insemination, which remain largely restricted to married couples; joint tax returns for PACS couples were only allowed after three years, changed in 2005. France became the thirteenth country to legalise same-sex marriage in 2013: the bill passed the National Assembly 329–229 on 12 February 2013, the Senate approved it on 12 April, the Constitutional Council upheld it on 17 May, President Hollande signed it on 18 May, and the first ceremony took place on 29 May in Montpellier. Same-sex couples have been able to adopt since May 2013, but implementation has been limited: only four same-sex couples had jointly adopted by April 2018 and 10 same-sex adoptions occurred in Paris between May 2013 and May 2019. Assisted reproduction was extended to lesbian couples and single women in legislation that took effect in September 2021, with the state covering the cost for women under 43 and children able to learn the donor's identity at 18. On surrogacy abroad, the Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born via surrogate can be adopted by the partner of the biological father, and in December 2019 ruled that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth-specific findings in the source: In 2019, the Ministry of Education launched the Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign against anti-LGBTQ bullying, which helps students report bullying, established a helpline for students and staff, and requires all French schools to provide guidance about LGBTQ issues, with 17 May (International Day Against Homophobia) set as a sensitisation day. In March 2008, Education Minister Xavier Darcos had announced a national priority fighting discrimination including homophobia in schools, and the high school student union FIDL has run anti-homophobia campaigns among young people. In February 2019 it was reported that French schools use 'parent 1' and 'parent 2' rather than 'mother' and 'father' on enrolment forms, provoking conservative outrage. In March 2019, Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced that all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms. Politically, a bill to ban medical transition under the age of 18 was introduced after The Little Mermaid Observatory report of March 2024 called youth transness a 'social contagion'; it passed the Senate in May 2024 but is unlikely to be passed by the National Assembly, is opposed by the Macron government, and has had no update since 23 July 2024. In late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology released the country's first guidelines for medical care of trans youth, recommending puberty blockers for patients who have reached at least Tanner stage 2 alongside calcium and vitamin D supplements. Historically, the discriminatory age of consent for homosexual relations stood at 21 versus 15 for heterosexual relations from 1942 until its equalisation at 15 in 1982.

WLF.name: Wallis and Futuna
WLF.summary:
Wallis and Futuna is a territorial collectivity of the French Republic and stands under the French national framework: the civil and criminal codes of France apply locally unless a local measure overrides them. No law in force criminalises trans people or same-sex relations, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity has been prohibited since the 2012 statutory extension covering employment, housing and access to services.

Legal gender-marker change is available on the basis of the 2016-17 French reforms, which removed the requirement for surgery or a psychiatric diagnosis. A trans visitor whose documents already reflect their lived gender can therefore present them without undergoing a separate local procedure. Non-binary recognition does not exist in French law, so a third-gender or X marker cannot be obtained. Nothing in the sources indicates trans-specific screening or questioning at the border; entry follows ordinary French procedure.

Practical exposure is shaped less by statute than by scale and social convention. The territory's roughly eleven thousand residents live in village settings where Catholic and Polynesian norms govern visibility and where anonymity is close to zero. A traditional third-gender role, fakafafine, is present in the community, but it coexists with stigma and concealment rather than open acceptance. There are no resident gender specialists, and residents travel outside the territory for any transition-related care; a visitor should assume no local capacity for routine or emergency gender-related healthcare.

No hostile state action toward trans visitors is documented. The one state-level adverse mechanism in evidence is the detention framework inherited from France. BuzzFeed News reported in January 2018 that trans women whose legal gender is marked male, largely those without sex-reassignment surgery, are held in all-male establishments in a documented legal grey area, citing the case of a trans woman transferred to a men's facility in Lille in 2014. The French national preventive mechanism, the CGLPL, concluded in its opinion of 25 May 2021 that serious violations of the fundamental rights of transgender persons persist in places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on referrals concerning around forty transgender detainees since 2010 and on interviews with associations and experts; that opinion extended its earlier opinion of 30 June 2010 on trans prisoners. As a French collectivity, Wallis and Futuna stands under that detention framework.
WLF.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the French prison placement practice described in 2018 reporting has occurred in Wallis and Futuna's own detention facilities is unresolved; the sources document the national framework but give no local case.

No local measure overriding French law on gender markers, and no customary or council decision restricting trans people's use of public facilities, is recorded in the inventory. Their absence here reflects the absence of sourcing, not a finding that none exists.

Statistics on violence against trans people, hate-crime reporting, or police handling of such incidents in the territory are not sourced. The assessment of exposure rests on demographic and social conditions rather than incident data.

Border and visa screening practice with respect to trans travellers is not described in any source; the statement that no trans-specific screening is indicated is an absence of evidence rather than a documented policy.

The scope of the CGLPL's mandate over the territory's own places of deprivation of liberty, and whether its 2021 opinion was applied locally, are not established by the inventory.

National law supplies anti-discrimination coverage and an administrative route to gender-marker change, while the country isolation, small population and dominant religious and customary norms leave healthcare and social acceptance as the binding constraints.

Reporting on national prisons and the preventive mechanism's 2021 opinion describe the same problem across a decade: the placement of trans detainees, particularly trans women recorded as male, remains unresolved in practice despite formal legal recognition of gender. The 2018 press account and the 2021 oversight opinion are consistent with each other rather than contradictory, and the 2014 transfer shows the issue arising in the parent nation's principal localities, not only in outlying state/province.

The presence of a customary third-gender role distinguishes the country from jurisdictions where gender diversity is purely a legal question, but the sources treat that role as coexisting with concealment rather than conferring protection. Comparison with mainland practice is limited by the absence of any local enforcement data.

BLM.name: Saint Barthélemy
BLM.summary:
Saint Barthélemy stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France proper.

No provision of that framework restricts a trans or same-sex visitor. Same-sex marriage has been available since 2013, the statute covering discrimination on grounds of gender identity is in force, legal gender-marker change requires neither surgery nor sterilisation, and the French ban on conversion practices adopted in 2023 applies. Gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery have been available under French law since 1975.

Two limits sit alongside that coverage. Non-binary identity is not recognised in French law, so a visitor whose documents record a non-binary status has no legal counterpart on arrival. Gender-affirming care is provided on a small island with very limited specialist capacity, which affects continuity of treatment rather than its legality.

Detention is the clearest downside risk. Saint Barthélemy falls within the French prison administration, where policy recognises only biological sex for placement. Reporting by the controller-general of detention places finds that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women assigned to men's facilities under birth-sex placement, suffer the most serious harm in the system; a 2011 case in Nantes sent a trans woman to a men's prison. The controller-general's opinion of 25 May 2021, drawing on some 40 referrals since 2010, concluded that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of deprivation of liberty. A trans visitor detained here would enter that same placement regime.

Visitor-facing accounts describe a discreet luxury culture rather than an organised scene. Guides report full legal equality on roughly 8 square miles with about 10,000 residents, a yacht-based economy long accustomed to gay couples, and same-sex couples drawing no attention; a luxury operator records no LGBTQ venues and no Pride-specific events, but also no hostility, with staff trained for diverse guests. An aggregate rights assessment scores the territory 7.7 out of 10, with nine positive indicators and one red flag covering limited healthcare access, and notes that no government issues LGBT+ travel advice for Saint Barthélemy while the UK Foreign Office shows no warnings.
BLM.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the controller-general of detention places conducts inspections of the detention facilities situated in Saint Barthélemy specifically is not sourced here; the 2021 opinion addresses France's places of deprivation of liberty generally.

The precise local availability of gender-affirming care, as distinct from its legality under French law, is unresolved: the sources establish limited specialist capacity on the island but do not set out which services are delivered locally and which require travel.

No government travel advice specific to LGBT+ visitors to Saint Barthélemy could be located, and no trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted for the territory, so the practical guidance rests on commercial guides and one aggregate rights rating.

Non-binary recognition is stated as absent under French law, but no source addresses how French consular or border staff handle documents issued by other states recording a non-binary or third gender marker.

ABW.name: Aruba
ABW.summary:
Aruba stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

On 8 September 2016 the Staten of Aruba passed a civil-code amendment opening registered unions to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5, with four abstentions. The amendment extends the marriage articles of the civil code to those registered unions and grants spousal pension succession and emergency medical decision-making rights. Aruba's own news service reported the vote as making the island the first in the Caribbean to act.

Marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognised throughout the Kingdom, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route. The Associated Press reported that religious and cultural opposition to the measure was strong, and that neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed such unions at the time.

GlobalGayz records that the Aruban government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until it was challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands.
ABW.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no material on legal gender recognition in Aruba, on changing gender markers on Aruban identity documents or passports, or on whether Netherlands procedures for gender-marker change extend to Aruba. This is unresolved and not sourced here.

No sourced information was available on entry or visa screening that could disclose a visitor's trans status, on hate-crime or hate-speech provisions covering gender identity, on access to gender-affirming healthcare, or on facilities and restroom rules. These remain not sourced rather than absent.

The safety claims on the tourism board page are self-description by the destination's marketer and are not independent verification of conditions on the ground. GlobalGayz is a cultural report rather than a legal source, and its statements on adoption and on the earlier government declaration were not corroborated against primary legal texts in this inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D3, D4, D5, D6, D7, D8.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity is legal in Aruba, for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16 and equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. The Aruba Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, is the governing penal framework cited. The source text does not address criminalisation on grounds of gender identity or gender expression. Wikipedia country coverage: The source describes a visible but discreet LGBTQ scene: several specific gay bars and clubs have opened in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as 'LGBT-friendly'. Local LGBT group Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba is quoted: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.' Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba. Harassment has nonetheless occurred: Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge (2004–2007). Wikipedia country coverage: The Aruba Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on various grounds, including 'heterosexual or homosexual orientation'. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as 'any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference, which has the purpose or effect of impacting or affecting recognition, enjoyment or the exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life.' Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year imprisonment. On 12 July 2024 the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation, in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba. The enumerated grounds cited cover sexual orientation only; gender identity is not mentioned. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition to LGBT rights. CUW.name: Curaçao
CUW.summary:
Curaçao stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here. It is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, holding full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

In April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed that LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights without delay, and a package of rights requests was delivered to ministers in The Hague. Curaçao's commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly endorsed equal rights for everyone.

That endorsement ran against organised opposition from within her own party. Winifred Raveneau's fierce resistance had already forced Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel after a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement, and parliamentary opposition to equal-rights measures continued even as the island's own government publicly backed the community.

Community infrastructure exists but is small. An LGBT centre, the Pink House, opened in Curaçao in 2010, and reporting from GlobalGayz (updated January 2017) treats Curaçao, Aruba and Bonaire as quietly gay-friendly places within the Kingdom while crediting Curaçao, with Sint Maarten and Aruba, as a driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites an IGLTA award naming the island the most gay-welcoming in the region.

For a trans visitor the composite reads as low legal risk with thin trans-specific infrastructure: no documented state hostility toward trans people, an active but negotiating community, and no sourced local gender-recognition pathway or trans-specific care capacity.
CUW.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses a gender-recognition pathway for trans people in Curaçao: whether a legal procedure exists, what it requires, or which authority decides is unresolved here.

Entry, visa and border-screening practices that could expose a visitor's trans status are not sourced, nor are document or marker rules for passports and identity papers issued in Curaçao or by the Netherlands.

Hate-crime or hate-speech protection covering gender identity, and any enforcement record under it, is not sourced. Nor is trans-specific healthcare capacity, its availability to visitors, or any exclusion of trans-related care.

Whether the Pride permit friction documented in 2013 recurred after that year, and whether the 2015 Kingdom equal-rights agreement has been implemented in Curaçao legislation, both remain unresolved on this inventory.

No sub-national variation within Curaçao is sourced; the island is treated as a single unit throughout.

BES.name: Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba)
BES.summary:
Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba) consists of three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Dutch national law governs civil status, marriage and anti-discrimination, and the same statutory framework that applies in the European Netherlands operates on the islands.

Same-sex unions have been registrable in the islands since 2012. On 4 December 2012 the Census Office in Saba registered the first such union in the Caribbean Netherlands, between Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez, an Aruban national aged 26, and Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto, a Venezuelan national aged 27. Both were visiting residents rather than local inhabitants, establishing that the registry performs civil ceremonies for persons without island residency.

Practical arrangements for a civil ceremony are documented on Saba. Saba Tourism identifies the Court Room in the Administrative Building as the most straightforward venue for an efficient civil ceremony, and records registrar Julieta Woods as flexible in accommodating couples' requests. The island maintains a functioning destination-wedding infrastructure, including caterers, florists and accommodation providers.

FRO.name: Faroe Islands
FRO.summary:
Faroe Islands stands under Denmark's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

The Faroe Islands are a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Domestic equality and family law are set locally, beneath a Danish human-rights framework. Same-sex marriage arrived only in 2017, late for the Nordics, after friction between church and state.

In 2006 LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures in a population of about 47,000, demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics. The territory had neither at that date. Surveys of the period found violence and discrimination against openly gay people not uncommon and legally unaddressed.

Religiously motivated opposition sits openly in Faroese politics. On 7 September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic prime minister Johanna Sigurdardóttir and her partner, citing his religion. The refusal concerned the presence of an openly gay head of government at an official table.

Opposition to public visibility continued. In July 2015, when av Rana demanded that Pride be banned from its position two days before the national holiday, singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him. His party remains formally opposed to homosexuality.

For a trans visitor the recorded hostility is political and rhetorical rather than physical. The named targets are openly gay public figures and a Pride event, and the actions on record are a refusal to sit at a banquet and a call for a ban. Violence risk appears low on the sourced material.

Population figures differ between sources, about 47,000 in the 2006 account and about 50,000 in later accounts.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when it was legalized across the Kingdom of Denmark; the age of consent was then set at 18 for male same-sex relations, and the Faroe Islands did not follow Denmark's 1977 move to a gender-neutral age of 15 until 1988. The only criminal penalties touching LGBTQ people in the text are under the anti-discrimination law: anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation is liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. That provision took effect on 1 January 2007, making the Faroe Islands the last Northern European country to ban discrimination and harassment based on sexual orientation. Wikipedia country coverage: Expression has been a recurring flashpoint: the first gay pride march in 2005 provoked much controversy, and in June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter to the editor, 'Hvar eru vit á veg?', attacking national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture', asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'. Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters and suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the centre. Public petitioning also figures: a petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures, while an internet petition after the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen collected 20,000 signatures and eight women in Tórshavn gathered a further 2,000 by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2006 openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out, and he and his family then received threatening telephone calls; police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, became mentally ill and died by suicide in 2012. In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn — nowhere else had the group been attacked. The 2007 law criminalises public threats, insults or degrading statements against LGBT people with a fine or up to two years' imprisonment.

GRL.name: Greenland
GRL.summary:
Greenland stands under Denmark's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here. It is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts for domestic law, while criminal law and official document rules remain Danish.

Same-sex relations are lawful, and the territory's record on partnership and marriage has been permissive for three decades. Partnership law was adopted from the Danish model in 1996 and passed with virtually no debate, and it has since been replaced by the marriage law.

Same-sex marriage came into effect in April 2016. Greenland adopted Danish legislation that had passed unanimously twice in Denmark, the first bill lapsing after Danish elections, and the local parliament enacted it without recorded opposition; it replaced the 1996 partnership law. The bishop of the established church supported it.

From 2016 Greenland has used a self-declaration approach to gender recognition, an approach adopted ahead of Denmark's own practice.

The social picture for a visitor is low-friction. Gay life is described as "almost a non-event": low-key, integrated and non-violent, with a modest Pride march since 2010. Organising is present but small in scale, and there is no record in this inventory of organised hostility toward LGBT people.

In August 2014 a new national association, LGBT Qaamaneq, was founded for lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people, pursuing political, cultural and social equality and open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters as well as to its members.

The practical counterweight is capacity rather than hostility. Some 56,000 people live across remote settlements, and specialist services are limited. A trans visitor is unlikely to meet legal obstruction and is more likely to meet limited provision, limited staff, and long distances to the next service point.
GRL.outOfScopeNotes:
Gender recognition procedure is only described in this record at the level of principle. The inventory does not document the administrative steps, the authority handling applications, name and marker change rules, or any medical or psychological prerequisites. That description remains unresolved by the sources here.

Nothing in the inventory addresses whether Danish hate-crime or hate-speech provisions extend to Greenland, or whether any local instrument protects gender identity from hostile acts. The non-violence characterisation rests on a 2015 cultural and travel account rather than an official or academic assessment.

No source covers entry, visa or border-screening practice for trans travellers, document-check experience, or the treatment of gender markers at ports of entry.

Facilities, prison placement, gendered accommodation and access to gender-affirming healthcare are not addressed. The only scale information available is the population of roughly 56,000 across remote settlements, which implies thin services but does not establish what those services are.

The single source on LGBT Qaamaneq dates from 2014. Its current activity, membership, funding and remit are not sourced here.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Since 2010 Greenland has outlawed hate speech, with Article 100 of the Criminal Code prohibiting speech that may deprive, threaten or demean people on the basis of sexual orientation among other categories, alongside penalty enhancements for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation. Public expression is also visible in the first pride parade held in Nuuk on 15 May 2010, attended by about 1,000 people. The source notes there is virtually no gay scene due to the small, scattered population, though some nightclubs and bars in Nuuk draw a mixed gay and straight crowd. Wikipedia country coverage: Transgender Greenlanders may change the sex designation on official identity documents; a law passed in 2016 by decree allows legal sex changes based on self-determination, with no requirement for sex reassignment surgery, hormone therapy, sterilization or a medical diagnosis. Applicants must be over 18 and state that they want to change their documentation, then observe a six-month reflection period to confirm the request. Greenlandic passports are available with an "X" sex descriptor in addition to male and female. Same-sex couples' relationship status changed on paper too: registered partnerships (nalunaarsukkamik inooqatigiinneq) ran from 1 July 1996 until application of that law was repealed the day the same-sex marriage law took effect on 1 April 2016. Wikipedia country coverage: Greenland's parliament passed a Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination in May 2024, taking effect on 1 July 2024, prohibiting all discrimination on the basis of "sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, [and] gender characteristics" among other characteristics. The law creates an Equal Treatment Board to manage discrimination complaints and an Equality Council to promote non-discrimination. Separately, since 2010 hate speech has been outlawed with penalty enhancements for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation under Article 100 of the Criminal Code. The state-funded Human Rights Council of Greenland works closely with the Danish Institute for Human Rights to promote and protect human rights.

PRI.name: Puerto Rico
PRI.summary:
Puerto Rico is a US territory, and the full United States federal framework applies on the island: statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, screening, federally funded care and federal custody. The territory's own legislation does not soften that framework; in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and the January 2025 executive order eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents presents a marker that may not match their appearance at inspection. Entry scrutiny is tightened further for one category of traveller: in February 2025 the United States State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Airport screening follows federal Transportation Security Administration procedure at Puerto Rico's airports. All luggage is screened and may be hand-searched; prosthetics including breast forms are treated as medically necessary items and are not subject to the three-liquid rule, and medical equipment is admitted through the checkpoint after screening. The National Center for Transgender Equality's guidance advises packing strategies that reduce the frequency of invasive searches, and a visitor should expect screening to be conducted on those terms.

Care access during a visit cannot be assumed. The January 2025 order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in Puerto Rico, and the territory's own statute compounds it: in July 2025 the governor signed a ban on trans youth care that reporting describes as the most severe such restriction in any US jurisdiction.

The 2025 law was pushed through non-public hearings and is deliberately vague, so clinicians and affirming parents who facilitate hormone therapy or top surgery risk prosecution. It mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the "risks" of trans-affirming care. The Health Secretary, Carlos Mellado...

sources.title: Executive Order 14168 ("Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government") - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Executive Order 14168 (signed 20 January 2025) directs US federal agencies, including the Bureau of Prisons, to recognize only two sexes, and federal practice has followed by placing transgender inmates in facilities congruent with their sex assigned at birth rather than their asserted gender identity. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order violates the Prison Rape Elimination Act's requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided on an individual safety assessment. Federal custody rules apply in Puerto Rico as a US territory; the search found no separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit, or ruling.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Puerto Rico's sodomy ban was upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002, but after the U.S. Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 struck down all state and territorial sodomy statutes for consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute. A separate criminalisation front emerged in July 2025, when Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for it, and threatened doctors who violate the ban with up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine, and permanent loss of their licenses; the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court. Wikipedia country coverage: An anti-discrimination bill (House Bill 1725) passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 and would have barred discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, public transportation and public facilities, business transactions and housing, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved. The 2013 law that did pass (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities remain uncovered. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses legally discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Governor Ricardo Rosselló in February 2018, and a similar 2019 bill was withdrawn by Rosselló on 13 June 2019 after House approval amid protests. Wikipedia country coverage: Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the U.S. federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. 2020 was the first year anyone in Puerto Rico was charged with a hate crime: Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged after Bonilla confessed that he and Díaz de León murdered two transgender women on 22 April 2020. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island. Separately, in 2013 the legislature passed House Bill 488 (signed 29 May 2013) extending domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.

GUM.name: Guam
GUM.summary:
Guam stands under the full United States federal framework as an unincorporated US territory. United States passports and other federal travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X gender marker was eliminated by a January 2025 executive order, so a trans visitor travelling on United States documents faces a mismatch between document and presentation at entry.

Screening at Guam's airport follows federal Transport Security Administration procedure. The agency's body-scanner and pat-down protocols can disclose a trans traveller's status to officers; travellers may request an alternative screening method and escalate problems on the spot, and most trans travellers pass screening without incident.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in Guam, so access to that care during a visit cannot be assumed.

In February 2025 the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports, a rule that applies to arrivals here.

Guam recognises same-sex marriage. Chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down the territory's prohibition on 5 June 2015, following an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero after they were denied a licence; the ruling took effect at 8am on 9 June 2015 and made Guam the first US territory to recognise such marriages.
GUM.outOfScopeNotes:
Two listed sources, a University of Hawaiʻi Pacific sexual identity guide and a Transgender Law Center Guam documents page, yield no usable finding for this record, so no claim rests on them.

Whether Guam's own territory-level statutes prohibit discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations is unresolved in this inventory; no Guam statute or local case is cited here.

The scope of the February 2025 visa-denial announcement is stated for athletes entering to compete in women's sports; its bearing on other visitor categories is unresolved and not sourced.

Local Guam police practice, hate-crime charging, and any territory-level complaint mechanism for trans residents are not addressed by the sources and remain unverified.

VIR.name: U.S. Virgin Islands
VIR.summary:
The U.S. Virgin Islands stands under the full United States federal framework, and that framework sets what a trans visitor faces at the border. United States travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker was eliminated by executive order in January 2025, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents faces a mismatch between document and presentation at entry. Airport screening follows federal procedure: Transportation Security Administration body scanners can flag trans bodies and trigger secondary screening and pat-downs, and travellers may request alternative screening or decline the scanner.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to that care during a visit cannot be assumed. In February 2025 the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

The territorial layer runs the other way. The Virgin Islands human-rights law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, and in March 2017 the Attorney General ruled that the territory's anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students, an official interpretation extending territorial protections. Same-sex marriage has been legal since a 2015 territorial Superior Court ruling struck down the denial of marriage licences to same-sex couples, later settled nationwide by federal recognition. The historic sodomy statute, applied from 1957, has been replaced. None of this alters federal document rules, federal screening, or federal funding decisions, and no territorial statute softens them.
VIR.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents how the January 2025 executive order eliminating the X marker has been applied in practice to documents issued to residents of the U.S. Virgin Islands, or whether any territorial court has considered it; that remains unresolved here.

The inventory does not establish whether the federal funding order on gender-affirming care has affected any specific territorial hospital or clinic, so the reach of that order within the territory is stated only at the level of federally funded institutions generally.

Enforcement of the territorial anti-discrimination law in relation to transgender adults, as distinct from the 2017 ruling on students, is not sourced, and no source in the inventory records trans-specific violence incidents, outcomes or police response in the territory.

ASM.name: American Samoa
ASM.summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies: EO 14168 on binary sex classification in documents, federal facilities and care funding; EO 14187 on gender-affirming care funding; and EO 14201 on athletic participation, the last paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all United States identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth; new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents; and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker, available from 2022, has been eliminated for new applications. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, with the policy contested in federal courts.

Marriage recognition is unsettled in practice. The Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it, so the territory declined a formal ban before Obergefell. In July 2015 the territory's attorney general said applicability of the federal marriage ruling was still under review, while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the CNMI moved to apply it. In January 2016 the newly confirmed District Court judge Fiti Alexander Sunia told the Senate he had not read Obergefell, that the district court does not deal with the ruling, and that he would not perform same-sex weddings absent a change in local law. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that Obergefell does apply and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied, while recording that no same-sex couple has applied to date and setting out a litigation route through the High Court of American Samoa, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, and then the US Department of the Interior. As of July 2024 an on-island survey by Miami University professor Daniel Hall was still testing whether the local ban would survive a 14th Amendment challenge, indicating that the ban is treated locally as operative and its durability as an open question, more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of marriages performed elsewhere.

Trans people in the territory have obtained protection through national enforcement machinery. In September 2023 the US Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, and in June 2023 a federal civil action had cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

Social conditions differ from the legal picture. Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, are described in university research material as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, with colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of indigenous gender identities; the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, re-anchored to cultural pride. Travel guidance describes homosexuality as widely accepted in Samoan culture, in contrast to Fiji, while noting that Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism and that reserved behaviour by people of all orientations is expected. Fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified at the 2003 committee hearing that Samoan fa'afafine do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing.
ASM.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Obergefell v. Hodges is operative in American Samoa remains contested and unresolved: the territory's own officials have said they had not read the ruling or that it was under review, while a 2026 law review article by practitioners in the territory concludes it applies. No court in the territory has ruled on the question, and no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage licence, so the practical position is untested.

The constitutional durability of the local same-sex marriage ban was still being surveyed in July 2024 and no published result of that survey is available in this inventory. The scope of the SWS25 visa restriction attached to EO 14201 as applied to entry into American Samoa is not sourced here, nor is the current status of the ACLU's challenge to the passport policy in the courts.

Guidance from Lambda Legal and HRC is a secondary summary of a policy under litigation and may lag court developments. The February 2023 sexual-abuse charge involving a transgender teenager is reported as a charge only, with no outcome recorded in this inventory.

sources.summary: The UH Manoa libraries research guide on Pacific gender identities, last updated 2026-07-23, states that the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride: 'we are fa'afafine Samoa'. It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture', and frames colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Out Traveler 'Ask the Expert' column (Ed Salvato, 2009-07-01) answering a honeymoon question about American Samoa: the two Samoan nations share the fa'amatai chiefly system; ASM's ~57,000 residents across seven islands/atolls; 'Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved behavior by people of all orientations is expected', yet 'unlike the homophobia rampant in Fiji, homosexuality is a widely accepted part of Samoan culture', with Western gay men reportedly courted by fa'afafine transgender locals and by officially straight men; local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands 'the homeland of fa'afafine culture'; ASM hotels skew business-travel (Tradewinds, Pago Pago).

The Independent (2015-07-10): American Samoa was then the only US territory unsure whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling applied — its AG said applicability was 'still being reviewed... I don't know' while Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam and CNMI moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made.

sources.title: American Samoa Senate rejects bill outlawing same sex marriages (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. The territory therefore deliberately declined a formal marriage ban before Obergefell, and the hearing records contemporaneous local fa'afafine views on the question.

sources.title: American Samoa judge objects to same sex marriage (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. The exchange shows that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise that the ruling did not automatically apply.

MNP.name: Northern Mariana Islands
MNP.summary:
The Northern Mariana Islands is a US commonwealth and stands under the national framework of the United States for travel documents, immigration and airport screening. United States passports and entry documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker option was eliminated by the January 2025 executive order, so a trans visitor travelling on United States documents presents a gender marker that may not match presentation at the port of entry.

Screening at the airport follows federal procedure, and the order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to such care during a visit cannot be assumed. In February 2025 the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

There is no criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct or of gender expression under Commonwealth law. Commonwealth Public Law 22-32, signed in January 2023, amends the Commonwealth Code to set criteria for enhanced sentencing in hate-motivated crimes, and the statute covers offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity; this is the principal local protection a visitor would be able to invoke after an identity-based assault, though the sources do not document how it has been applied.

Legal gender recognition exists in the territory, but only on condition that the applicant has undergone the specified medical process. A visitor relying on locally issued documents rather than a United States passport should expect that medical requirement to apply.

There is no comprehensive local nondiscrimination ordinance covering gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations. Beyond federal law, protection extends only to government employees, leaving private-sector and service-access discrimination to be pursued through federal EEOC recourse.
MNP.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not document any prosecution or enhanced sentence under Commonwealth Public Law 22-32, so its practical effect for a victim of an anti-trans assault is unresolved.

Whether the January 2025 federal marker restrictions govern documents issued by the Commonwealth itself, as distinct from United States passports, is not addressed in the inventory and remains unresolved.

No sourced material covers restroom or facility access, school policy, local healthcare-facility intake practice, or police conduct toward trans detainees in the territory. The Movement Advancement Project scores are dated 27 September 2026 and may not reflect later legislative action. The Pride attendance figure and the organiser's assessment come from a single local report.

COK.name: Cook Islands
COK.summary:
New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to the Cook Islands, while local criminal law governs conduct on the islands.

Sections 154 and 155 of the Cook Islands Crimes Act 1969 criminalised sexual activity between men and any indecent act with or upon another male, carrying maximum terms of seven years and five years respectively, with consent explicitly not a defence. Later coverage of the repeal cited a maximum of ten years for indecent acts between males. The penalty figures reported for the 1969 provisions differ across the sources, but all agree the offences were never enforced in living memory.

Parliament voted on Friday 14 April 2023 to strike the provisions from the Crimes Act through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023. A note attached to the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands, and the same bill added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. The repeal removed a colonial-era provision still on the statute books rather than an active prosecution threat.

Decriminalisation was stalled for years before 2023. A draft Crimes Bill, written with assistance from New Zealand, would have deleted sections 154 and 155, and a 2017 select committee recommended their removal; MPs subsequently backtracked on that recommendation. In 2020 parliament again deferred the bill's report by three months.

Same-sex marriage remains prohibited in the Cook Islands under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000. The islands' only LGBTI community organisation, the Te Tiare Association, campaigned for repeal across the whole period, and its members described the 1969 provisions as homophobia brought by colonisation into a society whose pre-contact history accepted same-sex relationships. The Cook Islands population was about 21,000 when the bill was drafted in 2017.
COK.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory addresses same-sex conduct only. It contains no information on the legal status of gender identity in the Cook Islands: no detail on legal gender recognition, on the marker requirements for Cook Islands residents travelling on New Zealand passports, or on how New Zealand identity-document procedures apply from the Cook Islands.

Nothing in the sources covers anti-discrimination protection, hate-crime provisions, restrictions or protections around bathrooms and other gendered facilities, or access to gender-affirming medical care for trans people in the Cook Islands.

The extension of New Zealand human-rights and human-rights-instrument protections to the Cook Islands is not addressed in the inventory; how much of New Zealand's framework applies to residents of a state in free association remains unresolved on this record.

Enforcement, sentencing and complaint-handling data after the 1 June 2023 repeal are not available here, as are entry and visa rules applying to trans visitors, or any reporting on anti-trans violence with dates or outcomes.

NIU.name: Niue
NIU.summary:
New Zealand nationality and passport rules govern entry into Niue, while criminal liability is determined by Niue's own statute law.

Sexual conduct between men was criminalised under ss.43-44 of the Criminal Law Code, which covered buggery, attempted buggery and indecent assault on males and carried penalties of up to ten years' imprisonment. Those provisions were inherited from New Zealand through the 1901 annexation, retained when Niue achieved self-governance in 1974, and left untouched by New Zealand's own decriminalisation in 1986, which amended New Zealand law only. The Niue Assembly subsequently passed the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act in May, in force in June, repealing them (Human Dignity Trust).

No source in the current inventory records criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct in Niue today, and none documents enforcement against queer people. The jurisdiction carries no statutory protection either: there is no non-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity, no recognition of same-sex relationships or marriages, and no recorded bias-motivated-violence framework.

The age of consent was equalised in May 2011 according to ILGA's State-Sponsored Homophobia survey. The Niue Act 1966, Part 21 (Marriage of Minors), still sets the age of majority at 21 for men and 19 for women, a sex-asymmetric threshold that remained on the statute books as of that survey and bears on capacity to marry and related legal thresholds.

UN Free & Equal's August 2015 information sheet for the Pacific lists Niue's fakafifine among the diverse pre-colonial gender identities of the area, described as "important parts of the cultural treasure of the region". The identity is documented as deeply embedded in family life, coexisting with a church-led conservative social environment.
NIU.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no sourced material on legal gender recognition or the rules for changing sex markers on passports and birth records; entry documents are governed by New Zealand nationality and passport rules, but marker-change procedure is not documented here.

No sourced information covers restroom or facility access, screening practices that could disclose a visitor's trans status, access to gender-affirming or general healthcare, or any public-health provision addressing gender identity or sexual behaviour. Whether such provisions exist is unresolved on this record.

Hate-crime or bias-motivated violence protections, and any enforcement statistics for them, are not sourced. The claim that no enforcement against queer people is documented rests on the absence of such material in the inventory, not on an affirmative finding of non-enforcement.

The year of passage and commencement of the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act is not stated in the sources; only the month of each is given. The precise current wording of the Niue Act 1966 marriage provisions, and whether later amendments altered the 21/19 ages of majority, is likewise unresolved.

HKG.name: Hong Kong
HKG.summary:
Hong Kong is a special administrative region running its own legal system under a constitutional settlement, and trans claims here have been settled by courts rather than by statute. Same-sex conduct is not prohibited outright: the Crimes Ordinance instead set the age of consent for male-male sex at 21 against 16 for heterosexual acts, and the Court of Appeal's September 2006 judgment in Leung TC William Roy v Secretary for Justice (CACV317/2005), brought by a 21-year-old who had been in same-sex relationships since 16, examined whether that facially neutral disparity unjustifiably discriminated. The case is the landmark precedent on equal age of consent in Hong Kong.

In February 2023 the Court of Final Appeal ruled that full sex-reassignment surgery must not be a prerequisite for changing the gender marker on the compulsory identity card, a far-reaching win for the transgender men in the Henry Tse litigation. That ruling reversed a February 2019 High Court loss in the same case, where Judge Thomas Au's 59-page judgment made full confirmation surgery the only objectively ascertainable criterion and rejected self-ID as leading to uncertainty and arbitrariness. The men had already changed legal gender in Britain, and their counsel argued the surgical requirement was out of proportion to the aim.

Recognition stops at the card. Beyond the identity-card marker, legal gender recognition in Hong Kong continues to require full sex-reassignment surgery, so the 2023 win does not carry across to other official records. Relationship recognition is also absent: in September 2025 the Legislative Council voted down the government's own registered-partnerships bill 71–14 after court deadlines, and no ordinance covering sexual orientation and gender identity equality has been enacted.
HKG.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not address entry, visa, or border-document screening as applied to trans visitors, and nothing here should be read as describing how a foreign passport or travel document with a changed marker will be handled on arrival. That question is unsourced.

No sourced incidents of violence against trans people in Hong Kong appear in the inventory, and hate-crime protection, healthcare access, and facilities or restroom rules are not covered by these sources. Their status is unresolved rather than known to be absent.

The current statutory age of consent in force after the 2006 Court of Appeal precedent is not separately confirmed by these sources; only the litigation and its standing as the landmark precedent on equal age of consent are documented.

The practical reach of the February 2023 identity-card ruling beyond the card, and the consequences of the September 2025 partnership-bill defeat for visiting partners of residents, are not sourced and remain unresolved.
