sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Cross-dressing per se is not illegal in Hong Kong. Hong Kong law allows change of legal documents such as the ID card and passport, but does not allow birth certificate changes; historically this required full sex reassignment surgery including removal of reproductive organs. Since April 2024, a revised policy allows individuals who have undergone specific gender-affirming surgeries (mastectomy for trans men; penectomy and orchiectomy for trans women) to apply for an ID gender marker change, provided they provide medical proof, live as their identified gender for at least two years, and undergo continuous hormone therapy. A 2019 CUHK survey found 59% agreed and 9% disagreed that transgender people should be able to freely express their gender. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex partners gained spousal visa rights through the Court of Final Appeal ruling of 4 July 2018 (QT case), which mandated immigration authorities to grant spousal visas to same-sex partners married or in civil unions abroad; this became effective on 19 September 2018 when the Director of Immigration announced favorable consideration of such applications. In 2013, trans woman Eliana Rubashkyn was discriminated against and sexually abused by Hong Kong airport customs officers, endured an invasive body search for more than nine hours, and became a stateless person requiring UN and NGO assistance. Wikipedia country coverage: The Rubashkyn case (16 September 2013) involved an invasive body search at Hong Kong airport customs lasting over nine hours on a trans woman, who was discriminated against and sexually abused by customs officers, leading to UN and NGO refugee assistance. No other border or customs screening findings appear in the source text. Wikipedia country coverage: On 23 July 2025, the High Court ruled in K v Secretary for Environment and Ecology that government regulation prohibiting trans people from using public toilets matching their lived gender identity was unconstitutional under the Basic Law's right to equality. A 2025 report concluded LGBTQ people face exclusion in various domains including personal security. The 2025 ruling on public toilets provides a new legal basis for facility access, though implementation details are not described in the source. Wikipedia country coverage: Since 2021, step-child adoption has been affirmed for same-sex couples in the Court of First Instance case AA v BB (S v KG), which granted a lesbian couple joint custody, shared care, and guardianship rights over their two children following separation, establishing a judicial mechanism for couples to obtain equal parental rights. Under Cap. 13 Guardianship of Minors Ordinance, the Court of First Instance has full control over appointing or removing guardians. Wikipedia country coverage: In July 2025, the government introduced the Registration of Same-sex Partnerships Bill granting limited medical decision rights including hospital visits, shared medical information, organ donation, and dealing with remains — but the bill was vetoed by the legislature in September 2025 (71 against, 14 for), leaving same-sex partners without recognized medical decision-making rights. A 2025 report concluded LGBTQ people face exclusion in domains including health. Trans youth seeking gender-affirming care face the requirement of continuous hormone therapy and specific surgical treatments to change ID gender markers, with no comprehensive gender recognition framework existing. Wikipedia country coverage: A 2025 report concluded LGBTQ people face exclusion including in domains of personal security and violence. Trans people report being susceptible to verbal, physical and sexual abuse in public toilets. Trans people face a high rate of rejection, victimization, and discrimination, with social marginalization leading to negative mental health effects — trans Hongkongers disproportionately experience moderate-to-severe depressive and anxiety symptoms. No hate crime legislation is mentioned; as of 2026 there are no laws against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Wikipedia country coverage: The Broadcasting Authority ruled in 2007 that the RTHK programme 'Gay Lovers' was 'unfair, partial and biased towards homosexuality' (later overturned by court in 2008). In May 2019, a Cathay Pacific advertisement featuring a same-sex couple was banned by Airport Authority Hong Kong and MTR Corporation, only reversed after widespread public criticism. Political opposition comes from social conservatives, often with evangelical Christian ties; around 80% of 10,775 written submissions on the proposed Registration of Same-sex Partnerships Bill were in opposition. As of 2026, there are no laws against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in Hong Kong. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognized in Hong Kong. The Registration of Same-sex Partnerships Bill was vetoed by the legislature on 19 September 2025 (71 against, 14 for). The Court of Final Appeal in September 2023 directed the government to establish an alternative recognition framework within two years but also ruled no constitutionally guaranteed right to marry exists. Same-sex couples gained spousal visa rights (CFA 2018), joint tax filing (effective 19 September 2018), limited domestic violence protection (2009), and equal public housing rights (Court of Final Appeal, 26 November 2024). Many Hong Kong residents who are British Nationals (Overseas) can register civil partnerships at British consulates in 22 countries. Wikipedia country coverage: A 2025 report concluded LGBTQ people face exclusion in domains including education. Attitudes toward trans acceptance are directly correlated with educational level. During the Legislative Council debate over unequal age of consent, conservative lawmakers argued legal inequality (21 for gay men vs 16 for heterosexuals) was necessary 'to protect youth and preserve tradition.' Younger people (18-40: 86% support fair treatment in 2022 poll) and non-religious people were more likely to support anti-discrimination protections and same-sex marriage. Trans youth seeking gender marker changes on ID cards must meet criteria including continuous hormone therapy and specific surgical treatment.

MAC.name: Macau
MAC.summary:
Macau is a Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China, standing under the national framework of its Basic Law while administering its own civil-law system of Portuguese derivation. Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1996, and no provision criminalises gender expression. The Basic Law's Article 25 list of protected grounds omits sexual orientation and gender identity, and statutory non-discrimination protection extends only to employment, under Article 6(2) of Law 7/2008.

There is no legal pathway to gender recognition. The Identification Bureau maintains no policy for changing the sex marker on Macau identity cards, and a 2015 study of gender-marker change never produced legislation. On 7 April 2026 the Justice Services Direction (DSAJ) stated that legal recognition of gender identity still requires "prudent study" of core societal values, civil law and family law, and that there are no plans to revise the framework — an answer issued after four trans residents filed an appeal on 31 March 2026. Macau is the only area in China without provisions for identity-card gender-marker change or sex reassignment; both are available in mainland China and in Hong Kong.

The first organised push came in February 2015, when Rainbow of Macau met Identification Bureau officials to discuss changing gender on identity documents. The individual making the request, identified as Avery, spoke from behind a screen. The practical consequence persists at the border: a trans man holding a Hong Kong identity card marked male remains registered as female in Macau, producing confusion when crossing.

Protection from violence is excluded along the same line. A 2012 draft of domestic-violence legislation dropped same-sex cohabitants for "lack of social consensus", and the law enacted in 2016 left out same-sex partners because they were not treated as "family members". Rainbow of Macau criticised the exclusion in May 2016. A statement issued by Jason Chao for the association recorded that the government enacted the law with knowledge of the UN Committee against Torture's 2015 concluding observations requiring protection without discrimination, and warned that the enactment signals that sexual-orientation discrimination is justifiable.

For a visitor: no exposure to prosecution, no recognition of gender or partnership, and no statutory recourse outside the employment sphere.
MAC.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether Macau has any hate-crime or aggravated-penalty provision covering anti-trans or homophobic violence, and no sourced statement covers facilities, bathroom access, or rules on gendered spaces.

No source addresses entry or visa screening of trans visitors, including whether immigration officers can question or refuse a traveller whose presentation differs from the sex marker on the document — the cross-border mismatch described here concerns a resident's identity cards, not border policy.

The content and recommendations of the 2015 gender-marker study are not sourced beyond the fact that it produced no law, and no timeline, legislative proposal or court ruling on gender recognition appears in the inventory. Enforcement of the employment protection in Law 7/2008 is likewise unverified here, as is any requirement, medical or otherwise, for persons seeking future recognition.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D6.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Macau
sources.summary: Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Macau': same-sex activity decriminalised 1996; no recognition of same-sex unions; Basic Law Art. 25 discrimination list omits sexual orientation — SOGI protection only in employment (Law 7/2008 Art. 6/2); the 2012 domestic-violence draft dropped same-sex cohabitants for 'lack of social consensus'; the 2015 gender-marker-change study never produced a law. Wikipedia country coverage: Media and public expression around LGBT people in Macau is constrained by stigmatising coverage: on 9 June 2015 the newspaper Exmoo ran a front-page story about a high school student allegedly molesting a 9-year-old, titling the perpetrator a "gay demon" (基魔), prompting Rainbow of Macau spokesperson Jason Chao to note the Penal Code treats homosexual and heterosexual sex offenders identically. Despite a surge in activism since the Macau LGBT Rights Concern Group was created in late 2012 and Rainbow of Macau was registered in April 2013, the source states that gay culture in Macau remains mostly invisible. The lesbian-themed film I'm here, directed by Tracy Choi, won the Macau Indies 2012 Jury's Award at the Macau International Film and Video Festival, depicting problems homosexuals face living in a small town like Macau. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised in Macau, and a March 2013 bill by Legislative Assembly member José Pereira Coutinho to recognise same-sex civil unions with the same rights as heterosexual couples was rejected 17 votes to 1 with 4 abstentions, and expressly excluded the right to adopt. The source states same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples remain ineligible for some legal rights available to opposite-sex couples. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex cohabitants were dropped from Macau's domestic violence law: after a 2011 public consultation included "same-sex cohabitants in an intimate relationship" in scope, the government's 2012 concluding report removed the reference citing "a lack of social consensus", and in 2016 it insisted on the exclusion. In October 2015 Rainbow of Macau complained to the UN Committee against Torture, which urged Macau to protect all domestic violence victims "without discrimination"; Rainbow of Macau called the resulting law discriminatory. Separately, on 16 August 2018 the deputy director of the Education and Youth Affairs Bureau (DSEJ), Leong Vai Kei, said students with "indications of homosexuality" would be referred to doctors or psychologists for medical examination, though she later apologised, claiming misquotation and mistranslation from Cantonese. Wikipedia country coverage: The general age of consent for both homosexual and heterosexual sex in Macau is 14, and under Penal Code Article 166 anal coitus with someone under 14 carries 3 to 10 years' imprisonment, while with a 14-to-16-year-old taking advantage of inexperience it carries up to 4 years. In February 2015 a transgender student, Avery (pseudonym), told Macau media about abuse and bullying experienced while studying at a local school. The 2015 Exmoo front-page story involved a high school student as alleged perpetrator and a 9-year-old victim, framed through the slur "gay demon". Wikipedia country coverage: Legal exclusion is repeatedly justified by "lack of social consensus": the government dropped same-sex cohabitants from the 2012 domestic violence report on that basis, and the UN Human Rights Committee noted in 2017 that Macau still does not allow transgender people to change gender markers on birth records and identity documents, reportedly for the same reason. Sexual orientation is absent from the non-exhaustive list of prohibited discrimination grounds in Basic Law Article 25, though sectoral protections exist in labour relations (Law No. 7/2008, fines up to MOP$50,000 per affected worker), personal data (Law No. 8/2005) and the ombudsman (Law No. 4/2012). Between 2004 and 28 February 2026 the Identification Services Bureau received eight written requests to change gender on ID documents, all rejected, and in April 2026 the Legal Affairs Bureau said there are "no plans" to revise the framework pending "prudent study" of core values, civil law and family relations.

MAC.blindSummary:
The state/province stands under the national framework of its Basic Law while administering its own civil-law system inherited from the administering state's legal tradition. Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1996, and no provision criminalises gender expression. The Basic Law's Article 25 list of protected grounds omits sexual orientation and gender identity, and statutory non-discrimination protection extends only to employment, under Article 6(2) of Law 7/2008.

There is no legal pathway to gender recognition. The Identification Bureau maintains no policy for changing the sex marker on identity cards, and a 2015 study of gender-marker change never produced legislation. On 7 April 2026 the Justice Services Direction (DSAJ) stated that legal recognition of gender identity still requires "prudent study" of core societal values, civil law and family law, and that there are no plans to revise the framework — an answer issued after four trans residents filed an appeal on 31 March 2026. The state/province is the only area under the national framework without provisions for identity-card gender-marker change or sex reassignment; both are available in the rest of the country and in the neighbouring state/province.

The first organised push came in February 2015, when a local association met Identification Bureau officials to discuss changing gender on identity documents. The individual making the request, identified as Avery, spoke from behind a screen. The practical consequence persists at the border: a trans person holding a neighbouring state/province identity card marked male remains registered as female at home, producing confusion when crossing.

Protection from violence is excluded along the same line. A 2012 draft of domestic-violence legislation dropped same-sex cohabitants for "lack of social consensus", and the law enacted in 2016 left out same-sex partners because they were not treated as "family members". The local association criticised the exclusion in May 2016. a statement issued by a local campaigner for the association recorded that the government enacted the law with knowledge of the UN Committee against Torture's 2015 concluding observations requiring protection without discrimination, and warned that the enactment signals that sexual-orientation discrimination is justifiable.

For a visitor: no exposure to prosecution, no recognition of gender or partnership, and no statutory recourse outside the employment sphere.

MAC.tangentialFactors:
Macau's position diverges sharply from both jurisdictions it is most often compared with. Gender-marker change and sex reassignment are legally possible in mainland China and in Hong Kong, leaving Macau as the sole area under the national framework where neither exists — a gap activists have pressed for years without a legislative result.

International scrutiny has produced commitments without effect. The UN Committee against Torture's 2015 concluding observations directed that protection from domestic violence be non-discriminatory; the 2016 law was enacted anyway, and the Justice Services Direction's April 2026 refusal to commit to reform shows the same pattern of review without revision.

Protection is narrow rather than absent: Law 7/2008 covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination in employment only, leaving housing, services, education and violence outside the statute, while the Basic Law's own discrimination list does not reach these grounds at all.

ESH.name: Western Sahara
ESH.summary:
Western Sahara is a disputed territory under military administration by Morocco, and the territory stands under Morocco's penal code wherever its security services operate. Same-sex intimacy is criminalised, carrying six months to three years of imprisonment, and the broad discretion police hold in applying morality provisions is the instrument turned on visibly trans people.

The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, a partially recognised state and African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara and separately records homosexuality as illegal for men and women, and illegal there for decades. A July 2017 global legality roundup lists it as a criminalising jurisdiction, so both claimed frameworks record criminalisation.

Rights reviews document involuntary outing of trans people, discrepancies in expression at checkpoints and in registry records, an absence of gender-affirming healthcare, and no legal gender recognition; a 2021 route to recognition covers intersex people only. Morocco's religious establishment has publicly condemned transition.

Enforcement stacks on top of the occupation. Morocco charged 170 people in a single year, an organised outing campaign ran in 2020, and rights defenders are prosecuted at the territory's own courts. Human Rights Watch reported on 9 December 2005 the trial of seven Sahrawi human-rights defenders charged with fomenting illegal protests, calling the charges dubious and demanding a fair trial. A 2018 legal study recorded LGBTI Sahrawis exposed to violations by state and non-state actors alike.
ESH.outOfScopeNotes:
Which penal code applies in the parts of Western Sahara administered by the Polisario Front rather than Morocco is unresolved in the sources; the inventory records Moroccan law for areas under Moroccan control and the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic's own criminalisation listing, without mapping the boundary of application.

No sourced material covers entry or visa rules for the territory, passport or gender-marker rules for foreign documents, hate-crime protection, or recognition of partners. These are not sourced rather than absent.

The figure of seven defendants in the 2005 trial comes from the Human Rights Watch dispatch alone and is not corroborated by a second source in the inventory. The 170-charged figure and the 2020 outing campaign are recorded for Morocco; their incidence inside Western Sahara is not separately quantified.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2, D3, D4, D5, D6, D8, D12, D13.

GMB.name: Gambia
GMB.summary:
Same-sex conduct has been a criminal offence in Gambia since the colonial era. The Criminal Code adopted in March 2025 removed the 2014 provision permitting life imprisonment for "aggravated homosexuality" and instead sets a five-year minimum sentence for "unnatural offences", defined in the statute as any homosexual act, with no stated maximum penalty; "gross indecency" carries three years. The offence attaches to conduct rather than to stated identity or expression.

The government of President Adama Barrow has not typically enforced these provisions. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report recorded no prosecutions under the statute while documenting significant societal stigma and police harassment of LGBT persons, and the 2020 report recorded arrests together with societal discrimination.

Official hostility was explicit under the previous long-term ruler. Human Rights Watch's September 2015 report "State of Fear" documents arbitrary arrest, torture and killings under Yahya Jammeh, including his anti-gay rhetoric and direct threats against LGBT people. Those findings describe the enforcement climate of the Jammeh regime rather than current practice.

Discrimination against LGBT people persists into the present political period. Freedom House rates Gambia "Partly Free" at 50/100 in Freedom in the World 2024, noting improved political freedoms after 22 years of Jammeh's rule while listing severe discrimination against LGBT+ people among the country's ongoing concerns.

Protection machinery exists on paper. The UK Home Office country information and policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity in Gambia, version 3.0 of February 2023, sets out a systematic assessment of risk, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with country information on the law and its treatment.
GMB.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no material on legal gender recognition, change of name or gender marker on passports or identity documents, entry or visa screening that could disclose a visitor's trans status, access to gender-affirming care, facility access, hate-crime enhancement, or recognition of partners. These elements of the record are not sourced here and remain unresolved rather than negative.

No trans-specific violence, arrest or homicide figures appear in the inventory. The available reporting is framed around sexual orientation and homosexual conduct; whether the statute's language has been applied against trans people specifically is not established by these sources.

Enforcement since the March 2025 Criminal Code took effect is not covered. The inventory's most recent enforcement data points are the 2020 and 2021 US State Department reports, and the Outright International profile's statement that the provisions have not typically been enforced carries no post-March 2025 case data behind it.

The dating of the pre-2025 aggravated-homosexuality provision differs between sources: one reference attributes the life clause to 2014, while the 2020 US State Department report describes a maximum of life under a 2013 amendment. This discrepancy is not resolved by the inventory.

No source in the inventory addresses whether a trans visitor's documents, presentation or prior record would attract screening at ports of entry, and no official Gambian statement on the treatment of gender-diverse travellers is included.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D3, D4, D5, D6, D8, D12, D13.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The Gambia does not allow citizens to change their legal gender and makes no provision for any official change of gender for its citizens. Since 2013, section 167 of the Criminal Code forbids men to dress "as women," punishable by up to 5 years in jail or a fine of 50,000 Gambian dalasi, effectively restricting gender expression. The country has no law or regulation protecting residents against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Wikipedia country coverage: Entry-related exposure is illustrated by the 23 December 2008 arrest of Frank Boers, a 79-year-old Dutch national, at Banjul International Airport when officials found him in possession of pornography including nude photos of himself and Gambian men; he was convicted of indecency and fined 100,000 dalasis in lieu of a two-year sentence. In May 2008 President Jammeh gave homosexuals 24 hours to leave the country and ordered the Inspector General of Police and the director of the Gambia Immigration Department to conduct mass patrols to "weed bad elements in society." The source text contains no LGBTQ-specific visa rules. Wikipedia country coverage: In June 2008 two Spanish men in their 50s, alleged to be gay, were arrested and detained at Kotu police station after taxi drivers reported them, and were released reportedly after the Spanish government intervened. Following the 2014 "aggravated homosexuality" law, state forces launched an investigation in November 2014 producing at least eight arrests — including at least four adult men, a 17-year-old boy, and nine women — with detainees held at the National Intelligence Agency headquarters in Banjul and allegedly tortured to compel confessions. On 10 April 2012 a court remanded 18 men (16 Senegalese, one Gambian, one Nigerian) arrested at a bar in the Tourism Development Area for "indecent practice" after police said they were wearing women's clothes; all charges were dropped on 1 August 2012. Arrests of gay people are believed to have been common during Jammeh's presidency, though data is lacking. Wikipedia country coverage: Jammeh's 15 May 2008 order threatened that "any hotel, lodge or motel that lodges this kind of individuals will be closed down," targeting accommodation providers hosting LGBTQ people. Post-2016, there are no LGBTQ+ organizations in the country because it is considered too dangerous. The 2014-era detentions took place at the National Intelligence Agency headquarters in Banjul, and further arrests occurred at Kotu police station. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2023 there were reports of healthcare workers refusing to honor LGBTQ+ people's privacy, which has negatively impacted HIV care for LGBTQ+ Gambians. The 2014 "aggravated homosexuality" law imposes a mandatory life sentence specifically on gay or lesbian people living with HIV, a direct barrier to testing and treatment. No incidents of conversion therapy or of surgeries on intersex children or non-consenting adults were reported. Youth-specific: a 17-year-old boy was among those apprehended in November 2014 on allegations of aggravated homosexual conduct. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in the Gambia, and the country prohibits LGBTQ people from adopting children. There is no discrimination protection law of any kind for LGBTQ residents. The Barrow government promised not to prosecute same-sex couples for consensual sexual acts, though it has stated there are no plans for liberalisation of homosexuality laws. Wikipedia country coverage: The 2014 Criminal Code (Amendment) Act defines "aggravated homosexuality" to include sexual acts with persons of the same gender under 18 years of age, carrying a mandatory life sentence — a direct legal exposure for LGBTQ minors. Children are raised within strict male and female gender norms, with non-conformity to the heterosexual norm treated as deviant and taboo, and the country's media promotes misinformation and harmful stereotypes toward LGBTQ+ people. In November 2014 a 17-year-old boy was among those arrested for alleged aggravated homosexual conduct. A 2021–2023 survey found 93% of Gambians would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbour, indicating the social climate LGBTQ youth grow up in; the source text contains no education-policy-specific findings.

GMB.tangentialFactors:
The legal change in March 2025 moved in two directions at once: it removed the life sentence introduced for aggravated homosexuality in 2014, yet raised the floor for any homosexual act to five years while leaving the ceiling unstated. The practical significance for a visitor turns on enforcement rather than on the length of the tariff, and enforcement has been irregular.

A political opening and a legal freeze coexist. Freedom House records gains in political freedoms under Barrow after more than two decades of authoritarian rule, while the criminal provisions targeting same-sex conduct remain on the books and LGBT discrimination remains a listed concern. The liberalisation of the wider political environment should not be read as an easing of the position of LGBT people.

The historical record is dominated by the Jammeh period. The most severe documented violence, including torture, killings and direct threats, belongs to the era covered by the 2015 Human Rights Watch report. Applying that description to current conditions would misstate the present enforcement picture, just as relying on the absence of prosecutions would understate the risk of arrest and police contact.

The 2020 and 2021 US State Department reports give a two-year window: arrests and discrimination recorded first, then no prosecutions but continuing stigma and police harassment. Together they suggest a regime of low-prosecution but persistent extralegal pressure.

The 2020 and 2021 external human rights reports give a two-year window: arrests and discrimination recorded first, then no prosecutions but continuing stigma and police harassment. Together they suggest a regime of low-prosecution but persistent extralegal pressure.
GMB.blindOutOfScope:
The source inventory contains no material on legal gender recognition, change of name or gender marker on passports or identity documents, entry or visa screening that could disclose a visitor's trans status, access to gender-affirming care, facility access, hate-crime enhancement, or recognition of partners. These elements of the record are not sourced here and remain unresolved rather than negative.

No trans-specific violence, arrest or homicide figures appear in the inventory. The available reporting is framed around sexual orientation and homosexual conduct; whether the statute's language has been applied against trans people specifically is not established by these sources.

Enforcement since the March 2025 Criminal Code took effect is not covered. The inventory's most recent enforcement data points are the 2020 and 2021 external human rights reports, and the statement that the provisions have not typically been enforced carries no post-March 2025 case data behind it.

The dating of the pre-2025 aggravated-homosexuality provision differs between sources: one reference attributes the life clause to 2014, while the 2020 external report describes a maximum of life under a 2013 amendment. This discrepancy is not resolved by the inventory.

No source in the inventory addresses whether a trans visitor's documents, presentation or prior record would attract screening at ports of entry, and no official statement on the treatment of gender-diverse travellers is included.
GMB.localsOnly:
Residents are subject to the same statute as visitors, with no distinction in the law between citizen and non-citizen in the definition of the offences. The five-year minimum for any homosexual act applies to conduct occurring in the territory.

Police contact is the routine form of pressure. The US State Department's 2021 report describes police harassment of LGBT persons alongside significant societal stigma, and the 2020 report records arrests. Prosecution is uncommon, but the exposure to stop, search, detention and informal penalty does not depend on a formal charge.

The community's visibility was shaped by the previous regime. Human Rights Watch recorded arbitrary arrest, torture and killings under Yahya Jammeh, together with his explicit threats against LGBT people, which established the intimidation baseline that the current period inherits.

Asylum and internal relocation questions are assessed under a defined framework. The UK Home Office country information and policy note of February 2023 addresses risk, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ claims, indicating that the conditions faced by LGBT residents have been examined in detail by an external state authority.
